descs.en: Lin Xiaoran is dramatic, affectionate, and impossible to handle. Zhou Yichen is patient, gentle, and hopelessly weak against her tears. Somehow, they fit together perfectly.

chapters.desc: He knew she was trouble the moment she started crying—and he still loved her too much to stop spoiling her.
chapters.title: The Boy Who Always Smiled at Her
chapters.content:
The winter sunlight spilled across the school rooftop, pale gold against the chilly afternoon air.

“Zhou Yichen, move.”

The boy sitting lazily on the bench looked up with his usual smile already waiting.

“You’re the one who came late, Xiaoran.”

Lin Xiaoran huffed dramatically and squeezed herself beside him anyway, shoulder shoving him hard enough that he nearly lost balance.

“You did that on purpose.”

“You’re too weak.”

“You literally attacked me.”

“But you’re still smiling.”

Because he always did. Whenever Lin Xiaoran was around, Zhou Yichen smiled like he forgot how to stop. He was the kind of boy girls whispered about in hallways—tall, calm, unfairly handsome, top student, captain of the basketball team. Yet the moment his girlfriend appeared, all that composed coolness disappeared into helpless indulgence. Especially when she pouted, and even more when she cried. And Lin Xiaoran cried easily.

“You brought milk tea?” she asked, eyes brightening.

Yichen handed her the warm cup from his coat pocket.

“Half sugar. No pearls.”

“Good boyfriend.” She pinched his cheek with satisfaction.

“You say that like you’re reviewing customer service.”

“I am.”

He laughed while she drank happily beside him, kicking her legs against the bench. From the rooftop door, their friends watched with disgust.

“Every day,” Chen Yuhao sighed.

Beside him, Tang Meilin rolled her eyes.

“You’re just jealous because you don’t have a girlfriend.”

Yuhao instantly straightened.

“That’s rude.”

Meanwhile, Xiaoran noticed them and waved.

“Why are you both standing there like divorced parents?”

“Because watching you two gives me diabetes,” Yuhao replied.

Yichen only smiled again. Meilin crossed her arms.

“Actually, Xiaoran, you should appreciate him more. If my future boyfriend tolerated even half your nonsense, I’d build him a temple.”

“I’m perfectly appreciative,” Xiaoran declared.

Yichen raised a brow.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She was cute in a way that made people forgive her far too easily. Yichen most of all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The problem started a week later. Basketball practice had just ended when Xiaoran came to the gym carrying snacks for Yichen. The gym still smelled of floor polish and sweat, and the last few players were dragging the ball cart back to the storeroom. But the moment she entered, she saw a girl from Class 2 handing him a towel. Pretty. Tall. Elegant. Exactly Xiaoran’s least favourite type. The girl smiled.

“Your game today was amazing.”

“Thanks,” Yichen replied politely.

That should have been the end. But inside Lin Xiaoran’s head, jealousy was loud. She walked over with a sweet smile that already made Yuhao—watching from nearby—mutter:

“Oh no.”

Xiaoran wrapped herself around Yichen’s arm possessively.

“Yichen,” she said brightly, “who’s this?”

The girl introduced herself politely. Xiaoran smiled even wider.

“Ohhh, you’re the girl who confessed to him last semester, right?”

Silence. The girl’s face stiffened. Yuhao covered his face with both hands. Even Yichen’s smile disappeared. Xiaoran continued casually:

“You’re still trying?”

“Xiaoran,” Yichen said.

That tone alone made her pause. The girl looked close to tears as she hurried away. And suddenly the gym felt cold. Yichen gently removed Xiaoran’s arms from his sleeve.

“You went too far.”

Her chest tightened.

“What? I was joking.”

“It wasn’t funny.”

“She likes you.”

“And? That doesn’t mean you get to humiliate her.” His voice stayed calm, which somehow felt worse.

Xiaoran’s eyes went red. Yichen sighed internally the second he saw it. Because there it was. The tears. Always so fast.

“I’m not scolding you,” he said, more gently.

“But you’re angry.”

“I don’t like what you did.”

“You care more about her feelings than mine?”

“That’s not what I said.”

But Xiaoran already looked devastated.

“I was jealous,” she whispered.

Yichen rubbed his forehead.

“I know. But jealousy isn’t an excuse to hurt someone.”

She bit her lip hard, eyes watery. And then the worst possible thing happened.

“You’re being mean to me…”

Yichen nearly lost the argument right there. Lin Xiaoran crying was the one thing he had no defence against. He made himself stay firm anyway.

“Xiaoran. Don’t avoid the point.”

The tears spilled over. Great. Now he felt like the villain in a tragic romance drama. She turned and ran out of the gym before he could stop her. Yuhao walked over slowly.

“…You survived longer than expected.”

“Shut up.”

“You made her cry.”

“I KNOW.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Xiaoran ignored him for two days. Which meant: no waiting for him outside the gym. No stealing his drinks. No dramatic good morning voice messages. No random “Do you love me more today or yesterday?” questions. Half the school noticed how miserable Zhou Yichen looked.

“He looks like a ghost haunting his own desk,” Yuhao commented.

“Go apologise already,” Meilin said.

“I’m not apologising for telling her she was wrong.”

“But you’re suffering,” Yuhao pointed out.

Yichen leaned back in frustration. The truth was, he missed her. He even missed being annoyed by her.

That evening, he finally found her sitting alone behind the library, hugging her knees, sleeves pulled down over her hands the way she always did when she was sulking. The moment she saw him, she looked away.

“I’m still angry.”

“I know. You said so in seventeen messages.”

Her lips twitched slightly before she hid it again. Yichen sat beside her. For a moment, neither spoke. Then he sighed.

“Xiaoran.”

Silence.

“I’m sorry I was harsh.”

She sniffed. Here we go again.

“But,” he said gently, “you really hurt her feelings.”

“I know…”

“And if someone treated you like that?”

“I’d cry for ten business days.”

Despite himself, Yichen laughed. Xiaoran finally looked at him, eyes still watery.

“I just hated seeing her near you.”

“I know.”

“She looked so pretty.”

“You’re prettier.”

“That answer was too fast.”

“Because it’s true.”

Her ears turned pink. Yichen reached over and pulled her closer by the sleeve.

“You can be jealous. But don’t become cruel because of it,” he murmured.

Xiaoran lowered her head guiltily.

“…Okay.”

“And no more embarrassing people publicly.”

“…Okay.”

“And no crying every time I correct you.”

“I can’t control that.”

“You absolutely can.”

“You said you wouldn’t scold me anymore.”

Yichen sighed with complete defeat before pulling her into his arms anyway. She melted against him like a satisfied cat.

“You spoil her too much,” Meilin called from somewhere nearby.

The two looked up to find Yuhao and Meilin holding convenience store snacks while spying openly. Yuhao pointed accusingly.

“See? THIS is why she acts like a menace.”

Yichen didn’t even deny it. Xiaoran looked extremely pleased with herself. Then she tilted her head up at Yichen sweetly.

“You still love me?”

He looked down at her. She knew exactly what she was doing to him.

“Unfortunately,” he said, kissing her forehead lightly, “way too much.”
chapters.epigraph: “Some people are impossible to handle—and impossible not to love.”

chapters.desc: A claw machine, a chance meeting, and one boy who smiled like he already knew she was meant to stay.
chapters.title: Strawberry Milk Confession
chapters.content:
It started with a claw machine. Lin Xiaoran stood in the arcade with her arms crossed, glaring at the stupid plush bunny trapped behind the glass like it had insulted her whole family. Around her, the machines flashed and jingled, and somewhere behind her a group of middle schoolers were screaming over a racing game.

“This machine is rigged.”

“It’s not,” said a calm voice beside her.

She turned. And for half a second, she forgot what she’d been about to say. The boy standing there was tall, clean-looking, dressed in their school uniform with his sleeves rolled up. Sharp brows. Pretty eyes. The kind of face that got talked about in group chats. Most annoyingly, he was smiling. Not smug, not teasing. Just warm. Lin Xiaoran recovered quickly.

“You work for the machine company or something?”

The boy laughed.

“No. You’re just grabbing the bunny wrong.”

“I’ve tried eleven times.”

“That explains the problem.”

“What does THAT mean?”

“You’re impatient.”

She narrowed her eyes. Who even was this guy? The boy stepped beside her.

“Move.”

“Excuse me?”

“You want the bunny or not?”

Xiaoran shuffled aside and watched him suspiciously. He fed in a coin, adjusted the claw once—and won the bunny on the first try. Xiaoran gasped in betrayal.

“That’s impossible.”

He picked up the bunny and handed it to her.

“There.”

She hugged the plush automatically before catching herself.

“…Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

Then he smiled again. And for some reason, her heart skipped. It was annoying.

“What’s your name?”

“Zhou Yichen.”

Oh. So this was THE Zhou Yichen. Top student. Basketball captain. Third-year legend. Girls from other schools literally waited outside games for him. Xiaoran’s guard went straight up.

“Hm. You’re overrated.”

Yichen blinked once. Then he laughed—properly, like she’d said something genuinely funny.

“You’re cute,” he said absentmindedly.

Lin Xiaoran nearly dropped the bunny.

“What?!”

“Nothing.”

His smile only deepened. And that was the first problem.

✦ ✦ ✦

After that, they somehow kept meeting everywhere. Library. Convenience store. Bus stop. School festival prep. It became suspicious enough that Tang Meilin accused fate of being too obvious.

“You like him,” Meilin declared.

“I absolutely do not.”

“You brushed your hair three times when he walked past.”

“That was wind maintenance.”

“That’s not a thing.”

Lin Xiaoran pretended not to hear. But secretly, she noticed things. Like how Zhou Yichen always looked relaxed around everyone else, but around her, he smiled more. How he remembered every tiny thing she said. How he once turned up with strawberry milk after hearing her complain that the cafeteria had been sold out for three days. How he never got annoyed even when she acted bratty on purpose. Which she did frequently.

“Move,” she’d say, shoving him aside in the hallway.

“You walked into me.”

“You exist in my path.”

“That sounds like a personal issue.”

“Hm.”

And somehow, he always looked amused instead of offended. It made her chest feel weird.

One rainy afternoon, Xiaoran forgot her umbrella after cram school.

By the time she reached the school gate, the rain was coming down in sheets, bouncing off the pavement.

“…Great.”

“You’ll get sick.”

She turned to find Zhou Yichen standing behind her holding a black umbrella. Again. Smiling, as usual.

“Were you waiting for someone?”

“You.”

Her heart stumbled so hard it was humiliating.

“…Why?”

“You texted the class group complaining about the rain.”

“That doesn’t mean come rescue me.”

“But you sounded pitiful.”

“I was NOT pitiful.”

“You used three crying emojis.”

“That’s expressive communication.”

Yichen laughed before opening the umbrella over her head.

“Come on.”

The walk home became dangerous for Lin Xiaoran’s emotional stability. Zhou Yichen was gentle in ways she wasn’t prepared for. He tilted the umbrella towards her side. Walked closer to the road so passing cars wouldn’t splash her. Listened carefully even when she rambled nonsense. And worst of all, he looked at her like she mattered.

By the time they reached her apartment building, Xiaoran already knew she was doomed. Yichen looked down at her.

“You should go inside before you catch a cold.”

“…Okay.”

But neither moved. Rain poured softly around them. Xiaoran clutched the plush bunny still attached to her bag. Then blurted—

“Do you like me?”

Silence. Yichen blinked, clearly surprised. Unfortunately for her pride, nerves only made Lin Xiaoran more reckless.

“Because if you DON’T, then you should stop acting so nice to me all the time because it’s confusing,” she rushed out.

Yichen stared at her for two seconds. Then, slowly, he smiled. The smile that always made her weak.

“What if I do like you?”

Xiaoran’s brain stopped working.

“Oh.”

Very intelligent response. Yichen stepped closer under the umbrella. Up close, she could see his knuckles had gone white around the handle.

“What if I’ve liked you since the arcade?”

“…That fast?”

“You called me overrated within thirty seconds.”

“And that made you fall in love?”

“I found it refreshing.”

She stared at him, ears turning pink. This was bad. Now she wanted to say it too. And Lin Xiaoran hated being vulnerable. But she also hated lying. So after a full minute of silent suffering, she mumbled—

“…I like you too.”

Yichen’s whole face softened.

“Yeah?”

“I think about you too much. It’s affecting my studies,” she confessed with deep annoyance.

He laughed. And suddenly Xiaoran realised something that scared her a little. Zhou Yichen looked happiest when he was with her.

“Lin Xiaoran,” he said gently.

“…What?”

“Do you want to go out with me?”

Her eyes widened.

“So suddenly?”

“You confessed first.”

“That’s true.”

“And I don’t want anyone else asking you before I do.”

Her heart did something alarming. She tried to act calm anyway.

“Hm. I’ll consider it.”

Yichen raised a brow.

“You confessed two minutes ago.”

“That was before. This is negotiation.”

He laughed again, lowering his head slightly closer to hers.

“Okay then. Please let me be your boyfriend,” he murmured.

Xiaoran lasted exactly three seconds before smiling shyly.

“…Fine.”

“Fine?”

“Don’t push your luck, Zhou Yichen.”

“Yes, girlfriend.”

And hearing him say it for the first time felt warmer than the umbrella over their heads.
chapters.epigraph: “He found her in chaos, and stayed like it was home.”

chapters.desc: The first strawberry milk of the day is finished before lunch. The second comes with a boy who is very bad at pretending he was just passing.
chapters.title: The Second Strawberry Milk
chapters.epigraph: “So you don’t have to drink two.”
chapters.content:
The first strawberry milk of the day was gone before lunch.

Zhou Yichen had put it on her desk before the morning bell, on his way down the aisle to his own seat three rows ahead, and had sat down and opened his physics book as if he had nothing to do with it. Lin Xiaoran drank it during morning reading with the carton held below the desk, which fooled nobody, and then kept the empty carton by her pencil case for the rest of the morning, because he had been her boyfriend for exactly six days and nothing he gave her could go in the bin yet.

Tang Meilin, who sat beside her and missed nothing, had opinions.

“You’ve looked at it four times since second period.”

“I was looking at the clock.”

“The clock is above the blackboard. The carton is next to your hand. Shall I ask him to buy you a second one? He seems good at it.” Meilin propped her chin on her fist.

Xiaoran hit her arm with the pencil case, not hard, and Meilin laughed into her textbook until the chemistry teacher looked over.

At lunch she sat with Meilin and Yuhao and Yichen at the long table under the canteen window, squeezed onto the bench so close to Yichen that their elbows knocked every time either of them lifted chopsticks. He had stopped pretending to mind on day two. She told the table about the milk in some detail: that the shop by the gate kept the strawberry ones at the back of the fridge where they were coldest, that you had to reach past the banana ones to get them, that the morning’s carton had been the perfect temperature, possibly a record.

“It’s milk,” Yuhao said.

“It’s the best one in the shop.”

“It’s the same one every day. They only have one kind.”

“Then it’s the best one every day.” She stole a piece of egg from Yichen’s tray to underline the point, and he moved the tray an inch closer to her so she wouldn’t have to reach.

Yuhao looked at him with pure disgust. “You used to have standards.”

“I still have standards,” Yichen said, and gave her the rest of the egg.

The second one arrived after lunch, and Yichen hadn’t bought it.

She came back from the canteen and there it was, beside her notebook, cold enough to have left a ring of water on the desk. Same pink label, same little printed strawberry. Her first, ridiculous thought was that he had found a way to do it twice without her seeing. Then she looked up and found him at his own desk, turned sideways to argue with Chen Yuhao about a basketball game, nowhere near the evidence.

“Who’s that from?” Meilin asked.

“I don’t know.”

“Oh,” Meilin said, in a voice Xiaoran didn’t like at all.

The answer walked over a minute later, scratching the back of his neck. Rong Hao sat two rows behind them, lent his notes to anyone who asked and carried the register for the class monitor when she was busy, and he was going pink in a way that made Xiaoran want to apologise before he’d said anything.

“You got it? The milk?”

“You bought this?”

“I heard you at lunch, telling Tang Meilin it was the best one in the shop. I was going down anyway. So.” He shrugged, too quickly.

To be fair to Rong Hao, she had described that milk at a volume meant for the whole canteen. She thanked him, properly, and he said it was nothing and went back to his seat, and the moment he sat down Meilin turned to her with a face that was doing a great deal of talking.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said a word.”

“Your face has said about forty.”

“Two strawberry milks. One morning. Lin Xiaoran, you’re a woman with options,” Meilin said reverently.

“I’m a woman with one boyfriend and a stomach.”

She opened the carton because leaving it shut felt rude, and took a sip, and it was sweet, a bit too sweet, not as good as the first one, which wasn’t a thing she was going to say out loud to anyone. And then she made the mistake of looking up.

Yichen had stopped arguing with Yuhao. He was looking straight down the classroom at her, at the carton in her hand, and his face did absolutely nothing, which was worse than if it had done something.

He got up, came down the aisle, and stopped by her desk with his hands in his pockets.

“Another one?”

Xiaoran nearly inhaled it. Meilin bent low over her pencil case.

“Rong Hao bought it. He heard me at lunch,” Xiaoran said.

“I see.”

He glanced back at Rong Hao, who had become extremely interested in his English vocabulary, and then back at her, and now there was something in the corner of his mouth that he wasn’t quite managing to hide.

“You must have been very convincing at lunch,” he said.

“I’m always convincing.”

“You are. You kept this?” He picked up the empty carton from the morning, the one she had been guarding all day, turned it round once in his fingers and raised his eyebrows at her.

“I forgot to throw it away.”

“Of course you did,” he said, and dropped it into the recycling bin by the wall on his way back, which felt like a small theft.

The bell went for the afternoon. On his way past Rong Hao’s desk he stopped, and the whole back half of the room went quiet, because everybody in Class 3 had seen at least one drama and knew what came next. All he said was, “Good choice. That’s the one she likes,” in the same pleasant voice he used to thank the canteen aunties. Rong Hao went red to the ears and said thank you for no reason anybody could identify, and Yichen sat down and opened his physics book again.

Meilin leaned over. “He’s smiling at his textbook.”

“He’s reading.”

“Nobody smiles at Newton’s second law.”

Ten minutes into the lesson, while the teacher had her back to them copying a diagram, Xiaoran’s phone buzzed against her leg. She slid it out under the desk.

Yichen: Is the second one as good as the first?

Xiaoran: It’s sweeter.

Yichen: Then don’t finish it. You’ll get a stomachache and blame me.

Xiaoran: Are you jealous of a carton of milk?

Three rows ahead, he didn’t turn round. The teacher finished the diagram and turned, and Xiaoran put on the face of someone who had been listening the whole time. When the teacher turned back to the board, the phone buzzed again.

Yichen: No.

Yichen: I’m reconsidering my strategy.

She coughed into her sleeve to cover a laugh. Up at the front, the back of his neck had gone pink, and she watched it for the rest of the lesson instead of the diagram, and copied the diagram from Meilin afterwards.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the afternoon break she went down to the shop and came back with a packet of sesame biscuits, the good kind in the gold wrapper, and put it on Rong Hao’s desk.

“For the milk. Thank you. Really,” she said.

Rong Hao looked at the biscuits and then at her, and something in his face settled. He laughed a little. “Okay. We’re even.”

“We’re even,” she agreed, enormously relieved.

“That,” Meilin said on the way back to their seats, “was the most polite rejection I’ve ever witnessed.”

“It wasn’t a rejection. It was biscuits.”

“It was a receipt.”

By the last bell the second carton was empty, mostly out of principle. Yichen was waiting for her by the classroom door with both their umbrellas, though it wasn’t raining, because he had decided at some point that week that her umbrella was also his responsibility. She hooked her arm through his before they’d even reached the stairs, which she had also decided at some point that week, and he let her.

“Finished it?”

“All of it.”

“Brave.” Somewhere between the second floor and the first, he said, without looking at her, “Tomorrow I’m buying it before anyone else gets the idea.”

“Why?”

“So you don’t have to drink two.”

She laughed so loudly that a first-year on the landing jumped, and leaned her whole weight on his arm for the rest of the stairs, and he complained about it and didn’t move his arm.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning there was a carton on her desk before the first bell, cold, with a yellow sticky note on the front in handwriting she was starting to know.

First.

Meilin read it over her shoulder and groaned so loudly that three people turned round. Xiaoran peeled the note off and pressed it inside the cover of her maths notebook, where nobody would look, and took out her phone.

Xiaoran: What time did you get here?

Yichen: Early enough.

Xiaoran: How early?

Yichen: The caretaker let me in.

She turned round in her seat. Three rows ahead, Zhou Yichen was looking at the blackboard with the face of a model student, and when she threw a balled-up corner of paper at the back of his head, he caught it without looking and put it in his pocket. She drank the milk slowly through morning reading and didn’t give Meilin a single sip.

chapters.desc: The first time he walked her home, it rained too hard to see the street. The second time the sun is out, and he takes the long way on purpose.
chapters.title: Walking Her Home
chapters.epigraph: “Then I’ll walk you home again.”
chapters.content:
The first time Zhou Yichen walked Lin Xiaoran home, it had rained so hard that he hadn’t seen the street. He remembered her face under the umbrella, the gate of her compound, and almost nothing in between.

The second time was a Friday a week later, and the sun was out.

“I’m walking you home,” he said at the bottom of the stairs, while half of Class 3 streamed past them towards the bike sheds.

Xiaoran already had hold of his sleeve. She’d taken it somewhere on the second floor, without asking, the way she had started taking his sleeve or his hand or the strap of his bag whenever they were walking anywhere, and he had stopped noticing when she did it and started noticing when she didn’t. “It’s not raining.”

“I know.”

“So you don’t have to.”

“You know where I live,” she pointed out.

“I know where your gate is. It was raining sideways. I couldn’t have found it again with a map. Show me.” He looked down at her.

Something happened in her face then, quick and pleased, that he wouldn’t understand for another twenty minutes. “That way,” she said, and pulled.

For a while nothing seemed unusual. They talked about the maths homework, which was unreasonable for a Friday, and about Yuhao, who had fallen asleep in politics with his eyes open and answered a question about the five-year plan with the word “rebounds.” Xiaoran was halfway through what Meilin had said about it when Yichen slowed down outside a fruit shop with a striped awning and a crate of peaches by the door.

An old man sat on a stool next to the crate, fanning himself with a folded newspaper. He lifted the paper at them like a flag.

“That shop has really good peaches,” Xiaoran said.

“You said that already.”

“Did I?”

“About fifteen minutes ago. Outside this shop.” He looked at the awning, then at the bus stop on the corner, which he also recognised.

“There are two fruit shops on this road.”

“With the same grandfather?”

The old man waved again, delighted. Xiaoran waved back, which didn’t help her case at all.

“Lin Xiaoran. Do you know the way to your own house?”

“Of course I know the way to my house.”

“Then why have we walked in a circle?”

She examined the peaches. “It’s a rectangle, technically.”

He shut his eyes. When he opened them he was laughing, the helpless, silent kind that he usually saved for Yuhao falling off things, and she put her forehead against his arm to hide her face.

“On purpose,” he said.

“You said you’d walk me home. You didn’t say how long it was allowed to take.”

The old man had stopped fanning to listen. Yichen bought two peaches from him, mostly out of embarrassment, and the old man told him that the girl’s mother bought from him every Sunday without fail, that she always picked the hard ones and let them soften on the windowsill, and that if he wanted to arrive anywhere before dark he should take the left at the corner.

“Thank you,” Yichen said, politely, and Xiaoran made a small noise into the collar of her uniform.

Out of earshot, he said, “Twenty minutes.”

“I know.”

“Past the same peaches twice.”

“They’re good peaches. Are you annoyed?” She was still holding his arm in both hands, as if he might try to make a run for it now that he knew.

“No.”

“You’re a bit annoyed.”

“I’m a bit impressed,” he said, and moved her hand down his arm until it was in his hand instead, which was what she’d been angling for since the gym.

The short way took eight minutes. She narrated every one of them. They turned left at the corner, crossed at the lights and went down a quieter street of low old buildings with washing strung between the balconies, and she pointed out everything as if she were conducting a tour for a foreign dignitary: the patch of pavement where she’d fallen off her bike at fourteen ( “Did you cry? For a reasonable length of time.” ), the noodle place that put too much vinegar in everything, the window of a lady who kept a parrot that could say Xiaoran, homework.

“It can’t.”

“It used to. Then she moved it to the back room. I think it was a complaint.”

Outside a small bakery she slowed down, and he understood before she said a word.

“Their strawberry buns are the best ones in the city.”

“Another strawberry?”

“It’s a theme. You started it.”

“Then I’d better finish it,” he said, and went in before she could tell him she’d been joking.

The bakery smelled of butter and hot sugar. He came out with a paper bag already going see-through at one corner, broke the bun in half on the step and handed her the bigger piece, and they sat down on the low step outside, between a parked bicycle and a pot of geraniums that had given up, with their schoolbags on their knees. The filling was too sweet and still warm. She got some on her thumb and licked it off without thinking, and he became interested in the traffic.

“Meilin and I usually get the 46. It goes round past the hospital. It’s faster,” she said, leaning into his shoulder.

“Then why walk?”

“The 46 doesn’t go past the peaches. And on the bus you can’t talk. Somebody’s grandmother always listens.” She brushed crumbs off her skirt and then, for good measure, off his.

“Somebody’s grandfather listened today.”

“He doesn’t count. He’s on our side.”

He folded the empty paper bag into a small square, then into a smaller square, because he was the kind of person who did that, and she watched him do it and thought with some alarm that she could probably watch him fold paper bags for an hour.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her compound was a plain gate with a security booth, a radio inside it playing opera, and a row of plane trees along the pavement. A bicycle was chained to the railing with a basket full of leeks. He looked at all of it with great attention, the booth and the trees and the leeks, and she realised he was memorising it, and had to look at her shoes.

“So this is what it looks like when it isn’t raining,” he said.

“It’s not much.”

“I wanted to see it. This one’s for your mother.” He held out the second peach.

“She’ll ask who it’s from.”

“Tell her a man on the corner insisted.”

She laughed, and didn’t let go of his hand, and he didn’t take it back. A woman with a shopping bag went through the gate and gave them a long look. Somewhere inside the compound a bicycle bell rang.

“Where do you live, anyway?” she asked, as if it had only just occurred to her, which it hadn’t. She had looked it up on the class contact sheet on the first night and then felt like a criminal.

He pointed back the way they had come, past the school, past the bus station. “That way. Twenty-five minutes.”

“Twenty-five minutes the other way?”

“About that.”

“Plus the rectangle.”

“Plus the rectangle,” he agreed.

She considered this with a guilty face for almost two seconds, and then held on to his hand a bit tighter. “Then you should stay for a while. Before you walk all that way. To rest.”

“I’ve been sitting on a step eating a bun.”

“That was a different kind of rest.”

“Do you usually come home on your own?”

“Sometimes. Sometimes with Meilin, when she’s not at her aunt’s.”

“Message me when you’re in.”

“I always message you when I’m in.”

“Message me anyway.”

She took a step back, then a step forward again, and caught his sleeve. “Next time I’ll take you the short way.”

“Next time?”

“If you want.”

He smiled. “Then I’ll walk you home again.”

She went in through the gate and looked back twice. He was still standing under the plane trees both times, with the peach bag in his hand, and the second time he lifted it at her the way the old man had lifted his newspaper.

He was halfway down the street when his phone went.

Xiaoran: I’m in! Mum says thank you for the peach and WHO is the old man

Yichen: Tell her it’s a long story.

Xiaoran: It’s a rectangle.

He put the phone away. A few steps later he took it out again.

Yichen: Why the long way?

The dots came up and went away twice.

Xiaoran: I wanted you to see all of it. Not just the gate in the rain.

He read it standing on the corner by the bakery, where the step still had crumbs on it.

Yichen: I’ll remember. The fruit shop, the parrot, the bakery.

Xiaoran: Mostly the bakery.

He walked home the long way. He went back past the fruit shop on purpose, to see if he could find the rectangle on his own, and he could, and the old man waved his newspaper at him. It was a completely inefficient way to spend a Friday. He was fairly sure she had planned that part too.

chapters.desc: Zhou Yichen noticed her long before she noticed him—loud, chaotic, impossible to forget—and quietly decided she would become his favourite coincidence.
chapters.title: All Our Coincidences Were Intentional
chapters.content:
Before Zhou Yichen ever spoke to Lin Xiaoran, he already knew three things about her. First, she was loud. Second, she was dramatic. Third, she could cry faster than anyone he had ever met.

The first time he noticed her was outside the teachers’ office. A girl in a slightly messy uniform stood there arguing with a teacher over confiscated snacks.

“But I need instant noodles,” she protested.

“You don’t.”

“What if I faint from heartbreak during math class?”

“You won’t.”

“How can you be so sure?”

At first, Yichen had only been walking past. Then the girl sighed and muttered under her breath—

“This school suppresses artistic souls.”

The teacher nearly laughed despite herself. Yichen did too. The girl was cute. Not just pretty—every single thing she felt showed on her face. That should’ve been the end of it. But after noticing someone once, somehow you kept seeing them everywhere. In the cafeteria complaining because her pudding was sold out. In the hallway fake-crying because her friend Tang Meilin refused to lend her lip gloss. In class presentations confidently speaking nonsense with full conviction.

“She’s ridiculous,” Chen Yuhao commented one afternoon while the basketball team walked past the courtyard.

Below them, Lin Xiaoran sat on a bench sulking while Meilin ignored her.

“What happened?” Yichen asked.

“She lost rock-paper-scissors.”

“…That’s why she looks heartbroken?”

“She takes competition seriously.”

Yichen watched as Xiaoran grabbed Meilin’s sleeve and whined something shameless enough to make Meilin shove her away. Instead of getting angry, Xiaoran just laughed, loud and careless, like she had never once worried what anyone thought of her. Yichen looked away after a second. For some reason, he was smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second time she truly caught his attention was during rain duty week. Students rushed through the corridors while teachers yelled about slippery floors. Yichen carried sports equipment back towards the gym when he noticed a familiar figure crouching beside the school garden. Lin Xiaoran was crouched in the rain with a tiny soaked kitten tucked inside her jacket, her own hair dripping.

“What are you doing?” Meilin asked beside her.

“It looked cold.”

“You’re also cold.”

“I’m tougher than him.”

The kitten meowed pitifully. Xiaoran looked devastated.

“Oh no. Don’t sound so pitiful,” she whispered, hugging it carefully.

Yichen laughed before he could stop himself. Xiaoran looked up. Their eyes met for the first time. Yichen saw her properly then. Soft features. Bright eyes. Pink lips slightly parted in surprise. For one second, Xiaoran simply stared. Then her eyes narrowed.

“…Why are you laughing?”

“Nothing.”

“You definitely laughed at me.”

“A little.”

“Hm. Rude.”

But she didn’t actually sound offended. Yichen walked away afterward. But he kept thinking about her. About how she held the kitten so gently. About how expressive her face was. About how alive she felt compared to everyone else around him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The arcade encounter one week later wasn’t exactly coincidence. Well. Not entirely. The basketball team had won a practice match nearby, and Yuhao suggested going to the shopping centre arcade afterward. Yichen normally would’ve refused. But walking past the claw machines, he stopped. There she was again. Lin Xiaoran. Standing before a claw machine with absolute fury on her face.

“I’ve already spent twenty-seven yuan,” she told Meilin.

“Then stop.”

“No.”

“The bunny looks ugly anyway.”

“Don’t insult him.”

Yichen watched silently from several machines away. Xiaoran failed again. And again. Then she crouched in front of the machine and pointed accusingly.

“You and I are enemies now.”

Meilin looked exhausted.

“You’re talking to a machine.”

“It started first.”

Yichen laughed. Before he knew it, he was walking towards her.

“You’re grabbing the bunny wrong.”

Xiaoran spun around. Yichen almost smiled. It was exactly the face she’d made defending instant noodles to the teacher.

“You work for the machine company or something?” she demanded.

And just like that, they were talking.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the arcade, the “coincidences” started piling up. Except most of them were caused by Zhou Yichen himself. He simply never admitted it. Like the convenience store encounter. Xiaoran entered after school craving strawberry milk only to discover the shelf empty.

“This country has failed me,” she sighed.

A hand appeared beside her, holding the exact drink.

“You can have mine.”

She turned. Zhou Yichen stood there as if this were fate, and not because he’d bought the last bottle ten minutes earlier, knowing the store was almost out.

“…Why are you here?”

“Buying water.”

“You bought strawberry milk.”

“I wanted this earlier. But not anymore.”

She laughed despite herself. Right then, Yichen decided he wanted to make her laugh as often as possible.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then came the library coincidence. Which was definitely not coincidence. Yuhao had mentioned that Xiaoran studied there every Wednesday, because her home WiFi died every week for “mysterious reasons.” The mysterious reason turned out to be her neighbour, who had been stealing it to download pirated games. So, naturally, Yichen started studying there every Wednesday too.

The first time Xiaoran spotted him, she squinted at him.

“You’re everywhere.”

“That sounds romantic.”

“That sounds creepy.”

He smiled lazily.

“Then I’ll leave.”

“…I didn’t say leave.”

Yichen sat back down. Xiaoran looked horrified at herself for saying that out loud. He nearly laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then came the bus stop coincidence. The café coincidence. The hallway coincidence. The school festival coincidence.

At first, Xiaoran genuinely believed fate kept pushing them together.

Meanwhile, Yuhao watched Yichen deliberately take the long way between classes just to “accidentally” run into Xiaoran near Building C.

“You’re actually shameless,” Yuhao said.

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“You changed your entire lunch schedule because she eats earlier.”

“Coincidence.”

“You hate the cafeteria before noon.”

“People change.”

Yichen rubbed the back of his neck, which was what he always did when he was lying. Yuhao stared at him in disbelief. Zhou Yichen—calm, rational, untouchable Zhou Yichen—was staging run-ins like the lead in a romance drama. And he looked happy doing it. The moment she came into view, his whole expression changed. His smile went warm and easy, like she’d brought the sun in with her and didn’t know it.

One afternoon, Yuhao finally asked the obvious question.

“What exactly do you like about her so much?”

Yichen looked towards the courtyard below. Lin Xiaoran was down there again, complaining about something while Meilin ate her lunch in peace. Probably another crisis. Yichen watched her, smiling without realising it.

“She makes everything feel less tiring.”

Yuhao blinked. Below them, Xiaoran happened to look up. Their eyes met across the courtyard. Her whole face lit up, like she was happy to see him and hadn’t noticed yet. Yichen smiled wider. And right then, he knew he was in serious trouble.
chapters.epigraph: “Before he ever spoke to her, he had already started choosing her.”

chapters.desc: Evening self-study seats are now assigned by exam rank, both classes together, and fourteen desks between her and Zhou Yichen is thirteen too many.
chapters.title: Seat Swap
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to rush.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had never cared about rankings. She cared about passing, about not spending her Sundays buried in revision, and about the stationery shop near the school gate getting the new gel pens in before Meilin did. The number beside her name on the monthly exam list was something that happened to her, like weather. Then Teacher Xu changed the seats.

For the first weeks of December, Class 3 had sat more or less where it liked, which meant Xiaoran had sat at the desk directly behind Zhou Yichen, close enough to put her chin on her folded arms and read his notes over his shoulder, close enough to poke his back with the end of her pen whenever a lesson got boring, which was most lessons. She had started to think of this as a law of nature.

On Monday morning their head teacher walked in with the exam results under her arm and the expression of a woman who had been looking at the back row for too long.

“From today,” Teacher Xu said, “seats go by the December monthly exam. First place chooses first. Then second. All the way down.”

The groan went round the room like a wave at a football match.

“Teacher, why?”

“Because some of you have been treating the back corner as a holiday resort,” Teacher Xu said, and looked at Chen Yuhao, who looked out of the window.

“First place. Zhou Yichen.”

He got up, picked up his books and walked down the aisle, and Xiaoran watched him go with the specific feeling of someone watching a train leave. He chose a desk in the third row, by the window, and sat down without looking back, and the names went on. Xiaoran was twenty-ninth.

By the time Teacher Xu reached her, the only desks left were at the back, and she ended up in the far corner by the mop bucket, next to the radiator that only worked on one side. She put her books down and looked up the room, past all the heads, to the third row by the window.

“How many people are between me and him?”

Meilin, who had come in thirty-first and ended up beside her, counted under her breath. “Fourteen. Fifteen if you count Chen Yuhao, who is basically two people.”

“I don’t like this.”

“You’ve never complained about your seat before.”

“My seat has never been in Siberia before.”

Meilin put her hand over her mouth.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“Your shoulders are shaking.”

“They’re cold. We’re in Siberia,” Meilin said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first day was survivable. The breaks were ten minutes long and she spent every one of them at his desk, perched on the edge of Yuhao’s chair while Yuhao stood beside it with the face of a man evicted from his own home. She stole Yichen’s eraser and gave it back. She drew a small star in the margin of his English workbook. When the bell went she trailed back down the room to the corner, and during physics she discovered that from the mop bucket you could see the back of his head and absolutely nothing else.

There were other problems. When he sighed at a hard question she couldn’t hear it. When the teacher stepped out she couldn’t poke him. When she finished an exercise she couldn’t lean forward and whisper the answer into the back of his collar to see if he’d got the same one, which had been one of her favourite parts of the day, because he always had and always pretended to check.

On Tuesday she sent him a message during the lunch break, from across the room.

Xiaoran: It’s very far back here. The radiator is making noises.

Yichen: What kind of noises?

Xiaoran: Lonely ones.

He turned round in his seat, found her in the corner, and gave her a look of such patience that Meilin had to leave the room.

On Wednesday, Meilin caught her copying history dates into a notebook in three colours.

“Since when do you revise history at lunch?”

“Since today.”

“The test’s in four weeks.”

“I know when the test is.”

Meilin sat back slowly. “Is this about Zhou Yichen?”

The pen stopped. “I want to improve my ranking.”

“Why?”

Xiaoran looked at the dates for a while. “I want to sit closer,” she said, so low it was nearly lost in the clatter of lunch boxes.

“How close?”

“Within two desks.”

Meilin laughed until the boy in front turned round, and then, to her credit, she stopped laughing, took the green highlighter out of Xiaoran’s hand, and started testing her on the Opium Wars.

By Thursday Xiaoran had done the arithmetic, which was the only arithmetic she did willingly. Mathematics was hopeless; she could study it for a month and gain four points. But history, English, Chinese and politics were subjects where effort turned into marks. There were four of them. She read English vocabulary on the bus, revised history at lunch, and spent self-study on the essay questions she usually left until the night before, sitting in the corner with her coat on because of the radiator.

She still took her maths to Yichen, because there was no point pretending she could do it alone. At Thursday’s long break she put her exercise book down on his desk and sat on his chair with him, half on and half off, which the chair wasn’t designed for.

“You changed the sign here.”

“Where?”

He pointed. She sighed and leaned into his shoulder while she fixed it, and he held the book steady for her so she could write without moving her head, which was the correct response.

“You’ve been working,” he said.

“How do you know?”

“I turn round sometimes. You’re always writing.”

“You turn round?”

“I check you’re not asleep. Try this way. It’s easier to remember.” He took a scrap of paper and wrote out a shorter method in his neat, quick hand.

She tucked the paper inside her exercise book as if it were a banknote. She had already stood up when he said, still looking at the problem, “You don’t have to rush.”

“What?”

“Your marks. There’s time before the next exam.”

She studied his face, trying to work out how much he knew, and got nothing. “I know,” she said, and went back to Siberia.

“Did he guess?” Meilin asked.

“No.”

“He’s the cleverest boy in the year. I don’t believe you.”

“Then don’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The days went by. She didn’t turn into a model student. She still got distracted, still spent too long choosing highlighters, still stared out of the window when the teacher talked about function graphs. But she tried, properly, in a way she never had before, and it was strange to discover that trying felt less like suffering and more like having somewhere to go.

The night before the January exam, Meilin rang her.

“Are you studying?”

“Yes.”

“Not watching a drama?”

“No.”

“Are you ill?”

“Meilin!”

Meilin laughed, and then her voice changed. “You know you don’t have to get into the top ten for him. He likes you in the corner too.”

“I know. But I want to sit near him. It’s my seat. I’m going to earn it,” Xiaoran said, after a while.

The results went up on the board outside the office the following Monday. She found Yichen first, because his name was always first. Then she went down the list with her finger, and further down, and there she was.

Her maths had gone up by three points, which was a rounding error. History had gone up by nineteen. English by eleven. Together they had moved her up thirteen places.

“Sixteenth. Sixteenth!” Meilin said, and grabbed her arm.

“Is that enough?”

Meilin counted along the seating plan in her head, lips moving. “If the people above you do what they always do, you’ll be right next to him. Or one desk away. Depends on Rong Hao.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Teacher Xu read the names out after lunch. Yichen went first, chose the same desk in the third row by the window, and sat down, then something odd happened.

The second-place girl looked at the empty desk beside him, the best desk in the room, and walked past it to the one behind. The third-place boy did the same. So did the fourth. By the eighth name the whole class had noticed, and by the twelfth it had become a sort of collective performance: people walked up to the empty desk beside Zhou Yichen, looked at it, and then sat somewhere else with enormous dignity. When it was Yuhao’s turn, he strolled past it and announced to nobody in particular, “Not that one. That one’s taken,” and three people clapped.

Teacher Xu looked up from her list. “What is going on?”

“Nothing, Teacher,” said Class 3, in unison.

“Lin Xiaoran,” Teacher Xu said, after a long pause, with the air of a woman who had decided she didn’t want to know.

Xiaoran walked up the aisle with her books held against her chest and her face on fire. She put them down on the desk beside his. He moved his pencil case two inches to the left to make room, which was the only thing that gave him away.

“Hi,” she said.

“Hi.”

“I improved.”

“Thirteen places. Nineteen points in history. I looked,” he said, in the voice other people used for football scores.

“You looked?”

“I looked first thing this morning. Before you did. You could have just told me you wanted to sit closer.” He was smiling now, the quiet smile that meant he had known about this for days.

She stared at him. “How did you know?”

“You told Meilin at lunch on Wednesday. At a volume.”

“Yichen!”

Teacher Xu cleared her throat, and the room went back to being a room. Xiaoran opened her textbook with her face still burning, and a minute later a folded piece of paper slid across the desk from his side, no longer a long journey through fourteen people.

Congratulations on your new seat.

She wrote underneath: It was a lot of work.

I know. I’ll try not to move too far away next time.

You’d better, she wrote, and then, because she could, she hooked her foot round his ankle under the desk and kept it there for the rest of the lesson. Mathematics, unfortunately, was still impossible. Everything else was much easier.

chapters.desc: Meilin notices that Lin Xiaoran’s sevens have started to look exactly like someone else’s.
chapters.title: His Handwriting in Her Notebook
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t have to change your handwriting. I liked it before, too.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had never thought about her handwriting. It was readable, mostly, and that seemed like enough. Her notes were a mixture of careful headings in three colours, hurried explanations that slid downhill towards the margin, small doodles, and stars beside anything important, or anything she liked, or anything on the lunch menu. Her letters leaned in different directions depending on her mood. Her sevens were two strokes and done.

Then, on a Thursday in early January, Tang Meilin looked over during maths and said, “Since when do you cross your sevens?”

Xiaoran kept copying from the board. “I don’t.”

Meilin tapped the page with her pen. At the end of the line, at the end of a calculation that was almost certainly wrong, sat a seven with a small neat bar through its middle.

“You used to do them like this. Now you do them like this. Since about Monday.” Meilin drew one on the corner of her own page, two strokes, a little lopsided. She drew the other kind, with the bar.

“People’s handwriting changes.”

“Does it.”

“All the time. It’s science.”

Meilin propped her chin on her hand and looked at her for so long that Xiaoran turned to a fresh page.

The truth was she hadn’t decided anything. It had just happened. On Monday, in evening self-study, she had borrowed Yichen’s maths notebook to copy a method, the way she borrowed it most evenings, and had sat with it open on her desk next to his while he did physics beside her. His notes were nothing like hers. Everything lined up. His numbers were the same shape every time. When he crossed something out he drew one straight line through it, so you could still read what he’d got wrong, whereas her crossings-out looked like small storms. His fours were closed at the top like little flags. His sevens had a bar through the middle.

She had found it oddly soothing, the way some people find it soothing to watch fish. And then she had gone back to her own page and written a seven with a bar through it, because it looked nice. Then another one. By Wednesday it was hers.

“It’s his. It’s Zhou Yichen’s seven,” Meilin said, reading her face like a menu.

“How would you know what his sevens look like?”

“Because you’ve been copying his homework method into your book every night for a month and I sit next to you. Oh my goodness. You’ve started writing like him.” Meilin’s smile widened.

“I have not.”

“You’re going to start drawing his little flags on your fours next.”

Xiaoran turned away with her cheeks heating up and decided, firmly, that from now on she would write her sevens the normal way. She lasted until the next maths lesson.

✦ ✦ ✦

He noticed that evening. She had pushed her exercise book over to his side of the desk at the self-study break so he could check a question, and leaned on his arm to watch him do it, which was how she watched him do most things.

“The answer’s right,” he said.

“Really?”

“Really.” He ran his pen down the working, and then the pen stopped. He looked at the seven at the end of the line. Then at the next one. Then the one after that.

“Why are you looking at it like that?”

“Your sevens have changed.”

She sat up so fast that his arm lost its support. “Have they?”

“Mm.”

“Maybe. Slightly. It happens.”

“Did you start writing them like mine?”

She grabbed the exercise book back and held it against her chest. He let her take it. He didn’t laugh, which was almost worse; he just looked at her with an expression of deep, quiet enjoyment, like a man who has been handed a present.

“Don’t smile,” she said.

“I’m not.”

“Your eyes are smiling.”

“Is it bad? Writing them like mine?” he asked.

She looked down at the book in her arms. “No.”

“Then it’s fine.” He went back to his physics.

She sat there, still hugging the exercise book. “You actually noticed?”

“Of course I noticed.”

“How?”

“I read your notes. Every time you leave them on my side of the desk. Which is always,” he said, as if this were the most ordinary thing in the world, and turned a page.

She put her forehead down on the cover of the exercise book and stayed there until the bell.

The next afternoon Meilin got her confirmation. Xiaoran had been trying, in history, to write sevens the old way, and every single one had come out with a bar through it.

“You could just admit it,” Meilin said.

“Admit what?”

“That you like his handwriting.”

“I think it’s neat.”

“Of course.”

“That’s all.”

“Of course, look. I’m doing it too. Solidarity,” Meilin said again, and wrote a seven with a bar through it in her own book.

Xiaoran looked. “Yours looks like a fork.”

“It needs practice.”

That Saturday she did her maths homework at the kitchen table with her mother’s radio on, and sent him a photograph of the finished page before her mother could see her doing it.

Xiaoran: 23 sevens. All crossed. All mine now. You can’t have them back.

Yichen: I don’t want them back.

Xiaoran: Good.

Yichen: Do you want my fours as well? They’re very reliable.

Xiaoran: Don’t push your luck.

Yichen: Question 6 is wrong, by the way.

She looked at question six, found the sign she had changed, fixed it, and sent him a photograph of the corrected answer with eleven exclamation marks. He sent back a single thumbs-up, which from Zhou Yichen counted as a standing ovation. Her mother asked from the stove why she was smiling at a maths book, and she said it was a good maths book, and her mother, who had been sixteen once, didn’t ask again.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next week, Chen Yuhao borrowed Yichen’s physics notes at the self-study break, because his own were mostly drawings of basketball shoes. He got four pages in before he stopped.

“Why is there a star here?”

Yichen didn’t look up. “It’s important.”

“You’ve never drawn a star in your life. There’s one on every page. Since Tuesday. Zhou Yichen. Are these her stars?” Yuhao flipped back a page, then another. He held the notebook up to the ceiling light.

Beside Yichen, Xiaoran had gone completely still, her pen hovering over a history date.

“They’re stars. Nobody owns stars,” Yichen said.

“She does. She puts them next to everything. She put one next to the lunch menu.”

“Then I’m borrowing them,” Yichen said, and held out his hand for the notebook, and Yuhao gave it back, because there was nothing else to be done with a person who said things like that in a calm voice in a full classroom.

Meilin leaned over from behind them and whispered, “He’s copying you back.”

Xiaoran didn’t answer. She drew a small star beside the date she had been about to write, neatly, the best star of her life. Then, under the desk, she found his free hand and held on to it for the rest of self-study, and copied the rest of the history notes left-handed, which made them nearly illegible and was entirely worth it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday they walked out together, her arm through his, her notebook pressed against her chest with her free hand.

“Did you finish the maths?”

“Almost. I got distracted by a star.”

He didn’t ask which one. Just before the stairs he said, looking straight ahead, “You don’t have to change your handwriting. I liked it before, too.”

It took her a second to understand. He had seen her trying to write the old sevens in history. He had seen her get embarrassed, and he had remembered, and now here he was on the stairs, reassuring her about something that was, objectively, not important at all.

“I wasn’t trying to change it,” she said.

“I know.”

“I just thought your sevens looked neat.”

“Thank you,” he said gravely.

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re teasing me.”

“A little.”

She thumped his arm with the notebook. He took it out of her hand, opened it as they walked, and looked for a while at the page she’d been working on: the calculations, the stars, the wandering headings, all the small barred sevens. Then he handed it back.

“Yours is easier to recognise than mine.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s yours. Even if you borrow a few of my numbers.” He waited a beat.

She laughed and leaned her whole weight against him, and he staggered half a step for her benefit on the landing. At the gate she made him hold out his palm and wrote a seven on it in blue biro, barred, neat, and he looked at it all the way to the bus stop and didn’t wash it off until Sunday. That evening, when she sat down to finish her homework, she didn’t change her sevens back.

chapters.desc: The rain starts at the last bell, there is one umbrella between them, and a great deal to negotiate about who holds it.
chapters.title: Umbrella Etiquette
chapters.epigraph: “I know. But let me.”
chapters.content:
The rain started as the last bell rang. It began as a few drops ticking against the classroom windows and turned, in the time it took Class 3 to pack its bags, into the kind of downpour that blurred the buildings across the road. Lin Xiaoran stood at the window with her bag half zipped and watched the courtyard fill with water.

“It’s raining,” she announced.

“Excellent observation,” said Tang Meilin, and took a small folding umbrella out of her bag with the smugness of a woman who checked the forecast.

“Can we share?”

“Where’s yours?”

“At home.”

“Why is it at home?”

“It wasn’t raining this morning.”

“That,” Meilin said, “is generally how weather works.” She pointed her umbrella across the room like a sword. “Go and ask your boyfriend. Mine’s for one person, and I’m the person.”

Zhou Yichen was by the back door, swinging his bag onto his shoulder and arguing with Chen Yuhao about whether a three-pointer counted if you’d stepped on the line, which apparently it didn’t, and which Yuhao was taking personally. He saw her coming across the room and took the umbrella out of the side pocket of his bag before she’d opened her mouth.

“You forgot yours.”

“How do you know?”

“You’ve got the face. Come on.” He shook it out at the top of the stairs.

It was a black umbrella, big enough for two people as long as the two people paid attention to each other. They went out through the gate under it, and for the first few minutes everything was fine. They talked about the history test, which had been unfair, and the canteen, which had run out of the sweet potatoes, which had also been unfair. Then Xiaoran looked up and frowned.

“Your shoulder’s wet.”

He glanced down. A dark patch had spread across the left shoulder of his uniform. “It’s fine.”

“You’re holding it too far over me.”

He moved the umbrella an inch. “Better?”

“Not really.”

“Then what do you suggest?”

“Hold it in the middle.”

“It is in the middle.”

“It’s not. Your hand’s over there. Give it to me.” She pointed.

He gave her the handle, because arguing with Lin Xiaoran about an umbrella was the kind of thing a person only did once. She adjusted it with enormous seriousness, half a centimetre at a time, until it was tilted well towards him, and nodded at her work.

“There.”

Thirty seconds later her own shoulder was soaked.

“You moved it,” he said.

“Because yours was wet.”

“And now yours is wet.”

“Then come closer,” she said, as if this were his fault, and he did, until their shoulders were pressed together all the way down. She didn’t need to be told twice; she leaned in so hard that he had to adjust his walk to stay upright, and then she looked up at the umbrella and said, with deep satisfaction, “See? Physics.”

The trouble was that Xiaoran had firm views about how an umbrella should be shared. Both people stayed dry. The handle stayed exactly in the middle. Nobody was a martyr. Yichen, on the other hand, seemed perfectly content to walk home with one side of himself underwater, and every time she looked away the umbrella drifted back towards her side.

On the quiet stretch past the bike repair shop, she caught him at it.

“You’re doing it again.”

“I know.”

“Why?”

He tipped his head down so she could hear him over the rain on the canvas. “Because I’d rather get wet than have you get cold.”

She stopped walking. He stopped with her, and the umbrella stopped, and they stood there in the middle of the pavement while a man on a scooter swerved round them and swore.

“That’s not fair,” she said.

“What isn’t?”

“You can’t say things like that when we’re arguing about an umbrella. Then I can’t argue properly.”

“Is that so,” he said, and took the handle back out of her hand, moved it over the middle of both of them, and put his free arm round her shoulders to tuck her under it, until there was no gap left to argue about. “Is it fair now?”

She checked. It was in the middle. They were both mostly dry. His arm was round her. “Yes,” she said, a little muffled, because her face was against his blazer.

A few minutes later she noticed that his other hand was carrying her schoolbag.

“Why have you got my bag?”

“You gave it to me.”

“When?”

“When you took the umbrella. You needed both hands for the steering.”

She tried to remember and couldn’t. “Do I want it back?”

“Do you?”

“No,” she decided, and hooked two fingers into his blazer pocket instead, so that she was holding on to him in two places, which seemed safer in this weather.

They stopped at the shop on the corner of the residential road, where the awning was wide enough for a crowd of schoolchildren, and Xiaoran went straight to the heated cabinet by the till and came back with two cartons of hot milk.

He was already reaching for his wallet. She put her hand flat over the cartons.

“I’ll pay.”

“Why?”

“Because you’ve got my bag and the umbrella and a wet shoulder.”

“That isn’t much.”

“I know. But let me.”

He stepped aside. She paid with two coins and a great deal of ceremony, and they stood under the awning drinking hot milk out of the cartons while the rain came down in sheets beyond the edge of the canvas. She looked at his shoulder, then at hers, and handed him her carton.

“Hold this.”

He held it. She reached up and brushed the water off his shoulder with the flat of her hand, frowning. He stood perfectly still and let her, looking down at her bent head, and when she glanced up he was smiling in a way that made her stop brushing.

“Xiaoran. It’s all right.”

“It’s not all right. You’ll get ill and then you’ll have to miss practice and you’ll be grumpy and it’ll be the umbrella’s fault.”

“The umbrella’s?”

“I can’t blame you. You were being nice.”

When the rain eased a little they went back out. This time she didn’t argue about where the handle was. She put her arm through his, pressed herself against his side, and stayed there, which turned out to solve the whole problem, because there was no longer any space between them for the rain to get into.

“If your shoulder gets wet,” she said, “you tell me.”

“All right.”

“And you don’t pretend it’s fine.”

“And if yours gets wet?”

“I’ll tell you. See? We have a system now.” She looked pleased.

At the turn where they usually split, she stopped and looked at his shoulder one last time. It was still damp.

“You’ll get wet again tomorrow if it rains.”

“Then I’ll bring a bigger umbrella.”

“You said that last time.”

“Then I’ll bring two.”

She laughed, and tugged his sleeve, and went off down her road. Halfway along she turned round and shouted over the rain, loud enough for the whole street, “Next time, hold my hand as well!”

“I was holding your bag!”

“Hold both!”

He stood at the corner with his left side wet through and laughed out loud, alone, in the rain, which a woman passing with her shopping clearly found alarming.

At nine that evening, while she was meant to be doing English, her phone lit up on top of the vocabulary book.

Yichen: Home. Dry.

Xiaoran: Prove it.

A photograph arrived: his school blazer hanging over the back of a chair next to a radiator, the left shoulder still a shade darker than the right.

Xiaoran: That shoulder is NOT dry.

Yichen: It’s drying. It’s in the process.

Xiaoran: Did you have a hot shower?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: Did you drink something hot?

Yichen: My mother made ginger tea. She asked why only one side of me got wet.

Xiaoran: What did you say??

Yichen: I said the umbrella was being held by someone with strong opinions.

She rolled over on her bed and pressed her face into the pillow and made a noise that brought her mother to the door to ask if she was all right.

Xiaoran: Tell her it was a fair system in the end.

Yichen: I’ll tell her it was your system.

Xiaoran: Goodnight. Keep the shoulder warm.

Yichen: Goodnight. Bring your umbrella tomorrow.

Xiaoran: No.

Yichen: Why not?

Xiaoran: Because then I’d have to walk on my own under it.

There was a long pause, long enough for her to wonder whether that had been too much and decide that it hadn’t.

Yichen: Leave it at home, then.

She did. It rained again on Thursday. She didn’t even pretend to look for it.

He bought a bigger umbrella that weekend, navy, with a wooden handle. The first time it rained, she stood under it, looked up at all that extra space, and moved closer anyway.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran thought she understood Zhou Yichen completely… until she saw what his silence looked like when someone else tried to take his place.
chapters.title: The Day Zhou Yichen Finally Got Jealous
chapters.content:
The first sign something was wrong was that Zhou Yichen stopped smiling. Not completely. Just… less. And for someone like Zhou Yichen, who usually looked at Lin Xiaoran like she personally invented happiness, the difference was obvious to everyone. Everyone except Lin Xiaoran.

“Yichen,” she announced proudly during lunch, “someone confessed to me today.”

Chen Yuhao choked on his drink. Tang Meilin slowly lowered her spoon. Across the table, Zhou Yichen looked up calmly.

“Oh?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“A first-year boy.”

“…Mm.”

“He said I’m cute.”

“…He’s right.”

Yuhao glanced at Yichen’s hand. He was holding his chopsticks a little too tightly. That answer was far too calm. Xiaoran carried on happily, with no idea what she was walking into.

“Then he asked if I wanted to watch a movie with him.”

“What did you say?” Meilin asked carefully.

“I told him I already have a boyfriend, obviously.”

Yichen nodded once.

“Good.”

“But then,” Xiaoran said while opening her yoghurt, “he got sad so I comforted him a little.”

Silence. Yuhao became interested in his food. Yichen smiled faintly.

“What does ‘comforted him a little’ mean?”

“Oh, nothing serious. I just told him he’ll definitely find someone prettier and kinder than me someday.” Xiaoran waved casually.

Yichen stared at her.

“Prettier than you?”

“Yes.”

“You told another guy that?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“…Should I not?”

Meilin closed her eyes briefly. Oh no. The problem with Zhou Yichen was that he almost never got jealous. Girls liked him, confessed to him, and texted him all the time. Xiaoran got jealous about it at least twice a month. Yichen stayed calm through all of it—secure, and endlessly patient with her. So when he finally did get jealous, nobody knew what to expect.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second sign something was wrong came after school. Zhou Yichen waited for Xiaoran at the classroom door every afternoon. Today, he wasn’t there. Confused, Xiaoran wandered around Building B looking for him. She finally found him near the basketball court, talking with his teammates.

“Yichen!”

He looked over. Same handsome face. Same small smile. But something about him felt cooler. Further away. Xiaoran didn’t like it at all. She walked over and grabbed his sleeve out of habit.

“Why didn’t you wait for me?”

“I was busy.”

That had literally never stopped him before. Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“…Are you angry?”

“No.”

That was a lie, even if he told it nicely. Before she could investigate further, another voice interrupted.

“Senior Xiaoran!”

Everyone turned. A younger boy jogged over with a can of coffee, looking nervous. The same first-year. He faltered when he saw Zhou Yichen standing beside her. But he worked up his courage and held the drink out to Xiaoran.

“Thank you for earlier. I bought your favourite flavour,” he said shyly.

Xiaoran looked surprised.

“How did you know my favourite?”

“You mentioned it.”

“Oh.”

She reached for it without thinking—only for another hand to take it first. Silence. Zhou Yichen held the can in one hand, smiling politely. It wasn’t a friendly smile.

“Thank you. But she doesn’t drink coffee after 5 p.m,” he said gently.

The younger boy froze completely. Xiaoran blinked.

“…I do sometimes.”

Yichen looked at her.

“You couldn’t sleep until two last time.”

“…Oh.”

The boy was starting to sweat.

“I-I just wanted to thank senior…”

“You already did. That’s enough.” Yichen’s voice stayed pleasant.

Even Yuhao, watching from nearby, nearly saluted. That was the most boyfriend move he had ever seen. The boy made his escape. As soon as he was gone, Xiaoran turned to Yichen.

“…You scared him.”

“He’ll survive.”

“…You’re definitely angry.”

“I said I’m not.”

“You’re doing your fake customer-service smile.”

Yuhao walked off. He didn’t want to witness whatever happened next.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, Lin Xiaoran lay sprawled across her bed, video calling Meilin.

“I think Zhou Yichen is malfunctioning.”

“He’s jealous.”

“…Huh?”

Meilin stared at her through the screen.

“You really don’t notice things unless they hit you with a chair.”

“What’s there to notice?”

“He’s obsessed with you.”

“Well, yes. Obviously.”

“And another guy openly approached you.”

“But I rejected him!”

“You also comforted him.”

“He looked sad!”

Meilin sighed.

“Xiaoran. Imagine a pretty girl confessed to Yichen, then Yichen comforted her gently and accepted gifts from her.”

Xiaoran sat bolt upright.

“…Oh.”

“Exactly.”

Suddenly, everything replayed in her head. Yichen not waiting after class. The weird smile. Taking the coffee. The calm voice that somehow felt colder than usual. Oh no. Zhou Yichen was jealous. And for some reason, knowing that made her chest feel warm. Which was probably not the right reaction.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Xiaoran arrived at school carrying two strawberry milks. One for herself. One peace offering. She found Zhou Yichen in the library before morning class, reading quietly near the windows. Sunlight fell across his face. He looked annoyingly good. Xiaoran crept over and set the drink down beside him.

“For you.”

Yichen glanced at it.

“Bribery?”

“Yes.”

He laughed quietly despite himself. Good. Progress. Xiaoran sat beside him, fidgeting slightly.

“…Are you still jealous?”

“I wasn’t jealous.”

He rubbed the back of his neck.

“Liar.”

“I was concerned.”

“You stole his coffee like a drama villain.”

“He bought it for my girlfriend.”

The way he said my girlfriend so naturally made her ears go warm. Yichen finally closed his book and looked at her properly.

“I trust you. I just don’t like other guys trying to take my place,” he said.

Xiaoran blinked slowly.

“…That’s kind of hot.”

For the first time, Yichen looked genuinely caught off guard. Then he laughed helplessly, covering his eyes briefly.

“You’re unbelievable.”

“No but seriously. You’re usually so calm. Seeing you jealous is kind of…” Xiaoran said, leaning closer.

“Kind of?”

“…Cute.”

Yichen stared at her.

“I was miserable yesterday.”

“You looked good being miserable.”

“That doesn’t help.”

Xiaoran giggled before hooking her pinky around his sleeve.

“Don’t worry. I only like you,” she said.

His expression softened. The look he only ever gave her, no matter how jealous, annoyed, or tired he was. Yichen sighed and pulled her chair closer to his.

“Next time,” he murmured, “don’t comfort random boys who like you.”

“What if I enjoy making you jealous?”

“You won’t enjoy the consequences.”

Yichen leaned in, his voice low.

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“…What?”

“If another guy buys you coffee again, I’m kissing you in front of him.”

Silence. Her whole face went red. And Zhou Yichen finally smiled properly again, looking satisfied with himself. That was when Lin Xiaoran realised, too late, that a jealous Zhou Yichen might be far more dangerous than she had ever been.
chapters.epigraph: “He was never jealous often—so when he was, even love felt dangerous.”

chapters.desc: She said it over a plate of shrimp, in front of witnesses, without meaning to—and Zhou Yichen was never going to let her take it back.
chapters.title: The First Time She Said “I Love You” Casually
chapters.epigraph: “The biggest words are sometimes the ones that slip out by accident.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran’s first “I love you” wasn’t romantic. There was no rain, no heartfelt confession, no background music. It happened at a crowded hotpot place near school, because Zhou Yichen was peeling shrimp for her.

“You’re actually amazing,” Xiaoran declared from across the restaurant table.

Yichen kept peeling.

“You say that every time someone feeds you.”

“That’s because acts of service are attractive.”

“You learned one psychology term and became unbearable.”

“I love you.”

Silence. Xiaoran kept drinking her juice peacefully. Across from her, Zhou Yichen froze. The shrimp stopped halfway to her plate. Chen Yuhao slowly looked up from his noodles. Tang Meilin closed her eyes. Oh no. Lin Xiaoran clearly had no idea what she had just said. Zhou Yichen was staring at her.

“…What did you say?”

Xiaoran blinked. “Hm?”

Yuhao kicked her chair under the table.

“Ow?! What’s wrong with you?!”

“You just said you love him.”

“…And?”

Everyone stared at her in disbelief. Then Xiaoran finally processed her own sentence. Her eyes widened slowly.

“Oh.”

Yichen still hadn’t moved. He was just looking at her, calmly. Xiaoran grabbed her juice cup with both hands.

“That slipped out accidentally.”

“You accidentally love me?”

“No—that’s not what I meant.”

“Then explain.”

Her face went red.

Meilin whispered to Yuhao, “This is the happiest day of his life.”

Yuhao nodded. “He’s pretending to stay calm, but inside he’s already planning the wedding.”

Meanwhile, Xiaoran was dying. Saying “I love you” by accident was somehow more embarrassing than any proper confession. Especially with Zhou Yichen looking at her like that—soft and focused, like nothing else in the restaurant existed.

“I got caught up in the moment,” she mumbled.

“You said you love me because I peeled shrimp.”

“That sounds shallow when you say it out loud.”

Yichen finally smiled—small at first, then wider. It was the smile Xiaoran secretly liked most.

“You’ve never said it before,” he said.

The teasing at the table died down a little. Xiaoran looked away.

“…You already knew.”

“I did.”

“Then why are you acting surprised?”

“Knowing isn’t the same as hearing it.”

Her chest tightened, because he was right. They’d been dating for months. She asked him “Do you love me?” almost every day, usually right after doing something annoying, and he always answered. But she had never once said it herself. And now everyone at the table was staring at her, waiting.

“This is horrible,” she whispered.

Yuhao looked delighted. “Say it again.”

“I’ll kill you.”

Meilin sipped her drink calmly. “Personally, I think it’s cute.”

“Traitor.”

Yichen rested his chin against one hand, eyes still fixed on her.

“…Did you mean it?”

Lin Xiaoran wanted to evaporate. It wasn’t fair of him to ask so softly.

“…Maybe.”

“That’s not an answer.”

She tried to glare. “Why are you interrogating me?”

“Because I’m happy.”

That was the problem with him. No teasing, no smugness. He was just happy, plainly and honestly, because she loved him. Xiaoran’s ears turned even redder.

“…Fine. I meant it,” she muttered.

Yichen’s whole face softened. And Xiaoran realised, a little alarmed, that hearing “I love you” from her might be Zhou Yichen’s biggest weakness. He looked absurdly happy.

“You’re smiling too much,” she accused.

“You caused it.”

“That sounds like a you problem.”

Yuhao made a gagging noise.

“Can you two stop being disgusting while I’m eating?”

“No,” Yichen said.

The table went quiet. Zhou Yichen was polite to everyone, always. He had just told Yuhao no, and he looked pleased about it.

Meilin looked impressed. “One accidental ‘I love you’ and he became arrogant.”

“I’m not arrogant,” Yichen said, still looking at Xiaoran like she was the only person at the table.

Xiaoran hid behind her menu.

“I regret speaking.”

“You can’t take it back. You said it in front of witnesses.”

“And I,” Yuhao said proudly, “will remember this forever.”

“I hate all of you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The teasing went on for three days. Every time Xiaoran complained about homework—

“Maybe Yichen can help. Since you love him so much.” Yuhao would say.

Every time she bought snacks—

“Such loving girlfriend behaviour,” Meilin would say.

Xiaoran nearly lost her mind. Zhou Yichen, meanwhile, was insufferable. He got even more affectionate than usual. Touching her head more. Holding her hand first. Smiling at her like she’d hung the moon. Worst of all, he kept bringing it up when they were alone.

“You love me,” he’d murmur out of nowhere.

And Xiaoran would go red all over again.

One evening after cram school, they walked home under an orange sky. Xiaoran kicked at pebbles while Yichen carried her bag, because apparently she was “too tired.”

“You’ve been smiling all week,” she accused.

“I wonder why.”

“I said it once accidentally.”

“You meant it.”

“…Unfortunately.”

Yichen laughed. He spoke again.

“I love you too.”

Xiaoran stopped walking. She had blurted hers out over shrimp. He said his carefully, on purpose, like he wanted her to hear every word. The evening breeze moved gently around them. Xiaoran’s chest felt strangely full.

“You can’t say things like that so suddenly,” she mumbled.

“Why not?”

“It’s bad for my heart.”

Yichen smiled and reached over to fix the crooked ribbon in her hair.

“But you already knew,” he teased.

Xiaoran stared at him. Then she buried her face in his shoulder.

“This relationship is ruining my cool image.”

“You never had one.”

“Mean.”

But she stayed where she was. Yichen held her close, smiling into her hair. He had a feeling he would remember that careless little “I love you” for the rest of his life.

chapters.desc: Zhou Yichen almost never gets angry. Then a teammate says the wrong thing about Lin Xiaoran, and he can’t let it go.
chapters.title: The One Time Zhou Yichen Lost His Temper
chapters.epigraph: “Gentle people have a line too. You just don’t see it until someone crosses it.”
chapters.content:
During basketball season, everyone knew to leave Zhou Yichen alone before a match. He got frighteningly competitive, and nobody was stupid enough to provoke him. Liu Zheng had never been good at reading a room.

“Pass the ball faster!”

Sneakers squeaked across the gym floor as the team ran drills before the regional tournament. Sweat dripped down Zhou Yichen’s neck as he snatched the ball back sharply.

“You were late to position,” he said coldly.

Liu Zheng scoffed. “You act like we’re professionals.”

“Then stop playing carelessly.”
