You’re allowed to look over here. We agreed.

She wrote underneath: I’m studying.

It slid back. You’ve been on that page since seven.

She turned her head. He was facing his physics book with a perfectly straight face, but the tips of his ears had gone pink, and she remembered that they had done exactly that on Friday too, right after, when he had seemed so calm and hadn’t been. It was the most comforting thing she had seen all day.

So she looked at him, on purpose, for the whole of the next minute, until he gave up and looked back. Then she slid her hand across the gap between the desks, palm up, under the edge of the table where Mr. Pan couldn’t see, and after a second his hand covered it.

Mr. Pan cleared his throat at the front of the room at nobody in particular. Behind them, Meilin made a noise into her sleeve that could have been a sneeze.

Xiaoran read the paragraph about the water cycle a fifth time, holding his hand, and this time it went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past nine he rang, and she answered before the first ring had finished.

“We spent the whole day not looking at each other. And then the whole of self-study looking,” he said.

“Don’t remind me.”

“And Yuhao knows.”

“Don’t remind me about that either.”

She lay back on her bed with the phone against her ear and her knees up and listened to him laugh. After a while she said, “Tomorrow can we just be normal?”

“We can try.”

“Really try. And I’m allowed to lean on you in self-study. Like before.”

“You were always allowed.”

“And no looking away.”

“That might be difficult.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re distracting.”

She pulled the blanket up over her head. “You’re doing that on purpose.”

“Good night, Xiaoran.”

“Say it again.”

“Good night, Xiaoran,” he said, more slowly, and she fell asleep that night with the phone still on the pillow.

The next morning at the school gate he said good morning and she said good morning, and they both looked straight at each other while they did it, and she took his arm with both hands the way she always had, and then she walked into the gatepost.

Behind them, Yuhao said “Normal” to nobody in particular, and kept walking.

chapters.desc: A grade trip, a shared bus, and a whole day of not holding hands in front of the teachers. He counts how many times she reaches for his.
chapters.title: Practising Not Holding Hands
chapters.epigraph: “No. I had to practice all day. Not holding your hand.”
chapters.content:
The grade trip was supposed to be educational. A day at the old county academy outside the city, the teachers said: the architecture, the stone tablets, a worksheet to fill in by group. Lin Xiaoran had been looking forward to it for a week, not because she cared about Qing dynasty roof brackets, but because it meant a whole day out of school with Zhou Yichen.

Then, at the briefing in the hall, the grade director read out the rules. Stay with your assigned group. No running. No shouting. And, he added, looking at no one in particular in a way that somehow looked at everyone, the school’s guidance on inappropriate closeness between students applied on trips as well.

There would be teachers everywhere. At the gate. On the bus. In every exhibition room. Probably in the bushes.

At seven-thirty in the morning, outside the school gate, she found Yichen with Chen Yuhao and a folded itinerary, and her hand went out towards his before she had decided anything, the way it did every morning. Halfway there she remembered. Her fingers stopped in the air between them.

He looked at her hand. Then at her face. He didn’t say anything, but his mouth did something at one corner that she recognised.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re laughing with your face.”

She took the hand back and examined a button on her sleeve with great interest until the bus came.

✦ ✦ ✦

The seating went by group. Xiaoran was with Meilin and two other girls in the middle. Yichen was across the aisle with Yuhao and two boys from the basketball team. It was, technically, about a metre.

“Stop looking like someone cancelled your birthday,” Meilin said, ten minutes out of the city.

“I’m not looking like anything.”

“You’ve turned round four times. You’ll get a neck injury.”

“I’m looking out of the window.”

“The window’s on the other side.”

“There’s scenery,” Xiaoran said, and Meilin looked past her at the view, which was a car park.

Across the aisle, Yichen glanced over. Their eyes met. Without thinking she lifted her hand off her knee, just slightly, palm towards him, a habit as automatic as blinking. He looked at it, then at the head teacher sitting in the front row facing backwards, and raised his eyebrows. She put her hand back down on her knee and sat on it.

“Are you two communicating in code?” Meilin asked.

“No.”

“Because that looked like a very complicated conversation.”

“Please go to sleep,” Xiaoran said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the academy the teachers split them into groups and handed out the worksheets. Twenty minutes in, Xiaoran was standing in front of a display board covered in small dense characters about a famous examiner when Yichen appeared at her shoulder.

“How’s it going?”

“Look at all these words,” she said tragically.

He leaned in to read. Their shoulders were almost touching. Her whole arm was aware of it. And then a voice from behind them said, “Students, keep moving, please, don’t block the display,” and they sprang apart like two magnets turned the wrong way round.

“We’re being watched,” she whispered, once the teacher had gone past.

“Apparently.”

“Everywhere.”

“Finish the worksheet. Then we can walk round the courtyard together. Within the designated area,” he said.

“Very responsible, Zhou Yichen.”

“Someone has to be.”

She finished the worksheet in record time. Most of her answers were correct, and one was a drawing of a roof bracket because she couldn’t remember the word.

At the back of the academy there was a row of old examination cells, narrow brick booths with a plank for a desk and a plank for a seat, where candidates had once been shut in for three days with their brushes and their dried food. A sign said you could step inside to experience the conditions. Xiaoran stepped inside to experience the conditions and announced from the plank that she would have failed the imperial examinations within an hour.

“You’d have done the poetry section,” Yichen said from the doorway.

“I’d have written a poem about how hungry I was.”

“They’d have passed you for honesty.”

She held out both hands towards him from the plank, the way she did on the bleachers after practice when she wanted pulling up, and he took a step forward before either of them remembered. Somewhere behind him a teacher’s voice said “Group three, this way,” and he turned on his heel and studied the brickwork with the intensity of an architect. She got up off the plank on her own, which was humiliating, and walked past him with her nose in the air, and he followed her out, laughing without making a sound.

The courtyard was big and shaded, with old trees and stone paths, and students drifted around it taking photographs. They walked side by side along the path, a sensible, school-approved distance apart, and her hand brushed his. Once. Twice. The third time he looked down at her.

“There’s a teacher,” she said, fast.

“I know.”

“So we can’t.”

“Then we won’t.”

They walked a few more steps. “But I want to,” she said, and it was mostly breath.

He didn’t take her hand. He let the back of his fingers knock against hers as they walked, once, deliberately, and kept walking as if nothing had happened, and that was so much worse than holding hands that she had to stop and pretend to look at a tree.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunch they sat at the stone picnic tables, groups facing groups. Yuhao was telling a long story about a goose he’d seen at a service station. Xiaoran couldn’t get the cap off her water bottle. Before she’d finished struggling, Yichen had reached across the table, taken it, opened it and handed it back, and their fingers touched for exactly as long as it took.

Yuhao stopped the goose story. “What was that?”

“What?”

“Why did you open it for her?”

“She couldn’t open it.”

“Her hands are broken?”

“Eat your lunch, Yuhao.”

“You’ve got no survival instinct,” Meilin told Yuhao, and he looked genuinely confused, which was the best part.

Under the table, Yichen’s shoe found hers. She looked up. He was listening to the goose story again with every appearance of interest. She pressed her foot against his and he pressed back, and they stayed like that for the rest of lunch, which was childish, and also the best thing that had happened to her since breakfast.

The class photo came after lunch, in front of the main gate. Girls in front, boys behind. Xiaoran stood beside Meilin. Yichen ended up directly behind her. Just as the teacher lifted the camera and said “Everyone look here!”, she felt something brush the back of her hand where it hung at her side.

His fingers, resting against hers. Not holding. Just there.

The camera flashed. She turned round as soon as the teacher said they were done.

“Was that allowed?”

“Technically we weren’t holding hands.”

“You’re finding loopholes.”

“Learning from you,” he said, and she was so delighted that she forgot to step away from him until Meilin pulled her by the sleeve.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the bus home she fell asleep almost at once, her head against the window. She woke when the bus stopped for the headcount and someone touched her shoulder. Yichen was standing in the aisle with a packet of biscuits.

“You didn’t eat much at lunch.”

She took it, and then, before he could go back to his seat, she caught the edge of his sleeve and held on for one second longer than any teacher would have called appropriate.

“See you when we get off,” she whispered.

“See you when we get off,” he said.

“You two are a public health risk,” said Meilin, as he went.

Back at school, the teachers made a final announcement about not leaving belongings on the bus, and the groups dispersed. Yichen was helping Yuhao carry a box of leftover worksheets back to the classroom. Meilin watched Xiaoran watching him.

“Go.”

“There’s—”

“There’s no teacher next to you anymore. Go.”

She didn’t need to be told twice. Yichen saw her coming, handed the whole box to Yuhao, and said, “Take this up.”

Yuhao looked at Xiaoran, then at Yichen, and smiled with every one of his teeth. “Of course. Of course I will. Take your time.” He staggered off under the box.

Yichen held out his hand. “Now?”

“Now,” she said, and grabbed it with both of hers, and let out a long sigh.

“Was it that difficult?”

“Yes. No. I had to practice all day. Not holding your hand.”

“How did you do?”

“Badly. I kept nearly doing it. In the bus, and the courtyard, and in front of the roof brackets.” She swung their hands.

“I counted. You reached for it twelve times,” he said.

“You counted? And you?” She looked up at him.

He considered lying. “Fourteen.”

She laughed out loud and swung their joined hands once, twice, all the way to the gate, where the grade director was standing with a clipboard, and let go so fast she nearly took his watch with her. Then, as soon as they were round the corner, she took it again, and didn’t let go until her bus came.

chapters.desc: Someone from Class 5 dedicates a song to her on the morning radio, and Zhou Yichen takes the news very calmly, for him.
chapters.title: The Radio Dedication
chapters.epigraph: “I hope you don’t feel embarrassed about the song. It was really thoughtful.”
chapters.content:
The first time Lin Xiaoran heard her own name over the school radio, she nearly dropped her pencil.

It was Wednesday, the morning after the trip, in the ten minutes before first period when the radio club played requests and birthday greetings through the speaker above the blackboard. Nobody in Class 3 ever listened. Xiaoran was using the time to finish the maths homework she had forgotten the night before, with her elbow on Zhou Yichen’s side of the desk and his exercise book open under it for reference, which he was pretending not to notice.

“Good morning, everyone! We have a special dedication today. This next song is for Lin Xiaoran in Class 3,” said the announcer, brightly.

Her pencil stopped. All around the room, heads came up.

“Someone would like you to hear this song. The message says, Hope you have a good day. Signed: Z.”

The opening bars of a famous love song came out of the speaker, all violins and longing, and Class 3, as one body, turned and looked at Zhou Yichen.

He was in the middle of drinking water. He lowered the bottle slowly. He looked at the speaker. Then he looked around at thirty-eight expectant faces and said, quite calmly, “It wasn’t me.”

“Liar,” said Chen Yuhao, delighted.

“It wasn’t.”

Xiaoran turned to stare at him. He met her eyes and gave a tiny shake of his head, and she knew him well enough by now to know he meant it. Something in her chest dropped a few centimetres, and then she was annoyed with herself for minding, and then she was annoyed with the violins.

Tang Meilin leaned over the back of her chair. “Someone dedicated a love song to you.”

“It’s probably a mistake.”

“To your exact name and class?”

“There might be another Lin Xiaoran.”

“In Class 3? Where? Point to her.” Meilin looked around the room with exaggerated care.

The song lasted four minutes and twelve seconds. Meilin watched Xiaoran for every second of it. Xiaoran watched her maths homework and didn’t write a single number. Beside her, Yichen took his exercise book back from under her elbow, gently, and went on with his English as if there were nothing in the room but English.

When the announcements moved on to the canteen menu, she leaned towards him until her shoulder was against his.

“Did you really not send it?”

“I really didn’t.”

“Not even as a joke?”

“If I sent you a song, I wouldn’t sign it with a Z. You’d know it was me.” He turned a page.

“How?”

“Because I’d use your whole name. And mine.”

She sat up and stared at him. He went on reading. Meilin, who had heard every word, put her head down on her desk and stayed there until first period.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the long break the dedication had become the most interesting topic in Class 3. Meilin had told two people. Those two had told the back row. By the time Xiaoran came back from the shop with a drink, three girls were gathered around her desk running an investigation.

“Maybe it’s someone from another class.”

“Maybe he’s liked her for years.”

“Maybe Z is his real initial.”

“Can everyone please stop?” said Xiaoran.

“She thought it was Zhou Yichen,” Meilin offered.

“Meilin!”

“Of course she did,” said one of the girls. “Who else signs things with a Z and sits next to her?”

Yichen, at his desk with his chin on his hand, said mildly, “It’s still not me.”

“You don’t seem very bothered,” said one of the girls, sounding disappointed.

“Should I be?”

“Someone dedicated a love song to your girlfriend!”

He thought about it. “It was a good song,” he said, which was so unsatisfying that all three girls left.

Xiaoran sat down, unscrewed her drink, and studied him sideways. He did look calm. He looked completely calm. But he had been on the same page of his English reader since the bell, and when she reached under the desk for his hand, he took it before she’d found it.

“Are you upset?” she whispered.

“No.”

“A bit?”

“I’m curious. Somebody knows your name and your class. I’d like to know who,” he admitted.

“I thought it was you. For a second. I hoped,” she said.

He looked at her then, properly, and his thumb moved over her knuckles once under the desk. “I’ll remember that,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The answer arrived after school. She was packing her bag when a boy appeared in the classroom doorway, a little out of breath, with his hands in his blazer pockets. Zeng Bowen, Class 5. She knew his name because he ran the radio club’s request box on Wednesdays, and for no other reason at all.

“Lin Xiaoran? Have you got a minute?”

Meilin’s head came up like a meerkat’s. Xiaoran went out into the corridor.

“Did you hear the song this morning?”

She understood before he finished. “That was you?”

“Yeah. I thought if I just put Z, it’d be less awkward.” He rubbed the back of his neck.

They had spoken perhaps four times, all of them about the banner for the sports festival.

“Thank you for the song. It was nice,” she said.

“I was wondering if you’d want to go to the new bookshop by the station sometime. On a weekend.”

She held on to the strap of her bag. She didn’t want to embarrass him. She also didn’t want him to wait for something that wasn’t coming.

“That’s kind of you. But I can’t.”

He nodded slowly, a little disappointed, not angry. “Because of Zhou Yichen?”

“Yes, I already have someone,” she said.

He laughed, a small surprised laugh at himself. “I thought so. Everybody says so. I wanted to try anyway.”

“I hope you don’t feel embarrassed about the song. It was really thoughtful.”

“Don’t worry. I knew it was a risk.” He gave her a last smile and went off down the corridor with his hands back in his pockets.

When she turned round, Meilin was in the doorway, and behind Meilin, at his desk, packing his bag with extreme slowness, was Yichen.

“You heard,” Xiaoran said.

“The door was open. And Meilin was standing in it, so the sound came straight through,” he said.

“I said no.”

“I heard that too.”

“And I said I already have someone.”

“I heard that part twice. I asked Meilin to repeat it,” he said.

Meilin nodded gravely. “I did a voice.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the gate Chen Yuhao and Tang Meilin were waiting for them, and Yuhao took one look at the two of them and put his hand on his heart.

“Lin Xiaoran in Class 3. This next song is for you,” he announced to the whole bicycle shed, in the announcer’s bright radio voice.

“I will end you,” said Xiaoran.

“From a mysterious Z,” Meilin said helpfully.

“It was Zeng Bowen. He’s in Class 5. He was dared. It’s over,” said Xiaoran.

“Is it, though? Brother. How did you feel. In your heart. When the violins started,” said Yuhao, and looked at Yichen, who was checking the strap of his schoolbag with great concentration.

“Fine,” said Yichen.

“Fine. Meilin. He says fine,” Yuhao repeated, delighted.

“He broke his pencil,” said Meilin.

Xiaoran turned and looked at Yichen. He had his back to her. The tips of his ears had gone red.

“You broke your pencil?”

“It was an old pencil.”

“You broke your pencil when they said my name.”

“It was a coincidence,” said Yichen, and started walking.

She caught up with him in two steps and took his arm with both hands and leaned on it, with her chin practically on his shoulder so she could see his face.

“Were you jealous?”

“No.”

“A little bit jealous?”

“Zeng Bowen was dared.”

“That’s not a no.”

He looked straight ahead. “A little bit,” he said, low, and she laughed so loudly that the boys by the bike rack turned round.

Behind them, Yuhao looked at the two of them, and then remembered urgently that he had to be somewhere else, and Meilin went with him, saying “Good night” in a voice that meant something else entirely.

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked home the usual way.

“Yuhao’s strange,” Xiaoran said.

“He’s been strange since we were eleven.”

She had her arm through his before they reached the bus stop. At the corner by the bakery she said, “Aren’t you going to ask why I said no?”

“Do I need to?”

“No.”

“Then I won’t. Who’s the someone, though? You didn’t say a name.” He walked a few steps.

She stopped dead on the pavement and stared at him. He looked perfectly serious, except for the corner of his mouth.

“Zhou Yichen,” she said.

“That sounds familiar.”

She dug her fingers into his arm. “Don’t be annoying.”

“I’m not being annoying. I wanted to hear you say it without Meilin doing a voice.”

That evening, while she was meant to be doing English, her phone lit up.

Yichen: Did you like the song?

Xiaoran: It was nice. The violins were a lot.

Yichen: I might dedicate one to you someday.

She sat up so fast she knocked her dictionary off the bed.

Xiaoran: Really?

Yichen: If I do, I’ll put your name on it.

Xiaoran: Not just Lin Xiaoran in Class 3?

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: Then what?

The reply took a while.

Yichen: Lin Xiaoran. My favourite person.

She pressed the phone flat against her chest and lay back on the bed and stared at the ceiling with a smile so wide it hurt.

Xiaoran: That’s not very anonymous.

Yichen: I don’t intend to be.

She took a screenshot. Then a second screenshot, in case the first one went missing.

chapters.desc: One weekend of romance dramas, one very specific request, and an empty hallway after practice.
chapters.title: Better Than the Drama
chapters.epigraph: “Real life has no background music. It has something better.”
chapters.content:
The problem started with a drama. Specifically, a forty-episode romance drama Lin Xiaoran had promised herself she would watch exactly one episode of on Saturday night. By Sunday afternoon she was on episode thirty-one, wrapped in Yichen’s stolen hoodie, eating shrimp crackers in the dark like a raccoon. Then episode thirty-two happened. Rain on a rooftop. The male lead tilting the female lead’s chin up. A pause long enough for the piano to swell, and then a kiss so slow and certain that Xiaoran had to pause the video and lie face down on her bed for a while.

She watched it four times. Then she thought about her own first kiss. The empty classroom. The way Yichen had asked first. The way it had been soft and warm for one perfect second—right before she lost her balance and nearly toppled off the chair, and he had to catch her mid-kiss. It had been sweet. It had been theirs. It had also had no background music whatsoever. At 11:40 PM she texted Tang Meilin.

Xiaoran: is it normal to be jealous of a fictional couple

Meilin: go to sleep

Xiaoran: their kiss had BACKGROUND MUSIC

Meilin: yours had a chair. you told me. twice

Xiaoran: I HATE THAT YOU REMEMBER

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday, Xiaoran couldn’t look Zhou Yichen in the eye. Nothing had happened. That was the problem. Somewhere around episode thirty-four she had made a decision: she wanted a proper kiss. A drama kiss. Slow, deliberate, no furniture involved. She just had no idea how to ask for one. Every time Yichen glanced at her in class, her brain started playing the piano music.

“You’re red,” he observed at lunch.

“It’s warm.”

“It’s raining.”

“Warm rain.”

Across the table, Chen Yuhao narrowed his eyes. “She’s been weird since homeroom.”

“She watched a drama all weekend,” Meilin said, without looking up from her planner.

“MEILIN.”

Yichen looked at her with sudden interest. Xiaoran stuffed an entire dumpling into her mouth so she wouldn’t have to answer. By the last period, she had drafted the request eleven different ways in the margins of her notebook and crossed out every single one.

✦ ✦ ✦

Practice ran late, so the school was nearly empty by the time Yichen came upstairs for his bag. Evening sun lay across the third-floor hallway in long gold stripes. Somewhere downstairs, a few students were still laughing. Xiaoran was waiting outside the classroom, holding his water bottle like a hostage.

“You didn’t have to wait,” he said, pulling on his hoodie.

“I did.”

“Why?”

She took a deep breath. All eleven drafts vanished at once.

“Kiss me like episode thirty-two.”

Yichen stopped with one arm still in his sleeve.

“…What?”

“Nothing.”

“You said episode thirty-two.”

“I said nothing.”

He finished pulling the hoodie on, slowly, and looked at her the way he looked at a math problem he already knew the answer to.

“Is this the drama?”

“There is no drama.”

“Meilin said—”

“Meilin is a liar.”

The corner of his mouth moved. Then, before she could escape, he leaned down and kissed her—quick and light, over before she had even closed her eyes. Xiaoran blinked.

“…That’s it?”

“Hm.”

“That wasn’t episode thirty-two.”

“What was it?”

“A trailer.”

That made him laugh, low and surprised. He set his bag down against the wall.

“So what happens in episode thirty-two?”

She should have said nothing. She should have run. Instead she grabbed the front of his hoodie with both hands, cheeks burning, and said the bravest thing she had said all year.

“…Again. Properly this time.”

Yichen smiled, then leaned down slowly, patiently, giving her plenty of time to panic and run away. This time, Lin Xiaoran didn’t run—even though her heartbeat sounded medically dangerous, even though he was close enough now that she could feel his breath, close enough that her fingers tightened in the front of his hoodie without her permission. That tiny movement softened his whole expression, like he found her nervousness cute instead of embarrassing. Which made everything worse.

“Still scared?” he murmured.

“A little.”

“You wanted this.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you trembling?”

“Because YOU’RE handsome.”

Yichen laughed under his breath, and that sound, this close, made her knees weak. His hand settled at her waist—not forceful, just enough to steady her when she leaned in. Warm fingers resting lightly against her side, like he was still making sure she was okay. He always made sure first. That bit of gentleness melted what was left of her panic. He kissed her again—slower this time, not teasing, not quick. A real kiss. His thumb brushed her waist without him seeming to notice, and Xiaoran finally understood why romance dramas were so popular. Her brain stopped working entirely.

She held on to his hoodie and kissed him back—awkwardly at first, then a little better when Yichen smiled against her lips like he was quietly encouraging her. That tiny smile in the middle of the kiss got to her more than the kiss itself. It was so… Yichen. Patient. Warm. Even this became gentle because it was him. Then he tilted his head and kissed her again—still soft, still careful, but longer, until Xiaoran’s knees nearly gave up.

One of her hands slid up and caught lightly at the back of his neck. Yichen went still for a fraction of a second—then his other hand steadied her waist more firmly. Not intense. Just instinctive. Protective. When they finally pulled apart, Xiaoran looked completely dazed—eyes unfocused, breathing uneven—while Zhou Yichen somehow still looked calmer than her. Slightly flushed, maybe. But infinitely more composed. Unfair.

“…Oh my god,” Xiaoran whispered weakly.

Yichen’s lips twitched.

“What?”

“That drama ruined my life.”

He laughed quietly again before brushing hair away from her face carefully.

“You’re cute.”

“That’s not the issue.”

“The issue is—”

She stopped abruptly. Because Yichen leaned closer again. Not kissing her yet—just close enough that she forgot the sentence entirely.

“…You were saying?” he murmured.

Nothing. Lin Xiaoran no longer had thoughts.

“I forgot what I was saying,” she admitted honestly.

That finally broke Yichen completely. He laughed properly this time, lowering his forehead briefly against hers. Somehow that felt even more intimate than the kissing.

“You spent the entire day panicking over this?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“You’re unbelievable.”

“You kissed me like a drama lead.”

Yichen smiled helplessly and kissed her cheek instead—gentler, familiar—and that small kiss made her chest ache in a completely different way. Dramatic kisses were exciting. This felt affectionate. Real. Then after a moment, Yichen looked at her.

“…Disappointed?”

Xiaoran blinked rapidly.

“What?”

“You watched those drama scenes all weekend. So?” A tiny teasing smile appeared again.

Silence. Xiaoran grabbed his sleeve.

“Zhou Yichen. You’re never allowed to ask questions like that after kissing someone.”

“So you WERE comparing.”

“I was… curious.”

“Results?”

She stared at him for two full seconds. Then honestly—

“…Better than the drama.”

Yichen froze. Just slightly. But Xiaoran noticed, and her confidence came roaring back.

“AHA.”

She had finally found a way to embarrass Zhou Yichen. His ears were faintly red. Victory. Beautiful victory.

“You’re blushing,” she whispered.

“No I’m not.”

“Oh my god you ARE.”

Before she could keep bullying him, Yichen pulled her closer by the waist—smoothly, effortlessly—and Xiaoran forgot how to speak for the second time.

“You’re getting brave now,” he murmured near her ear.

“That’s because I won.”

“There was a competition?”

“There’s always competition.”

Yichen laughed softly again.

“You know what your problem is? You say things confidently. Then you panic the second I respond.” His thumb brushed lightly against her waist again.

True. Painfully true. Xiaoran buried her face in his shoulder.

“I hate this relationship.”

“No you don’t.”

“…Okay maybe not.”

The hallway stayed quiet. Gold evening light stretched across the floor by the windows, and somewhere downstairs, a few students were still talking. Neither of them moved—mostly because Xiaoran refused to look him in the eye after that kiss, and Yichen looked suspiciously comfortable holding her there.

“Xiaoran, you know you can just kiss me whenever you want, right?”

Silence.

“WHAT KIND OF SENTENCE IS THAT.”

Yichen only smiled, completely unbothered, like he had said something perfectly reasonable. Xiaoran glared at him. Then, before she could lose her nerve, she rose onto her toes and kissed him—quick, clumsy, and entirely her own idea. This time, it was Zhou Yichen who forgot how to speak.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran wanted one proper date. She didn’t expect a street band to describe her relationship out loud.
chapters.title: The Song That Knew Too Much
chapters.epigraph: “Some songs sound like they were written about you. Some actually were.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen and Lin Xiaoran’s dates usually ended in chaos, not romance. Most weekends meant Chen Yuhao screaming at video games in somebody’s living room while Tang Meilin judged everyone from the couch. Yichen would sit beside Xiaoran. Xiaoran would steal his hoodie. And the whole afternoon would disappear without either of them noticing. So when Xiaoran announced—

“We’re going on a REAL date tomorrow.”

—everyone reacted differently. Yuhao nearly choked. Meilin looked suspicious. Zhou Yichen just looked amused.

On Saturday morning, sunlight filled Xiaoran’s bedroom while she tore through her wardrobe. Today mattered. Not that she would admit it. Okay, maybe a little. The problem was Douyin. All week, her feed had been full of ridiculously aesthetic couples walking down pretty streets, holding hands, soft music playing. Now Xiaoran wanted that too. Just once. A proper date. Just the two of them. No basketball, no friends, no Yuhao screaming “GET A ROOM” every ten minutes. And sometimes she missed him, even though she saw him almost every day. Which sounded insane. But it was true.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You look nervous,” Yichen said the second Xiaoran climbed into the car he’d borrowed from his dad.

“I’m not nervous.”

“You changed outfits three times.”

“How do YOU know that?”

“You posted mirror selfies accidentally.”

“…Oh.”

Yichen laughed and handed her a milk tea. Half sugar, no pearls. Of course he remembered. Xiaoran’s carefully prepared cool image cracked a little.

“You’re bribing me already,” she accused.

“It’s 10 a.m.”

“Exactly.”

Yichen smiled at the road. Zhou Yichen out of his school uniform was a problem. Grey sweater. A watch loose around his wrist. Hair a little messy from the wind. It was upsetting. Xiaoran stared too long. Yichen noticed.

“You’re doing it again.”

“I’m observing.”

“What’s your conclusion?”

Xiaoran turned to the window.

“…My boyfriend looks like a perfume ad.”

Yichen nearly laughed into the steering wheel.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first half of the date went surprisingly well. They wandered through shopping streets, shared snacks, and argued over claw machines. Xiaoran lost six tries at a plush rabbit before Yichen won it on his first—exactly like the day they met.

“Show-off,” she muttered, hugging it anyway.

“You spent twenty yuan.”

“It was a strategic investment.”

At one point they stopped at a tiny café Xiaoran had found on Douyin. The desserts were beautiful. The portions were microscopic.

“People online lied to me,” Xiaoran whispered while staring at her tiny cake.

“You wanted aesthetics.”

“I also wanted survival.”

Yichen pushed half of his towards her without a word. Zhou Yichen always remembered things. He noticed things, and quietly took care of her before she even asked: picking the cilantro out of her noodles, catching her wrist when she drifted towards the road, carrying her bag after she complained exactly once. Those tiny things softened her heart more than any grand gesture could.

✦ ✦ ✦

By evening, the streets had gone quiet. Golden light stretched across the sidewalks, and the little shops switched on their warm lights one by one. Xiaoran walked beside Yichen, swinging their joined hands.

“Tired?” he asked.

“No.”

“You walked slower.”

“I’m preserving the date.”

Yichen looked amused. “That’s not how time works.”

“You don’t know romance.”

Then music drifted down the street. A small student band was playing outside a café on the riverside corner. Nothing fancy—a guitarist, a keyboard player, and a singer laughing shyly at the little crowd that had gathered. Xiaoran stopped walking.

“Ooooh.”

She tugged Yichen to the back of the crowd. The singer adjusted the microphone and smiled.

“This next song is dedicated,” he said lightly, “to people who accidentally fell in love with someone troublesome.”

The crowd laughed. Beside Yichen, Xiaoran gasped.

“Wow. That’s targeted harassment against you,” she whispered.

Yichen glanced down.

“Interesting. I thought it sounded like you.”

“Rude.”

Then the guitar started, soft and warm, the kind of melody that belonged to sunsets. The singer began—

“She talks too much when she gets excited,
Gets angry over things that don’t matter,
Cries when I tease her even a little—
But somehow the world gets quieter beside her.”

Xiaoran blinked once.

“…Wait.”

Yichen’s lips twitched. The singer continued.

“She steals my jackets like they belong to her,
Complains every day but still waits for me after class,
Everyone says she’s hard to handle—
So why do I keep smiling when I see her?”

That line was a little too accurate. Yichen laughed under his breath. Xiaoran turned slowly.

“…Why are you laughing.”

Yichen looked away, still smiling.

“This song is weird.”

“What does that mean?”

“It knows too much.”

Xiaoran squinted at him as the music softened into the chorus.

“Maybe love isn’t peaceful after all,
Maybe love is noisy and clingy and impossible,
But if she disappeared for even one day—
I think my whole life would feel empty.”

Silence. A breeze moved down the street. Cars passed. Somewhere behind them, people were laughing. But Zhou Yichen couldn’t really hear any of it anymore. Every lyric kept turning into Lin Xiaoran: her dramatic voice, the way she’d clung to him before his family trip, her tiny angry face when she was jealous, the way she filled every silence without trying, the way even the worst days got lighter once she showed up. And the chorus was painfully true. If Xiaoran disappeared from his life now, everything really would feel emptier.

Beside him, Xiaoran had stopped joking too. When she looked up, Yichen was already looking at her—like the song had just told everyone his secrets.

“…Stop looking at me like that,” she muttered.

“Like what?”

“Like YOU wrote the lyrics.”

Yichen smiled a little, then leaned in just enough that only she could hear—

“The chorus is true though.”

Xiaoran’s face went red.

“Zhou Yichen, you can’t suddenly say romantic things during public music events.”

Yichen laughed and laced his fingers through hers a little tighter. The singer moved into the last verse—

“She’ll probably never realise this,
But every ordinary day became brighter after meeting her,
So if loving her means losing my peace forever—
Then honestly… I don’t mind at all.”

And for the first time that whole day, Lin Xiaoran understood why people loved romance songs so much. Not because the lyrics were dramatic. Because when you were standing next to the right person, every line sounded true.

chapters.desc: Her cousin and her boyfriend are spending Saturday together. Lin Xiaoran has concerns.
chapters.title: Lin Jun Stole Her Boyfriend for a Day
chapters.epigraph: “The scariest meeting isn’t meeting the parents. It’s meeting the cousin who knows everything.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran knew something was wrong the moment Zhou Yichen smiled at his phone during lunch. Not a normal smile. A suspicious one. She narrowed her eyes.

“Who are you texting.”

Yichen glanced up. “Lin Jun.”

“My cousin?” Xiaoran repeated slowly.

“Hm.”

“…Why.”

“He asked if I wanted to hang out Saturday.”

A longer silence. Then Xiaoran pointed at him.

“Absolutely not.”

Across the table, Chen Yuhao looked delighted. “Oho.”

Tang Meilin didn’t even look up from her phone. Everyone had seen this coming. Ever since Lin Jun moved back from Shanghai for a new job, he and Zhou Yichen had gotten along disgustingly well. It made no sense. One was Xiaoran’s emotionally exhausted older cousin. The other was her emotionally exhausted boyfriend. Apparently shared suffering created male friendship. Traitors. Both of them.

“Why are YOU two hanging out?” Xiaoran demanded.

Yichen looked unbothered. “He wants to know me better.”

“That sounds like an interrogation.”

Yuhao nodded seriously. “It probably is.”

Meilin sipped her drink calmly. “Honestly fair.”

“WHOSE SIDE ARE YOU ON?”

Nobody answered, because Lin Jun investigating Zhou Yichen was extremely understandable. If Xiaoran dated some random guy, her family would absolutely run a background check. Still, Xiaoran hated it. Somehow, she felt left out. Which was ridiculous. But true.

“You’re stealing my boyfriend,” she told Jun on a video call that evening.

Lin Jun looked completely relaxed.

“He’ll survive.”

“That’s not the issue.”

“What is the issue?”

“You two are bonding without supervision.”

Jun laughed.

“Why do you sound like a worried mother?”

“Because you’re suspicious.”

From the corner of the screen, Yichen sipped his water and watched the argument unfold, thoroughly entertained. Traitor.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday came, and Lin Xiaoran became the most restless person alive.

“This feels wrong,” she muttered, pacing Meilin’s bedroom.

Meilin, lying on her bed with a face mask on, already looked exhausted.

“It’s one afternoon.”

“My cousin and boyfriend are going on a date.”

“It’s not a date.”

“How do YOU know.”

“Because one of them basically raised you.”

“That doesn’t stop men from being weird.”

Across the city, Zhou Yichen was finding the whole thing interesting. He liked Lin Jun. Calm, sharp, easy to talk to. And dangerously observant. The two of them were walking through a riverside shopping district with iced coffees.

“You know,” Jun said eventually, “Xiaoran thinks I’m stealing you.”

Yichen laughed.

“She told me that too.”

Yichen smiled. Very Xiaoran. For a while, the conversation stayed easy—basketball, university, Jun’s years working in Shanghai. Then, naturally, it turned to Xiaoran.

“How long have you liked her?” Jun asked.

Yichen thought about it.

“…Longer than she realised.”

Jun nodded, like that made sense.

“She’s difficult sometimes.”

Yichen laughed.

“That’s true.”

“But. She’s sincere.” Jun glanced sideways briefly.

“I know.”

“She gets attached deeply to people.”

Yichen knew that too, probably better than anyone now. Lin Xiaoran loved loudly, clingily, like she had never learned how to hold back. Maybe that was why he liked her so much.

“She talks about you constantly,” Jun said.

Yichen sighed. “Apparently everyone knows that.”

“Trust me. You have no idea.”

Jun stopped outside a small convenience store.

“You know what she used to do as a kid?”

Yichen sensed danger.

“What?”

“She cried because I went on a school trip for three days.”

“Oh my god,” said Xiaoran’s voice behind them.

Both men turned. There she was, three metres away with Meilin, looking deeply betrayed.

Jun blinked. “What are you doing here?”

“You shared your location accidentally.”

Then Yichen laughed so much he nearly dropped his drink. Jun looked horrified.

“You TRACKED me?”

“I was worried!”

“You’re insane.”

“You STOLE MY BOYFRIEND.”

A woman walking her dog gave them a wide berth. Meilin covered her face.

“I told her not to come.”

“You participated willingly,” Xiaoran accused.

“I was kidnapped.”

Jun sighed and looked at Yichen.

“…You see what we dealt with growing up?”

Yichen smiled.

“Every day.”

Xiaoran marched over and grabbed Yichen’s sleeve.

“Are you done bonding?”

Jun looked offended.

“He likes me more than you now.”

“That’s fake.”

“You sure?”

Xiaoran turned to Yichen.

“Yichen. Choose carefully.”

The threat would have been scarier if she weren’t holding his sleeve like an angry kitten. Yichen looked from one cousin to the other. Then he answered—

“He buys me coffee.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

Jun nearly collapsed laughing. Xiaoran looked devastated.

“Wow, my cousin and my boyfriend,” she whispered.

Yichen finally smiled and pulled her closer by the wrist. Then, near her ear—

“You know no one replaces you.”

Instant recovery. Meilin watched them over her face mask.

“Disgusting.”

Jun nodded solemnly. “Actually unbearable.”

But Xiaoran had already cheered up. Maybe Lin Jun and Zhou Yichen getting along wasn’t the worst thing. Especially since they both already looked equally exhausted from dealing with her. A true family connection, really.

chapters.desc: Two weeks at her grandparents’ house in the town, a television with four channels, and a phone that rings at exactly nine every night.
chapters.title: The Holiday Call Schedule
chapters.epigraph: “No. I miss seeing you.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran spent the last two weeks of the summer holiday at her grandparents’ house in the small town four hours from the city, where she had lived until she was twelve. There was a persimmon tree in the courtyard, a television that got four channels, and a bedroom she shared with her grandmother, because the other one was full of her grandfather’s fishing gear.

On the first night, Zhou Yichen rang at nine.

Exactly nine. She had been waiting since a quarter to, sitting cross-legged on her bed in her biggest T-shirt with the phone beside her pillow, picking it up every few minutes to check the screen and putting it down again. Her grandmother, folding washing on the other bed, had been watching this for fifteen minutes.

“Are you waiting for someone?”

“No.”

“Then why do you keep looking at it?”

“I’m checking the time.”

“The clock’s on the wall,” said her grandmother, and Xiaoran had no answer to that.

At nine precisely, the phone rang. Xiaoran’s whole face lit up and she reached for it. Her grandmother, unfortunately, was closer.

“Oh, someone’s calling.”

“Grandma!”

But her grandmother already had it to her ear. “Hello?”

There was a short pause, and then a polite voice, which Xiaoran could just hear across the room. “Hello, Grandma. This is Zhou Yichen.”

Her grandmother looked at Xiaoran. Xiaoran looked back in horror.

“Ah! Yichen!”

Xiaoran’s mouth fell open. She had never told her grandmother his full name. She had mentioned him. Several times. Possibly every day since she’d arrived. But that wasn’t the point.

“How are you, child?”

“I’m well, thank you. How are you?”

“Good, good. Have you eaten?” Her grandmother held up one finger at Xiaoran, who was crawling across the bed towards her with her hand out.

“Yes, Grandma.”

“Good. Are you studying over the holiday?”

“Yes. We have quite a lot of homework.”

“Good. You must work hard. Now. You’re ringing for Xiaoran?” Her grandmother settled back against the headboard, which Xiaoran knew from long experience was a bad sign.

“Yes, Grandma.”

“Then let me ask you a few things first.”

Xiaoran shut her eyes. She knew that tone. It was the tone her grandmother used on the man who sold eggs at the Sunday market, and the egg man had once taken forty minutes to get away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eight minutes later she was sitting on the edge of her bed watching what appeared to be a formal interview. Out in the courtyard, her grandfather turned his radio up, which was what he always did when an interview started.

“How long have you known my granddaughter?”

“Since the start of high school.”

“Are you in the same class?”

“Yes, Grandma. I sit next to her.”

“Next to her! Since when?” Her grandmother looked at Xiaoran over the top of the phone with enormous interest.

“Since January.”

“Ah. And she’s a good desk-mate?”

There was a pause on the line. “She lends me her eraser. And she never gives it back when I lend her mine,” said Yichen.

“Hey!” said Xiaoran.

Her grandmother laughed so much she had to put her hand on her chest. “That’s her. That’s exactly her. When she was six she took her cousin’s eraser and buried it in the courtyard.”

“Grandma, please,” Xiaoran mouthed, and her grandmother gave her a reassuring smile and carried straight on.

“What subjects do you like?”

“Maths and physics.”

“Good. Maths is important. Xiaoran isn’t good at maths.”

“She’s getting better,” said Yichen.

Xiaoran put a pillow over her face. Four hours away, Yichen was sitting at the desk in his bedroom with his back straight. He had expected to hear Xiaoran. Instead he had now been talking to her grandmother for nearly ten minutes, and he had the feeling, which he recognised from oral exams, that the hard questions hadn’t started yet.

“Do you play any sports?”

“Basketball.”

“Basketball! Does Xiaoran come to watch?”

“Every game. She sits in the third row,” he said, and his voice changed a little.

“Does she understand it?”

“She’s learning.”

Xiaoran lifted her head out of the pillow. “I understand basketball!”

On the other end of the line, Yichen laughed. She could hear it. He was enjoying this.

✦ ✦ ✦

By a quarter past, the questions had got more personal.

“What do your parents do, Yichen?”

He told her, and politely.

“Does your mother cook?”

“Sometimes.”

“Do you help her?”

“When I’m home.”

“Good. Boys should be able to look after themselves. Can you cook?”

“A little.”

Xiaoran’s head snapped round. A little? She had watched him make fried rice exactly once, in the school’s home economics room, and the teacher had opened all the windows.

“A few simple things,” he amended.

“That’s very good. Xiaoran can’t cook at all.”

“Grandma!”

“It’s true. The last time you made eggs here, you left the gas on.”

“That was one time!”

“She’s careless sometimes. You must remind her,” her grandmother told the phone.

“I will.”

“Don’t agree with everything she says!” Xiaoran shouted across the room.

“See? She’s always like this,” said her grandmother.

“I know,” said Yichen.

Xiaoran stopped. She turned slowly towards the phone. I know?

Her grandmother looked absolutely delighted. “So you’re used to her temper.”

“Yes, Grandma.”

Xiaoran pressed the pillow back over her face and decided she would remember this for the rest of her life.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-five minutes she finally got a word in. “Grandma, can I talk to him now?”

“In a moment. Yichen. Do you have a girlfriend?” Her grandmother turned back to the phone with an air of great innocence.

There was a silence. Xiaoran nearly dropped the pillow.

“GRANDMA!”

Her grandmother waited calmly. On the other end, there was a short pause.

“Yes, Grandma,” said Yichen.

Xiaoran went completely still.

“Ah! You do! Is she a good girl?”

“Very good.”

“Does she work hard?”

“She does.”

“Is she obedient?”

A pause. Xiaoran stared at the phone with her eyes as wide as they would go, sending him a silent message about what would happen to him if he answered that carelessly. He seemed to receive it.

“She’s kind,” he said.

Her grandmother laughed. “That’s not what I asked.”

“She’s also quite playful.”

“Don’t!”

“Ah, I see. You two must get on very well,” said her grandmother, beaming at Xiaoran.

“Yes, Grandma,” he said, without hesitating at all, and Xiaoran forgot for a second to be embarrassed.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past nine her grandmother finally held the phone out. “Here. Talk to him.”

Xiaoran took it as gently as she could manage, which wasn’t gently, and turned to face the wall.

She dropped her voice to a hiss. “Why didn’t you tell her you wanted to talk to me?”

“I did.”

“When?”

“At the start.”

“And then?”

“She asked me a question.”

“One question?”

“Several,” he admitted, and she could hear him smiling.

She lay back on the bed. “How long has it been?”

“About thirty-five minutes.”

“Thirty-five minutes?”

“Mm.”

“I’m so sorry. My grandmother interviewed you.”

“She was very nice.”

“She asked if you had a girlfriend.”

“I noticed. I didn’t know what you’d told her.” He was quiet.

“Nothing! I’ve told her nothing. I said you were a friend from school.”

“I’m sorry. I should have said I was a friend.”

“No. No. It’s fine. It’s just that she’ll want to know everything tomorrow,” she said, too fast.

“Is that bad?”

“It’s embarrassing.”

“Did you mind that I said yes?”

She turned onto her side and picked at the edge of the blanket. Across the room, her grandmother was busily folding a towel she had already folded.

“No, I didn’t mind,” she said, small.

“Good.”

“Did you mind? All those questions?”

“No.”

“She asked about your parents.”

“Yes.”

“And cooking.”

“Yes.”

“And whether you—”

“You’re repeating the questions,” he said.

“Because there were too many!”

“I liked talking to her.”

She went quiet. “Really?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because she’s important to you,” he said, and she lay there looking at the ceiling with nothing at all to say. That was so unfair. He always found something to say that made her forget what she’d been complaining about.

“You’re too good at answering questions.”

“Was I being tested?”

“Maybe.”

“Did I pass?”

“Not sure yet,” she said, and he laughed.

They talked for another fifteen minutes. She told him about the dumplings her grandmother had made, and the neighbour who’d come round that afternoon purely to look at her and say she’d grown, and how she’d fallen asleep in front of one of the four channels during a program about pigs. He told her about training and the homework he hadn’t finished and the history essay he hadn’t started. It was easy. It was like the conversations they had walking out of school every afternoon, except there was no bell to cut it off.

A little before ten her grandmother started getting ready for bed, and Xiaoran cupped her hand round the phone.

“Grandma’s going to sleep.”

“All right.”

“Tomorrow I’m answering it myself.”

“Okay.”

“Unless she gets there first.”

“Then I’ll talk to her again. I don’t mind. She might ask something worse tomorrow. I’ll answer politely,” he said.

“Good night, Yichen.”

“Good night.” Then, before she could hang up: “Did you have a good day?”

She smiled at the wall. “Yes.”

“Good. Sleep early.”

When she’d put the phone down, her grandmother spoke from the dark on the other side of the room.

“He’s a polite boy.”

“Grandma. You talked to him for forty minutes.”

“He’s easy to talk to,” said her grandmother, and turned over, and was asleep in about two minutes, and Xiaoran lay awake with the phone on her chest.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next night she prepared. By five to nine she was on the bed with the phone in her hand and the volume checked, and her grandmother was safely in the kitchen. At nine exactly it rang, and she had it to her ear before the first ring finished.

“Hello!”

“Hello.”

“I got it.”

“Congratulations. Is she asleep?”

“She’s in the kitchen.”

“Should I prepare myself?”

“Yes, be very careful,” she said, giggling.

They managed four minutes. Then footsteps came down the corridor, and her grandmother appeared in the doorway drying her hands on a tea towel.

“Is that Yichen?”

Xiaoran shut her eyes.

“Good evening, Grandma,” said the phone.

“Ah, Yichen! Have you eaten?”

By the fourth night it was a routine. Nine o’clock meant Yichen. Sometimes Xiaoran answered first; sometimes her grandmother did. Once her grandmother was already sitting next to the phone at ten to nine with her reading glasses on, as if there might be something to read. He learned that she liked to ask whether he’d eaten, whether he’d studied, and whether training was tiring. He answered every question. On the sixth night she made him say hello to her husband, and he spent four minutes shouting pleasantries at a man who was holding the phone upside down and saying “What? What?” until her grandmother took it back.

On the fifth night Xiaoran protested.

“Grandma, you can’t keep interviewing him every night!”

Her grandmother looked up from her knitting. “Why not?”

“Because he’s ringing me!”

“Then you can talk to him when I’ve finished.”

“Finished what?”

“Talking,” said her grandmother. She counted stitches. “He’s a nice boy. What’s wrong with getting to know him?”

Xiaoran opened her mouth. There wasn’t really a good answer to that, so she shut it again.

“Besides,” said her grandmother, “he always rings at nine. Never one minute past. Your grandfather has never been on time for anything in fifty years.”

From the courtyard, her grandfather said, “I heard that,” and turned the radio up.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the ninth night Xiaoran answered first, and her grandmother was watching a costume drama in the other room with the volume up, and for twenty minutes it was just the two of them. She was telling him about the market, and the hair clip shaped like a little persimmon she’d nearly bought, and the snacks her grandmother had insisted on buying for him that she was supposed to take back to the city, when he said, “Your grandmother asked me something yesterday. Before you got the phone.”

She sat up. “What?”

“She asked whether I was going to keep ringing you when the holiday’s over.”

Xiaoran went still. “What did you say?”

He was quiet.

“That I’d like to.”

She looked down at the blanket. Something warm and slow went through her chest.

“Oh.”

“Is that all?”

“No.”

“Then what?”

She pulled the blanket up to her chin and spoke into it. “I’d like that too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last night she was sitting next to her half-packed suitcase when the phone rang at nine. Her father was driving up in the morning to fetch her. School started the day after that.

“Are you ready to come back?” he asked.

“Yes. I miss school.”

“Really?”

“No. I miss seeing you.”

There was a short silence on the line.

“I miss you too,” he said.

They talked about the first day back, and whether he’d be at the gate before the bell, and what she wanted to eat first when she got back to the city, which was the noodles from the stall by the school. Then her grandmother appeared in the doorway.

“Is Yichen there?”

Xiaoran sighed. “Yes, Grandma.”

Her grandmother came over and bent down to the phone. “Yichen. Does your school start on Monday as well?”

“Yes, Grandma. It’s the same school.”

“Of course it is. Make sure you eat breakfast.”

“I will.”

“And take a jacket. It might get cold.”

“All right.”

Her grandmother straightened up, and then, as if it had just occurred to her: “Tell him to come and visit us. At New Year.”

“Grandma!”

But Yichen answered before Xiaoran could object. “I’d like that very much, Grandma.”

“Good. You’re always welcome.” And she went off to bed.

Xiaoran sat still. Neither of them said anything.

“You’re really going to come?” she whispered.

“If your grandmother invites me.”

“She just did.”

“Then I’ll come,” he said, and she hid her face in her knees and smiled into them where nobody could see.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father’s car came up the lane at ten the next morning. Her grandmother packed a bag of persimmons into the boot, and then a bag of dried mushrooms, and then a jar of chili oil wrapped in three layers of newspaper, and then held Xiaoran’s face in both her hands at the gate.

“Tell Yichen to eat breakfast.”

“Grandma, I don’t see him at breakfast.”

“Then tell him at lunch.”

She let go of Xiaoran’s face and turned to Xiaoran’s father, who had been loading the boot and listening to all of this with a slowly changing expression.

“He rings at nine. Very punctual,” she said.

Her father shut the boot. He said nothing at all for the first hour of the drive. Somewhere past the second toll gate, he said, “Who rings at nine?”

Xiaoran pretended to be asleep for the next three hours, and it was the hardest performance of her life.

chapters.desc: One bad landing in a close game, and Lin Xiaoran learns what real fear feels like.
chapters.title: Don’t Scare Me Like That Again
chapters.epigraph: “Some people love quietly. She loved like a fire alarm.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran hated basketball injuries. Not normal hate. Personal hate. Basketball injuries meant blood, limping, bruises, and Zhou Yichen saying “I’m fine” while obviously not fine. And Zhou Yichen got hurt often enough that Xiaoran had developed a small trauma response to the word “injury.” Usually it wasn’t serious. A sprained wrist. A bruised shoulder. A sore ankle. Things athletes shrugged off, and things Xiaoran absolutely didn’t. Still, even she knew basketball was rough. So normally, she saved the drama for afterward.

Today was different.

✦ ✦ ✦

Final quarter of the city league semifinal, and the gym was deafening. The score was close. Everyone was screaming. Xiaoran sat beside Meilin in the bleachers, clutching Yichen’s jacket in both hands.

“He looks tired,” she muttered, for the tenth time.

“He’s played three quarters nonstop,” Meilin said.

“But he looks EXTRA tired.”

“He’s sweating because he’s a human being.”

Xiaoran ignored her. Something felt wrong today. The game had turned rough early. One player on the other team kept going after Yichen—nothing technically illegal, just too physical. And Yichen, competitive Yichen, only got colder each quarter. More intense. More reckless. Eventually, Meilin noticed too.

“…He’s getting irritated.”

On the court, Yichen blocked a shot and drove forward again, fast and sharp. The crowd roared. Then it all happened too fast. One shove. One bad landing. The horrible screech of sneakers skidding across the floor—and Zhou Yichen went down. Hard. The gym went silent. Xiaoran froze—her whole brain froze—because Yichen wasn’t getting up. He stayed down, gripping his leg, while players crowded around him. Coach Wang ran onto the court. A whistle. Someone in the crowd gasped.

And somewhere nearby, someone whispered—

“That looked bad.”

That sentence alone broke something in Xiaoran.

“Yichen.”

Her voice came out small. Then louder—

“YICHEN.”

Meilin grabbed her wrist before she could run onto the court.

“Xiaoran wait—”

But Xiaoran couldn’t breathe properly. Yichen still wasn’t standing. Worse, he looked like he was in real pain—the kind he usually hid in a second. His face was pale, his jaw tight, his breathing uneven.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time Yichen had been helped to the bench, Xiaoran was crying. Not dramatic crying. Real tears. The medical staff examined his ankle while Coach Wang argued with the referees.

“It’s probably a bad sprain,” Meilin said gently.

Probably. Xiaoran hated that word. Probably still meant maybe not. Finally, Yichen looked up—straight at the bleachers, straight at her. The second he saw her crying, the pain on his face gave way to something else: worry. For her. Even now. Idiot. He mouthed something: I’m okay. Xiaoran nearly cried harder, because he was so obviously NOT okay.

✦ ✦ ✦

The game ended eventually. Xiaoran didn’t remember the score, or the crowd leaving, or anyone talking to her. She only remembered rushing to the medical room afterward with shaking hands and pushing the door open. Yichen was sitting on the examination bed while the doctor wrapped his ankle. He looked up when she came in.

“…Hey.”

That one word nearly undid her.

“You scared me,” she whispered.

Yichen paused. Then his expression softened. He could tell she’d been genuinely terrified. Xiaoran walked closer, trying hard not to cry again. She failed.

“Does it hurt badly?”

“A little.”

“That means yes.”

“A reasonable amount.”

“What does THAT mean?!”

Yichen managed a weak smile, which somehow made it worse. Why was he comforting her? He was the one who was hurt. The doctor finished and stood.

“No fractures. But severe sprain. He needs proper rest,” he explained calmly.

Rest. Thank god. Not surgery, not the hospital, not permanent damage. The second the doctor left, Xiaoran let out a shaky breath, maybe her first in an hour. Then she hit Yichen’s shoulder. Not hard.

“I hate you.”

Yichen blinked.

“That seems harsh.”

“You fell like you were dying.”

“I twisted my ankle.”

“You scared me to death.”

Her voice cracked on the last word, and Yichen’s face went soft. This wasn’t Xiaoran being dramatic. She had genuinely panicked—probably imagined the worst possible ending in the first three seconds.

“…Come here,” he said.

Xiaoran was beside him before he finished saying it. Yichen pulled her carefully against him, one hand at the back of her head. Only then did Xiaoran notice how cold her hands had gone.

“I’m okay,” he murmured into her hair.

“You weren’t moving.”

“I know.”

“You looked hurt.”

“I was hurt.”

“That’s worse.”

Yichen laughed under his breath—then hissed when he moved wrong. Xiaoran pulled back.

“SEE.”

“Relax.”

“DON’T RELAX.”

He smiled helplessly. This was exactly why he hid injuries from her sometimes. When something happened to someone she loved, Lin Xiaoran didn’t do anything halfway. Sometimes he found that a little overwhelming. But never unwanted. Never that.

“You know,” he said after a while, “players get injured all the time.”

“I know.”

“Then why were you crying like someone announced my funeral?”

“Because it was YOU.”

She said it without even thinking, and it hit harder than he expected. Yichen looked at her for a second—her red eyes, the worry she still couldn’t hide—then gently brushed his thumb under her eye.

“You really got scared huh?”

Xiaoran tried to glare.

“You think?”

“I’m sorry.”

Zhou Yichen rarely apologised for getting hurt. It usually wasn’t his fault. But he meant this one, like he regretted scaring her more than the injury itself. Xiaoran sniffed.

“You better recover properly.”

“Hm.”

“And no pretending you’re okay just to practice again.”

“Hm.”

“And no acting cool.”

“That one’s difficult.”

She hit his shoulder again. Yichen laughed and caught her hand this time, lacing their fingers together. Comforting her again, without even thinking about it. Outside the medical room, the evening light was fading across the empty gym. The match was long over. The crowd was gone. Everything had finally gone quiet. Only then did Xiaoran realise something embarrassing: her heartbeat had only calmed down once she was holding Zhou Yichen’s hand again.

chapters.desc: A sprained ankle in the city semifinal, a week on crutches, and a girlfriend who carries everything until he asks her to ask first.
chapters.title: Crutches
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t want you to get hurt.”
chapters.content:
On Saturday, in the last quarter of the city league semifinal, a boy who had been leaning on Zhou Yichen all game finally shoved him hard enough, and Yichen came down on the side of his right foot.

Severe sprain, the doctor said. No fracture. Crutches for two days, no basketball for three weeks, and rest. Yichen heard the rest as a suggestion. Lin Xiaoran heard it as a law of physics.

On Monday morning his mother dropped him at the school gate. Xiaoran was already there. She had been there, Meilin told him later, since ten past seven, in a wind that had turned her ears red, holding a carton of milk that had gone warm in her hand.

She watched him get out of the car crutches first, and her face did something complicated.

“Does it hurt?”

“Not much.”

“That means a lot.”

“It means not much. Good morning.” He got the crutches under his arms.

She crouched down right there by the gate, in front of everyone coming in for morning reading, and looked at the bandage as if she could see through it. On Saturday night in the medical room she had cried and hit his shoulder and said she hated him. This morning she didn’t do any of that. She just looked.

“You’re going to be okay. Right?”

“Yes.”

“Promise.”

“I promise,” he said, and only then did she stand up, and the first argument of the week began.

“I’ll take your bag.”

“I can carry my own bag.”

“You’ve got crutches.”

“I’ve got a bag with straps. It goes on my back. The crutches go under my arms. It’s a whole system.”

She had already taken his schoolbag off the back seat and put it on. Then she took the plastic bag his mother had packed, which held an ice pack, his lunch, and a cushion for his ankle that he had specifically asked his mother not to pack. Then she picked up her own bag with her other hand.

“Give me yours, at least,” he said.

“Absolutely not.”

He looked to Tang Meilin for help. Meilin shrugged. “Don’t look at me. She decided last night. She rang me about it.”

Chen Yuhao arrived on his bicycle, braked, and stopped to enjoy the view. “Wow. Xiaoran. Very devoted.”

She turned on him. “Where were you on Saturday while that boy was pushing him all game?”

“On the bench. With a broken finger. As you know.”

“Then go and be useful with nine fingers somewhere else.”

He went, wheeling his bicycle, with Meilin, who was laughing so hard she had to hold on to the handlebars.

“Come on,” Yichen said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Class 3 was on the third floor. By the second flight, Xiaoran was beginning to see the flaw in her plan.

His schoolbag was heavier than it looked, because he carried every textbook every day like a lunatic. The plastic bag kept sliding down her wrist. Her own bag was digging into her other shoulder. Yichen went up beside her one step at a time, placing the crutches carefully.

“Give me something.”

“I’m fine.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I’m fine,” she said again, and hitched the bags up, and one of his books started sliding out of the top of his schoolbag. She grabbed for it without letting go of anything else, and her foot landed on the edge of the step instead of the middle.

For one long second she tipped backwards.

“Xiaoran!”

He let go of one crutch and caught her arm. The crutch clattered down three steps. The plastic bag dropped. Two books went skidding across the landing. She stood still with her heart going like a drum, and he stood with his hand clamped round her arm and his whole weight on his good leg and the banister.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Your ankle?”

“It’s fine. Yichen, your ankle—”

“Give me the bags.”

“I—”

“Now.”

He didn’t raise his voice. He never did. But he said it in a way that made her stop, and she slid his schoolbag off and leaned it against the wall, and collected the books, and handed him the crutch, and then stood there not looking at him.

“You nearly fell.”

“But I didn’t.”

“That’s not the point.”

“I was only trying to help!”

“I know.”

“Then why are you angry?”

He breathed out. “I’m not angry that you wanted to help. I’m frightened because you were carrying four bags down the edge of a staircase and you almost went backwards down it.”

“Three bags.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I wanted to,” she said, to the floor.

“I know you did. But wanting to help doesn’t mean you have to get hurt doing it. I don’t want you to get hurt.” He leaned the crutch against his side and reached out and pushed her hair back off her face, where it had come loose.

Yuhao, who had heard his name shouted from two floors below, came back up and took the bags without saying anything clever, which was how she knew she had frightened everybody. She walked the last flight beside Yichen with nothing in her hands at all, looking at his crutches on every step. Outside the classroom door, he stopped.

“Are you upset?”

“No.”

He waited.

“A bit,” she said.

“Because I told you not to carry everything?”

“Because you keep telling me not to do things. Don’t carry the bag. Don’t stand in the wind. Don’t cry in the medical room. Sometimes I feel like you don’t need me to do anything.” She looked up.

“Is that what you think?”

She shrugged one shoulder.

He leaned towards her, carefully, all his weight on the crutches. “I like that you look after me. I like that you worry. I like that you stood at the gate for twenty minutes until your ears went red. But I don’t want you to think you have to prove it by carrying everything. You can just walk next to me. That’s enough.” Her ears went red again.

“That’s not enough.”

“For me it is.”

She looked at his hands, both of them busy holding crutches, and then she hooked one finger through his belt loop, low, where the corridor couldn’t see.

“Can I at least hold this?”

He laughed. “Yes.”

“Even if I’m not carrying anything?”

“That’s what it’s there for.”

She smiled properly then, for the first time that morning, and held on to his belt loop all the way to his desk, and sat down beside him, and spent the whole of morning reading watching his ankle instead of her book.

“I can feel you looking at it,” he said, without turning a page.

“I’m checking it’s still there.”

“Where would it go?”

“I don’t know. Somewhere I can’t see it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

All day she was impossible. At the first break she moved his chair so he wouldn’t have to. At lunch she went to the canteen and came back with two trays, balancing them like a waitress, and wouldn’t let him get up even to fetch chopsticks. In PE she sat on the bench next to him instead of running laps, and told the teacher she had a stomachache, and the teacher looked at her and then at Yichen’s foot on the bench and said, “Of course you do,” and let her stay.

“You’ll get in trouble,” Yichen said.

“I’ve got a stomachache.”

“Since when?”

“Since Saturday,” she said, and let her head drop onto his shoulder, and watched Class 3 run laps in the cold.

That night at nine, her phone rang.

“Is it up?” she said, before he could say hello.

“Is what up?”

“Your foot. The doctor said up.”

“It’s up.”

“On what?”

“On the cushion my mother packed. Which you carried to school and back, so it’s been on a field trip.”

“Send me a picture.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Send me a picture or I’ll come round.”

“You don’t know where I live.”

“I know where you live. I looked at the class contact sheet in December,” she said darkly.

There was a pause. Then her phone buzzed against her ear, and she took it away and looked at the screen: a photograph of a foot in a white sock and a bandage, propped on a cushion with a pattern of small yellow ducks, and beyond it the edge of a desk and a physics textbook.

“Ducks,” she said.

“My mother bought it.”

“I love it. I love your mother’s taste.”

“I’ll tell her.”

“Don’t tell her! Does it still hurt?” She lay back on her bed with her own feet up on the wall, out of solidarity.

“A bit.”

“You said not much this morning.”

“It was not much this morning. Now it’s a bit.”

“That’s worse.”

“It’s the same amount. I’m just telling you the truth now because you’re not standing in a wind.”

She was quiet for a while, listening to him breathe on the other end, and the scratch of his pen on paper; he was doing homework with his foot on the ducks.

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

“I’m sorry about the stairs.”

“I know.”

“I’ll ask first. Tomorrow.”

“I know. Go to sleep. You’ve got to be at the gate at twenty past seven,” he said again.

“How do you know I’ll be at the gate?”

“Because you’re you,” he said, and she fell asleep that night with the duck photograph open on her screen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning she was at the gate again at twenty past seven with a small bag of snacks and a determined expression.

His mother’s car pulled up. It was the last day of the crutches. His ankle was still swollen, and he looked inconvenienced and otherwise fine.

“Good morning.”

“Morning.”

“For you. Things you can eat at break. There’s fruit. And biscuits. And milk. And vitamins, because Meilin’s mother says vitamins.” She held out the bag.

He looked inside. Then at her. “Thank you.”

She reached for his schoolbag, stopped halfway, and looked at him. He raised one eyebrow. They stared at each other in the middle of the gate.

“Fine,” she said. “I’ll ask first. Can I carry your bag?”

He considered it. “Yes.”

Her whole face lit up.

“Only the schoolbag,” he said.

“You’re negotiating.”

“I’m being reasonable.”

“You’re very difficult to look after.”

“Then you should reconsider.”

She looked at him. “You’re stuck with me,” she said.

She carried his schoolbag up all three flights. It was too heavy for her, and he let her, because she had asked.

At lunch Meilin found them on the second-floor landing, Yichen on the step with his crutches propped beside him and Xiaoran one step below, both eating biscuits out of the same bag.

“You carried it,” Meilin said.

“He let me,” said Xiaoran, with enormous dignity.

Meilin looked at Yichen, who didn’t deny anything, and went away again, shaking her head at both of them.

chapters.desc: Three weeks off the court. One girlfriend in full nurse mode. Zhou Yichen may not survive his own recovery.
chapters.title: Don’t Limp. I’ll Cry Again.
chapters.epigraph: “The injury healed in weeks. The worry took longer.”
chapters.content:
The aftermath of Zhou Yichen’s injury was unbearable for exactly one reason: Lin Xiaoran, treating him like a critically endangered patient.

“Walk slower.”

“I am walking.”

“You limped.”

“I didn’t.”

“It looked painful.”

Yichen was standing by his locker while Xiaoran hovered nearby like an anxious ghost. It had been three days since the injury, and somehow she had gotten worse instead of calmer. The sprain meant no basketball for at least three weeks, which annoyed Yichen enough already. Xiaoran was acting like he’d come back from a war. Yesterday she’d carried his bag, even though it was clearly too heavy for her. This morning she’d bought him breakfast, water, AND vitamins. At lunch she’d pulled out his chair for him.

“Xiaoran, I injured my ankle.”

“Yes.”

“Not my entire body.”

“You don’t know how interconnected health is.”

Across the classroom, Yuhao looked deeply entertained.

“She’s entered nurse mode.”

Meilin nodded. “It only gets worse from here.”

“I can hear both of you,” Xiaoran snapped.

Two seconds later—

“Yichen don’t stand too long.”

Yichen sighed into his hand. The worst part was that he couldn’t stop her. Every time he said he was fine, her eyes went watery. It wasn’t fair.

✦ ✦ ✦

Things got worse after school, because Zhou Yichen made one terrible mistake: he forgot Xiaoran was behind him on the stairs and walked a little faster than usual.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

The entire hallway turned. Yichen stopped. Behind him, Xiaoran looked genuinely horrified.

“Why are you moving like that?!”

“…Like a human?”

“You’re injured.”

“My legs still function.”

“Not correctly.”

Before he could argue, Xiaoran took his arm. Not dramatically, this time. Carefully, like she was afraid too much pressure might hurt him. Yichen felt guilty instead of amused. She still looked shaken from that day.

“You know,” he said more softly as they went down the stairs, “I’m recovering fine.”

“I know.”

“But?”

Xiaoran looked away. Then, quieter—

“When you fell… You really scared me.” She swallowed slightly.

Oh. Again, the fear she couldn’t hide. Yichen remembered it too: the crying, her shaking hands, the way she’d looked at him like the world had almost ended. Part of him still felt bad for putting that look on her face.

“You know I’d tell you if it was serious right?” he murmured.

Xiaoran nodded. Then, after a pause—

“But you also always say you’re fine even when you’re not.”

That was fair. Yichen sighed.

“I hate when you’re reasonable.”

“I learned from Meilin.”

“Of course you did.”

Finally, Xiaoran smiled a little, small and relieved, and somehow that smile made Yichen less annoyed about the whole injury.

✦ ✦ ✦

The peace lasted about twelve hours. The next morning, Xiaoran was back in full disaster mode.

“Why are you carrying THAT.”

Yichen blinked. He was holding a bag of basketballs outside the gym storeroom.

“…Because Coach asked?”

Yichen stared at her. Xiaoran stared back. Then she marched over and took the bag right out of his hands.

“Xiaoran.”

“You need rest.”

“It weighs five kilograms.”

“Exactly.”

“Then why are YOU carrying it?”

Silence. Xiaoran made it two steps before she started struggling. Nearby, Yuhao nearly collapsed laughing.

“This relationship is incredible.”

Meilin looked exhausted. “One of them has no survival instincts. The other has no logic.”

“WHICH ONE.”

“Both.”

Yichen took the bag back before Xiaoran hurt herself instead. Then, without thinking, he crouched and retied the shoelace she’d been stepping on all morning. It happened so casually that neither of them noticed. Yuhao did. Yuhao never missed a chance to be annoying.

“Oh my god. You two are disgusting,” he whispered.

Xiaoran went red.

“We literally did nothing.”

“He bent down like a husband in a drama.”

“SHUT UP.”

Yichen just smiled, stood up, and tapped her forehead.

“You’re worrying too much.”

“I’m not.”

“You almost cried because I carried basketballs.”

“That was a reasonable reaction.”

It was exhausting. It was also cute.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon, it started pouring after class. Most students waited by the entrance for parents or buses. Xiaoran sat beside Yichen and watched the rain hammer the courtyard. For once, she wasn’t talking. No complaining. Just quiet.

“Does it still hurt?”

Yichen glanced at his wrapped ankle.

“A little.”

“See.”

Yichen smiled helplessly and lifted his arm. Xiaoran shifted closer, and Yichen rested his chin on her hair, holding her hand loosely.

“I’m okay,” he murmured again.

This time, Xiaoran didn’t argue. She leaned into him and whispered—

“…You can’t get seriously hurt.”

“Hm?”

“I don’t like it.”

It sounded so simple. Almost childish. But Yichen knew what she meant. She couldn’t stand seeing him in pain, or not knowing, or the idea of something bad happening to him. That kind of love scared him sometimes. Nobody had ever worried about him that fiercely before. Not even himself.

“You fell for three seconds and I already imagined widowhood.”

Yichen choked on a laugh.

“WIDOWHOOD?”

“I panicked.”

“We’re in high school.”

“That doesn’t stop tragedy.”

Yichen laughed until his ankle shifted wrong again.

“DON’T MOVE.”

“Okay okay.”

“See? SEE?”

He was still smiling while she scolded him. And for the first time since the injury, the fear they had both been carrying started to fade.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran overhears that she’s holding Zhou Yichen back—and starts to wonder if they’re right.
chapters.title: Should We Break Up?
chapters.epigraph: “The cruelest words are the ones we quietly agree with.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran usually ignored rumours. Not because she was emotionally strong. She just didn’t care enough. People talked all the time anyway—about grades, relationships, appearances. Half the school practically ran on gossip. So whenever Xiaoran overheard someone talking about her, she usually rolled her eyes and walked away. This time, they mentioned Zhou Yichen too. And that changed everything.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened on a Thursday after class. Xiaoran had stayed late helping Meilin decorate classroom boards for school festival week.

By the time she finished, the hallways were almost empty. She was heading for the back staircase, texting Yichen, when she heard it.

“…Honestly, Zhou Yichen could do way better.”

Xiaoran slowed down. Girls’ voices, somewhere around the corner by the storage room. Normally she would have kept walking. Then—

“I don’t even understand what he sees in Lin Xiaoran.”

Silence. Xiaoran stopped. She didn’t mean to. Her feet just stopped. The voices went on.
