“I heard he rejected training invitations because she wanted attention.”

“That’s ridiculous.”

“No seriously. My friend from Class 3 said he skipped extra practice before because Xiaoran was upset.”

“She’s honestly holding him back.”

“And he used to be way more focused before dating.”

The girls laughed—not loudly, not cruelly. Just casually, like they really believed it. Somehow that was worse. Xiaoran stayed frozen, because the worst part was that some of it was technically true. A few weeks ago, Yichen really had turned down an extra match. But not because of her. She knew that. His ankle hadn’t fully healed, and Coach Wang had told him not to overdo it. Still, hearing people say she was dragging him down lodged painfully in her chest. Especially because… what if other people thought so too?

✦ ✦ ✦

After that day, something changed. Not dramatically. Quietly enough that only the people closest to Xiaoran noticed. She still smiled, still joked, still clung to Yichen. But sometimes she went quiet afterward, especially when basketball came up.

Like now: Saturday afternoon at Meilin’s house, everyone eating snacks while Yuhao rambled excitedly about an upcoming invitational tournament. Apparently several schools had asked for Yichen by name.

“Coach says scouts might come too,” Yuhao said proudly.

Meilin nodded. “That’s huge.”

Normally Xiaoran would have bragged like she’d personally trained Zhou Yichen herself. Today, she only smiled and looked down at her drink. Yichen noticed, of course. Later that evening, walking her home, he finally asked—

“What’s wrong?”

Xiaoran blinked innocently.

“Hm?”

“You’ve been weird for two weeks.”

“I’m always weird.”

“Not like this.”

Silence. The evening wind moved through the quiet street. Then, more quietly—

“You stop talking whenever basketball gets mentioned.”

Oh. So he had noticed that too. Of course he had. Zhou Yichen noticed everything about her, even the moods she worked hardest to hide.

“…Nothing’s wrong,” she said eventually.

“Liar.”

He said it so simply, so certainly, that Xiaoran nearly cried right there. He knew her too well now. Yichen slowed down and looked at her properly.

“Did someone say something?”

The question landed too close. Xiaoran’s fingers tightened around her sleeve, and Yichen understood. His expression cooled.

“Who?”

“No one.”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked away. She didn’t want him angry. That wasn’t the point. The point was that the words wouldn’t leave her head. Holding him back. Distracting him. Making him less focused. She knew how talented Yichen was, how seriously everyone talked about his future. Meanwhile she still got lost near school and cried over math. The comparison suddenly felt unbearable.

“So what if they’re right?”

Yichen stopped walking.

“…What?”

Xiaoran stared straight ahead.

“I mean… You were already doing so well before me.” She forced a small laugh.

“Xiaoran.”

“And everyone expects so much from you.”

His expression changed. Serious now. Actually serious. But Xiaoran kept going before she could lose her nerve.

“What if dating me really makes things harder for you?”

Silence. Then, quietly—

“Should we break up?”

The world went still. Even Xiaoran felt strange after saying it, like the sentence didn’t belong to her. Just thinking it already hurt. Zhou Yichen just looked at her. He wasn’t angry or shocked, only deeply focused, like he was trying to work out how she’d gotten there on her own.

“Who told you that?”

Xiaoran looked down.

“No one directly.”

“What exactly did they say?”

“…That I hold you back.”

Out loud, it sounded embarrassingly small. Yichen was quiet for two seconds. Then he laughed—not mocking, just disbelieving—and that confused Xiaoran even more.

“You’re laughing?”

“I’m trying very hard not to get angry.”

“Oh.”

Then he took her hand, lacing his fingers through hers.

“Look at me,” he said.

Slowly, Xiaoran did, and immediately regretted it. He was looking at her far too softly.

“You think I’d choose basketball over you?”

“That’s not what I mea—”

“If dating you affected me negatively,” he said calmly, “I would’ve ended things already.”

Xiaoran blinked. That was painfully logical.

“But instead,” he said more quietly, “you’re the person I want beside me after every game. You’re the first person I look for in crowds.”

Another silence.

“And you think that makes my life worse?”

Xiaoran’s chest ached. Hearing him say it so directly was almost too much.

“But your future—”

“My future is my responsibility.”

He said it like he’d decided that a long time ago. Yichen sighed and stepped closer.

“You know why I skipped that extra match?”

Xiaoran nodded weakly. “Your ankle.”

“Exactly. Not because of you.” His thumb brushed lightly across her knuckles.

“I know.”

“Then why believe strangers over me?”

That question hurt the most, because she didn’t know. Maybe loving someone that talented made insecurity grow. Like one day he might realise he deserved someone better. More mature. Less troublesome. Maybe Yichen understood that already, because he pulled her into his arms.

“You know what actually distracts me? You crying over imaginary breakups,” he murmured into her hair.

“I hate you.”

“No you don’t.”

Unfortunately, he was right. Now Xiaoran just felt ridiculous—for overthinking alone this long, for almost believing strangers over Yichen. After a while, she muttered into his hoodie—

“…You really don’t want to break up?”

Yichen pulled back just enough to look at her properly. Then, flatly—

“Absolutely not.”

“Oh.”

“And honestly,” he said calmly, “you’re not escaping me that easily.”

Xiaoran laughed—her first real laugh in weeks.

“Finally,” Yichen murmured.

And just like that, Lin Xiaoran finally felt like herself again.

chapters.desc: The Monday after she asked whether they should break up, a folded note on her desk answers her in one word.
chapters.title: One Word
chapters.epigraph: “I know. But I’d like you not to say it unless you do.”
chapters.content:
The question hadn’t been planned. That was the first thing Lin Xiaoran wanted to make clear, if anyone ever asked, which she hoped nobody would.

She hadn’t gone to Meilin’s on Saturday meaning to ask her boyfriend whether they should break up. She had gone for the snacks. But for two weeks she had been carrying around what the girls by the storage room had said, holding him back, he used to be more focused, and on the walk home the question had fallen out of her.

He had laughed. He had said he was trying hard not to get angry, and asked why she believed strangers over him. And when she asked again, into his hoodie, whether he really didn’t want to, he had said “Absolutely not,” so flat and certain that she had laughed for the first time in weeks.

She went to bed happy. At two in the morning she woke up and thought about the storage room again.

She typed are you sure? and looked at it, and deleted it, because he had already answered twice and a third time would be embarrassing. Then she lay awake until four, being embarrassed anyway.

Sunday was normal. They messaged about a drama and a cat video and the invitational on Saturday, and underneath the normal the question sat there like a stone in a shoe.

On Monday morning she sat down at her desk, reached into the drawer for her chemistry book, and found a folded sheet of paper on top of it.

No name. One word in the middle of the page, in handwriting she knew better than her own.

No.

And underneath, much smaller, as if added after some thought:

(In case you ask again.)

She read it four times. Then she looked at the desk beside hers. Zhou Yichen was sitting there with his English book open, his strapped ankle stretched out under the desk in front, looking at a vocabulary list.

“When did you put this here?”

“Put what?”

“Yichen.”

“Before you came in. Yuhao kept watch.” He turned a page.

At the desk behind them, Chen Yuhao raised one hand without looking up, like a man taking credit for a goal.

✦ ✦ ✦

She folded the note along its crease and held it in her lap all through morning reading, and when the bell went, Tang Meilin leaned over the back of her chair.

“You’re doing the face.”

“What face?”

“The one where you’ve lost something or found something and you can’t decide which.”

Xiaoran gave her the note. Meilin read the word, read the small line, and looked up.

“No to what?”

Xiaoran told her, in a whisper, while Yichen went to the front to hand in the homework. The storage room, the girls, the friend from Class 3 who apparently reported on everyone, the walk home, the question. Meilin’s face went through several stages. It ended on an expression Xiaoran had only seen once, when a boy in primary school had thrown Xiaoran’s lunch box into a pond.

“You asked Zhou Yichen if you should break up. Because of three girls by a mop cupboard.”

“It was a storage room.”

“Which three?”

“Meilin.”

“I only want their names. For research. He wrote it down so you’d have it in writing.” Meilin looked at the note again and her face changed back.

“I know.”

“So you’d stop asking.”

“I know.”

“He knows you. Talk to him at break. And don’t cry in class, it’s festival week, people will talk,” Meilin said, not entirely as a compliment, and handed it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the long break he went out to the corridor, his ankle still strapped but steady now, no limp unless he forgot, and she followed him, and they ended up at the window at the end by the fire door where nobody ever went.

“You already answered. On Saturday,” she said, holding up the note.

“I know.”

“Twice.”

“You asked twice. So I thought you’d probably ask a third time. Late at night. When I wasn’t there to say it. So I wrote it down.” He leaned his shoulder on the wall.

She thought about two in the morning and are you sure? and the delete key, and didn’t say anything. He watched her not say anything.

“Two o’clock?” he said.

“Ten past.”

He nodded, as if that were about what he’d expected.

“Xiaoran. On Saturday I laughed because you were standing right in front of me and I could see you were fine. Then I went home. It wasn’t funny at home.” He looked at the paper in her hand.

She hadn’t thought about that. Not once, in two days of thinking. She had thought about the girls, and about herself, whether she was too much, whether she was in his way. She hadn’t thought about him walking home on Saturday night with that sentence in his ears.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“I know you didn’t mean it.”

“I didn’t.”

“I know. But I’d like you not to say it unless you do. If you ever mean it, say it, and we’ll talk properly. If you don’t, ask me something else. Ask me if I’m sure. Ask a hundred times. I’ll write it on every page of your notebook.” He said it without any heat at all, the way he told her to eat breakfast.

“Every page?”

“Even the maths pages.”

Her eyes had started to sting. Meilin had specifically said not to cry.

“I’m not crying.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were thinking it.”

He laughed, and held out his arm, and she walked straight into it and pressed her face into his shoulder, in the corridor, in festival week, where people would talk.

“Those girls,” he said into her hair.

“Don’t.”

“I wasn’t going to do anything. I was going to ask Coach Wang to put the real reason for my rest days on the team noticeboard. In large print.”

She laughed into his shirt. “That’s doing something.”

“It’s a noticeboard. Noticeboards are neutral.”

They stood there until the bell. She didn’t let go of him the whole time, and he didn’t ask her to, and when two girls from Class 5 came round the corner and saw them and turned round again, she held on tighter.

“Is the invitational on Saturday?” she asked, as they went back in.

“Is that a silly question?”

“It’s a test question. To see if you still answer.”

“Yes. It’s on Saturday. Sit behind the bench. Coach already said,” he said.

At lunch the four of them squeezed onto the end of the long table under the canteen window. Xiaoran sat so close to Yichen that she was half on his side of the bench, eating from his tray as much as hers, and nobody commented, because nobody ever did anymore.

Meilin put down her chopsticks and looked across at him. “I want their names.”

“No,” said Yichen.

“I’m only going to look at them.”

“You’re going to look at them for three weeks in the canteen until they move schools.”

“That’s a type of looking.”

“Whose names?” said Yuhao, with his mouth full.

“Nobody’s,” said Xiaoran.

“Three girls said she was holding him back. By the storage room. And she believed them for two weeks,” Meilin said.

Yuhao swallowed. He looked at Xiaoran with genuine bewilderment. “Holding him back? From what? He did eleven hours of practice last week. He does physics for fun. Somebody needs to hold him back. I’ve been trying since we were eleven.”

“See. Even Yuhao,” said Meilin.

“Even me. Hang on,” Yuhao agreed, then frowned.

Xiaoran burst out laughing so hard she had to put her hand over her mouth, and leaned against Yichen’s shoulder until she’d stopped. When she sat up, he moved the last dumpling from his tray onto hers without comment.

“I asked once. Twice. I won’t ask again,” she told Meilin, defensively.

“You will. Ten past two. Some night,” said Yichen.

“Then you’ll answer?”

“I’ll answer. I’ve got a lot of paper,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday morning there was a new sheet on the basketball noticeboard outside the gym, in large print, pinned at eye level between the training schedule and a poster about dental hygiene.

TEAM NOTICE. Z. Yichen: rest days 4, 6, 11 and 13 (right ankle, doctor’s instructions). Not optional. — Coach Wang

It was the most boring notice anyone had ever pinned to that board, and by lunchtime half the grade had read it, because the other half had told them to.

Meilin took a photograph and sent it to Xiaoran with no caption at all. Then she sent a second message.

Meilin: Large print.

Xiaoran: He said noticeboards are neutral.

Meilin: Your boyfriend is terrifying and I support him.

At the afternoon break, Xiaoran stood in front of the board for longer than necessary. Two of the girls from the storage room came down the corridor, slowed, read it, and looked at each other, and one of them said “Oh” in a small voice, and they walked on a little faster.

Xiaoran didn’t say anything. The noticeboard was neutral. When she got back to her desk there was a second folded note on top of her chemistry book. She hadn’t seen him do it, and he had been sitting next to her all lesson.

Still no.

“How?” she said.

“Trade secret.”

“Was it Yuhao?”

From the desk behind, Yuhao raised his hand again.

That night she put both notes inside the clear back cover of her phone case, where they stayed for the rest of high school, two small white squares going soft at the folds. She didn’t take them out often. Knowing they were there was enough.

Once, much later, at two in the morning, she did take them out. She read them, put them back, and went to sleep.

The rest days, for the record, were the fourth, the sixth, the eleventh and the thirteenth. He rested on all of them. On each one he sat at the side of the gym with his ankle up on a chair, doing physics homework, in full view of anyone who cared to look, and on every one of them Xiaoran sat beside him doing her history, with her head on his shoulder, in full view as well.

chapters.desc: Zhou Yichen eats chili oil like water. Lin Xiaoran decides to build a tolerance. It goes about as well as expected.
chapters.title: You’re Crying Over Chili Oil?
chapters.epigraph: “Love is wanting to share someone’s world, even when it burns.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen had one frightening talent: he could eat spicy food like his tongue had signed a legal immunity contract. Not normal spicy. Unhinged spicy. The kind that made other people reconsider their life choices after one bite. And Zhou Yichen stayed calm, unbothered, completely fine. Lin Xiaoran absolutely hated it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“It’s literally red.”

“That’s usually what chili oil looks like.”

“No. That’s not food. That’s lava,” Xiaoran whispered, staring at his noodles in horror.

The four of them were at a noodle shop near school after basketball practice. Rain was pouring outside. Yuhao was happily demolishing a plate of fried rice, Meilin looked spiritually exhausted as always, and Zhou Yichen was calmly adding MORE chili oil to an already dangerous bowl of noodles.

“You’re trying to impress someone.”

“I’m eating dinner.”

“That cannot taste good.”

Yichen glanced at her lazily. “Want to try?”

“Absolutely not.”

Three minutes later, Xiaoran stole a bite anyway, because curiosity always won. Instant regret.

“WATER.”

Yuhao choked laughing.

“She’s dying.”

“IT BURNS.”

“You took half the spoon,” Meilin pointed out.

“I THOUGHT HE WAS EXAGGERATING.”

Yichen pushed his drink towards her before she could combust.

“Slow down.”

“YOU EAT THIS WILLINGLY?”

“It’s not that spicy.”

Meilin stared at him blankly. “You’ve lost human sensation.”

The noodle shop owner wandered over and set a glass of milk in front of Xiaoran without a word, like he’d seen this before. Accurate. Zhou Yichen kept eating peacefully while Xiaoran sat there blinking back tears from one bite. One. His bowl looked like lava.

“This relationship won’t survive long-term,” Xiaoran whispered afterward, clutching her iced tea.

“Because of chili oil?” Yichen asked.

“Yes.”

“That feels unreasonable.”

“No, actually dietary incompatibility destroys marriages,” Yuhao interrupted seriously.

“Why are you talking like a divorced uncle?” Meilin asked tiredly.

✦ ✦ ✦

After that, the spicy food situation got personal, because Zhou Yichen started teasing her about it. Subtly. Constantly. Very annoyingly. At lunch the next day—

“Want some?”

“No.”

“It’s mild.”

“You’re a liar.”

Yichen smiled a little and ate the noodles himself. No reaction. No suffering. No weakness. That annoyed Xiaoran most of all. How was he so handsome while casually eating lava? It felt biologically unfair. One afternoon after school, Xiaoran finally snapped.

“I’m building spice tolerance.”

Yichen looked up from his homework.

“…Why.”

“So I can understand your world.”

Meilin looked concerned.

“Please don’t.”

“Too late.”

Yuhao grinned. “This’ll be funny.”

It wasn’t funny. Not even slightly.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first attempt was a disaster. Xiaoran bought “mild” skewers from a street stall after school. “Mild,” the vendor promised. Lies. Cruel lies.

Halfway through the second skewer, Xiaoran’s eyes were already streaming. Yichen sighed and handed her tissues.

“You don’t need to force yourself.”

“I can do this.”

“You’re crying.”

“That’s temporary weakness.”

She took another bite out of pure stubbornness and coughed so hard she had to sit down on the kerb. Yuhao had to lean against a wall to laugh.

“She’s crying over a skewer.”

Meilin rubbed her forehead. “I knew this would happen.”

Yichen watched her—the stubborn face, the watery eyes, the way she kept going anyway. Hopelessly cute.

“Okay, enough,” he said, taking the skewer from her.

“No.”

“You stopped breathing earlier.”

“I’m adapting.”

“You’re dying.”

Xiaoran glared at him over her carton of milk. Then,

“…How are you eating this normally?”

Yichen shrugged. “I grew up with it.”

“That explains a lot.”

He laughed under his breath, then wiped a bit of sauce from the corner of her mouth with his thumb. Small. Automatic. Xiaoran’s heartbeat betrayed her anyway. Stupid handsome boyfriend.

✦ ✦ ✦

A week later, Xiaoran tried again. And again. And slowly, her tolerance actually improved. Not much, but enough that she could eat medium-spicy noodles without crying in public, which she considered a historic achievement.

“Wow, love really changes people,” Yuhao said one lunch break.

“Exactly,” Xiaoran said proudly over her spicy hotpot.

Then her expression changed. Meilin narrowed her eyes.

“…Too spicy?”

Xiaoran’s eyes went watery.

“No.”

“Liar.”

“I’m fine.”

Then tears started rolling silently down her face. Yuhao lost it.

“She’s crying again.”

“I HATE ALL OF YOU.”

Yichen looked helpless as he pushed her drink closer.

“You pushed too hard again.”

“But I almost survived.”

Yichen laughed and handed her more tissues. Then, more softly—

“You know you don’t actually need to like spicy food because of me.”

Xiaoran sniffed.

“But you love it.”

“Hm.”

“And I wanted to experience things you like too.”

Oh. That one caught him off guard. Yichen looked at her for a second—flushed cheeks, watery eyes, all that stubborn sincerity she never bothered hiding. Then he smiled.

“You already do,” he said.

Xiaoran blinked.

“Hm?”

“You already understand my world enough.”

Yuhao gagged. “Oh my god.”

Meilin nodded tiredly. “Actually unbearable.”

But Xiaoran was too busy staring at Yichen to care, her heart melting embarrassingly fast. Then, after a pause—

“…I’m still learning spicy food.”

“Why?”

“So one day we can eat extra spicy hotpot together romantically.”

Yichen laughed and squeezed her hand under the table.

“Okay. But we’re bringing milk,” he said.

chapters.desc: A double date with the rival captain and the girl Xiaoran once fought on the café street. What could go wrong?
chapters.title: Should We Even Be Sitting Together?
chapters.epigraph: “Peace treaties are usually signed over food.”
chapters.content:
A double date with Zhou Yichen and Song Kai was already a terrible idea. Adding their girlfriends? Disaster. Especially because, technically, Lin Xiaoran and Xu Hani still hated each other after the Hair-Pulling Incident. Not publicly, just spiritually. Which was somehow worse. So when Song Kai suggested—

“Why don’t the four of us eat together once so things stop being awkward?”

—nobody was thrilled. Xu Hani looked offended. Xiaoran looked ready to commit crimes again. And Zhou Yichen immediately got a headache.

✦ ✦ ✦

“This is stupid,” Xiaoran hissed, fixing her hair outside the restaurant.

“It’s just dinner.”

“It’s diplomatic negotiations.”

Beside her, Yichen sighed. She wasn’t entirely wrong. Song Kai had picked a barbecue place by the river. Neutral territory, apparently. Very strategic. Yichen watched her mentally prepare for war.

“Remember,” he said calmly, “you promised not to fight.”

“I only fight when provoked.”

“That sentence inspires zero confidence.”

Xiaoran crossed her arms.

“Why are YOU calm? Your rival is literally inside.”

“Basketball rival,” Yichen corrected.

“That’s still testosterone tension.”

Inside, Song Kai already looked exhausted.

“Hani,” he warned carefully, “please don’t provoke Xiaoran.”

“I don’t care about her enough to provoke her.”

Song Kai sighed. This dinner was going to kill him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Five minutes later, all four of them were sitting together. Painfully awkwardly. The restaurant was warm and noisy, meat sizzling on the grill in the middle of the table. Their table, though, was pure tension. Xu Hani drank water elegantly. Lin Xiaoran stabbed her grilled mushrooms like they’d wronged her. The two boys exchanged an exhausted look.

“Great atmosphere,” Song Kai muttered.

“No one’s bleeding yet,” Yichen answered.

“Amazing progress.”

Across the table, Hani suddenly spoke.

“So. Still fighting people over your boyfriend?” She looked at Xiaoran lazily.

Silence. Yichen closed his eyes. Here we go. Xiaoran smiled sweetly.

“Still talking too much?”

Song Kai grabbed his drink. Oh no. Yichen calmly put more meat in Xiaoran’s bowl before she could escalate. A distraction tactic. Very experienced boyfriend behaviour. It only worked for a while.

“You know,” Hani said casually, “people at my school still talk about that fight.”

“Good, at least someone found meaning in your hair loss,” Xiaoran answered.

Song Kai choked on his water. Yichen lowered his head, trying hard not to laugh.

“Hani,” Song Kai warned tiredly.

“What?” Hani replied innocently.

“You too,” Yichen said quietly towards Xiaoran.

“I’m literally peaceful.”

“You threatened her hairstyle.”

It should have exploded already. Somehow it didn’t—mostly because the boys had gotten weirdly good at crisis management since dating these two. At one point, Hani complained about university applications and Xiaoran accidentally agreed with her. Both girls paused, like neither had expected common ground. The boys watched in silence, afraid to break the spell. Then a waiter set a plate of extremely spicy meat in front of Hani instead of Xiaoran. Hani took a casual bite. Instant regret.

“…Why is this so spicy?!”

Xiaoran blinked—then burst out laughing. Not mocking. Genuinely helpless laughter.

“OH MY GOD.”

Hani glared with watery eyes.

“Why are you happy.”

“You look exactly like me last month.”

Yichen sighed. The spicy food incident. Traumatic memories. Song Kai looked more and more entertained as Xiaoran pushed a glass of milk towards Hani without thinking.

“Drink this before you pass away.”

“…Thanks.”

“You’re still annoying though.”

“Same to you.”

Progress. Questionable, but still progress. Later, the conversation drifted back to basketball. Unfortunately. Song Kai smirked at Yichen.

“You still owe me a proper rematch.”

“You sound obsessed,” Yichen answered calmly.

“Because you got lucky.”

Xiaoran sat up straighter. Danger. Hani noticed too.

“Oh my god. Look at her face,” Hani muttered.

“What face?” Song Kai asked.

“The ‘don’t insult my boyfriend’ face.”

“I DON’T HAVE A FACE.”

“You absolutely do.”

Under the table, Yichen took Xiaoran’s wrist and gave it a gentle squeeze. Calm down. Song Kai laughed openly.

“She really gets angry over you instantly.”

“That’s because he’s talented,” Xiaoran said stubbornly.

Yichen looked tired.

“Xiaoran.”

“No. I’m serious.”

Hani looked at her strangely. Not mocking this time. Thoughtful.

“…You really like him huh?”

The whole table paused. The question sounded unexpectedly sincere, and even Xiaoran blinked, like the obviousness of the answer had surprised her for a second.

“Of course I do.”

No embarrassment, no joke. Just honest. The mood at the table shifted after that—softer, less hostile. Even Hani looked calmer, like she’d understood something. Beside her, Yichen had gone quiet. Hearing her answer like that, so naturally, still got to him every time. Then Song Kai ruined it.

“Disgusting,” he muttered.

Hani rolled her eyes.

“Your relationship is honestly exhausting to watch.”

“Thank you,” Xiaoran answered proudly.

“That wasn’t a compliment.”

“I accepted it anyway.”

Yichen finally laughed and put more meat on her plate, the way he always did without thinking. Watching that made Hani glance at Song Kai beside her. Song Kai looked horrified.

“…Don’t start.”

Too late. Across the table, Xiaoran noticed. A slow, dangerous smile spread across her face.

“Oh,” she whispered delightedly. “NOW who’s on a weird double date?”

chapters.desc: Fourteen days to find the perfect gift for a boy who already has everything—and remembers everything.
chapters.title: The Birthday Gift Problem
chapters.epigraph: “The best gifts aren’t bought. They’re remembered.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had exactly fourteen days before Zhou Yichen’s birthday. Which should’ve been enough time. Unfortunately, she was Lin Xiaoran, which meant a simple birthday present turned into a national crisis.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I don’t know what to buy him.”

Xiaoran lay face-down across Tang Meilin’s bed, suffering. Meilin kept doing her homework.

“You’ve been repeating that sentence for forty minutes.”

“Because LOVE is difficult.”

“Buying gifts isn’t love. It’s shopping.”

“Not for soulmates.”

Zhou Yichen was incredibly easy to please. Too easy. That was the problem. Basketball shoes? He’d smile. A hoodie? He’d smile. A handwritten note? He’d probably smile like an idiot. Which made choosing harder. Xiaoran wanted it to feel special. Not expensive. Just… important. Something that would make him think, Ah. This is so Xiaoran. Every idea felt stupid after five minutes.

“He already has shoes.”

“Then buy something else.”

“He has everything.”

“He doesn’t own a spaceship.”

“That’s because I’m poor.”

Meilin’s phone buzzed. She glanced at it.

“Oh. Yichen asked if you’re alive.” Meilin looked up.

Xiaoran groaned into the blankets.

“No one understands my suffering.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen, meanwhile, supposedly had no idea. Which was impressive, because Xiaoran was terrible at hiding things, especially excitement. Three days before his birthday, she followed him around school like a suspicious little criminal, disappeared at lunch, and came back looking stressed. Yuhao noticed.

“She’s planning something.”

“Obviously,” Yichen answered calmly.

“She looked at your wrist for thirty seconds earlier.”

Yichen paused. Interesting. Later, at basketball practice, Yichen was sitting courtside with a water bottle when Xiaoran appeared out of nowhere. Too cheerful. Suspiciously cheerful.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Hypothetically.”

“Bad start already.”

“If someone gave you a birthday gift… What would mean the most to you?” She sat down beside him casually.

Yichen looked at her, then smiled a little.

“You’re asking for yourself?”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Okay maybe.”

He laughed and wiped the sweat from his neck with a towel, which distracted Xiaoran for three full seconds. Ridiculously handsome athlete boyfriend. Very inconvenient. Then he answered honestly—

“Anything from you.”

“That’s NOT HELPFUL.”

Yuhao, who had overheard everything, called over—

“Buy him matching underwear.”

“GET OUT.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The real problem was that Zhou Yichen remembered everything. Her milk tea order. Her exam schedule. The exact bakery she liked. Random things she’d said months ago. Meanwhile, Xiaoran regularly lost her own phone. How was she supposed to compete with someone that thoughtful? Then one evening, sorting through old photos, Xiaoran froze. Inside a storage box was something she’d almost forgotten: the claw machine bunny. A little faded now. A tiny white rabbit. And she remembered.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first thing Zhou Yichen ever won for her, back before they were even dating. She had failed eleven times in a row; he’d stepped in and won it on the first try. Later, after they got together, she’d waved it at him and joked—

“If we ever break up in the future, I’m keeping this.”

And Yichen had said, completely calmly—

“We’re not breaking up.”

At the time, she’d laughed. Now, remembering it made her chest ache, because he had meant it, even back then. And suddenly Xiaoran knew exactly what to give him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen’s birthday arrived. No big party. Just close friends having dinner at Yuhao’s house. Very normal. Very warm. Yuhao gave him basketball accessories. Meilin gave him practical stationery, because she valued function over romance. Then everyone looked at Xiaoran, who had suddenly become nervous.

“Oh? Special girlfriend gift.” Yuhao grinned.

“Shut up.”

Yichen watched as she pulled out a medium-sized paper bag, her sleeves tugged down over her hands.

“…It’s not expensive,” she muttered.

“No one asked.”

“I’m managing expectations.”

Then she handed it to him. Yichen expected something cute. Maybe handmade. Maybe dramatic. Instead, he went still when he opened the box. Inside was the old white rabbit, carefully cleaned, with a simple silver bracelet around its neck. Small. Minimal. Exactly the kind he would actually wear every day. For a second, he said nothing, which made Xiaoran panic.

“Oh no.”

Yichen looked up.

“…You kept this?”

“Of course I kept it.”

Silence.

“You remembered?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“…The claw machine?”

“No. What you said afterward.” His voice went soft.

Oh. That. Xiaoran’s face went hot. He remembered that too? The others looked lost.

“What are you two talking about?” Yuhao asked.

“History,” Meilin answered wisely.

Then Xiaoran looked at Yichen again.

“You said we wouldn’t break up. So I thought… maybe the rabbit should stay with the original owner for your birthday.” She tried laughing lightly.

The room was quiet for exactly two seconds. Then Yuhao grabbed Meilin’s sleeve.

“WHY ARE THEY LIKE THIS.”

“Quiet.”

Zhou Yichen was still looking at the bracelet, the rabbit, Xiaoran sitting there pretending not to panic. No expensive gift could have hit him harder. Lin Xiaoran always managed to give him things that felt frighteningly sincere. He reached over and took her hand.

“You know,” he murmured, “this might be my favourite gift ever.”

Xiaoran went red.

“Don’t say things like that publicly.”

“It’s my birthday.”

“That’s not how birthdays work.”

Yichen laughed, then put the bracelet on right there. Somehow that hit Xiaoran embarrassingly hard. It looked right on him, like it had always belonged there. Yuhao stared at them.

“I’m single because the universe hates me.”

Meilin nodded sympathetically.

“Correct.”

chapters.desc: Their first anniversary lands a week after his birthday, and Lin Xiaoran has three coins to her name. So they make a rule: nobody spends anything.
chapters.title: One Year, Exactly
chapters.epigraph: “Then I’ll pay it back next year.”
chapters.content:
The problem with celebrating an anniversary one week after a birthday was that, apparently, love was expensive. At least, that was Lin Xiaoran’s conclusion.

She had discovered this while sitting at her desk on a Monday evening, staring at the contents of her wallet.

Three coins, a receipt from the stationery shop, and a discount coupon for a drink she didn’t even like.

She turned the wallet upside down, as if a forgotten banknote might fall out if she shook it hard enough. Nothing. Xiaoran stared at it.

Then she looked at the calendar beside her desk, where December 6 had a red heart drawn round it. Their anniversary was tomorrow. She closed her eyes.

A week ago, she had been perfectly happy with her financial decisions. Zhou Yichen’s birthday had been a success. She had spent fourteen days panicking about his gift and every yuan she had saved on the silver bracelet round the rabbit’s neck. And he had loved it. That was the important part.

He had looked at her with that rare, unguarded expression that always made her feel. But the bracelet had taken everything.

Yichen, on the other hand, had never been broke in his life, and his idea of a small present came in a box inside another box. Whatever he had planned for tomorrow, she couldn’t match it.

She hadn’t thought about that when she bought the bracelet. She’d been busy being in love. Xiaoran picked up her phone.

Xiaoran: Yichen.

Yichen: Hm?

Xiaoran: What are you doing tomorrow?

Yichen: School.

Xiaoran: After school.

Yichen: Nothing planned.

She narrowed her eyes.

Xiaoran: Nothing?

Yichen: Should there be something?

Xiaoran: No.

A pause.

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: What?

Yichen: What happened?

She looked at her wallet again, then typed.

Xiaoran: Hypothetically, if someone had no money, would you still love them?

His reply came almost immediately.

Yichen: Depends.

Her eyes widened.

Xiaoran: Depends on WHAT?

Yichen: Whether they’ve been spending it on something unnecessary.

She stared at the screen.

Xiaoran: You’re a terrible boyfriend.

Yichen: I’m joking.

Yichen: I love you even when you’re broke.

Xiaoran smiled despite herself, then another message arrived.

Yichen: Is this about tomorrow?

She hesitated.

Xiaoran: Maybe.

Yichen: Go to sleep. We’ll talk tomorrow.

She put her phone down, still feeling vaguely unsettled.

He knew. Of course he knew, and that made her more nervous.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Xiaoran arrived at school with a plan. It wasn’t an impressive plan. In fact, it consisted of three steps:

1. Don’t mention the anniversary.
2. Don’t look disappointed.
3. Hope Yichen hasn’t prepared a surprise.

The third step was the most difficult. Because Zhou Yichen was the sort of person who could make arrangements and somehow produce something she hadn’t expected.

He might have reserved a restaurant. He might have bought her something. He might have planned a date. And she had absolutely nothing.

She was standing near the classroom entrance when he arrived.

He was carrying his schoolbag over one shoulder, his uniform neat as usual. His eyes found her almost immediately.

“Morning.”

“Morning.”

He leaned down slightly and pressed a kiss into her hair. She smiled. Then he looked at her face.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re thinking too loudly.”

“I’m not.”

“All right.”

He reached for her hand. She took it, but her expression remained suspiciously serious. Yichen studied her for another moment.

“Did you sleep?”

“Yes.”

“Properly?”

“Yes.”

“Then why do you look like you’re about to negotiate a business contract?”

She met his eyes.

“Maybe I am.”

“With whom?”

“You.”

“What’s the proposal?”

She hesitated. Then she said, “We shouldn’t spend money today. Either of us.”

Yichen looked at her. He said nothing. Then he smiled.

“That’s the proposal?”

“Yes.”

“Accepted.”

She blinked.

“Just like that?”

“Would you like me to negotiate?”

“No.”

“Then we’re done.”

She stared at him, searching his face for signs that he was hiding something. He squeezed her hand.

“Happy anniversary, Xiaoran.”

Her heart gave a small, unexpected flutter. She looked down at their joined hands.

“Happy anniversary.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The school day was almost unbearable. Not because of the lessons. Well, partly because of the lessons.

But mostly because Xiaoran kept remembering that today was their anniversary.

She had been dating Zhou Yichen for exactly one year. Three hundred and sixty-five days. She had counted. Not that she would admit it.

She remembered the first time he had walked her home. The first time he had held her hand. The first time he had called her his girlfriend, and how she had spent the rest of that evening smiling at absolutely nothing.

She remembered their first disagreement, their first proper date, the first time she had fallen asleep on his shoulder, and the first time she had realised that being with him wasn’t just exciting. It was comfortable. He had become part of her ordinary days.

And she liked that more than she knew how to explain.

During lunch, she found herself staring at him across the table.

Yichen was listening to Chen Yuhao talk about something, occasionally responding with a few words. His expression was relaxed, his attention divided between the conversation and the food in front of him. Then, as if sensing her gaze, he turned. Their eyes met. He raised an eyebrow. She looked away. A moment later, her phone vibrated.

Yichen: What?

He was still listening to Yuhao, but his phone was in his hand beneath the table.

Xiaoran: Nothing.

Yichen: You’ve been staring.

Xiaoran: Can’t I look at my boyfriend?

Yichen: You can.

Yichen: You’re making me nervous.

She smiled.

Xiaoran: Good.

This time, he smiled too. Across the table, Tang Meilin noticed the exchange and rolled her eyes.

“Can you two communicate normally for five minutes?”

Xiaoran put her phone away.

“We are communicating normally.”

“You’re texting each other while sitting across the table.”

“That’s normal.”

Chen Yuhao leaned forward.

“Actually, I think they’re celebrating their anniversary by pretending the rest of us don’t exist.”

Yichen calmly took a sip of water.

“You’re welcome to leave.”

Yuhao stared at him.

“On their anniversary? You can’t even pretend to be polite?”

“Why would I?”

Meilin laughed. Xiaoran kicked Yichen lightly beneath the table. He glanced at her, looking entirely innocent. She mouthed, Be nice. He mouthed back, I am. She shook her head. He smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

After school, they didn’t go anywhere immediately. Yichen walked her to the small convenience store near the school gate. Xiaoran stopped in front of the entrance.

“Why are we here?”

“Are you thirsty?”

“A little.”

He opened the door for her.

“Then choose something.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“Didn’t we agree not to spend money?”

“We did.”

“Then—”

“We’re not buying anything.”

He walked inside. She followed him, increasingly confused. Yichen went straight to the refrigerated section, took out two bottles of water, then walked towards the cashier. Xiaoran watched him.

“Yichen.”

He met her eyes.

“What?”

“Those cost money.”

“I know.”

She folded her arms. He placed the bottles on the counter.

“Two, please.”

She looked at him in disbelief. When they stepped outside, she immediately confronted him.

“You said we wouldn’t spend money.”

“We won’t.”

“You just bought water.”

“Three yuan.”

“That’s still money.”

He handed her one bottle.

“Then I’ll pay it back next year.”

She stared at him. He unscrewed his own bottle and took a drink.

“Besides, you said you were thirsty.”

Xiaoran looked at the water in her hand, then at him.

“You’re impossible.”

“Happy anniversary.”

She laughed, unable to remain annoyed. They started walking.

Their route was familiar. Past the school gate, down the street lined with small shops, across the pedestrian crossing, and towards the little neighbourhood park where they had spent time together before. It wasn’t a special place.

There was a playground, a few benches, a small pond, and a path that circled the trees.

But it was one of the first places where they had spent time together without needing an excuse.

They had come here after school during the early months of dating, sometimes with snacks, sometimes with homework, sometimes because neither wanted to go home yet. Yichen led her towards their usual bench. Xiaoran stopped.

“Wait.”

He turned.

“What?”

“Are we going to sit here?”

“Unless you have somewhere else in mind.”

She looked around. The park was quiet. A few children were playing near the swings, and an elderly man was walking his dog. Then she smiled.

“I like here.”

“I know.”

They sat down. For a while, neither said anything.

Xiaoran placed her schoolbag beside her and opened her water bottle. Yichen sat close enough that their shoulders touched. She looked at him.

“Did you really not prepare anything?”

He turned towards her.

“What do you mean?”

“Anything.”

He considered her expression. Then he reached into his schoolbag and took out a folded piece of paper. Her eyes widened.

“Yichen!”

He turned to her.

“What?”

“You said—”

“I didn’t buy anything.”

He handed it to her. She accepted it carefully.

The paper was folded into a neat rectangle. Her name was written on the outside in his familiar handwriting. She unfolded it.

Inside was a short letter in his slanted handwriting, with a few words crossed out and rewritten.

Xiaoran,

One year ago, you agreed to be my girlfriend.

I remember being nervous that day. I didn’t think you noticed, but you probably did.

This year has been good. Better than I expected, actually.

I like that you tell me about things I don’t understand. I like that you ask me questions even when you already know the answer. I like that you get excited over small things and that you sometimes talk so much you forget what you were saying.

I like walking you home. I like saving you a seat. I like knowing you’ll look for me when you enter a room.

I don’t know what next year will be like. We have exams, university applications, and a lot of things ahead of us. But I hope I get to spend it with you.

Thank you for this year.

I love you.

—Yichen

Xiaoran read it once, then again. Her lips pressed together.

She looked down at the paper, trying hard not to let her expression give her away. Yichen watched her.

“Too much?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Then?”

She looked up.

“You’re so unfair.”

He frowned slightly.

“How?”

“You can’t just write things like this.”

A small smile appeared on his face.

“Why not?”

“Because I don’t have anything.”

He held her gaze. Then he reached over and gently took the letter from her hands, folded it along its original creases, and placed it back in her palm.

“You don’t need to.”

“But—”

“Xiaoran. I wanted to write it. That’s all.” He brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

She looked at the letter again. “You were nervous. That night. Your knuckles were white on the umbrella,” she said.

“You noticed.”

“I notice things too, Zhou Yichen.”

Then she leaned over and rested her head against his shoulder.

Yichen shifted slightly, making it easier for her to settle there.

“Thank you,” she whispered.

He kissed her hair.

“You’re welcome.”

A few minutes passed before Xiaoran sat up again.

“Wait.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“What?”

“I have something.”

He looked at her with mild surprise.

“You said you didn’t have anything.”

“I don’t.”

“Then what is it?”

She took out her phone. He watched as she opened the photo gallery.

She scrolled for a while, then turned the screen towards him.

It was the first photograph she had taken after he asked her out: the plush bunny on her bag, dripping wet, photographed in the lift because she hadn’t known what else to do with her hands.

The next one was the two of them outside the bakery a week later. Meilin had taken it. Yichen was looking at her, and Xiaoran was smiling at the camera. Yichen studied it.

“I remember.”

“Of course you do.”

She swiped to the next picture. Another one, then another.

There were pictures from their first few months together. A blurry photo of their hands. A picture of him carrying her books. A photograph of them sitting together after school, with her head resting on his shoulder. Some were poorly framed. Some were blurry.

Some were so ordinary that she had almost forgotten taking them. But she had kept all of them.

“I made an album,” she said.

Yichen looked at her.

“When?”

“Over the past few days.”

She continued scrolling.

“I wanted to give you something, but then I remembered I’d spent everything on your birthday. So I thought maybe I could just put together the pictures I already had.”

She looked slightly embarrassed.

“It’s not very good.”

He didn’t answer immediately. He was looking at the screen. At their first picture.

At all the little moments she had collected without making a big deal of them. Then he looked at her.

“Can I have it?”

She blinked.

“You want it?”

“Of course.”

“It’s just pictures.”

“I know.”

She hesitated, then sent him the album. His phone vibrated. He opened it. She had called it One Year.

Beneath it were dozens of photographs, arranged in chronological order. The first picture was the wet bunny.

The last one was from his birthday, taken only a week ago.

He was holding the rabbit, the bracelet already on his wrist, looking at her with an expression she had caught without realising how much it gave away. Yichen stared at that picture for a while. Then he looked at her.

“You kept all of these?”

“Mhm.”

“Even the blurry ones?”

“The blurry ones, yes.”

“Why?”

“Because they’re memories.”

He smiled. She watched him scroll.

“Do you like it?”

He locked his phone and put it away. Then he turned towards her fully.

“I love it.”

Her smile appeared. He reached for her hand.

“Thank you.”

She leaned forward and hugged him. He wrapped both arms around her, holding her close. They stayed like that.

There was no music and no dinner reservation, only a park bench after an ordinary school day, and Xiaoran thought it was exactly right.

The sun was beginning to set when they finally stood up. Yichen picked up both schoolbags. Xiaoran reached for hers.

“I can carry it.”

“I know.”

“Then give it to me.”

He looked at her.

“Do you want it?”

She paused, then smiled.

“No.”

“Thought so.”

They walked towards the park entrance, their hands joined. A few steps later, Xiaoran slowed down.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Do you think our first year was good?”

He studied her.

“Yes.”

“Even when we argued?”

“Yes.”

“Even when I got upset over silly things?”

“Sometimes.”

She stopped walking.

“Sometimes?”

He turned towards her, his expression perfectly composed.

“Some things weren’t silly.”

She studied his face.

“You’re supposed to say all of them were understandable.”

“That would be dishonest.”

She gasped. He laughed and tugged gently at her hand, bringing her closer.

“But I liked this year. All of it. Even the difficult parts,” he said.

Her expression softened.

“Why?”

“Because it was with you.”

She was quiet. Then she pulled him down by the collar and kissed his cheek.

“You’re getting better at saying things.”

“Was I bad before?”

“A little.”

“That’s unfortunate.”

She laughed. They continued walking. After a while, Yichen glanced at her.

“Do you know what I think?”

“What?”

“Next year, we should save some money.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“For what?”

“Our second anniversary.”

She considered it, then shook her head.

“No.”

“No?”

“We’ll save money for other things.”

“Like what?”

“Food.”

He considered her.

“Food?”

“And dates.”

“Those are the same thing.”

“Not necessarily. We can save for a trip. Or go somewhere we’ve never been. Or buy something together. Maybe we’ll have more money next year.” She was getting animated now.

“Maybe.”

“And we should save for your birthday too.”

He looked at her.

“You’re already planning my next birthday?”

“Of course.”

“That’s a long way away.”

“It’s never too early.”

He laughed.

Then, after a moment, he said, “I don’t need anything expensive.”

She turned to him.

“I know.”

“Just so you remember.”

“I know, Yichen.”

He squeezed her hand.

“Then we’re fine.”

At the crossing, they had to stop for the red light.

Xiaoran stood beside him, rocking slightly on her heels. She looked down at their hands.

Then at the date on her phone. December 6. One year, exactly.

She felt the urge to say something, though she wasn’t quite sure how to put it into words.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“I’m glad you asked me out.”

He turned towards her. She looked ahead, a little embarrassed.

“I mean... I’m glad we started dating.”

His expression softened.

“So am I.”

“I didn’t know what it would be like, you know? Having a boyfriend.”

“Was it disappointing?”

She turned to him immediately.

“No!”

“Good.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re teasing me.”

“A little.”

She leaned against his arm.

“I just mean... I didn’t know that it would feel like this.”

“Like what?”

She thought about it.

“Like having someone I can tell everything to. Someone I want to see even when I’ve already seen him all day. Someone who makes boring days better. And someone who steals my food.”

“I don’t steal your food.”

“You do.”

“You offer it.”

“That’s different.”

He smiled. She held his gaze.

“And I didn’t know I’d like ordinary things this much.”

He was quiet. Then he lifted their joined hands and kissed her fingers.

“I think ordinary things are the best part.”

The traffic light turned green. But neither moved immediately. Xiaoran smiled.

“Happy first anniversary, Zhou Yichen.”

He looked at her with that quiet, familiar warmth.

“Happy first anniversary, Lin Xiaoran.”

Then he bent his head and kissed her, slow and warm, while the traffic went round them and the last of the sun lay across the pavement. Her stomach did something ridiculous. She held on to his sleeve so she wouldn’t float off the kerb. When he pulled away, Xiaoran’s cheeks were pink. She looked at him.

“One year.”

“One year.”

“Exactly.”

He smiled.

“Would you like another?”

“Another what?”

“Year.”

Her expression changed. Then she smiled so brightly that he couldn’t help laughing.

“Yes.”

“All right.”

He took her hand again.

“Then let’s go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, Xiaoran lay on her bed with Yichen’s letter beside her pillow.

She had read it so many times that she could almost remember every sentence. Her phone buzzed.

Yichen: Did you get home safely?

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: Good.

Xiaoran: I read your letter again.

Yichen: And?

Xiaoran: I like it.

Yichen: That’s good.

Xiaoran: I love you.

A short pause.

Yichen: I love you too.

She smiled at the screen, then another message appeared.

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: Hm?

Yichen: Next year, let’s not worry so much about buying each other things.

She looked at the message.

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: Because I think we already have enough.

She read it twice. Then she typed.

Xiaoran: What do we have?

His reply came a moment later.

Yichen: Each other.

Xiaoran pressed her phone against her chest. It was such a simple answer.

She liked it anyway. He had written her a letter because he wanted to, she had given him a folder of blurry photographs because she wanted to remember, and they had walked home along the same streets as always. Nothing had felt missing.

A week ago she had spent everything she had on his birthday. Today the whole anniversary had cost three yuan, and he had promised to pay it back.

She fell asleep with the letter under her pillow.

chapters.desc: The first cold morning of the year, a navy scarf, and a grandmother who is asked, at some length, how to embroider letters.
chapters.title: Winter Uniform
chapters.epigraph: “Tell your mother I like her scarf.”
chapters.content:
The first properly cold morning of the year arrived without warning. On Monday Lin Xiaoran had been complaining that the classroom was too warm. On Tuesday she was standing at the school gate with her hands pulled up inside her sleeves, wondering what she had done to deserve this.

Her coat was buttoned to the chin and the wind still found the gaps. She blew into her fists and stamped her feet and waited for Zhou Yichen, because she always waited for him at the gate, even though he had told her a dozen times to go inside.

He came round the corner with his bag over one shoulder and a navy scarf wound round his neck.

“You’re wearing a scarf.”

“Observant.”

“I’m serious.”

“So am I.”

She stepped right up to him and took the end of it in her fingers. It was soft and plain, deep navy, and near the end, in a slightly lighter blue, someone had stitched three small letters.

Z.Y.C.

“Is this yours?”

“No. I borrowed it.”

“Your initials are on it.”

“Then you have your answer.”

She turned it over to look at the stitching. Small, neat, perfectly even. “Who made it?”

“My mother.”

“Your mother made this? By hand?”

“Would you like me to arrange an interview?”

She ignored him, still running her thumb over the letters. “That’s so nice.”

“She made it last winter. She said I’d never remember which scarf was mine if I left it somewhere.”

“And was she right?”

“Twice a winter, on average.”

Xiaoran laughed, and then he looked at her hands, which had gone pink at the knuckles, and frowned.

“You’re freezing.”

“I’m fine.”

“Your hands disagree.” He was already unwinding the scarf.

“What are you doing?”

“Giving you a scarf.”

“You’ll be cold.”

“I’ve got a coat.”

“So have I.”

“Your coat isn’t doing a very good job.” He wrapped it round her neck twice and tucked the end inside her collar. It was still warm from him, and it smelled of his washing powder, and she couldn’t think of a single thing to say.

It was too long for her. One end came almost to her waist. She looked down at the stitching.

“People will know it’s yours.”

“That’s generally what initials are for.”

“Then they’ll know I’m wearing your scarf.”

“I don’t think anyone’s going to mistake you for me. You’re considerably shorter,” he said.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed and she shoved his arm, then hooked her own arm through his and held on to it with both hands, partly from cold and partly from habit, and they went in through the gate like that.

“Does your mother know you’re giving it away?”

“I’m not giving it away. It’s a loan.”

“What if I don’t give it back?”

“Are you planning to steal it?”

She considered it. “Maybe.”

“Then I’ll have to tell my mother.”

“You wouldn’t.” She had met his mother exactly twice, once at an airport and once in a car, and both times Mrs. Zhou had been so kind to her that she had gone home afterwards and lain on her bed with a pillow over her head for an hour.

“She’d probably be pleased. She made it so I wouldn’t be cold, and it turns out I know someone who needs it more,” he said.

At the classroom door she stopped him, unwound the scarf and held it out.

“You’re giving it back already?”

“You’ll need it. Your mother made it for you.”

He took it, but instead of putting it on he folded it over his arm. “Then here’s an arrangement. You can borrow it whenever you’re cold.”

“Really?”

“As long as you return it.”

“That’s a very strict borrowing policy.”

“I might make exceptions for reliable borrowers.”

“How do I become a reliable borrower?”

“Start by not stealing it. And don’t stand at the gate waiting for me tomorrow. Go inside.” He reached out and straightened her collar.

“Then how will you know I’m here?”

“I’ll look for you,” he said, so that she nearly missed what it meant.

She nearly missed it. She didn’t, quite. She went to her desk with her face warm, and he sat down next to her, and before the bell she leaned over and said, low, “Tell your mother I like her scarf.”

“I will.”

“Tell her she’s got good taste.”

“She’ll be pleased.”

“Tell her I’ll give it back.”

He gave her a long, slow, amused look. “I’ll leave that part out.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon the temperature dropped again. Yichen came out of the gym after practice and found her at the gate anyway, in exactly the place he’d told her not to stand, with both hands up her sleeves and her nose pink.

“I said go inside.”

“I was inside. Then I came out.”

He didn’t argue. He just unwound the scarf and put it round her neck again, and tucked the end in, and she looked up at him from inside it.

“Your mother will think you can’t look after yourself.”

“Then I’ll tell her I’ve been looking after someone else,” he said, and she pulled the scarf up over her nose so he couldn’t see her face.

The next morning, in morning reading, she forgot to take it off. Rong Hao came past her desk with the homework register, read the stitching at the end of it, and said “Z, Y, C,” out loud, like a man reading a number plate. Half the row turned round.

“You’re wearing his name,” Tang Meilin said, without looking up from her English.

“I’m wearing a scarf.”

“With his name on it.”

Beside her, Yichen turned a page of his English reader and said nothing, and the back of his neck was red.

She took the scarf off and folded it in her lap under the desk, and kept her hand on it through two lessons.

At lunch she put it back on to walk to the canteen, because the corridor was freezing, and Chen Yuhao saw it from the other end of the queue and came over with his tray.

“Is that your mother’s scarf?”

“It’s my scarf. My mother made it,” said Yichen.

“It’s on her.”

“It’s a loan.”

Yuhao looked at Xiaoran, wrapped up to the nose in navy wool with Z.Y.C. hanging down her front like a label in a shop. “My mother knitted me a hat once. Red. With a bobble. I lost it in two days and she still brings it up at Spring Festival.”

“That’s because you lost it,” said Meilin.

“I’m just saying. If that scarf goes missing, Auntie Zhou is going to know exactly where to look.”

“It won’t go missing. I’m a reliable borrower,” Xiaoran said, offended, and pulled it up higher.

“You’ve had it a day and a half.”

“And I’ve been reliable the whole time.”

Yuhao turned to Yichen. “Aren’t you cold?”

“No.”

“Your ears are red.”

“It’s warm in here.”

“It’s three degrees in here. The windows are steamed up. You used to be a sensible person. You used to wear a coat that zipped.” Yuhao shook his head sadly.

“He’s still sensible,” said Xiaoran, and put her cold hands inside Yichen’s blazer pockets, both of them, with his hands still in there, and leaned against him in the queue to keep warm, and Yuhao looked at the ceiling of the canteen as if asking it for strength.

“I’m going to sit with the basketball team. They don’t do this,” he announced.

“Give them a year,” said Meilin.

“Nobody does this,” said Yuhao, and went.

On the way home that afternoon, with the scarf back round her neck, she had an idea.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she rang her grandmother.

“Grandma. How do you embroider letters?”

There was a pause on the line, the sound of a woman putting down her knitting. “Which letters?”

“Just letters. Initials.”

“Whose initials?”

“Mine.”

“On what?”

Xiaoran looked at the navy scarf, which she hadn’t returned, which was folded on her pillow. “On something.”

“Is this the boy who rang every night at nine in the summer?”

“Grandma.”

“The one who talked to me for forty minutes about the persimmon tree?”

“How do you embroider letters, Grandma?”

It took forty minutes. Her grandmother explained backstitch, then satin stitch, then told her to forget satin stitch because she would only make a mess of it, then asked whether the boy was still eating breakfast, then explained backstitch again. Xiaoran found a needle in her mother’s sewing tin and a reel of white thread, and at one in the morning, on the other end of the scarf, inside the fold where nobody would see, she had stitched three crooked letters.

L.X.R.

The R had a tail that went somewhere it shouldn’t. She had pricked her finger twice. She looked at it under her desk lamp and thought it was the worst embroidery in the history of China and also the best thing she had ever made.

She gave the scarf back at the gate the next morning, folded so the inside end was hidden.

He found it at the self-study break that evening, when he unwound it to hang on the back of his chair. She watched him find it out of the corner of her eye without turning her head. He turned the end over in his fingers and looked at it. Then he folded it back so the letters were on the inside again, the way she had left them, and put it back on, and didn’t take it off for the rest of the evening, although the radiators in Class 3 were the only ones in the school that worked.

A note slid across the desk at quarter to nine.

Your R is drunk.

She wrote underneath: Give it back then.

No.

✦ ✦ ✦

For the rest of the winter the navy scarf went back and forth between them. Some days he wore it. Some days she did. On the cold mornings he walked through the gate already unwinding it, because he knew where she’d be standing.

In February, when she finally went to his house properly for the first time and sat at his family’s table in a state of controlled terror, the scarf was hanging by his front door. When she left, Mrs. Zhou took it down to put round Xiaoran’s neck, and turned the end over, and saw the crooked white letters inside the fold.

She didn’t say anything. She only smiled, and tucked the end in.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran has never cooked. Zhou Yichen’s parents are out on Saturday. She’s going to cook anyway.
chapters.title: This Tastes Suspiciously Edible
chapters.epigraph: “The secret ingredient is stubbornness.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran decided to cook for Zhou Yichen because of one dangerous thought: How hard could it be? Historically, that thought had ruined many lives.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’ve never cooked before.”

Tang Meilin said it in the tone of someone watching a preventable tragedy. They were in the supermarket, Xiaoran pushing the cart with terrifying confidence.

“I can learn.”

“You almost burned instant noodles last year.”

“That was a microwave issue.”

“You put METAL inside.”

“Technicality.”

Xiaoran kept tossing things into the cart: eggs, tomatoes, beef, green onions. Whatever she’d seen in cooking videos.

“…Do you even know what you’re making?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

Silence.

“Love.”

“Okay we’re doomed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It had started innocently. Yesterday at lunch, Yichen had mentioned—

“My parents won’t be home Saturday.”

Xiaoran’s drama-poisoned brain immediately translated that into: perfect romantic cooking opportunity. Realistically, she should have ordered takeout and lied. But Lin Xiaoran had too much pride. If she was going to cook for her boyfriend, she was going to actually cook, even if civilisation collapsed. So Friday night was preparation night: three hours of cooking tutorials, two breakdowns, and one nearly catastrophic knife incident.

“Your fingers are more important than romance,” Meilin warned over video call.

“I know.”

“Why are you holding the knife like that.”

“…Like a warrior?”

“Like a threat to society.”

Xiaoran kept chopping, badly. Cooking looked so much easier in videos. Why did onions require suffering? Why was the oil attacking her? Why did garlic burn in three seconds?!

“This is impossible.”

“It’s fried rice, not nuclear engineering.”

“You don’t understand pressure.”

Meilin understood perfectly. The pressure was Lin Xiaoran desperately wanting Zhou Yichen to like something she’d made herself. Which made the whole thing kind of cute. Dangerous. But cute.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday came too fast, and now Xiaoran was standing in Yichen’s kitchen in an apron, questioning every decision she had ever made. Yichen sat at the counter, watching. Too.

“Why are you staring at me.”

“You invited me here.”

“To EAT. Not observe.”

“Hm.”

That calm little hm irritated her, mostly because he looked far too good sitting there in a grey hoodie, chin propped on one hand, watching her cook. Very distracting.

“You’re nervous,” he said after a while.

“I’m NOT nervous.”

“You added salt twice.”

Silence. Xiaoran looked down at the bowl. Oh no. OH NO. Yichen laughed under his breath while Xiaoran panicked.

“This is a disaster.”

“It’s fixable.”

“How.”

“We start over.”

No annoyance, no disappointment. Just calm. And somehow that made Xiaoran feel less stressed right away. Then Yichen got up and came over, close enough that Xiaoran forgot how to breathe normally. Stupid handsome boyfriend.

“You missed some eggshell too,” he murmured.

“…Where.”

Instead of answering, Yichen reached past her shoulder and carefully picked the tiny piece of shell out of the bowl. Warmth flooded Xiaoran’s face. Domestic Zhou Yichen was a problem. Then he glanced down at her.

“…Cute apron.”

“Don’t mock me.”

“I’m serious.”

“You’re smiling.”

“Because it’s pink.”

“It was the only one Meilin had.”

Unfortunately, the pink apron had tiny strawberries on it, and Zhou Yichen was visibly fighting a laugh every five minutes. Unbearable man.

✦ ✦ ✦

The cooking actually improved after that, mostly because Yichen stopped sitting there and helped. Not taking over. Just helping—washing vegetables beside her, passing things, stopping her from committing seasoning crimes. At one point, Xiaoran frowned at the pan.

“Does this look cooked?”

Yichen leaned in to check. Way too close. Xiaoran could smell his shampoo again. Disaster.

“Hm, almost,” he murmured thoughtfully.

Then he reached around her to turn the heat down—one arm beside her, his chest almost touching her shoulder—and Lin Xiaoran forgot about cooking entirely.

“…You’re distracting.”

“I’m fixing your fire hazard.”

“That’s not what I mean.”

Yichen smiled a little, then looked down at her in that quiet, soft way. The one that ruined her every time.

“What are you saying, then?” he asked.

Nothing. Her brain had stopped working again. Meanwhile, the rice was burning.

“OH MY GOD.”

Romance, interrupted. Tragic.

✦ ✦ ✦

An hour later, the food was done. And it looked… surprisingly normal. Actual edible-looking food. Xiaoran stared at the table.

“…Why does this look successful.”

Yichen sat across from her calmly.

“You worked hard.”

“That doesn’t guarantee quality.”

Then came the most terrifying moment of Xiaoran’s life: Yichen picking up the spoon. She watched him like a criminal awaiting sentencing.

“Be honest. If it’s bad, just say it,” she warned.

“Hm.”

“No boyfriend lies.”

“Hm.”

“And don’t force yourself.”

“I understand.”

Then he took a bite. Silence. One second. Two seconds. Three—

“…Wait.”

Xiaoran stopped breathing.

“It’s bad?”

“No.”

He looked genuinely surprised. He looked at the food, then at her.

“…This is actually really good.”

“…What.”

“The beef’s seasoned properly. The rice texture’s good too.”

Then Lin Xiaoran screamed.

“OH MY GOD.”

Yichen started laughing as Xiaoran grabbed his sleeve.

“YOU’RE NOT LYING?”

“I’m not.”

Xiaoran dropped into her chair and covered her face.

“I’m talented.”

“You almost poisoned the kitchen earlier.”

“BUT NOT THE FOOD.”

The pride all over her face was adorable, and Yichen couldn’t stop smiling as she celebrated over fried rice like she’d won a national award.

“You know,” he said, taking another bite, “I thought this would taste terrible.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

“I still came prepared to eat everything.”

“That’s NOT ROMANTIC.”

“It is from my perspective.”

Xiaoran glared at him. Yichen laughed again. Casually, he reached over and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear. Xiaoran forgot the entire conversation. Yichen looked at her flushed face and smiled.

“…You should cook for me again sometime.”

Somehow, that meant more to her than the food turning out well.

chapters.desc: A sudden downpour, a useless umbrella, and one sentence Lin Xiaoran really didn’t mean to say out loud.
chapters.title: Holding Hands Is Warm, But Hugging in the Rain Is Dangerous
chapters.epigraph: “Some storms are worth getting caught in.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran hated rain. Not emotionally. Physically. Rain ruined hair, shoes, makeup, moods, dignity, and occasionally public transport. Zhou Yichen, strangely, loved it. Not in a poetic way. He just liked the quiet, the cooler air, the way the basketball court smelled afterward. Today, though, the rain was dangerous for a completely different reason.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Run faster!”

“I AM RUNNING.”

“You’re WALKING. Your legs are just long.”

They were sprinting through a sudden evening downpour after leaving the arcade downtown. Ten minutes ago, the weather had been perfect. Now? Total betrayal from the sky. Xiaoran held her bag over her head while Yichen tried to angle their one umbrella against a wind that seemed to have a personal grudge.

“This umbrella is decorative,” Xiaoran complained loudly.

“It’s trying its best.”

“WE’RE STILL DYING.”

Yichen laughed and pulled her closer by the wrist so she wouldn’t slip on the wet sidewalk. Even drenched, that small thing made her heart go soft. Very annoying. Finally they ducked under the awning of a closed bookstore, both breathing hard. Rain came down in silver sheets around them, headlights smeared across the wet street. And suddenly the whole thing felt unfairly romantic. Xiaoran noticed. Unfortunately. Rain still clung to Yichen’s hair. His sleeves were pushed halfway up, his shoulders soaked from shielding her. He looked like a scene from one of her dramas.

Zhou Yichen looked down at her.

“…Why are you staring.”

“Nothing.”

“You’ve been quiet for thirty seconds.”

“That’s because rain lowers my IQ.”

“Hm.”

His thumb brushed across her knuckles absentmindedly. A small, automatic thing. But suddenly Xiaoran was hyperaware of everything: the sound of the rain, how close he was, how warm his hand was. Maybe because the weather felt softer, her chest did too.

“Holding hands is warm,” she mumbled.

Yichen glanced at her.

“What?”

Oops. Accidental thought leak. Xiaoran looked away.

“Nothing.”

But Zhou Yichen always got curious at the worst possible times.

“What did you say?”

Silence. Then, defiantly—

“I said holding hands is warm.”

“And?”

She hesitated. Why did this suddenly feel embarrassing? Then—

“…But hugging feels warmer.”

Silence. When Xiaoran finally looked up, Yichen was watching her. He wasn’t teasing or laughing, just looking at her with that soft expression that always made her weak. Then, slowly, he let go of her hand. Xiaoran blinked.

“Hm?”

Instead of answering, Yichen stepped closer and, without a word, pulled her into his arms. Warmth wrapped around her. Not sudden. Just steady. His hoodie smelled faintly like rain and laundry detergent, and one hand settled at the back of her head. Xiaoran understood something then. Holding hands was warm. But this was dangerous. Hugging Zhou Yichen in the cold rain made the whole world quietly disappear—the noisy street, the weather, the passing cars—until there was only the steady beat of his heart under her cheek.

Above her head, Yichen murmured—

“Better?”

His voice was lower like this. Closer. Xiaoran tightened her arms around him.

“…A little.”

“A little?”

“Okay maybe a lot.”

He laughed under his breath, and she felt it against her forehead. Outside their little shelter, the rain kept pouring. Neither of them moved. After a while, quietly—

“You’re cold,” he murmured.

“That’s because SOMEONE gave me fake umbrella protection.”

“Hm.”

“That hm means guilt.”

Yichen smiled and rubbed her arm through her damp cardigan, trying to warm her up. That small thing got to her more than any grand gesture could. Then thunder cracked overhead. Xiaoran flinched, and Yichen’s arms tightened around her before he even thought about it. The realisation hit her embarrassingly hard. Being loved by Zhou Yichen was genuinely unfair sometimes. Then—

“Yichen, I think rain might actually be romantic.”

“Only now?”

“I’m growing as a person.”

He laughed softly again. Yichen looked down at her. Close. Way too close. The rain blurred behind him and the yellow streetlights caught in his eyes, and Xiaoran’s heartbeat went ridiculous again. This was exactly like the drama scenes she screamed over. Except better, because it was real.

“You say things like that way too easily,” Yichen murmured.

“I do not.”

“Hugging is warmer?”

Silence. Okay. Maybe she did. Xiaoran buried her face deeper in his chest.

“I take it back.”

“Too late.”

“Delete the memory.”

“Impossible.”

After a second, he kissed the top of her damp hair. Soft and quick. And that tiny kiss destroyed whatever dignity she had left.

“This relationship,” she whispered weakly, “is making me too happy.”

chapters.desc: A teacher’s wedding, one cream-coloured dress, and the evening Zhou Yichen forgot how to talk.
chapters.title: Xiaoran Looks Beautiful Today
chapters.epigraph: “He had seen her every day. He had never seen her like this.”
chapters.content:
At exactly 5:42 p.m., Zhou Yichen realised Lin Xiaoran looked too beautiful today. Not everyday cute. Dangerous. The kind that made him briefly forget how conversations worked. Which irritated him a little, because he prided himself on composure. That composure disappeared the second Xiaoran stepped out of Tang Meilin’s room.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You can breathe now.”

Yuhao’s voice snapped him back to reality. He looked deeply entertained, because Zhou Yichen had frozen. For three full seconds. They were waiting downstairs at Meilin’s apartment before heading to Teacher Su’s wedding banquet. Teacher Su taught literature and had somehow become everyone’s emotional support teacher, so a few of her closest students had been invited—including some unfairly attractive teenagers. Specifically, Lin Xiaoran. She came down the stairs slowly, fiddling with one small earring, and Yichen’s brain stopped working again.

Xiaoran almost never dressed up. Usually it was oversized sweaters, school uniform, hoodies—his, often. Tonight she wore a soft cream dress that fell just below her knees. Simple. Elegant. Not trying to look older. Just pretty. Her hair was curled at the ends, framing her face. Tiny pearl earrings. Light makeup. She still looked completely like herself, just prettier, in a way that felt unfair to society. Xiaoran looked nervous the second she noticed everyone staring.

“…Why are you all acting weird.”

Meilin crossed her arms proudly.

“Because I worked hard.”

“Meilin spent forty minutes fixing your hair,” Yuhao said.

“I almost lost my life,” Meilin corrected.

Then she looked at Yichen, and paused. Her boyfriend was staring. Openly. Completely focused on her.

“…Why are YOU acting weird?”

Yichen blinked. Twice. Still staring. Yuhao nearly collapsed laughing beside him.

“Oh my god.”

Then, Yichen said—

“You look beautiful.”

Zhou Yichen almost never gave compliments that directly. His were usually smaller, softer, private. This one came out on instinct, before he could think, and it hit Xiaoran harder than any dramatic flirting could. Her whole face went red.

“…Oh.”

Brilliant response. Yichen seemed a little calmer now that he’d said it. His eyes kept moving over her face anyway, still taking her in, and Xiaoran noticed, which only made it worse.

“Stop looking at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like… Like THIS.” She gestured helplessly.

Yuhao cut in—

“He looks like he just discovered women.”

“Shut up.”

Meilin sighed.

“Can we leave before these two combust.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The banquet was warm and lively: golden lights, soft music, round tables full of chatting relatives and teachers. The students sat together off to one side, trying to behave. Keyword: trying. Teacher Su looked so happy that it made everyone emotional, especially when she nearly cried at the sight of her former students all dressed up.

“You all grew up so fast,” she sniffed.

Xiaoran hugged her carefully, then ruined the moment immediately—

“Teacher, you look like a movie star today.”

Teacher Su laughed through tears.

“Still talking nonsense.”

Yichen stood nearby holding the gift bag. And once again, he looked at Xiaoran and lost his train of thought. It kept happening all evening—the way she smiled politely at older relatives, the way she laughed, the way the warm light caught her earrings.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He blinked. Teacher Su smiled knowingly.

“You’ve been staring at Xiaoran all evening.”

Xiaoran nearly dropped her tea. The other students choked trying not to laugh. Even Meilin looked delighted. Outwardly, Yichen stayed calm. Inwardly, not at all. The tips of his ears gave him away. Teacher Su continued smiling warmly.

“You two are very cute together.”

Xiaoran buried her face in her hands.

“This wedding is attacking me personally.”

Yichen looked away, the corner of his mouth lifting, which only made everything worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that night, as the guests began to leave, a light rain started outside the hotel entrance—soft enough not to matter. The others waited for their rides while Xiaoran and Yichen stood a little apart under the decorative lights by the garden path. A quiet moment. Warm night air. Everything felt softer. Xiaoran looked down at her shoes. Yichen glanced at her, then didn’t look away.

“You look beautiful tonight.”

Xiaoran looked away fast. Why did simple compliments from him feel so dangerous? Yichen stepped closer, close enough that his suit jacket brushed her sleeve. He looked unfair tonight too. Black formalwear should be banned for teenage boys. Especially Zhou Yichen.

“I think everyone noticed,” Xiaoran mumbled.

“What?”

“That you kept looking at me.”

“It’s hard not to.”

Silence. Was he trying to kill her tonight? Yichen looked thoughtful, like he wanted to say something else. Then, quietly—

“You know what scared me earlier? When you came downstairs.”

“…Why?”

Yichen looked at her calmly.

“Because for one second,” he admitted, “I genuinely forgot how to talk.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

chapters.desc: One secondhand poetry book. One very dramatic girlfriend. One week nobody at school will ever forget.
chapters.title: Xiaoran Became a Poetry Menace
chapters.epigraph: “Even ordinary afternoons become literature.”
chapters.content:
It started because Lin Xiaoran bought one old poetry book at a secondhand bookstore. One book. That was all it took to destroy the peace.

✦ ✦ ✦

“It smells intellectual.”

Tang Meilin stared at the dusty hardcover in horror. The four of them were at a café on Saturday while Xiaoran proudly showed off her purchase: an old, faded hardcover of translated classical poetry and romantic prose. She already looked like a changed woman.

“It’s vintage,” she corrected seriously.

“It smells like someone’s grandfather.”

“That’s called history.”

Yichen glanced at it, stirring his iced coffee.

“Do you even like poetry?”

“I’m evolving.”

Yuhao looked suspicious.

“Last month you said philosophy was fake.”

“That was before literature entered my soul.”

Meilin sighed.

“We’re doomed.”

Unfortunately, she was right.

✦ ✦ ✦
