By Monday morning, Lin Xiaoran was unbearable. Not normal unbearable. Poetic unbearable, which was worse. She leaned against her desk in the morning sun.

“Some people,” she sighed, “are like moonlight reflected across water.”

Silence. Meilin looked up from her homework.

“…What.”

Xiaoran turned to Yichen.

“Beautiful but impossible to hold.”

Yuhao stared. Zhou Yichen stopped writing and slowly looked at her. Where was this coming from? Then, calmly—

“Good morning to you too.”

Xiaoran nodded wisely.

“The moon also rises gently.”

“I hate this already,” Meilin muttered.

It got worse. Much worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunch, Yuhao stole a dumpling off Xiaoran’s plate. Instead of yelling like a normal person, she narrowed her eyes and whispered:

“Greed is a fire that consumes friendship.”

Yuhao froze.

“…What.”

“Ancient wisdom.”

“That was a threat.”

“That dumpling had meaning.”

Yichen nearly smiled into his drink. Watching Xiaoran weaponize poetry all day was getting more entertaining by the hour, especially because she so clearly felt intelligent now. Then she turned to him. Danger.

“What,” Yichen said.

Xiaoran pointed her chopsticks at him.

“You know,” she murmured, “there’s a phrase here that reminds me of you.”

Silence. Yichen leaned back.

“Hm?”

“‘The pine tree does not bend easily before winter winds.’”

Meilin gagged. Yuhao looked horrified. Xiaoran went on proudly—

“It means someone calm and steadfast.”

“I know what pine trees symbolize,” Yichen answered calmly.

“Oh.”

“But thank you.”

He said it simply, gently, and it got to Xiaoran embarrassingly hard. Zhou Yichen always took her nonsense seriously. Even poetic nonsense.

“You’re not making fun of me?”

“Should I?”

“No.”

“Then no.”

Meilin watched the interaction with dead eyes.

“I’m dropping out of school.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The real problem started on Wednesday, because Xiaoran had memorised too many lines. Way too many. Now she ambushed people with them all day. At PE class—

“The wind today feels lonely.”

During math—

“Numbers are humanity’s attempt to organise chaos.”

While eating crackers—

“Crisp sounds remind us life is fragile.”

Yuhao finally snapped.

“WHO GAVE HER THIS BOOK.”

In afternoon study hall, Yichen sat beside Xiaoran while she copied poetry into a notebook—concentrating hard, a tiny frown on her face, completely serious. Dangerously cute. Then, without looking up—

“Yichen, if I died young, would you compare me to flowers?”

Silence. Yichen slowly turned towards her.

“…What kind of sentence is that.”

“It’s literary.”

“It’s creepy.”

Xiaoran finally looked up.

“In poetry, beautiful people always die tragically.”

“You’re not dying.”

Xiaoran smiled—small and soft, like that answer pleased her far too much. Yichen noticed, and that tiny expression got to him too.

“What would you compare me to then?” she asked.

Yichen thought about it for a second, while nearby Meilin and Yuhao braced for emotional damage.

“You remind me of sunlight.”

No teasing, no hesitation. Just honest. Xiaoran blinked rapidly.

“…That was way too romantic.”

“You asked.”

“But you answered TOO well.”

Yuhao grabbed Meilin’s arm.

“I can’t survive this.”

Yichen went back to his notes like he hadn’t just destroyed everyone. He said—

“Sunlight’s noisy too.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

“And she’s back.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By Friday, the poetry phase should have been over. Instead, it evolved. Xiaoran started leaving tiny folded notes in Yichen’s notebooks. Not love letters, exactly. Just random lines—some romantic, some threatening, some completely incomprehensible. For example:

“The stars tonight resemble your emotional unavailability.”

“Even mountains erode eventually, unlike your stubbornness.”

And:

“If abandoned, I will haunt you artistically.”

In chemistry, Yichen opened his notebook and found another one. He unfolded it calmly.

“When I look at you, even ordinary afternoons become literature.”

Slowly, the corner of his mouth lifted. Across the room, Xiaoran saw it and hid behind her textbook. Writing the lines had been fine. Watching him read them was embarrassing. Beside her, Meilin looked spiritually exhausted.

“You’re both becoming worse.”

“No we’re becoming cultured.”

“You’re becoming insane.”

Fair criticism. Then a folded note landed on Xiaoran’s desk. She opened it. Inside, in Zhou Yichen’s neat, slightly slanted handwriting:

“You should keep reading poetry.”

And below that, one more line:

“Because you sound cute when you talk like this.”

Xiaoran put her forehead down on the desk with a thunk. Across the room, Zhou Yichen smiled a little and went back to work, completely unaffected. On the outside. Terrible man.

chapters.desc: Mock exams are coming, and Xiaoran makes a rule for library study that turns out to be mostly a rule against herself.
chapters.title: Mock Exam Season
chapters.epigraph: “You’re not going to tell me I should study harder?”
chapters.content:
The rule was Lin Xiaoran’s idea, which, looking back, was why it was such a bad one.

It was three weeks before the mocks, and the whole of the final year had turned into a place where people whispered, carried spare pens, and flinched at the word revision. Xiaoran had spread her notes across the long table in the library, arranged her highlighters by colour, written a list of topics she needed to review, and then spent fifteen minutes looking at Zhou Yichen.

Not on purpose. He was just there, beside her, going through a practice paper with one hand flat on the page and the other writing in the margin, wearing the face of a person to whom mathematics had never done anything wrong. Every time she looked up from her notes, there he was. It was a design flaw in the seating.

“You’ve been staring,” he said, without lifting his head.

“I haven’t.”

He put his pen down and looked at her. “All right.”

He said it in a way that meant he was kindly allowing her to lie, which was worse.

“You’re distracting,” she said.

“How?”

She couldn’t say because I like looking at you and I keep forgetting what I’m meant to be doing, so she said, “You keep moving.”

He looked at his own hand. “I was writing.”

“Exactly.”

The corner of his mouth went up. She regretted everything.

“Fine, new rule. We’re not allowed to look at each other,” she said, sitting up straight.

“At all?”

“For nine minutes.”

“Why nine?”

“Ten sounds like a punishment. Nine sounds like a challenge. Promise.” She held out her hand across the corner of the table.

He shook it. “Promise.”

✦ ✦ ✦

For the first thirty seconds it went beautifully. She read the first question, wrote down the formula, started working through it. She was a focused, serious person preparing for an important exam.

Then she remembered he was sitting next to her.

She could see the edge of his sleeve. She could hear his pen. She knew exactly where he was without looking, which was the whole problem. At the end of the second minute he shifted in his chair and her eyes went to him on their own, and she wrenched them back to the page so fast her neck clicked.

Beside her, slightly, he smiled. She could feel him doing it.

“Stop it,” she whispered.

“I’m not looking at you.”

“You’re smiling at me.”

“Smiling isn’t looking. You didn’t make a rule about smiling.”

At four minutes her eraser rolled off the edge of the table. He caught it without turning his head and put it down by her notebook.

“Thank you,” she muttered.

“You’re welcome.”

“You’re not supposed to talk to me.”

“You said look. You didn’t say talk.”

At six minutes she made a mistake in a calculation. She rubbed it out and made the same mistake again. She rubbed that out.

“You’ve dropped a two,” said Yichen, to his own paper.

She went rigid. “We’re not supposed to look at each other.”

“I didn’t. I saw it with my peripheral vision.”

“You’re not supposed to help me, either.”

“That’s a different rule.”

“You’re inventing loopholes.”

“I’m pointing out an error. Would you rather I looked?”

“No!”

His shoulders shook once. The librarian looked over. At seven minutes she caught herself watching his reflection in the dark window, and looked away so fast she banged her knee on the table leg. He didn’t say anything about it, which was kind, and also unbearable.

At eight minutes she started counting down under her breath. Forty seconds: she turned a page she hadn’t read. Twenty: he leaned across to reach for his water bottle and his arm brushed hers, and she stared at her notebook so hard her eyes began to water. Ten. Nine. Eight.

“Done,” he said.

She turned to him so fast her chair scraped.

He was already looking at her. He had been waiting. He didn’t say anything; he just smiled, the slow one that started at the corner of his mouth and took its time getting to his eyes, and she felt her whole face go hot.

“Why are you looking at me like that?”

“You said I wasn’t allowed to. Now I’m allowed.”

“Was it hard?”

“Very,” he said. “How much did you get done?”

She looked down. One finished question. Half a calculation. A small drawing of a cat in the corner of the page, wearing what looked like a crown.

He studied it. “Productive.”

“Don’t.”

“I only said one word.”

“It was a mean word. New rule. You’re not allowed to tease me until after the mocks.” She folded her arms.

“That’s three weeks.”

“Then you’d better be careful.”

He slid a scrap of paper across to her. On it, in his small neat writing, was the calculation she’d been fighting, with the two circled in red.

Here. Try again.

She tried again. She got it right. She turned the page so he could see and he nodded, and she sat a little taller in her chair.

“Next rule. You’re not allowed to look at me until you’ve finished the next five questions,” he said.

“That’s not fair. You’re making the rules now.”

“You started it.”

“I make the rules. You follow them. That’s the system.”

“Five questions,” he said, and went back to his paper, and after a long glare at the side of his head, which he ignored, she picked up her pen.

✦ ✦ ✦

When the librarian started switching off the lights at the far end, she had done four questions, fixed two mistakes and written a full page of notes. She packed up with a pleased little hum.

“One more question,” he said.

“Tomorrow.”

“You said you’d finish the chapter today.”

“I’ve changed my mind.”

He closed his book. “All right.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re not going to make me stay?”

“No.”

“You’re not going to tell me I should study harder?”

“No.”

“You’re not going to say the mocks are important?”

He stood up and put his bag on his shoulder. “They are important. But you’ve been working for two hours. We can do the rest tomorrow.” She groaned.

She looked at him for a second, at how easily he’d said it, without making her feel guilty about the question she hadn’t done, and something in her chest went warm and stupid. She got up, came round the table and put her arms round his waist from behind while he was zipping his bag.

“What’s this?”

“A hug.”

“In the library?”

“The lights are off at that end. It doesn’t count.”

“The librarian’s watching.”

“She’s seen worse. Yuhao fell asleep on the reference books last week and drooled on the atlas,” Xiaoran said, into his blazer.

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked out to the gate with her hand in his.

“Actually,” she said, “I think I could have lasted longer.”

“Could you?”

“Easily. Twenty minutes.”

“Let’s test it tomorrow.”

“No.”

“I thought you were confident.”

“I was. Then I reconsidered. Nine minutes is a very reasonable limit. Scientists agree,” she said.

“Which scientists?”

“Me.”

“Then nine minutes,” he said, and swung their joined hands once, which he almost never did, and which she counted as a win.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the morning of the first mock, the whole year stood in the corridor outside the exam rooms clutching transparent pencil cases, looking like people waiting for a ferry in bad weather.

Xiaoran was gripping hers with both hands. “I’ve forgotten everything.”

“You haven’t.”

“I have. The quadratic formula has left my body. I can feel the space where it was.”

“Say it.”

She said it, all of it, in one breath, with her eyes shut.

“It’s still there,” Yichen said.

“Only because you asked. In the room it’ll be gone.”

He took her pencil case out of her hands, opened it, and checked it the way he checked his own kit bag before a game: two pencils, sharpened; eraser; ruler; black pen; spare black pen; her student card. He took one of the pencils out, looked at the point, frowned, and swapped it for one of his own.

“That one was blunt.”

“It was lucky.”

“It was blunt. This one’s lucky now. Don’t look at the whole paper first. Start with the bits you know. If you get stuck, skip it and come back.” He gave the case back.

“What if I get stuck on everything?”

“Then you draw a cat,” he said, “and come back.”

She laughed despite herself, and then the invigilator opened the door and started calling names, and her laugh went away. He was in a different room, by surname. She held on to his sleeve until the last possible second, until Meilin physically detached her and steered her through the door by the shoulders.

At the lunch break between papers her phone, which she had been forbidden to take into the room and had kept in her bag in the corridor, had one message on it.

Yichen: Did the quadratic formula come back?

Xiaoran: It came back!!! Question 14!!! I used your pencil!!!

Yichen: Told you it was lucky.

Xiaoran: I drew a cat on the rough paper. Only a small one. In the margin. For luck.

Yichen: Did you go back to the question afterwards?

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: Then the system works.

She found him at the end of the corridor ten minutes later, eating a sandwich standing up, and walked straight into him and put her arms round his middle and her face against his chest, and he finished the sandwich over her hair.

“Two more papers,” he said.

“Don’t say numbers. I’ve had enough numbers.”

“After that, nothing till the real thing.”

“Don’t say the real thing either,” she said into his blazer, and felt him laugh.

The results came out three weeks later. Mathematics up six points. History the highest in the year. On the front of her maths paper, beside the mark, the teacher had written in red pen: Better. Stop drawing cats.

She showed it to him at the gate. He read it, looked at her, and said she had probably drawn the cat in the ninth minute.

“The eighth. In the ninth I was counting,” she said.

chapters.desc: His first game back after the injury. Scouts in the stands. Lin Xiaoran, holding nothing.
chapters.title: The Game the Scouts Came to See
chapters.epigraph: “Some people worry with their whole body.”
chapters.content:
The invitational was on a Saturday, and Lin Xiaoran hadn’t slept properly since Wednesday. It wasn’t the scouts. Everyone at school had been talking about the scouts for two weeks—how many were coming, which universities, whether one of them was from Beijing. Yuhao had a theory that one of them was secretly a former national team player. Nobody knew where he’d heard it. Xiaoran didn’t care about any of that.

She cared about his ankle.

“It’s fine,” Yichen said on Friday, for what had to be the fortieth time.

“Show me.”

“We’re in a convenience store.”

“Show me anyway.”

He sighed, put down the onigiri, and rolled his ankle slowly in a full circle, right there between the drinks fridge and the instant noodles. The cashier watched them over the counter with open interest.

“See?”

“It made a noise.”

“That was my shoe.”

“Shoes don’t make noises.”

“These are basketball shoes. They squeak. Coach Wang cleared me. The physio cleared me. I’ve practised for ten days.” He picked the onigiri back up.

Xiaoran tugged her sleeves down over her hands and said nothing.

Yichen studied her. Then he bought her a strawberry milk she hadn’t asked for, stuck the straw in for her, and said more quietly, “I won’t do anything stupid.”

“You said that last time.”

“Last time someone pushed me.”

“What if someone pushes you again?”

“Then I’ll fall better.”

That wasn’t the reassurance he thought it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

The gym on Saturday was louder than the semifinal had been. Students from four schools packed the bleachers, and someone had hung a hand-painted banner for their team that spelled “invitational” with two Ls. Near the scorer’s table, three adults in plain jackets sat with clipboards, not cheering for anyone. Everyone kept looking at them. Xiaoran sat between Meilin and Yuhao, gripping nothing this time. She’d decided that on the way in. No jacket to strangle, no water bottle to wring. If she held something, she would only hold it harder.

“You’re very calm,” Meilin said.

“I am extremely calm.”

“Your knee is bouncing.”

Xiaoran put a hand on her knee to stop it. Down on the court, the teams were warming up. Yichen moved through the layup line like he always did—easy, unhurried, a little bored-looking, which Xiaoran had learned meant he was concentrating. Then, on his way back to the end of the line, he glanced up at the bleachers, found her, and tapped the tape on his left ankle twice with two fingers.

It took her a second to understand. See? Fine.

“Oh my god. Did he just send you a signal?” Yuhao said.

“No.”

“He did. He sent a signal.”

“It was a cramp.”

“In his fingers?”

Two rows behind them, a pair of girls had gone quiet. Xiaoran recognised one of their voices before she recognised the face—the storage-room voice. She’s honestly holding him back. The girl looked away the second their eyes met. Xiaoran turned back to the court and found, to her own surprise, that she didn’t care what the girl thought anymore. She had a much more important job today, which wasn’t passing out.

✦ ✦ ✦

For the first quarter, Yichen played carefully. Too carefully. He passed when he could have driven. He landed on both feet every time, like someone stepping off a kerb. Xiaoran noticed, and so did the other team, and by the end of the quarter they were down by six. At the break, Coach Wang said something to him that nobody in the stands could hear. Yichen nodded once, wiped his face on his shirt, and walked back on.

Then he stopped being careful. It wasn’t reckless—Xiaoran knew reckless now; reckless was the semifinal, cold and angry and going straight through people. This was different. He looked like himself again. He read a pass before it happened and took it the length of the floor. He pulled up for a jumper with a defender in his face and didn’t even watch it go in. When a player from the other team bumped him on a drive, he stumbled, caught himself, and kept going, and Xiaoran forgot to breathe for that entire second and remembered all at once when he scored.

“He’s okay,” Meilin said, quietly, like she knew.

“I know,” Xiaoran said, and her voice came out wobbly.

By the fourth quarter, the three adults by the scorer’s table had stopped writing and started just watching. They won by eleven. Yichen played the whole second half and didn’t limp once.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterward, the gym emptied slowly. Xiaoran waited by the side door with Meilin and Yuhao, which was where she always waited, except today it took much longer than usual, because Yichen was talking to one of the men in plain jackets. Then to a second one. Coach Wang stood beside him the whole time with his arms folded and the expression of a man trying hard not to look proud.

“That’s Beijing, I’m almost sure that one’s Beijing,” Yuhao whispered.

“You don’t know that.”

“I have a feeling.”

When Yichen finally came over, he had two business cards in his hand and his hair was still damp from the showers.

“Well? Were they impressed? Did they cry?” Yuhao demanded.

“Nobody cried.”

“Did they say ‘generational talent’?”

“No.”

“Did they say anything?”

Yichen thought about it. “One of them asked about my grades.”

Yuhao looked personally betrayed by higher education. Meilin dragged him off to buy drinks, which was the most obvious exit Xiaoran had ever seen, and suddenly it was just the two of them by the side door, the evening coming in cool around them. Xiaoran looked at his ankle. Yichen looked at her looking at his ankle.

“Still fine,” he said.

“I didn’t ask.”

“You were going to.”

She was. She bit her lip instead. Then, because there was no point pretending, she said, “You were really good today.”

“Hm.”

“Not normal good. Scary good.”

“You noticed the first quarter.”

“You were scared. I saw,” she said.

He didn’t deny it. That surprised her more than anything else. Zhou Yichen, who said “I’m fine” about everything, turned the business cards over in his fingers and said, “A little.”

“What changed?”

He watched her, like he was deciding how much to say.

“Coach told me to stop playing like I was afraid of getting hurt. And I looked up, and you weren’t holding anything,” he said.

Xiaoran blinked. “What?”

“Last time you held my jacket so hard you stretched the sleeve. Today your hands were empty. So I figured you weren’t that worried.” The corner of his mouth lifted.

“I was VERY worried.”

“I know that now.”

“I was worried with my whole body. I just didn’t hold anything.”

He laughed, and took her hand—the empty one—and laced his fingers through hers.

“Then thank you,” he said, “for worrying without strangling anything.”

She leaned her forehead against his arm and let out a breath she felt like she’d been holding since Wednesday. A few weeks later, the first recruitment letter arrived. By the end of the month there were four, spread across his desk in a neat, terrifying row, and Xiaoran started to understand that the future everyone kept talking about had an address now. But that came later.

That evening, they just walked home slowly, at his pace for once, while she told him in great detail every moment of the game she had almost died during. He listened to all of it.

chapters.desc: Walking her home after the game the scouts came to see, he gives her one of the two cards that were pressed into his hand.
chapters.title: The Scout’s Card
chapters.epigraph: “When you become a really good basketball player, can I still keep it?”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran told him the whole game again on the walk home: the first quarter, when he’d looked nervous; the second, when he hadn’t; the steal in the third that had made Chen Yuhao stand up on his seat and get shouted at by a parent. By the time they turned into her street she had run out of game and moved on to the scouts.

“Will you have to travel? Do they make you do trials? What about school? What did they say? What did you say?”

“Breathe,” said Zhou Yichen.

“I am breathing. Answer the questions.”

“One of them asked about my grades. The other one asked if my parents would come to a meeting. Neither of them promised anything.”

“But they gave you cards.”

“They gave me cards.”

“Two cards. Two different men. Yuhao says one of them is Beijing.” She had his arm in both hands and was more or less steering him along the pavement by it.

“Yuhao says a lot of things.”

“Is it Beijing?”

He didn’t answer, which was an answer. She squeezed his arm so hard he winced.

At her gate, under the plane trees, he reached into his jacket and took out one of the two cards. The one Yuhao had sworn was Beijing.

“Here.”

“What?”

“Keep it.”

She stared at it, then at him. “Why?”

“You seem more interested in it than I am.”

“That’s not true.”

“Isn’t it?”

She took it as if it might break. It was white, slightly bent at one corner from his pocket, with a man’s name, a youth development program in Beijing, and a phone number. Yuhao had been right.

“You’re really giving me this?”

“I’ve got the other one. And the number’s in my phone.”

“Then why give me this one?”

He shrugged. “Because you’ll look after it better than I will.”

She looked down at it. It was such an ordinary thing, the kind of little card that ended up between the pages of a textbook or at the bottom of a bag. But somebody had watched him play tonight, in front of a full gym, and had come down from the stands afterwards and seen something worth stopping for. Not the boy who sat next to her in Class 3 and forgot his physics homework once a term and fell asleep on her shoulder on the bus. A basketball player.

She wanted to keep that.

“Don’t lose it,” he said.

“I won’t.”

“I know.”

“I mean it.”

“I know you mean it, Xiaoran.”

She unzipped the small inside pocket of her bag, the one she never used, put the card in it and zipped it shut, and pressed her hand flat over the pocket for good measure.

“You’re treating it like it’s valuable.”

“It is valuable.”

“It’s a business card.”

“It’s your business card.”

“Technically it’s his.”

She ignored this. “Do you think you’ll do it?”

He knew what she meant. “I’ll find out more first.”

“But you want to.”

“Of course I want to.”

“Then I think you should.”

He looked at her. “You don’t think it’ll be too much? With school?”

She thought about it properly, because he’d asked properly. “I think you find out what it is. And then if you want it, you don’t say no just because it might be hard. You don’t say no to things because they’re hard. You never do. It’s annoying.”

He laughed. “That’s sensible.”

“I can be sensible.”

“Sometimes.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

He took her face in both his hands, in the dark under the plane trees, and kissed her temple, quickly, because the security guard in the booth had a radio on and a clear view. “I’ll think about it.”

“Good,” she said, unsteadily, and went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t do her maths homework that night. She sat at her desk with the exercise book open and a pen in her hand and the card propped up against her pencil case, and she looked at it. She read the name again. The program. The number. She turned it over, although there was nothing on the back.

She thought about him at a trial somewhere, playing against people he’d never met. Getting better. Not that she thought he needed to be better. She already thought he was the best person on any court she had ever sat beside. But she had seen him stay behind after practice doing the same movement over and over until it was right, and listen to Coach Wang with his whole face, and come out to the gate afterwards red-cheeked and quiet and happy. Sometimes she wondered if he ever let himself enjoy being good at something.

At ten her phone buzzed.

Yichen: Have you finished studying?

Xiaoran: Almost.

Yichen: That’s not an answer.

Xiaoran: I’m thinking.

Yichen: About maths?

She looked at the card.

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: You’re lying.

Xiaoran: I’m thinking about your card.

Yichen: I thought you were keeping it safe.

Xiaoran: I am. It’s right here. I’m guarding it.

Yichen: By looking at it?

Xiaoran: I’m happy, okay? Somebody noticed you. That’s already something. You should be proud.

There was a long pause.

Yichen: Good night, Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: That’s it?? You’re avoiding my compliment.

Yichen: I’m accepting it. I’ll say it properly tomorrow.

Xiaoran: Promise?

Yichen: Promise. Go to sleep.

At bedtime she put the card inside the small notebook beside her bed. Then she took it out again, because the notebook was in the drawer and the drawer was too far away. In the end she slipped the card into a clean paper sleeve and put it under the edge of her pillow, flat, where it couldn’t bend, and lay down on her back and stared at the ceiling.

It wasn’t her achievement. She hadn’t played the game. She hadn’t spent all those evenings practising. But she had been there, before anyone else noticed. And he’d handed her the card at the gate without even thinking about it. She fell asleep smiling into her pillow.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning he was at the gate before her, which almost never happened.

“You look pleased with yourself,” he said.

“I am pleased with myself.”

She took his arm and pulled him down until she could whisper in his ear. “I put your card under my pillow.”

He stood up straight and looked at her. “Under your pillow?”

“To keep it safe.”

“Your bag has a pocket.”

“I know.”

“Your desk has a drawer.”

“I know.”

“But you put it under your pillow.”

“It’s important,” she said, completely unembarrassed.

“It’s a business card.”

“Why does everyone keep saying that?”

He laughed, and then he stopped laughing, and reached out and pushed a piece of her hair back behind her ear. “Then I’m glad you’re keeping it.”

“Really?”

“Really. Just don’t bring it to school loose.”

“I’m not an idiot.”

“You put it under your pillow.”

“That’s different. That’s love.”

He looked at her. She heard what she’d said, and went red all the way up to her hairline, and he didn’t tease her about it, which was how she knew he’d heard it too.

They walked towards the building. After a few steps she slid her hand down his arm into his.

“Yichen. When you become a really good basketball player, can I still keep it?”

“When. Not if,” he repeated.

She nodded, as if that had been obvious all along.

“Then you can keep it.”

“Even if you get more important cards?”

“Even then.”

“Even if you get famous?”

“Then you’ll need a safe.”

At lunch, Yuhao wanted to talk about nothing else.

“Beijing. Beijing. I told you. I said it in the car park. Nobody listened,” he said, waving his chopsticks.

“We listened. You said it nine times,” said Meilin.

“Because nobody was listening. You’re going to go to Beijing and become famous and forget about us. You’ll have a driver. You’ll wear sunglasses indoors.” He pointed the chopsticks at Yichen.

“I’ll finish school first,” Yichen said.

“With sunglasses.”

“Leave him alone. He hasn’t decided anything. He’s finding out more,” said Xiaoran. She was sitting so close to Yichen that she was sharing his half of the bench and most of his rice.

“Look at her. Look at her defending him. Do you know where she keeps the card?” Yuhao said to Meilin.

“Don’t—” said Xiaoran.

“Where?” said Meilin.

Yichen looked at his food. Xiaoran looked at Yichen. “You told him?”

“He asked why you looked so pleased this morning. I’m a bad liar,” Yichen said.

“You’re an excellent liar. You lie to Teacher Xu about your homework every week.”

“I’m a bad liar to Yuhao. It’s different. He can tell.”

“Under her pillow,” said Yuhao, to Meilin, with relish.

Meilin put her hand over her heart. “Lin Xiaoran.”

“It’s a safe place,” Xiaoran said, with dignity, and went pink to the ears.

Later, on the way back up to the classroom, when the other two had gone ahead, Yichen slowed down on the stairs until she was level with him.

“I said I’d say it properly.”

“Say what?”

“Last night. You said someone noticed me. You said I should be proud. Thank you. For noticing first. Before them.” He stopped on the landing and looked at her.

She stood still on the step.

“Say it again.”

“Thank you for noticing first,” he said, and she launched herself at him so hard he had to grab the handrail, and a teacher coming down the stairs said “Ahem,” loudly, and walked round them.

Three weeks later the first proper letter came to his house, and she was sitting at his family’s dining table when he opened it, and she didn’t say a word about the card. But that night, when she got home, she took it out from under her pillow and put it in the back of the notebook where she kept things that were going to matter: behind a pressed leaf from the evening he’d asked her out, and a strawberry milk label she would never, ever have admitted to keeping.

chapters.desc: University offers are arriving for Zhou Yichen. Lin Xiaoran is quietly terrified of where they might take him.
chapters.title: Which Future Includes You?
chapters.epigraph: “Plans change. People stay.”
chapters.content:
Choosing universities should have been exciting. Lin Xiaoran treated it like impending doom.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re staring at the same page.”

Tang Meilin looked up from her laptop. Xiaoran hadn’t moved in a while. University brochures covered the whole café table—prestigious schools, scholarship pamphlets, department rankings. And in the middle of it all, Zhou Yichen’s basketball recruitment letters. Apparently being tall, smart, and athletic wasn’t enough. Universities wanted him too. Annoying, honestly.

“I hate higher education,” Xiaoran muttered.

“That’s because applications started.”

“No. It’s because adulthood is scary.” She slumped across the table.

Meilin sighed. Fair. Lately everyone talked about the future constantly—majors, dorms, career plans, cities. It scared Xiaoran more than exams did. Not because she didn’t have dreams. Because for the first time, she realised dreams could pull people in different directions. And Zhou Yichen had so many options, while she still changed her mind about careers every three weeks.

✦ ✦ ✦

The real problem had started yesterday, when Xiaoran overheard teachers talking about Yichen after basketball practice.

“He could definitely enter Beijing.”

“Or Shanghai.”

“His coach said sports universities are contacting him too.”

“He has a strong future.”

Strong future. The words lodged in her chest. Suddenly the future wasn’t abstract anymore. It was real, and terrifyingly far away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen noticed the change right away, because Lin Xiaoran physically couldn’t hide her feelings. At lunch she sat beside him, poking at her rice. Quiet. Too quiet.

“You failed a test?” Yichen asked.

“No.”

“You lost something?”

“Yes.”

Yichen paused.

“What.”

“My peace.”

“You’ve been weird since yesterday.”

“I’m reflecting on life.”

Across from them, Yuhao was eating noodles peacefully. Then he decided to get involved.

“She’s probably thinking about universities.”

Silence. Traitor. Xiaoran glared.

“How do YOU know?”

“You’ve been reposting sad quotes.”

Meilin nodded from beside him.

“One literally said ‘distance turns even stars into strangers.’”

Yichen blinked, then slowly turned to Xiaoran. Now he understood. Xiaoran immediately regretted existing. Out loud, it sounded dramatically pathetic.

“Forget I ever spoke,” she muttered.

But Zhou Yichen looked thoughtful now, which only made her more nervous.

“Come with me after school.”

“Where.”

“You’ll see.”

“Every time someone says that in a drama, something terrible happens.”

“Hm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After school, Yichen took her to the old outdoor court behind campus, the quiet one that was usually empty in the evenings. The sky was cloudy, the wind cool. Peaceful. Xiaoran sat beside him on the bench, bracing for devastation. What if he really wanted a university far away? What if he left? What if—

“What university do YOU want?”

His question cut her spiral short.

“Hm?”

Yichen looked at her calmly.

“What do you want?”

Silence. Nobody had asked her that yet. Everyone asked about scores, options, being practical. Not what she wanted.

“I don’t know yet.”

“That’s okay.”

“But you do. You already have plans.”

Yichen leaned back against the bench.

“Not really.”

“You literally have recruitment offers.”

“That’s basketball.”

“That’s your future.”

He glanced at her, then said calmly—

“You’re part of my future too.”

He said it so naturally, like it was obvious, like there had never been another possibility. Xiaoran’s chest ached.

“But what if your best opportunity is somewhere far?”

Yichen didn’t answer right away. He looked out at the empty court for a moment.

“Do you know why I haven’t accepted anything yet?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“…Why?”

“Because I’m waiting for your applications first.”

Silence.

“WHAT.”

He said it so calmly, like it wasn’t a completely insane boyfriend thing to say. Xiaoran stared at him in horror.

“You can’t make life decisions around me!”

“I can.”

“That’s unhealthy.”

Finally, Yichen laughed—warm and quiet—while Xiaoran kept short-circuiting beside him. Then he looked at her again.

“I’m serious. I’ll choose the place that makes the most sense for both of us.”

That scared Xiaoran more than distance did. Because suddenly she understood that Zhou Yichen loved her in frighteningly serious ways. Quietly and steadily. Real. Shaped like a future.

“What if I don’t get into good schools?”

“You will.”

“But WHAT IF.”

“Then we’ll figure it out.”

Simple again. It always was with him, like nothing was frightening if they faced it together.

“I don’t need everything perfectly planned right now, Xiaoran.”

The wind moved through his hair as the evening light faded behind the court, and somehow he looked older. Not in age. Just steadier.

“I just know I don’t want a future without you in it.”

Silence. Then the tears came, because Lin Xiaoran always cried when she was overwhelmed.

“Why are you crying?” Yichen sighed.

“You said things.”

Even crying, she shifted closer until her shoulder pressed against his arm. Quietly—

“What if we fight more in university?”

“We will.”

“What if we get busy?”

“We will.”

“What if you meet prettier girls?”

Yichen looked deeply unimpressed.

“Seriously?”

“I’m planning ahead.”

“You’ll still be annoying there too.”

“Oh.”

“And I’ll still love you there too.”

Xiaoran covered her face.

“This conversation is a personal attack.”

Yichen smiled and gently pulled her hands away from her face. Then—

“Stop being scared alone.”

Somehow, that comforted her most of all. Maybe the future really was uncertain. Maybe university would change things. Maybe growing up would be messy. But sitting beside Zhou Yichen, his hand warm around hers under the evening sky, the future didn’t feel quite so frightening anymore.

chapters.desc: One internet question. One very serious girlfriend. Zhou Yichen was not prepared.
chapters.title: Would You Still Love Me If I Was a Capybara?
chapters.epigraph: “Real love answers ridiculous questions sincerely.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen should have known peace never lasted long around Lin Xiaoran, especially when she went quiet. Quiet usually meant one of three things: she wanted something, she had done something, or she had discovered internet nonsense. Today, it was the third one.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen was doing homework at Xiaoran’s house while she lay upside down across the bed beside him, scrolling through videos. A normal, safe afternoon. Or so he thought.

“Yichen, would you still love me if I was a capybara?”

Yichen’s pencil slowed to a stop. What kind of question was that? Xiaoran was watching him from upside down, waiting. Completely serious.

“…A capybara.”

“Yes.”

Yichen blinked. Twice.

“…The giant rodent?”

“Don’t call me that.”

“I’m asking for clarification.”

Xiaoran sat up.

“You’re stalling. That means hesitation.”

“There SHOULD be hesitation.”

Across the room, Tang Meilin looked up from her phone with dead eyes.

“Oh no.”

Yichen set his pencil down. Experience had taught him that this kind of conversation could get dangerous. Then, calmly—

“Why specifically a capybara?”

“They’re calm.”

“You’re not calm.”

“They’re cute.”

“Hm.”

“And they sit in hot springs with oranges.”

“Important trait.”

“Exactly.”

Yichen considered her. Then—

“Yes.”

Xiaoran blinked rapidly.

“…Really?”

“You asked.”

Meilin groaned.

“You people are impossible.”

But Xiaoran wasn’t finished.

“What if I was an ugly capybara?”

Yichen sighed.

“There’s no such thing.”

“Wrong answer. Some capybaras definitely look unemployed.”

“That’s oddly judgmental.”

“I’m asking seriously.”

Yichen leaned back in his chair. Then, calmly—

“You’d still be Xiaoran.”

Simple and warm, and Xiaoran’s whole face softened. Disaster. Zhou Yichen always answered ridiculous questions sincerely.

“What if I couldn’t talk anymore because I was a capybara?”

“You already say nonsense half the time.”

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

Meilin nearly collapsed laughing. Yichen finally smiled a little.

“You’d still follow me around.”

“That’s true.”

“And steal my food.”

“ALSO TRUE.”

“See?”

Xiaoran stared at him suspiciously now.

“…You’ve thought about this too comfortably.”

“I adapted quickly.”

Meilin cut in tiredly—

“Can I ask why this conversation exists.”

Xiaoran grabbed her phone and shoved a video at them. On screen, a capybara sat peacefully while tiny ducklings climbed onto its head. Yichen watched.

“…Okay.”

“LOOK AT THEM.”

“Hm.”

“They look so calm.”

Fair. Even Yichen had to admit the capybara looked weirdly at peace. Then Xiaoran pointed accusingly.

“See? If I became one, you’d live a calmer life.”

“No.”

“No?”

“You’d still create problems somehow.”

Silence.

“…That’s true.”

Meilin nodded.

“You’d become the first capybara banned from libraries.”

“Why specifically libraries.”

“You’d chew the books.”

“That’s species discrimination.”

Yichen went back to his homework. Conversation over, probably. Unfortunately, Lin Xiaoran still had thoughts. Too many thoughts.

“Would you pet me?”

The pencil stopped again.

Meilin got up and headed for the kitchen. “I need water.” Coward.

Yichen looked back at Xiaoran, who was now sitting cross-legged, hugging a pillow, waiting seriously. Then, calmly—

“Yes.”

“…Really?”

“Hm.”

“How.”

Yichen considered it. Then he reached over and patted her hair. Once. Twice.

“Like that,” he answered.

Silence. Xiaoran completely malfunctioned. Why did the simplest affection from him always hit harder than expected? Yichen looked suspiciously amused.

Xiaoran crawled over until her head was resting on his shoulder. Very capybara behaviour, somehow. Yichen glanced down.

“What now.”

“I’m testing if you’d still cuddle me.”

“You’re already doing that.”

“Oh.”

“Would you still date me publicly?”

“Yes.”

“What if society judged you.”

“I already date you now.”

“ZHOU YICHEN?!”

Meanwhile Meilin shouted from the kitchen—

“HE GOT YOU THERE.”

chapters.desc: Lunch at Zhou Yichen’s house, with both his parents home. Lin Xiaoran is not emotionally prepared.
chapters.title: I’m Invited to Zhou Yichen’s House?
chapters.epigraph: “You learn the most about someone from the people who raised them.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran knew something was wrong the moment Zhou Yichen casually said—

“Come over tomorrow.”

Silence.

“…Where.”

“My house.”

A longer silence. Excuse her? His house? While his parents were HOME?

✦ ✦ ✦

That Friday night, Xiaoran sat frozen on her bed while Tang Meilin watched her spiral.

“He invited me casually.”

“Hm.”

“CASUALLY.”

Meilin looked up from her phone.

“You’ve already met his parents before.”

“That was different.”

Technically true. The first time Xiaoran met the Zhou family was the airport goodbye before their trip. The second was the ride home when Yichen came back. Both times were short, sweet, and polite. Mrs. Zhou smiled warmly. Mr. Zhou seemed calm and gentle. Nobody asked serious relationship questions. It had almost felt like they saw her as just a cute high school girlfriend. Young. Temporary, maybe. Which had actually made her less nervous.

But now he had invited her over on a Saturday, with both his parents home. Then Xiaoran sat bolt upright.

“Oh my god.”

“What now.”

“What if this is evaluation day.”

“…Evaluation day.”

“What if his mother secretly observes whether I can become a daughter-in-law.”

Meilin stared at her.

“You’ve watched too many dramas.”

“YOU DON’T KNOW RICH FAMILY CULTURE.”

“The Zhou family is literally normal.”

“That’s what makes them scarier.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday came too fast, and Lin Xiaoran spent TWO HOURS choosing clothes. Not too pretty—suspicious. Not too casual—lazy. Not too cute—impossible.

Meanwhile Zhou Yichen received seventeen messages during basketball practice.

Xiaoran: Does your mother prefer elegant girls or cheerful girls

Yichen: Normal girls.

Xiaoran: That didn’t help.

Then later—

Xiaoran: What if your father hates me

Yichen: He won’t.

Xiaoran: How do you know

Yichen: Because you’re cute.

Xiaoran lost focus for the next fifteen minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time Yichen met her at his front gate that afternoon, Lin Xiaoran looked one small inconvenience away from collapse. She was holding a cake box awkwardly—hair carefully done, white top, soft pink skirt. Yichen almost smiled. She had clearly tried hard.

“You’re nervous.”

“No I’m not.”

“You nearly walked into the mailbox.”

“…It came out of nowhere.”

Before Yichen could answer, the front door swung open and Mrs. Zhou appeared.

“Oh, Xiaoran’s here!”

Warm smile, gentle voice, no scary mother-in-law aura whatsoever. Which somehow made Xiaoran MORE nervous.

“Hello, Auntie, I brought cake,” she said quickly, with a small bow.

“You’re so polite. Come inside quickly,” Mrs. Zhou laughed.

In the living room, Mr. Zhou looked up from his newspaper.

“Yichen finally stopped hiding his girlfriend from us.”

Xiaoran froze. Yichen sighed.

“Dad.”

Mrs. Zhou laughed, and the air softened a little.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Zhou house felt exactly like Yichen. Clean, comfortable, quiet but warm. Neatly organised bookshelves. Basketball photos along the hallway, including one of a gap-toothed little Yichen holding a ball almost as big as he was. Soft music coming from the kitchen. Seeing him in his own home got to Xiaoran more than she expected. This was his real space. The place he grew up. The place he became himself.

“Xiaoran, sit beside me,” Mrs. Zhou said warmly from the sofa.

“Oh.”

Yichen looked suspiciously amused. Traitor boyfriend. So Xiaoran sat down carefully beside Mrs. Zhou while Yichen disappeared into the kitchen. Abandoned.

“He talks about you a lot.”

Silence. Xiaoran blinked rapidly.

“…He does?”

Mrs. Zhou smiled knowingly.

“Hm.”

“Oh.”

Her ears went pink. Zhou Yichen talked about her at home? What did he say? Had he mentioned the time she cried over math homework?

“You don’t need to be nervous around us.”

Her voice was soft, like she really meant it.

“We already met you before. You’re exactly what I expected,” she said.

Silence. Somehow that made Xiaoran even more nervous.

“…Good expected?”

Mrs. Zhou laughed lightly.

“Very cute expected.”

Yichen came back from the kitchen with drinks just in time to see Xiaoran quietly malfunctioning beside his mother. It almost made him laugh. Lin Xiaoran, who talked nonstop around everyone else, was sitting perfectly upright with both hands in her lap, trying desperately to behave. Then Mr. Zhou spoke from across the room.

“So.”

Oh no. Xiaoran sat up straighter.

“Does Yichen bully you at school?”

“Yes.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“He judges my math.”

“You failed two quizzes.”

“See? Bullying.”

Unexpectedly, Mr. Zhou laughed. Actually laughed. And the whole room relaxed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was easier after that. Not because Xiaoran stopped being nervous, but because the Zhou family was surprisingly normal. Mrs. Zhou kept putting food in her bowl. Mr. Zhou calmly asked about university plans. Nobody interrogated her. Nobody acted weird. At one point, Mrs. Zhou sighed fondly, watching Yichen peel shrimp for Xiaoran without even thinking about it.

“He really likes you.”

Yichen paused. Xiaoran nearly dropped her chopsticks. Adults really just SAID things.

“He spoils her too much,” Mr. Zhou added.

“That’s true,” Mrs. Zhou agreed.

Yichen finally looked a little helpless.

“You’re both making her nervous.”

“We’re telling the truth,” his mother replied calmly.

Then she turned towards Xiaoran again.

“He’s been calmer since dating you.”

Xiaoran blinked, holding her bowl.

“…Calmer?”

Mrs. Zhou smiled.

“Hm. Yichen used to stay in his room a lot more.”

Across the table, Yichen paused—a tiny pause, almost invisible. But Xiaoran noticed. Mrs. Zhou went on—

“He was always a good child. Responsible. Quiet. Never caused trouble.”

“That sounds accurate,” Xiaoran nodded automatically.

“But sometimes,” Mrs. Zhou added, “he carried things by himself too much.”

The table went quiet, and Xiaoran was curious. She knew Zhou Yichen at school—basketball captain Zhou Yichen, calm boyfriend Zhou Yichen, the boy who spoiled her endlessly while staying perfectly composed. But what had he been like here, before her? Before she could stop herself—

“What was Yichen like at home?”

Yichen looked up slowly.

“…Xiaoran.”

Too late. Mrs. Zhou was already smiling.

“Oh, he was very serious.”

“Mum.”

“He’d come home, finish homework, practice basketball, study again.”

“That still sounds like him.”

“Hm, but now he laughs more.”

Yichen actually looked a little embarrassed. A rare sight. Xiaoran stared at him.

“…You didn’t laugh before?”

“I laughed.”

Both his parents looked unconvinced.

“Not often,” Mr. Zhou corrected calmly.

“Oh my god.”

Xiaoran turned to Yichen.

“You were a robot.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“It’s TRUE.”

Yichen sighed while Mrs. Zhou laughed.

“He laughs a lot when he talks to you at home.”

Xiaoran froze.

“…At home?”

“Hm. Sometimes we hear him on calls with you.” Mrs. Zhou nodded casually.

Across the table, Yichen closed his eyes. Complete defeat. Xiaoran’s ears went pink.

“WAIT.”

“He’d be sitting there looking normal,” Mrs. Zhou continued gently, “then suddenly smiling at his phone.”

“Mum.”

“And once,” she said thoughtfully, “he laughed so hard because of you that his father thought something happened.”

Mr. Zhou nodded once.

“I was concerned.”

Xiaoran turned slowly to Yichen, who looked deeply resigned.

“…You laugh like that because of me?”

“You say stupid things constantly.”

“That’s not the important part.”

Xiaoran’s chest went painfully soft. Picturing Zhou Yichen alone at home, smiling at her messages, got to her more than she expected—especially because at school he always looked so composed. Apparently he carried little pieces of her into his private world too.

“What else does he do?”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“No, I want to know.”

Mrs. Zhou nearly laughed again. Mr. Zhou added calmly—

“He checks his phone more now.”

“Oh my god,” Xiaoran whispered.

Yichen looked exhausted.

“You’re all enjoying this too much.”

It felt unfair. At school, Zhou Yichen had dignity. Respect. Control. Meanwhile his parents were casually revealing that yes, he smiled at her texts alone. Yes, he waited for her calls. Yes, he was happier now. Mrs. Zhou looked at Xiaoran warmly.

“Thank you for taking care of him.”

That made Xiaoran go still. Nobody had ever put it that way. People always talked about how much Yichen took care of HER—protected her, spoiled her, loved her patiently. But his mother was thanking her, like she mattered just as much in his life.

“I don’t think I do much,” Xiaoran admitted honestly.

Across the table, Yichen looked at her, and before anyone else could speak—

“You do.”

Xiaoran’s heart stumbled. Then, holding her gaze—

“You make things lighter.”

Mrs. Zhou smiled. Mr. Zhou looked unsurprised. Xiaoran forgot how to breathe. He’d said it in front of his parents, so naturally. No teasing. No joking. Just honest. Under the table, her fingers found his hand. And this time, Yichen held on first.

chapters.desc: One Friday in March, while his son is in a meeting about his future, Mr. Zhou drives her home and asks about hers.
chapters.title: His Father’s Question
chapters.epigraph: “I hope you get to do what you want.”
chapters.content:
Being driven home by somebody else’s father, Lin Xiaoran discovered, was a completely different sport from being driven home by your own.

With her own father she put her feet on the dashboard and changed the radio station and complained about the traffic. In the back seat of Mr. Zhou’s car she sat up straight with her schoolbag on her knees and her hands folded on top of it and tried not to touch anything, including the seat. Mr. Zhou seemed determined to make this impossible.

“Have you eaten?” he asked, as he turned out of the school gate.

“I had something at the break, Uncle.”

“Something?”

“A bun.”

“A bun isn’t dinner. Yichen says you’ve been studying hard.” He glanced at her in the mirror.

She wasn’t sure what Yichen had said to his father about her, or how much, and the thought of the two of them discussing her at a dinner table made her want to slide down into the footwell. “A bit. The first mock’s in two weeks.”

“Then don’t stay up too late. Studying is important. Sleep is also important.”

“Yes, Uncle.”

Yichen wasn’t in the car. He was still upstairs in Coach Wang’s office with the man from the Beijing youth program, the one whose card was under her pillow, and the meeting had already run an hour over. Mr. Zhou had come to join it at six, been told it would be at least another hour, and found Xiaoran on the bench outside the gym, where she’d been sitting since five with her coat buttoned up and her maths homework on her knees.

At half past five Yichen had come down the stairs for the first time, still in his training top, and found her there.

“You’re still here.”

“I said I’d wait.”

“It could be another hour.”

“Then I’ll wait another hour. I’m being productive.” She held up her maths book.

He looked at the page. “You’ve done one question.”

“It’s a hard question. What are they saying? Is he nice? Is it really Beijing? Are you nervous?” She caught his sleeve before he could go back up.

“He’s nice. It’s really Beijing. I’m not nervous.”

“You’re a bit nervous. Your ears.”

He touched his ear without meaning to, and she laughed, and he looked down at her sitting on the bench with her coat buttoned to the chin and her maths book on her knees, and something in his face went quiet and soft.

“Go home, Xiaoran. It’s getting dark.”

“I want to hear how it went.”

“I’ll ring you.”

“I want to hear it with your face.”

He went back upstairs because Coach Wang called him, and at six his father arrived and went up too, and at a quarter to seven Yichen came down for the second time, for thirty seconds between one question and the next, and stood in front of the bench.

“My father’s going to drive you home.”

“I don’t need—”

“It’s dark. He’s got the car. He’ll come straight back. Please. I’ll ring you the minute it’s finished. With my voice, if not my face.” He crouched down so their faces were level, which he only did when he meant something.

She had said no twice by then. She didn’t say it a third time.

So here she was. Mr. Zhou would drive her home across half the city and drive back again, and he had said it as if it were nothing.

For a while neither of them spoke. She watched the streets go by. Then he said, “Xiaoran, have you thought about what you’d like to study?”

Teachers asked that question every week now. It still made her think before she answered.

“Media, I think. Communications. Something where you make things.”

“Media,” he repeated.

“I like putting ideas together. Telling a story so people understand it. Working out why someone feels something when they see a picture or hear a sound. I’m not completely sure which direction yet.” She stopped, embarrassed at how much she had said.

“You don’t have to decide everything now.”

“I know. But I want to understand it before I choose.”

“That’s sensible. Do you enjoy school?” He stopped at a red light.

“Some of it. Literature. Anything with a project.”

“And mathematics?”

There was a pause from the back seat.

“That bad?” said Mr. Zhou.

She laughed in spite of herself. “I’m trying.”

“Trying is good. Don’t tell Yichen I said this, but he’s been studying a lot too. More than usual.” His eyes crinkled in the mirror.

“Really?”

“He’ll think I’m reporting on him.”

“You are reporting on him, Uncle.”

“I am,” Mr. Zhou agreed, and she liked him a great deal at that moment.

“He spends so much time on basketball,” he went on, “that sometimes I have to remind him there are other things in the world. And then, lately, I find him at the kitchen table at eleven at night doing chemistry. I asked his mother what had happened. She said, ‘Lin Xiaoran is studying for the mocks.’”

Xiaoran made a small strangled noise.

“He tells his mother everything. And his mother tells me everything. It’s how our family works. He tells me you’re keeping one of the cards,” said Mr. Zhou.

“He told you about that?”

“He told his mother.”

She put her face in her hands in the back seat, and Mr. Zhou laughed, a warm, surprised laugh that sounded so much like Yichen’s that she looked up.

“He’s excited. About Beijing. He’s trying not to show it,” she said, when she could.

“That sounds like him.”

“He’ll want to do it properly. He won’t want to just go because someone asked.”

Mr said, “No. He won’t. We’ll talk about it properly tonight. It’s an interesting opportunity. There are a lot of things to think about. And your parents? What do they think about media?” Zhou. He was quiet, watching the road. The light changed.

“They’re supportive. They want me to do well at school first.”

“Naturally.”

“My mother asks about my marks a lot.”

“Because she cares.”

“I know. Sometimes I think she worries more than I do.”

“Parents are very good at that,” he said, so matter-of-factly that she laughed again. “What does your mother do?”

“She’s an accountant.”

“Then she’ll understand why I asked about the mathematics.”

He was quiet for a stretch of road, and then he said, in a different voice, as if it were something he’d been turning over for a while, “It’s good that you have something you’re interested in. Not everyone your age knows. Even if you change your mind later, it gives you somewhere to start. Look at the courses. Find out what the work is really like. Think about what kind of life you want, not only which job. And don’t choose something just because someone tells you it’s a good choice. Even someone you like very much.” He met her eyes in the mirror.

She understood that he meant Yichen. She also understood, from his face, that he wasn’t warning her off; he was telling her something he’d probably told his son.

“I’ll remember,” she said.

“Good.”

At the corner of her road she sat forward. “Uncle, you can stop here. It’s only a short walk.”

“I can take you to the gate.”

“It’s okay. Really.”

He pulled in. She unbuckled her seatbelt, gathered her bag, opened the door, and then stopped.

“Uncle? Thank you for asking. About what I want to study.”

He looked surprised. “Why thank me?”

“Because sometimes when adults ask, it feels like there’s already a right answer and you’re supposed to guess it.”

Mr. Zhou looked at her in the light from the street lamp.

“I’m glad you told me the real one. Go on in. And tell your mother not to let you study too late,” he said.

He waited with the engine running until she was through the gate.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen rang at half past ten, from his bedroom, sounding tired.

“Did you get home all right?”

“You know I did. Your father texted you.”

“He said you were polite, you’re afraid of mathematics, and you thanked him for asking about your future.”

“All true.”

She was lying on her bed with her maths book open on the pillow beside her, untouched. “Your father’s lovely.”

“He likes you.”

“How do you know?”

“He doesn’t normally drive people across the city and interview them about their careers.”

“It wasn’t an interview!”

“He told my mother it went very well.”

She pulled her pillow over her face. “What about you? What happened with the man?”

He was quiet for a while. She could hear him moving around his room.

“He wants an answer by summer. My father wants me to finish school and choose a university, and do the program after, if they’ll wait. My mother wants me to eat. I don’t want to decide before I understand what I’m saying yes to.”

“That’s sensible.”

“Sometimes I’m sensible.”

“Your father said you’ve been doing chemistry at eleven at night.”

“Of course he did.”

“He said your mother said it was because of me.”

There was a long silence on the line.

“My family,” Yichen said, “has no loyalty.”

She laughed until she had to hold the phone away from her ear. Then she lay on her back and looked at the ceiling and said, more quietly, “Yichen. I hope you get to do what you want.”

“I hope you do too.”

“Even if it’s not the same city?”

“Even then. But I’d like it to be,” he said.

When they hung up, she did two maths questions, because she had promised, and then, because it was nearly midnight and nobody was watching, she opened her laptop and typed media and communication degree and read for an hour about a future she hadn’t chosen yet, in a city she hadn’t chosen either.

chapters.desc: A photograph from the New Year gala, hidden badly in a mathematics textbook, and an accountant mother who finds it.
chapters.title: Her Mother Finds the Photo
chapters.epigraph: “You’re not going to tell me I shouldn’t date him?”
chapters.content:
The photograph wasn’t well hidden. That was the first mistake. The second was hiding it in a maths textbook, which was the one book in the flat her mother regularly opened.

It was a small print from the New Year gala in January. Meilin had taken it on her phone and Xiaoran had paid two yuan to have it printed at the shop by the school gate. In it, Zhou Yichen stood next to her in his white shirt with one hand resting lightly behind her shoulder. She was smiling at the camera with her head tipped towards him. He wasn’t looking at the camera at all. He was looking at her.

She had taken it out on Tuesday night to look at it, slipped it between the pages of the textbook meaning to put it back in her notebook, and forgotten.

On Wednesday afternoon she came home, dropped her bag in the hall and was washing her hands when her mother called from the kitchen.

“Xiaoran? Can you come in here a moment?”

Nothing unusual about it. And yet. Her mother was sitting at the kitchen table with a glass of water and a stack of school papers. On the table, in front of the papers, face up, was the photograph. Xiaoran stopped in the doorway.

“Is this yours?” said her mother.

“Yes.”

“Who took it?”

“Meilin.”

Her mother picked it up and studied it, holding it a little away from her face the way she did with receipts. “And who’s this?”

Xiaoran knew perfectly well that her mother knew. She had mentioned Zhou Yichen a hundred times. Her father had been asking since last summer, at intervals, who it was that rang at nine o’clock every night. But hearing about a boy was one thing. Finding a photograph of your daughter standing beside him in a white shirt was another.

“Zhou Yichen,” she said.

“The basketball boy.”

“Yes.”

Her mother looked at the photograph again. “He’s handsome.”

Xiaoran nearly choked on air. “Mum.”

“What? He is.”

“That’s not the point!”

“Then what is the point? Sit.” Her mother put the photograph down and pushed out the chair opposite with her foot.

Xiaoran sat. She looked at the edge of the table.

“Are you two close?”

“Yes.”

“How close?”

“Mum.”

“I’m asking a question. I’m allowed to ask questions in my own kitchen.”

Xiaoran could have said friends. It would even have been true, in a way. But she had never actually wanted to hide him, not from her mother, and the photograph lying there on the table between the electricity bill and the school newsletter seemed to be asking her to be honest.

“He’s my boyfriend.”

Her mother didn’t say anything. She took a sip of water.

“How long?”

“A while.”

“How long is a while?”

Xiaoran told her. Her mother’s eyebrows went up. “Fifteen months?”

“Yes.”

“Since before the summer. Since before Grandma’s. The boy who calls at nine.” Xiaoran watched her mother put it together with the speed of a woman who did other people’s tax returns for a living.

“Yes.”

“Your father has asked me four times who calls at nine. I told him it was a study group.”

“You knew?”

“I knew there was a boy. I didn’t know there was a boyfriend. There’s a difference, Xiaoran. One of them gets a lot more questions. Why didn’t you tell me properly?” Her mother put the glass down.

“I thought you knew.”

“You thought I knew, so you didn’t tell me. That’s your father’s logic.” Her mother shook her head slowly.

“Sorry.”

Her mother reached across the table and put her hand over Xiaoran’s. “I’m not angry.”

“You’re not?”

“I’m surprised. That’s all. Does he treat you well?” She looked at the photograph again.

“Yes.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes, Mum.”

“What’s he like?”

There were so many answers that choosing one felt impossible. “He’s kind. He’s patient. He listens even when I’m talking about something stupid. He works really hard. And he— He makes me laugh. He’s very serious and then he says something and I can’t breathe,” Xiaoran said.

“You sound fond of him.”

“I am.”

“Does he make you happy?”

“Yes.” That one came without thinking.

Her mother tapped the photograph with one finger. “He’s looking at you.”

“What?”

“In the picture. You’re looking at the camera. He’s looking at you.”

Xiaoran leaned over. She had looked at that photograph perhaps two hundred times and somehow never noticed. Her face went hot.

“Maybe he didn’t hear Meilin say smile.”

“Maybe,” said her mother.

“Mum.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your eyebrows did.”

Her mother laughed. Then she glanced at the stack of school papers, and Xiaoran knew what was coming the way you know a train’s coming from the hum in the rails.

“How are your marks?”

“Fine.”

“Fine?”

“Mostly fine.”

“Your first mock is in two weeks.”

“I know.”

“Have you been revising?”

“Yes. Mostly.” Her mother looked at her.

Her mother said, “I’m not telling you not to see him. I’m not going to lock you in your room. But I want you to keep your priorities straight. Having a boyfriend isn’t a problem. Forgetting your own future is.”

“I won’t forget.”

“What does that mean, to you?”

“It means I’ve still got my own things. School. The exams. Deciding what I want to study.”

“Good. And him? What does he want?” Her mother sat back.

“He studies too. More than me. And he’s got basketball. There’s a scout from Beijing who wants to talk to his parents. He’s not the kind of person who’d want me to give anything up. He’d be cross if I did.” She looked at the photograph.

Her mother looked at her for a while, then nodded, slowly.

“You’re not going to tell me I shouldn’t date him?” Xiaoran asked.

“Would you listen if I did?”

Xiaoran started to answer and didn’t.

“That’s what I thought. I’m not giving you permission to neglect your studies. But liking someone isn’t something to be ashamed of. Just remember you’re still growing up. You’ve got your own plans and your own life. Don’t make every decision around another person, however much you like him. And if anything ever makes you unhappy, you tell me. You don’t hide things because you think I’ll be upset,” said her mother, and laughed. She pushed the photograph back across the table.

“Okay.”

“Promise.”

“I promise.”

Her mother reached out and pushed the hair off her forehead, the way she had when Xiaoran first came back from her grandparents’ at twelve and wouldn’t talk to anyone for a week. “Good.”

Xiaoran picked up the photograph and checked the corners for bends.

“Does he know you’re keeping this?” her mother asked.

“Of course.”

“Has he got one?”

“Yes.”

“Where does he keep his?”

Xiaoran considered lying. “In his phone case. Behind the phone.”

Her mother made a small sound, not quite a laugh, and looked out of the window as if something had touched her that she hadn’t expected. “Well. Then I suppose it’s a nice photograph,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening Xiaoran sat at the kitchen table with her maths workbook while her mother cut fruit beside her.

“Is that where it lives now?” her mother asked, nodding at the notebook where the photograph had been tucked inside the cover.

“Yes.”

“Not in the maths book.”

“You knew it was in the maths book. You found it there.”

“I did. Next time, find a better hiding place. Or don’t hide it. And next time you take a picture with him, get someone to take one where you’re both looking at the camera,” her mother agreed. She put a plate of orange segments down by Xiaoran’s elbow.

“Why?”

“Because I want to see his face properly. And because your father will want to see it too. I’ll tell him tonight. Gently. He cries.” She paused in the doorway with the knife in her hand.

“Mum!”

Her mother laughed all the way down the hall.

Xiaoran sat with her face warm and her phone in her hand.

Xiaoran: My mother found our photo.

Yichen: The gala one?

Xiaoran: In my maths book.

Yichen: Why was it in your maths book?

Xiaoran: That’s not the important part!!

Yichen: What did she say?

Xiaoran: She said you’re handsome.

There was a pause.

Yichen: Your mother has good judgment.

Xiaoran: You’re SO shameless.

Yichen: What else?

Xiaoran: She asked if you treat me well. I said yes. She asked how long. I said fifteen months. She’s telling my dad tonight.

Yichen: Is that bad?

Xiaoran: He’ll cry.

Yichen: Happy crying?

Xiaoran: He cries at weather forecasts. It’s hard to tell.

Yichen: Did she ask about your marks?

Xiaoran: WHY are you like this.

Yichen: Because I’d ask about your marks.

Xiaoran: You’re supposed to be on my side.

Yichen: I am on your side. That’s why I’m telling you to finish your maths.

She made a face at the phone, and then she looked at the photograph inside the notebook cover, the one where he was looking at her and not at the camera, and found that it looked different now that her mother had seen it. Not less private. Just less hidden.

She finished the maths. It took forty minutes and she got two wrong, and when she took it into the living room to be checked, the way she had every evening since she was twelve, her mother marked it in red pen at the coffee table and said, without looking up, “Tell the boy who calls at nine that his girlfriend can’t add.”

chapters.desc: For her first birthday as his girlfriend, Zhou Yichen plans everything—and remembers something she forgot.
chapters.title: The Birthday Where Zhou Yichen Lost Financial Control
chapters.epigraph: “He remembered the things she forgot she wanted.”
chapters.content:
Three days before Lin Xiaoran’s birthday, Chen Yuhao noticed something suspicious.

“…Why are there shopping bags in your locker.”

Zhou Yichen closed the locker calmly.

“Nothing.”

“Those are luxury brand bags.”

“Basketball-related.”

“Are basketballs sold in jewellery stores now?”

Nearby, Tang Meilin looked exhausted.

“He’s gone.”

“What.”

“He entered rich devoted boyfriend territory.”

Zhou Yichen had been acting strange all week—checking his phone constantly, leaving practice early, ignoring his teammates. At one point he’d turned down basketball plans because he had “important things to prepare.” Terrifying. Finally, Yuhao cornered him at break.

“What did you buy her.”

“Nothing excessive.”

Silence.

“…That answer means it’s excessive.”

Yichen looked away. A tiny pause. A bad sign.

“She mentioned wanting it once.”

“Oh no.”

“And forgot about it afterward.”

“Oh NO.”

Yuhao clutched his chest.

“This man is too far gone.”

“Stop being weird.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Xiaoran had no idea, mostly because she’d spent the whole week invested in one question: would Zhou Yichen do something romantic? Not expensive. Not huge. Just… romantic. It was their first birthday together. Then, on Friday night, she got a message.

Yichen: Tomorrow morning. Wear something comfortable.

Xiaoran screamed into her pillow.

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday arrived with suspiciously perfect weather—warm sun, a soft breeze, a bright blue sky. Romantic conditions. Xiaoran spent ninety minutes choosing an outfit. Something cute but effortless, which took tremendous effort. She settled on a pale blue dress with tiny ribbons at the sleeves. Soft. Pretty. Very girlfriend. Then the doorbell rang, and the second Xiaoran opened the door, her heartbeat betrayed her. Zhou Yichen looked unfair today. Black long-sleeve shirt. Relaxed jeans. Hair a little messy from the wind, one hand in his pocket. And the way his eyes went soft the second he saw her.

Yichen blinked.

“…You dressed up.”

“You noticed too fast.”

“You’re pretty.”

Xiaoran turned around.

“No. Restart the greeting.”

Yichen laughed softly near the doorway.

“Okay. Take two.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first half of the date was surprisingly normal: lunch, wandering downtown, holding hands, stealing each other’s drinks. At one point Xiaoran dragged him into a stationery shop and judged notebooks for twenty minutes.

“This one looks smart.”

“It’s paper.”

“You don’t understand aesthetics.”

Later, they wandered through crowded shopping streets, sunlight bouncing off the shop windows, a comfortable quiet between them. Until Yichen stopped walking.

“Hm?”

“Wait here.”

Before she could investigate, he disappeared into a nearby store and came back a few minutes later with another shopping bag.

“…What’s that.”

“Nothing.”

“That’s a boyfriend lie.”

“It’s your birthday.”

“That doesn’t answer the question.”

Yichen just smiled and kept walking, which only made her more curious.

✦ ✦ ✦

As evening came, Yichen took her to the riverside—golden sunset on the water, street musicians playing, warm lights coming on along the walkway. Beautiful. Dangerously romantic. Then Xiaoran noticed a small cake box on a reserved table by the river. Beside it, her favourite flowers.

“…You planned this?”

“Hm.”

“By yourself?”

“I had help.”

“From who.”

“Unfortunately Yuhao.”

Xiaoran sat down, staring at it all. Nothing extravagant. Warm lights, a pretty view, a small cake, the exact desserts she liked. Somehow that made it feel even more sincere.

“This is really pretty.”

Yichen relaxed a little. He’d spent two weeks planning this—not because Xiaoran demanded grand gestures, but because she deserved the effort.

“Oh wait.”

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes suspiciously.

“…What’s inside the shopping bag.”

Silence. Yichen looked away. Another bad sign.

“Open it later.”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“NOW.”

With visible resignation, Zhou Yichen handed over the bag, and Xiaoran froze. Inside was the necklace she’d pointed at MONTHS ago while window shopping—a delicate silver chain with a tiny star charm. She’d looked at it and said—

“Way too expensive.”

And then she’d forgotten all about it. Apparently, Zhou Yichen hadn’t.

“You remembered?”

Yichen looked oddly calm, which usually meant he was nervous.

“You liked it.”

“That was months ago.”

He shrugged. But his heart was already racing. He’d worried about this gift too much—too romantic, maybe, too serious. The moment Xiaoran touched the necklace and her eyes went soft, relief hit him all at once.

“I wanted your first birthday gift from me to be something you’d keep for a long time.”

Silence. Xiaoran’s eyes went suspiciously watery.

“Oh no. Don’t cry,” Yichen sighed immediately.

“I’m NOT crying.”

“You literally are.”

“It’s because you’re acting too much like a husband.”

“…That’s your complaint?”

“Yes.”

Yichen laughed despite himself, and that familiar laugh made the evening warmer. He held out his hand.

Xiaoran leaned closer. Carefully, Yichen lifted the necklace and fastened it around her neck himself—warm fingers brushing her skin, close enough that she could smell his cologne, close enough to hear him breathe. Her heart started racing too. Then, near her ear—

“Pretty.”

That one word was too much. The necklace mattered less than the way he looked at her wearing it, like she was precious long before the gift was.

“Do you like it?”

Xiaoran looked at him for a long second—the boy who remembered things she forgot herself, who planned, who spoiled her endlessly without ever making it feel heavy. Her chest felt too full. Before Yichen could say anything else, Xiaoran stood up and hugged him tight. No warning. No speech. Just her arms around him and her face pressed against his shoulder. Yichen froze for a second. Then his arms closed around her waist, holding her steady. The riverside lights shimmered around them while music drifted through the evening air.

“I really like it,” Xiaoran mumbled against his shoulder.

Yichen smiled softly near her hair.

“Hm.”

“You’re too good at this boyfriend thing. My heart can’t take it.”

He laughed—the soft laugh only she ever heard this close. Xiaoran pulled back a little, hands still loosely gripping his sleeves, eyes suspiciously emotional. Then she tugged him down and kissed his cheek. Soft. Quick. Enough to make Zhou Yichen go completely still. Lin Xiaoran almost never started things this directly. Usually she got shy halfway through. But maybe it was the lights, or her birthday, or just loving him too much—she kissed him first anyway. Then her face went red.

“…Oh no.”

Yichen looked at her, quietly. Something in his eyes had changed—softer, darker, more focused. And Xiaoran realised that kissing her boyfriend out of nowhere beside a romantic river might have been a tactical error.

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“How am I looking at you.”

“Like you’re planning crimes.”

Yichen laughed under his breath before pulling her back closer lightly by the waist again.

“Too late.”

“Zhou Yichen, this is MY birthday. You’re supposed to behave.”

“No one told me that rule.”

Xiaoran hid her burning face against his chest again while Yichen held her there. With the necklace resting against her skin and his heartbeat steady under her ear, Lin Xiaoran felt dangerously happy. Too happy. Which usually meant Zhou Yichen was about to make things worse. She was right. After a few quiet seconds, Yichen tilted her chin up, slow and careful.

“…What?” she whispered.

Yichen just looked at her. The riverside lights caught in his eyes, the night breeze moved around them, and he looked unbearably handsome again.

“You kissed me first.”

“That was a mistake.”

“You should forget it happened.”

“I don’t think I will.”

Xiaoran’s ears went even redder. The way he was looking at her felt unfair—focused, warm, like she was the only thing worth paying attention to tonight.

“Can I kiss you back?”

He usually just kissed her by now—her forehead, quick kisses, small affections. Asking like this felt much more dangerous. Much more intimate. Xiaoran forgot how speaking worked.

“…You’re asking?”

“I’m being polite.”

“That’s somehow worse.”

Yichen laughed under his breath.

“Hm?”

That stupid calm hm, the one that always made her surrender. So, weakly—

“…Okay.”

Yichen’s whole face softened. Then he leaned down slowly—enough time for Xiaoran to panic, for her fingers to tighten on his sleeves, for her heartbeat to become completely ridiculous. His lips met hers—warm, gentle, unhurried, like he wanted the moment to last. That made it worse. Zhou Yichen kissed exactly the way he loved her. Patiently. Carefully. Completely. Xiaoran melted, eyes closing, his hand resting light and steady at her waist. The city lights blurred behind them, music drifted from somewhere by the river, and for a few quiet seconds nothing else existed but him.

Then he kissed her again, a little deeper. Still gentle. Still controlled. But enough to make Xiaoran’s knees feel unreliable. He pulled back slowly, their foreheads almost touching, both of them breathing quieter now. Xiaoran immediately hid her face against his chest again. Total failure.

“…I can’t survive this birthday,” she mumbled.

Yichen laughed while holding her closer.

“You started it.”

“I was being affectionate.”

He smiled against her hair.

“Happy birthday, Xiaoran.”

Hearing him say it like that, still holding her by the glowing river, felt more special than every gift combined.

chapters.desc: Xiaoran wants to follow him to university. Yichen says no. Their first real fight about the future.
chapters.title: Somewhere Between Your Dream and Mine
chapters.epigraph: “Love isn’t following someone. It’s finding the place where both of you can grow.”
chapters.content:
The fight started because they both loved each other too much, which felt deeply unfair.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I said I can follow you.”

“And I said no.”

Lin Xiaoran stood in the empty classroom after school, glaring at Zhou Yichen. Outside, the evening sun stretched across the desks. Inside, it was war. University applications were real now. Painfully real. And the closer the deadlines got, the more careful Zhou Yichen became around her. Too careful. The kind of careful that got on Xiaoran’s nerves.

“I don’t understand why you’re acting difficult,” she complained.

“I’m not.”

“You literally ARE.”

“No, I’m thinking realistically.”

“And realistically. I can just apply wherever you go,” Xiaoran crossed her arms stubbornly.

Silence.

“No.”
