Too fast. Too firm. Xiaoran’s chest tightened. That hurt more than she expected.

“…Why not.”

Yichen sighed and pressed his fingers to his temple. This conversation scared him too—more than basketball, more than entrance exams—because their future suddenly felt fragile in ways neither of them understood yet.

“Because I don’t want you choosing your future around me.”

“But you literally said you were considering MY applications.”

“That’s different.”

“How is that different?!”

Good question. Terrible question. The real answer was simple: Zhou Yichen trusted himself to give things up for her. He didn’t want her giving things up for him. Not this young, and not before she’d even figured herself out. Xiaoran looked upset now. Not dramatic upset. Hurt. Yichen immediately regretted his tone.

“I’m not saying I don’t want us together.”

“But that’s what it sounds like.”

“It’s not.”

“Then explain properly.”

For a moment, neither of them spoke. Somewhere outside, a basketball thudded against the court. Then Yichen sat down in one of the chairs by the window, tired and thoughtful. After a second, Xiaoran sat beside him. Still upset. But closer anyway. Always closer anyway.

“When I think about university,” Yichen admitted, “I get scared too.”

Xiaoran blinked. Zhou Yichen almost never admitted to being afraid. Especially not this calmly. Then he said—

“What if basketball stops working out. What if classes become too hard. What if we fight more. What if we grow differently.”

His voice was steady, but she could hear the uncertainty underneath. Her anger softened. He wasn’t pushing her away. He was scared of failing both their futures somehow.

“I don’t even know what dream I want yet,” she admitted.

It was embarrassing to admit. Everyone else seemed so sure—medicine, business, law, engineering. Xiaoran changed interests depending on her mood and whatever drama she was watching. Last month it was interior design. Before that, psychology. Before THAT, she’d nearly decided to open a café because the aesthetic felt healing.

“I just know I want you there.”

It made Yichen’s chest ache, because he wanted the same thing. More than anything. He took her hand carefully between both of his.

“Okay. Then let’s think about this differently,” he murmured.

Xiaoran looked at him.

“How.”

“We stop choosing FOR each other.”

Silence.

“And instead?”

“We choose somewhere both of us can grow.”

Something gentler than sacrifice or compromise. Something shared. Then Yichen pulled a folded brochure from his bag. Xiaoran blinked in confusion.

“…What’s this.”

“A university halfway between our options.”

She looked down at it. A strong school. Good academics. A decent basketball program. Not the farthest, not the closest. Balanced. Then Xiaoran looked back up.

“You researched this already?”

“Hm.”

“When?”

“Last week.”

He really had been thinking about it seriously. Not avoiding it. Trying to solve it on his own.

“You idiot,” she whispered.

“Hm.”

“You made me think we were breaking up.”

“We were discussing universities.”

“Same thing.”

Yichen laughed under his breath.

“It doesn’t have to be this exact place.”

“But…”

“I just wanted us to find a middle ground together,” Yichen said.

That sentence fixed something in Xiaoran. Suddenly the future didn’t feel like losing or following. It felt shared—something they’d build slowly, together.

“What if we both get rejected.”

“We’ll cry. Then we apply somewhere else.”

“What if we become long distance anyway?”

Yichen looked at her calmly.

“Then we try.”

He said it so simply. Not because life was simple, but because loving her wasn’t something he ever questioned first.

“I don’t care if we end up in different cities temporarily. I just don’t want either of us regretting our choices later,” he admitted.

Silence. Xiaoran leaned against his shoulder. Warm evening light filled the classroom, and for the first time in weeks, the future stopped feeling like something trying to pull them apart.

“You know what’s annoying?”

“Hm?”

“You sound mature today. It’s annoying.”

Yichen smiled slightly. Meanwhile Xiaoran looked down at the brochure again before mumbling—

“…I like this school.”

Yichen’s fingers tightened gently around hers.

“Me too.”

Then after a second—casually—

“If we go there together,” Xiaoran said thoughtfully, “you’ll still buy me snacks, right?”

Yichen looked deeply unimpressed.

“This is your priority?”

“Yes.”

“…Then yes.”

Immediate satisfaction.

“Okay. Now I feel ready for adulthood.” Xiaoran nodded seriously.

chapters.desc: Forty days before the gaokao, a sticky note appears under her pencil case. Every morning after that, the number changes.
chapters.title: Forty Days Left
chapters.epigraph: “It’s never not been there.”
chapters.content:
The countdown began with a sticky note. Lin Xiaoran found it on a Monday morning at the end of April, tucked under the corner of her pencil case: a small yellow square with 40 written in the middle, and under it, in handwriting she knew better than her own, Forty days. Don’t panic.

She looked at the desk beside hers. Zhou Yichen was taking out his chemistry book as if he had only just arrived, which was a lie, because his bag was already hung on the back of his chair and his water bottle was already half empty.

She held up the note. “What’s this?”

“A note.”

“I can see it’s a note.”

“Then I don’t think there’s a problem.”

“Did you put it there?”

“Maybe.”

“Why?”

He nodded at the number. “Because there are forty days left.”

“I know there are forty days left.”

“Good. Then it’s working.”

“You’re making a countdown?”

“So are you.”

He tipped his head at the little calendar she’d taped to the inside of her desk lid, where she had been crossing off days in red pen since the first of the month, and hadn’t told him, and hadn’t thought he’d seen.

“We’re doing the same thing,” he said.

“Mine’s more organised.”

“Yours is a calendar. Mine has a message.”

She folded the note in half and put it in her pencil case, and he watched her do it with a look she pretended not to see.

“Don’t lose it.”

“I won’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After that, there was one every morning. He was always in before her, and the note was always there under the pencil case. On Sundays, when school was shut, the number arrived by text at seven, with nothing else, and she would send back a thumbs-up and go back to sleep.

39. One day closer. One chapter at a time.

38. Eat breakfast.

37. You know more than you think you do.

36. Don’t spend twenty minutes worrying about one question.

“That one’s personal,” she said, holding it up at him.

“That one’s accurate.”

She started keeping them in an envelope in her desk. On the morning of thirty-five she got in early, for once, before him, and slid a note of her own into the front pocket of his schoolbag where it hung on his chair.

35. You eat breakfast too.

He found it at the first break. He turned round in his seat, holding it between two fingers.

“What’s this?”

“A note.”

“I can see it’s a note.”

“Then I don’t think there’s a problem,” she said sweetly, and he stared at her for a second and then laughed out loud in the middle of the classroom, which he almost never did, and Rong Hao turned round to see what had happened.

34. I ate breakfast. Did you?

She wrote underneath: Yes. Mum checked. Mum also asked who leaves you notes.

33. Good. Keep listening to her.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the morning of thirty, the note wasn’t under her pencil case. It was in Mr. Pan’s hand.

The self-study supervisor patrolled the corridors before homeroom every morning with a thermos and an expression of permanent suspicion. At ten to seven he had looked through the window of Class 3 and seen Zhou Yichen alone in the empty classroom, bent over Lin Xiaoran’s desk, doing something to her pencil case. He had drawn his own conclusions.

He walked into morning reading, went to the front, and held the yellow square up between finger and thumb. Xiaoran felt the blood leave her face. Beside her, Yichen sat straight.

“Thirty. Sleep is also revision,” Mr. Pan read aloud.

He looked at the class over the top of his glasses. Thirty-eight students looked back. Nobody breathed.

“Correct,” said Mr. Pan.

He walked down the aisle, put the note on Xiaoran’s desk without looking at either of them, and left. He never mentioned it again.

Tang Meilin put her head down on her arms and stayed there until the bell. Chen Yuhao, behind them, made a sound like a kettle. Xiaoran put that note in a separate pocket of the envelope, and that evening, in self-study, she leaned against Yichen’s shoulder for the full two hours, which Mr. Pan walked past four times and pretended not to see.

✦ ✦ ✦

As the days went by, the notes got less about the countdown and more about the small things.

29. You don’t have to get every question right.

26. Your handwriting goes downhill when you’re tired. Go to bed.

21. I’ve watched you work harder this month than I’ve worked all year.

That one she read twice, and then she turned and looked at him, and he was doing physics with his ears red, and she didn’t say anything because if she had said anything she would have cried in the middle of morning reading.

She waited until evening self-study, when the room was quiet and Mr. Pan was at the far end with his thermos, and then she pushed her chair a few centimetres closer to his and whispered, “That’s not true.”

“What isn’t?”

“Twenty-one. You work harder than anyone. You did physics on the bus to the semifinal.”

“I did physics on the bus because Yuhao was singing.”

“You did physics at the noodle shop on Saturday.”

“The noodles were slow. I’ve watched you, Xiaoran. You used to put your pen down after twenty minutes and draw a cat. Now you don’t put it down at all. You fell asleep on your history book on Thursday and woke up with a date printed backwards on your cheek.” He didn’t look up.

“Which date?”

“1911.”

She put her hand to her cheek. “You didn’t tell me!”

“You looked very revolutionary.”

She laughed, too loudly, and Mr. Pan looked up from the far end of the room, and she bent over her book. But under the desk she found his hand and held on to it, tight, and after a moment he turned his over so their palms fitted.

“You did that. That’s all twenty-one means,” he said, low, to the physics book.

She didn’t let go of his hand for the rest of self-study, and did her history reading one-handed, turning the pages with her elbow when she had to.

They were both busier than they had ever been. The teachers piled on practice papers. Their conversations shrank to homework and formulas and have you eaten. But they still walked to the gate together every evening, her arm through his, and on the bad days she put her forehead against his back in the queue at the canteen and stood there like that, and he let her, and on his bad days he put his chin on her hair at the gate for a minute before he let her go. They didn’t need every minute. They only made sure they didn’t disappear from each other’s days.

On the morning of fifteen there was no number. Just a sentence.

When this is over, we’ll have time to do something other than study.

At the gate that evening she said, “What’s the plan?”

“What plan?”

“For after.”

“We haven’t discussed it.”

“Then discuss it.”

“What do you want to do?”

“Sleep.”

“Reasonable.”

“Eat something nice.”

“Also reasonable.”

“Go somewhere without textbooks. And you’re not allowed to talk about training.”

“That’s very restrictive.”

“One day. One whole day,” she said.

“One day. Let’s get through these fifteen first,” he agreed. He took her hand and held it in his coat pocket all the way to her bus stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the morning of twelve there was no note.

She lifted her pencil case. Then her textbooks. Then her whole bag. She checked under the desk, and under Meilin’s desk, and was on her way to the bin when Meilin caught her wrist.

“It’s one note.”

“It’s never not been there.”

“Maybe he overslept.”

“He doesn’t oversleep. He’s never overslept in his life.” She looked at his empty chair. His bag wasn’t on it.

He hadn’t overslept. Halfway through first period the classroom door opened and he came in with a mask over his face and a voice like gravel, apologised to the teacher, and sat down beside her. On the back of his left hand, in blue pen, was written 12, and underneath, smaller, fever, clinic, sorry.

“Go home,” she whispered, horrified.

“After lunch. My mother’s coming.”

“You’ve got a fever! Why are you here?”

“Twelve days left,” he said, as if that explained everything, and to him it did.

She put her hand flat on his forehead under the desk, felt how hot it was, and took her hand back and glared at him, and at lunch she sat with him in the corridor by the window with his head on her shoulder until his mother’s car came, and walked him down to the gate holding his arm.

The next morning there were two notes. 12 and 11. The 12 said: Don’t come to school with a fever. (Do as I say, not as I do.)

✦ ✦ ✦

7. One week. Trust yourself.

She wrote underneath: I do. Mostly.

6. Mostly is enough.

She laughed so loud that Meilin looked over and read it upside down.

“Is this the daily boyfriend correspondence?”

“Don’t read it.”

“I didn’t read it. I just have eyes. If someone left me notes every morning, I’d probably marry him.” Meilin leaned back in her chair.

“Don’t say things like that!”

“Then stop looking so happy about it.”

3. Three days. Don’t let the last stretch scare you.

It’s not the last stretch. It’s the actual exam.

2. Then just do the question in front of you. Not the whole exam.

On the last morning there was one more note.

1. Tomorrow, just do your best. I’ll see you after.

She looked at it. Then she turned to him and said, “Will you?”

“Will I what?”

“See me after.”

“I’ll be at your gate. Your exam finishes at five. Mine finishes at five. I’ll be there by half past,” he said.

“It’s across the city.”

“Half past,” he said.

There were thirty-five notes in the envelope by then, and five text messages she had screenshotted and printed at the shop by the gate for one yuan each, so the set was complete. She had counted twice. She put the envelope in her drawer at home, under her pyjamas, where her mother would never look, and laid four pens out on top of her admission card, in case three of them stopped working.

chapters.desc: The gaokao: two exam venues across the city, one fraction question, and a taxi that took thirty-one minutes.
chapters.title: Two Days in June
chapters.epigraph: “You always know the first step. Write that.”
chapters.content:
The night before the gaokao, Lin Xiaoran packed her exam bag four times. Admission ticket. ID card. Two black pens, two spare black pens, two pencils, an eraser shaped like a strawberry that she had been told wasn’t technically allowed and was bringing anyway for morale. A clear plastic pencil case, because the rules said clear. A watch without a screen, because the rules said no screens. She unpacked it all, checked it, and packed it again.

At 9:30 her phone lit up.

Yichen: Stop repacking your bag.

Xiaoran: how do you know

Yichen: Because it’s 9:30.

Xiaoran: that’s not evidence

Yichen: Call me.

She called. He picked up on the first ring, sitting at his desk with his study glasses pushed up into his hair, a single lamp on behind him. He didn’t look nervous. He never looked nervous. It was one of the most irritating things about him.

“What if I forget how fractions work,” she said, instead of hello.

“You won’t.”

“They’re arrogant. I told you. They think they’re better than whole numbers.”

“You scored a hundred on the final.”

“That was a different me. That me had you sitting beside her for three weeks.”

He was quiet for a second. “That me is still you. I didn’t do the test,” he said.

She pulled her knees up to her chest and didn’t answer, because there was a lump in her throat that had appeared out of nowhere. They weren’t even going to be in the same building tomorrow. The exam venues were assigned by student number: Xiaoran at the middle school on the east side, Yichen across the city near the river. She had looked it up on the map three times. Forty minutes by car.

“You’ll be fine,” he said.

“You can’t know that.”

“I know you. Go to sleep. Don’t look at notes.”

“I already put the notes away.”

“Where?”

“…Under my pillow.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

She moved them to her desk while he watched, then lay down with the phone on the pillow beside her. Neither of them hung up. At some point she fell asleep listening to him turn pages, and when she woke at six the call had ended just before twelve and there was one message.

Yichen: Eat breakfast. I’ll see you after math.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother drove her to the exam site herself. Mrs. Lin wasn’t a soft woman. She was an accountant, and she approached the gaokao the way she approached the end of the tax year: with a checklist, a thermos, and no patience for nonsense. On the way she quizzed Xiaoran on the contents of her bag without once looking away from the road.

“Admission ticket.”

“Yes.”

“ID.”

“Yes.”

“Pens.”

“Four.”

“Why four?”

“In case three stop working.”

Her mother sighed through her nose, which in Mrs. Lin meant she was trying not to laugh. Xiaoran’s father hadn’t come, because her father cried at things like this, and her mother had decided that crying outside an exam gate was bad for morale. Instead he had sent fourteen messages since six a.m., most of them stickers of cartoon rabbits holding banners. The street outside the school was already full. Parents three deep along the barrier. Police directing traffic. A row of mothers in red qipao for luck, a few fathers holding sunflowers. Someone had set up a tent handing out free water. When the gates opened, the students went in one by one past the ID check, and the parents stayed outside, holding thermoses, not talking much.

Before Xiaoran got out of the car, her mother reached over and straightened the collar of her shirt. It was the only soft thing she did all morning.

“Don’t leave anything blank. Even if you don’t know. Write something,” Mrs. Lin said.

“I know.”

“And don’t look at the clock every two minutes. You do that.”

“I don’t do that.”

Her mother just looked at her. Xiaoran got out of the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chinese in the morning was fine. Better than fine—the essay prompt was about a small thing that had changed how you saw someone, and Xiaoran wrote eight hundred words about a boy at an arcade who won a stuffed bunny out of a claw machine on the first try and then pretended it had been luck. She changed his name and the setting. She didn’t change the bunny. Math in the afternoon was a war.

She hit the first fraction question twenty minutes in and froze completely. Her mind went blank and white like a fresh page. The girl at the next desk was writing fast. The clock on the wall said 3:21. Don’t look at the clock every two minutes. She put her pen down. Closed her eyes for one breath. Then she heard it, absurdly clearly—a calm voice across a study table, three weeks before the final, pushing a sheet of paper back towards her: Slow down. You always know the first step. Write that.

She wrote the first step. Then the second. She didn’t finish every question. There was one near the end she only half understood, and she wrote everything she knew about it anyway, because her mother had said to, and because leaving it blank felt like giving up out loud. When the bell rang at five, her hand ached and her shirt was stuck to her back and she had no idea how it had gone.

She walked out into the sunlight with two hundred other students, and the crowd of parents outside surged against the barrier, and somewhere in the middle of all of it—Zhou Yichen was standing by the tent with the free water, holding a strawberry milk. Xiaoran stopped dead. He wasn’t supposed to be here. His exam had ended at the same time as hers, forty minutes away, across the river.

“How,” she said, when she reached him.

“Taxi.”

“You can’t have—it’s forty minutes—”

“Thirty-one. The driver was motivated. How was it?” He put the strawberry milk in her hands and studied her face.

She opened her mouth to say terrible, and what came out instead was:

“I didn’t leave anything blank.”

Something in his expression went soft.

“Good,” he said.

Behind him, Mrs. Lin was getting out of the car. She looked at Yichen. She looked at the strawberry milk. She looked at her daughter, who was obviously about to cry in public. Then she got back in the car and waited, and for once didn’t honk.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second day passed in a blur of English and science, and by the time the last bell rang on the evening of the eighth, Xiaoran didn’t feel happy or sad or relieved. She just felt empty, like someone had carefully poured everything out of her and set her down.

That night the four of them met at the noodle shop near school, because none of them could think of anywhere better. Yuhao ate three bowls and announced he would never read a book again. Meilin, who had already worked out her expected score to within five points, refused to tell anyone the number. Xiaoran fell asleep against Yichen’s shoulder halfway through her noodles and woke up to Yuhao filming her.

Afterward, Yichen walked her home. The streets smelled like rain that hadn’t come yet.

“It’s done,” she said, at her building’s gate.

“Hm.”

“Whatever happens, it’s done.”

“It is.”

She looked up at him. He had come straight from his own exam, crossed a city in a taxi, and stood outside a school gate in June heat with a strawberry milk going warm in his hand. He had never once told her he was nervous for himself.

“Were you scared? Today?” she asked.

He thought about it honestly, which was one of the things she loved about him.

“During my exam, no. Waiting outside your gate, a little,” he said.

“Why?”

“Because if it went badly, you’d have walked out alone.”

Xiaoran stared at him. Then she hugged him, hard, right there at the gate, where her father could absolutely see from the fourth-floor window and was absolutely watching.

“Thank you for the taxi,” she mumbled into his shirt.

“Thank the driver.”

“I’m thanking you.”

He rested his chin on her hair. “Then you’re welcome. Now go inside. Your dad is waving,” he said.

chapters.desc: Neither father goes to the gaokao. On the second evening, one of them takes out the rubbish.
chapters.title: Two Fathers
chapters.epigraph: “He brought her a strawberry milk.”
chapters.content:
Lin Hongwei didn’t go to the gaokao.

“I’m going. I’ll stand outside. Lots of fathers stand outside,” he had said in the kitchen three weeks before.

His wife had looked at him over the top of her reading glasses. “You cried at her primary school graduation.”

“That was different.”

“You cried when she got her ears pierced.”

“She was very brave.”

“You cried at the dentist. Her dentist. Not yours.”

“The dentist was rough with her.”

“You’re not going,” said Mrs. Lin, and turned a page of the electricity bill, and that was that.

So on the seventh of June, at half past six in the morning, he stood at the fourth-floor window in his vest and watched his wife’s car turn out of the compound with their daughter in the passenger seat, and then he went into the kitchen and made braised fish for a family of nine.

He had worked at the city water bureau for twenty-three years. He liked things that ran where they were supposed to. He didn’t know what to do with a day in which his only child was sitting in a room he couldn’t see, answering questions he couldn’t help her with. So he cooked. He cleaned the kitchen. He cooked again. At eleven he rang his wife.

“Is she in?”

“She’s in.”

“Did she have breakfast?”

“She had breakfast. She had two pens in her hand and two in her pocket and she gave me a thumbs-up at the door. Stop ringing me.”

At twelve he rang again.

“What now?”

“Is it hot there? It’s hot here. Is there shade?”

“Hongwei.”

“I’m only asking about the shade.”

“There’s shade,” said his wife, and hung up, and he stood in the kitchen with the phone and a pot of rice for nine and didn’t know what to do with either.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second evening, a little after five, his phone rang, and it was Xiaoran.

“Dad. It’s finished.”

“How was it?”

“Fine.”

“Fine?”

“Fine fine. Good fine. I don’t know. I don’t want to talk about it. We’re going for noodles. Me and Meilin and Yuhao and—” Her voice was hoarse and tired and somehow lighter than it had been for months.

“And the boy,” he said.

There was a pause on the line.

“Yes, and Yichen. He came by taxi from his venue. He got here before me. He had a strawberry milk,” she said.

“Of course he did,” said Lin Hongwei, and she laughed, a startled, exhausted laugh, and said she’d be home by half past nine.

He had known about the boy since March. His wife had told him in the end, in bed, with the light off, so that he couldn’t see her face and she couldn’t see his.

“The one who rings at nine. It isn’t a study group,” she had said.

“I know it isn’t a study group.”

“You do?”

“Study groups don’t ring at exactly nine o’clock every night for two weeks while she’s at your mother’s. And study groups don’t talk to your mother for forty minutes about persimmons.”

“How do you know about the persimmons?”

“Your mother told me. At New Year. She said he was a very polite study group.”

They had lain there in the dark for a while.

“Are you all right?” his wife had asked.

“I’m thinking,” he’d said, and she had passed him a tissue in the dark without being asked.

He had decided eventually that a boy who rang at the same time every night and was polite to his mother-in-law was probably not the worst thing that could happen. He hadn’t met the boy. He’d seen him once from this window, at a distance of four floors, carrying an umbrella.

At half past nine he was at the window again.

“You’re going to wear a groove in the floor,” said his wife from the sofa.

“I’m checking the weather.”

“It’s June. The weather is hot.”

“They’re there,” he said.

She came and stood beside him. Down at the building door, under the streetlight, their daughter was talking with her hands, the way she did when she was too tired to make sense, and the boy was standing still, listening to her, with his whole face. Then she put her arms round him, hard, and he put his chin down on her hair as if he’d done it many times and still thought about it every time.

“Oh,” said Mrs. Lin, under her breath.

Lin Hongwei raised his hand and waved, because his daughter would want to know he was there. The boy saw it first. He said something, and Xiaoran let go and looked up and waved back, embarrassed, and went in.

They listened to her on the stairs, four flights, slow. The door. “Shoes,” said Mrs. Lin. “I know,” said their daughter. The bathroom door. The water.

He went back to the window, because he had seen something else and wanted to be sure. At the compound gate, under the plane trees, a dark car had pulled in and stopped with its headlights off. The boy hadn’t walked away. The boy had got into it.

Lin Hongwei looked at the car. Then he went into the kitchen, opened the cupboard under the sink, and looked at the rubbish bag, which was perhaps a third full.

“Where are you going?” said his wife, when he came through with it.

“Rubbish.”

She looked at the bag. She looked at him, in his vest and slippers. She looked, at the window.

“Take your time,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Mingyuan hadn’t gone to the gaokao either.

“Don’t come. If you’re outside, I’ll think about you being outside,” his son had said at breakfast a week before. Not unkindly.

“Lots of fathers wait outside.”

“I know. I’ll think about all of them.”

“Let him be. He knows what he needs,” said his wife, putting a boiled egg in front of each of them.

“What if he needs a lift?”

“Then he’ll ring you. I’ll ring you. I promise,” said Yichen.

So Zhou Mingyuan went to his office instead, closed the door, and spent two days not reading the same quarterly report. At five past nine on the second evening, his phone lit up.

Yichen: Can you pick me up from Xiaoran’s building? I don’t think I can walk home.

He drove across the city faster than he would ever have admitted, and parked at the compound gate under the plane trees, and his son came out of the dark and got into the passenger seat.

“Thank you.”

“How was it?”

“Fine.”

“Fine?”

“I’ll tell you tomorrow,” Yichen said, and was asleep before the seatbelt clicked.

Two days of exams. A taxi across the city in the June heat between his last paper and her gate, with a strawberry milk. Noodles. Whatever had happened by her building door. He had his head against the window and his mouth slightly open, and he looked twelve years old.

Zhou Mingyuan didn’t start the engine. He sat in the dark with his hands on the wheel looking at his son. Then he got out, because it was a warm night and his back hurt, and stood by the car.

A man came out of the building carrying a bag of rubbish.

He was in his fifties, in a vest and slippers, and he walked to the bins by the gate slowly, the way people walk when the rubbish isn’t the reason. He put the bag in the bin. He looked at the car. He looked at the boy asleep in the passenger seat, and then at the man standing beside it, and Zhou Mingyuan understood who he was at the same moment the other man understood who he was.

There was a pause in which neither of them knew what to do with his hands.

“Zhou. Yichen’s father,” said Zhou Mingyuan.

“Lin. Xiaoran’s.”

They shook hands over the bonnet. Lin Hongwei’s hand was damp; he had been washing a great many dishes.

“Long two days,” said Zhou Mingyuan.

“Long two days,” said Lin Hongwei.

They both looked through the window at the sleeping boy. Somewhere in the compound a television was playing the evening news, and a woman on a balcony was calling a child in.

“Did he say how it went?” Lin Hongwei asked.

“He said it was fine. He says everything is fine.”

“So does she.”

“Do you believe her?”

“No,” said Lin Hongwei. “Do you believe him?”

“No.”

They considered this, two men who had each, separately, been told for two days that everything was fine.

“He came by taxi. From his own venue. To meet her,” said Zhou Mingyuan.

“I know. She told us. Twice. He brought her a strawberry milk.” Lin Hongwei looked at the boy a little longer.

“That’s what he does. Since December before last. Every morning. His mother thought he’d started drinking it himself. She bought him a crate,” said Zhou Mingyuan, as if it were a family failing.

Lin Hongwei made a sound that might, in another man, have been a laugh. “Xiaoran’s stopped eating breakfast twice. Because of the milk.”

“I’ll tell him.”

“Don’t. She’d know I said something,” said Lin Hongwei.

That was all. He nodded once, and said, “Drive carefully,” and Zhou Mingyuan said, “Good night,” and Lin Hongwei went back across the dark courtyard in his slippers and didn’t look back, although on the fourth floor a curtain moved.

Zhou Mingyuan got into the car and started the engine as gently as he could, so as not to wake his son.

Yichen woke at the second red light, all at once, the way he always had as a child.

“Was I asleep long?”

“Nine minutes.”

His son looked out at the road, and then at him. “Did anything happen?”

Zhou Mingyuan considered the question. “A man took out his rubbish,” he said, and the light changed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, Mrs. Lin was on the sofa with her feet up for the first time in two days. Xiaoran was in the shower, singing badly.

“Well?” said Mrs. Lin.

Her husband sat down next to her.

“His father,” he said, after some thought, “drives a very clean car.”

Mrs. Lin waited.

“And the boy was asleep. He was so tired he couldn’t keep his eyes open. And he still walked her to the door first.”

She looked at him. His eyes were wet. She handed him a tissue from the box on the coffee table, which she had brought out of the bedroom at eight o’clock for exactly this reason.

The bathroom door opened and Xiaoran came out with a towel round her hair, pink and damp and singing, and stopped.

“Dad? Why are your eyes red?”

“Onions,” said Lin Hongwei.

“We had fish.”

“Fish onions.”

She looked at her mother. Her mother looked at the television. Xiaoran shrugged and padded off to bed, still singing, which she hadn’t done since February.

Neither of them told her. Mrs. Lin, who had been told about the car, kept it to herself on principle, and across the city Mrs. Zhou was told nothing at all, because her husband had decided it didn’t count.

chapters.desc: Eight days until the scores come out, a girl who refreshes the page every four minutes, and a capybara café.
chapters.title: Waiting for Scores
chapters.epigraph: “Do you think we’ll be okay?”
chapters.content:
Sixteen days after the gaokao, with eight still to go before the scores came out, Lin Xiaoran had developed a habit that was beginning to worry everyone around her.

She checked her phone. She refreshed the results page. She checked the official announcement schedule, which hadn’t changed since it was published. She refreshed the results page again.

“They might come out early this year. Half the class is posting estimated marks in the group chat. Rong Hao found a website that says it can predict the release time to the minute,” she told Zhou Yichen on the phone at nine in the morning.

“Have you eaten?”

“That’s unrelated.”

“Have you?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Breakfast.”

“What breakfast?”

She sighed. “A sandwich. Half a sandwich. Some of a sandwich.”

“Good. Eat the rest of it.”

She could hear him moving around his room, opening a drawer, closing it. He sounded maddeningly rested.

“Yichen. Do you think they’ll come out today?”

“I don’t know.”

“What if they do?”

“Then we look.”

“What if the website crashes?”

“Then we wait.”

“What if—”

“Xiaoran. You’ve checked that page six times since I rang.” His voice was calm and a bit amused.

“How do you know?”

“Because you’ve told me six times. Come out with me tomorrow.”

“Where?”

“Somewhere.”

“That’s not a place.”

“A café.”

“What kind of café?”

“You’ll see. Two metro lines and a short walk. You’re going to sit down and look at animals. I’ll be at your gate at ten.” Another pause, during which she was almost sure he was smiling.

He hung up before she could interrogate him, which she found deeply unfair, and then she checked the results page again.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten the next morning he was at her compound gate under the plane trees, standing a careful distance from the door of her building, because her mother was home and he hadn’t yet been introduced to her mother in any way that counted.

She came out in a cardigan and a skirt with her small shoulder bag. Her phone was already in her hand.

He looked at it, then at her. “Good morning.”

“Good morning. Where are we going?”

“Metro.”

“You’re being suspicious.”

“Thank you.”

She held his hand on the metro, and leaned into his shoulder when they got a seat, and checked her phone only twice, which he counted aloud each time. They changed lines once and walked ten minutes down a street of closed bicycle shops, and stopped outside a small café tucked behind a dry cleaner’s. Through the window she could see people sitting on cushions around low tables.

She read the sign. She looked at him. She read the sign again.

“Capybara?”

“That’s what it says.”

Months ago, on a bench after practice, she had asked him whether he would still love her if she turned into a capybara, and he had thought about it for an unreasonably long time before saying yes.

“You remembered.”

“It took me a long time to answer. I felt I owed you.”

Her whole face lit up, and she dragged him through the door by the hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside it was warm and quiet. In a fenced area at the back, four capybaras sat about on wooden platforms looking as if they had never had a worry in their lives.

“Oh, look at it. That one,” Xiaoran breathed.

“I see it.”

“It’s so round.”

“Yes.”

“It looks like nothing has ever gone wrong for it.”

“That’s why I brought you here,” he said, and she turned and looked at him before the staff member came over with a cup of pellets and a set of rules.

She read the rules with total seriousness, washed her hands with total seriousness, and crouched down by the fence holding out a pellet on her flat palm, the way the sign said. The round one considered her. Then it ambled over and took the pellet with a soft, whiskery mouth and stayed, leaning its whole weight against the fence next to her knee.

“It’s leaning on me. Yichen. It’s leaning,” she whispered, as if it might hear and stop.

“I know. I’m taking a picture.”

“Don’t take a picture, look at it!”

“I’m looking at you,” he said, and showed her the screen: her crouching by the fence, beaming at the capybara with her whole face, a stray pellet stuck to her cardigan.

“Send it to me.”

“Later.”

She reached for her own phone. He held out his hand.

“What?”

“Your phone.”

“Why?”

“Because we’re here.”

She looked at the capybara. She looked at him. “Are you confiscating it?”

“Temporarily.”

“What if the results come out?”

“Then you’ll find out in an hour.”

“What if someone messages me?”

“They’ll wait.”

“What if—”

He kept his hand held out. She looked at it. Then she sighed so heavily that a man at the next table looked over, and put the phone in his palm.

“Don’t read my messages.”

“I won’t.”

“Don’t turn it off.”

“I won’t.”

“If the results come out, tell me immediately.”

“I will.”

He put it in the inside pocket of his jacket and zipped the pocket up, and she pointed at him. “You’re responsible for that.”

“Understood.”

“Very responsible.”

“Go and see your friend,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next hour went faster than any hour since the exam. She fed the capybaras. She watched one of them fall asleep in a patch of sun with its chin on another one’s back. She spent a long time arguing with him about whether they looked more like enormous guinea pigs or small, unusually peaceful bears, and he took the guinea pig side purely to annoy her, and when she copied the capybara’s expression, perfectly calm, eyes half shut, he took another photograph and said, “Peaceful. It’s frightening.”

“Then I should be a capybara.”

“You’d get bored. You’d have to sit still all day.”

“So would you.”

“I’d be a very fast capybara. Training every morning,” he said.

They ordered drinks and a plate of small cakes and sat on cushions by the window, and she leaned against his side with her shoes off and her feet tucked under her, and for a while she didn’t look at the clock or reach for her bag. She was still thinking about the scores. Of course she was. But they had moved over and made a bit of room.

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

“Do you think we’ll be okay?”

He looked at her. She wasn’t asking about the capybaras.

“Whatever the results are?”

“Yes.”

He took his time, which was the thing she loved most about him and found most unbearable. “I think there might be choices to make. Some might be hard. But we both worked, and we’ll deal with whatever comes.”

“What if I don’t get the course I want?”

“Then we look at the others.”

“What if I have to go somewhere far away?”

“Then we work out how to manage it.”

“You’re not worried?”

“Of course I’m worried. I’m not made of stone. But worrying today won’t change them. And I don’t want you to spend eight days being frightened of something that hasn’t happened yet.” He found her hand on the cushion between them.

She looked down at their hands. “Okay.”

“Besides,” he said, “you’ve got an important job today.”

“What job?”

“Keeping the round one company.”

She laughed, and turned her face into his shoulder, and stayed there. Then she lifted her head.

“Wait. What about you?”

“What about me?”

“Your score. You never talk about it. Have you checked the page?”

He hesitated for a fraction of a second too long.

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Once.”

“When?”

“Last night. At two.”

“At two in the morning?”

“I couldn’t sleep. I don’t need a big number. I need one number. The program will wait for me if I go to university first, but only if the university is a good one. And Huaining’s business school takes the top six percent in the province, and I was ninth in our class in the last mock.” He looked out of the window, at the dry cleaner’s sign across the street.

“You were ninth because the chemistry paper was unfair. Everyone said so.”

“The gaokao doesn’t care what everyone said.”

She looked at him, at the calm face that had been telling her all morning not to worry, and climbed out of her own corner of the cushions and into his, so that she was more or less sitting in his lap, and put both arms round his neck.

“Xiaoran. There are people.”

“I don’t care. You’ve been carrying my phone in your pocket all day so I wouldn’t look at it, and you’ve been looking at yours at two in the morning.”

“That’s different.”

“It’s exactly the same. You’re going to be fine. You’re going to get your one number. And when you get it you’re going to tell me first, before your father, before Coach Wang.” She pressed her cheek against his.

“Before my mother?”

“Your mother can be second.”

He didn’t argue. After a while she felt his shoulders come down, the way they did after a long practice, and his arms went round her waist, and they sat there like that with the cakes going stale until the round capybara wandered over to the fence and stared at them, and she laughed into his neck.

“It’s judging us.”

“It’s jealous,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside, the afternoon was warm. He unzipped his pocket and gave her phone back, and she looked at the screen with her heart in her mouth: messages in the class group, two missed calls from Tang Meilin, and a notification from the results website.

She opened it so fast she nearly dropped the phone.

“Anything?”

“It’s a reminder. About the release schedule. Nothing yet.”

“All right.”

She put the phone in her bag, and zipped her bag, and he raised an eyebrow.

“You’re not checking again?”

“No, I’ll check tomorrow. At breakfast. After I’ve eaten a whole sandwich,” she said.

“A whole one.”

“An entire sandwich.”

At the corner she stopped and looked back at the café. “I want to come again. With Meilin. And I want to feed the round one again.”

“We can.”

Her legs had gone tired from crouching, and he flagged down a taxi instead of walking to the metro without asking whether she minded. She looked at him as he got in beside her.

“Thank you.”

“For what?”

“For bringing me. I didn’t check my phone for nearly two hours.”

“Very impressive.”

“Don’t make fun of me.”

“I’ll put it on your CV. Under achievements,” he said.

She fell asleep before they reached her street, for the first time in sixteen days, with her head on his shoulder and a smear of capybara pellet dust on her skirt. Yichen leaned forward and asked the driver, quietly, to turn the radio down.

chapters.desc: Applications are in, results are coming, and four friends are refreshing their portals in the same hour.
chapters.title: The Day Our Futures Arrived
chapters.epigraph: “Some futures arrive all at once.”
chapters.content:
Application season turned their whole class a little unhinged. Some students got motivational. Some got religious. Some got frighteningly competitive. Lin Xiaoran got dramatic. Naturally.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I think I’m going to faint.”

“You said that yesterday too.”

“This is a CONTINUOUS faint.”

Xiaoran was lying across the cafeteria table while Tang Meilin calmly worked through practice questions beside her. All around them, people were talking about applications—interviews, scholarships, majors, cities. The future was everywhere now, and it exhausted Xiaoran. She still couldn’t believe they were old enough for this. Then Zhou Yichen walked over with drinks—tall, calm, unfairly reliable-looking—and Xiaoran sat up a little, like a flower turning towards the sun. Embarrassing, honestly.

Yichen handed over her usual drink without a word and sat down beside her.

“You ate lunch?”

“Yes.”

“She ate fries,” Meilin corrected.

“Fries are a vegetable.”

“They are not,” Meilin said.

Yichen sighed, opened the lunchbox beside her, and put the chopsticks in her hand.

“Eat properly.”

Watching him do that without thinking made Xiaoran’s chest ache a little these days. University meant that one day, this wouldn’t happen every afternoon anymore. Yuhao dropped into the seat across from them.

“I’ve decided.”

“Hm?”

“If university life doesn’t give me romance, I’m suing society.”

Meilin didn’t even look up.

“You’d lose the case.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After weeks of discussions, tears, arguments, and spiraling, Xiaoran and Yichen had finally chosen their universities. Together, without either of them giving something up. Zhou Yichen applied mostly to universities with strong business programs and good basketball teams. Basketball mattered to him, but he thought realistically about the future too—something Xiaoran admired, even if she teased him for being “too mature.” Xiaoran chose media and communication studies, which surprised nobody. Lin Xiaoran physically couldn’t stop talking. But more than that, she loved stories, people, ideas. Even her random obsessions somehow fit.

When she told Yichen, he didn’t look surprised at all.

“You were always going to choose something people-related.”

“What does THAT mean.”

“You make strangers tell you their life stories in cafés.”

“That’s charisma.”

“That’s weird.”

Still, he smiled afterward—soft and proud—and that meant more than any compliment. In the end, they both applied to Huaining University in Shanghai: a respected school with strong programs and a competitive basketball team. Yichen could have chased a higher-ranked school and she could have picked an easier one, but this was the place that felt right. The middle ground they’d found together. They both applied to backup schools too, because unlike romance dramas, real life required common sense.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then results day arrived, and peace died immediately.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I can’t open it.”

“You literally have to.”

“I’d rather disappear.”

Xiaoran sat frozen in Yichen’s bedroom, staring at her laptop like it might bite. Yichen sat beside her, much too calm.

“How are you not nervous?” she demanded.

“I am nervous.”

“No you’re not. Your face looks normal.”

“My heart rate is elevated.”

“That’s not normal.”

Across the room, Yuhao was pacing and Meilin had gone pale, because somehow all four of them were getting results within the same hour. Terrible planning by the universe. Yuhao screamed.

“I GOT IN.”

Immediate chaos. Meilin grabbed his laptop.

“YOU ACTUALLY DID.”

“I’M EDUCATED.”

Xiaoran’s anxiety went up about five hundred percent.

“Oh my god.”

Yichen reached over and squeezed her hand.

“Open it with me.”

It made breathing a little easier. Slowly, Xiaoran clicked into the portal. Loading. Loading. Loading—silence. Dead silence. Yichen leaned closer.

“What.”

Xiaoran blinked. Twice. Then she covered her mouth, because there it was. Admission confirmed. Huaining University. Media and Communication Studies. For a full second, she couldn’t process it.

“OH MY GOD.”

Screaming. Tears. Total collapse. Yichen caught her when she launched herself at him.

“I GOT IN.”

“I know.”

“YICHEN I GOT IN.”

His arms tightened around her while she nearly cried into his shoulder from relief. Then she froze. Wait.

“…Your results.”

“Hm.”

“You didn’t check yours yet.”

Silence.

“Oh no.”

Now they were both nervous. Yuhao and Meilin watched like sports commentators.

“This relationship controls my blood pressure,” Yuhao whispered.

Then Yichen opened his own portal. Quiet room. One second. Two. Three— Accepted. Business Administration. Huaining University. Xiaoran started crying again.

“Why are you crying more than me?” Yichen laughed.

“BECAUSE THIS IS CINEMATIC.”

Xiaoran grabbed his face with both hands.

“We’re going together.”

“Hm.”

“ZHOU YICHEN WE’RE GOING TO UNIVERSITY TOGETHER.”

His eyes went soft at the happiness all over her face. And—

“So we are.”

It felt bigger than anything. Suddenly the future wasn’t blurry anymore. Dorms. Classes. A new city. Adult life. Together. Xiaoran looked at him again.

“We survived.”

“Application season, yes.”

“No. The future.” She smiled shakily through tears.

And for the first time, Zhou Yichen let himself believe that maybe they really would make it there together.

chapters.desc: Two dining tables across the city, a spreadsheet with weightings, a slideshow with transitions, and one first choice.
chapters.title: The Application Form
chapters.epigraph: “Is she good? At her subject.”
chapters.content:
On the last Sunday of June, two dining tables on opposite sides of the city looked exactly as serious as each other.

At the Lins’, there was a laptop, a printer that had been carried in from the bedroom, three highlighters, and a spreadsheet. Mrs. Lin had built the spreadsheet herself over four evenings, after work, with the study door shut. It had a column for each university on Xiaoran’s list, a row for everything that mattered, and a final row labelled WEIGHTED SCORE, which nobody was allowed to look at until the end.

At the Zhous’, there was a folder for each option, a second folder for the youth program in Beijing, and a laptop on which Mr. Zhou had prepared, Yichen would later tell her in a tone of real distress, a slideshow.

Xiaoran sat opposite her parents with her hands folded on the table, as if she had been summoned. Her phone was in her lap, under the table. It buzzed once.

Yichen: My father has made slides.

She turned the phone over under the edge of the table.

Xiaoran: My mother has made a spreadsheet. With weightings.

Yichen: Slides beat weightings.

Xiaoran: Weightings have formulas.

Yichen: Slides have transitions.

“Xiaoran, phone,” said her mother, without looking up from the laptop.

She put it back in her lap.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Media and communication. Four options. Two in Shanghai, one in Hangzhou, one here,” Mrs. Lin said, running her highlighter down the first column.

“Huaining first,” Xiaoran said.

“I know Huaining is first. You’ve said Huaining is first eleven times since April. We’re not discussing which is first. We’re discussing why. If you can tell me why, I’ll put it first. If you can’t, the spreadsheet will.” Her mother looked at her over the reading glasses.

Xiaoran had been preparing for this, in a sense, since she was nine, when her mother had made her explain the reasoning behind a request for a hamster. She took a breath and explained. The practical modules. The second-year production project, the one where you made a real film for a real client. The teacher whose documentary she had watched three times. The internship placements in the final year. The fact that, of the four, it was the only one where she had read the course list and wanted to start that afternoon.

Her father, who had said nothing so far, wrote something on the corner of the printout.

“And the boy,” her mother said, in exactly the same voice.

Xiaoran went still.

“He’s applying there too,” her mother went on, highlighting. “Business. I’m not stupid. Is that the reason?”

“No,” Xiaoran said. And then, because her mother would know if it wasn’t the whole truth, “It’s not the first reason. It’s not in the top three.”

“Where is it?”

Xiaoran thought about it honestly. “Fifth.”

Her mother looked at her, then typed something into the spreadsheet. Xiaoran couldn’t see what.

Her father spoke for the first time. “How far is it from the station?”

“Forty minutes by metro. Then a bus.”

“How often is the bus?”

“Dad.”

“It’s a reasonable question.”

It was, she supposed. She looked it up for him on her phone, since the phone was now evidently allowed. Every twelve minutes, until eleven at night. He wrote that down too, under whatever he had already written in the corner, and underlined eleven twice, and she knew without asking that he was already working out what she would do if she ever missed the last one.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the city, Mr. Zhou had reached slide nine.

He said, “The program will wait one year. Possibly two. I asked. Their man was very clear that they would rather have you at nineteen with a university behind you than at eighteen with nothing.”

Yichen nodded. He had known this since March; he had stood on the stairs outside Coach Wang’s office and heard most of it. But it was different on a slide.

“So the question isn’t basketball or university. The question is which university lets you keep basketball properly. Your father and I would like you to have both,” his mother said, from the end of the table, where she was peeling a pear in one long spiral.

“I’d like that too.”

“Then,” said Mr. Zhou, and clicked, and slide ten came up with four logos and a comparison of their basketball programs, their business schools, and their distance from home in hours by train.

Huaining was in the middle. Not the highest-ranked business school on the slide; not the strongest team. The only one where both columns were green.

His father had coloured them himself, with a green highlighter he had bought specially, which was still on the table beside the laptop with its cap off.

Yichen looked at the slide for a while. Under the table, his phone buzzed.

Xiaoran: My mother asked if you’re the reason.

Yichen: What did you say?

Xiaoran: Fifth.

He laughed out loud, and both his parents looked at him, and he said “Sorry” and put the phone in his pocket.

“Is something funny?” his father asked.

“No. Huaining. First,” Yichen said.

“Why?”

He gave the reasons. The coach. The business school’s internship scheme. The fact that the team trained in the mornings, so lectures weren’t sacrificed. He gave them clearly and in order, the way his father liked, and his father nodded at each one.

“And Xiaoran,” his mother said, setting down the pear.

He had known it was coming. His mother always got there eventually, by a more direct road than his father.

“She’s applying there too.”

“We know.”

Yichen said, “It’s not the reason. We agreed. Neither of us chooses for the other. If she’d wanted Hangzhou, I’d have said go. It’s on the list. It’s not near the top.”

“Where?”

“Fifth,” he said, and his mother looked at him for a second, and then laughed, without explaining why, and started on another pear.

“There is one more slide,” Mr. Zhou said.

Slide eleven was white, with a single word in the middle: Questions?

Yichen looked at it. “Do you have any?”

“One. Is she good? At her subject.” His father folded his hands on the table, the way he did in meetings he intended to win.

Yichen thought of the short films she made on her phone and showed nobody but him, and the documentary she had watched three times, and the way she went quiet and certain behind a camera, like someone else entirely.

“Yes, better than I am at mine,” he said.

His father looked at him. Then he nodded, as if a column of figures had finally balanced, and closed the laptop.

“Then she’ll be all right anywhere. And so will you,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past nine, Mrs. Lin turned the laptop round.

WEIGHTED SCORE. Huaining: 8.7. Next highest: 7.1.

“Well, there we are. It’s first because it’s first. Not because of the boy,” she said.

Xiaoran looked at the spreadsheet. Near the bottom, in the row her mother had added while she was talking, in small grey type, was a line she hadn’t been meant to see.

Someone sensible nearby: +0.2.

She looked up. Her mother had already taken her glasses off and was cleaning them on her sleeve, with great concentration.

Her father cleared his throat. “Your mother’s very thorough,” he said, and got up, and went into the kitchen, and ran the tap for longer than washing one cup required.

While he was gone, Xiaoran picked up the printout. In the corner, in her father’s small, square handwriting, the kind he used for meter readings at the bureau, he had written three words while she was talking.

She wants to start.

Underneath, in her mother’s pen, there was a tick.

✦ ✦ ✦

They filled in the forms online at ten, both families, within twenty minutes of each other. First choices: Huaining, Huaining. Backups chosen by the spreadsheet and the slideshow respectively, because both families had been sensible about the backups and argued only about the first line.

At eleven, Xiaoran sat on her bed with the confirmation screenshot open.

Xiaoran: Submitted.

Yichen: Submitted.

Xiaoran: My mother gave you 0.2 points.

Yichen: Out of what?

Xiaoran: I don’t know. I think it’s a lot.

Yichen: My father coloured your university green.

Xiaoran: It’s your university too.

Yichen: He coloured it before he knew which one you’d picked. He did it in April.

Xiaoran: What did your mother laugh at?

Yichen: I told her you were fifth.

Xiaoran: I told mine the same.

Yichen: I know. I think that’s what she was laughing at.

She read that twice. Then she rang him, because messages weren’t enough, and he picked up before the first ring had finished.

“You were waiting.”

“I had the phone in my hand. That’s not the same as waiting,” he said.

“It’s exactly the same. Did your father really do slides?” She pulled the duvet up to her chin.

“Eleven. The last one said Questions?”

“Did you have any?”

“He had one. He asked if you were good at your subject.”

She went still under the duvet. “What did you say?”

“I said yes.”

“Just yes?”

“I said you were better at yours than I am at mine.”

“That’s not true.”

“It’s true. I’ve seen the film you made of the canteen queue. The one where the auntie drops the ladle and you held the shot until she laughed. I can’t do anything like that.”

“You can shoot a three-pointer with your eyes shut.”

“Not with them shut.”

“Nearly shut.”

“Nearly shut,” he agreed.

She lay there listening to him breathe. On his side she could hear a television, and his mother’s voice saying something about pears.

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

“If I’d wanted Hangzhou. Would you really have said go?”

“Yes.”

“You’d have been sad.”

“I’d have been very sad. I’d have taken the train every weekend and complained about it the entire way. But I’d have said go.”

“I didn’t want Hangzhou.”

“I know. You wanted the one where you make a real film for a real client in second year. You’ve told me eleven times.”

“Mum said eleven too!”

“Your mother and I keep the same records,” he said, and she was laughing too much and had to put her face in the pillow so her father wouldn’t hear through the wall.

When she’d stopped, she said, “I want to see you tomorrow.”

“I’ve got training at eight.”

“After training.”

“After training I’ll be disgusting.”

“I don’t care. I’ll bring you a drink. I’ll sit on the bench and watch, and then you can be disgusting at me for an hour.”

“That’s very romantic.”

“I know. Good night. Tell your father his slides won,” she said.

“They didn’t win. It was a draw.”

“Then tell him it was a draw,” she said, and hung up before he could argue, and lay in the dark with the phone on her chest, smiling at the ceiling like an idiot.

chapters.desc: One summer gap, one campus in Shanghai, and a café they’ve already decided is theirs.
chapters.title: Practising Our Future
chapters.epigraph: “Practice makes the future less frightening.”
chapters.content:
After results came out, something strange happened. Everyone suddenly had nothing to do. School was technically over, but graduation hadn’t happened yet, and university hadn’t started. They were stuck in a weird one-month gap where life felt paused. No uniforms. No exams. No schedules. Just waiting. Lin Xiaoran loved it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“This feels wrong.”

They had taken the train into Shanghai for the day, and Xiaoran was walking beside Zhou Yichen near Huaining University’s main gate, iced coffee in hand. The summer air was warm and breezy, sunlight glinting off glass buildings and tree-lined paths. Students wandered past with laptops, skateboards, books. Adult-looking people. Terrifying, honestly.

Yichen glanced down at her. “What feels wrong?”

“We’re here without homework.”

“That’s called freedom.”

“I don’t trust it.”

It was their third unofficial “future practice date”: visiting the campus, exploring nearby streets, pretending they already belonged here. Xiaoran was enjoying it far more than she’d expected. The more familiar the campus became, the less frightening adulthood felt. Then she stopped walking.

“Oh.”

“What.”

Xiaoran pointed at a café across the road: floor-to-ceiling windows, warm lighting, bookshelves along the walls, soft music drifting outside. And, most importantly, cute desserts.

“That’s OUR café.”

Silence. Yichen followed her gaze.

“…You decided that in three seconds.”

“Yes.”

“Based on what criteria.”

“The vibe.”

“That’s not a system.”

Ten minutes later, they went in anyway, because Zhou Yichen indulged her too much.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside smelled like coffee and vanilla—warm, comfortable, university. Students typed on laptops while couples shared desserts by the windows. Xiaoran was immediately moved.

“Oh my god.”

“What now.”

“We’re becoming adults aesthetically.”

She grabbed a menu and sat down across from him.

“No matter what happens,” she announced seriously, “this is our meeting spot.”

“Hm.”

“After classes.”

“Hm.”

“If we fight, you still have to come here.”

“You’re planning future arguments already?”

“I’m realistic.”

Yichen watched her over the menu. Hearing her talk so easily about their future got to him more than he expected. Months ago, she’d cried over applications. Now she was casually planning which café they’d go to after lectures. Growth. Very cute growth.

“What if the drinks are bad?” Yichen asked.

Xiaoran froze. Oh. Good point.

“This relationship depends entirely on beverage quality.”

“Thought so.”

So, naturally, they ordered far too much: two drinks, three desserts, and a sandwich neither of them planned to share and both of them did. About fifteen minutes later, Xiaoran put both hands flat on the table.

“It’s perfect. The strawberry cake is perfect.”

Yichen looked around the café—sunlight through the windows, Xiaoran across from him talking happily about nothing—and the future suddenly felt close. Real, not abstract anymore.

“You’re excited,” he observed.

Xiaoran blinked, then smiled a little.

“…I think I am.”

It made Yichen smile too. For weeks he’d worried that all the university talk only stressed her out. Now she looked genuinely happy imagining what came next. Xiaoran leaned forward.

“We should choose more places.”

“What places.”

“Important relationship infrastructure.”

“…Infrastructure.”

“Yes.”

So that was the rest of the afternoon: future practice.

✦ ✦ ✦

They started with a bookstore, where Xiaoran found the communication shelves and immediately started judging textbook covers.

“This one looks arrogant.”

“It’s a grammar book.”

“Exactly.”

Then Yichen dragged her to the sports centre—huge courts, training rooms, bright indoor gyms. Watching him there made Xiaoran pause. He already fit here somehow. Tall under the university banners, confident, comfortable, like the future had been waiting for him. Then he turned around.

“What.”

Oops. Caught staring again.

“…Nothing.”

“You’re staring again.”

Then he reached over and fixed the twisted strap of her bag. A small, automatic thing. Xiaoran’s chest went painfully soft. Adulthood might change a lot of things, but she couldn’t imagine him ever stopping these tiny ways of caring.

“You know what’s weird? I used to think university would feel super romantic.”

“And now?”

“It mostly feels expensive.”

Yichen laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, the sky turned orange above the campus while they sat by the lake behind the library, drinks half-finished beside them, a warm summer wind moving through the trees. Xiaoran rested her head on Yichen’s shoulder. Not dramatically, this time. Just comfortably. And

“Do you think we’ll change a lot?”

Silence. Yichen looked out at the water.

“…Probably.”

“Oh.”

“But I don’t think that’s bad.”

Somewhere nearby, students were laughing.

“My mum said people change after university.”

“They do.”

“What if you become too cool for me.”

Yichen looked unimpressed.

“You ask strange questions.”

“I’m serious.”

“No matter what university does to me,” he said, “you’ll still be the first person I call when something happens.”

Xiaoran groaned into his shoulder.

“Why are you suddenly romantic again.”

“You started it.”

She looked around slowly—at the paths they’d walk, the café they’d chosen, the buildings waiting for them—and instead of scared, she felt warm. Like this future already held little pieces of them.

“We’re really growing up.”

“Hm.”

“Still,” Xiaoran said thoughtfully, “we should try every dessert here before the semester starts.”

“Obviously.”

chapters.desc: On graduation day, Lin Xiaoran accidentally asks Zhou Yichen to marry her. His answer is worse.
chapters.title: Yichen, Will You Marry Me?
chapters.epigraph: “Some questions are asked too early. Some answers are not.”
chapters.content:
Graduation day felt strange. Too loud. Too emotional. Too bright, somehow. The school grounds were full of students taking pictures while teachers pretended not to cry. Uniforms for the last time. Classrooms for the last time. High school ending under the summer sun. Lin Xiaoran didn’t handle emotional transitions well.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Don’t cry before photos.”

“I’m NOT crying.”

“Your eyes say otherwise.”

Tang Meilin was fixing Xiaoran’s graduation ribbon while Xiaoran blinked through suspiciously shiny eyes. Nearby, Yuhao took about fifty group selfies nobody had asked for. Across the courtyard, Zhou Yichen was talking with a few teachers outside the basketball building. Tall in the afternoon sun. Calm. Steady. Still exactly Zhou Yichen, even today. And Xiaoran got emotional all over again. They had really survived high school. Meilin noticed her staring.

“…She’s doing it again.”

“What.”

“You’re doing the boyfriend-staring thing.”

Yuhao zoomed in with his phone camera.

“Look at her face.”

“DELETE THAT.”

“You look like a wife seeing her husband return from war.”

“That’s literally just graduation.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The ceremony was emotional chaos: teachers giving speeches, students crying, parents taking far too many photos, and one boy confessing publicly and getting rejected on the spot. A historic disaster. Xiaoran spent most of it leaning sleepily against Yichen, because it was too warm. At some point, without thinking, she found his hand under the sleeve of her gown, and his fingers closed around hers right away. Everything softened—the noise, the crowd, the fear of growing up—because Zhou Yichen still felt exactly the same beside her.

“We’re graduating.”

“Hm.”

“That sounds fake.”

“A little.”

“What if university secretly sucks.”

“We’ll survive.”

After the ceremony, everyone scattered across campus for photos—classrooms, hallways, the basketball courts, the old staircase behind the library. Ordinary places turning into memories much too fast. Xiaoran and Yichen walked slowly along the empty sports field as the evening light turned gold, their gowns loose around their shoulders, a warm wind moving through the trees. Then Xiaoran stopped walking. Yichen looked back at her.

She looked at him for a second. He looked really handsome today. Not just physically. Older, maybe. More certain. Like the future already suited him. And before her brain caught up—

“Will you marry me?”

Silence. Even the wind seemed to go quiet. That had come out WAY too naturally. Xiaoran froze.

“…Wait.”

Zhou Yichen was looking at her calmly. Not shocked, exactly. Just deeply focused.

“Is this a proposal.”

“No.”

“You asked me to marry you.”

“I didn’t mean NOW.”

“Hm.”

“Oh my god.”

Xiaoran covered her face. What kind of graduation sentence was that?

“I meant… someday. Maybe. In theory.”

“That clarified nothing.”

And, unfortunately, Yuhao and Meilin showed up at exactly the wrong moment.

“What clarified nothing?” Yuhao asked immediately.

Dead silence. Xiaoran’s survival instincts kicked in.

“NOTHING.”

Too late. Yichen turned to them calmly.

“Xiaoran asked me to marry her.”

“WHAT?!” Yuhao yelled.

“LIN XIAORAN,” Meilin said.

“YOU PROPOSED BEFORE UNIVERSITY STARTED?” Yuhao went on.

Xiaoran slumped against the fence in embarrassment.

“I HATE EVERYONE.”

Yuhao looked revived.

“This graduation just became incredible.”

Meilin stared at Xiaoran in disappointment.

“You couldn’t even wait until adulthood.”

“It wasn’t serious!”

Then Yichen said—

“I’d say yes though.”

Everyone froze, Xiaoran included. Slowly, she turned to him.

“…What.”

Yichen looked completely, suspiciously calm.

“If you asked seriously later,” he said casually, “I’d probably say yes.”

Yuhao screamed loud enough to scare the birds out of the trees. Meilin grabbed Xiaoran’s arm before she could slide down the fence. Xiaoran stared at Yichen like he had personally destroyed her future.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

“What.”

“YOU CAN’T SAY THINGS LIKE THAT CASUALLY.”

“You proposed first.”

“I WAS JOKING.”

“Hm.”

That hm again—the terrible, calm hm that meant he was secretly enjoying this. Yichen reached over and straightened her crooked graduation ribbon. Small. Careful. Somehow it felt more intimate than the entire accidental proposal.

“Still,” he murmured, “you’d look good marrying me.”

Xiaoran covered her face again while Meilin nearly collapsed laughing beside her.

“This relationship is ridiculous,” Meilin declared.

Yuhao wiped away fake tears.

“Young love survived graduation.”

And while Xiaoran malfunctioned beside him, Zhou Yichen smiled at the sunset-lit campus. The future didn’t feel far away at all anymore.

chapters.desc: The graduation-day question, from the side of the boy who heard it.
chapters.title: Will You Marry Me? — Zhou Yichen’s Side
chapters.epigraph: “He stayed calm on the outside. He always did.”
chapters.content:
The problem with loving Lin Xiaoran for this long was that she said terrifying things casually and expected him to survive them normally. Which was impossible.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Will you marry me?”

For one second, Zhou Yichen forgot how to breathe. Not visibly. Never visibly. Years of basketball, exams, responsibility, and Xiaoran’s personality had trained him to stay calm on the outside. Inside, it was a complete disaster. It came so suddenly. So naturally. Like she really could imagine a future with him that far ahead. Marriage. Her. Him. Together. The picture hit his chest before logic could, and his heart reacted first. Fast. Much too fast.

He looked at her in the evening light—her gown, her hair moving in the wind, her eyes still wide from realising what she’d said. She looked younger and older at the same time. Still his dramatic Xiaoran. But not just a high school girl anymore. Someone standing at the edge of adulthood with him. His heart beat even harder. Because the first thing he wanted to do wasn’t laugh, or tease her. He wanted to pull her close. He wanted to hear her ask again, properly. He wanted to kiss her stupid forehead and ask—

“Do you even understand what you just said to me?”

But he didn’t, because Lin Xiaoran would combust on the spot. So he stayed calm. He always stayed calm first.

“Hm,” he answered. “Is this a proposal?”

Outwardly relaxed. Inwardly, not even slightly. Because part of him wished it was real. That surprised him. Not because marriage sounded impossible—but because with Xiaoran, he could imagine it far too easily.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran panicked.

“No. I didn’t mean NOW.”

Yichen watched her—the flustered face, the embarrassed eyes, the way she wouldn’t look at him when she was overwhelmed. His chest tightened. This girl trusted him with her future so naturally already. Even as a joke.

Then Yuhao and Meilin arrived and chaos broke out. Yichen barely heard half of it. His mind was stuck on one thing. Will you marry me? Such a ridiculous sentence. Such a dangerous one. Especially today, when the future had suddenly become real. Then Xiaoran shouted—

“It wasn’t serious!”

Yichen looked at her, and before he could think too carefully—

“I’d say yes though.”

Silence. The moment he said it, he knew he meant it. Completely. Without a trace of a joke. That scared him a little. Zhou Yichen wasn’t impulsive. He thought things through. Planned. Protected. But with Xiaoran, the truth sometimes got out before he could stop it. And the truth was simple: if Lin Xiaoran ever seriously asked him someday, he couldn’t imagine saying no. Xiaoran looked at him in total horror.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

His heart sped up again. She looked devastatingly cute when she was flustered, especially with the graduation sunlight on her face.

“You can’t say things like that casually.”

Yichen almost smiled. The irony was unbelievable. This girl had accidentally proposed first—and now SHE was overwhelmed? But instead of teasing her, he looked at her for another second. Really looked. At the girl who cried easily. Who got lost constantly. Who annoyed him every day. Who loved him loudly without realising how deeply. And a frighteningly soft thought settled in his chest: I really could spend my whole life with her.

It didn’t feel dramatic. It felt calm. Certain. Like something he’d known for a long time. Then Xiaoran complained weakly—

“I was joking.”

Yichen stepped closer and straightened her crooked graduation ribbon, slow and careful—something to do with his hands so she wouldn’t notice his heart still hadn’t calmed down. If he held her hand right now, he might not want to let go.

“You’d look good marrying me.”

Again, the tiny sharp breath, the flustered face, the look of someone who couldn’t decide whether to hit him or hug him. Yichen finally smiled to himself. Maybe she didn’t know yet. Maybe she really had been joking. But Zhou Yichen knew one thing clearly now: someday, if Lin Xiaoran ever asked him again for real, he would probably say yes before she finished the sentence.

chapters.desc: Tang Meilin has been hiding something for three months. Lin Xiaoran is a professional investigator.
chapters.title: Tang Meilin Had a Boyfriend?!
chapters.epigraph: “The quiet ones always have the best secrets.”
chapters.content:
They found out by accident, which somehow made it worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Wait.”

Lin Xiaoran lowered her spoon and narrowed her eyes across the café table. It was one of their usual summer-break afternoons. Normal. Peaceful. Until—

“Why are you smiling at your phone.”

Tang Meilin froze for half a second. Almost invisible. Unfortunately, Lin Xiaoran was a professional at detecting suspicious behaviour.

“…I always smile.”

“No you don’t.”

“She literally doesn’t,” Yuhao said.

Meilin glared at both of them. Xiaoran leaned forward.

“WHO IS IT.”

“There’s no one.”

“You looked happy. You’re never happy.”

Yichen sipped his drink and watched. When Xiaoran went into investigation mode, survival rates dropped sharply. Meilin’s phone buzzed again, and Xiaoran saw the preview. [Did you eat already?]

“OH MY GOD.”

Several customers looked over. Yuhao nearly choked on his drink. Meilin looked like she wanted to disappear.

“Lower your voice.”

“YOU HAVE A BOYFRIEND?”

“No.”

“Then why does someone text like a husband.”

“Maybe they’re polite.”

“NO ONE SAYS ‘did you eat already’ POLITELY.”

Even Yichen looked mildly interested now.

“…Who is it.”

Meilin stared at all three of them with betrayal.

“This is why I keep secrets.”

“You kept THIS secret? From ME?” Xiaoran gasped dramatically.

“Yes.”

“Betrayal.”

Yuhao nodded seriously.

“She’s right.”

“You’re both insane.”

Another notification appeared: [Call me later.] And under it, a heart emoji. Silence. Xiaoran grabbed Meilin’s arm.

“TANG MEILIN.”

“STOP SHAKING ME.”

Even Yichen was smiling now—a small, rare smile—which only encouraged Xiaoran.

“How long has this been happening?!”

“…Three months.”

“THREE MONTHS?!”

Yuhao looked genuinely wounded.

“You hid a whole man.”

“It wasn’t serious yet.”

“THERE ARE HEART EMOJIS.”

Meilin finally sighed and put her phone down. Escape was impossible.

“Fine.”

All three of them leaned in. Nosy vultures.

“We met during volunteer tutoring last semester.”

Xiaoran blinked rapidly.

“THAT quiet guy?”

“Hm.”

“The tall one with glasses?”

“Hm.”

“The one who looked like he paid taxes already?”

“…That description feels disrespectful.”

Yuhao snapped his fingers. “Wait, I know him. Shen Zixu, right?”

Meilin nodded once. Xiaoran stared. Tang Meilin—the stable one, the friend who judged everyone else’s romantic decisions—had secretly been dating someone for THREE MONTHS. This was historically significant.

“You held hands before telling us?”

Meilin looked exhausted.

“Yes.”

“Kissed?”

“Xiaoran.”

“ANSWER THE COURT.”

Yichen covered his mouth, clearly hiding a laugh. Traitor boyfriend. Then Meilin crossed her arms defensively.

“At least I’m normal about relationships.”

Silence. Then all three looked at her together.

“…What.”

“You hid a whole boyfriend for three months. That’s not normal,” Yuhao said.

Meilin glared harder.

“At least I don’t ask people if they’d still love me as capybaras.”

Xiaoran immediately pointed at Yichen.

“He answered yes.”

“That’s not helping your case.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Once Xiaoran had information, she was impossible. The interrogation went on for TWO HOURS.

“How did he confess.”

“He didn’t.”

Dead silence.

“What.”

“I confessed first.”

Even Yichen looked surprised. That didn’t sound like Meilin at all. Meilin looked down at her drink and mumbled—

“I got tired waiting.”

The mood at the table softened. That sounded unexpectedly sincere. Xiaoran blinked.

“…That’s kinda romantic.”

“Hm.”

“What did you say exactly?”

Meilin immediately looked horrified.

“No.”

“PLEASE.”

“No.”

“MEILIN PLEASE I RAISED YOU.”

“You absolutely did not.”

Three against one was impossible. After several minutes of suffering, Meilin gave up.

“I said… ‘If you keep looking at me like that, eventually I’m going to misunderstand things.’” She paused briefly.

Xiaoran slammed both hands on the table.

“THAT’S SO GOOD.”

Even Yichen looked impressed—one small nod, which from him was high praise. Meilin covered her face.

“I hate all of you.”

Yuhao looked deeply emotional.

“Why is everyone around me accidentally romantic.”

Meilin’s phone rang. [Shen Zixu calling] All three of them turned to look at her. Meilin stared back with visible regret.

“…Don’t make this weird.”

“No promises,” Xiaoran whispered immediately.

With the face of someone deeply unfortunate, Tang Meilin answered. And instantly, her voice softened. Just a little. But enough. Enough that Xiaoran gasped again.

“Oh my god she likes him FOR REAL.”

“XIAORAN.”

Beside her, Zhou Yichen laughed into his drink while Xiaoran glowed with pure gossip happiness.

chapters.desc: A tiny studio in Shanghai, four flights of stairs, and Lin Xiaoran’s mother has questions for Zhou Yichen.
chapters.title: Moving Day Comes With Parents
chapters.epigraph: “Check twice. She lies the first time.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had met Zhou Yichen’s parents three times. Zhou Yichen had met hers exactly once, for forty seconds, outside an exam gate, while holding a strawberry milk. Moving day was going to fix that whether anyone was ready or not.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car was packed so full that Xiaoran rode the whole way to Shanghai with a lamp across her knees and a rice cooker wedged against her ankles. Her father drove. Her mother sat in the passenger seat with a printed list titled MOVING — XIAORAN, ticking things off whenever they passed a toll gate, as if the items might escape between cities.

“Bedding.”

“In the back.”

“Winter coat.”

“It’s August.”

“Winter coat.”

“…In the back.”

“Medicine box.”

Xiaoran didn’t answer. Her mother turned around in her seat.

“I’ll buy medicine there,” Xiaoran said.
