“Shanghai has changed you,” Yuhao declared.

Xiaoran, who was sitting on the low wall outside the convenience store with a cold drink in her hand, looked at him.

“How?”

“You’ve become more expensive.”

Meilin snorted.

“She was always expensive. You just couldn’t afford her standards.”

“Exactly! Thank you.” Xiaoran pointed at Meilin.

Yuhao looked between them. “I see. Two against one. This is why I don’t come home.”

“You came home yesterday,” Meilin reminded him.

“That was before I knew you two were here.”

Xiaoran laughed. It felt strange, in a good way, to be back in the same place with the same people after a year of university. They had spent months exchanging messages, sending pictures of campus life, complaining about assignments, and arranging video calls whenever their schedules aligned.

But sitting together like this, with Meilin stealing her drink and Yuhao talking nonsense, was different. There was no need to explain anything.

They could pick up where they had left off. Yichen arrived a little later.

He was wearing a plain white T-shirt and dark trousers, his hair slightly damp from the summer heat. His basketball bag hung over one shoulder. Yuhao spotted him first.

“Look who finally decided to visit us.”

Yichen glanced at him. “I live here.”

“Temporarily.”

“Still longer than you.”

Meilin laughed. Xiaoran had already stood up.

“You’re late.”

“By five minutes.”

“Seven.”

He looked at her, then at the drink in her hand.

“Have you eaten?”

“Lovely to see you too.”

“Hello. Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Something.”

He gave her a look.

She sighed. “A sandwich.”

“When?”

“At lunchtime.”

“It’s almost four.”

“I know how clocks work, Yichen.”

He reached for her hand, taking her empty drink bottle with the other.

“Come on. I’ll get you something.”

Yuhao watched them walk towards the shop.

“One year of university. And they’re still like this,” he said thoughtfully.

Meilin crossed her arms.

“Some things never improve.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The city-league game was on Saturday evening. Yichen had been invited to play for a local team during the summer break. It wasn’t a professional competition, but it was a proper city-league tournament, with teams from different districts, regular spectators, referees, and enough local pride to make every match competitive. He hadn’t planned to play at first.

He had university training to consider, and the summer was supposed to be a break. But the invitation came through an old coach who knew his playing history, and Yichen had agreed after checking the schedule.

Xiaoran found out about the game when he mentioned it casually over dinner.

“You’re playing on Saturday?”

“Yes.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I just did.”

She stared at him. He looked back, entirely composed.

“That’s not what I meant.”

“I know.”

“Yichen.”

He smiled slightly.

She pointed her chopsticks at him. “I’m coming.”

“I assumed you would.”

“Good.”

Across the table, Yuhao leaned forward.

“Can we come too?”

Yichen nodded. “Of course.”

Meilin looked at Xiaoran.

“Are you going to become one of those basketball girlfriends who scream every time their boyfriend touches the ball?”

Xiaoran considered this.

“Probably.”

Yichen continued eating.

“Please don’t.”

She turned to him.

“Why?”

“I’d like to hear the coach.”

Yuhao burst out laughing.

“He’s already regretting inviting us.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday arrived with an oppressive summer heat. The outdoor court had been set up for the tournament, though the main playing area was covered by a roof. There were rows of plastic seats along the sidelines, small stalls selling drinks and snacks, and a crowd that had begun gathering well before the first game. Xiaoran arrived with Meilin and Yuhao.

She was wearing a loose summer dress, sneakers, and a cap to keep the sun off her face. In her bag were tissues, a bottle of water, sunscreen, and a small towel. Meilin looked inside.

“Are you preparing for a basketball game or a three-day expedition?”

“Yichen sweats a lot.”

“He’s playing, Xiaoran. That’s generally what happens.”

“I know.”

Yuhao leaned over.

“Did you bring a first-aid kit too?”

She met his eyes.

“No.”

“Disappointing.”

“Would you like me to bring one for you?”

“Why? Are you planning to get injured?”

“Your mouth is going to get you injured.”

Meilin laughed as they found their seats. Yichen was already warming up. Xiaoran spotted him almost immediately.

He was moving through a shooting drill with his teammates, his attention fixed on the basket. His posture was relaxed but focused, the ball leaving his hands with a familiar rhythm.

She watched him make a shot, then another, then another. Yuhao followed her gaze.

“He’s gotten better.”

Meilin nodded. “He looks stronger too.”

Xiaoran smiled, pleased by their observation.

“He trains a lot.”

“We know. You’ve told us,” Yuhao said.

“I have not.”

Meilin gave her a flat look.

“You sent us a video of him practising at eleven at night.”

“Because he made a really good shot!”

“And then you sent another one.”

“That was a different shot.”

Yuhao shook his head.

“Love is a disease.”

Xiaoran ignored him. On the court, Yichen finished his warm-up and glanced towards the seats. His eyes found her. She lifted both hands and waved.

He smiled, a small one, then raised his hand in acknowledgment. Meilin leaned towards Xiaoran.

“That smile.”

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“Meilin.”

“He’s looking at you like he has a whole separate game happening over there.”

Xiaoran’s cheeks warmed.

“Stop.”

Yuhao nodded solemnly.

“Very serious competition. One opponent. One girl. One hand wave.”

“Both of you are unbearable.”

The game started at six. Yichen’s team had a difficult opponent.

The first quarter was fast and physical, with both sides trading baskets. Yichen played as a guard, helping organise the offence and moving between the perimeter and the paint depending on the defensive setup.

Xiaoran didn’t understand every tactical decision, but she had watched enough of his games to recognise when something was going well.

She knew the difference between his relaxed expression and the one he wore when he was fully locked in. Tonight, he was serious.

He communicated constantly with his teammates, calling out screens, directing movement, and adjusting when the opposing team changed its defence. He wasn’t the loudest player on the court. But his teammates listened.

In the second quarter, he intercepted a pass and drove towards the basket. A defender stepped across his path. Yichen changed direction, slipped past him, and finished with a layup. Xiaoran stood up.

“Yes!”

Yuhao clapped.

Meilin laughed. “There she goes.”

Xiaoran didn’t sit down immediately. Yichen jogged back on defence, expression unchanged. Then he glanced towards the stands. She was still standing. He shook his head, almost smiling.

“He’s looking at you,” Meilin whispered.

“He’s not.”

“He is.”

Xiaoran sat down, trying to look composed. A few minutes later, Yichen made a three-pointer. She stood up again. This time, Yuhao joined her.

“THAT’S MY GUY!”

Yichen turned his head towards the stands. His expression suggested he was reconsidering his friendship with all three of them.

Meilin laughed so much she had to cover her mouth. Mr. Zhou arrived midway through the third quarter. Xiaoran noticed him before Yichen did.

A tall man in a light shirt stepped into the seating area, accompanied by another older man. He spoke to someone near the entrance, then looked towards the court.

He didn’t appear rushed. He didn’t appear interested in finding a seat, either.

He went straight to a chair in the back row without looking for a better one. Xiaoran recognised him immediately.

She had met Yichen’s father several times. He was always polite, measured, and difficult to read. Unlike Yichen’s mother, who was warm and openly affectionate, Mr. Zhou rarely expressed much through his face. Xiaoran nudged Meilin.

“Yichen’s father is here.”

Meilin turned.

“Oh.”

Yuhao glanced over.

“Didn’t know he was coming.”

“Neither did I.”

On the court, Yichen was preparing to receive a pass when his eyes moved towards the stands. He saw his father. There was no obvious reaction. No smile, no wave, no change in posture. He looked away and continued playing. Xiaoran watched him carefully.

She wondered whether he had known his father might come. The game continued.

Yichen’s team was trailing by four points. Their opponents had become more aggressive defensively, forcing several turnovers. Yichen adjusted.

He slowed the pace, called for a screen, and moved the ball around rather than forcing a difficult shot. On the next possession, he found a teammate cutting towards the basket. The pass was clean. The teammate scored. Xiaoran clapped.

Then, a little later, Yichen drove towards the baseline and passed to the opposite corner. Another basket.

The gap narrowed. The final minutes became increasingly tense. The opposing team called a timeout. Players gathered around their coach.

Yichen stood with his hands on his hips, listening.

From the stands, Xiaoran noticed his father checking his watch. She didn’t think much of it.

When play resumed, Yichen received the ball near the top of the key. His defender pressed close, leaving little room to move. A teammate cut towards the basket. Yichen passed. But the pass came a fraction too early.

The teammate hadn’t completed his movement. The ball travelled behind him, and the opposing team intercepted it. A fast break followed. The crowd groaned.

Yichen immediately turned and sprinted back, but the opponent scored before his team could recover. Xiaoran’s fingers tightened around her water bottle. He didn’t look frustrated. Not outwardly. He took his position again.

The game ended with Yichen’s team losing by three points. A respectable loss, which was still a loss.

The players shook hands, exchanged a few words, and gathered near their bench.

Xiaoran was already making her way down the steps.

“Yichen!”

He turned when he heard her. His expression changed slightly when he saw her approaching, the tension in his shoulders easing.

“Hey.”

She stopped in front of him.

“You’re sweaty.”

He met her eyes.

“I just played a game.”

“I know.”

She held out the towel. He accepted it, wiping his face.

“How was it?”

“Good.”

She tilted her head.

“Good?”

“We lost.”

“I saw.”

He glanced at her.

“You don’t have to pretend.”

“I’m not pretending. You played well.”

“Not perfectly.”

“No one plays perfectly.”

He smiled.

“That’s a very generous assessment.”

“It’s an accurate one.”

He looked at her, then reached out and touched the brim of her cap.

“Did you enjoy watching?”

She nodded.

“Very much.”

He laughed. Before he could say anything else, Yuhao appeared behind her.

“That was a good game, man.”

Yichen nodded. “Thanks.”

“That pass in the fourth quarter, though.”

Meilin elbowed Yuhao.

“Can you let him breathe first?”

“What? I’m discussing basketball.”

“You’re discussing his mistake.”

Yichen shook his head.

“It’s fine.”

Yuhao raised both hands.

“See? He’s fine.”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

“Have you eaten?”

He sighed.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Can I change first?”

She blinked.

“Oh. Yes.”

He smiled and brushed his fingers against hers.

“I’ll be back.”

By the time Yichen returned, the crowd had begun to disperse.

Xiaoran was standing beside the small refreshment stall with Meilin and Yuhao. They had bought cold drinks and were arguing about where to eat. Yichen joined them, carrying his basketball bag.

“Hotpot,” Yuhao declared.

“It’s too hot for hotpot,” Meilin said.

“Hotpot is never too hot.”

“You’re the reason people lose their appetite.”

Xiaoran turned towards Yichen.

“What do you want?”

He looked at the three of them.

“Anything.”

Yuhao groaned.

“Why are you all so difficult?”

“Because you ask questions without accepting answers,” Yichen replied.

Xiaoran laughed. They eventually agreed on a small noodle restaurant near the old commercial street.

But before they left, Xiaoran noticed Mr. Zhou standing near the edge of the court.

He was speaking to the older man who had arrived with him. Yichen noticed him too. His steps slowed.

“Yichen,” Xiaoran said.

He turned to her.

“Your father.”

“I see.”

Mr. Zhou turned towards them. His gaze settled on his son.

“Yichen.”

“Dad.”

The greeting was brief. Mr. Zhou looked at the basketball bag over his shoulder.

“Finished?”

“Yes.”

“How did it go?”

“We lost by three.”

His father nodded once. Then his eyes moved towards the court.

“Your fourth-quarter possession. You passed too early.” He waited, and when Yichen said nothing, he finished it.

There was no anger in his voice, only a short, precise observation. Yichen’s expression remained composed.

“The cut wasn’t finished.”

“Then you should have waited.”

“I know.”

His father looked at him for another moment. Then he checked his watch.

“I have to go.”

Xiaoran looked at the man. He had arrived late.

He was leaving before the players had even finished packing up. Mr. Zhou nodded to her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Good evening, Uncle Zhou.”

“Good evening.”

He turned back to Yichen.

“Keep training.”

Then he left. He hadn’t said well played, or asked how university was going. One observation, a reminder to keep training, and then his back going out through the gate. None of them spoke. Yuhao was the first to break the silence.

“Well.”

Meilin gave him a warning look. He closed his mouth. Xiaoran looked at Yichen. His face was unreadable.

She wasn’t sure whether he was disappointed, irritated, or used to it.

“Yichen?”

He adjusted the strap of his bag.

“Hm?”

“Do you want to go?”

He nodded.

“Let’s go.”

She reached for his hand. He took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was noisy. Yuhao complained about the restaurant’s portion sizes. Meilin accused him of ordering too much. Xiaoran tried to steal a piece of food from Yichen’s bowl, and he moved it away just far enough to make her protest. For a while, everything returned to normal.

But Xiaoran noticed that Yichen was quieter than usual, even for him.

But there were moments when she caught him looking at his phone without actually doing anything, or staring at the table while Yuhao told a story.

Eventually, Meilin and Yuhao started arguing about an old high-school incident. Xiaoran leaned closer to Yichen.

“Are you okay?”

He held her gaze.

“Yes.”

She studied his face.

“Really?”

He smiled slightly.

“Really.”

She didn’t push. Instead, she slipped her hand beneath the table and found his. He looked down. Then his fingers closed around hers. He leaned towards her.

“Don’t worry.”

She looked at him.

“I’m not.”

His expression suggested he didn’t believe her. She gave his hand a small squeeze.

“I just wanted to hold your hand.”

His gaze softened.

“All right.”

He brought her hand to his lips and kissed her knuckles beneath the table. Across from them, Yuhao was still talking. Meilin noticed.

She smiled to herself and returned to her food. They walked home together after dinner.

The summer evening was warm, the streets illuminated by shop signs and the occasional passing motorcycle. Yuhao had gone in the opposite direction, while Meilin had been picked up by her parents. Xiaoran and Yichen took the longer route.

They passed the old primary school, the small park, and the bakery street where she had once got hopelessly lost trying to buy him pastries. Yichen carried both their bags.

Xiaoran walked beside him, occasionally brushing her shoulder against his.

After a while, she asked, “Did you know your father was coming?”

“No.”

She nodded.

“Did you want him to?”

Yichen was quiet.

Then he said, “It doesn’t matter.”

Xiaoran looked up at him. It wasn’t quite an answer.

But she understood that he wasn’t ready to give her a different one. She looked ahead.

“Your pass wasn’t bad.”

He studied her.

“What?”

“The pass. In the fourth quarter.”

He gave her a faint smile.

“You don’t have to defend me.”

“I’m not defending you.”

“Then?”

“I’m telling you what I saw. You saw the opening. You made the pass. Your teammate wasn’t ready. It happens.”

Yichen’s gaze returned to the road.

“That’s why it’s a mistake.”

“Yes.”

She said it so plainly that he looked at her again. She smiled.

“You’re allowed to make mistakes, you know.”

He laughed.

“Thank you for the permission.”

“You’re welcome.”

They walked a little further.

Then he said, “He was right.”

Xiaoran turned towards him.

“About the pass?”

“Yes.”

She nodded.

“Then you can work on it.”

He considered her.

“That’s it?”

“What else?”

“Nothing.”

She smiled.

“You’re very good at basketball, Yichen. That doesn’t mean you can’t improve.”

He was quiet. Then he reached down and took her hand.

“I know.”

She leaned against his arm. She asked, “Are you disappointed?”

He considered the question.

“Not about the game.”

She waited. He didn’t elaborate. She didn’t ask him to.

Instead, she lifted their joined hands and swung them gently between them.

“Come on.”

“Where?”

“Home.”

He looked down at her. Then he smiled.

“All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that night, Yichen returned to his room after showering. His basketball bag sat beside his desk.

He took out his shoes, towel, and water bottle, placing each item where it belonged. Then he checked his phone. There was a message from his father.

Dad: Review the fourth-quarter footage if you can get it.

Yichen looked at the message. A few seconds later, another one arrived.

Dad: Your footwork is better than at the invitational.

He read it twice. His father hadn’t been at the invitational. He must have found the footage. He typed a short reply.

Yichen: I’ll review it.

He put the phone down. Across the room, an old drawer stood slightly open. Inside were school certificates, photographs, a few medals, and things he hadn’t looked at in years. He pushed it shut.

Then he returned to his desk, opened his laptop, and searched for the game footage.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next afternoon, Xiaoran found him at the small basketball court behind the community centre. She had expected him to be there.

He was alone, wearing a dark training shirt, shooting from the perimeter. The ball hit the rim. He retrieved it. Took another shot. This time, it went in.

Xiaoran stood by the fence, watching him for a while before calling out.

“Excuse me.”

He turned. His expression softened when he saw her.

“You’re here.”

“Am I interrupting?”

“No.”

She walked over, holding a plastic bag.

“I brought something.”

He glanced at it.

“What?”

“Food.”

“For me?”

“For you. I ate mine on the way.”

He laughed. She placed the bag on the bench.

“Your mother said you might be here.”

“She told you?”

“She asked me to bring you something.”

He shook his head, smiling. Xiaoran took out a small container.

“Fruit.”

“Thank you.”

“And a sandwich.”

“Thank you.”

“And—”

“Xiaoran.”

She stopped. He looked at her, amused.

“What else?”

She took out a small packet of tissues.

“You’re welcome.”

He laughed and accepted it. She sat on the bench while he finished a few more shots. After a while, he came over, drinking water.

“How long have you been here?”

“Long enough.”

“Watching?”

“Yes.”

“Did I play well?”

She tilted her head.

“Do you want an honest answer?”

“Always.”

“You do a little bounce on your toes before you shoot when you’re annoyed. You did it four times.”

He stared at her. Then his mouth curved.

“Who taught you that?”

“Me. I don’t watch the ball. I watch you.”

“Impressive.”

She smiled proudly. He sat beside her. For a while, they ate in comfortable silence. Then Xiaoran looked at him.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Last night you told me it doesn’t matter.”

He didn’t answer.

“You don’t have to tell me everything straight away. Just don’t say it doesn’t matter and then come out here on your own the next day.”

He looked at the hoop, and then at her. Then he lifted her hand and pressed a kiss against her fingers.

“I’ll remember.”

“Good.”

He leaned back against the bench. The court was quiet, with only the occasional sound of a ball bouncing from the far end.

After a while, Xiaoran let her head drop onto his shoulder.

“By the way.”

“Hm?”

“You’re playing again next week?”

“Probably.”

“Then I’ll come.”

“All right.”

“And Meilin and Yuhao.”

He closed his eyes.

“Do we have to invite Yuhao?”

She laughed.

“Yes.”

“Unfortunate.”

“He cheered for you.”

“He shouted at the wrong time.”

“That’s because he’s enthusiastic.”

“He’s loud.”

“Same thing.”

Yichen smiled and kissed her temple.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, when Yichen returned home, he found his father in the study. Mr. Zhou was reading through some documents. Yichen stood at the door.

“Dad.”

His father looked up.

“Yes?”

“About yesterday.”

Mr. Zhou put down his pen. Yichen entered and stood across from the desk.

“The pass was early.”

His father nodded.

“I know.”

“I saw the cut, but I didn’t wait for him to finish.”

Mr. Zhou watched him.

“Then you know what to correct.”

“Yes.”

A brief silence followed. Yichen looked at his father.

“Did you watch the whole game?”

Mr. Zhou’s expression remained neutral.

“Most of it.”

“You arrived during the third quarter.”

“I had something to attend to.”

Yichen nodded. His father returned his gaze to the documents.

“Your mother said you’re staying here for the summer.”

“Yes.”

“Don’t neglect your training.”

“I won’t.”

“Good.”

That was the end of the conversation. Yichen left the study. He didn’t expect anything more.

But as he walked down the corridor, he heard his father’s voice again.

“Yichen.”

He stopped and turned. Mr. Zhou was still seated behind the desk.

“Your defence has improved.”

Yichen looked at him. A small pause.

“Thank you.”

His father nodded once. Yichen returned to his room.

✦ ✦ ✦

A few days later, Xiaoran found herself in Yichen’s room while he was downstairs.

She had come over to return a book, and his mother had told her she could leave it on his desk.

The room looked much the same as she remembered. Neat, quiet, with everything in its place. She put the book down.

Then she noticed an old metal box on the shelf, a little dusty, with a faded basketball sticker on the lid. The lid wasn’t quite shut. When she reached up to push it closed, a photograph slid out onto the shelf.

A boy of about twelve in a jersey far too big for him, holding a small trophy in a school gym. In the front row of the stands behind him, Mrs. Zhou was waving with both hands.

Xiaoran smiled and laid the photograph back on top of the medals inside.

When Yichen came upstairs, he found her sitting on the edge of his bed.

“Your book’s on the desk.”

“Thank you.”

He glanced at the shelf, then at her.

“Did you find something?”

“You at twelve. In a jersey like a dress. Your mum was in the front row.”

“She came to everything.”

“And your dad?”

He took the box down and closed the lid properly.

“He never had time.”

He said it the way people mention the weather, and she didn’t ask again. Instead, she smiled and held out her hand. She held out her hand. He walked over, taking her hand. She pulled him down beside her.

“You’re very handsome.”

He glanced at her.

“That’s unrelated.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you telling me?”

“Because I want to.”

He smiled and leaned down to kiss her forehead.

“All right.”

She rested against him. Downstairs, his mother called them for dinner. Neither of them moved until she called twice.

chapters.desc: A typhoon comes up the coast on the night of his first dinner inside her family’s home, and her mother makes up the spare room.
chapters.title: Summer Dinner, Her House
chapters.epigraph: “Thank you for inviting me.”
chapters.content:
The rain had started at four, sideways, the way it did in July when a typhoon was coming up the coast, and by the time Zhou Yichen had climbed the stairs to the fourth floor his umbrella had turned inside out twice.

The first thing he noticed when Xiaoran opened the door was the pair of guest slippers waiting by the shoe rack. The second was that her mother was standing directly behind her, smiling as if she had been waiting for this moment all afternoon.

“Yichen! You’re here.”

“Good evening, Auntie. Sorry to bother you.”

“Bother me? Come in, come in. Why are you standing on the landing like a delivery man?”

“Mum,” said Xiaoran, “let him take his shoes off first.”

“I know how people take their shoes off, Xiaoran.”

“Then why are you rushing him?”

“Because the fish is getting cold.”

He stepped in and held out the paper bags. “Thank you for having me, Auntie. It’s only some fruit and pastries.”

“You shouldn’t have. Very thoughtful. Your uncle’s in the living room.” She took the bags and disappeared towards the kitchen, and Xiaoran watched her go with a growing sense of unease.

Her mother was being much too pleasant.

She had met him exactly twice before: forty seconds outside a gaokao gate, and one whole moving day in Shanghai, during which she had watched his posture, his handwriting on the box labels, and the way he carried a rice cooker up four flights of stairs. Afterward, in the car, she had said only, “He labels things properly,” which from Mrs. Lin was high praise. But this was the first time he’d come through their front door. For two years he had been the boy at the compound gate, the boy who rang at nine, the boy her father had watched once from the window. Now he was standing in the hallway in her father’s spare slippers, as her boyfriend, and her mother had evidently decided to make the most of it.

“Come on,” Xiaoran muttered, and took his hand.

He looked down at their hands and then at her. His face was perfectly composed, but the corner of his mouth told her he’d noticed how nervous she was.

He bent his head. “Should I let go?”

She gripped harder. “No.”

“All right,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father was on the sofa watching the typhoon warning on the news: a red map with a white spiral crawling slowly up towards their city. When he saw Yichen he switched it off, which Xiaoran had never seen him do during a weather forecast in her life.

“You’re here.”

“Good evening, Uncle.”

“Sit, sit.”

She had expected awkwardness. A few questions about university, or basketball, or his family. Instead her father talked about the weather, which tonight was at least relevant; then the traffic, which tonight was hopeless; then the Huaining basketball team’s last season, which he had evidently been reading about. Yichen answered all of it easily. He was good at this. He talked to adults. After a while Xiaoran sat down on the arm of the sofa next to him, and then slid down onto the cushion, and her knee ended up against his.

Her mother came out with a plate of cut peaches. “Yichen. Eat.”

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“Eat more. You’ve been training.”

“A few times a week.”

“Then you need to eat properly.”

“Mum,” said Xiaoran, “he’s not starving.”

“I didn’t say he was.”

“You’re feeding him like he’s been lost in the mountains.”

Her father laughed. Yichen bent his head, hiding a smile.

“Don’t laugh,” Xiaoran hissed at him.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He held out a piece of peach on a toothpick. “Would you like some?”

“You’re changing the subject.”

“Would you?”

She took it. Her mother watched the two of them with an expression of deep satisfaction. It was going to be a long evening.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was worse. Not because of the food; the food was wonderful. Her mother had cooked enough for twelve, and Xiaoran was fairly sure she’d been planning it for a week. There were dishes Yichen liked, and dishes Xiaoran liked, and at least two that her mother announced were especially good for someone who played basketball. Yichen thanked her every time she put something in his bowl. Xiaoran, meanwhile, was being entirely ignored.

“Yichen, have some more fish.”

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“Do you like it?”

“Very much.”

“As much as the dumplings on moving day?”

“Those were the best thing I ate that week, Auntie.”

“They were frozen,” said her mother, delighted.

Xiaoran put down her chopsticks. “Hello? I’m also sitting here.”

“We can see you,” said her father.

“Then why is nobody asking if I want more?”

“You’ve got hands,” said her mother.

Yichen moved the fish dish across the table towards her without a word.

“Thank you,” said Xiaoran, with dignity.

“See? Yichen’s more thoughtful than you are,” said her mother.

“Mum!”

Her father laughed into his tea, and then had to put the cup down and wipe his eyes, because he was a man who couldn’t laugh without also, slightly, crying. Yichen, to his credit, didn’t look pleased with himself. He went on eating. But his eyes were full of it.

Later her father turned to him over the soup. “Business, isn’t it?”

“Yes, Uncle.”

“How do you find it?”

“It’s interesting. There are a lot of group projects.”

“And with basketball?”

“I have to plan the week carefully.”

“And Xiaoran? Does she study properly?” said her father.

Xiaoran stopped with the spoon halfway to her mouth. “Dad.”

“She leaves things until the last minute.”

“Dad!”

Yichen considered it. “She works hard. When she cares about something, she doesn’t stop until it’s right. She gets distracted sometimes. But she always makes her deadlines. She stays up too late to make them,” he said.

Her father looked at him, and nodded slowly.

“That’s true,” he said.

Xiaoran looked at Yichen. He had defended her without telling a single lie. She pressed her knee against his under the table, hard, and he glanced at her with a perfectly innocent face. He was being much too good at this.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner her mother asked Yichen to help her fetch some things from the cupboard in the hallway. Xiaoran stood up at once.

“I’ll do it.”

“You can clear the table.”

“I can carry things.”

“I know. That’s why I want you to clear the table.”

“It’s all right, Auntie. I’ll help,” said Yichen, getting up.

They went off down the hallway. Something was definitely going on. Xiaoran cleared the table faster than she ever had in her life and followed them.

She found them outside the spare room. Her mother was standing by the open door. Yichen was holding a folded blanket. And the room—

The spare room had been made up. Not tidied. Made up. Fresh sheets. Two pillows. A folded towel on the end of the bed. A little lamp on the bedside table, and next to it a bottle of water and a new toothbrush still in its packet.

“Mum.”

Her mother turned round. “What?”

“What is this?”

“A room.”

“I can see it’s a room. Why does it look like a hotel?”

Her mother looked at the room, and then at Yichen, and then at the window at the end of the hall, which the rain was hitting like handfuls of gravel.

“The metro stops at nine when there’s a typhoon warning. It’s twenty to. The buses stopped at seven. His mother can’t drive across the river in this, and I’m not putting him in a taxi on the bridge either. I’ve been watching that storm since Tuesday. I made the bed on Wednesday.” She said it without any fuss at all.

Yichen went still. Xiaoran stared at her.

“You made it on Wednesday? Before you’d even asked him?”

Her mother looked genuinely puzzled. “Would you rather he slept on the sofa?”

“No, but—”

“Then what’s the problem?”

“Thank you, Auntie. That’s very kind. I’ll message my mother,” said Yichen.

“I already did. On Wednesday. I sent her the forecast. She sent a thumbs-up,” said Mrs. Lin.

She turned to go.

“Xiaoran, show him where the bathroom is,” said Mrs. Lin.

And she walked off to the kitchen, leaving the two of them in the hallway outside an obviously prepared spare room.

Xiaoran turned slowly to look at him. He was looking at the room. Then at her. The corner of his mouth was starting to go.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face is saying something.”

He looked down at the blanket in his arms. “Your mother is very thoughtful.”

“Yichen.”

“She’s even put out two pillows.”

“Stop.”

“Would you like to inspect it?”

She put both hands over her face. “I hate this.”

“No, you don’t,” he said, and she peeked at him through her fingers, and he was still smiling, and somehow that was worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

When her mother had finished showing him where the towels lived, Xiaoran pulled him by the sleeve to the end of the hallway, by the window, where the rain was loudest.

“You’re not actually staying, are you?”

He looked at her. “Would you like me to leave?”

“No! I mean, you don’t have to. I just didn’t know she had a whole plan.” She heard herself, and went red.

“She had the forecast.”

“And you just said yes?”

“Would saying no have been more polite?”

She had no answer. He laughed, and took her hand.

“Xiaoran. Your parents know we’re together. They’ve invited me into their home. They’ve made up a room for me. I don’t think there’s anything to worry about.”

She looked down. It wasn’t that she minded him being here. She wanted him here. She liked him at her family’s table, and on the sofa next to her father, being treated as somebody who belonged. It was only strange. For two years he had been the boy outside. Tonight he was standing in her hallway holding her mother’s towel, with the storm throwing rain at the window, and everyone in the flat knew exactly who he was.

“Are you nervous?” she said.

He thought about it. “A bit.”

“Really?”

“Your father’s been looking at me very carefully all evening.”

“He likes you.”

“I know. That’s why. I want him to keep liking me.” He turned her hand over in his.

She stopped arguing. She stepped closer and put her forehead against his chest, just for a second, in the corner of the hall where the kitchen door couldn’t see.

“And your mother,” he said into her hair.

“She already likes you more than me.”

“That might be true.”

She jerked her head back. “You’re supposed to deny it!”

He laughed. “Come on. Living room. Before your mother comes looking.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was tea and more fruit. Her father asked about the team’s preseason, and then her mother went into the bedroom and came back with a photograph album.

Xiaoran recognised it from the doorway. “Mum. No.”

“What?”

“Put it away.”

“Why?”

“Because I know what’s in it.”

“What is it?” said Yichen.

“Nothing,” said Xiaoran.

Her mother sat down on the other side of him and opened it on her knees. “Here. This is Xiaoran when she was small.”

Xiaoran lunged for the album. Her mother moved it out of reach without looking up. “Don’t disturb me.”

Yichen leaned in. A little girl with a bowl haircut and a fierce round face was standing behind a birthday cake under a persimmon tree, in her grandparents’ courtyard, with her cheeks puffed out, apparently mid-argument with someone outside the frame.

“That’s you?”

“Unfortunately.”

“You were cute.”

“Don’t encourage her. She was very stubborn,” said her mother.

“Was?” said her father, and Xiaoran glared at him.

Her mother turned a page. “Oh, this is her first day at the new school. In the city. Twelve years old. New school, new everything. That morning she told me she wanted to go back to her grandmother’s and keep chickens.”

The photograph was of a girl in a uniform that was too big for her, outside a gate Yichen didn’t recognise, holding her mother’s hand and looking at the camera with total despair.

“That sounds familiar,” said Yichen.

“Excuse me?”

He looked at her, amused, and said nothing at all, and her mother laughed.

“She’s still like that sometimes.”

“Mum!”

He turned the pages slowly. He didn’t laugh loudly or make a fuss. He looked at each one as if it mattered, and every so often asked her mother a quiet question, and her mother told him things Xiaoran had forgotten herself: the year she’d refused to wear anything but red, the time she’d tried to post a letter to her grandmother by putting it in the fridge.

Xiaoran watched him. There was something strange and close about seeing him here, on her parents’ sofa, learning about the little girl who’d lived in this flat long before she met him. He knew her in ways her parents never would: what she was like when she was tired, how she sounded when she was trying not to cry over something small, the version of her that existed outside these walls. And now, page by page, he was getting the one that came before.

At some point her father’s phone rang and he went to answer it, and her mother took the teapot back to the kitchen. Yichen shut the album.

“Your childhood photos are very cute.”

She groaned. “Please forget them.”

“Why?”

“I have an image to maintain. A sophisticated university student.”

“I see.”

“Don’t look at me like you know me.”

His face changed. “I do know you,” he said.

She went quiet. Under the edge of the album he found her hand, and laced his fingers through hers, and the strange, enormous feeling of having him here in her family’s home got a little smaller.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven her mother came out with a small plate of fruit for him to take to his room.

“Don’t stay up too late, either of you.”

“Okay.”

“Yichen, if you need anything, knock.”

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“Xiaoran, you too.”

“Yes, Mum.”

At the kitchen door she paused. “And don’t keep him awake talking all night.”

Xiaoran made a noise like a stepped-on cat. “Mum!”

“Good night,” said her mother serenely, and shut the kitchen door.

Yichen waited until it was shut. Then he looked at Xiaoran, who pointed a warning finger at him.

“Don’t.”

His shoulders were moving.

“You’re laughing.”

“I’m not.”

“You are!”

He gave up and laughed without a sound, with his hand over his mouth, and she hit his arm.

“You’re enjoying my suffering.”

“A bit.”

“You’re terrible.”

He took the hand that had hit him and kissed her knuckles. “Good night, Xiaoran.”

He started towards the spare room. She watched him go, and then said, “Yichen?”

He turned round.

“Thank you for coming.”

The teasing went out of his face. He came back down the hallway and pushed a piece of hair off her cheek.

“Thank you for inviting me.”

He bent and kissed her, briefly, there in the hallway under the light, where anyone could have seen. “Go to sleep. I’ll see you at breakfast.”

She watched him go into the room her mother had made up on Wednesday, and heard the door close.

At some point after midnight the wind changed, and something on a balcony across the courtyard came loose and banged for an hour. In the morning her mother said she hadn’t heard a thing. Her father said he hadn’t either. But at breakfast he put the last fried egg on Yichen’s plate without asking anyone, and that was how Xiaoran knew he’d been awake too, lying in the dark, listening to the flat with one more person in it.

chapters.desc: The next evening she takes him to the Friday market by the river, the one her family went to every week the year they moved to the city.
chapters.title: The Hometown Night Market
chapters.epigraph: “I like seeing where you grew up. The second half of it.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen had lived in this city his whole life and had never once been to the Friday night market by the river.

Xiaoran’s family had gone every week the first year after they moved here from the town, when she was twelve and knew nobody, and her father had walked her up and down the stalls every Friday night to make the city feel smaller. The typhoon had blown through in the small hours and gone out to sea by noon, and the air had that washed, flattened feeling it always had afterward. By six the stalls were back up.

“Come on. Two streets,” she said, pulling him by the hand off the bus.

“Why are you walking so fast?”

“Why are you walking so slow?”

“You’re pulling me in three directions.”

“Because there are three things I want to show you.”

“Which one first?”

She considered it, walking backward in front of him with both his hands in hers. “Food.”

“Good choice.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The market ran along the embankment under strings of yellow bulbs, two long rows of stalls with a crowd shuffling between them, and it smelled of charcoal and chili oil and frying dough and something sweet she couldn’t name. Xiaoran stopped dead in front of a stall with a smoking griddle and a hand-painted sign.

“That one.”

“What is it?”

“Egg pancake with the spicy sauce. I used to have it every single week. Dad and I would share one and he’d let me have the middle.”

“Do you want one?”

“I want two.”

He ordered two. While the woman cracked the eggs she leaned against his arm and pointed out everything around them as if he’d asked for a tour.

“That noodle stall’s been there since forever. That one used to sell goldfish, now it’s phone cases, it’s a tragedy. That dessert stall used to be better.”

“How long ago?”

“Years.”

“Maybe the owner changed.”

“The owner’s the same. The taste changed.”

“I see,” he said gravely.

“You’re not taking me seriously.”

“I am.”

“You’re agreeing with everything.”

“Would you prefer I argued?”

She thought about it. “No.”

“Then I’m doing well.”

The woman handed over the pancakes in paper. Xiaoran bit into hers immediately and made a strangled sound and flapped her free hand in front of her mouth.

“Too hot?”

She nodded, eyes watering, cheeks puffed. He uncapped the water bottle from his bag and gave it to her.

“Careful.”

“It’s still good. Try,” she said, when she could talk. She tore off the middle of her pancake, the soft bit with the most sauce, and held it up to him.

He bent down and ate it out of her fingers.

“Good?”

He chewed, and nodded, and reached for more, and she pulled it out of reach.

“That’s the middle. That’s the best part. I’m giving you the best part.”

“I know. Your father would be furious,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They bought far more than either of them meant to. She kept saying she hadn’t had something since she was fourteen, and then she’d have it, and he ended up carrying four paper bags while she walked beside him with her hand through his arm and stole from whichever bag was nearest.

At the quieter end, under the trees, there were stalls with handmade jewellery and hair clips laid out on velvet. She stopped at one and leaned over the tray.

“Do you like something?”

“I’m just looking.”

She picked up a clip and put it down. Picked up another. He stood beside her with the bags and watched her not decide. In the end she chose a small hair clip in the shape of a silver persimmon with one leaf, and asked the price, and got her purse out.

“I can get that,” he said.

“I know you can. But I want to buy it.” She paid the woman and took the clip.

“All right.”

“I’ve got my own money. I’ve been saving my allowance since May.”

“I know you have.”

“You can buy the next egg pancake,” she said generously, and clipped it into her hair above her left ear without a mirror, crooked.

He looked at it, then reached over and moved it a centimetre so the leaf sat straight.

“There’s a persimmon tree at my grandmother’s. In the courtyard. You saw it in the photo last night. The one with the birthday cake,” she said.

“You were nine.”

“I’d just fallen out of it.”

“That explains the expression.”

“I was being brave,” she said, and pulled him on towards the game stalls.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a ring toss with a row of green bottles and a wall of prizes behind them, and in the middle of the prizes, on a hook, was a small plush rabbit with one ear folded down.

“Look.”

“Do you want it?”

“It’s so cute.”

She tried first. Her first ring landed beside a bottle. Her second bounced off the counter. Her third went sideways into a box of spare rings.

“This game is unfair.”

“How?”

“The rings are too small.”

“Would you like me to try?”

She stepped aside at once and gave him the space in front of the counter like a stage. “Yes.”

He took the three rings and looked at the bottles the way he looked at the basket on a free throw. Still. Weighing it. His first ring hit the neck of a bottle and bounced off. His second landed beside one of hers. His third went somewhere behind the stall entirely, and the man running it said, “Ah,” with real sympathy.

She stared at him. “You play basketball.”

“Basketball has a bigger ring.”

“Yichen!”

“I’m aware,” he said, with dignity.

She bought three more rings out of pity and took them herself, frowning. The first missed. The second missed. The third dropped round the neck of a green bottle with a small, perfect clink.

“I did it!”

The man unhooked the rabbit and gave it to her, and she turned round and held it up to Yichen in both hands like a trophy, and he bent down and kissed her cheek right there, in front of the stall and a family of four.

“Well done.”

She went red to the ears, and hid her face in the rabbit.

✦ ✦ ✦

They found a bench at the end of the embankment where the stalls ran out and the river was black and wide, with the lights of the far bank shaking on it. She sat down with the rabbit on her knee and leaned against him. He gave her the last of the soy milk and put the bags down by his feet.

“Did you come here a lot?”

“Not anymore. When I was younger, nearly every week. At first with Dad. Then with Meilin. We used to cut through there to get home faster. Mum never let me walk it on my own after dark.” She pointed across the road at a narrow alley between two buildings.

“Did you listen?”

“Of course.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Most of the time.”

He laughed, and she tucked herself against his shoulder.

“I used to think it was so big. The whole market. I used to get lost and cry and the egg pancake lady would give me a sweet and wait with me till Dad came.”

“And now?”

“Now it’s small. It’s two streets.”

“Because you grew up.”

“Maybe. I’m glad you came. I wanted to show you properly. Not just tell you about it.” She was quiet, watching the river.

He rubbed his thumb over the back of her hand. “I like seeing where you grew up. The second half of it.”

“Why?”

“Because I know the Xiaoran who studies too late, and takes pictures, and complains about group projects. I didn’t know the one who came here every week and fell out of trees and argued about which dessert stall was better.”

“I still argue about that.”

“I’ve noticed. I like knowing her too,” he said.

She didn’t answer that. She just turned her face into his neck and stayed there, with the rabbit squashed between them, until the man at the nearest stall started putting his shutters down.

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked back to her building at half past nine, her with the rabbit, him with the bags. Her mother was out on the fourth-floor balcony taking in the washing that had survived the typhoon, and she leaned over the railing when she saw them at the gate.

“You’re back!”

“We went to the night market!”

“Did you eat properly?”

“Yes!”

“How much?”

“Quite a lot, Auntie,” Yichen called up.

“What’s that?”

Xiaoran held the rabbit up over her head. “I won it! He missed all three!”

Her mother looked at Yichen over the railing. “Basketball player,” she said, to no one in particular, and went inside with the washing.

He didn’t go up. His own home was twenty minutes away on the metro, and the metro was running again, and the spare room had been for the storm. They sat instead on the low wall by the gate, where she had sat with Meilin and Chen Yuhao when she was sixteen, and the guard in the booth turned his radio down a little, out of tact or curiosity.

She sat the rabbit on the wall between them, facing the street like a chaperone. He moved it out of the way and put his arm round her.

“Would you come again?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Even if I make you walk round for two hours?”

“Yes.”

“Even if I make you play the ring toss again?”

“That depends.”

“On what?”

“Whether you let me win.”

She laughed into his shoulder. Then, after a while, more quietly: “I like having you here. In this city. At my house. With my parents. It feels like I don’t have to keep everything separate anymore.”

“You don’t.”

“University me and home me and you.”

“It’s all the same you. I’d like to be part of all of it,” he said.

She kissed him then, on the wall by the gate, short and then not so short, and when she pulled back he was smiling.

“You’ve got that face. The one where you’re thinking something.”

“I was thinking your half of the city is quite nice.”

“That’s all?”

“And that I’m coming back at eight.”

“Why eight?”

“Your mother’s taking us to breakfast.”

She sat bolt upright. “She told you?”

“At the door this afternoon. While you were looking for your shoes.”

“Why does my mother tell you things before she tells me?”

“Maybe she trusts me more,” he said, and she hit him on the arm with the rabbit, and he caught it before it fell and gave it back to her.

From four floors up, a voice said, “Eight o’clock. Not five past,” and the balcony door slid shut.

chapters.desc: That summer he is in and out of her family’s home so often that one evening her mother says hello to the door.
chapters.title: The Door Says Hello
chapters.epigraph: “My mother said hello to a door.”
chapters.content:
By the middle of that summer, Zhou Yichen had been in and out of the Lins’ flat so often since the night of the typhoon that he knew where the guest slippers lived, which cupboard had the good cups, and that Mrs. Lin would offer him a third helping of everything no matter how many times he said he was full. He was comfortable there. Possibly too comfortable. He had certainly never expected to end up hiding in it.

It happened on a Saturday afternoon. Xiaoran had asked him over to work on their summer reading, and had told him with total confidence that they’d have the place to themselves.

“You’re sure she’s not coming back?” He was at the dining table with his laptop. She was lying on the sofa with her feet up on the armrest and a printout on her stomach.

“She’s gone to Auntie Hui’s.”

“All afternoon?”

“Until dinner. They’re making dumplings. They always make dumplings and it always takes four hours because Auntie Hui pleats them twelve times.”

“All right.”

She turned her head on the cushion. “Why are you asking so many questions?”

“Because of the rule.”

She laughed. Since the spring of the gaokao year, her mother had had one rule about Zhou Yichen, delivered at the kitchen table with a red pen in her hand: not in this flat when there’s no adult home.

“That rule was for high school.”

“It was never formally repealed.”

“I’m nineteen.”

“The rule doesn’t have an age on it. I checked,” he said.

“How did you check?”

“I asked your father.”

She sat up so fast the printout slid onto the floor. “You asked my father?”

“In June. When he was showing me the fish tank. I asked if the rule still applied now we were at university.”

“What did he say?”

“He said, ‘Ask her mother.’”

“And did you?”

“No, I’m not brave,” said Yichen.

She lay back down, laughing, and then got up and came over and sat on the arm of his chair and leaned on his shoulder to read his screen, which was an essay on supply chains, and said it was the most boring thing she had ever seen, and stayed there anyway for twenty minutes with her chin on his head while he worked.

“My mother likes you. She wouldn’t mind,” she said into his hair.

“She’d mind.”

“She sends you home with food.”

“She sends me home with food and instructions. Last time the instructions were to make sure you ate it.”

“She does like you, though.”

“Good. Then let’s keep it that way. Go and read your book,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They worked. It was a quiet, pleasant afternoon, with the fan turning and the cicadas going in the plane trees outside. Every so often she turned her laptop round to show him something, and he’d lean over and point at a paragraph and say, “That’s your argument. The rest is decoration,” and she’d say “It’s nice decoration,” and move it anyway.

At ten past three the front door opened. She heard it first. She went completely still on the sofa. He looked up.

“Xiaoran? I’m home! Auntie Hui’s got a migraine!”

Xiaoran sat bolt upright. “Hide,” she whispered.

He blinked at her. “What?”

“Hide.”

“Xiaoran—”

“Please!” She was already off the sofa and pulling him up out of his chair by the wrist. A year of that rule did things to a person. The nearest door was the little storeroom off the living room, where the mop and the spare rice and fifteen years of boxes lived. She opened it.

He looked inside. He looked at her.

“Just for a minute,” she said, with her hands clasped under her chin.

He looked at her for one more second with the face of a man accepting that this was now his afternoon, and stepped in among the brooms. She shut the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother came into the living room with a shopping bag in each hand.

“Why are you standing there like that?”

“I’m studying.”

“Standing up?”

“I was stretching.”

Mrs. Lin put the bags down on the table. Next to two laptops. And two cups of tea.

She looked at the second cup. Xiaoran looked at the second cup. Then at her mother. Then at the cup again.

“Did you have someone over?”

“No.”

“Then who drank this?”

“Me.”

“Out of two cups?”

“I was very thirsty.”

“And the second laptop?”

“It’s for... comparing.”

Her mother looked at her for a long, long moment. “I see. I’m going to put these away,” she said.

“Okay!”

Her mother went down the hall towards the kitchen with the bags. Xiaoran let her breath out and turned towards the storeroom, and from behind its door came a small, distinct rustle, followed by the hollow clonk of a mop handle falling against a bucket. She shut her eyes.

Her mother came back without the bags. She stopped in the doorway. She looked at the storeroom door.

“Why is that shut?”

“Because I shut it.”

“Why?”

Xiaoran looked at the door, and at her mother, and at the door. “Because it’s a door?”

The living room was silent. Outside, a cicada stopped and started again.

Then her mother’s eyes went past her, to the shoe rack by the front door. There, beside Xiaoran’s slippers, sat a pair of size forty-four trainers with their laces tucked neatly inside, the way only one person in the world tucked in his laces.

“Mum! Do you want some tea? I’ll make you tea!”

“That would be nice,” said Mrs. Lin, and walked straight past her to the storeroom, and stopped in front of it, and said to it, in a perfectly pleasant voice:

“Hello, door.”

Silence.

“Hello, Yichen.”

The door opened from the inside. Yichen was standing among the brooms with a folded umbrella in one hand. He inclined his head, exactly the way he did to professors and old ladies on the metro.

“Hello, Auntie.”

Her mother looked at him. She looked at the umbrella.

“What are you doing in there?”

A sensible man might have said that he’d been invited, and that Xiaoran had panicked, and that he’d gone along with it to keep the peace. Yichen looked at the umbrella in his hand as if it might have an opinion.

“I was looking for something.”

“An umbrella?”

“Yes.”

“In the storeroom.”

“Yes.”

“Did you find it?”

He looked down at the umbrella. “Yes, Auntie.”

“Good,” said Mrs. Lin. She turned round. “Xiaoran. Why didn’t you tell me he was here?”

Xiaoran was in the kitchen doorway with the kettle in her hand, and she could feel her ears burning. “I was going to.”

“When?”

“Later.”

“Is he a secret?”

“No!”

“Then why was he in with the mop?”

Xiaoran put the kettle down and covered her face with both hands. Yichen, to his enormous credit, didn’t laugh. He came out of the storeroom and shut the door behind him.

“I’m sorry, Auntie. I should have said hello when you came in. I knew you were out. I shouldn’t have come when you weren’t home.”

Her mother looked at him, and something in her face changed.

“You know about the rule,” she said.

“Yes, Auntie.”

“Who told you?”

“Xiaoran. And Uncle said to ask you.”

“He said that, did he. Well. You tucked your laces in. At least you’re tidy. Sit down. Both of you. I’m making the tea. Xiaoran, you’re useless, give me that kettle.” She glanced at the shoe rack. She waved a hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

The three of them ended up at the dining table. Yichen had put the umbrella back. Her mother had brought out a plate of peaches and some biscuits, and was asking him about his summer training schedule and his reading list and whether he’d eaten lunch, and he answered each question politely and in full.

It was all completely normal, which made it much worse. Xiaoran sat next to him and kicked his ankle under the table every time her mother looked. Her mother saw every kick and ignored them all.

“So you were studying together?”

“Yes, Auntie.”

“That’s good. She’s been working hard this summer.”

“She has,” said Yichen.

Xiaoran looked at him. There was the smallest curve at the corner of his mouth. Don’t you dare, she thought at him, as hard as she could. He looked down at his peach.

“You should both take breaks. Studying all day isn’t healthy. Yichen, have another peach,” said her mother.

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“And you can come round whenever you like. When I’m here. Then you won’t have to hide.” Her mother put the peach on his plate.

Xiaoran made a strangled noise.

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“And next time,” said Mrs. Lin, as if she were remarking on the weather, “take your shoes in with you.”

Yichen finally laughed. He tried not to, put his hand over his mouth and turned it into a cough, and failed, and her mother laughed too, and Xiaoran put her forehead down on the table between the biscuits and stayed there.

✦ ✦ ✦

When her mother had gone back to the kitchen, Xiaoran lifted her head and glared at him. “You laughed.”

“I did.”

“You weren’t supposed to.”

“I’m sorry.”

“You’re not sorry at all. You could have just come out.” She lowered her voice to a hiss.

“You told me to hide.”

“Because I panicked!”

“I noticed.”

He reached over and moved her hands away from her face, one at a time, and held them on the table.

“Don’t be embarrassed.”

“My mother said hello to a door.”

“She was being polite.”

“She’ll remember this forever. She’ll tell Auntie Hui. She’ll tell my grandmother.”

“Probably. She was right, though. I shouldn’t have come when she wasn’t here. I knew the rule,” he agreed.

“It’s a stupid rule.”

“It’s her rule. In her flat. She made it because she trusts me a bit. Not all the way. I’d like it to be all the way one day. Hiding with the mop doesn’t help.” He turned her hand over and looked at it.

She looked at him. Then she leaned sideways until her head was on his shoulder.

“You’re so annoying when you’re right.”

“I know.”

“For what it’s worth,” he said, after a while, “your storeroom has a very good umbrella.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

From the kitchen, her mother called: “Yichen! More peaches?”

“Yes, please, Auntie.”

Xiaoran sat up and stared at him. “You’re too comfortable here.”

“Your mother invited me.”

“After she found you in a cupboard.”

“Storeroom,” he said, and she hit his arm, and he caught her hand and held on to it under the table while her mother came back in with a second plate of peaches and looked at the two of them, and at their hands, and pretended not to see, and put the plate down in front of him.

chapters.desc: Three years together, and Lin Xiaoran has never once seen Zhou Yichen watch basketball. Until 8 AM on a Saturday.
chapters.title: The Terrifying Discovery That Zhou Yichen Was a Nerd
chapters.epigraph: “It’s not nerd things. It’s an organised binder.”
chapters.content:
For almost three years, Lin Xiaoran believed she understood Zhou Yichen completely. Basketball. Business major. Good grades. Annoyingly handsome. Secret softie. Simple. Reasonable. Normal. Then one Saturday morning, she discovered a side of him that genuinely frightened her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It began because Xiaoran was bored. She had claimed one corner of Yichen’s sofa at eight in the morning, supposedly to study, and was mostly drawing pandas in the margins of her media theory notes. Yichen sat at the other end with his laptop. Peaceful. Normal. Then the laptop let out a roar—a full arena of people screaming at once. Xiaoran looked up.

“…What was that?”

“Hm?”

“That.”

Yichen glanced at the screen. “Oh. The game started.”

“What game? It’s eight in the morning.”

“It’s eight in the evening in New York.”

She stared at him. “You get up at eight on a Saturday to watch basketball?”

“Sometimes seven.”

“You never told me.”

“You never asked.”

Fair. Annoyingly fair. She already knew he loved basketball. Everyone knew. She had watched him play for three years, held his jacket through tournaments, researched potassium for him. But she had never once seen him watch it. So she climbed across the sofa and sat beside him, curious. That was her first mistake.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the screen, players ran up and down a court under blinding lights while two commentators talked fast. Xiaoran understood the basics: ball, hoop, tall men. Then she noticed something horrifying. Yichen was paying attention. Not casual attention, not background-noise attention. The kind of focus he usually reserved for his own games, elbows on his knees, eyes moving across the whole court instead of following the ball. One play ended in a missed shot. Immediately—

“He should have switched.”

Xiaoran turned slowly. “…What?”

“The big man stayed in drop coverage. That gave the guard the whole pull-up.”

“What.”

“And the weak-side help was late, so the corner was open anyway.”

“What.”

“They’ve been doing it all quarter. His shooting numbers off the dribble are the best in the league this month.”

“WHAT.”

Yichen finally looked at her, and paused, because she was staring at him like he had grown a second head.

“…You know what all of that means?” she asked.

“Hm.”

“ALL of it?”

“Hm.”

She grabbed both his shoulders. “WHO ARE YOU?”

✦ ✦ ✦

It got worse, because once she started asking questions, he answered them.

“How do you know they’ll lose?”

“They’re losing the possession battle. Too many turnovers.”

“The what battle?”

“And their spacing is terrible. Look—four guys on one side of the floor.”

“Yichen, you’re speaking wizard.”

“It’s basketball.”

“It is NOT the basketball I know. The basketball I know is you running around looking handsome and me screaming.”

“That’s also basketball.”

The terrifying part was that he wasn’t even trying. It just came out of him, the way math did, the way finding her in a crowd did. Then, during a commercial break, Xiaoran discovered the bookshelf. Huge mistake. Behind the business textbooks, filling an entire shelf, was a row of thick notebooks with years written on the spines in his neat handwriting, starting from when he was thirteen. She pulled one out. Inside were hand-drawn diagrams—circles and arrows and dotted lines—with notes in the margins. Backdoor cut works if the wing over-helps. Try in practice. Dad says I always pass too early.

Under the notebooks was a shoebox full of ticket stubs from city league games, a dog-eared book called Spacing, Tempo and the Modern Offence, and a binder of printed shot charts with coloured highlighter on every page. She held up the binder like evidence in a courtroom.

“What is THIS.”

Yichen glanced over. “Shot charts.”

“You PRINTED them. And HIGHLIGHTED them.”

“It’s easier to see on paper.”

“You did this for FUN?”

“Hm.”

Silence. Her boyfriend was a nerd. An actual nerd. Not a basketball player who happened to be smart—a basketball nerd, with a filing system. Yichen looked confused by her reaction. To him this was obviously normal.

“My dad used to watch games with me. He’d pause the replay and ask what I would’ve done,” he said, by way of explanation.

“THAT DOESN’T EXPLAIN THE HIGHLIGHTER.”

He looked at the binder, then at her, then back at the binder, genuinely puzzled about where the problem was.

✦ ✦ ✦

When the game came back, the calm, composed Zhou Yichen disappeared entirely.

“Why would you take that shot? No. NO. There’s twenty seconds on the clock.”

“They just threw the game away.”

Xiaoran stared at him. This man was emotionally invested. Deeply, aggressively invested in a team on the other side of the planet that didn’t know he existed. Then, in the last minute, one player made a cut so clean the defence didn’t even turn around in time, caught the pass in stride, and laid it in. Yichen sat bolt upright.

“THAT was beautiful.”

Xiaoran had never heard him call anything beautiful except a basketball play of his own, and her. Apparently, now there were three things.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rest of the morning became educational suffering, because every time she asked one question, he answered with a lecture.

“What’s a pick-and-roll?”

Twenty minutes.

“What’s drop coverage?”

Fifteen minutes, with diagrams on the back of her media theory notes.

“Why does everyone keep yelling about spacing?”

Thirty minutes. She regretted that one deeply. When the game finally ended, Xiaoran sat slumped against the cushions, mentally exhausted. Yichen looked perfectly happy.

“…You really love this,” she said.

“Hm.”

Simple answer. But it landed differently, because she rarely saw him like this. No competing, no looking after everyone around him: just excited, the way a kid gets excited. A little nerdy.

“I didn’t know,” she said.

“Know what?”

“That you could talk this much.”

He laughed—properly laughed.

“You asked questions.”

“YOU HAD ANSWERS READY. You had DIAGRAMS.”

She leaned against his shoulder anyway, warm and comfortable.

“It’s cute,” she said.

“What is?”

“You. Getting this excited about nerd things.”

“It’s not nerd things.”

“You have a binder.”

“It’s an organised binder.”

“SEE.”

He laughed again, helplessly, and put an arm around her waist. Xiaoran smiled into his shoulder. Three years, and she was still finding new parts of him—especially the parts nobody else got to see.

“Want to watch the game tomorrow?” he asked.

She looked up, suspicious. “Are you trying to convert me?”

“Maybe.”

“Will there be another lecture?”

“Probably.”

“Then no.”

“Understandable.”

But for the rest of the week, Lin Xiaoran kept asking—completely out of nowhere, in the middle of lunch, in the library, once during a movie—“What’s drop coverage again?”

Just to watch Zhou Yichen accidentally turn into a basketball nerd all over again.

chapters.desc: She mutes a girl who posted about Yichen. He mutes an account that posted about her. Fang Ze finds out about both.
chapters.title: Blocked
chapters.epigraph: “Because they don’t know you.”
chapters.content:
The first account Lin Xiaoran muted belonged to a girl from Economics she had never met.

She only knew the girl’s name because it was under a photograph of Zhou Yichen coming out of the sports centre with his kit bag on his shoulder, and the caption made her stop with her spoon halfway to her mouth.

Zhou Yichen is honestly unfairly good-looking. How does anyone look like this after training?

Underneath, the comments:

I saw him at the gym yesterday, he’s even taller in real life

is he single

I heard he’s not

doesn’t mean we can’t look

Xiaoran put her spoon down. She wasn’t angry. The girl hadn’t done anything wrong. Yichen was good-looking; Xiaoran had known that before the rest of the university had apparently taken a vote on it. She just didn’t want to read about it over her breakfast. She pressed the three dots. Mute.

The post vanished. She went back to her congee. Problem solved.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon they were at the halfway vending machine, in the twelve minutes between her media lecture and his seminar. She had an iced tea. He had water. He was scrolling through his phone, and after a while he said, without looking up, “You’re reading my screen.”

“I’m not.”

He tipped the phone towards her. She looked hard at a tree.

“Did you see the post?”

“What post?”

“About the team. With my photo.”

“No.”

He looked at her. She looked back with an expression of perfect innocence.

“Interesting,” he said.

“Why are you asking?”

“Someone sent it to me. They said I’m getting popular.”

She choked on her tea. He took the bottle out of her hand before she dropped it.

“Careful.”

She coughed and glared at him. “You’re enjoying this.”

“A bit.”

“You’re not popular.”

“Thank you.”

“I mean you were already popular.”

“That’s better,” he said, and gave her the tea back, and didn’t ask about it again. He didn’t need to.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second account she muted had posted a video. It was a clip from the October game against Tongji: a few passes, a jump shot from the corner, the moment he turned round to his teammates after it went in. She watched it twice. Then she read the caption.

The Business faculty’s number one reason to come to basketball games

And the comments.

came for the game stayed for him

his girlfriend must be so lucky

wait he has a girlfriend??

apparently but nobody’s ever seen her

She stopped on the last one. Nobody’s ever seen her. She went to nearly every home game. She sat in the third row with Ning and shouted his name until she was hoarse. His teammates knew her. Half of them called her team manager. It was only that she and Yichen didn’t post each other much.

She looked at nobody’s ever seen her for a while. Then she muted that one too.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen’s turn came the next day. He was waiting outside the Media building when a notification came through from the university confession account. Somebody had posted a photograph of Xiaoran.

It was from the student exhibition the week before. She was standing by a display board holding her camera, her hair tied back, looking at something outside the frame with total concentration. He had been there that afternoon. She hadn’t noticed him for ten minutes, until he turned up beside her with a drink.

Who is this girl from Media? Saw her at the exhibition, she’s so pretty

He knew he shouldn’t. Since last spring he had a rule about comments: he didn’t read them. He read them anyway.

I think she’s second year

does anyone know her name

she’s always around the media building

heard she has a boyfriend

lucky guy

He looked at the screen. Then he tapped the account. Mute. And put the phone in his pocket as she came through the doors at a run.

“Yichen!”

He took her bag off her shoulder. “Slow down.”

“I thought you’d gone.”

“I said I’d wait.”

She took his hand and they started walking. After a few steps she looked up at him.

“Did you see the post?”

“What post?”

She stopped. So did he. For two seconds they looked at each other.

Then her eyes narrowed. “You muted it.”

“Did you?” he said.

She opened her mouth, and closed it, and looked away, and he laughed out loud on the path.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took another week for them to realise what was going on.

They were in the library at a table by the window, her with a presentation, him with lecture notes. His phone buzzed. He looked at it and slid it under his notes.

“Who’s that?”

“Fang Ze.”

“What does he want?”

“He sent me a post.”

“About what?”

“About someone asking about you.”

She sat up. “Me?”

He turned the phone round. It was a screenshot: the confession account again, and this time a picture of her taken from behind, walking across the main square with her camera bag.

Does anyone know the girl who’s always taking photos around the Media faculty?

she’s so pretty

I think she’s dating someone in Business

isn’t that Zhou Yichen’s girlfriend??

wait really

“How did Fang Ze even find this?”

“He follows the account.”

“Why?”

“Entertainment, he says.”

She looked at the screenshot. Then at him. “Did you mute it?”

He didn’t answer straight away, which was answer enough.

“Yichen. Did you mute the account?”

“Yes.”

A slow smile came over her face. “You did.”

“So did you.”

“How do you know?”

“Because you haven’t mentioned it once in two weeks,” he said, “and every time somebody brings it up you go very calm.”

“I’m naturally calm.”

“Of course.”

“I don’t care about things like that.”

“Naturally.”

“Stop agreeing with me like that.”

“All right,” he said, and went back to his notes.

They worked for four minutes. Then she leaned across the table and whispered, “Wait.”

“What?”

“Are we both muting people who talk about each other?”

He thought about it. “It seems that way.”

She put her hand over her mouth. Her shoulders started to shake. He watched her try to hold it in for as long as she could, which was about five seconds, and then she put her head down on her laptop and laughed into the keyboard until the boy at the next table turned round.

“We’re ridiculous,” she whispered.

“A bit,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fang Ze found out properly over dinner, at the hotpot place by the north gate, because Fang Ze always found out about everything eventually.

“By the way,” he said, fishing a slice of lamb out of the pot, “I sent you that post last week.”

“I saw it.”

“You muted the account, didn’t you?”

“Yes.”

“I knew it. I sent you another one yesterday and you didn’t say anything. Normally you at least tell me the photo’s bad.”

“Most of the photos are bad.”

“See? That’s what I mean.”

He turned to Xiaoran. “And you,” he said.

“What about me?”

“You muted it too.”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen. Yichen looked at Xiaoran. Neither of them said anything.

Fang Ze put his chopsticks down. “Oh my God.”

“Don’t,” said Yichen.

“You’re both doing it? You’re both going round muting everyone who posts about the other one?”

“It’s not like that,” said Xiaoran.

“Then what’s it like?”

She thought about it honestly. “Sometimes I just don’t want to read strangers talking about him.”

“And you?” Fang Ze said to Yichen.

Yichen took a piece of tofu out of the pot. “Same.”

Fang Ze looked from one of them to the other, and then he laughed until he had to hold onto the table.

“That’s insane. There are thirty thousand students at this university and you two have personally decided to protect each other from the internet.”

“We’re not jealous,” said Xiaoran.

“I didn’t say jealous!”

“You were thinking it.”

“Eat your dinner,” said Yichen.

“Look at you! You’re not even denying it!”

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked back afterward along the river path with their hands in his coat pocket.

“Do you think we’re strange?” she said.

“Compared to Fang Ze?”

“Generally.”

“No.”

“Good. Does it bother you? When people talk about me?” A few more steps.

“Sometimes.”

“Why?”

“Because they don’t know you.”

She met his eyes.

He said, “They see one photograph. Or a few seconds of a video. And they decide they know something about you. They talk about you like you’re someone they’ve met. I don’t like it. I know that’s not very generous.” He was quiet.

“It’s a bit possessive.”

“I’ve been called worse. Does it bother you that I’m possessive?”

She considered it. “No, I don’t like the ones asking if you’re single,” she said, and squeezed his hand inside the pocket.

“Why?”

“Because you’re not.”

“How do you know?”

She gave him a look that said it was the stupidest question in the world. “Because you’re going out with me.”

He laughed. “Right.”

“If they want to know if you’ve got a girlfriend they could just ask you.”

“That would mean talking to me.”

“Exactly. You could wear a sign.”

“What would it say?”

“Taken. Admire from a distance.”

“I don’t think I need a sign. The person I want to know I’m taken is already holding my hand,” he said, and stopped on the path, and pulled her round to face him by their joined hands.

She looked at him under the streetlight for a second. Then she tugged him down and kissed him, there on the river path where anyone could have taken a photograph, and didn’t care at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she was in bed when her phone buzzed.

Yichen: Have you muted Fang Ze?

Xiaoran: what? why?

Yichen: He’s just sent me another one.

Xiaoran: about you?

Yichen: About us.

A screenshot arrived. Someone had taken a photograph on the river path that evening: the two of them under the streetlight, her looking up at him, him looking down at her. The caption said: Campus’s most obvious couple, spotted again. She looked at it.

Xiaoran: I’m muting Fang Ze

Yichen: He’s not an account.

Xiaoran: he should be

Xiaoran: actually don’t. I want to see what else he finds

Yichen: I thought you didn’t like people posting about us.

Xiaoran: I don’t. but I like pictures of us

He opened the screenshot again and looked at it for a while. It wasn’t that anyone had posted it, or that people thought they looked good together. It was the way she was looking at him: the particular way she did when she’d forgotten anyone else existed.

Yichen: I’m keeping this one.

Xiaoran: why

Yichen: I like how you’re looking at me.

She buried her face in her pillow. A minute later she typed you’re so annoying, and he typed I know, and she lay there smiling into the dark. Then, for the first time in two weeks, she opened the confession account, found the photograph, saved it, and muted the account again.

chapters.desc: Fang Ze unlocks Yichen’s phone with her birthday on the first try, and a Saturday in October turns into a conversation about passcodes.
chapters.title: The Passcode Swap
chapters.epigraph: “Because I made you tell me your passcode.”
chapters.content:
The argument started over a phone, and the phone wasn’t even hers.

It was a Saturday afternoon in October of second year. Lin Xiaoran was sitting cross-legged on Zhou Yichen’s sofa, in his flat across the road from her building, waiting for him to get ready for dinner, and she had just been told something deeply offensive.

“He did what?”

“He unlocked it. At training. I left it on the bench. The coach wanted the schedule, so Fang Ze picked it up and got in on the first try,” said Yichen from the bedroom.

“How?”

Yichen came out with his wallet in his hand and looked at her the way he did when the answer was sitting in front of him in socks.

“Your birthday.”

She stared at him. “Your passcode is still my birthday?”

“It’s been your birthday since I was seventeen.”

“And Fang Ze knows my birthday?”

“The whole team knows your birthday. You brought a cake to training.”

She had. She hadn’t realised that a cake made her birthday public information.

“Change it,” she said.

“Why?”

“Because if Fang Ze can get into your phone, anyone can. That’s basic security. My mother would be horrified.”

He considered this. “Your mother would be horrified,” he agreed, and turned slightly away from her and did something with his thumb.

“What did you change it to?”

“Something else.”

“What?”

“If I tell you,” he said reasonably, “Fang Ze could get it out of you.”

Her mouth fell open. “I would never tell Fang Ze.”

“You told him your birthday.”

“With a cake!”

He put the phone in his pocket, entirely unbothered. She looked at her own phone. She unlocked it with his birthday. Then, because she wasn’t going to be the only person in this relationship who could be bribed with cake, she changed hers too.

“What’s yours now?” he said.

“Something else.”

He smiled. “Fair.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The real problem showed up at dinner. They were at the noodle place by the east gate, sharing a plate of smashed cucumber, and she was halfway through a story about her media theory seminar when his phone lit up on the table. He glanced at it and put it in his pocket.

“Who was that?”

“Fang Ze. Asking if I’m coming to training tomorrow.”

“Then answer him.”

“In a minute.”

She ate a mouthful of noodles. Then, casually: “Can I use your phone?”

“For what?”

“To check something.”

“What?”

“Something.”

He slid it across the table. She picked it up. The screen was locked. She looked at it. She looked at him. He looked back, perfectly calm, and drank some water.

“What’s the passcode?”

“You told me to change it.”

“I didn’t mean from me!”

“You didn’t specify. I’m being thorough. Your mother would approve,” he said.

She put the phone down and crossed her arms. “You’re unbelievable. What’s the new one?”

“That would rather defeat the purpose.”

“Yichen!”

He laughed, and that was how it began.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, running late for her nine o’clock, she discovered that she had no idea what she’d changed her own passcode to. She had done it in a temper, to something she’d been sure she’d remember. She didn’t. After three wrong tries she stood in the middle of the walkway staring at the screen, and rang him.

“Good morning.”

“What’s your birthday?”

A pause. “My birthday?”
