“I’ve forgotten my passcode.”

There was a short silence on the line, and then a low, amused laugh that made her regret ringing him at once.

“You’re laughing?”

“I’m sorry.”

“No, you’re not.”

“Not especially. Try the day we first met,” he said.

She frowned. “That’s not what I used.”

“Try it anyway.”

She tried it. The phone unlocked. She took it away from her ear and stared at it, and then put it back.

“You guessed?”

“Educated guess.”

“That’s cheating.”

“How is it cheating?”

“Because you know me.”

“That’s generally how it works,” he said, and she hung up on him.

Yichen: Have a good lecture.

Xiaoran: I don’t like you

Yichen: You remembered your passcode.

She looked at that for a while. Then she smiled at it, against her better judgment, and ran.

✦ ✦ ✦

For the first week it was mostly funny. They’d never been secretive with each other. They knew each other’s friends and schedules and habits; they’d never had any reason to go through each other’s phones. But they’d always just picked up whichever one was nearest. He’d use hers to take a picture when his was in his bag. She’d use his to look up an address. She’d send herself photographs out of his camera roll when he’d taken one of her that she liked.

Now everything had to be asked for.

“Can you send me that?”

“Which?”

“The photo from yesterday. The one on the bridge.”

“From my phone?”

“Obviously from your phone.”

He sent it. She looked at it, and at him. “You could have just let me use your phone.”

“You could have just asked me to send it.”

“You’re so annoying.”

He kissed her temple. “Thank you.”

In the library she asked to see his screen, just to check the time. He tilted it towards her. She looked at the lock screen. He looked at her. Neither of them said anything at all. Then he put it away, and she went back to her notes looking deeply wronged, and kept her foot hooked round his ankle under the table for the rest of the afternoon anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the second week, Fang Ze had noticed. They were having lunch in the canteen, and Xiaoran leaned across the table.

“Can you look at the message I just sent you?”

Yichen unlocked his phone, opened their chat, and read it out loud.

“I wanted you to see the picture,” she said.

He forwarded it back to her. She opened it on her own phone. Fang Ze watched this happen with his chopsticks halfway to his mouth.

“Why don’t you just let her use your phone?”

“She doesn’t know the passcode,” said Yichen.

“Why not?”

“Because he changed it,” said Xiaoran.

“Why?”

“Because I changed mine.”

“Why?”

Xiaoran sat back. “Because he—”

“Because she—” said Yichen, at the same moment.

They both stopped. Fang Ze put his chopsticks down slowly.

“Have you two had a fight?”

“No,” said Xiaoran.

“Yes,” said Yichen.

She turned to him. “Excuse me?”

“Haven’t we?”

“No!”

A huge grin spread over Fang Ze’s face. “Oh, this is excellent. How long?”

“How long what?”

“How long have you been refusing to tell each other your passcodes?”

“Nineteen days,” said Yichen.

“You’re counting?”

“No.”

“You answered very fast.”

“I have a good memory.”

Xiaoran groaned and put her forehead on Yichen’s shoulder.

Fang Ze said, “I need to understand this. You two have been together for years, you sit on each other’s laps in the library, and you’re fighting about passwords?”

“We’re not fighting,” said Xiaoran into Yichen’s sleeve.

“Of course not,” said Yichen.

“Then why do you sound like you’re enjoying it?”

“Because I am,” said Yichen, and Xiaoran kicked him under the table, and he didn’t even flinch.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the third week it became genuinely ridiculous. She had a group presentation and needed to send him a file she’d downloaded on her phone. Her arms were full of books and a coffee and her laptop, so she held the phone out to him without thinking.

“Can you send this to yourself?”

He took it. They both looked at the locked screen.

She shut her eyes. He looked down at her.

“Would you like me to guess?”

“No.”

She put everything down on a bench, unlocked it, gave it back to him. He sent the file. As he handed it back she caught his sleeve.

“Actually. Wait. What’s your passcode?”

He looked at her. “Do you really want to know?”

She hesitated. “Maybe.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s annoying.”

“That’s not a very strong reason.”

“Yichen.”

He bent his head towards her. “Are you asking because you want to know? Or because you want to win?”

She opened her mouth, and closed it, and he nodded as if she’d answered.

“I thought so.”

“You’re enjoying this far too much.”

“Perhaps. Come on. You’ll be late,” he said, and kissed her and picked up her books for her.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the fourth week neither of them mentioned it at all. They still used each other’s phones, but they asked first. They sent pictures instead of passing phones across the table. And somewhere in there they had both worked out that neither of them actually cared about the other’s passcode in the slightest. The only problem was that neither of them wanted to be the one who said so.

On the Thursday her phone died in the library. She dug her power bank out and found the cable was broken, and sighed, and he looked up.

“Use mine. There’s a cable in my bag. You can charge yours off it.” He slid his phone across the table.

She picked it up. She looked at the lock screen. She looked at him. He had already gone back to his case study.

“You’re giving me your phone?”

“Yes.”

“Without changing the passcode first?”

He glanced up. “Do you need to unlock it?”

She paused. “No.”

“Then there’s no problem,” he said, and went back to his reading.

She put it down slowly. That was it? After nearly a month of this, he was just going to hand it over?

“You’re not going to ask for mine?”

“Do you want me to?”

“No.”

“Then I won’t.”

“You’re being very mature.”

“Thank you.”

“I don’t like it.”

“That’s unfortunate,” he said, and turned a page.

She tried to go back to her presentation and couldn’t concentrate at all. After a few minutes she put her hand under the table, and found his knee, and he turned his hand palm up without looking away from his book and let her fingers slide between his.

✦ ✦ ✦

It ended on a Sunday. They were at her flat doing nothing at all; she was lying on her sofa with her head in his lap, scrolling her phone, while he read. At some point she reached over and picked his phone up off the coffee table.

“What do you need?”

“Nothing. Can I ask you something?” The screen lit up. She looked at the lock screen. Then up at him.

“Of course.”

“Are we still doing this?”

He closed his book. “Doing what?”

She held up his phone. “The passcode thing.”

He looked down at her. “Are you tired of it?”

“Yes.”

“Then we can stop.”

She turned onto her back to see him properly. “Just like that?”

“Would you like a formal announcement?”

“Maybe,” she said, laughing.

He put the book aside and held out his hand. “Give me your phone.”

She gave it to him. He unlocked it, first try, with the code she’d been using since the second morning.

“You remember it?”

“Of course I remember it. The day we met.”

“How do you even remember that?”

He gave her a look. “Xiaoran.”

She went a bit pink. He gave her phone back, and she held his up.

“What’s yours?”

He told her. One, two, zero, six. She typed it in, and the phone unlocked, and she lay there looking at it. The sixth of December. The night of the umbrella and the stuffed rabbit and please let me be your boyfriend.

“I tried your birthday. And mine again. And your student number, and four zeros, and the date of your first game,” she said.

“I know. You tried in the library. I watched.”

“I never tried this.”

“No, I noticed that too,” he agreed.

She didn’t say anything for a while. She held his phone against her chest with both hands and looked up at him, and he looked down at her, and neither of them felt any need to fill the quiet.

He put both phones on the coffee table. “Are we finished?”

“Yes. I think I won, actually.” She smiled up at him.

“How?”

“Because I made you tell me your passcode.”

“You asked.”

“And you answered.”

“Would you like a medal?”

“Yes.”

He bent down and pressed a kiss into her hair. “There.”

“That’s not a medal.”

“It’s what I’ve got.”

She hooked her arms round his neck and pulled him the rest of the way down and kissed him properly, and when he finally lifted his head he was still smiling.

“Anything else?”

“Don’t change it again.”

“Why would I?”

“Just checking. But if you do, I’m changing mine too.”

“I assumed as much,” he said.

The phones stayed on the coffee table, unlocked and forgotten, until it was dark.

On Monday at training Fang Ze picked up Yichen’s phone off the bench, tried her birthday, tried it again, and put it down, wounded. Nobody on the team ever found out what the new number meant.

chapters.desc: Zhou Yichen says he doesn’t need anything for his birthday. Lin Xiaoran remembers one sentence from three months ago.
chapters.title: Two Tickets to the Garden
chapters.epigraph: “Of course I remembered.”
chapters.content:
For most people, buying Zhou Yichen a birthday gift was difficult, because he already had everything. A family with money. Good grades. Basketball. Expensive watches, expensive shoes, expensive everything. Whenever his birthday came around, he said the same thing.

“I don’t need anything.”

Annoying answer. Especially for Lin Xiaoran, because this year she wanted the gift to matter.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three months before his birthday, she found out what it should be. It was another early weekend morning on his sofa. Since discovering that her boyfriend was secretly a basketball nerd, Xiaoran had become slightly interested in watching games—not much, just enough to understand when he started speaking wizard. She was eating crackers. He was explaining things nobody had asked about. Normal relationship activities. Then the broadcast cut to a wide shot of the arena: an enormous round ceiling, a sea of people, the court glowing in the middle like a stage.

“That’s the Garden,” Yichen said.

“Hm?”

“Madison Square Garden. New York. One day I want to watch a game there.” He was quiet for a second.

Xiaoran looked over, because Zhou Yichen almost never said things like that. He was still watching the screen, completely casual, as if he hadn’t just told her a dream.

“Really?”

“Hm.”

“Why that one?”

“It’s the Garden.”

“That explains nothing.”

He laughed. “The history. The building. The way the crowd sounds. Dad and I used to say we’d go. When I was a kid. He never had the time.” By the end his voice had gone quieter.

“Why not now?”

He shrugged. “Season’s during school. Tickets. Flights. Planning. Maybe someday.” He said it lightly.

Then he went back to explaining spacing, like the conversation had never happened. Lin Xiaoran remembered every word.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three months later, his birthday arrived. Yichen expected something small. A handmade gift, maybe. Clothes. One of Xiaoran’s chaotic, sincere little presents with a card covered in stickers. Instead she handed him an envelope.

“What is this?”

“Open it.”

He was immediately suspicious, because she looked far too excited. Inside were two tickets. For several seconds, Zhou Yichen’s brain stopped working. He read them, then read them again, then a third time. New York. Madison Square Garden. A Saturday night in January, during winter break. Two seats, high up, in a section number that began with a two.

“…Yichen?”

Nothing. He was staring at the tickets like they might disappear.

“What is this,” he finally said, quietly.

Xiaoran blinked. “…Your birthday gift?”

“No.”

“What do you mean, no?”

“No. Xiaoran. These are tickets to the Garden.” He sounded genuinely stunned. A rare event.

“I know.”

“I can read.”

“Good.”

“LIN XIAORAN.”

She started laughing, because he looked so shocked, and the famous calm Zhou Yichen had apparently stopped functioning entirely.

“How,” he said.

So she explained. The prize money from the competition. The freelance video jobs she’d taken on weekends, editing a bakery’s promotional clips and a classmate’s cousin’s wedding. Three months of birthday budget. Learning far more about game schedules and seat maps than she had ever wanted to. Waking up at four in the morning to buy them the minute they went on sale. All because of one sentence on a Saturday morning.

“I wanted to surprise you,” she said.

He didn’t say anything. Suddenly Xiaoran felt nervous. Maybe it was too much. Maybe the seats were too high, or January was a bad time, or he’d rather go with his father, or—Yichen stood up. He walked around the table, pulled her to her feet, and hugged her. Hard. So suddenly that she almost squeaked.

“Yichen?”

He didn’t answer. He didn’t let go, either.

“…Are you okay?”

Then he laughed—soft, disbelieving, almost helpless—against her hair.

“You’re insane.”

“I know.”

“You’re actually insane.”

But he still wasn’t letting go, and that told her everything. Zhou Yichen wasn’t a dramatic person. He didn’t get emotional easily or react loudly. Right now, he looked completely overwhelmed.

“You remembered,” he said.

“Hm?”

“The Garden thing.”

And suddenly she understood. The tickets, New York, even basketball mattered less than this: she had listened. One random morning, one casual sentence, one small dream he’d said out loud and then put away—and she had remembered.

“Of course I remembered,” she said.

He looked down at her, and for once his calm expression was nowhere to be found. The girl he loved had spent three months working and saving for this, just to make him happy. How was anyone supposed to stay calm after that?

“If someone asked me,” he said, “what the best birthday gift I’ve ever gotten was—”

His hand found hers.

“It would be this.”

Xiaoran looked extremely pleased.

“Better than your car?”

“Yes.”

“Better than your watch?”

“Yes.”

“Better than—”

“Stop comparing yourself to objects.”

She laughed. Then a thought hit her.

“Wait. You’re taking me, right? I bought two.”

He finally smiled—the real one, the one that only showed up for her.

“Obviously.”

He laced his fingers through hers.

“You bought the tickets. The least I can do is take the girl I love to New York to use them.”

She kissed him for that, on the mouth, on his sofa, with the game still paused behind them and both his arms round her before she’d finished.

For the next three days, Chen Yuhao became extremely tired of hearing Zhou Yichen talk about Madison Square Garden over the phone. This was impressive, because normally talking too much was Xiaoran’s job.

chapters.desc: Her first paid job earns her two thousand yuan, and she spends every cent of it on a lens.
chapters.title: Her First Paid Gig
chapters.epigraph: “Because I worked for it.”
chapters.content:
The first time Lin Xiaoran was paid for something she had made herself, it was two thousand yuan, and she spent all of it on a lens before it had been in her account for a full day.

It started with a message from a third-year in her faculty. A small fashion label in the old French Concession was shooting its winter collection and needed someone cheap and good: half a day, three models, a few setups indoors and out, enough pictures for a month of posts. The third-year had seen the photographs Xiaoran took for the film society’s autumn screening and given them her name.

She read the message three times. Then she looked the label up to make sure it existed. Then she rang Tang Meilin, four hundred kilometres away.

“Meilin.”

“What? I’m in a lab.”

“I think someone wants to pay me to take pictures.”

“Congratulations?”

“No, listen. They actually want to pay me. Money. Two thousand yuan.”

“That’s what being paid generally means, Xiaoran.”

“For one shoot.”

“Still good.”

Xiaoran sat up on her bed, four floors up in the building with the broken lift, and stared at the wall. “Meilin. I could buy the lens.”

“You haven’t done the job yet.”

“I know. But I could.”

“Maybe earn the money before you spend it in your head,” said Meilin, and somebody behind her said something about a centrifuge, and she hung up.

Xiaoran ignored the advice entirely.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told Zhou Yichen that evening on the phone, lying on her stomach with her feet in the air.

“They want me on Saturday. Half a day.”

“That’s great.”

“I know!”

“Are you nervous?”

“No. Yes. A bit. I’ve never done it for someone who’s going to use them. What if they’re bad?”

“They won’t be bad.”

“You can’t know that.”

“I’ve seen the film society ones. You made Professor Hu look like he enjoys his job.”

She laughed into the duvet. “That was the lighting.”

“Then use the lighting again,” he said. “What time’s Saturday?”

“Nine till two. Why?”

“I’ll bring you lunch at two.”

“You’ve got training at two.”

“I’ll bring you lunch at two-fifteen,” he said, as if training were a minor detail, and she smiled at the ceiling after he’d hung up.

On Friday night she charged every battery twice, cleaned the sensor with the little rubber blower, wrote a shot list on an index card, rewrote it, and messaged him at half past eleven.

Xiaoran: what if I forget how a camera works

Yichen: You won’t.

Xiaoran: what if my hands shake

Yichen: Then hold it with both hands. Go to sleep.

Xiaoran: call me for five minutes

He called her for twenty. Mostly he read her bits of his marketing textbook in a flat voice until she started laughing and then stopped laughing and then fell asleep, and he heard her breathing change, and said “Good night” to nobody and hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

The shoot was in a converted townhouse with peeling green shutters. The creative director was a woman in her thirties called Fei who talked fast and drank iced coffee in November. The models were two girls and a boy not much older than Xiaoran, and the styling was simple: wool, cream and rust, a lot of scarves.

Xiaoran spent the first twenty minutes not taking a single picture. She walked around the rooms watching where the light came from, which windows were good, which corner had the ugly radiator in it. Fei watched her do it with her coffee and didn’t say anything.

Then she started, and after the first ten frames her hands stopped shaking and she forgot to be nervous.

“Could you look towards the window? Not at it. Towards it.”

“Chin down a little.”

“There. Stay there. Don’t move. Don’t breathe.”

The boy model laughed, and she caught that, too.

At eleven Fei came and looked over her shoulder at the screen.

“These are good.”

Xiaoran looked up. “Really?”

“You’re using the window. Most people your age just put a light on everything. I like this one. The laugh.” Fei scrolled.

“Thank you. Can we try the stairs before we finish? There’s a good bit of light on the landing at about one.”

Fei looked at her, then at her watch. “How do you know what time the light’s on the landing?”

“I watched it. While you were doing makeup,” said Xiaoran.

At two-fifteen exactly, while she was packing up, there was a message on her phone.

Yichen: Outside. Green door?

She ran down the stairs with her camera bag banging against her hip and found him on the pavement in his training kit, with his coat over it and two boxes of noodles in a plastic bag.

“You skipped training.”

“I left early. I told the coach my girlfriend was working.”

“You did not say that.”

“I said it in those words. He said, ‘Go.’. Did it go well?” He held up the bag.

She took the bag out of his hand, put it on the step, and hugged him hard enough that he took a step backward, in the middle of the pavement, with Fei watching through the window.

“It went well. It went really well. She liked the one with the laugh,” she said into his coat.

“Of course she did,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The money came through on Tuesday. She was sitting with him in the café by the east gate after his training, his hair still wet from the shower, and her phone buzzed on the table between them, and she looked at it and went completely still.

“Something happened,” he said.

“How do you know?”

“You’ve stopped breathing.”

She turned the screen round. Received: ¥2,000.00.

He looked at it and then at her. “Your shoot.”

“My shoot. That’s mine. I made that.” She was grinning so widely her face hurt.

He reached across the table and put his hand over hers. “Two thousand yuan. For your own pictures,” he said, the way he’d read out a final score.

It was such a simple thing to say. She felt her face go hot anyway, and she turned her hand over under his and held on.

“What are you going to do with it?”

“Buy something.”

“Something?”

“The lens.”

He knew which one. It was a secondhand portrait lens in the window of a camera shop near the station, two thousand and forty yuan, and she had gone to hold it three times in October and sent him a photograph of it every time.

“Then you should get it.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re not going to tell me to save it?”

“Do you want to save it?”

“No.”

“Then buy the lens.”

“You’re very supportive of my financial decisions.”

“I’m supportive of you buying the thing you’ve wanted for two months with money you earned.”

She was quiet for a second. “That’s why I want it.”

He waited.

“Because I worked for it.”

“I know.”

“If you’d given it to me for my birthday I’d have loved it. But it wouldn’t be the same.”

“I know. You don’t have to say it.”

“I’m not saying you were going to—”

“Xiaoran. You don’t have to explain it to me.” He ran his thumb across the back of her hand.

She looked at him. Then she nodded, and her shoulders came down.

“Now show me the lens again. I want to make sure you’re not buying something ridiculous,” he said.

“Excuse me?”

“It’s a reasonable question.”

“You don’t know anything about photography!”

“I know what an expensive box looks like,” he said, and she kicked his ankle under the table, and he didn’t move his foot away.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went to the shop the next afternoon. She’d watched four reviews and read enough forum threads to have opinions about things she hadn’t known existed a week earlier. She held the display lens up to the light. She asked the man behind the counter about autofocus and the little scratch on the barrel and whether the boxed one was the same, and he answered.

Yichen stood a step behind her with his hands in his pockets and didn’t say a word. She could feel him watching. She glanced back once and found him looking at her the way he looked at film of a game, still, paying total attention.

“What?”

“Nothing. Carry on.”

When the man asked if she’d like to take it, she looked at the price tag once more.

“Yes, please.”

She paid with all two thousand and forty yuan of her own, and checked the receipt twice, and held the box against her chest all the way out of the shop. He didn’t say anything about the receipt. He only held the door.

On the bus she sat with the box on her knees and went quiet.

He looked sideways at her. “Regretting it?”

“No. I just can’t believe it’s mine. I keep thinking someone’s going to come and take it off me.” She turned the box over in her hands.

“Who?”

“I don’t know. The lens police.”

“Do you think it’s silly?”

“Being this happy about a lens? A bit.”

“Why would it be silly?”

“It’s only a lens.”

“Then why did you want it?”

“Because it’ll make my pictures better.”

“And you like making pictures.”

“Yes.”

He said, “Then it’s not only a lens. It’s the thing you wanted, that you worked for, that helps you do what you love. You’re allowed to be happy about that.”

She looked at him. Then she let her head drop onto his shoulder and kept it there for the rest of the ride, holding the box in both arms.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she tested it on everything in her flat: the light coming through the curtains, the ceramic cup on her desk, the tangerines in the bowl, the view across the road to his building. Then she turned round.

He was on the floor with his back against her bed, looking at the team’s game schedule on his phone.

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

“Look here.”

He looked up. Click. She looked at the screen and went quiet. The window light had fallen across one side of his face and caught the small curve at the corner of his mouth, the one he had when he thought nobody was paying attention. He looked like himself. She took another.

“Am I your test subject?”

“Yes.”

“Should I charge you?”

“You’re getting free professional photographs.”

“Then I’d like to be paid another way.”

“How?”

He put his phone down and held out his hand.

She came. He took her by the waist and pulled her down into his lap, camera and all, and kissed her, and when she tried to sit up he kept a hand on her back.

“One more.”

“You said one.”

“I’ve changed my terms.”

“Professional photographer. I have boundaries,” she said against his mouth.

“Understood,” he said, and kissed her again anyway, and she didn’t enforce any of them.

Later, while he read on her bed, she sent Meilin a picture of the lens on her desk.

Xiaoran: Bought it

Meilin: How much did you spend

Xiaoran: All of it. And 40 of my own

Meilin: Of course you did. Did your boyfriend chip in

Xiaoran: He bought noodles. I bought my own lens

Meilin: Good. At least one of you has financial sense

She laughed out loud. He looked up from the bed.

“What?”

“Meilin.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Probably. Yichen. One more,” she said, and lifted the camera again.

This time he looked straight down the lens and smiled at her, on purpose, and she pressed the shutter and knew before she looked that it was the one she’d keep.

chapters.desc: A week after the Garden tickets, Lin Xiaoran turns up to their third anniversary with two packets of instant noodles. Zhou Yichen notices more than she thinks.
chapters.title: Three Years, Quietly
chapters.epigraph: “We’re together. We had dinner. You’re sitting on my sofa. I don’t see the problem.”
chapters.content:
By the time their third anniversary arrived, Lin Xiaoran had become exceptionally skilled at pretending she wasn’t broke.

It was a skill she had been building since a Tuesday morning in October, when she woke up at four to buy two tickets the minute they went on sale.

She had learned to walk past cafés without looking at the menus. She had become good at saying she wasn’t hungry when her friends suggested ordering dessert. She had discovered that the university cafeteria’s cheapest meal was actually quite acceptable if she added enough chilli oil.

And she had become an expert at refusing Zhou Yichen’s offers to buy her things without making it sound like she was refusing him.

The problem was that Zhou Yichen knew her well.

He noticed things. He noticed that she had stopped ordering her usual milk tea after class. He noticed that she had begun checking prices before choosing what to eat. He noticed that she had once taken a considerable amount of time deciding whether she really needed a new notebook. He also noticed that, whenever he suggested going somewhere, she became interested in staying home. He hadn’t said anything. Not yet.

But he was beginning to suspect something. And today, of all days, she had arrived at his apartment carrying a plastic bag containing two packets of instant noodles. Yichen opened the door. He looked at the bag, then at her.

“Happy anniversary.”

Xiaoran smiled brightly.

“Happy anniversary!”

He stepped aside to let her in. She walked past him, took off her shoes, and headed straight for the kitchen. Yichen closed the door.

“What’s in the bag?”

“Dinner.”

He looked at the plastic bag again.

“That’s dinner?”

“Yes.”

“Interesting.”

She turned around.

“Don’t say it like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re judging my culinary choices.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He followed her into the kitchen. Xiaoran placed the two packets on the counter with the seriousness of someone presenting a carefully prepared menu.

“Tonight’s special.”

Yichen looked at the packaging.

“Instant noodles.”

“Correct.”

“Two servings.”

“Very good.”

“With what?”

She paused, then lifted a finger.

“Eggs.”

“Anything else?”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“Why?”

“Just asking.”

“Green onions.”

“Anything else?”

“You’re asking too many questions for someone who hasn’t offered to cook.”

He smiled.

“All right. I’ll cook.”

She immediately handed him the packets.

“Thank you.”

He looked at her, amused. It wasn’t that he disliked instant noodles. He had eaten them plenty of times, especially during busy periods at university.

But their third anniversary dinner was apparently going to be prepared in his kitchen with two packets of noodles and whatever ingredients they could find in his refrigerator. He looked at Xiaoran.

She was already opening the refrigerator, examining its contents.

“Do you have eggs?”

“Yes.”

“Green onions?”

“Top drawer.”

“Vegetables?”

“Some.”

She glanced over her shoulder.

“You’re surprisingly well-stocked.”

“I live here.”

“That’s not a guarantee.”

He leaned against the counter, watching her. She took out two eggs, a small bunch of green onions, and a container of vegetables. Then she looked at him.

“Don’t just stand there.”

“What would you like me to do?”

“Wash these.”

He accepted the vegetables.

“Yes, chef.”

“Good assistant.”

The noodles were Xiaoran’s idea. The decision to eat at his apartment had been hers too. She had told him she wanted something simple, that she didn’t feel like dressing up, and that they had both been busy enough lately without making a big occasion of it. All of that was true.

What she hadn’t told him was what the tickets had really cost.

He knew about the prize money and the weekend editing jobs. She’d told him at his birthday dinner a week ago, while he was still holding the envelope. She hadn’t told him that the seats had gone up in price on the morning of the sale, or that the difference had come out of everything else: her milk tea, her phone top-up, the new tote bag she’d been going to buy in November, and most of December.

She didn’t regret a single yuan. She just hadn’t expected their third anniversary to arrive one week later.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up.

“Hm?”

“Your noodles are boiling over.”

Her eyes widened.

“Oh!”

She hurried towards the stove. Yichen moved aside, letting her take over.

“You’re supposed to watch them.”

“I was watching.”

“You were thinking.”

“That’s the same thing.”

“Not when the water is escaping.”

She looked at the pot, then at him.

“You’re very talkative today.”

He smiled and handed her the chopsticks. She stirred the noodles, muttering something about how difficult it was to cook with an audience.

Yichen didn’t tell her that he had already noticed the way she had been calculating expenses in her head whenever they went out.

He didn’t tell her that he had seen her hesitate before buying a drink last week.

And he certainly didn’t tell her that, when she had arrived earlier, he had noticed she was carrying the same old tote bag she had been using for months, even though its strap was beginning to fray. He had considered asking. But he had also noticed something else.

She was happy, the plain kind, nothing like the bright show she put on when she wanted to distract him from something. She had been smiling since she arrived.

And he didn’t want to turn their anniversary into an interrogation. So he let her stir the noodles. They ate on his sofa.

The coffee table had been cleared, leaving enough space for two bowls, two pairs of chopsticks, and a small plate of sliced fruit. Xiaoran had insisted on arranging everything herself.

She had even found two matching glasses for their drinks. Yichen looked at the table.

“Very elaborate.”

She sat down beside him.

“Don’t underestimate my preparation.”

“I wouldn’t dare.”

She handed him his bowl.

“Happy anniversary.”

He accepted it.

“Happy anniversary.”

They touched their glasses together. Then Xiaoran took her first bite. She closed her eyes.

“Mmm.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Good?”

“Very.”

He tasted his own.

“It’s good.”

She smiled proudly.

“See?”

“Although I suspect the chef had something to do with it.”

“Obviously.”

He leaned back against the sofa. She settled beside him, her legs folded beneath her, and began eating as if it were a banquet. Yichen watched her.

“You’re hungry.”

She met his eyes.

“Of course. It’s dinner.”

“You could have told me earlier.”

“Why?”

“I could have prepared something.”

She waved her chopsticks.

“This is prepared.”

He smiled.

“All right.”

She continued eating. After a while, she looked at him.

“You’re looking at me.”

“Am I not allowed?”

“You’re making me nervous.”

He tilted his head slightly.

“Why?”

“You’re doing that thing.”

“What thing?”

“Looking at me like you’re trying to figure something out.”

He smiled.

“Maybe I am.”

She looked down at her bowl.

“Don’t.”

“All right.”

He returned to his noodles. She watched him for a second, then moved a piece of egg from her bowl into his. He looked down.

“What’s this?”

“Your share.”

“You gave me the bigger piece.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s our anniversary.”

He met her eyes.

“Does that mean I get the bigger piece every anniversary?”

“Of course.”

“That’s a generous tradition.”

“I’m a generous girlfriend.”

“I know.”

She smiled, pleased. He picked up the egg and ate it. After dinner, Xiaoran insisted on washing the dishes. Yichen told her he could do it. She told him that he had cooked.

He reminded her that she had brought the ingredients. She said that was hardly a contribution. Eventually, they compromised. She washed. He dried. It was a familiar arrangement.

Their shoulders occasionally brushed as they worked. Sometimes she passed him a plate without looking, and he took it without needing to ask. When she reached for the dish towel, he handed it to her before she could.

At one point, she turned around too quickly and almost bumped into him. He caught her by the waist.

“Careful.”

“You’re standing too close.”

“This is my kitchen.”

“That’s not an excuse.”

He smiled. She remained where she was, his hand still resting at her waist. Then she lifted her wet hands.

“Don’t.”

He looked at them.

“What?”

“I know what you’re thinking.”

“I’m not thinking anything.”

“You’re going to wipe your hands on me.”

He looked at her. Then his smile grew.

“That’s a good idea.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed and released her. She pointed a wet finger at him.

“Don’t you dare.”

He stepped away, still smiling. She shook her head, returning to the sink.

A few minutes later, he came up behind her and rested his chin on her shoulder. She leaned back against him.

“Done?”

“Almost.”

He wrapped his arms around her waist. She rinsed the last bowl and placed it on the rack. Then she turned within his arms. She smiled. He lowered his head and kissed her.

It was a soft kiss at first, familiar and affectionate. She rested her hands against his chest, then slid them around his neck when he kissed her again. When they separated, she stayed close.

“Three years,” she whispered.

“Three years.”

“That’s quite a long time.”

“Is it?”

She nodded.

“We’ve known each other for so long.”

“Not long enough.”

She turned to him. His expression was calm, but there was something warm in his eyes. She smiled.

“That’s a good answer.”

“I thought so.”

She laughed and kissed his cheek. They returned to the sofa.

Xiaoran curled up beside him, her head resting on his shoulder. Yichen picked up the remote and opened a streaming service.

“What do you want to watch?”

“Something.”

“That’s helpful.”

“Something romantic.”

He turned to her.

“Do you want to watch a romance?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s our anniversary.”

He nodded.

“Reasonable.”

He scrolled through the options. She watched him for a while before speaking.

“Actually, I don’t mind what we watch.”

He looked over.

“Then why did you say romance?”

“Because I wanted to.”

He smiled and selected a film. The opening scene began.

Xiaoran settled more comfortably against him, pulling a cushion into her lap. Yichen put one arm around her shoulders. For the first twenty minutes, she watched attentively. Then she started commenting on the characters.

“Why would she believe him?”

Yichen glanced at the screen.

“Maybe she likes him.”

“That’s not a reason to be stupid.”

He laughed. A little later, she complained about the male lead’s inability to communicate.

“See? This is why people should talk.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“Do you think we communicate well?”

She considered it.

“Most of the time.”

“Most?”

“Sometimes you just look at me.”

“That’s because you usually know what I’m thinking.”

She smiled.

“Not always.”

“Then ask.”

She looked at him.

“All right. What are you thinking now?”

He held her gaze.

“That you’re comfortable.”

She blinked.

“That’s all?”

“And that I like having you here.”

Her expression softened. She shifted closer, resting her cheek against his chest.

“Me too.”

He kissed her hair. Halfway through the film, Yichen noticed that Xiaoran was scrolling through her phone. She wasn’t really reading anything.

She opened an app, closed it, checked the time, then returned to the home screen. He didn’t ask.

A few minutes later, she put the phone down, then picked it up again. He glanced at the screen. She was looking at a banking app.

Her thumb hovered over something before she locked the phone. Yichen looked back at the television. He had seen enough. She was worrying about money.

He remembered the way she had declined his offer to take her shopping last weekend. The way she had insisted on splitting a meal when he offered to pay. The way she had become interested in cooking at home.

He had a fair idea why. A week ago she had handed him two tickets to the Garden and told him, glowing, about the prize money and the bakery videos. She hadn’t said a word about what came after. He didn’t want to embarrass her by asking. So he did something else.

He reached for the fruit on the table and offered her a slice. She held his gaze.

“Thank you.”

He nodded.

A moment later, he asked casually, “Have you been busy lately?”

She blinked.

“With what?”

“Everything.”

“University?”

“Among other things.”

She considered the question.

“Not especially.”

“All right.”

She looked at him.

“Why?”

“Just asking.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re suspicious.”

“Am I?”

“Yes.”

“Then I should be careful.”

She laughed and took another piece of fruit. He didn’t ask about the banking app again. A little later, Xiaoran sat up.

“Wait.”

Yichen paused the film.

“What?”

She looked around the living room.

“Did you prepare anything?”

He studied her.

“What kind of thing?”

“For our anniversary.”

He considered her.

“Does dinner count?”

“Yes.”

“Then I prepared dinner.”

“That’s cheating. I brought dinner.”

“I cooked it.”

“With my ingredients.”

“Which I cooked.”

She laughed.

“Honestly.”

He leaned back.

“Would you like something else?”

She shook her head quickly.

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

He watched her face. She smiled.

“Really. I don’t need anything.”

He believed that she meant it. At least, he believed that she didn’t need something expensive.

But he wondered whether there was something she wanted and was deliberately avoiding.

He didn’t know how to ask without making it sound like he was questioning her financial situation. So he reached for her hand.

“Then stay here.”

She tilted her head.

“That’s the plan.”

“Good.”

He pulled her gently closer. She laughed as she settled against him. At around ten, Xiaoran’s phone rang. It was Tang Meilin. Xiaoran answered.

“Hello?”

Meilin’s voice came through immediately.

“Happy anniversary!”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Thank you!”

“Where are you?”

“At Yichen’s.”

“What did you do?”

“Nothing much.”

“Nothing much?”

“We ate.”

“What did you eat?”

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen. He was looking at the paused film, listening without appearing to listen.

“Instant noodles.”

There was a silence.

Then Meilin said, “You’re joking.”

“No.”

“On your third anniversary?”

“Yes.”

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Did he forget?”

Yichen looked over. Xiaoran immediately shook her head.

“No! He didn’t forget.”

“Then why are you eating instant noodles?”

“Because we wanted to.”

Meilin sounded unconvinced.

“Are you sure?”

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen again. He was still looking at her, his expression unreadable. She smiled.

“Of course.”

Meilin sighed.

“Fine. Enjoy your romantic noodles.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Goodnight.”

“Goodnight. Tell him I said happy anniversary too.”

“I will.”

She ended the call. Yichen looked at her.

“Meilin?”

“Mhm.”

“What did she say?”

“She thinks we’re strange.”

He smiled.

“She’s not wrong.”

Xiaoran leaned against him.

“She asked why we ate instant noodles.”

“And what did you say?”

“That we wanted to.”

He looked down at her.

“Good answer.”

She smiled.

Then, after a moment, she asked, “Do you think it’s strange?”

“What?”

“Our anniversary.”

He considered the question.

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“Why would it be?”

She shrugged.

“I don’t know. Three years is a long time. People usually do something special.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Is this not special?”

She blinked. He gestured vaguely towards the room.

“We’re together. We had dinner. You’re sitting on my sofa. I don’t see the problem.”

She smiled.

“You’re making it sound very simple.”

“It is simple.”

He reached over and tucked her hair behind her ear.

“I want to spend today with you. I am.”

She looked at him. Then she leaned forward and kissed him.

“All right.”

Later, they moved to his bedroom. Xiaoran wanted to lie down and finish the film on his tablet.

Yichen sat against the headboard, and she settled beside him with her legs across his lap.

He played with her fingers while the film continued. After a while, she spoke.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“What’s your favourite memory from the past three years?”

He looked down at her.

“That’s difficult.”

“Why?”

“There are too many.”

She smiled.

“Choose one.”

He thought.

“Probably the day we started dating.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I was waiting for you to say yes.”

She laughed.

“You made me say it first.”

“You said it first all by yourself. I was just holding the umbrella.”

She looked at him with a soft expression.

“I remember.”

He brushed his thumb across her knuckles.

“What about you?”

She thought about it. There were so many. The first time he had held her hand. The first time he had kissed her. Their first anniversary, when they had spent almost nothing and somehow ended up with a day she remembered more fondly than many expensive dates.

His birthday a week ago, and the look on his face when he opened the envelope.

“I think... I like the ordinary days.” She smiled.

He considered her.

“Why?”

“Because there are so many of them. Special days are nice. Birthdays, anniversaries, holidays. But most of our time isn’t spent doing something special. It’s just... this.”

She gestured towards the room.

“Watching something. Eating. Talking. Sometimes studying. Sometimes doing nothing.”

“And you like that?”

“Very much.”

He leaned down and kissed her temple.

“Then we’ll have more.”

She studied his face. It was nearly midnight when Yichen walked her to the door.

Xiaoran had put on her shoes and found her keys, and left her tote bag on his sofa without noticing. She turned towards him.

“Today was nice.”

“Yes.”

“Even though we didn’t do anything.”

“We did plenty.”

“Like what?”

“Eating.”

She laughed.

“That’s not enough.”

“Watching a film.”

“Still not enough.”

“Talking.”

She smiled.

“Better.”

He reached for her waist and pulled her closer.

“Being with you.”

She looked up at him.

“That’s enough.”

He kissed her. Then her forehead. Then her cheek. She rested her hands against his chest.

“Happy anniversary.”

“Happy anniversary.”

She hesitated.

Then said, “I love you.”

His expression softened.

“I love you too.”

She smiled and finally left. Yichen watched until she disappeared into the elevator. Then he closed the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found the notebook the next morning. It had slid out of the tote bag she’d left on his sofa and fallen open at a page headed GARDEN in her round handwriting. He hadn’t meant to read it. He read it anyway.

Competition prize. Bakery clips, four weekends. Wedding edit. Birthday budget. Every line had a number beside it, and the numbers added up to the price of two seats in a section that began with a two.

Under that, in smaller writing, was a second list.

Milk tea: no.
Phone top-up: next month.
New tote: after New York.
New York food: 300 (pretzel??)

He sat down on the sofa with it. So that was the instant noodles. And the frayed strap, and the milk tea, and the way she checked prices in the canteen. She’d given him the best birthday present of his life and was planning to eat on three hundred yuan for five days in New York.

He felt surprised first, then something warmer, then an ache in his chest he didn’t have a name for.

He closed the notebook, slid it back into the tote bag exactly where it had been, and picked up his phone. The Garden’s website took a while to load. He read about the seats closest to the court, and then about something called a pregame tour. Then he opened his banking app and typed in the amount she had paid, copied from the top of her page.

✦ ✦ ✦

When Xiaoran arrived that evening, Yichen was in the kitchen.

She walked in, placed her bag down, and immediately looked at him.

“Why are you smiling?”

He glanced over.

“Maybe I’m happy.”

“Why?”

He turned off the stove.

“Can’t I be happy?”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re suspicious again.”

He laughed. She walked towards him.

“What are you cooking?”

“Dinner.”

“What kind?”

“Something better than instant noodles.”

She gasped.

“Are you insulting yesterday’s dinner?”

“Never.”

He handed her a plate. She looked at it, then at him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Why are you being so nice?”

He smiled.

“Because it’s Saturday.”

“That makes no sense.”

“Does it need to?”

She studied him. He looked perfectly normal. Too normal, perhaps. But she couldn’t work out what was different.

He placed another plate on the counter and came closer, brushing a strand of hair behind her ear.

“Eat first.”

She glanced up at him, then smiled.

“Okay.”

He kissed her hair. She didn’t notice his eyes staying on her a second longer than usual, or know that he’d read a page of her notebook that morning. He served her dinner, listened to her talk about her week, and let her believe he hadn’t noticed anything at all.

She had been perfectly happy with the trade. He could see that, and he wasn’t going to take it from her. Yichen looked at her across the table.

She was telling him a story, her hands flying, about something that had happened in class that week. He listened. Smiling.

When she finished, he reached across the table and took her hand.

“What?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me again.”

“I like looking at you.”

Her cheeks warmed.

“That’s not fair.”

“Why?”

“Because I can’t concentrate when you say things like that.”

He laughed. Then he lifted her hand and kissed her fingers.

“Happy third anniversary, Xiaoran.”

She blinked.

“That was yesterday.”

“I know.”

She smiled.

“Then happy third anniversary, Yichen.”

He held her hand a little longer. He couldn’t wait to see her face in New York. Until then he let her keep her secret, and kept his.

He pretended not to notice, and she pretended instant noodles were all she had wanted. They were both excellent at it.

chapters.desc: Snow, a pretzel the size of her head, and an envelope that makes Lin Xiaoran shout in a Chinatown noodle shop.
chapters.title: New York Before Tip-Off
chapters.epigraph: “The gift was never the money.”
chapters.content:
The day before the game, Lin Xiaoran discovered two things. First, New York was absurdly big. Second, Zhou Yichen was richer than she remembered.

✦ ✦ ✦

The moment they stepped out of the hotel, Xiaoran stopped walking. Completely. It had snowed overnight. The street was a canyon of buildings so tall she had to tip her head all the way back to see where they ended. Yellow taxis honked at nothing. Steam rose out of a grate in the road like the city was breathing. A man walked past carrying a Christmas tree, three weeks after Christmas, as if that were normal.

“…Xiaoran?”

She pointed at everything at once.

“It looks fake.”

“It’s a city.”

“No. It looks like someone built a movie set and forgot to take it down.” She pointed again, at a building with a gold roof.

Yichen smiled. Watching her see New York, he decided, was better than seeing it himself. Every five minutes she discovered something new. Every ten minutes she took another photo. Every fifteen minutes she stopped dead in the middle of the sidewalk to stare up at something and got gently steered aside by a New Yorker who didn’t have time for this. They walked until their faces went numb. They watched skaters go around the rink under a giant gold statue. They shared a hot pretzel the size of Xiaoran’s head, which she declared “a little disappointing but still important.” They got lost twice—once in Central Park, once inside a single department store.

By evening they were sitting in a tiny noodle place in Chinatown, because a long flight and one hotel breakfast had already made Xiaoran homesick for broth, and the conversation finally turned to tomorrow. The game. The reason they had flown halfway around the world.

“I’m excited. Even though I still only understand half of what’s happening,” Xiaoran said.

“Hm.”

“You’ll explain.”

“Hm.”

“No lectures longer than ten minutes.”

“…Hm.”

She narrowed her eyes. “Why are you so happy?”

Yichen looked away. Which was already suspicious.

“There’s something I need to tell you.”

Uh oh.

“What happened?”

“Nothing.”

“That sounds like something happened.”

“Not really.”

Then he slid an envelope across the table.

“…What is this.”

“Open it.”

Now it was her turn to be suspicious. Inside were documents. New tickets. Not their tickets—their tickets were safely in her bag, in a plastic sleeve, because she had checked them every hour since Shanghai. These had different section numbers. A lot lower. The row said A. Xiaoran read them twice.

“…Yichen.”

“Hm.”

“These are not our tickets.”

“Hm.”

“These say courtside.”

“Hm.”

She looked up, slowly.

“ZHOU YICHEN.”

The tone that meant I know exactly what you’ve done. He stayed calm, mostly because he had known this was coming.

“You upgraded them.”

“Hm.”

“You upgraded EVERYTHING. Yichen, I know how much these cost.” She flipped through the rest. Courtside seats. A pregame arena tour. Access to watch the teams warm up from the tunnel.

“Hm.”

“I WORKED FOR MONTHS.”

“I know.”

“I SAVED FOR MONTHS.”

“I know.”

The noodle shop owner glanced over from behind the counter. Two tables away, an elderly couple had stopped eating to watch. Then Xiaoran found the actual crime, tucked at the very back: a bank transfer receipt for exactly the amount she had paid for the original tickets. Silence.

“…No.”

Yichen sighed. Yes. This part. Always this part.

“No?”

“No. Absolutely not.” She folded her arms.

“Xiaoran.”

“No.”

“Listen first.”

“No.”

He took her hand across the table. He said, “You gave me the best birthday gift I’ve ever had. You worked weekends for it. You saved your competition money. You got up at four in the morning to buy those tickets.”

She stayed quiet.

“And because I know how hard you worked,” he went on, thumb moving over her knuckles, “the last thing I want is for you to spend everything you saved on me.”

That made the argument harder. Much harder.

“The gift was never the money. It was that you remembered. That you wanted me here,” he said.

It was exactly the kind of answer Xiaoran couldn’t fight, because he wasn’t brushing her effort aside or replacing it. He understood what it had meant.

“You don’t get it,” she said, quieter.

“Then explain.”

She looked away. “…I wanted to give you something myself.”

Not the money. The feeling. Yichen lifted her hand and pressed a kiss to her fingers, right there in the noodle shop, in front of the elderly couple, who looked thrilled.

“You did. The moment you bought those first tickets, you already did,” he said.

Xiaoran felt her heart give way a little. Then she pointed at him across the noodles.

“You still upgraded everything.”

“Hm.”

“You didn’t have to.”

“I wanted to.”

“Show-off.”

“Hm.”

At least he admitted it. She kept the original tickets anyway. She wasn’t going to use them, but she folded them carefully back into their plastic sleeve and put them in the inside pocket of her coat, where they stayed for the rest of the trip.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, on the arena tour, they walked out of the tunnel onto the empty court. The ceiling rose above them, enormous and round, rows and rows of empty seats climbing towards it in every direction. A lone janitor was polishing the floor. Their guide was saying something about history and famous nights. Xiaoran forgot she was annoyed. Beside her, Zhou Yichen stood at the edge of the court with his hands in his coat pockets, still, looking like the happiest man on Earth.

Actually—no. The happiest man on Earth wasn’t looking at the court. He wasn’t looking at the ceiling or the banners or the famous floor. He was looking at her. Because somehow, the best part of the whole trip wasn’t the Garden. It was watching Lin Xiaoran see it with him.

chapters.desc: Back from New York, she is wide awake at seventeen minutes past three. Across the road, so is he.
chapters.title: Jet Lag
chapters.epigraph: “If it’s dark, I go back to sleep.”
chapters.content:
It was seventeen minutes past three in the morning, and Lin Xiaoran was wide awake.

Not the useful kind of awake, the kind that came with ideas or a sudden urge to tidy her desk. The kind where she lay in bed in her fourth-floor studio staring at the ceiling and felt, with total certainty, that she ought to be eating breakfast in Manhattan.

They had flown back from New York two days earlier. Zhou Yichen had adjusted to the time difference the way he adjusted to everything, by deciding to. She had apparently brought New York home in her suitcase. She was asleep at four in the afternoon, alert at midnight, and increasingly convinced that the correct time to eat was somewhere between two and four in the morning.

She picked up her phone.

Xiaoran: are you awake

A minute went by.

Yichen: I am now.

Xiaoran: sorry

Yichen: Jet lag?

Xiaoran: I think my body is still at the Garden

Yichen: Are you hungry?

She thought about it honestly.

Xiaoran: a bit

Yichen: What do you want?

Xiaoran: noodles?

Yichen: Instant?

Xiaoran: yes

Yichen: Ten minutes.

He knocked in eight. He was in a hoodie and the slides he wore to take the rubbish out, with his hair squashed flat on one side, holding a plastic bag.

“You came.”

“You said noodles. I brought fish balls. You never have any.” He held up the bag.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her kitchen was a strip of counter along one wall, one metre wide, and the light over the sink was far too bright for that hour. She stood in front of the cupboard in an old T-shirt and shorts with her hair in a lopsided knot while he filled the pot.

“You’re really making noodles. At three in the morning.”

“You asked for them.”

“I thought you’d tell me to go back to sleep.”

“I thought about it.”

“Would I have listened?”

“No.”

“Exactly,” she said, and hopped up to sit on the counter next to the hob.

He opened her fridge. It contained a bottle of soy sauce, two eggs, and a lemon. He looked at it for a while in silence.

“Egg?”

“Yes.”

“Vegetables?”

“There’s the lemon.”

He shut the fridge. “We’ll have egg.”

“And the fish balls.”

“We’re making instant noodles, not hotpot.”

“You brought them.”

“I brought them because I knew you’d ask,” he said, and tipped them in.

By half past three there were two bowls on the counter. He gave her chopsticks and she took one mouthful and shut her eyes.

“Oh.”

“Well?”

“Perfect.”

He tasted his own. “It’s instant noodles.”

“Don’t ruin the moment.”

She ate steadily, swinging her heels against the cupboard door, and every so often reached over and took a fish ball out of his bowl. After the third time he looked down at it.

“Are you planning to eat mine as well?”

“Yours looks fuller.”

“Because you keep taking from it.”

“That’s not how it works.”

He pushed the bowl along the counter towards her. “Here.”

“Really?”

“I’m not going to win.”

She took another fish ball. “Thank you.”

“This is a habit now. Being awake at three,” he said, leaning back against the fridge.

“It’s not my fault.”

“Whose fault is it?”

“New York’s.”

“I see.”

“And the flight.”

“Of course.”

“And the fact that I slept for four hours this afternoon.”

“That might be relevant,” he said, and she pointed her chopsticks at him.

“Don’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next night she woke at five to three. She lay still for ten minutes, eyes shut, being disciplined. Then she reached for her phone.

Xiaoran: are you awake

Yichen: No.

She put her hand over her mouth so she wouldn’t laugh out loud in the dark.

Xiaoran: then who’s typing

Yichen: A very tired person.

Xiaoran: noodles?

There was a pause.

Yichen: Five minutes.

He knocked in six. By the fourth night it was a routine. At three she woke up. At five past she was looking at the ceiling. At ten past she decided whether she was hungry, and at a quarter past someone eleven floors up in the building across the road got a message, and at twenty past they were both standing in her one-metre kitchen with the pot on.

On the fourth night she opened the cupboard and found a neat stack of noodle packets, her favourite flavour, eight of them, and in the freezer compartment a bag of fish balls she definitely hadn’t bought.

She turned round slowly. “Yichen.”

He was filling the kettle. “Mm.”

“Why are there so many?”

“Because we keep eating them.”

“You bought them?”

“Yes.”

“For us?”

“Who else?”

She went over and slid her arms round him from behind, her cheek against his back, and held on.

“You’re cute.”

“I’m buying groceries.”

“Exactly.”

He laughed and put his free hand over hers on his stomach. “Go and wash your hands.”

“One more minute.”

He let her have it. He let her have several, standing at the counter with the kettle in one hand, waiting for it to boil, and didn’t move until it clicked off.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the sixth night he had training at seven. He’d gone to bed at ten trying to get back to a normal week, and she’d made him promise not to answer if she messaged.

Just after three she woke up, as usual. She picked up her phone and put it down again. She wasn’t going to message him.

She got up instead, carefully, as if he could hear her from across the road, and turned on only the little light over the sink, and opened the cupboard. Two packets left. She took one. She was running water into the pot when somebody knocked on her door, lightly, twice.

He was standing in the corridor with his hair sticking straight up and his eyes barely open.

“Why are you awake?” she said.

“Why are you making noodles?”

She looked at the packet in her hand. “Because I’m hungry?”

He rubbed his face with both hands. “You could have messaged.”

“You’ve got training.”

“I know. Too much. Move.” He came past her into the kitchen, took the pot out of her hand, and poured some of the water away.

“You need to sleep.”

“So do you.”

“I’m not the one with training.”

“Then you can keep me company,” he said, and she sat up on the counter and watched him cook with her knees pulled up to her chin.

When the noodles were in the bowls, she said, “How did you know?”

He turned the hob off. “Your light.”

She blinked at him.

“I can see your window from mine. It’s the only one on this side of the street that’s ever on at three. Usually I don’t wake up. Tonight I did,” he said, as if he were confessing to something.

“You look?”

“I always look. If it’s dark, I go back to sleep.” He put her bowl beside her on the counter.

She was quiet. “And if it’s on?”

“Then you’re up. And I’d rather be up too,” he said.

He sat down on the step by the front door, because there was nowhere else in the flat to sit, and picked up his chopsticks. “Now eat. I’ve got training in four hours.”

She didn’t eat. She slid down off the counter and sat on the step beside him instead, which wasn’t wide enough for two, so that she was squashed against his side with her bowl on her knees, and leaned into his shoulder.

“Eat your noodles,” he said, into his bowl.

“I’m eating them.”

“You’re not.”

“I’m about to,” she said, and stayed exactly where she was.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the seventh night she woke at three and there was already a message waiting.

Yichen: Your light’s off. Are you asleep?

She looked at the message, and at her dark window, and typed.

Xiaoran: no. I’m trying to be

Yichen: Me too.

Xiaoran: are you hungry

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: me neither

Yichen: Then go back to sleep.

Xiaoran: ok

Thirty seconds went by.

Xiaoran: but what if we made noodles

There was a long pause. Then her phone rang, and when she picked up he was laughing, the low, helpless laugh he only did when nobody else could hear.

“Two small bowls.”

“Two!”

“Small.”

“Deal,” she said, already out of bed, and switched the light on so he’d see it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, when she opened the fridge for the lemon, there was a note stuck to the door with her dumpling-shaped magnet, in his handwriting.

3 A.M. Noodle Club
Members: 2

That evening she held it up at him when he came in. “What’s this?”

“An official club.”

“Does it have rules?”

“Yes. One: no noodles if nobody’s hungry.”

“Reasonable.”

“Two: no waking the other person up if they’ve got an early morning.”

“That one’s hard.”

“I know. Three: whoever finishes the last packet buys more.”

“Agreed.” She took a pen off her desk and wrote underneath, in her own big handwriting: 4. Yichen always brings fish balls.

“That’s not a rule.”

“It is now,” she said, and stuck the note back up with the magnet, squarely in the middle of the door.

The jet lag wore off in the end. The three o’clock wake-ups came less often, and then stopped. But the note stayed on the fridge. A few weeks later, on an ordinary Friday, she was at her desk finishing an essay at eleven when he looked up from her bed, where he had come to study and given up.

“Are you hungry?”

“A bit.”

“Noodles?”

“What time is it?”

“Eleven.”

“That’s too early. For the club,” she said.

“Then we’ll wait.”

She shut her laptop. “Actually, let’s make them now.”

“Why?”

She took his hand and pulled him up off the bed. “Because we don’t need jet lag to have noodles.”

He walked home at midnight. Down on the road he looked up, the way he always did. Her light was on. He stood on the pavement until it went off, and then he crossed.

chapters.desc: Game day at Madison Square Garden. But first, a fashion crisis on Fifth Avenue.
chapters.title: The Day Lin Xiaoran Wanted to Look Grown-Up
chapters.epigraph: “Not cute. Not pretty. Beautiful.”
chapters.content:
Game day. Saturday. The day the whole trip had been building towards. The day Lin Xiaoran discovered a completely unexpected crisis. The crisis wasn’t basketball. It wasn’t New York, or the fact that she still understood about forty-seven percent of what Yichen said about defensive schemes. The crisis was fashion.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started at breakfast, in a café on Fifth Avenue, where Xiaoran made the mistake of looking out of the window. Every woman who walked past looked effortless. Long wool coats. Leather gloves. Scarves wrapped like they’d been styled for a magazine. Sleek hair, good boots, the kind of confidence that made a grey sidewalk look like a runway. Then Xiaoran looked down at herself. Puffy white jacket. Comfortable jeans. Sneakers. A small panda keychain hanging from her bag.

She looked like a university student. Because she was a university student. But today, for some reason, she suddenly felt young. Across the table, Yichen looked up from his coffee and noticed her face immediately.

“What happened?”

Xiaoran pointed at a woman outside the window. “Look.”

He looked. “…Okay.”

“She looks like an adult.”

He looked at the woman, then at Xiaoran, then at the woman again.

“I don’t understand the problem.”

“I look like someone’s daughter.”

Yichen nearly laughed. “Xiaoran.”

“No, seriously. Look at her. She looks sophisticated. I look like I got lost on a school trip.” Another woman passed—camel coat, red lipstick, coffee in one gloved hand.

That was when he did laugh—a real one—which only made her more offended.

“THIS IS SERIOUS.”

“It isn’t.”

“YICHEN.”

His smile widened. The idea of Lin Xiaoran having an identity crisis on Fifth Avenue was, to him, extremely funny.

Unfortunately, once she decided something, she was impossible. Thirty minutes later they were shopping—not because Yichen suggested it, but because Xiaoran had announced, “I am becoming elegant today,” and apparently this was non-negotiable.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next three hours were chaos. The first dress was too mature. The second was too fancy. The third made her look, in her own words, like she was attending someone’s divorce. The fourth almost worked, except for the sleeves, which had opinions. Yichen followed behind, carrying more and more shopping bags. Patient. Hopelessly supportive.

At one point, a saleswoman smiled at Xiaoran and said, “Your husband is very patient.”

Xiaoran nearly choked. Yichen looked suspiciously pleased. Neither of them corrected her. Then Xiaoran found it: a soft burgundy knit dress with a simple neckline and long sleeves, warm enough for January, and a long camel coat to wear over it. Feminine without trying too hard. When she looked in the mirror, she paused.

“…Oh.”

The saleswoman smiled. “That’s the one.”

Even Xiaoran couldn’t argue. She looked older, somehow. Softer. More sure of herself. Still herself—just slightly different. Then she looked over at Yichen. Big mistake. He had gone completely silent.

“…Yichen?”

Nothing.

“Yichen?”

The saleswoman smiled knowingly. “Oh.”

Finally he cleared his throat. “…It looks good.”

Short answer. Too short. Which told Xiaoran everything, because Zhou Yichen only got this brief when he was completely compromised. She smiled in triumph. Success. Unfortunately, the next problem appeared at the register. Yichen paying. Again.

“No.”

“Yes.”

“Yichen.”

“Xiaoran. You bought me the Garden. Let me buy you a dress. You got up at four in the morning for those tickets. Let me win one argument this trip.” Then he made his winning argument.

Deeply annoying. But sensible. So the dress became Yichen’s purchase, a fact he looked suspiciously happy about for the rest of the afternoon.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, they took a yellow cab to the arena, and the city outside the window was all lights. Inside, the Garden was nothing like the empty building from the tour. It was full and loud and alive, twenty thousand people under that enormous round ceiling, music thumping, the court shining like it was lit from underneath. Their seats were so close to the floor that Xiaoran could hear the players’ sneakers squeak during warm-ups and see the sweat on the referees’ foreheads.

She stood by her seat in the burgundy dress and the new coat, holding her phone, not even taking photos, just looking. Then she caught her reflection in the glass of the scorer’s table. The dress. The coat. Her hair, which she had spent forty minutes on in the hotel bathroom. For once, she didn’t see a girl who had gotten lost on a school trip. She saw a woman.

It felt nice. Then she noticed Yichen looking at her. Again.

“…What.”

Nothing.

“Yichen. What.”

He looked away. Then—

“You look beautiful.”

Somehow, after years together, it still worked on her every single time. And this time, the way he said it felt different. Not cute. Not pretty. Beautiful. The word stayed with her. Then the lights went down, the crowd roared, and the game began, and the atmosphere changed completely. Even Xiaoran felt it—the pressure, the speed, how much every possession seemed to matter. And beside her, Yichen changed too. He leaned forward, elbows on his knees, eyes moving across the whole floor at once, tracking every screen and rotation the way he did on the sofa at eight in the morning, except now it was right in front of him. Every time a play worked exactly the way he had explained it on the back of her notes, he made a small sound under his breath, like a man watching a magic trick he already knew the secret to and loved anyway.

He looked ridiculously handsome. Xiaoran decided basketball was dangerous. Not playing it—watching someone you love fall in love with it all over again, three feet from the court. Late in the fourth quarter, a player went flying out of bounds after a loose ball and landed in the second row, two seats down. The whole crowd gasped. Yichen shot to his feet with everyone else. Xiaoran wasn’t watching the player.

She was watching him. He looked happier than she had seen him all year. Without thinking, she slipped her hand into his. He glanced down, surprised for half a second. Then he laced their fingers together and turned back to the game, and didn’t let go. The final minutes went by in a roar. The buzzer sounded. Confetti didn’t fall, because it was a regular season game in January, but it felt like it should have.

And standing there together, in the loudest building Xiaoran had ever been in, both of them realised the same thing. Years from now, when they remembered New York, they probably wouldn’t remember the final score. Or who made which shot, or the defensive schemes, or the forty-seven percent. They would remember this. Her first grown-up dress. His inability to stop looking at her. The noise, the lights, the snow waiting outside.

And the hand he didn’t let go of the whole way home.

chapters.desc: A few comments read at 2 AM, two weeks of skipped meals, and a date that ends in a quiet café.
chapters.title: The Day Zhou Yichen Found Out Lin Xiaoran Was Dieting
chapters.epigraph: “Who told you that you needed to change?”
chapters.content:
There were many things Zhou Yichen worried about. Basketball injuries. Exams. Career plans. Whether Xiaoran remembered her student card. Normal, reasonable concerns. One concern had never crossed his mind, because it sounded impossible: Lin Xiaoran dieting. The girl who once ate three desserts on a single date. The girl who considered bubble tea a personality trait. The girl who treated snacks as emotional support. Dieting? Impossible. Which was exactly why he didn’t notice at first.

It started with social media. Again. Always social media.

✦ ✦ ✦

A month earlier, Xiaoran had posted photos from New York: the burgundy dress, the city lights, a version of herself that looked a little more woman than girl. The response was overwhelmingly positive. Some of it wasn’t. Nothing cruel. Nothing dramatic. Just enough.

“She’s pretty but she’d look even better if she lost a little weight.”

“Her face is beautiful.”

“A slimmer figure would be perfect.”

Stupid, unimportant comments—the kind most people would ignore. Except Xiaoran read them at 2 AM, scientifically the worst time to read anything. And somehow they stayed with her. Not because she hated herself. She didn’t. But for the first time, she started wondering: what if? So Lin Xiaoran made a terrible decision. She started dieting, secretly. The bad kind: skipping breakfast, tiny lunches, coffee instead of food, water whenever she was hungry—the kind of diet guaranteed to make everyone miserable, especially her.

The strange part was that nobody noticed right away. Xiaoran acted mostly normal, and university was busy—deadlines, projects, practices, exams, life. Even Zhou Yichen missed it, for almost two weeks.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then came Saturday. Date day. The plan was simple: lunch, shopping, walking around the city, dinner. Xiaoran woke up feeling awful. Her stomach had spent two weeks surviving on disappointment and caffeine, and it was finally protesting. Violently. She still said nothing, because she didn’t want Yichen to worry. Terrible decision.

✦ ✦ ✦

By noon the stomachache was worse. Walking hurt. Standing hurt. Existing hurt. Somehow she kept smiling—until Yichen stopped walking.

“Xiaoran, what’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

A terrible lie. She looked pale—pale—and Zhou Yichen knew her too well.

“No.”

“What?”

“Something hurts.”

Dead silence. Caught. Again.

“…My stomach.”

Everything changed, because Zhou Yichen’s expression changed. Worry. Always worry first.

“When did it start?”

“A little while ago.”

“How long.”

She hesitated.

“Xiaoran.”

“…This morning.”

The truth, finally. She’d been hiding it all morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ten minutes later they were sitting in a quiet café. A warm drink in front of her. Food in front of her. Food she wasn’t touching. And finally, Yichen actually noticed.

“…Why aren’t you eating.”

Silence. Then more silence.

“…I’m not hungry.”

Wrong answer. Very wrong answer. Suddenly the pieces connected: the smaller meals, the constant coffee, the weight she’d lost, how tired she’d been. Everything. Dead silence.

“Have you been dieting?”

Uh oh. Xiaoran looked away. The universal sign of guilt. Zhou Yichen became angry. The worst kind: quiet angry.

“Lin Xiaoran.”

She winced. He had used her full name. Maximum danger.

“Answer me.”

“…A little.”

“A little.”

Xiaoran said nothing.

“You’ve barely been eating for two weeks.”

Oops. Of course he knew. Nothing stayed hidden from him forever.

“Why.”

Suddenly Xiaoran felt stupid. The comments sounded ridiculous now. Embarrassing. Small.

“…I wanted to look prettier.”

The anger disappeared. Completely. That answer hurt worse. Much worse.

“Xiaoran.”

She didn’t look up. Couldn’t. A hand touched her forehead, warm. Then a kiss—right on her forehead, soft and lingering. Xiaoran blinked, confused. She had expected a lecture. Not that.

“Look at me.”

She did. Big mistake. His eyes looked sad. Actually sad. Somehow that was worse than anger.

“Who told you that you needed to change?”

Xiaoran shook her head.

“Don’t do that.”

Another kiss to her hair, gentle and patient.

“Who.”

“…Nobody.”

A lie. But he let it go. That wasn’t the point. Then another kiss against her temple. And another. Each one impossibly gentle.

“What am I supposed to do with you?”

His voice sounded helpless.

“Yichen—”

Another kiss.

“You skip meals.”

Kiss.

“You drink coffee instead.”

Kiss.

“You get sick.”

Kiss.

“And somehow you’re surprised your stomach hurts.”

By now, Xiaoran’s ears were red. Being scolded while being repeatedly kissed was confusing.

“I just wanted to look prettier.”

Then Yichen laughed. His hand moved to hold her cheek, gently.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“You took me to New York. You worked for months to buy those tickets. You won competitions. You make everyone around you happier. And somehow the thing you’re worried about is losing weight?”

She looked down, because it sounded ridiculous when he said it.

“I just…”

Nothing came out. She didn’t even know anymore. Yichen sighed—the sigh he saved for her alone—and pushed the food towards her.

“Eat.”

Xiaoran didn’t move.

“Eat. Or I’m carrying you home.”

He sounded completely serious, which made it believable.

“You won’t think I’m ugly?”

Yichen leaned forward and kissed her cheek again, longer this time, then whispered,

“You’re beautiful when you’re eating. You’re beautiful when you’re studying. You’re beautiful when you’re talking too much. You’re beautiful when you’re annoying.”

“That’s rude.”

“Accurate.”

Then, more seriously: “If comments like that get in your head again, tell me. Don’t fix it by not eating.”

A tiny smile appeared. There she was—the real Xiaoran. Watching her finally pick up her fork made Zhou Yichen more relieved than winning a basketball game. He still spent the rest of the date kissing her forehead every twenty minutes, just to make sure she remembered. And every single time, he said:

“Eat your food.”

Which was considerably less romantic.

chapters.desc: A month after the dieting weeks, a photograph of his lunch arrives every day at noon. He never asks about hers.
chapters.title: Lunch, Every Day
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t want you to feel like you have to prove anything to me.”
chapters.content:
The first photograph arrived at 11:48. Lin Xiaoran was in a lecture on visual language, half listening, when her phone buzzed against the desk. It was from Zhou Yichen: a canteen tray, photographed from directly above. Rice, grilled chicken, some greens, a bowl of soup. The chopsticks were laid exactly parallel to the edge of the tray.

Xiaoran: ?

Yichen: Lunch.

Xiaoran: I can see that

Yichen: Good.

She shook her head and put the phone away. She didn’t know yet that it would happen every day.

✦ ✦ ✦

It had started, as far as he was concerned, a week before. A month after the dieting weeks, the ones he had found out about in the worst possible way, he had noticed that she was skipping meals again. Not dramatically. She was busy: a media competition, two group projects, a seminar paper. She drank coffee in the morning and ate half of something in the afternoon and told herself in the evening that she wasn’t really hungry.

The first time, he’d asked if she had eaten, and she’d said yes. The second time, he’d found her having a packet of biscuits for dinner at her desk. The third time, she’d said, lightly, that she was trying to be “more disciplined about food,” and he hadn’t liked the way she said it at all.

“Disciplined how?”

“Just. Not eating rubbish.”

“Biscuits for dinner is rubbish.”

“That was one time.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I’m fine,” she’d said, and changed the subject, and he had let her, because the last time he had pushed, she had cried in the stairwell and said she felt like he was watching her chew.

So he’d thought about it for two days. And then he’d started with a photograph.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next one came at five past twelve the following day. A bowl of beef noodles with a boiled egg.

Yichen: Lunch.

Xiaoran: you eat noodles a lot

Yichen: They’re quick.

Xiaoran: you should eat more vegetables

Yichen: There are vegetables.

She zoomed in. There were, technically, three leaves of pak choi.

Xiaoran: three leaves don’t count

Yichen: I’ll tell the canteen.

He didn’t ask what she was having. He didn’t ask whether she’d had anything. There was only the photograph.

By the end of the first week she knew the pattern. Some time between half eleven and half twelve, depending on his lectures, a picture arrived. Rice and chicken. Noodles. A sandwich from the café by the gym. Once, a bowl of grey porridge.

Xiaoran: what happened to your lunch

Yichen: It’s porridge.

Xiaoran: it looks like cement

Yichen: It’s good.

Xiaoran: are you eating building materials

He sent a close-up of the spoon.

Yichen: Would you like evidence?

She laughed so loudly in the library that the girl next to her turned round.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Monday of the second week she was in the canteen with Ning and Luo Jiayi when the picture came: a chicken rice bowl. She looked at it. Then at her own tray, which had a sandwich and a yoghurt and an iced coffee. She took a photograph of it and sent it before she could think about it.

Xiaoran: mine

Yichen: Looks good.

She waited. Nothing else came.

Xiaoran: that’s it?

Yichen: What else?

Xiaoran: you’re not going to ask if I’ve eaten?

Yichen: You’ve just sent me a picture of your lunch.

She stared at the screen and then started laughing.

“You’re smiling at your phone,” said Ning.

“Yichen’s sending me his lunch.”

“He’s sending you food?”

“Pictures of his food.”

Jiayi looked up from her noodles. “Why?”

Xiaoran opened her mouth to say she didn’t know. Then she closed it, because she had a feeling she did.

Yichen: Enjoy it.

✦ ✦ ✦
