By the third week she was looking forward to them. Once, during a group meeting that had been going round in circles for forty minutes, a picture of ordinary fried rice arrived and she looked at it.

Xiaoran: your lunch looks happier than my group

Yichen: It doesn’t have a deadline.

Another day she beat him to it. A proper lunch for once: rice, steamed fish, greens, soup.

Xiaoran: I ate. A real one

Yichen: I can see that.

Yichen: Looks nice.

She smiled at the screen for so long that her soup went cold, and then she drank it anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of the third week she asked him. They were sitting under the big camphor tree outside the Business building on a dry, bright day in March, in the gap between his lecture and her seminar. He’d brought her a little cup of mango pudding on the way over, and she was eating it with the plastic spoon while he read his notes.

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

“Why do you send me your lunch every day?”

He looked up. “Don’t you like them?”

“I love them.”

“Then what’s the problem?”

“There’s no problem. You never ask about mine.” She scraped the side of the cup.

“No.”

“Aren’t you curious?”

“Do you want me to be?”

“That’s not what I mean.”

“Then what do you mean?”

She thought about it, spoon in her mouth. “You used to ask. Every day. Have you eaten.”

He was quiet. Then he reached over with his thumb and wiped a bit of pudding off the corner of her mouth.

“I know. And I think it made you feel like I was checking. Like you had to give the right answer.”

She looked down at the cup.

He said, “I didn’t want to be someone you had to report to. So I thought I’d tell you what I was doing instead. If you wanted to tell me what you were doing, you could. If you didn’t, that was fine.”

“That’s sneaky.”

“How is it sneaky?”

“You made me curious about your lunch so I’d think about mine.”

He considered that. “Did it work?”

“Don’t look so pleased with yourself.”

“I’m not saying anything.”

“Your face is saying something.”

He laughed. Then he stood up, brushed the back of his jeans, and took her empty cup off her. “Go to your seminar.”

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

“What’s for dinner?”

“You’re asking me?”

“I’m curious,” she said, and he looked at her for a second longer than he needed to, and said, “We’ll decide later,” and she watched him walk all the way to the door of the Business building before she got up.

✦ ✦ ✦

It became part of the day. Neither of them called it anything. When he had training at lunch, the picture came late. When there was a game, it was sometimes a sandwich on top of his kit bag in the changing room. When he tried something new, he sent it before he’d taken a bite, so she could see it whole.

Xiaoran: Yichen what IS that

Yichen: Lunch.

Xiaoran: you keep saying that like it explains everything

Yichen: It does.

She sent a laughing sticker. Then, without stopping to think, she sent her own: a bowl of wonton soup from the stall by the east gate.

Yichen: Looks good.

That was all. He never made it into anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

One Thursday in April everything went wrong at once. Her group project fell apart, the lecturer sent back the draft with red all over it, and she spent the whole lunch break in the computer room rewriting a section that wasn’t even hers. When she finally looked up it was ten to two. Her stomach hurt. She was too cross to move. Her phone buzzed.

Yichen: Lunch.

It was a rice bowl with grilled fish. She looked at it. Then she put the phone away. A few minutes later it buzzed again.

Yichen: Better than yesterday’s.

She picked it up. She looked at the little picture, and then she typed, slowly, and nearly didn’t send it.

Xiaoran: I haven’t eaten yet

It felt strange to admit. Like taking off a coat in the cold.

Yichen: Busy?

Xiaoran: very

Yichen: Have you got ten minutes now?

Xiaoran: I suppose

Yichen: Canteen by the library. I’ll wait.

Xiaoran: you don’t have to

Yichen: I know.

She laughed, despite everything, and shut the laptop, and went.

He was at a table by the window with his own empty bowl pushed to one side and his notes open. He moved the notes to make room when she put her tray down. He didn’t look at the tray. He didn’t say anything about it at all.

“You really don’t ask,” she said.

“Ask what?”

“If I’ve eaten.”

“You’ve just told me,” he said.

She ate. While she ate she told him about the project, and the red pen, and the boy in her group who had developed the ability to vanish whenever there was work, and he listened, and asked two questions, and didn’t try to fix it. When the bowl was empty she pushed the tray aside and put her chin in her hand and looked at him.

“You’re really good at this.”

“At what?”

“Taking care of me without making me feel like I’m being taken care of.”

He looked at her. Then he leaned over and tucked a piece of hair behind her ear.

“I don’t want you to feel like you have to prove anything to me.”

She caught his hand before he took it back and held it against her cheek, in the middle of the canteen, until a boy at the next table coughed pointedly and she let go.

Then she picked up her phone and took a picture of his empty bowl.

“What are you doing?”

“Sending you mine.”

“That’s my bowl.”

“Exactly,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

By June the pictures were so ordinary she almost forgot they hadn’t always been there. She scrolled back through the chat one evening and found dozens of them. Beautifully arranged trays. Blurry ones taken in a hurry. One that was mostly his kit bag with a sandwich just visible in the corner. And in between them, almost as many of hers.

Xiaoran: do you know how many lunch pictures you’ve sent me

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: loads. you should start a food account

Yichen: Would you follow it?

Xiaoran: obviously

Yichen: Then I’ll keep going.

The next day at twelve, there was a bowl of noodles. She zoomed in. There were fish balls in it.

Xiaoran: fish balls!!

Yichen: The Noodle Club has standards.

She took a picture of her own lunch, which was rice and egg and tomato from the stall by the gate, and sent it back.

Yichen: Looks good. Enjoy it.

He had never once asked her to send one. He had only let her into an ordinary part of his day, every day, until she started letting him into hers. She didn’t tell him that she had started eating lunch partly so she’d have something to send back. She suspected he knew.

chapters.desc: A thirteen-day family vacation. Lin Xiaoran is a mature adult. Day Three is concerning.
chapters.title: Two Weeks Was Apparently Too Long
chapters.epigraph: “I hate family vacations.”
chapters.content:
When Zhou Yichen announced he was leaving on a thirteen-day family vacation, Lin Xiaoran laughed. Actually laughed.

“That’s fine.”

“Hm.”

“I’m a mature adult.”

“Hm.”

“I can survive two weeks.”

“Hm.”

Tang Meilin, who had been there for the One-Week Clingy Disaster of high school, looked deeply suspicious. Whenever Xiaoran claimed she was emotionally stable, disaster usually followed. Day One wasn’t bad at all. Yichen left in the morning. Xiaoran went to class, worked on assignments, had dinner with friends. Perfectly normal. At 10 PM she called him, for three hours. Still normal. Probably. Day Two was manageable. She sent him pictures of lunch, of campus, of a cat near the media building. Then another cat. Then another. Then a cloud that vaguely resembled a cat. Yichen replied: You sent me six cats today.

Xiaoran: You’re welcome.

Day Three was concerning, because after class she walked towards the business building out of habit—then remembered Yichen wasn’t there. He was several countries away. It hit surprisingly hard.

“…Oh.”

For the first time, campus felt a little bigger. A little emptier. Which was ridiculous, because she had survived sixteen whole years before meeting him. Yet somehow the place felt wrong without him. Day Four, things escalated.

“You’re staring at your phone.”

One of her classmates pointed it out.

“I’m not.”

“You checked it six times.”

“I received messages.”

“Not from him.”

Xiaoran had no answer.

Caught. Yichen, meanwhile, appeared to be having the time of his life. At least, that’s what his photos suggested: beaches, resorts, family dinners, mountain views. Every picture looked amazing, which only made Xiaoran more annoyed. How dare he enjoy himself while she suffered? A completely unreasonable thought. But still. Day Five, she stole one of his hoodies. Again. Not because she missed him. Obviously. It just happened to smell faintly like his cologne, which was entirely unrelated.

Day Six, the video calls got longer. Day Seven, even longer. At one point, Mrs. Zhou wandered into the background and laughed.

“Still talking?”

Dead silence. They had been talking for two hours.

“Mum.”

“What?”

Mrs. Zhou looked delighted. She waved at Xiaoran.

“He’s been carrying his phone around all day waiting for your messages.”

Dead silence. Yichen looked horrified.

“Mum. Please leave.”

Xiaoran was trying hard not to smile. That information was valuable. Very valuable. Day Eight, the suffering peaked. Not dramatically. Quietly.

That afternoon, Xiaoran won a small media competition. Normally Yichen was the first person she’d tell—not because she had to, but because she wanted to. But it was the middle of the night where he was. Suddenly the win felt slightly incomplete, which surprised her. Later that night, his reply arrived. Three words. Proud of you. She stared at them for five minutes. Day Nine, Chen Yuhao called.

“Are you alive?”

“Barely.”

“It’s been nine days.”

“Feels like nine years.”

“You’re ridiculous.”

“Correct.”

Day Ten, she started counting. Three days left. Then two. Then one. Every conversation somehow included, “When are you coming back?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Eventually, even Yichen noticed.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You asked me that six times.”

“I’m just checking.”

“Xiaoran.”

“…Fine. I miss you.”

Silence.

“I know.”

Simple and soft, the kind of answer that made missing him worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

The final day arrived. Thirteen days. Long enough for Xiaoran to decide she hated extended vacations. The airport felt familiar now—she had done this once before, in high school, for one single week. This time she wasn’t dramatic. Not visibly. No clinging, no pouting, no speeches. Just waiting. Patiently. Okay—not patiently. She checked the arrival board twelve times. Finally the doors opened, and there he was. Black shirt. Travel backpack. Slightly messy hair. The same Zhou Yichen—and somehow not, because after almost two weeks, seeing him in person felt strangely unreal.

Then he spotted her and smiled, and just like that, everything felt normal again. Yichen walked towards her.

“Hi.”

Xiaoran threw herself at him. Without any grace at all, hard enough that Yichen took a step back catching her. Her arms tightened, and for a while neither of them said anything. Thirteen days wasn’t forever. But it had been long enough for Xiaoran to realise something: she didn’t just like spending time with Zhou Yichen. He had quietly become part of what made ordinary days feel complete. Finally she muttered into his shoulder,

“I hate family vacations.”

Yichen laughed—the familiar laugh, the one she had missed most.

“I noticed.”

His arms tightened around her. Warm. Safe. Home. After a pause, near her ear, he whispered,

“You know… I missed you too.”

She leaned back just far enough to kiss him, in the middle of arrivals, while her suitcase fell over beside them and neither of them picked it up.

Xiaoran hugged him even tighter, which made Zhou Yichen laugh again. Apparently two weeks apart had only made his girlfriend clingier—an outcome that surprised absolutely nobody.

chapters.desc: A lost French couple, a café near campus, and a language Lin Xiaoran forgot to mention.
chapters.title: The Day Zhou Yichen Discovered His Girlfriend Secretly Spoke French
chapters.epigraph: “The same thing she’d been telling him all along—just in a different language.”
chapters.content:
There were many surprising things about Lin Xiaoran. Some were expected: her ability to get lost in places she’d visited twenty times, her talent for creating problems out of nothing, her habit of asking questions like:

“Would you still love me if I became a refrigerator?”

A follow-up, apparently, to the capybara question. Normal Xiaoran behaviour. What Zhou Yichen didn’t expect—was discovering she spoke French. Not badly, either. Fluently enough to make people stare. And she had apparently been practising for months without telling him. The betrayal was unbelievable. It started on a random Saturday. They were having lunch at a café near campus. Nothing unusual. Just a quiet date—until Xiaoran froze.

“Hm?”

Yichen looked up.

“What happened?”

Xiaoran’s eyes widened, and she sat up straighter. Very suspicious. Across the café, a middle-aged French couple stood looking lost—the man holding a map, the woman holding a phone. Xiaoran stood up.

“I’m back in a minute.”

And walked towards them. Yichen blinked. Okay. Probably helping with directions. Then Xiaoran opened her mouth. French came out. Perfect French. Not textbook French, not app French—real, conversational French. Dead silence. Because WHAT. The French couple immediately brightened. A full conversation followed—questions, answers, directions, recommendations, laughing. Zhou Yichen sat there, staring. Who was this woman? That was his girlfriend. Supposedly. Yet somehow she had unlocked an entire language pack without informing him.

The conversation continued for several minutes. Then Xiaoran smiled, said goodbye, came back, sat down, and went straight back to her juice. Like nothing had happened. Dead silence. Finally Yichen spoke.

“What.”

“What?”

“You speak French.”

“Oh.”

OH? That was the response?

“Since when?”

“Recently.”

“Recently enough to have a whole conversation?”

Xiaoran went quiet. Caught. A guilty smile appeared.

“A few months.”

Dead silence.

“A FEW MONTHS?”

She had hidden an entire language. Like a criminal.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

Xiaoran looked genuinely confused.

“I wanted to surprise you.”

Mission accomplished. Yichen was absolutely surprised. Then suspicious.

“When did you learn?”

“Every night.”

“Every night.”

“Mhm.”

“You already have assignments. And competitions.”

“Mhm.”

“You already watch random documentaries about things nobody cares about.”

“Mhm.”

“So when exactly did you have time?”

Xiaoran proudly pointed at herself.

“I am gifted.”

“No.”

“Okay maybe I sacrificed sleep.”

“Thought so.”

The truth. It was always sleep deprivation.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eventually the story came out. Months ago, Xiaoran had watched a French film for one of her media courses. Then another. Then another. Then she had become obsessed, which was on-brand: when Xiaoran liked something, she liked it aggressively. Normal people watched movies. Xiaoran accidentally learned a language. Then Yichen had an idea. His eyes narrowed.

“Say something.”

“What.”

“In French.”

“No.”

“Why.”

“Embarrassing.”

“You were just speaking confidently.”

“That was practical French.”

“This is boyfriend French.”

Yichen refused to let it go. For twenty whole minutes. Until Xiaoran surrendered.

“Fine.”

Very, she said something in French—soft, fast, beautiful, and completely incomprehensible to him.

“What did you say?”

Xiaoran looked away. Very suspicious.

“Nothing.”

“That’s a lie.”

“It’s not important.”

“Xiaoran.”

“No.”

Now he was definitely curious. If she refused to translate, it meant something. After several more minutes of interrogation, she gave up.

“…I said you’re handsome.”

Yichen smiled. Not a big smile. The dangerous one—the one that always caused problems.

“Oh. That’s all?”

“Yes.”

“Only handsome?”

“YICHEN.”

His smile widened. Xiaoran secretly learning French and then using it to compliment him was absurdly adorable. Then he leaned closer.

“Teach me.”

“What?”

“French.”

“No.”

“Why.”

“Because you’ll immediately use it against me.”

Correct. His face confirmed it immediately. Three weeks later, he had learned enough French to recognise one specific phrase—one Xiaoran muttered while studying, thinking he wasn’t paying attention. Thinking he couldn’t understand. A terrible mistake. He heard it perfectly, and this time he understood.

“Je t’aime.”

I love you. Simple. Soft. Unconscious. The kind of thing she probably didn’t realise she’d said out loud. Then Yichen closed his textbook.

“What.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“What?”

“You love me?”

Xiaoran froze. No. NO. He wasn’t supposed to understand that yet. Yichen looked unbearably pleased. From that day on, whenever Xiaoran forgot herself and slipped into French, Yichen paid close attention. His girlfriend had spent months on French, and the first important thing she had learned to say was the same thing she had been telling him all along. Just in a different language.

chapters.desc: A peaceful Saturday at the Zhou house, until Mrs. Zhou’s best friend’s daughter walks in calling him “ge.”
chapters.title: The Worst Visitor in Zhou Family History
chapters.epigraph: “The real problem had always been Xiaoran’s own imagination.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran wasn’t nervous. She had visited the Zhou family house several times already. Mrs. Zhou liked her. Mr. Zhou liked her. Even the neighbours’ cat that slept on the Zhou family wall liked her. Everything was fine. Then Jiang Meimei arrived, and nothing was fine anymore. The disaster started on a Saturday afternoon. Xiaoran was curled up beside Zhou Yichen on the living room sofa, stealing his snacks. Mrs. Zhou was chatting happily, Mr. Zhou was reading, and Yichen was pretending to study. Life was peaceful.

Then the front door opened. Mrs. Zhou brightened at once.

“Oh! Meimei is here!”

Dead silence. Who? The answer appeared five seconds later. A girl walked into the living room—beautiful, elegant, perfect posture, perfect makeup, perfect smile. The kind of woman who had clearly never tripped over her own feet. Unlike Xiaoran, who had once gotten lost inside a shopping mall. Twice.

“Hello Auntie.”

The girl smiled sweetly. Mrs. Zhou immediately hugged her.

“Meimei!”

Uh oh. Xiaoran’s instincts went off like an alarm, then came the fatal sentence.

“Xiaoran, this is Jiang Meimei. She’s my best friend’s daughter,” Mrs. Zhou said with a smile.

Dead silence. BEST FRIEND’S DAUGHTER? That phrase alone carried terrifying power.

“Meimei practically grew up with Yichen.”

Dead silence. WHAT. Xiaoran slowly turned towards her boyfriend. Yichen looked completely normal, which made it worse. He clearly wasn’t surprised. Meaning he already knew her. Meaning they had history. Meaning—

“Yichen ge.”

Jiang Meimei smiled. Ge. The dreaded honorific. Meanwhile Yichen simply nodded.

“Meimei.”

HE KNEW HER NAME. Xiaoran sat up straighter. This was serious. Then the conversation started, and somehow everything got worse.

“Oh, Yichen ge, are you still playing basketball?”

“Yes.”

“I saw your tournament photos.”

“Mm.”

“I showed them to my parents.”

“Mm.”

Their families were connected. Xiaoran hated everything. Jiang Meimei sat elegantly across from them, perfect in every way. The killing blow. Mrs. Zhou laughed.

“You know, when they were children, everyone thought Meimei and Yichen would become a couple.”

Xiaoran nearly inhaled a potato chip wrong. Jiang Meimei laughed politely. Mrs. Zhou laughed. Mr. Zhou laughed. Even the cat on the wall looked suspicious. Only Yichen looked exhausted—he had clearly heard this story a thousand times. Xiaoran hadn’t, and now she was suffering. Greatly.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next hour was torture—not because Jiang Meimei did anything wrong. That was the problem. She was nice. Kind, polite, friendly, impossible to dislike. Which made Xiaoran dislike the situation even more. Then, over tea, Jiang Meimei casually mentioned—

“I still have the birthday gift Yichen gave me years ago.”

A birthday gift. HE BOUGHT HER GIFTS. Xiaoran was spiraling. Internally. Externally she was smiling—a normal smile. Definitely not dying. A hand landed on her knee—warm, steady. Yichen. Without even looking at her, he squeezed once. A warning. He could apparently feel the jealousy radiating off her. Traitor. The real disaster happened later. Mrs. Zhou asked Yichen to help carry something upstairs, and Xiaoran was left alone with Jiang Meimei.

The moment he was gone, panic set in. Now they would have to talk. Woman to woman. Nightmare. Jiang Meimei smiled. Xiaoran prepared for battle. Then, unexpectedly, Meimei laughed.

“You look terrified.”

“…What?”

“You’ve been staring at me for two hours.”

Caught. Immediately. Meimei smiled again, genuinely amused.

“You’re much cuter than I expected.”

“…Expected?”

“Mrs. Zhou talks about you constantly.”

“She does?”

“All the time.”

Then Meimei leaned closer.

“And honestly, I understand now.”

Xiaoran blinked. What was happening? Meimei laughed again.

“You know, Yichen ge never liked any girls growing up. Never.”

Then she pointed upstairs.

“The fact he looks at you the way he does is honestly shocking.”

Now Xiaoran wanted details. Many details.

“What way?”

Meimei stared at her, then burst out laughing.

“Oh my God.”

“What?”

“You don’t know.”

Know what? Before Xiaoran could ask, footsteps sounded on the stairs. Yichen was back, and both girls immediately looked at him—one amused, one confused. Yichen looked instantly suspicious.

“…What happened?”

“Nothing,” Jiang Meimei said.

“Nothing,” Xiaoran said, in exactly the same tone. Very dangerous.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, after Jiang Meimei finally left, Xiaoran cornered her boyfriend.

“What way?”

Yichen blinked.

“What.”

“Jiang Meimei said you look at me differently.”

Realisation, followed immediately by annoyance. Meimei had started problems on her way out. Wonderful. Yichen sighed.

“Forget it.”

“No.”

“Please.”

“NO.”

Several minutes of relentless pestering later, he finally surrendered.

“The way someone looks at the person they love.”

Direct hit. Xiaoran froze completely. Yichen looked away, slightly embarrassed. Xiaoran scooted closer. Then closer. Then leaned into his shoulder, smiling.

“Okay.”

“Okay?”

“I’ve decided.”

“What.”

“I don’t hate Jiang Meimei anymore.”

“…You hated her?”

“Briefly.”

“Why.”

“She was too pretty.”

Yichen laughed. And just like that—the greatest threat in Lin Xiaoran’s imagination was over—mostly because Jiang Meimei had never been a rival at all. The real problem had always been Xiaoran’s imagination, which, unfortunately for everyone involved, was far more dangerous.

chapters.desc: Lunar New Year at her grandparents’ house, and one uncle with opinions about why she’s dating Zhou Yichen.
chapters.title: The One Thing Lin Xiaoran Could Never Tolerate
chapters.epigraph: “I chose him because he’s Zhou Yichen.”
chapters.content:
There were many things Lin Xiaoran disliked. Early classes. Group projects. Spicy food stronger than her tolerance, which was most spicy food. People who walked slowly in crowded places. But there was one thing she genuinely hated: gold diggers. Not because she was rich. She wasn’t. Her family lived comfortably—her mother an accountant, her father an engineer—not wealthy, not poor. Enough for food, for school, to get through a month without worrying. Nothing more, nothing less.

So it always made Xiaoran uncomfortable when people assumed she was dating Zhou Yichen for his money—especially since she had liked him long before she knew how wealthy his family actually was. Not everyone understood that. Including Uncle Deng: a distant relative from another city, the kind who appeared once every few years and somehow had opinions about everyone’s lives. It happened at Lunar New Year, at her grandparents’ house. Lots of relatives, lots of food, lots of noise, lots of gossip. A normal family gathering—until someone mentioned Zhou Yichen.

Everyone became interested.

“That’s the boyfriend in the business program at Huaining University, right?”

“Very handsome.”

“Excellent grades.”

“Good family.”

It was harmless—until Uncle Deng laughed and said, casually,

“Well, Xiaoran certainly found herself a rich boyfriend.”

The room quieted slightly. Xiaoran paused.

“Smart girl. Nowadays girls know how to choose,” Uncle Deng went on.

Dead silence. No. Not that. Not that. Across the table, her mother frowned and set down her cup with a small, sharp click. Uncle Deng didn’t notice. Or didn’t care.

“Honestly, if I were young again, I’d choose someone wealthy too.”

A few relatives looked uncomfortable. The implication was obvious. Xiaoran hated it. Not because it embarrassed her—because it insulted everything she felt for Yichen. Every late-night study session, every tournament, every argument, every moment, reduced to money. Xiaoran put down her chopsticks. Quietly.

“Uncle, if Yichen wasn’t rich, I’d still date him.”

The room went silent. Everyone knew that tone. The dangerous Xiaoran tone. Uncle Deng laughed.

“Of course you’d say that.”

Xiaoran smiled. It wasn’t a friendly smile.

“Actually, when we started dating, I didn’t know his family was wealthy.”

Silence.

“He was just annoying.”

Several cousins burst out laughing. Accurate.

“He studied with me. He helped me. He listened to me complain. He stayed beside me when I failed things. He celebrated when I succeeded.”

Then she looked directly at Uncle Deng.

“So no. I didn’t choose him because he’s rich.”

The room got quieter. Nobody was joking anymore.

“I chose him because he’s Zhou Yichen.”

Dead silence. Even her grandmother looked moved. Uncle Deng looked a little embarrassed, but still tried to defend himself.

“I wasn’t criticising you.”

“Maybe not. But it sounded like you were criticising him,” Xiaoran replied.

That surprised everyone. Most people would have defended themselves first. Xiaoran defended Yichen first. Always. Without thinking.

“You know what bothers me?”

Nobody answered.

“People think money is why someone stays.”

Her fingers tightened slightly around her teacup.

“But I’ve seen people with money treat others terribly. And I’ve seen people with nothing give everything.”

Then she smiled. A small smile. The real one this time.

“Yichen just happens to have both.”

Her grandmother laughed first.

“That’s a good answer.”

The tension broke. Conversation resumed, food returned, and the family gossip moved on.

Later that evening, as Xiaoran walked home, her phone rang. Yichen.

“Hm?”

“Lin Jun told me what happened.”

Family networks were terrifying.

“What part?”

“The part where you defended my honour.”

Then she heard him laughing.

“No, tell me.”

“I just think it’s nice.”

Xiaoran rolled her eyes.

“It wasn’t nice.”

“It was.”

“He was being annoying.”

“And?”

“And nobody gets to talk about you like that.”

A softer silence, the kind Yichen only ever had around her.

“So if I lost everything tomorrow…”

“No.”

“What?”

“No hypothetical questions.”

“Answer.”

She sighed. Then finally said:

“If you lost everything tomorrow, I’d still be there. Unfortunately.”

Yichen laughed—a real laugh, the kind she loved most. Somehow it felt worth more than all the money in the world.

chapters.desc: Grandma Lin wants to see the boy up close. Uncle Deng will be there. So will the dumplings.
chapters.title: Zhou Yichen Meets the Relatives
chapters.epigraph: “That one’s acceptable.”
chapters.content:
The invitation came from her grandmother, which meant nobody could refuse it.

Three days after Uncle Deng’s comment at New Year dinner, Grandma Lin called Xiaoran’s mother, and Xiaoran’s mother called Xiaoran into the kitchen, and said, without turning around from the sink, “Your grandmother wants the boy at dinner on the fifth.”

Xiaoran froze with a mandarin halfway to her mouth.

“…The boy?”

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Why?”

“She says if you’re going to defend someone in front of the whole family like that, she wants to see what he looks like up close. Your uncle will be there.” Her mother turned off the tap.

“Uncle Deng?”

“He’s staying until the seventh.”

Xiaoran put the mandarin down. “Mum. That’s a trap.”

“It’s dinner,” said Mrs. Lin, which in her language meant yes, and you’re both walking into it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen arrived at five, exactly on time, which Xiaoran had known he would. What she hadn’t expected was how he arrived. No black car. He came up the lane from the bus stop on foot, in a plain dark coat, carrying a fruit basket in one hand and a paper bag in the other. Inside the bag were a tin of good tea for her grandfather, a box of pastries from the old bakery near their high school, and a small pot of narcissus for her grandmother, because Xiaoran had once mentioned, months ago and only once, that her grandmother liked them.

She met him at the gate.

“You took the bus.”

“Hm.”

“You never take the bus.”

He looked at the house—the red couplets on the door, the paper lanterns, the sound of a dozen relatives talking over a television—and then back at her.

“Your uncle thinks I’m a rich boyfriend. I didn’t want to give him a parking space to prove it,” he said.

Xiaoran stared at him. Then she reached up and fixed the collar of his coat, which didn’t need fixing, mostly so she’d have something to do with her hands.

“You’re nervous,” she said.

“Very.”

That surprised her so much she forgot to be nervous herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside, it was exactly as bad as she’d feared and also completely different. Her grandmother took one look at the narcissus and said “Hm,” in a tone Xiaoran had only ever heard her use for good melons. Her father shook Yichen’s hand for too long and then had to go stand in the kitchen for a minute. Lin Jun, lounging on the sofa with a beer, raised it in Yichen’s direction like they were old war buddies, which, after the day he’d “stolen” him, they sort of were.

Then the questions started. The aunties wanted to know his height, his major, his grades, and whether he could cook. The uncles wanted to know what business he planned to go into and whether he’d thought about the civil service. Two small cousins wanted to know if he could dunk, and when he said yes, they wanted proof, immediately, in the courtyard, and had to be held back by the hoods of their jackets.

Yichen answered all of it. Calmly. Politely. Without once mentioning his family’s company, or his car, or anything he owned. When one auntie asked what his parents did, he said “My father runs a business, and my mother keeps him from working too much,” and the auntie laughed and moved on. Across the room, Uncle Deng watched all of this over his teacup and didn’t say anything. Xiaoran watched Uncle Deng.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened at the dumpling table. Every year on the fifth, the whole family folded dumplings together, and every year it was a competition nobody admitted was a competition. Grandma Lin sat at the head of the table, folding perfect pleated dumplings at terrifying speed. Xiaoran’s were lopsided but sealed. Lin Jun’s were somehow perfect, which was annoying. Yichen’s were a disaster. He held the wrapper like it was an exam question. He put in too much filling. He pinched the edges with enormous concentration, and the dumpling burst at the seam and lay there on the board, looking injured.

One of the little cousins burst out laughing. So did Grandma Lin.

“Again,” she said, and pushed another wrapper towards him.

He tried again. It was worse.

“You’re better at basketball,” Xiaoran told him.

“I’m better at everything than this.”

Uncle Deng put down his teacup.

“Must be strange,” he said, “doing things with your own hands for once.”

The table didn’t go silent, exactly. But it got quieter. Xiaoran felt her mother go still beside her. She opened her mouth.

Under the table, Yichen’s knee touched hers. Wait. He picked up a third wrapper.

He said, “It is. My dad says money is the easiest thing to have and the easiest thing to lose. He made me work in one of his warehouses the summer I was fifteen so I’d understand that. I was bad at that too. For the first week.” He spooned in less filling this time.

Uncle Deng raised his eyebrows.

“And,” Yichen said, still looking at the dumpling, “Xiaoran told me what she said to you at New Year.”

Now the table really did go quiet.

“I’m not sure I’ve earned all of it yet. But I’m trying to,” he said.

He pinched the edges closed. It held. Grandma Lin picked it up, turned it over, and put it on the tray with her own.

“That one’s acceptable,” she announced.

Across the table, Uncle Deng looked at Yichen. Then he picked up his teacup again, and said, gruffly, to nobody in particular, “Too much filling’s a common mistake.”

It was the closest thing to an apology anyone in the family had ever heard from him.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner, the cousins dragged everyone out into the courtyard for sparklers. The air smelled like gunpowder and cold. Somewhere down the lane, someone was setting off firecrackers, and the little cousins screamed and ran in circles, writing their names in light. Xiaoran stood by the door with Yichen, holding a sparkler she’d forgotten to light.

“You didn’t have to say that. About earning it,” she said.

“I meant it.”

“I know. That’s why you didn’t have to say it.”

He didn’t answer. He just took her sparkler, lit it from his own, and handed it back. Behind them, the door opened. Xiaoran’s mother came out, wrapped in her coat, holding something red. She walked straight up to Yichen and held out an envelope. He looked at it. Then at Xiaoran. Then back at the envelope, completely lost.

“Auntie, I can’t—”

“Take it. It’s New Year,” said Mrs. Lin.

He took it with both hands, the way you were supposed to, and bowed. Mrs. Lin nodded once, brisk as always, and went back inside without another word. Yichen stared at the red envelope in his hands.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm.”

“What does it mean? When the parents give it to—” He stopped.

Xiaoran looked at the door her mother had just closed, at the warm light behind the paper lanterns, at the shape of her grandmother at the window pretending not to watch. She knew exactly what it meant. In her family, the first red envelope from her mother didn’t go to friends, or classmates, or a boy someone was dating for now. It went to someone they expected to see at this table next year. And the year after that.

“It means,” she said, and her voice wobbled, “you have to come back next year and fold better dumplings.”

He looked at her for a long time in the flickering light. Then he tucked the envelope carefully into the inside pocket of his coat, over his heart, and didn’t say anything at all. He didn’t have to.

chapters.desc: A weekly viewing report, eleven hours of dramas, and the most dangerous thing Zhou Yichen has ever done: change a password.
chapters.title: Netflix vs Zhou Yichen
chapters.epigraph: “You violated my human rights.”
chapters.content:
There were many ways to start a relationship conflict. Jealousy. Miscommunication. Trust issues. Different life goals. Lin Xiaoran and Zhou Yichen managed to have one over Netflix—specifically, because Zhou Yichen accidentally found out how much Netflix Xiaoran watched in a single day. The discovery happened on a Tuesday. Yichen paid for the subscription. Not because Xiaoran couldn’t—because he’d insisted.

“Just use mine.”

At the time, Xiaoran thought that was sweet. A mistake.

One afternoon, Yichen got a notification: weekly viewing activity. Normally he ignored those. This time, he opened it—and froze.

“…What?”

The watch history went on. And on. Episodes one through seven of one show. Then another show. Then another. Dead silence. According to Netflix, Lin Xiaoran had spent almost eleven hours watching dramas on Sunday. Eleven. Hours. Yichen messaged her.

Yichen: How many hours were you on Netflix Sunday?

Seen. Typing. Stopped typing. Typing again.

Xiaoran: Why.

Yichen: Answer the question.

Xiaoran: Approximately.

Yichen: How many.

Xiaoran: The number isn’t important.

The number was important.

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: …

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: Maybe.

Yichen: Maybe?

Xiaoran: Nine?

Yichen: The report says eleven.

Dead silence. She had forgotten Netflix tracked things. Traitors, all of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen showed up at her apartment holding groceries, concern, and judgment.

“Eleven hours?”

“It was a weekend.”

“Eleven hours.”

“It sounds worse when you say it.”

“Because it is worse.”

Xiaoran crossed her arms.

“It was educational.”

“What was educational?”

“The romance.”

“No.”

“The character development.”

“No.”

“The cinematography.”

“No.”

Dead silence. Then Yichen opened her refrigerator and discovered she had skipped lunch. The atmosphere got much worse. After the diet incident, skipped meals were the one thing he never joked about.

“Xiaoran. You skipped meals.”

“I forgot.”

“You remembered fourteen episodes.”

Xiaoran had nothing to say to that. Then came the betrayal. The greatest betrayal.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Netflix logged her out. Because what? WHAT? She tried again. Nothing. Again. Nothing. Then her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Temporary restriction.

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

Xiaoran: You did WHAT?

Yichen: One week.

Xiaoran: ONE WEEK?

Yichen: You need sunlight.

Xiaoran: I HAVE SUNLIGHT.

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: I SAW SUNLIGHT THROUGH THE WINDOW.

Yichen: That’s not the same thing.

The war began. For the first time in months, Lin Xiaoran ignored Zhou Yichen completely. No messages. No calls. No random photos. No good morning, no good night. Nothing. Yichen lasted exactly six hours before he got uncomfortable. Normally his phone held three cat photos, two random observations, one complaint, five unrelated thoughts, and at least one look at this cloud. Today: nothing. The silence was deeply unsettling. Evening came. Still nothing. The next day, nothing. Day three, nothing. By then, even Chen Yuhao had noticed.

“What did you do?”

“I blocked Netflix.”

“You idiot.”

“She watched eleven hours.”

“That’s not the point.”

“Then what’s the point?”

“You touched her freedom.”

Yuhao shook his head.

“She’s going to hold this grudge forever.”

A terrifying possibility.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen found Xiaoran in the media building working on an assignment. She looked up, saw him, and looked straight back down. The audacity.

“Xiaoran.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

Nothing. Finally Yichen sat down beside her, close enough that their shoulders touched. Still ignored. Five minutes passed. Then ten. Finally, Yichen sighed.

“Are you done?”

“No.”

Her first words in three days. Progress.

“You’re really angry.”

“Correct.”

“It was for your health.”

“You violated my rights.”

Her rights. Netflix had apparently become a legal issue. Then Xiaoran turned—actually turned—and pointed at him.

“I was three episodes away from the confession.”

“The confession?”

“Three episodes.”

The heartbreak in her voice almost made him laugh. Almost. Yichen rubbed his forehead. The whole argument was ridiculous.

“I was worried.”

Her anger wavered. That tone was unfair—the genuine one, the honest one.

“You skipped meals. You slept at three.”

More silence.

“You watched until your eyes hurt.”

Xiaoran looked away. Caught. Again.

“I know.”

The fight lost all momentum. The truth was, she knew. And Yichen knew she knew. He took out his phone, opened Netflix, changed the password, and handed it over.

Her anger vanished. Completely. Like magic. Traitorous woman. She grabbed his sleeve—the universal sign of peace.

“Thank you.”

“Conditions.”

“What.”

“No eleven-hour marathons.”

Xiaoran said nothing.

“Xiaoran.”

“Ten?”

“No.”

“Nine?”

“No.”

“Eight?”

“No.”

She tucked herself against his shoulder. The ultimate negotiating strategy, and unfortunately the most effective one, because Zhou Yichen immediately knew he had already lost. Just like every other argument with Lin Xiaoran.

“Six hours maximum,” he said.

Xiaoran gasped.

“Victory.”

“That’s not a victory.”

“It is to me.”

Then she smiled—the bright one, the one that made Yichen forgive things far too easily. As she happily logged back into Netflix, Yichen realised blocking her had been a mistake. Not because she was angry—because a drama-deprived Lin Xiaoran was much harder to handle than a drama-addicted one. A lesson he never repeated.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran is “extremely busy.” Her lie lasts approximately three minutes.
chapters.title: The World’s Worst Liar
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody who was actually busy sent updates about how busy they were.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran was many things. Cute. Dramatic. Smart. Chaotic. A good liar wasn’t one of them. The problem wasn’t that she couldn’t make up stories. She absolutely could. The problem was that Zhou Yichen knew her far too well, which was why her latest lie lasted approximately three minutes. A personal record. The disaster started on a Wednesday afternoon. Yichen had practice. Normally Xiaoran waited for him afterward. Today she wasn’t there. Instead, he got a message.

Xiaoran: I’m busy.

Dead silence. The message already looked suspicious. Not busy with what. Not talk later. Just: I’m busy. Then another message arrived.

Xiaoran: Extremely busy.

Yichen smiled. Nobody who was actually busy sent updates about how busy they were.

An hour later, he found her at the campus café, looking guilty. The moment she saw him, she sat up straight. Too quickly. Like a criminal.

“Hi.”

“Hi.”

Silence. Yichen sat down across from her—calm, patient—and waited. Eventually, Lin Xiaoran always confessed. She simply couldn’t help herself. And right on schedule, she started talking.

“Today was productive.”

“Oh?”

“Very productive.”

“Hm.”

“I was studying.”

The first lie. Tiny, harmless. But Yichen noticed—not because of the words, but because she tugged her sleeves down over her hands, the way she had for years whenever she was nervous.

“Very serious studying.”

“Hm.”

“Educational.”

“Hm.”

“Academic.”

“Hm.”

Yichen’s mouth twitched. Now she was overexplaining. Another sign. Xiaoran kept talking, and the more she talked, the worse it got.

“I definitely wasn’t doing anything strange.”

The self-report. Nobody had accused her of anything, and she was already defending herself. Yichen was enjoying himself enormously. Watching Xiaoran lie was one of life’s simplest pleasures—not because she was convincing, but because she wasn’t. At all.

“I spent the entire afternoon being responsible.”

“Responsible.”

“Very.”

“Hm.”

“I would never waste time.”

Now Yichen had to look away, because his smile was becoming noticeable. Xiaoran noticed anyway. Uh oh. She knew that smile—the one that appeared whenever he caught her doing something ridiculous. And suddenly she was flustered. Not because she’d been caught. Because he looked unfairly handsome. There was something deeply dangerous about Zhou Yichen when he knew something she didn’t know he knew. Relaxed, confident, amused—the slight smile, the calm eyes, the feeling that he was letting her dig her own grave and enjoying every second. A disaster.

Yichen leaned back, comfortable, watching.

“So. What exactly were you studying?”

Dead silence. Details. The enemy of every liar. Xiaoran panicked.

“Media.”

“What part?”

“…Media media.”

Yichen’s smile widened, just slightly, and somehow that made her heart beat faster. Not because of the interrogation. Because he looked ridiculously attractive. This was terrible.

“Which assignment?”

“The assignment.”

“Which one?”

“The… important one.”

“Hm.”

The smile grew, slowly, until Xiaoran wanted to hide under the table. Not from embarrassment. From him. Why was he looking at her like that? Yichen folded his arms, still smiling, still patient, obviously entertained.

“Xiaoran.”

“What.”

“Look at me.”

“No.”

Yichen laughed, which made things worse. He leaned forward, close enough that she could see the amusement in his eyes.

“Why not?”

“Reasons.”

“What reasons?”

“Personal reasons.”

“Such as?”

He was enjoying this far too much. Xiaoran pointed at him.

“Stop smiling.”

“What smile?”

THAT smile. The teasing one, the one that showed up whenever he felt completely in control. Which was unfortunately right now. Yichen tilted his head, still smiling, still impossible, and asked,

“How long were you watching dramas?”

Direct hit. The truth. And the worst part? He had known from the very first sentence. The entire conversation had been a trap. A cruel, cruel trap. Xiaoran covered her face, defeated.

“Four hours.”

“Hm.”

“Maybe five.”

“Hm.”

“…Six.”

Exactly the six-hour limit from the Netflix treaty. Technically she hadn’t even broken the rule. She had just lied about getting close to it, which was somehow more embarrassing. The confession. As always. Yichen laughed—victorious, annoyingly handsome—and Xiaoran peeked through her fingers, only to regret it immediately. He was still smiling at her like that. Still far too attractive for someone who had just interrogated her.

He reached over and gently moved her hands away from her face.

“Hi.”

Xiaoran groaned.

“I don’t like you.”

“Liar.”

The worst part was that he was right about that, too.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran has discovered a new research topic. It has categories, lists, and ratings. Zhou Yichen would like it to stop.
chapters.title: The Internet Was a Mistake
chapters.epigraph: “Do you know how dangerous you are?”
chapters.content:
There were many things Zhou Yichen feared. Basketball injuries. Losing important tournaments. Lin Xiaoran attempting to cook without supervision. But one thing caused problems more consistently than all of them: the internet. Every time Xiaoran discovered a new interest online, everyone suffered. This week’s victim was Zhou Yichen. It started on a Thursday evening. Yichen was studying. Peacefully. Productively. A rare event. Then his phone vibrated.

Xiaoran: Question.

Every message that started with “Question” was dangerous.

Yichen: What.

Xiaoran: Did you know there are different types of kisses?

Dead silence.

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: There are SO MANY.

Yichen: Why are you researching this.

Seen. No reply. Which was somehow more alarming.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next day, Yichen found out why. Xiaoran showed up outside his lecture hall carrying a notebook. Not suspicious normally. Extremely suspicious when carried by Lin Xiaoran.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“I have information.”

“About?”

“Kisses.”

Dead silence. Several students nearby walked away. Smart people. Xiaoran opened the notebook. It had notes. NOTES.

“Look.”

Yichen looked, and immediately regretted it. She had clearly spent hours on this. There were categories. Lists. Observations. Ratings.

“Why.”

“Educational purposes.”

“No.”

“Fine. Curiosity.”

At least that was honest. Xiaoran pointed at the page.

“Apparently there are forehead kisses.”

“You know that.”

“You do those.”

“Correct.”

“Cheek kisses.”

“You know that too.”

“Hand kisses.”

Yichen didn’t answer.

“Eskimo kisses.”

Then she flipped another page.

“And French kisses.”

Dead silence. The real reason. Yichen understood everything. He closed the notebook, slowly.

“No.”

“What.”

“No.”

“You haven’t even heard my proposal.”

“I don’t need to. I know exactly where this conversation is going.”

He was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three hours later, in a quiet corner of the campus garden, Xiaoran was still talking about it. Relentlessly.

“Why does it have that name?”

“I don’t know.”

“Who invented it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Why is it famous?”

“Xiaoran. Please stop interviewing me.”

She pouted. It had absolutely no effect. Mostly. She rested her chin on his shoulder, thinking. Dangerous.

“I think couples probably try different things naturally.”

Yichen sensed disaster approaching. Rapidly. Xiaoran looked up—curious, innocent, hopelessly unaware.

“…Do you?”

Sometimes Yichen wondered how one person could be so smart and so clueless at the same time. She could analyse media campaigns, win competitions, research anything—and still completely fail to understand the effect she had on him. Very, Yichen sighed.

“Xiaoran, do you have any idea what you do to me?”

“What does that mean?”

Exactly. She didn’t know. Not even slightly. He reached over and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear—a familiar gesture that made her smile right away.

“There.”

“There what?”

“That smile.”

“…What about it?”

“You do things like that. You ask questions. You get curious. Then you look at me like everything is simple.”

Xiaoran blinked, completely confused. Yichen laughed. Of course she was. Then he leaned in and pressed a kiss into her hair—gentle, warm, familiar. The kiss he always gave her, the one that calmed her down every time.

“There.”

“What was that for?”

“Because I like that one.”

Xiaoran smiled again.

“So that’s a no?”

“Absolutely.”

“This relationship has no freedom.”

Yichen actually laughed—a real laugh, the kind she loved hearing. Xiaoran leaned against him, happy. The internet might have introduced her to dozens of kinds of kisses, but her favourite was still the simplest: Zhou Yichen looking at her like she was the best thing that had ever happened to him, and kissing her forehead like he was quietly reminding himself she was real. Even if she occasionally came up with terrifying research topics.

chapters.desc: In his dream, Lin Xiaoran is a famous idol who has never met him. He does not take it well.
chapters.title: The Dream That Made Zhou Yichen Hug Xiaoran at 3 AM
chapters.epigraph: “The one who knew exactly who Zhou Yichen was.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen rarely remembered his dreams. Most disappeared the moment he woke up. This one didn’t. Unfortunately. The dream started normally. At least—normal by dream standards. He was on campus. Walking towards the media building. Looking for Xiaoran. People started screaming. Not scared screaming. Excited screaming. The kind of screaming usually reserved for celebrities. Yichen stopped. Confused. Then he heard it.

“XIAORAN!”

“LIN XIAORAN!”

“SHE’S HERE!”

Dead silence. Because what? A black van pulled up. Security appeared. Cameras. Hundreds of fans. And out stepped—Lin Xiaoran. Except not his Xiaoran. Well—still his Xiaoran. Different. Much different. Her hair was longer and perfectly styled, her makeup flawless, her clothes designer. Beautiful. Actually breathtaking—the kind of beautiful that made entire crowds stop moving. And apparently—In this dream—she was a famous idol. Dead silence. Dream Yichen was just as confused as real Yichen.

Then Xiaoran smiled. The crowd lost their minds. People screamed louder. Phones everywhere. Security closed in around her. A terrifying realisation appeared. Nobody was acting strange. Meaning this was normal. For her. Then Xiaoran walked past him. Completely past him—without stopping, without smiling, without even looking. Like he didn’t exist. Dead silence. That felt awful. Then Yichen followed. Because apparently dream logic said that was acceptable. The next several days became increasingly horrifying.

Because Dream Xiaoran genuinely didn’t know him. Not as a boyfriend, not as a friend, not at all. Meanwhile, Yichen was still himself—still a university student, still a basketball player, still hopelessly in love with her. Only now his girlfriend was an international celebrity who had never met him. Worst dream ever.

Then came the truly evil part. The fan meeting. Because somehow—dream Yichen ended up there. Standing in line like everyone else. Holding merchandise like everyone else. Waiting his turn like everyone else. The humiliation was unbelievable. He reached the table. And there she was. Beautiful, smiling, perfect—and completely unfamiliar.

“Hello.”

Her idol smile appeared—professional, warm, practised. The one she gave thousands of people. Not the real one, not his, and somehow that hurt. Then she looked up.

“What’s your name?”

What kind of nightmare was this?

“My…”

His voice actually failed. Dream Xiaoran waited politely. Completely unaware she was destroying him.

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Nice to meet you.”

And that was somehow worse. Much worse. Because no. No it wasn’t. She was supposed to know him. She was supposed to steal his hoodies, send him forty messages a day, hug him out of nowhere while he studied. Not this. Never this. Then Dream Xiaoran signed his album.

“Thank you for supporting me.”

Support. Not boyfriend. Not Yichen. Not idiot. Not mine. Support. The dream became increasingly absurd afterward. Yichen somehow went to her concerts. Watched her interviews. Watched her get more famous, watched millions of people love her—and every single time, she looked right through him like a stranger. Then one day in the dream—things became unbearable. Because an interviewer asked:

“What kind of man is your ideal type?”

Dream Yichen paid close attention. Obviously. And Xiaoran thought carefully. Then smiled.

“I think someone gentle.”

Good.

“Someone patient.”

Good.

“Someone who makes me feel safe.”

Excellent. Then she laughed.

“I don’t know though. I’ve never met someone like that.”

Dream Yichen almost had a breakdown. WHAT DO YOU MEAN. HE WAS RIGHT THERE. The dream jumped again. Now he stood backstage after a concert. Watching her from a distance. Dream Xiaoran turned. Actually turned. Their eyes met, for the first time. She walked towards him. Closer. Closer. Until she was standing right in front of him. Finally.

“Do I know you?”

The world exploded. Zhou Yichen woke up immediately. 3:17 AM. Dark room. Heart pounding. Genuine irritation. That dream had been cruel. Then he felt something warm and heavy against his side. Lin Xiaoran. They had both fallen asleep on his sofa halfway through a movie, under the same blanket, and she was still there—completely real. No idol, no fame, nothing out of reach. Just Xiaoran. His Xiaoran, drooling slightly on his shoulder. Very glamorous. It was the first time she’d ever still been at his place after midnight. Her own studio was across the road, and somewhere around the second film neither of them had wanted to walk her there.

Yichen stared at her for several seconds. He wrapped both arms around her, tight enough that she made a confused, sleepy noise.

“Hm?”

Half asleep. Barely conscious.

“What happened?”

Nothing. How was he supposed to explain? Sorry, I had a dream where you were a celebrity and didn’t know me, so now I’m emotionally damaged. Impossible. Then Xiaoran opened one eye.

“…Yichen?”

He was still hugging her. Not letting go.

“You okay?”

“…Bad dream.”

Her sleepy expression softened.

“Oh.”

Without even waking up properly, she wrapped her arms around him too.

“There.”

“What.”

“Better.”

Half asleep, and completely unaware she had just fixed everything. Then she yawned.

“You’re my favourite person.”

Sleepy Xiaoran was dangerous. Two seconds later, she was asleep again. Zhou Yichen lay staring at the ceiling, his heart finally calming down. The dream version had been beautiful. World-famous. Perfect. But he preferred this one—the clingy one, the dramatic one, the one who stole his hoodies and never stopped talking. The one who knew exactly who Zhou Yichen was. Before falling asleep again, he tightened his arms around her, just to make sure. In case Dream Xiaoran got any more ideas.

In the morning she woke up under his blanket with a crease from his shirt on her cheek and a cup of warm milk on the floor beside the sofa. He kissed her good morning before she could be embarrassed about the drooling. It worked, mostly.

After that it stopped being an accident. By spring there was a toothbrush in his bathroom, a drawer that was hers, and a spare key on her ring. She slept at his apartment on Fridays and most Saturdays and went back across the road on Sunday nights, because her studio, she said, still needed her. It mostly needed her laundry.

chapters.desc: Jiayi and Ning want a night out by the river. Lin Xiaoran has never been to a club. Zhou Yichen has, exactly twice.
chapters.title: The First Night Out
chapters.epigraph: “Since we were seventeen.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had never been to a club. Not once. Not in high school, when some of her classmates had started sneaking into places with fake confidence and borrowed jackets, and not in her first year at Huaining either, because clubs had always sounded to her like somewhere you went to shout at people you could already text. Then on Friday afternoon her phone lit up.

Jiayi: We’re going out tonight. The place by the river. Ning’s coming. You’re coming.

Ning: You are actually coming this time.

Xiaoran: What do people even DO there

Jiayi: Dance. Drink. Exist loudly.

Xiaoran: That’s suspiciously vague

Ning: PLEASE

She stared at the screen. She was curious. A little intimidated. Mostly curious. Meilin and Yuhao were at universities hours away now, and Jiayi and Ning were the first friends she’d made here on her own, the two who’d lost her in the festival crowd in her first month and then spent ten frantic minutes looking for her. She wanted to do things with them.

She just didn’t know what to expect. So naturally she rang the person who knew almost everything.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Have you ever been to a club?”

A short pause. “Yes.”

She sat up on her bed. “When?”

“The one by the river? Twice. Once after the spring league final, and once for Fang Ze’s twentieth birthday.”

“You never told me that.”

“I told you both times. The first time you were asleep by ten and sent me a sticker of a sleeping panda at eleven. The second time you were up finishing your competition slides and sent me nine stickers and a photo of your face mask.” She could hear him smiling.

She remembered the face mask. She didn’t remember the club.

“You said the team’s going out.”

“The team went out. To a club. I drove three of them home at half past eleven, because I don’t drink when I’m driving, and I was in bed by midnight. Why?”

“…I’m going tonight. With Jiayi and Ning.”

“Your first time.”

“How do you know?”

“Because you just asked me what people do there.”

“That’s not evidence.”

“It’s fairly convincing evidence.”

She ignored that. “Would you come?”

“Of course.”

She smiled at the ceiling. “Really?”

“Did you think I’d say no?”

“I thought you might have training.”

“Not on a Friday. And not tonight,” said Zhou Yichen.

At half past seven he knocked on the door of her studio. Black shirt, dark trousers, the plain watch he always wore. Nothing special. Unfortunately he had the kind of face that made nothing special look expensive.

She’d chosen a fitted top, a short skirt, boots, a small bag, a little more eyeliner than usual, and an hour on her hair.

He looked at her for a second longer than he needed to. “Beautiful.”

Then his eyes went to the bag. “What’s in there?”

“Important things.”

He looked when she opened it. Phone, wallet, lip gloss, powder, a hair tie, a tiny perfume, two packets of tissues, a stuffed panda keyring, and an amount of miscellaneous items that defied classification.

“Are you going to a club or moving house?”

“Don’t judge me.”

He took out the perfume, handed it to her to use now, and put the panda keyring on her desk. “Less in the bag. You’ll put something down somewhere.”

“I’m not that careless.”

He looked at her. She looked back. A few seconds passed.

“…Sometimes.”

He checked that her phone was charged, did up the strap of her bag where it had twisted, and didn’t say one word about the skirt.

“If you feel uncomfortable, tell me. We’ll leave whenever you want. And you don’t have to drink because everyone else does.”

“I know.”

“I know you know,” he said, and held out his hand.

The club was much louder than she’d imagined. The bass came up through the floor into her boots. Lights swung across the ceiling and the dance floor was a single moving animal made of people.

She stopped in the doorway, and he stopped with her.

“Too much?”

“No. Just— Wow.” She looked round.

“First impression?”

“Very loud.”

“That’s generally the point.”

Jiayi saw them first and screamed her name across the room, then saw who she’d brought, and her mouth fell open. “You brought the basketball one?”

“My personal guide,” said Xiaoran proudly.

At the bar she spent five minutes reading the menu as if it were an exam paper. “What’s this one?”

“A cocktail.”

“And this?”

“Also a cocktail.”

“What’s the difference?”

“The ingredients.”

“Very helpful,” she said, and he laughed, and then explained properly: which were sweet, which were strong, which tasted like juice and weren’t. He ordered himself water with lemon, because the car was outside. When she chose something pink he put a glass of water beside it without comment.

She took a sip and her eyes went wide. “It tastes like juice.”

“Be careful with those.”

“Why?”

“Some drinks are much stronger than they taste.”

She looked at the glass with deep suspicion. “That’s dishonest.”

“Very,” he agreed.

When the music changed, Jiayi grabbed her hand. “Come and dance.”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen.

“Go. I’ll watch your things,” he said.

At first she was awful. She didn’t know what to do with her hands, wasn’t sure whether she was on the beat, and laughed every time she bumped into someone, which was often. Ning showed her a step. Jiayi showed her another. Somewhere around the third song she stopped thinking about it, and started having fun.

From the edge of the floor, Yichen watched. He wasn’t interested in the dancing. He was interested in the way her face changed every time she got a step right, and the way she looked over her shoulder every minute or two to check he was still there, and lit up every time she found him.

She came back breathless. “I danced.”

“I saw.”

“Was I good?”

“Very.”

“You’re biased.”

“Completely.”

She took his hand. “Come with me.”

He put the water down. He wasn’t an enthusiastic dancer. He was, unfairly, a good one: one hand at her waist, the other holding hers, moving. She stared up at him.

“You can dance.”

“Can I?”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“You never asked. Stop watching your feet. Follow the music,” he said, and bent his head so that she could hear him over the bass.

She did. It was much less frightening with him.

Later, sitting in the quiet corner he’d found without seeming to look for it, she studied him over her water.

“How do you know all this? Where the quiet seats are. Which drinks. Where the bathroom is. How to get the bartender’s attention without waving.”

“I’ve been here twice.”

“Twice is not enough to know where the bathroom is.”

“It’s exactly enough to know where the bathroom is.”

She narrowed her eyes. “Did girls come up to you? Those two times?”

The real question.

“A few.”

“And?”

“And I said I had a girlfriend, and showed them the photo of you in the face mask.”

She gasped. “You did not.”

“Fang Ze has it on his phone. The team manager is quite famous on the team.”

She hid her face in his shoulder, which was where she’d been going to put it anyway. Then she lifted it. “Have you ever brought a girl here?”

He smiled slowly. “I’ve only ever had one girlfriend, Xiaoran. Since we were seventeen. She’s never been to a club before tonight.”

Her cheeks went pink. “…I’m here now.”

“Exactly,” he said, and kissed her temple, and she forgot her next question.

By midnight she was pleasantly exhausted. Jiayi hugged her at the door and made her promise to come again. Ning took a photograph of the two of them under the sign that Xiaoran made her delete and then made her send.

In the car she leaned back against the seat and turned her head towards him. “I had fun.”

“I know. You’ve been smiling for three hours.”

A few streets later she said, “Did you? Have fun? Even though you were looking after me the whole time?”

He kept his eyes on the road. “I didn’t spend the evening looking after you instead of having fun. I spent it having fun with you.”

She went quiet. Then she reached across the console and took his free hand.

“Next time I want to go with your team.”

“All right.”

“And dance more.”

“All right.”

“And try a different drink.”

“We’ll see.”

“You’re not going to stop me?”

“I’m going to make sure you know what’s in it.”

“Deal. Wait. Those two times. How long did you stay?” She thought for a moment.

“About two hours each.”

“And you drove everyone home.”

“Somebody had to.”

“So you’ve been to a club twice, drunk water both times, and gone to bed before midnight.”

“Yes.”

“Zhou Yichen,” she said, delighted, “you’re the most boring man in Shanghai.”

“Probably. But tonight I wasn’t bored at all,” he said.

She kissed his cheek at a red light. He drove the rest of the way home with one hand on the wheel and the other holding hers, already certain that tomorrow would bring a detailed review of everything she’d seen, and at least forty more questions. He wasn’t complaining. Not even slightly.

chapters.desc: Her father’s fiftieth birthday lunch, and an aunt from the town who would like to know exactly what a media degree pays.
chapters.title: The Aunt Who Asks About Salaries
chapters.epigraph: “No. It means I know you’ll take it seriously.”
chapters.content:
It was supposed to be a nice family lunch. It was her father’s fiftieth birthday, on the second Saturday in March, and Lin Xiaoran and Zhou Yichen had taken the early train back from Shanghai for it. Her mother’s younger sister had come in from the town on the bus, with a bag of dried mushrooms and the determination of a woman who had missed New Year with flu and intended to catch up on everything she’d missed, including the boy.

Everyone else had seen him at New Year. Uncle Deng had made his remark, Grandma had summoned him to dinner on the fifth, and the whole family had decided he would do. Auntie Hui had seen none of it. She’d been in bed with a hot water bottle, hearing about it all on the phone.

Yichen had arrived at eleven with a box of pastries from the old bakery by their high school, greeted every single person in the room correctly, and settled on the sofa next to her father, who was wearing a new shirt and pretending he didn’t know it was his birthday. Xiaoran had sat on the arm of the sofa beside Yichen with her hand on his shoulder, and stayed there through two cups of tea.

Everything had been perfectly normal until lunch.

“So, Yichen,” said Auntie Hui, putting a piece of fish into her bowl. “Business, isn’t it?”

“Yes, Auntie.”

“That’s good. Lots of opportunities in business. Finance. Management. Very practical.”

“There are quite a few paths, yes.”

“And basketball as well?”

“For the university team.”

“You must be very busy.”

“It’s manageable.”

Auntie Hui nodded, satisfied, and turned to her niece. “And you, Xiaoran? Media?”

Xiaoran swallowed. “Yes.”

“What will you do with it?”

“I’m still working it out. I like production. Advertising, maybe. Making things for brands.”

“Ah,” said Auntie Hui.

It was only one syllable, but it made Xiaoran look up.

“That’s interesting,” said her aunt. “But is it stable?”

“I think it can be.”

“Can be.”

Her mother, beside her, kept eating. Xiaoran smiled the smile she kept for relatives.

“There’s a lot you can do with a media degree, Auntie.”

“Of course, of course. But you know, these days, everyone wants to work in media. Everyone wants to be a content creator.”

Her aunt turned back to Yichen.

“Business is different. At least you know where you’re going,” she said.

Yichen put his chopsticks down. He didn’t say anything yet.

Xiaoran knew where this was going. She’d been here before. It was never really a question about what she wanted. It always turned into a comparison: her subject against someone else’s, the practical against the supposedly uncertain.

“It’s still early. I’ve got time,” she said.

“That’s true. You’re young. But when you’re choosing a career, you have to think about the future. About a family. It’s hard if both people have unstable jobs. It’s good to have your own career, of course. But a girl should be practical. If your boyfriend has a good job, you don’t need to put so much pressure on yourself to earn a lot.” Her aunt reached for the greens. She smiled kindly at her niece.

Xiaoran’s chopsticks stopped in the air. Across the table, her father looked up from his soup.

“Auntie, I’m not choosing my career based on what he earns,” Xiaoran said.

“I’m only giving advice.”

“I know. But I’m not. I’m going to earn my own money. I already have. I don’t want—” She heard her own voice go thin and hated it.

“Auntie,” said Yichen, at the same moment, and both of them stopped.

He looked at Xiaoran. She looked at him. He gave her the smallest nod, as if to say go on, and she found she’d lost her place.

“Xiaoran’s right. Her career should be about what she wants to build. Not about what I might earn,” he said into the gap.

His voice was calm. It wasn’t loud. But the whole table went quiet.

“Oh, of course. I didn’t mean—” said Auntie Hui.

“I know. But I don’t think her future should be treated as something that depends on mine. She’s very good at what she does. She already has paid work outside her course. I’d like her to have the chance to do it properly.” He picked up his chopsticks again.

Her aunt’s expression shifted slightly. “Yes, I’m sure she’s capable. But I’m talking about practical things. You two are together. You’ll have to think about money eventually.”

“Eventually, perhaps. But I haven’t graduated yet. It would be quite ambitious of me to talk about my salary as if it’s already in my bank account.” A faint smile.

Her father coughed into his soup. Xiaoran nearly laughed.

“Well, that’s true,” said Auntie Hui, a little uncertainly. Then, rallying, to Xiaoran: “But you should still have a number in mind. How much do you expect to earn when you graduate?”

Yichen said, “She doesn’t have to decide that today, Auntie. And I don’t think it’s fair to ask her to justify her future salary when nobody’s asked me to justify mine.” There was no edge in it at all. Only a quiet, unmistakable refusal to let the conversation go any further that way.

For the first time, Auntie Hui didn’t seem to know what to say next.

Her mother finally put her chopsticks down. “Exactly. They’re students. Let them enjoy it.”

“Plenty of time to worry about salaries,” said her father, and reached across and put a piece of fish in Xiaoran’s bowl, which he hadn’t done since she was nine.

The conversation moved on. But under the table Xiaoran found Yichen’s hand on his knee and held on to it, hard, through the whole of the next dish, and ate left-handed, badly, and didn’t let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

She caught him in the kitchen afterward. He’d volunteered to carry the plates, and she’d followed him on the excuse of getting more water, and as soon as the door swung shut she leaned back against the counter.

“Yichen.”

He put the plates down by the sink. “Mm.”

“You answered for me.”

He turned round. He didn’t look pleased with himself. If anything he looked.

“Was that all right?”

“I’d started answering.”

“I know. I’m sorry. I came in on top of you.”

“I could have finished.”

“I know you could. I wasn’t answering because I thought you couldn’t. I just didn’t think you should have to explain yourself to the whole table on your father’s birthday,” he said at once. Not you didn’t need to, not I had to protect you. Just that he knew.

She looked at him. Then she let out a breath and stepped forward and wrapped her arms round him and her face against his chest.

“Thank you,” she said into his shirt.

He put his arms round her. “You’re welcome.”

“But next time let me finish.”

“Next time I’ll let you finish.”

“And then you can help.”

“Then I’ll help,” he said, and she felt him smile against her hair.

She tipped her head back to look up at him. “The thing about your salary being in your bank account was funny.”

“Good. I was hoping someone appreciated it. Your father did. He coughed.”

She laughed, and then stopped. “Do you really think it’ll work out? My career?”

“Yes.”

“You’re very confident.”

“I’ve seen you work.”

“That doesn’t mean I’ll succeed.”

“No. It means I know you’ll take it seriously. You don’t have to know where you’ll end up. You just have to keep choosing what you want to do.” He looked down at her.

“And if I never earn very much?”

“Then you’ll earn what you earn. And it’ll be yours. I don’t want you choosing anything because you’re worried about depending on me. Or because someone thinks your degree isn’t practical enough. Choose what you want.” He tucked her hair behind her ear.

She held on tighter. “Okay.”

“Now,” he said, “are you getting water, or did you bring me in here for a private meeting?”

“Both.”

“Very efficient,” he said, and she laughed into his chest, and her mother pushed the kitchen door open with a tray, looked at them, and backed straight out again.

✦ ✦ ✦

When they came back to the table, Auntie Hui was asking her father about the water bureau’s new building. Xiaoran sat down next to Yichen and pulled her chair a few centimetres closer to his. A few minutes later her aunt turned to her again.

“Xiaoran. Are you doing an internship this summer?”

“I’m applying to a few creative studios.”

“That’s good. Get experience early.”

“I’ve already done a shoot for a fashion label. Last November.”

“Oh? Paid?”

“Yes,” said Xiaoran, and couldn’t keep the pride out of her voice.

“That’s nice. How much did they pay you?” Her aunt considered it.

Xiaoran nearly choked on her water. Yichen, beside her, reached calmly for the teapot.

“Enough about money, Hui,” said her mother.

“What? I’m only curious!”

Xiaoran put her cup down. This time she got there first. “Two thousand, Auntie. For half a day. I spent all of it on a lens.”

Auntie Hui blinked. “All of it?”

“All of it. It’s the best thing I’ve ever bought.”

There was a pause. Then her aunt laughed, properly, for the first time all lunch. “You’re your mother’s daughter. She spent her first month’s wages on a bicycle and didn’t eat meat for three weeks.”

“Hui,” said her mother.

“It’s true!”

Yichen put the teapot down and poured Xiaoran’s tea without looking at her. She pressed her lips together hard. This time she was definitely going to laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

The party ended in the late afternoon. Yichen helped her father carry the folding chairs back into the storeroom and said goodbye to everyone, one by one. Her mother packed fruit for him to take home. Auntie Hui, perhaps sensing that she’d been a little persistent, came over to the door and pressed half her dried mushrooms on him for his mother.

“It was nice to meet you, Yichen.”

“And you, Auntie.”

“Come again.”

“Thank you.”

She looked at Xiaoran. “And you. Send me a picture of this famous lens.”

“I’ll send you a picture taken with it,” said Xiaoran, and her aunt laughed again and went back in.

Xiaoran walked him to the bus stop at the end of her road; he was going to his own parents’ for the night. She held his arm with both hands the whole way, and leaned on him at the crossing.

“That was the first time you’ve done that. In front of everyone,” she said.

“I know.”

“Usually you let me handle things.”

“I still do. I came in too early. I’m sorry.”

“I’m not cross. I liked it. I liked that you said what I might earn. Dad’ll talk about that for weeks.” She swung his arm a little.

“Will he?”

“He’ll say it shows modesty.”

“It wasn’t modesty. I genuinely don’t know.”

“That’s what modesty is,” she said. The light changed. “Do you think she’ll ask again? Next New Year?”

“Probably.”

“You’re not even going to pretend otherwise.”

“Would you like me to lie?”

“No. Next time I’m answering her myself. The whole thing.” She looked up at him.

“All right.”

“But if she starts comparing us again—”

He waited.

She smiled at him sweetly. “Then you can help.”

“Understood,” he said, and at the bus stop he kissed her, quickly, because there was an old man on the bench pretending not to watch, and she didn’t let go of his sleeve until the bus doors were actually closing.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she was on her childhood bed with her notes when her phone buzzed.

Yichen: Home.

Xiaoran: good

Xiaoran: I was thinking

Yichen: Dangerous.

Xiaoran: when I’m a very successful creative director I’m going to buy Auntie Hui a lens. so she understands

Yichen: That’s very generous.

Xiaoran: and if I’m NOT very successful I’ll buy you dinner

Yichen: Just dinner?

Xiaoran: a good dinner. with my own money

Yichen: I’ll hold you to that.

Yichen: For the record. I’m looking forward to seeing what you become. Not what you earn.

She read it twice. Then she typed:

Xiaoran: I’m looking forward to seeing what you become too

Yichen: I know. Good night, Xiaoran.

She lay back with the phone on her chest. Through the wall she could hear her father in the next room telling her mother, at great length, that the boy had said what I might earn and not what I will earn, and that this showed modesty, and her mother telling him to go to sleep, it was his birthday and he was fifty.

chapters.desc: Three rejections in one week, deleted before anyone can ask. She stops saying “guess what” at dinner. He notices.
chapters.title: The Emails She Didn’t Forward
chapters.epigraph: “I made an exception.”
chapters.content:
The first rejection arrived on a Tuesday, at 11:04 in the morning, in the middle of a lecture on audience segmentation.

Dear Ms. Lin, thank you for your interest in our Summer Associate Program. After careful consideration…

Lin Xiaoran read it under the desk. Then she read the first line again, as if it might have changed its mind. It hadn’t. She deleted it.

She looked at the empty space where it had been. Then she looked at the back of the head of the boy in front of her, who was asleep, and at the lecturer, who was explaining the difference between a demographic and a persona.

Then she went to the deleted folder and deleted it from there too, which felt better, and wrote audience segmentation neatly at the top of a fresh page, and underlined it twice, and didn’t hear another word for forty minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had applied to nine places.

This had been a sensible number in January. In January she had still been the girl who’d won a national media strategy competition the year before. There had been a trophy shaped like a speech bubble on her shelf and a photograph of her holding it on the faculty noticeboard, and Zhou Yichen had looked at that photograph for so long, every time they walked past it, that Jiayi had started calling it the shrine.

In January, nine applications had felt like nine doors that were already a little bit open.

By the end of March, four of them had said nothing at all. On the Tuesday, one said no. On the Thursday, two more did.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Guess what,” said Xiaoran every evening at dinner, normally.

It was how she started. She had started every dinner that way since high school. Guess what, the professor wore odd socks. Guess what, a pigeon walked into the lecture hall and nobody did anything. Guess what, Ning said something so mean to a boy in our group that he apologised to her.

Yichen never guessed. That wasn’t the point. The point was that she said it, and he put his chopsticks down, and she told him.

On Thursday night, at the noodle place behind the sports hall, she didn’t say it.

She told him about the lecture. She told him about Jiayi’s new earrings. She ate all her noodles. She stole two of his dumplings, which was normal, and didn’t make a speech about it, which wasn’t.

He noticed. He didn’t say anything. He moved the dumplings closer to her side of the table. On Friday she didn’t say it either.

On Saturday he put his chopsticks down before she’d started.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Nothing’s wrong. I’m tired. Assignments.” She smiled at him. It was a good smile. She’d practised it in the lift.

He looked at her. Then he nodded, and picked his chopsticks up again, and let her have it.

That was the worst part. He believed her, or he let her think he did, and she sat there being believed and felt terrible.

✦ ✦ ✦
