The thing was, she couldn’t tell him. Not because he’d be unkind. He would be the opposite of unkind. He would be so kind it would be unbearable.

He would say their loss. He would say you won a national competition. And then, because he was Zhou Yichen and because his family owned a great many warehouses and knew a great many people, he would say, carefully, I could ask someone. And she would have to say no.

She had sat at her grandparents’ table at New Year and listened to Uncle Deng explain, in front of everyone, why a girl from an ordinary family dated a boy like that. She had heard the word he hadn’t quite used. She had held Yichen’s hand under the table so hard her knuckles hurt.

She wasn’t going to get her first internship because somebody knew somebody who knew Mr. Zhou.

So she didn’t tell him. She just stopped saying guess what, because there wasn’t anything to guess.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Thursday night, after the second and third emails, she sat on the stairs outside her studio at midnight, on the fourth floor, because her room felt too small to be disappointed in. She rang Meilin.

Meilin answered on the second ring from a dormitory four hundred kilometres away, sounding exactly as she had at sixteen.

“You only ring at midnight when something’s wrong.”

“Nothing’s wrong.”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

So she told her. The nine applications. The three noes. The four silences. The trophy shaped like a speech bubble, which she now couldn’t look at.

Meilin listened to all of it, which was rare, because Meilin usually interrupted by the second sentence.

“Does Yichen know?”

“No.”

“You’re sitting on a staircase at midnight so your boyfriend who lives across the road won’t see your face.”

“…Maybe.”

“Xiaoran. You’re not scared he’ll fix it. You’re scared he’ll see you lose,” said Meilin, in the voice she’d used in the noodle shop the winter before, the one that had made the four of them promise not to drift.

Xiaoran didn’t answer. A moth knocked against the stair light.

“He’s seen you lose before. He watched you get forty-three in maths. He stayed,” said Meilin.

Xiaoran laughed, which hurt, and went back inside, and didn’t tell him the next day either.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ning found out first, because Ning found out everything.

“You’ve been refreshing your email like it owes you money,” she said on Monday, in the library, without looking up from her own laptop.

“I’m checking for a group assignment.”

“We don’t have a group assignment.”

“Then I’m checking for nothing.”

Ning turned her screen round. On it was the Summer Associate Program page of a large agency in the financial district, with a large red banner across the top that said APPLICATIONS CLOSED.

“They rejected me too,” said Ning. “On Tuesday. I laughed for ten minutes. Did they reject you?”

Xiaoran looked at her.

“And two others. And four haven’t answered,” she said, quietly.

Ning considered this.

“Does Captain Zhou know?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because he’d fix it.”

Ning was quiet for longer than usual. Then she said, “He can’t fix it. He’s a business student. They don’t even know what a content calendar is.”

Xiaoran laughed, a little wetly, into her sleeve, and Ning pushed a packet of tissues across the desk without comment, which was the kindest thing Sun Ning had ever done in public.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found out on Wednesday. Not from Ning. Ning would have died first.

He found out because Xiaoran came out of a one-to-one with her portfolio tutor and walked straight into the campus café, and straight through it, and into the bathroom at the back, and stayed there for nineteen minutes.

He knew it was nineteen minutes because he was sitting at their table by the window waiting for her, the way he did every Wednesday at four, with her milk tea already bought and going warm.

When she came out her eyes were red and she had powdered over it, badly, and she sat down and picked up the milk tea and said, “Sorry. Long queue.”

There was no queue. There was never a queue. There was one bathroom and he had watched the door the entire time. He didn’t say that.

He said, “Okay.”

She drank half her milk tea through the straw without breathing. He waited.

He was good at waiting. He had waited for her outside exam halls and dressing rooms and once, memorably, outside a bookshop for an hour and ten minutes while she read the first chapter of nine different novels to decide which one she deserved.

“My tutor says my portfolio’s too safe. She says I win competitions because I’m good at telling a panel what it wants to hear, and agencies can smell that. She says I should send them something I’m scared of,” she said, to the milk tea.

“Is that why you were in the bathroom?”

“No. I was in the bathroom because three companies have said no and four haven’t bothered and I haven’t told you, and I didn’t want you to find out from my face.” She put the cup down.

Then he said, “Which three?”

She told him. He nodded slowly, as if she’d given him a list of patients and he was deciding which to see first. He didn’t say their loss. He didn’t say you won a national competition.

He said, “And you didn’t tell me because you thought I’d ask someone.”

She looked up.

“How do you know that?”

Yichen said, “Because I thought about it on Saturday. When you didn’t say guess what. I thought, if it’s what I think it is, I know three people I could call. And then I thought, she’d never forgive me.”

Her mouth opened.

“You knew on Saturday?”

“I guessed on Saturday.”

“You never guess! That’s the whole point! You never guess!”

“I made an exception,” he said.

She stared at him across the table with her ruined powder and her half a milk tea, and then she started laughing, and then the laugh turned into something else halfway through, and she put her face down on her folded arms on the table and cried properly, in the middle of the campus café, at four in the afternoon.

He didn’t come round the table. He reached across it and put his hand on the back of her head and kept it there, warm and still, until she’d finished.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I’m not calling anyone. I want you to know that first,” he said later, walking her home.

“Good.”

“Not my father. Not my father’s friends. Not my father’s friends’ daughters, who all work in marketing, apparently, and all went to the same famous university.”

“How do you know that?”

“My mother tells me. Every holiday.”

She snorted.

“But I’ll do one thing. If you let me,” he said.

“What?”

“Your tutor said send something you’re scared of. What are you scared of?” He stopped at the bottom of her stairs.

She thought about it. Then she told him.

There was a campaign she had never shown anyone. Not the competition one, all neat charts and audience personas. A real one. For the old noodle shop near their high school, the one with the soft menu and the owner who still gave her milk instead of chili. She’d made it last winter, after she’d sat in that shop with Meilin and Yuhao and been afraid for the first time that the four of them would drift apart. Photographs. A short video. Copy written in the owner’s own words. It was messy and sentimental and it wasn’t strategic at all.

“It’s embarrassing,” she said.

“Is it good?”

She hesitated.

“…It’s the best thing I’ve made.”

“Then send that,” said Yichen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He kept his word. He didn’t call anyone. What he did was worse.

He became, for nine days, the most unpleasant mock interviewer in the history of Huaining University.

“Why should we hire you instead of the other two hundred applicants?”

“Because I’m—”

“Don’t say passionate.”

“I wasn’t going to say passionate.”

“You were going to say passionate.”

“…I was going to say passionate.”

“Everyone says passionate. Again.”

He sat at his desk in a shirt with the sleeves rolled up, looking at her over his laptop as if she were a quarterly forecast that didn’t add up, and asked her the worst questions he could find. What’s your biggest weakness. Tell me about a time you failed. Why do you want to work in a city where you don’t know anyone. Why should we believe a competition win wasn’t luck.

On the fourth evening she said “passionate” by accident and he simply looked at her over the laptop until she threw a cushion at him. On the sixth she cried halfway through tell me about a time you failed, because the honest answer was this week, and he waited, and when she’d finished he said, “That. Say that. But without the crying,” and she laughed so much she couldn’t breathe.

The last one made her so angry she answered it perfectly. He wrote something down.

“What did you write?”

“Nothing.”

She leaned over the desk and looked. He had written that one and underlined it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the tenth day she rewrote the noodle shop campaign for the fourth time and sent it, with a new cover letter, to a media company in Beijing that she had found at one in the morning and not mentioned to anyone, not even Ning or Jiayi. Not to Yichen. It wasn’t a secret, exactly.

It was just that if it said no, she wanted to be the only one who knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three weeks later she was sitting cross-legged on his bed on a Thursday evening with her laptop on her knees, pretending to edit a group presentation, when the email came in. She saw the company name. Her stomach did something complicated.

Yichen was at his desk with a textbook open, reading the same page he’d been reading for twenty minutes because she’d been humming. She opened the email. She read the first line. She read it again, slowly.

Then she read the whole thing three times, and opened two more tabs to check the company was real, and that the program was real, and that she was real, and looked at the address at the bottom, which was in Beijing, more than a thousand kilometres from this bed and this boy and this terrible, wonderful, too-quiet room. She looked up at him.

He was still reading the same page. She took a breath.

“Yichen.”

chapters.desc: She has told Yichen about the internship in Beijing. Now she has to tell her mother, who will tell her father, who will cry.
chapters.title: Telling Her Parents About Beijing
chapters.epigraph: “You’re my daughter. How could I not worry?”
chapters.content:
She had told Zhou Yichen the night the email came, sitting cross-legged on his bed with her laptop on her knees, in a voice that came out much higher than she meant it to. He had put his textbook down and said her name, and then congratulations, and then nothing at all for a while, because he was holding her too tightly to talk.

Eight weeks. A media company in Beijing, more than a thousand kilometres from his bed and his books and his too-quiet flat. A summer program she’d found at one in the morning and applied for without telling a soul. Telling him had been the easy part.

“Tell your mother the way you told me. Start with the part you want,” he said at the door the next morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

She rang her mother the following evening from his dining table. He was in the kitchen making tea. She hadn’t asked him to leave the room; he’d known it was a conversation she needed to have on her own, and gone, and left the kitchen door open so she could see his back at the counter.

“Hello, Mum.”

“Xiaoran? Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Rice.”

“With what?”

“Mum.”

Her mother laughed. “All right. What is it? You sound serious.”

Xiaoran looked down at the notes she’d written. She’d prepared everything: the program dates, the accommodation, the flights, the contact details, answers to questions her mother hadn’t even thought of yet.

“I wanted to tell you something. I applied for a summer internship.”

“Oh?”

“At a media company. Real production work. Campaigns. Real clients. They emailed me on Thursday. I got in.”

“Really? That’s wonderful! Congratulations!”

Xiaoran smiled at the table. “Thank you.”

“Which company?”

“It’s in Beijing.”

Silence.

It went on, and on, with nothing in it: no breath of a laugh, no next question. Xiaoran’s smile faded slowly. She took the phone from her ear and looked at it to make sure the call hadn’t dropped. It hadn’t.

“Mum?”

Nothing. Then a small sound, as if her mother had put something down.

“It’s only eight weeks. They arrange accommodation for all the interns. They’ve sent the details. I’ve checked the schedule. I’ll send you everything,” Xiaoran said quickly.

“Beijing?”

“Yes.”

“Why Beijing?”

“Because that’s where the company is.”

“I know that. I mean, why did you choose something so far away?”

“It’s a good opportunity.”

“Couldn’t you find something here? Or in Shanghai?”

She had expected that one. She’d even written down an answer. But hearing it in her mother’s voice made her feel about nine years old.

“I applied to three places in Shanghai. They said no. This one said yes,” she said carefully. She hadn’t told her mother that either.

Her mother didn’t answer straight away. Then: “When did you apply?”

“A few weeks ago.”

“And you’re only telling me now?”

Xiaoran shut her eyes. “I didn’t know if I’d get it.”

“So you applied without discussing it with us.”

“I wanted to try first.”

Another silence. This time Xiaoran knew her mother was upset. Not angry, exactly. But something had shifted in her voice.

“Have you already decided to go?”

Xiaoran hesitated. Then she told the truth. “I want to.”

The silence that followed was longer. She could hear movement on the other end; perhaps her mother had gone into the bedroom and shut the door.

“Mum? Are you angry?”

“No.”

It came too fast. Xiaoran’s throat went tight.

“Then why aren’t you saying anything?”

Her mother let out a breath. “I’m thinking.”

“Okay.”

“You’re still young, Xiaoran.”

“I’m at university, Mum.”

“I know you’re at university. Beijing isn’t next door. And eight weeks is a long time.”

“I know.”

She looked at the edge of the table. In the kitchen, Yichen had stopped moving. She had imagined this conversation differently. She’d imagined her mother being excited, asking what she’d learn, whether she’d meet interesting people, what she’d bring home. Instead she was explaining why she wanted to leave.

She felt the familiar pull to make it easier. She could say it didn’t matter. She could say there were other programs. She could say she hadn’t decided. She didn’t want to. For once, she didn’t want to make her excitement smaller just because it frightened someone else.

“Mum. I really want to go.”

A pause. “I know.”

“I’ve wanted to do something like this for ages. I want to see how people work somewhere else. I want to learn production properly. I think it’ll help me work out what I want to do after university. I’m not going because I want to leave home. I just want to try.” She lowered her voice.

Her mother didn’t say anything.

“Let me think about it.”

“Okay.”

“Send me the details. And don’t book anything.”

“I won’t.”

A pause. “Have you eaten properly today?”

Xiaoran let out a small, helpless laugh. “Yes, Mum.”

“All right. Good night.”

“Good night.”

The line went dead. She kept the phone against her ear for a few more seconds anyway. Then she put it down on the table and looked at it. She didn’t cry. Not straight away. She just sat there feeling as if she’d been carrying something heavy for fifteen minutes without realising how much it weighed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen came out of the kitchen and put a cup of tea in front of her and sat down in the chair beside hers, close enough that their knees touched.

“How did it go?”

“She said she’ll think about it.”

“All right.”

“She didn’t say yes.”

“She didn’t say no.”

“She went quiet. After I said Beijing she just stopped talking. I knew she’d worry. I didn’t think she’d go completely silent.” Xiaoran turned the cup round and round.

He didn’t tell her everything would be fine. He knew better than to promise something he couldn’t. “What did you tell her?”

“Everything. The program, the dates, where I’d live. Why I want to go. She kept asking why I couldn’t find something here.”

“Did you tell her why this one matters?”

“Yes.”

“Then you’ve done your part for today.”

“That’s it?”

“For today.”

“I should have prepared better. I should have told her before I applied.”

“Maybe.”

She turned and glared at him. “You’re not helping.”

“I’m not going to tell you every decision was perfect. But applying for something because you wanted it isn’t something you need to apologise for.” He took her hand off the cup and held it.

“I don’t want her to think I’m being careless.”

“Then show her you’re not. Send her everything. Let her read it. Answer her questions. You don’t have to win her over in one phone call.”

“What if she still says no?”

“Then you’ll have another conversation.”

“You’re not going to tell me to go anyway?”

“Do you want me to?”

She thought about it. “No.”

“Then I won’t. But I want you to go, if it’s what you want. I want that very much.” He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

She looked at him. “Even though it’s far?”

“Because you worked for it.”

“You’ll miss me.”

“Yes.”

“Very much?”

“Probably.”

“Probably?”

“Do you need me to exaggerate?”

“Yes.”

“Terribly. I’ll be miserable. I’ll forget how to eat. I’ll stare out of windows,” he said.

She laughed, and it came out wet, and she climbed out of her chair into his lap and put her face in his neck, and he held her while her tea went cold.

“You’ll call me,” he said into her hair, after a while.

“Obviously.”

“Video?”

“Obviously.”

“Every day?”

She leaned back to look at him. “Are you going to miss me that much?”

“Would you like an honest answer?”

“Yes.”

“Yes. But I don’t want you spending your time in Beijing worrying about whether I’m lonely,” he said.

“I won’t. I’ll worry about whether you’re eating.”

“That’s reasonable.”

“And sleeping.”

“Less reasonable.”

“And whether you’re training too much.”

“You’ll be very busy,” he said.

“I’ll have a lot of responsibilities,” she agreed, and put her face back in his neck.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning she sent her mother everything: a long message, the PDF, the official schedule, the accommodation details, the coordinator’s email. At the bottom she wrote, I really hope I can go, Mum. I think it’ll be good for me. I’ll answer anything you’re worried about.

No reply came. She put her phone in her bag and went to her lecture. At the afternoon break there was a message.

Mum (Accounts Dept.): I have read the information.

Her heart jumped.

Mum (Accounts Dept.): The accommodation details are clear. I want to know who is responsible for you while you are there.

It wasn’t a yes. But it was a question. A real one. She sent the coordinator’s details and explained how the interns would be supervised, and how often they’d check in.

Mum (Accounts Dept.): All right. I’ll look at it properly.

She sent a screenshot to Yichen.

Xiaoran: she replied

Yichen: She’s asking about the arrangements. That’s a conversation now.

Xiaoran: you think so?

Yichen: I’m usually right.

Xiaoran: don’t ruin the moment

✦ ✦ ✦

Four days later her mother rang again. Xiaoran was sitting on the steps outside the Business building waiting for Yichen’s seminar to finish.

“Are you busy?”

“No. I’m waiting for someone.”

Her mother had a list. Would anyone else from her university be going? How would she get from the airport? What would she do if she got ill? What would she eat? Xiaoran answered every question patiently. She’d already found out most of it. For the rest, she promised to check and send it on.

Then her mother went quiet again, and Xiaoran’s fingers tightened round the phone.

“Mum? Are you still worried?”

“Of course I’m worried. You’re my daughter. How could I not worry?” Her mother sighed.

Something in Xiaoran’s chest gave way a little. “I know.”

“You’ve never been away that long.”

“I know.”

“And Beijing’s far.”

“I know, Mum.”

A pause. “But you seem to have thought about it properly.”

Xiaoran went completely still.

“I’m not saying I’m not worried. And I still want to check some things. But if everything’s arranged properly—” her mother stopped, and Xiaoran didn’t breathe “—then I suppose you can go.”

She couldn’t say anything at all.

“Mum? Are you saying yes?”

Her mother gave a small laugh. “I’m saying you can go if it’s all arranged properly. Don’t make me say it twice.”

The smile came so fast it almost hurt. “Okay.”

“Call me when you land.”

“I will.”

“And when you get to the accommodation.”

“I will.”

“And don’t go wandering around on your own at night.”

“Mum.”

“I’m serious. Keep your phone charged. Eat properly. And send me pictures.”

“Pictures?”

“Of the places you go. I want to see them.”

Xiaoran looked down at her shoes. Her eyes had started to sting. “Okay, Mum.”

“Have you told Yichen?”

“Not yet.”

“Tell him. He’s been on your side, hasn’t he?”

Across the courtyard the Business building doors had opened, and Yichen was coming down the steps with his bag over his shoulder, phone in hand, looking round for her.

“Yes,” she said.

“Then tell him. And your father is going to cry. I’m telling you now so you’re ready.” Her mother paused.

Xiaoran’s face crumpled. “Mum—”

“Don’t you cry as well.”

“I’m not crying.”

“Your voice sounds strange.”

“I’m fine.”

Her mother laughed. “Go on. Go and do your things. Look after yourself.”

“I will. Love you.”

“Love you too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When she looked up, Yichen was standing in front of her. He’d seen her face from across the courtyard.

“What happened?”

She looked at him. Then the smile broke through.

“She said yes.”

His whole face changed. “Really?”

“She said I can go. I can go to Beijing.”

He crouched down on the step below her and took both her hands. “Congratulations.”

“Again?”

“Again,” he said, and she put her arms round his neck and her face into his shoulder and held on. For a few seconds she didn’t say anything. Then, muffled against his shirt: “I thought she was going to say no. She went so quiet. I thought—”

“I know. She needed time.” He rubbed her back.

She sat back, and he brushed his thumb under her eye and caught the wet there.

“She wants pictures,” she said.

“Then take lots.”

“I’ll send you all of them.”

“I’d expect nothing less.”

“And you have to answer when I ring.”

“I will.”

“Even if you’re training?”

“After training.”

“What if I ring because I miss you?”

“Then I’ll answer as fast as I can,” he said.

“Are you going to miss me?”

“We’ve discussed this.”

“I want to hear it again.”

“Terribly,” he said, and she laughed and kissed him, quickly, on the steps of the Business building, in front of half his seminar.

He stood up and held out his hand. “Come on. We’re celebrating.”

“Where?”

“Anywhere you like.”

She took his hand and let him pull her up, and kept hold of it. “Noodles. And dessert. And you have to listen to me talk about Beijing for the whole of dinner.”

“That sounds manageable.”

“Without complaining.”

“That might be harder.”

She hit his arm. He caught her hand and kissed it. “Come on, future Beijing intern.”

At nine her father rang. He didn’t say much. He said congratulations twice, and asked about the weather in Beijing in July, and whether she had a good umbrella, and then her mother took the phone back and said, “He’s fine. He’s gone to the bathroom. He’ll be fine,” and Xiaoran laughed with her face against Yichen’s shoulder, and the noodles went cold, and she didn’t care at all.

chapters.desc: A summer internship in Beijing. A training camp outside the city. Eight weeks and more than a thousand kilometres.
chapters.title: The Internship in Another City
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t want you to go tomorrow.”
chapters.content:
The first time Lin Xiaoran mentioned Beijing, Zhou Yichen thought she was talking about a drama.

She was sitting cross-legged on his bed, laptop balanced on her thighs, hair tied into a messy ponytail. There were three open tabs on her screen, a half-finished cup of milk tea beside her, and an expression he had learned to recognise. Excitement. The kind that made her forget to blink.

“Yichen.”

He looked up from his textbook. “Hm?”

“I got an offer.”

His eyes moved to her face. “For what?”

She turned the laptop around. A media company in Beijing. A summer internship program. Eight weeks. A competitive placement, with opportunities to work on real campaigns, assist with production, and contribute to editorial projects. He read the page carefully. Then he looked at her.

“Xiaoran.”

“I know.”

“You got it?”

“I got it.”

He closed his textbook. For a moment, she thought he might say something practical. Ask about accommodation, the company, the schedule, whether she had checked the transportation arrangements. Instead, he smiled. A proper smile.

“Congratulations.”

Her face brightened. “Really?”

“Why would I not congratulate you?”

“I don’t know. Maybe because it’s in Beijing.”

He glanced at the laptop again. “It’s a good opportunity.”

“It’s very far.”

“I know.”

“Eight weeks.”

“I can read.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re not helping.”

He reached over and gently tugged the end of her ponytail.

“I’m trying to understand why you’re looking at me like I’ve personally arranged for Beijing to be on the other side of the country.”

“You could have arranged for it to be closer.”

“Unfortunately, my influence has limits.”

She laughed, and he pulled her closer by the waist, pressing a kiss against her temple. He was genuinely happy for her.

He knew how much work she had put into building her portfolio, from last year’s competition to the two campaign samples she had rewritten four times since. He remembered the nights she had stayed up revising projects, the frustration when her first applications went unanswered, and the way she had pretended not to care when a company rejected her. This was something she had earned.

He wasn’t going to make her feel guilty for receiving it.

But later that night, when Xiaoran had fallen asleep beside him, he found himself looking at the internship page again. Eight weeks. Beijing. He calculated the distance without meaning to.

Then he locked his phone and turned towards her.

She was sleeping with one hand curled near her cheek, her hair scattered across his pillow. He gently moved a strand away from her face.

“Eight weeks,” he whispered.

She didn’t hear him. He kissed her hair anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

The training camp call came three days later. Yichen was in the university gym when his coach asked him to stay behind after practice.

The invitation was for a summer training camp outside the city. A chance to train with a more competitive group, work with experienced coaches, and potentially secure a place in a larger university-level tournament roster. Coaches from other programmes usually came to watch the final week.

It was the kind of opportunity he had been working towards since joining the basketball team. He listened, asked a few questions, and accepted.

When he told Xiaoran, she was sitting across from him in a café, enthusiastically explaining the internship’s orientation schedule. She stopped mid-sentence.

“Wait.”

He looked at her.

“Training camp?”

“Mm.”

“When?”

“Same period as your internship.”

She stared at him. He nodded. For a few seconds, neither of them spoke. Then Xiaoran slowly lowered her straw.

“So we’re both leaving.”

“Looks like it.”

“Different cities.”

“Yes.”

“For almost two months.”

“Eight weeks.”

She gave him a wounded look. “Why are you repeating the number?”

“Because you keep asking.”

“Maybe I’m hoping you’ll say something different.”

He reached across the table and touched her fingers.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked down at their hands.

“It’s a good opportunity for you. And the training camp is important to me,” he said.

“I know.”

“Then we should go.”

She nodded. It was the reasonable answer. The correct answer.

The answer they would both have given if they were discussing anyone else’s relationship. But she didn’t smile. And he noticed.

✦ ✦ ✦

They spent the next two weeks preparing for their separate departures.

Xiaoran researched accommodation, transportation, nearby convenience stores, and the safest routes between her apartment and the company. She made a spreadsheet with far too many tabs. Yichen checked the details with her, pointed out two things she had overlooked, and helped her compare the available options. He even accompanied her to buy luggage. She chose a pale blue suitcase. He thought it was too small.

She thought he was being dramatic. They compromised by buying a slightly larger one.

At the training camp, Yichen would be staying in shared accommodation with the other players. He packed his sportswear, shoes, recovery equipment, and a few personal belongings. Xiaoran watched him fold his clothes.

“You’re very efficient.”

“Someone has to be.”

“I packed my suitcase yesterday.”

“You packed it three times.”

“Because I kept remembering things.”

“You brought four pairs of shoes.”

“They’re different.”

“They’re all white.”

She looked offended. “They are not.”

He glanced at the suitcase. She followed his gaze.

“Fine. Three are white.”

He smiled. She threw a T-shirt at him. He caught it easily.

For all their teasing, the packing days were strangely difficult.

They had always been together in the small, ordinary ways that made a relationship feel effortless. A quick visit after class. Dinner after practice. A message asking whether the other had eaten. A hand reaching across a table without needing to ask.

Now, every small thing seemed to have an ending attached to it.

The last time they would shop together before leaving. The last dinner at their usual place. The last evening studying in the same room.

The last night she could fall asleep with her head against his shoulder. Neither of them said it aloud.

✦ ✦ ✦

The night before Xiaoran’s flight, she went to Yichen’s apartment. She arrived with a small paper bag.

“What’s that?” he asked.

“Something for you.”

He took it. Inside was a compact photo album.

Not an expensive one. Just a simple little book with photographs she had printed over the past few months.

Their first university basketball game. A picture of him looking away while she took a photograph. A café receipt with a ridiculous doodle she had drawn. A photo of them in Chengdu, standing in front of the panda enclosure. A blurry picture of his hand holding hers inside a car. There were captions written in her handwriting. Some were silly. Some were embarrassingly sentimental. He turned each page slowly.

At the end, there was a small note.

For when you miss me. Which will probably be often, because I’m lovable.

He looked at her. She was suddenly interested in the sleeve of her sweater.

“It’s not a big gift.”

“Xiaoran.”

“You don’t have to say anything. It’s just something I thought—”

He closed the album and set it carefully on the table. Then he pulled her into his arms.

She went willingly, pressing her cheek against his chest.

“Thank you,” he murmured.

“You like it?”

“I love it.”

“Really?”

He leaned back just enough to look at her.

“I’ll take it with me.”

She smiled. Then, after a moment, her expression softened.

“Don’t lose it.”

“I won’t.”

“Don’t let your teammates borrow it.”

“Why would they borrow my photo album?”

“I don’t know. Maybe they’ll want to see how pretty your girlfriend is.”

He laughed.

“Very confident.”

“It’s a fact.”

He kissed her cheek. She closed her eyes. For a while, they stayed like that, holding each other in the quiet apartment.

Eventually, she whispered, “I’m going to miss you.”

His arms tightened slightly.

“I know.”

“That’s all?”

He lowered his head, his cheek brushing her hair.

“I’m going to miss you too.”

She pulled away to look at him.

“That’s still not enough.”

He studied her face for a second. Then he cupped her cheek.

“I don’t want you to go tomorrow.”

Her expression changed. He rarely said things like that.

Not because he didn’t feel them, but because he usually preferred to make her feel secure rather than burden her with everything he was thinking.

But tonight, he was tired of pretending the distance was something he could simply calculate and manage.

“I know you should go. I know it’s important. And I want you to have it,” he said.

She swallowed.

“But I don’t want you to go.”

Her eyes became glossy.

“Yichen…”

He brushed his thumb beneath her eye before a tear could fall.

“I’m not asking you to stay.”

“I know.”

“I just want you to know that wanting you here and wanting you to succeed aren’t mutually exclusive.”

That was when she finally cried. A few tears she couldn’t quite stop. Yichen pulled her back against him.

“Hey.”

“I’m fine.”

“You’re crying on my shirt.”

“Then don’t wear such a nice shirt.”

He let out a small breath of laughter, kissing her hair.

“That’s my solution?”

“It’s a very practical one.”

He held her until she stopped trying to hide her tears.

✦ ✦ ✦

The airport was worse than either of them expected.

Xiaoran had insisted she was going to be fine.

She had said it while brushing her teeth, while checking her ID card, while eating breakfast, and again in the car.

By the time they reached the departure hall, she had become unusually quiet. Yichen pulled her suitcase beside him.

“Have you checked everything?”

“ID card, phone, wallet, charger.”

“Laptop?”

“Yes.”

“Internship documents?”

“Yes.”

“Medicine?”

She nodded.

“Good.”

She looked up at him.

“You sound like my father.”

“Your father probably has excellent judgment.”

“Don’t agree with me.”

He smiled faintly. They stood near the entrance to the security area.

People moved around them, dragging suitcases and talking on their phones. Announcements echoed overhead.

Xiaoran looked at the entrance, then at him, then back at the entrance.

“Can you come with me?”

“I can accompany you to the security line.”

“I mean…”

She stopped. He understood. He stepped closer and wrapped his arms around her. She buried her face against his chest.

“I don’t want to leave you.”

His hand moved slowly over her back.

“I know.”

“What if I get lonely?”

“Call me.”

“What if you’re training?”

“I’ll call you back.”

“What if I’m busy?”

“Then I’ll wait.”

“What if—”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up. He touched her cheek.

“We’ll figure it out.”

She nodded, but her lips trembled. He pressed a kiss into her hair. Then her left cheek. Then her right.

Finally, he kissed her lips, gently and without rushing, as if he were trying to give her something to carry with her.

When he pulled away, she held onto his jacket.

“Don’t forget me.”

His expression changed. For the first time that morning, he looked almost offended.

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You think eight weeks is enough to make me forget you?”

She tried to smile. He lowered his forehead to hers.

“I’ve spent years getting used to having you around. I’m not going to suddenly become unfamiliar with you because you’re in another city.”

“Okay.”

“Go make something of this opportunity.”

She sniffed.

“Okay.”

“And eat properly.”

“Okay.”

“Don’t skip meals because you’re busy.”

“Okay.”

“Don’t walk around with your phone out in unfamiliar places.”

“Okay.”

“Don’t—”

She pressed a finger against his lips.

“I’m going to miss you even more if you keep giving me homework.”

He kissed her fingertip.

“Then go.”

She hugged him one last time. And when she finally walked towards security, she turned around twice. He was still there both times. The third time, he raised his hand. She waved. Then she disappeared into the crowd.

Yichen remained where he was for a little longer than necessary. His phone vibrated.

Xiaoran: Don’t look so handsome when I leave. It’s unfair.

He looked at the message. A small smile appeared.

Yichen: I’ll try to look worse next time.

Xiaoran: You can’t. It’s genetic.

He laughed under his breath. Then he put his phone away and went home. The apartment was quiet. Her cup was still on the table. A hair tie was on the sofa.

One of her slippers had somehow ended up beneath his desk.

He picked it up and placed it beside the other one. Then he opened the little photo album.

He looked at the first photograph for a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first week was easy. Or at least, they tried to make it easy. Xiaoran sent him photographs of Beijing. The office building. The view from her apartment.

A bowl of noodles she claimed was the best thing she had ever eaten.

A photograph of herself wearing her internship identification card, looking pleased with her own reflection.

Xiaoran: Do I look professional?

Yichen: Very.

Xiaoran: Really?

Yichen: You look like someone who knows what she’s doing.

Xiaoran: I don’t.

Yichen: They don’t need to know that.

She laughed at her phone in the middle of the office.

He sent her pictures of the training camp in return. The court. His teammates. A photograph of his shoes after practice.

She complained that he was terrible at taking pictures.

He told her that he was documenting his surroundings, not producing a magazine. Their video calls were frequent. Sometimes they spoke for an hour. Sometimes only ten minutes.

Sometimes Xiaoran would call him while walking home, and he would stay on the line until she reached her apartment.

She would tell him about the people she met, the projects she was assigned, the things she learned.

He would tell her about practice, his teammates, the training schedule, and the coach who seemed to believe that sleep was a privilege rather than a biological necessity. They were busy. But they were happy. Until the second week. It happened on a Thursday.

Xiaoran had been working on a campaign proposal for most of the day. Her supervisor had asked her to revise several sections, and she had stayed late to finish the changes.

By the time she got back to her apartment, it was nearly ten. She showered, ate something small, and called Yichen. No answer. She assumed he was still training. She sent a message.

Xiaoran: Are you done?

No reply. She changed into her pyjamas and sat on the bed. Then she opened their chat again. Still nothing. She knew he was busy. She knew the training camp was demanding. She knew he couldn’t always answer. But she missed him. That was all. She wanted to hear him say her name.

She wanted to complain about her supervisor, tell him about the ridiculous coffee machine at work, and ask whether he had eaten. She wanted to hear his voice. At 10:47 p.m., her phone finally rang. She answered immediately.

“Yichen?”

“Sorry.”

His voice sounded tired.

She sat up. “It’s okay. Are you done?”

“Just finished.”

“Did you eat?”

“Mm.”

“What did you eat?”

“Dinner.”

She frowned. “That’s not an answer.”

He gave a quiet laugh.

“Rice, chicken, vegetables. Happy?”

“Very.”

There was a pause.

Then he asked, “How was your day?”

She opened her mouth. And, she didn’t know where to start.

She had been waiting all evening to tell him everything. But now that he was finally there, she could hear the exhaustion in his voice.

“Fine,” she said.

“Just fine?”

“Mm.”

“Anything interesting?”

She looked down at her blanket.

“Not really.”

He was quiet.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hmm?”

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Then sleep early.”

She nodded, although he couldn’t see her.

“Okay.”

“I’ll call you tomorrow.”

“Okay.”

“Goodnight.”

“Goodnight.”

The call ended. She stared at the screen. It had been less than four minutes. She knew he was tired. She knew he had done nothing wrong. Still, the disappointment settled in her chest.

She put her phone down and turned off the light.

For the first time since arriving in Beijing, she cried herself to sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next few days were worse. Not because anything terrible happened. That was the problem. Nothing terrible happened.

Xiaoran continued going to work. She completed her assignments, attended meetings, learned how to navigate the city, and gradually became more comfortable with her colleagues. Yichen continued training.

His schedule became more intense as the camp approached its final evaluation. There were additional sessions, recovery work, and team meetings. Their calls became shorter. Their messages became less frequent. They still said good morning. They still said goodnight. They still told each other to eat. But something had changed. Xiaoran stopped sending him every little thing.

She stopped taking photographs of her lunch just to show him. She stopped calling him when she walked home.

When something funny happened, she sometimes opened their chat, typed a message, and deleted it.

She didn’t want to become another responsibility in his day. Yichen noticed. Of course he noticed. He knew her habits too well.

He knew that when Xiaoran was excited, she sent messages in clusters. When she was annoyed, she sent voice notes. When she was sleepy, she used fewer punctuation marks.

And when she was trying not to bother him, she became excessively considerate. It was the last one that worried him.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday night, he called her after practice. She answered after several rings.

“Hello?”

“Busy?”

“No. I was just washing my hair.”

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Rice.”

“With?”

She paused.

“Food.”

He closed his eyes briefly.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I’m asking because I care, not because I’m conducting an investigation.”

She laughed.

“I had beef noodles.”

“Good.”

There was a silence. He sat on the edge of his bed, phone against his ear.

“How was your week?”

“Good.”

“Work?”

“Good.”

“Your supervisor?”

“Good.”

He leaned forward, resting his elbows on his knees.

“You’ve become very fond of that word.”

She smiled faintly.

“It’s a useful word.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I’m really okay.”

“I didn’t say you weren’t.”

She looked out of the window. The city lights blurred slightly.

“I just don’t want you to worry.”

His jaw tightened.

“Why would I not worry?”

“Because you’re busy.”

“I’m aware of my schedule.”

“And the training camp is important.”

“So is your internship.”

She didn’t answer. He waited.

Then, he asked, “Are you lonely?”

Her eyes stung. She wanted to say no. She wanted to be mature about it. She wanted to be the girlfriend who supported him without needing anything in return. But she was tired of being mature.

“A little,” she admitted.

His expression softened.

“How little?”

She laughed weakly.

“Quite a lot.”

He leaned back against the wall.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because I know you’re tired.”

“I’m tired, Xiaoran. I’m not unavailable.”

She pressed her lips together.

“I don’t want you to feel like you have to call me.”

“I don’t.”

“Or like you have to make time for me.”

“I want to make time for you.”

“Yichen…”

“Listen to me.”

His voice was gentle, but firm enough to make her stop.

“You’re not asking me to abandon training. You’re asking your boyfriend to spend time with you.”

She looked down.

“That’s different?”

“Very.”

A tear slipped down her cheek. He exhaled slowly.

“Are you crying?”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Maybe.”

He closed his eyes. He hated being unable to reach her.

He hated that there were more than a thousand kilometres between them, that he couldn’t take her face in his hands, couldn’t wipe the tears away, couldn’t pull her against his chest and let her complain until she felt better.

“Show me your face,” he said.

She turned on her camera. Her eyes were red. He stared at her. Then he smiled gently.

“Hello, pretty girl.”

She sniffed.

“Don’t.”

“Why?”

“I’m crying.”

“I can see that.”

“Then don’t call me pretty.”

“Would you prefer I call you a disaster?”

She laughed despite herself.

“Better,” he murmured.

Her smile faded again.

“I miss you.”

His gaze softened.

“I miss you too.”

“I miss you so much.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

He was quiet. Then he said, “You’re right. I probably don’t know exactly how much.”

She looked at him.

“But I know that when I finish training, the first thing I do is check my phone to see whether you’ve messaged me. I know that I keep looking at the time because I want to know whether you’re awake. And I know that I have been sleeping with your ridiculous photo album beside my bed.”

Her lips parted. He glanced away for a moment, almost embarrassed by his own confession.

“Is that enough evidence?”

She covered her mouth.

“Yichen…”

“I’m not asking you to pretend this is easy.”

He looked directly into the camera.

“It’s not easy for me either.”

chapters.desc: Shorter calls, one missed night that matters, and a station where this time she’s the one waiting.
chapters.title: The Internship in Another City (Part 2)
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t make yourself smaller just because I’m far away.”
chapters.content:
The next week, they tried something different. They stopped treating their calls like appointments that had to be squeezed into the end of the day. Instead, they began sharing their ordinary lives again.

Yichen would send her a photograph of his breakfast before practice.

Xiaoran would send him a voice note while walking to work.

He would call her for five minutes during his lunch break, even if all he had to say was that the training session had been exhausting.

She would send him a photograph of the sky outside her office. Sometimes they didn’t even have anything to say.

They simply stayed on the phone while doing their own things.

One evening, Xiaoran was working on a presentation when Yichen called.

“Hi.”

“Hi.”

“What are you doing?”

“Working.”

“Still?”

“Almost done.”

He heard the sound of her keyboard.

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

She told him. He was quiet.

Then he said, “I miss you.”

Her fingers stopped. She looked at the phone.

“Why are you saying that suddenly?”

“Because I do.”

She smiled at the screen.

“I miss you too.”

He opened his arms. She blinked.

“What?”

He reached for her. She looked at the phone again.

“Yichen, we’re on a video call.”

“I know.”

She laughed.

“Then how?”

“Use your imagination.”

She leaned towards the camera and pressed a kiss against the screen. He watched her. Then he smiled.

“That’s not very convincing.”

“It’s all you get.”

“Unfortunate.”

She laughed again. And for the first time in days, the distance felt a little less cruel.

✦ ✦ ✦

But the hardest moment came during the sixth week.

Xiaoran had been selected to assist with a presentation for a major client.

It was a small role, but a meaningful one. She had worked hard on the research and was excited about the opportunity. She wanted to tell Yichen. She wanted him to be proud of her.

She wanted to hear him say that he had known she could do it.

But the presentation was scheduled on the same day as the training camp’s final evaluation. They had discussed it beforehand. He had promised to call her afterward.

She had promised to send him a message once the presentation ended. The day went well. Better than well.

Her supervisor praised her work in front of the team. One of the senior staff members even asked whether she would be interested in assisting with another project.

Xiaoran walked out of the office feeling almost weightless. She took out her phone. There was a message from Yichen.

Yichen: Finished. Going into evaluation soon. I’ll call you when I’m done.

She smiled and typed.

Xiaoran: Good luck! Don’t injure yourself. I’ll tell you something later.

She waited. Then she decided to send a photograph of herself outside the building.

She was smiling so brightly that her cheeks hurt.

Xiaoran: I did well today :)

He reacted with a heart. Then he went into evaluation. Hours passed.

She went back to her apartment, showered, ate dinner, and waited. At 9:30 p.m., there was still no call.

A little after ten at night, she sent a message.

Xiaoran: How did it go?

No reply. At eleven at night, she finally called. His phone rang. And rang. And rang. No answer.

She told herself he was probably with the team. She told herself he might be celebrating.

She told herself there was no reason to be upset.

At midnight, she fell asleep with her phone beside her. The next morning, she woke to a message.

Yichen: Sorry. The evaluation ran late, then we had a team meeting. I just got back. Are you awake?

She read it. Then she read it again. She knew it was reasonable. She knew he had a demanding day.

But she couldn’t stop the small, ugly thought that had appeared in her mind.

I had something important to tell you.

She typed. Deleted. Typed again.

Xiaoran: It’s okay. Hope everything went well.

She put the phone down. A few minutes later, it rang. She stared at his name, then answered.

“Morning.”

“Morning.”

His voice was tired.

“Did you sleep?”

“Mm.”

“I’m sorry I missed your call.”

“It’s okay.”

He was quiet.

“Xiaoran, how was your presentation?”

She swallowed.

“Good.”

“Just good?”

She smiled faintly.

“It went well. My supervisor liked it.”

“That’s great.”

“Mm.”

“What did they say?”

She told him. She explained the praise, the possible next project, the way she had managed to answer a difficult question without freezing. Yichen listened carefully. He asked questions.

He remembered the names of the people she mentioned.

He told her that he was proud of her. And she believed him. But she still felt sad.

When she finished, he said, “I wish I could have heard about it last night.”

She looked down.

“It’s okay.”

“I wanted to.”

“I know.”

“Xiaoran.”

She closed her eyes.

“I’m not angry with you.”

“I know.”

“Then what is it?”

She was silent.

Finally, she whispered, “I just wanted you there.”

The words were small. But they carried everything.

“I wanted to call you after the presentation. I wanted to tell you while I was still excited. I wanted to hear you say you were proud of me before I went to sleep.”

Her voice trembled.

“I know you had your evaluation. I know it was important. I know you didn’t do anything wrong. But I still wanted you.”

Yichen didn’t speak. She continued, trying to hold herself together.

“And I hate that sometimes I feel like I’m waiting for the little pieces of your day that are left over. I know that’s not fair, because you’re probably feeling the same way. But I miss being part of your ordinary day.”

He sat still. Then he looked down at his hands.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hmm?”

“I think I’ve been trying too hard to make sure you don’t feel like you’re sacrificing anything for me.”

She listened.

“I keep telling myself that if I work hard enough, if I finish training properly, if I don’t complain, then these eight weeks will pass quickly. And I thought that was what you needed from me.”

He paused.

“But I might have forgotten that you don’t need me to be impressive from another city.”

Her eyes filled.

“You need me to be your boyfriend.”

He looked at the camera.

“I’m sorry.”

She shook her head.

“Don’t.”

“I should have called.”

“You were busy.”

“I could have sent a message before the meeting.”

She didn’t answer.

“I can’t always be available. But I can do better at making sure you don’t feel like you’re waiting for me to remember you,” he said.

She pressed her lips together.

“And you don’t have to be considerate every time you miss me. You can be selfish sometimes,” he said.

She laughed through her tears.

“I’m already quite selfish.”

“I know.”

“Excuse me?”

“Very.”

She wiped her cheek. He smiled faintly.

“That’s one of the things I like about you.”

“I like that you want me. I like that you tell me when you miss me. I like that you still want to tell me every little thing, even when you think it’s unimportant.”

His voice softened.

“Don’t make yourself smaller just because I’m far away.”

That broke her. She covered her face and cried.

Yichen watched her, wishing desperately that the screen would disappear and leave him with the real girl instead.

“Come here,” he murmured.

She lowered her hands. He held his palm against the camera. She placed hers against it. It was ridiculous. It was insufficient. But they stayed that way for a while.

✦ ✦ ✦

The final two weeks passed more gently. Not because they missed each other less. They simply became better at admitting it.

Xiaoran began calling him whenever she wanted, without apologising for it.

Yichen started sending her voice messages when he knew he wouldn’t be able to answer immediately.

He told her when he was going into practice. She told him when she had a deadline.

They made plans for the day they would see each other again. She wanted to eat hotpot. He wanted to sleep. She wanted to go shopping.

He wanted to hold her hand and do absolutely nothing. They compromised. Hotpot first, then shopping, then nothing.

One night, Yichen called her after a particularly difficult practice.

He was lying on his bed, hair still damp from his shower.

Xiaoran was sitting at her desk, wearing an oversized T-shirt.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Do you think we’ll be different when we come back?”

He looked at her.

“Different how?”

“I don’t know. Maybe we’ll get used to being alone.”

He was quiet. Then he said, “I hope we get used to being apart when we have to.”

She blinked.

“But not because we prefer it.”

Her expression softened.

He said, “I don’t want us to become people who need to be together every second to feel secure. But I also don’t want us to pretend we don’t miss each other.”

She nodded slowly.

“I think that’s fair.”

He studied her.

“Are you worried?”

“A little.”

“About what?”

She hesitated.

“About going back to normal and realising how much we missed.”

He smiled gently.

“Then we’ll make up for it.”

“How?”

“Start with dinner.”

She laughed.

“That’s your plan?”

“It’s a good plan.”

“What about kissing?”

“Also included.”

“Cuddling?”

“Obviously.”

“Will you hold my hand?”

He looked at her as if the question were absurd.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I’ve been waiting eight weeks.”

She smiled.

Then, softly, she said, “Me too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her internship finished three days before his camp did, so this time she was the one waiting.

The day Yichen returned, Xiaoran arrived at the station nearly forty minutes early. She checked the arrival board three times. She checked her phone. She bought a bottle of water. She didn’t drink it.

When the train finally arrived, she stood near the exit with her hands clasped together. People began coming out. One after another. Then she saw him.

A black duffel bag over one shoulder. A backpack in one hand. His hair slightly longer than when he left. His expression tired, but his eyes searching. He saw her almost immediately. And smiled. Xiaoran didn’t walk. She ran.

He barely had time to put his bag down before she threw her arms around him.

“Yichen!”

He caught her, laughing as he wrapped both arms around her.

“Careful.”

“I missed you.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

He pressed his cheek against her hair.

“I missed you too.”

She tightened her arms around his waist. For a moment, neither moved. The station was noisy. People were passing them. His bag was on the floor. None of it mattered. She drew back to look at him. Then she frowned.

“You’re thinner.”

“You’re imagining things.”

“You have been training too much.”

He smiled.

“You’ve been worrying too much.”

“That’s because you don’t take care of yourself.”

“I do.”

“Not enough.”

He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“Hello.”

She blinked.

“What?”

“I’m home.”

Her face crumpled. He saw it immediately and pulled her back into his arms. She buried her face against his neck.

“Don’t say things like that.”

“Why?”

“I’ll cry.”

He kissed her temple.

“Then cry.”

And she did. Not because she was sad. Not because the distance had broken anything.

Because she had spent eight weeks missing the weight of his arms, the warmth of his body, the sound of his voice without a speaker between them.

She had missed him in ways she hadn’t known how to explain. Now he was here.

And she could finally stop imagining what it would feel like to hug him again.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went to dinner that evening. As promised, hotpot. Xiaoran sat opposite him, watching him eat. He noticed after the third time.

“You’re staring.”

“I’m observing.”

“Anything interesting?”

She nodded solemnly.

“Your face.”

He laughed. She smiled. Then she reached across the table and touched his hand.

He turned his palm upward, letting her fingers slide into his. They ate slowly.

They talked about the internship, the training camp, the people they had met, the things they had learned, and all the small details they had saved for each other.

At some point, Xiaoran told him about the presentation again.

This time, he was sitting right across from her. He listened without looking at his phone. He asked questions. He laughed at the parts she found funny.

When she finished, he said, “I’m proud of you.”

She looked down at their joined hands.

“You already said that.”

“I know.”

“Then why say it again?”

“Because I wanted to say it while I was here.”

She looked up. He smiled. She squeezed his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner, they went back to his apartment. Xiaoran took off her shoes and walked straight to the sofa. Then she turned around and opened her arms. Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

She opened her arms. He put his keys down.

“I’m coming.”

She held her arms out wider. He walked over, bent down, and let her wrap herself around him. She kissed his cheek, then the other. Then his jaw. He laughed.

“What’s this?”

“Eight weeks of missed affection.”

“That’s quite a lot.”

“I haven’t finished.”

“I can tell.”

She pulled back, looked at him, and kissed his lips. This time, he didn’t tease her.

He held her face gently and kissed her properly, slowly, with the kind of affection that had been difficult to fit into a phone call.

When they separated, she rested her forehead against his.

“Can we stay like this?”

He brushed her hair behind her ear.

“As long as you want.”

“Even if I don’t let you move?”

“Then I’ll have to negotiate.”

She smiled.

“I’m a difficult negotiator.”

“I’ve noticed.”

She rested her head against his chest. His arms settled around her. For a while, they said nothing.

Then Xiaoran murmured, “I thought the distance would make everything feel different.”

He looked down at her.

“Does it?”

She thought about it.

“Not really.”

“Good.”

She traced a small circle on his shirt.

“I think I understand something now.”

“What?”

“I don’t need you to be beside me all the time.”

He listened.

“But I really, really like it when you are.”

He smiled.

“That’s convenient.”

“Why?”

“Because I really, really like being beside you.”

She grinned. Then she leaned up and kissed him again. He held her a little closer.

Eight weeks ago, they had stood at an airport entrance, both pretending that the distance would be manageable. It had been difficult.

There had been lonely evenings, missed calls, quiet disappointments, and moments when loving each other from far away felt like trying to hold water in their hands. But they had learned something. They could be ambitious without abandoning each other.

They could be lonely without being ashamed of it.

They could miss each other without making the other person feel guilty.

And most importantly, they could keep choosing each other even when their lives were moving in different directions. Xiaoran eventually fell asleep against his chest. Yichen looked down at her. Her hand was still curled into his shirt. He gently kissed her temple.

“Eight weeks,” he whispered.

She stirred.

“Don’t count anymore.”

“Okay.”

“I’m home now.”

He watched her. Then he kissed her hair.

“Me too.”

chapters.desc: A point guard from Hangzhou posts one photograph from camp. The whole team sees it. Captain Zhou may never recover.
chapters.title: The Photograph in His Training Bag
chapters.epigraph: “I held it anyway.”
chapters.content:
The photograph had been posted at 1:12 a.m. on the last night of the summer training camp, by a point guard from a university in Hangzhou whom Zhou Yichen had shared a room with for eight weeks and would now never forgive.

It showed Yichen asleep on a narrow dormitory bed, one arm thrown over his eyes, still in his training shirt.

On his chest, held flat under his other hand as if someone might try to take it, was a small photo album.

The caption said: every night for eight weeks. every single night. we have suffered.

By the first university practice of the autumn semester, the entire Huaining basketball team had seen it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen knew something was wrong the moment he walked into the changing room, because it went quiet.

The Huaining changing room was never quiet. It was twelve men, a speaker playing three songs at once, and Fang Ze explaining something about his own calves. Now it was silent.

Twelve faces turned towards him with expressions of enormous, innocent interest.

“Afternoon, Captain Zhou,” said Fang Ze.

“Afternoon.”

“How was camp?”

“Fine.”

“Fine,” said Fang Ze, nodding slowly. “Did you sleep well?”

Yichen put his bag down on the bench.

“Who sent it to you.”

“Sent what?”

“Fang Ze.”

Fang Ze held up his phone. On it was the photograph, enlarged so that the album filled the screen. Someone had circled it in red.

“Every night. Every single night,” said Fang Ze, in a voice of great tenderness.

The room collapsed. Somebody fell off the bench. Somebody else started reading the caption aloud in a high, trembling voice, like a poem at a funeral, and had to stop halfway because he was crying with laughter.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran heard about it forty minutes later, when she arrived at the gym with two drinks, which had become her habit since first year, and found the entire team doing a warm-up lap with the clear intention of passing as close to her as possible.

“Afternoon, team manager!”

“Hello?”

“Team manager, quick question.”

“Yes?”

“Is it true you made Captain Zhou a book?”

She stopped walking. At the far end of the court, Yichen, who had been stretching his hamstrings with tremendous concentration, closed his eyes.

“What book?”

Fang Ze jogged past backwards. “The one he slept with. For eight weeks. Every night.”

Xiaoran turned slowly and looked across the court at her boyfriend. Her boyfriend didn’t look back.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Every night?” she said in the corridor afterwards.

“He’s exaggerating.”

“There’s a photograph.”

“It was one night.”

“The caption says every night.”

“The caption was written by a man from Hangzhou who snores,” said Yichen, “and has no credibility.”

She looked at him. He looked at the vending machine.

She had been home from Beijing for five days. She had been told, by him, at the station, with his arms round her, that he had missed her. She had been told, on the phone, at the worst point of the internship, that he’d been sleeping with her ridiculous photo album beside his bed. Beside. Not on.

“You held it. While you were asleep. Like a teddy bear,” she said.

“I fell asleep reading it.”

“Every night?”

“Xiaoran.”

“Did you read the captions?”

He didn’t answer.

“The one on the Chengdu page? This panda eats more than me but don’t tell him?” She stepped closer.

The corner of his mouth went.

“I read the captions,” he said.

“Every night?”

He looked at her then, properly, the way he did when he’d decided there was no point lying.

“Most nights. The other nights I was too tired to open it. I held it anyway,” said Zhou Yichen.

She hadn’t expected that. For a moment she couldn’t say anything at all. She stood in the corridor outside the Huaining gym with two cups of iced tea sweating in her hands and her face doing something she couldn’t control.

Then she said, “Show me where it is now.”

“No.”

“Yichen.”

“It’s in my bag.”

“You brought it to practice?”

“It was in my bag at camp. I haven’t unpacked,” he said, with dignity.

“You’ve been home two days.”

“I’ve been busy.”

She put both drinks down on top of the vending machine, the old one by the gym door that had once eaten a whole week of Fang Ze’s change, unzipped the front pocket of the sports bag on his shoulder before he could stop her, and there it was: her little album, the corners a bit soft now, one page loose. A café receipt was tucked inside the back cover that hadn’t been there when she’d given it to him.

She took it out. It was from the camp canteen, dated the second week, the night she’d cried herself to sleep in Beijing. On the back, in his neat handwriting, it said: Call her at lunch tomorrow, not after. She says fine when she means not fine. She looked up at him.

He held out his hand for it, and she didn’t give it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The team saw them come back into the gym. She was holding his hand. He was holding both drinks. Neither of them was saying anything.

“Oh no. She’s crying. Captain, you made the team manager cry,” said Fang Ze, delighted.

“She’s not crying,” said Yichen.

“I’m a little bit crying,” said Xiaoran.

The whole team went “Ohhhh” at once, like a single enormous embarrassing animal.

Coach blew his whistle so hard a ball rolled off the rack.

“Zhou! Lin! Out of my gym if you’re going to do that. Everyone else, line. Now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came out of practice at seven. She was sitting on the low wall outside the gym with the album on her knees, turning the pages slowly, the way he must have done in a narrow bed in a dormitory two hours outside the city. He sat down next to her.

“Coach wants to see me tomorrow,” he said.

“Because of the crying?”

“Because the man who ran the camp rang him. Somebody watched the last week. Asked for my name.” He was quiet for a second.

She turned her head.

“Somebody who?”

“He didn’t say.”

He was looking straight ahead at the car park, but she knew that face. It was the face he’d worn at seventeen, the night before the game the scouts came to see.

“Probably nobody,” he said.

“Probably somebody.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Probably somebody,” she said again, and let her head drop onto his shoulder, and held his hand on top of the album, and he didn’t argue.

A minute later his phone buzzed in his pocket. He took it out and looked at it and laughed under his breath.

Fang Ze: team group chat has voted. the album is now an official team mascot. it travels to away games. this is not a democracy

“Absolutely not,” said Yichen, and typed it.

Fang Ze: too late captain. we’ve ordered it a jersey

✦ ✦ ✦

The jersey arrived the following Tuesday. It was navy blue, the size of a postcard, with HUAINING across the front and a number eleven on the back, and Fang Ze presented it in the changing room before practice with the solemnity of a man handing over a medal.

“For the album. Since it’s clearly a member of this team,” he said.

“It isn’t coming to away games.”

“It’s already on the travel list. Coach signed it.”

“Coach did not sign it.”

Fang Ze unfolded a sheet of paper. At the bottom, under twelve names and one that said Album (Lin), in Coach’s terrible handwriting, was the word Fine. Yichen looked at it.

Then he took the tiny jersey, without a word, and went to his locker.

When Xiaoran came in at the end of practice with two drinks, the locker door was open. On the top shelf, between his spare shoes and a roll of tape, sat her photo album, its soft corners propped against the metal wall, wearing a navy blue jersey with a number eleven on the back.

She stopped in the doorway with both hands over her mouth.

“Don’t,” said Yichen, from the bench.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face said something.”

“My face,” said Xiaoran, coming over and sitting down beside him with the drinks, “is saying that you are the most embarrassing boyfriend in the history of this university, and that I’m going to tell everyone, and that I love you.”

The changing room, which had gone quiet, made the noise again: one enormous, embarrassing ohhhh. Yichen closed his eyes.

But he didn’t take the jersey off the album. Not that day, and not when the team travelled to its first away game of the season, and not three weeks later, when a man in a dark jacket sat at the back of the gym and wrote something down.

chapters.desc: A man in a dark jacket at the back of the university gym, a message from a professional club, and a very small basketball keychain.
chapters.title: The Scout at the Back of the Gym
chapters.epigraph: “Then you’ll still be Zhou Yichen.”
chapters.content:
The first person to notice Zhou Yichen wasn’t his coach. It wasn’t his teammates, either.

It was a man sitting at the back of the university gym, wearing a dark jacket and holding a tablet on his lap. Yichen didn’t know who he was. He didn’t even notice him.

At that moment, he was too busy trying to win a practice game, three weeks into the autumn semester. The score was 78–76. There were twenty seconds left.

His teammate called for the ball, but Yichen had already seen the opening. He moved past the defender, changed direction, and drove towards the basket. Another player stepped in to block him. Yichen didn’t hesitate. He jumped.

The ball left his fingertips just before the defender’s hand reached it. Two points. The gym erupted.

His teammates shouted. Someone slapped his back. The coach blew his whistle, looking thoroughly pleased with himself.

Yichen merely jogged back, expression composed, as if he hadn’t just made the winning shot.

From the back of the gym, the man in the dark jacket looked down at his tablet. Then he wrote something.

Xiaoran was waiting outside the gym with two drinks.

She had originally planned to watch the entire practice, but after nearly an hour, her attention had wandered to her phone, then to the vending machine, then to a conversation with one of Yichen’s teammates who had come out to refill his water bottle. Still, she had watched the final game.

And she was proud of herself for not shouting when Yichen made the winning shot. She had only clapped. Quite loudly.

When Yichen finally emerged, his hair was damp, his training shirt clinging slightly to his shoulders, and his sports bag hanging from one hand. Xiaoran immediately held out a drink.

“Congratulations.”

He took it.

“For what?”

“For winning.”

“It was practice.”

“You still won.”

He glanced at her. “You were watching?”

“Of course.”

“From the beginning?”

She hesitated. He smiled.

“Xiaoran.”

“I watched the important parts.”

“What happened in the first quarter?”

“Basketball.”

He laughed. She followed him towards the benches, talking about how one of his teammates had nearly fallen over during a particularly dramatic attempt at defending him.

Yichen listened, occasionally correcting her interpretation of what had happened. Then he stopped.

“Wait here a moment.”

“Why?”

“I need to speak to Coach.”

She nodded and sat down. Yichen walked back into the gym.

Xiaoran watched him approach the coach, who was standing near the scorer’s table with another man. The man in the dark jacket.

She noticed him because he looked strangely out of place among the students. He wasn’t wearing sportswear, wasn’t carrying a gym bag, and didn’t seem particularly interested in the rest of the team. He was speaking to the coach. Then he looked at Yichen. Xiaoran tilted her head.

Something about the way the man shook Yichen’s hand made her curious.

When Yichen returned, she immediately asked, “Who was that?”

“Someone Coach knows.”

“Someone important?”

“Maybe.”

“Yichen.”

He looked at her. She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re hiding something.”

He smiled slightly.

“Am I?”

She stared at him. He took a sip of his drink.

“Let’s go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The message arrived two days later. Yichen was in the middle of a lecture when his phone vibrated. An unfamiliar number. He almost ignored it. Then he saw the message.

Hello, Zhou Yichen. This is Lou Wei from the player recruitment department of the Shanghai Herons Basketball Club. We met briefly at your university gym on Tuesday. I would like to discuss a potential trial opportunity with you.

He read it twice. Then he put his phone down.

For the next twenty minutes, he tried to pay attention to his professor. He failed. After class, he called the number. The conversation lasted nearly fifteen minutes.

The club had been observing university-level competitions and had received recommendations from several coaches, including the one who had run his summer camp. They were interested in inviting him for a trial session. It wasn’t an offer. It wasn’t a contract.

It was an opportunity to be evaluated by a professional club. A serious one.

Yichen asked about the schedule, the training expectations, and what would happen after the trial. He listened carefully.

When the call ended, he stood outside the lecture hall for a while. Then he opened Xiaoran’s chat.

Yichen: Are you free tonight?

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: I have something to tell you.

Xiaoran: Are you injured?

He stared at the message.

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: Did you fail an exam?

Yichen: No.

Xiaoran: Did you buy another car?

He laughed.

Yichen: Come have dinner with me.

Xiaoran: You’re making me nervous.

Yichen: Good. You’ll be more curious when you see me.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran arrived at the restaurant ten minutes early. Yichen was already there.

He had changed into a simple dark shirt, his hair neatly styled, and his expression was unusually thoughtful. She sat down immediately.

“Tell me.”

He pushed the menu towards her.

“Order first.”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I’m not eating until you tell me.”

He considered her, then gave a quiet laugh.

“Someone from the Herons contacted me.”

She blinked.

“The basketball club?”

“They want me to attend a trial.”

She didn’t respond. Then her eyes widened.

“Wait. A professional club?”

“It’s a trial.”

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“A professional club.”

“I heard you the first time.”

“They want you?”

“They want to evaluate me.”

She placed both hands on the table.

“That’s amazing.”

He smiled. She was already leaning forward, her excitement practically spilling across the table.

“When?”

“Next month.”

“How long?”

“A few days initially. Depending on the evaluation, there may be further opportunities.”

“Are you going?”

He looked at her.

“Yes.”

She nodded immediately.

“Of course you’re going.”

He watched her.

“You’re not surprised?”

“I am surprised.”

“You look very calm.”

“I’m trying to behave like a supportive girlfriend.”

He laughed.

“That’s a new development.”

She ignored him.

“I’m serious. You should go. You worked so hard to get here.”

He reached across the table and touched her hand.

“Thank you.”

She squeezed his fingers. Then, as if remembering something, she suddenly sat straighter.

“Wait.”

“What?”

“Does this mean you’ll become a professional basketball player?”

“Not necessarily.”

“But you could?”

“It’s possible.”

Her eyes shone.

“Yichen…”

He smiled at her expression. She looked so happy that he almost forgot how carefully he had been considering the invitation. Almost.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next few weeks were different. Yichen’s training schedule became more demanding.

He spoke with his university coach about the opportunity, adjusted his routine, and began preparing specifically for the trial. His shooting drills became more precise. His conditioning sessions became longer.

He studied footage of the club’s previous games and familiarised himself with their style of play. He was serious about it. Very serious. Xiaoran noticed.

She noticed the way he sometimes stayed behind after practice to repeat a drill. She noticed how carefully he managed his meals and sleep. She noticed that his usual relaxed evenings were increasingly occupied by recovery sessions and reviewing game footage. She tried to be supportive. She really did.

She even learned how to prepare a few simple meals that suited his training schedule.

Unfortunately, she was still not particularly good at cooking.

The first time she made chicken breast, it was so dry that Yichen needed two glasses of water to finish it. She watched him chew.

“Is it bad?”

He swallowed.

“No.”

“Really?”

“It’s edible.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“That’s not a compliment.”

He smiled and reached for her hand.

“It’s good that you tried.”

She looked at the plate.

“I wanted to make something useful.”

“You already do.”

“Don’t say that just because you don’t want to hurt my feelings.”

“I’m not.”

He leaned over and kissed her cheek.

“Besides, I like having you around.”

She smiled. Then she pushed the plate towards him.

“Finish it.”

He looked at the chicken, then at her.

“Yes, ma’am.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The night before the trial, Xiaoran came over. Yichen was reviewing footage on his laptop when she arrived.

She had brought food, a small paper bag, and an expression that suggested she had been planning something. He glanced at the bag.

“What did you buy?”

“Nothing.”

He looked at her.

“Xiaoran.”

“It’s a surprise.”

She placed the bag on the table and sat beside him.

“Have you finished reviewing?”

“Almost.”

“Then stop.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Why?”

“Because your brain needs rest.”

He looked at the screen.

“Five more minutes.”

She stared at him. He stared back. She reached over and gently closed the laptop.

“Your five minutes are over.”

He laughed.

“Very authoritative.”

“I’m serious.”

“I know.”

She took his hand and examined his fingers. His palms were rough from training. There was a small patch of redness near one knuckle. She brushed her thumb over it.

“Does it hurt?”

“No.”

“Are you nervous?”

He looked at her.

“A little.”

It was an honest answer. She seemed surprised.

“Really?”

“It’s a professional trial. I’d be more concerned if I weren’t nervous.”

She nodded thoughtfully. Then she opened the paper bag. Inside was a small keychain.

A miniature basketball, with his initials engraved on the back. He looked at it.

“What’s this?”

“Good luck charm.”

He turned it over in his hand.

“You made this?”

“I ordered it. But I chose the design.”

He smiled.

“Very thoughtful.”

“Don’t lose it.”

“I won’t.”

She hesitated. Then she said, “I know it’s just a trial. And I know there are lots of things that can happen. But I hope you get what you want.”

He looked at her.

She said, “I hope they see how good you are. Not just because you’re tall or handsome or because you can jump very high.”

He laughed.

“Thank you for including my height and appearance.”

“I’m being serious.”

“I know.”

She looked down at their hands.

“I’ve watched you work so hard. Sometimes I think you don’t even realise how much you’ve improved.”

His expression softened.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hmm?”

She reached for him. He pulled her closer until she was sitting against him. She leaned into his shoulder. For a while, neither spoke.

Then he said, “Do you know what I’m thinking?”

“What?”

“That I should have asked you to come with me.”

She lifted her head.

“To the trial?”

“Mm.”

“Can I?”

“Of course.”

Her eyes widened.

“Really?”

“If you want to.”

She tried not to look too excited. Failed.

“Then I’ll come.”

He laughed and kissed her hair.

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The trial took place at the club’s training facility. It was much larger than the university gym.

The court was polished, the equipment was professional, and the atmosphere was noticeably different. There were no casual conversations between drills, no students wandering in and out, no teammates joking around while waiting for their turn. Everyone seemed focused.

Xiaoran sat in the spectator area with her hands clasped around a bottle of water.

She had dressed comfortably, but she had spent an unreasonable amount of time deciding what to wear. She wanted to look presentable.

She also wanted to avoid looking like someone who had come merely to watch her boyfriend.

Although, technically, that was exactly what she had come to do. Yichen had told her not to worry. She had worried anyway.

When he walked onto the court, she immediately sat straighter. He was wearing the trial uniform. A simple training jersey with his assigned number.

His hair was neatly arranged, his expression composed, and his posture confident. She had seen him play countless times. At university. During tournaments. During casual games with friends. But this felt different.

He wasn’t playing in front of people who already knew him. He was being evaluated. And he knew it.
