Then she whispered, “Look at you.”

His expression softened.

“Thank you.”

“Not because they invited you to the next stage.”

He looked down.

“Why, then?”

“Because you didn’t let one unfair day change the way you approached the next one.”

She said, “You still worked hard. You still played properly. You didn’t become arrogant just because they finally gave you a chance.” She looked up at him.

“And you didn’t become bitter just because someone else had an easier way in.”

Yichen smiled faintly.

“That’s a very generous assessment.”

“It’s true.”

He bent down and kissed her. A gentle kiss, then another, just above her cheek. She smiled against him.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen received a message from his university coach.

Coach: Heard about today’s evaluation. Well done.

Yichen replied.

Yichen: Thank you, Coach. I appreciate your recommendation.

A few minutes later, his phone rang. He answered.

“Coach.”

“Zhou. How did it go?”

“They’ve invited me to the next development stage.”

There was a brief silence, then the coach laughed.

“Good. I knew they’d see it.”

Yichen smiled.

“Thank you for helping me.”

“Don’t thank me too much. I only gave them your records and told them what I’ve seen.”

“You also contacted the athletic director.”

“Of course. You’re one of our players. If there’s an opportunity for you to develop, the university should support you.”

Yichen looked down. The coach continued.

“Listen. I want you to remember something.”

“Yes?”

“Don’t let the professional club become the only place where you measure your value. You have a good future in basketball, but you still have to develop. Keep your academics in order. Keep your training consistent. Don’t let the attention distract you.”

“I understand.”

“Good. And don’t become too proud.”

Yichen laughed.

“I won’t.”

“Your teammates will become unbearable if they hear you’re getting special attention.”

“I’ll keep it quiet.”

The coach chuckled.

“Too late. The sports office already knows.”

Yichen closed his eyes briefly.

“Already?”

“Of course. The Director of Athletics has been asking about you since the first evaluation.”

Yichen laughed.

“Understood.”

“Good. Keep working.”

The call ended. Yichen sat. Then he opened his messages and sent Xiaoran a screenshot.

Yichen: Coach called.

Xiaoran: WHAT DID HE SAY

Yichen: Told me not to become arrogant.

Xiaoran: That’s because he knows your girlfriend is already very proud of you.

Yichen: Is that so?

Xiaoran: Extremely.

Yichen: Then I should be careful.

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: I might become arrogant.

She sent him a series of angry stickers. He laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that night, Xiaoran called him. She was already in bed, her hair tied loosely, and her face looking slightly sleepy.

“Yichen?”

“Mm?”

“I was thinking.”

“About?”

“Your university.”

He smiled.

“What about it?”

“I didn’t know they would support you like that.”

He leaned back against his pillows.

“Neither did I.”

“Do you think they really believe you’ll become a professional player?”

He thought for a moment.

“I think they believe I deserve the chance to find out.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“That’s even better.”

He looked at her through the screen.

“Why?”

“Because they’re not promising you anything. They’re just making sure you aren’t overlooked.”

She said, “Your coach saw your potential. The athletic director supported the recommendation. Your professor wanted to make sure your studies wouldn’t be a problem. And the sports office helped organise everything.” She paused.

“That’s a lot of people believing in you.”

Yichen smiled faintly.

“Apparently.”

She rested her chin on her pillow.

“You know what I think?”

“What?”

“I think you should invite all of them to your first professional game.”

He laughed.

“All of them?”

“Yes.”

“That’s quite a large audience.”

“Good. They should see you play.”

He watched her. Then he said, “You’ll be there too.”

She smiled.

“Obviously.”

“Front row?”

“Of course.”

“Will you shout?”

She nodded seriously.

“Very loudly.”

“Then I’ll have to make sure I play well.”

She laughed.

“No pressure.”

He reached towards his phone, adjusting the angle slightly.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hmm?”

He opened his arms. She leaned closer to the screen.

He kissed his fingertips and touched them lightly against the camera. She giggled.

“That’s not a real kiss.”

“It’s all I can give you right now.”

“Then you owe me one.”

“I owe you several.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, a formal email arrived from the club. The subject line read:

Invitation to Development Training Program – Zhou Yichen

It outlined the next stage, including training dates, fitness assessments, performance reviews, and a possible longer-term development arrangement. It wasn’t a contract. It wasn’t a guarantee. But it was real progress. Yichen read the email carefully. Then he forwarded it to his university coach. A few minutes later, his coach replied.

Good. Now earn the next one.

Yichen smiled. He saved the email. Then he opened Xiaoran’s chat.

Yichen: It came.

Xiaoran: THE EMAIL?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: SEND ME A SCREENSHOT.

He sent it. She replied almost immediately.

Xiaoran: I’M SO PROUD OF YOU.

Then another message.

Xiaoran: Wait.

Xiaoran: Does this mean I should start learning how to be a professional basketball player’s girlfriend?

Yichen laughed.

Yichen: What does that involve?

Xiaoran: Looking pretty. Supporting you. Bringing water. Not embarrassing you.

Yichen: You’re already doing three out of four.

Xiaoran: WHICH ONE AM I NOT DOING?

He smiled.

Yichen: The last one.

She sent him an angry sticker. Then:

Xiaoran: Fine. I’ll embarrass you even more when you become famous.

Yichen looked at the message. He could almost picture her saying it, cheeks puffed out, eyes bright, entirely convinced that she had the right to tease him regardless of how far his career went. He typed back.

Yichen: I’ll look forward to it.

And he meant it. Because the club had finally given him a proper chance. His university had stood behind him. The evaluators had recognised his performance.

But the part he would remember most wasn’t the meeting, the recommendation letters, or the invitation to the next stage.

It was the girl who had watched him sit on the sidelines, who had stayed when he didn’t get to play, and who had been just as proud of him on the difficult day as she was on the day he finally proved himself. He hadn’t needed her to defend him. He hadn’t needed her to fight his battles.

He only needed to look towards the spectator seats and know she was there. And she always was.

chapters.desc: A new sponsor’s logo on his sleeve, and Zhou Yichen is ready to walk away. Lin Xiaoran goes to dinner with his father instead.
chapters.title: Not Number Seventeen
chapters.epigraph: “I’m going to earn it.”
chapters.content:
The new training kit arrived on the Monday of Zhou Yichen’s second week with the development group, in a stack of plastic bags on the bench outside the Herons’ changing room.

Navy, like the old one. Same heron on the chest.

And on the left sleeve, a new patch. A small square logo in grey and white that he had seen every day of his childhood: on the side of trucks, on the gates of warehouses, on the corner of the letterhead his father used for everything, including birthday cards.

He stood there with the shirt in his hands.

“New sponsor. Logistics company. Big one. Signed on Friday. You’ll see their people at the game on Saturday,” said the kit man cheerfully.

Behind him, somebody laughed. Yichen turned.

Number seventeen was sitting on the bench, lacing his shoes. The director’s nephew. The boy who’d played a full scrimmage on his first day while Yichen sat and watched. He’d been polite since. Careful. He looked at the patch on the sleeve, and at the name on the shirt in Yichen’s hands, and at Yichen’s face, and he worked it out a second after Yichen did.

“Zhou. Oh,” he said slowly.

Then he smiled. It was almost relieved.

“So you’re one of us now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran knew something had happened the moment he got into the car.

He didn’t say anything. That wasn’t unusual. He drove her back from the training facility most Mondays without saying much, because he was tired and she was talking.

But he didn’t put his hand on her knee at the first red light.

He always put his hand on her knee at the first red light.

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

“What happened?”

He told her at the second red light, in about forty words, in a voice so flat that she didn’t understand at first how bad it was. Then she did.

“Your father’s company is sponsoring the Herons.”

“Yes.”

“Did he know you were there?”

“I don’t know.”

“Did you tell him?”

The light changed. He drove.

“I didn’t tell my parents about the trial. Any of it. The scout. The evaluations. The development group,” he said at last.

She stared at him.

“Why?”

Yichen said, “Because my father knows half the people on that club’s board, and I wanted to find out if I was good enough without him knowing any of them. And now everyone in that changing room thinks the same thing about me that I thought about number seventeen.” His hands were still on the wheel.

She opened her mouth.

He said, “I’m going to turn it down.”

“What?”

“The development program. I’ll write to them tomorrow.”

“Yichen—”

“I won’t be that, Xiaoran. I sat on that bench for three hours. I watched him play because somebody’s father rang somebody. I am not going to walk into that gym on Saturday with my father’s name on my arm.” He still hadn’t raised his voice. He never did.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang his father that night. She sat on the end of his bed and listened to one side of it, which was enough.

“…No. I’m not angry. I’m asking you to cancel it.”

A long silence.

“Then don’t cancel it. Move it to another club.”

Another silence.

“Forty jobs. Yes. I heard you. Then I’ll leave the club.” He was standing at the window with his back to her, one hand flat on the glass, the way he stood at the free-throw line when he was counting.

A shorter silence.

“Because it’s mine, Dad. It was the only thing that was.”

He ended the call. He stood at the window for a while. Then he came and sat down beside her on the bed, and she put her arms round him from the side, and he let her, and didn’t say anything else that night at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t, technically, plan to have dinner with Mr. Zhou.

What she planned was to find out which hotel he was staying at for the signing week, which took one message to Mrs. Zhou, who adored her and asked no questions. Then she meant to leave him a polite note. The note turned into a phone call.

The phone call turned into “Come and eat with me, Xiaoran. I’m on my own and the hotel restaurant is very sad.”

So at seven on Wednesday she was sitting in a hotel dining room with white tablecloths and a view of the river, across from a calm, grey-haired man in a cardigan who had once told his son he always passed too early. He poured her tea himself.

“He doesn’t know you’re here,” said Mr. Zhou. It wasn’t a question.

“No.”

“He’ll be angry.”

“He’s already angry.”

“With me.”

“With himself,” said Xiaoran, and then, because she’d decided in the taxi that she wasn’t going to be polite for the whole of dinner, “and with you, a bit.”

Mr. Zhou smiled. It was the first time she’d ever seen where Yichen got it from: the smile that happened only at one corner, as if the rest of the face hadn’t been told.

He said, “I didn’t know he was there. I want you to know that, even if he doesn’t believe it. The board’s chairman mentioned it at the signing dinner. Your son’s in our development group, you must be very proud. I said yes. I didn’t know what he was talking about. My son has a whole life I find out about from other men at dinners.” He turned his teacup a quarter turn.

She didn’t know what to say to that. So she said the thing she’d come to say.

“Uncle. Can I tell you about the first day?”

He looked at her.

She told him. All of it. The lineup announced, and Yichen’s name not in it. The assistant coach saying just watch. Three hours on a bench. Number seventeen missing pass after pass and staying on the court. The two staff members by the cafeteria, his father called this morning. Yichen in the car park afterwards saying I’m not going to let that be the only thing I take from today, and then going home and watching the footage until two in the morning.

“He sat on a bench for three hours,” said Xiaoran, “because of somebody’s father.”

Her voice wobbled. She ignored it.

“Please don’t make him the next one.”

The restaurant was quiet. Somewhere a waiter put down a tray.

Mr. Zhou looked at her. She made herself look back. She was five years old in a kindergarten playground, planted in front of a boy twice her size. She was nineteen at her grandparents’ table holding Yichen’s hand so hard it hurt. She was twenty in a hotel dining room with her tea going cold. She didn’t look away.

“My wife said you’d do this,” said Mr. Zhou finally.

“Auntie said—?”

“She said, that girl will go and stand in front of you, and you had better listen. I’m not cancelling the contract, Xiaoran. There are forty people in that warehouse in Pudong whose jobs depend on it. My son is right about almost everything, and he is wrong about that.” He put his cup down.

Her heart sank.

“But,” said Mr. Zhou.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday afternoon the Herons’ general manager called Yichen into his office and closed the door.

He came out twenty minutes later with a sheet of paper in his hand and drove straight to the media building, where Xiaoran was in a seminar, and waited outside it for fifty minutes, which he hadn’t done since first year. When she came out he held it up.

It was a copy of a letter, on his father’s letterhead, to the club’s board. Two paragraphs. The second one said that the sponsorship agreement was conditional on one thing: that every selection decision concerning Zhou Yichen would be made by the technical staff alone, recorded in writing with the reasons, and that the sponsor would never be told any of them. If that was ever broken, the money stopped.

At the bottom, in his father’s small square handwriting: He’s yours to judge. Not mine. Please judge him properly.

“He sent it on Wednesday night. At eleven. After a dinner. With you,” said Yichen. He looked at her.

“Ah,” said Xiaoran.

“You went to dinner with my father.”

“It was a very sad hotel restaurant. He was on his own.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I didn’t ask him to do that! I just told him about the bench. That’s all. I told him about the first day, and I told him not to make you the next one, and then I ate a very small fish and went home.” She held up both hands.

He looked at her. He looked at the letter. He looked at her again.

“You stood in front of him,” he said.

“…A bit.”

He didn’t say anything else. He folded the letter in half and put it inside his jacket, against his chest, the way he’d held a photo album in a dormitory bed for eight weeks.

✦ ✦ ✦

The development scrimmage on Saturday was open to staff and families, which in practice meant eleven people in a stand built for four hundred.

Xiaoran sat in the third row with two drinks.

Yichen played. He started. He didn’t do anything spectacular. He did a hundred small correct things, and once, late in the second half, he made a pass to number seventeen that was so clean the boy scored without having to think, and looked at him afterwards with an expression Xiaoran couldn’t read from the stand.

In the corridor at half-time she heard number seventeen say to him, “Your dad’s the sponsor?”

“Yes.”

“Mine’s on the board. He sits in the front row. Every time.”

Yichen looked at him. Something passed between them that Xiaoran couldn’t name and wasn’t meant to.

“Then play like he isn’t there,” said Yichen, and went back out.

It was only at the final whistle that she saw him look up past her, to the very back of the stand, and stop. She turned round.

In the last row, on his own, in a grey cardigan, sat Mr. Zhou. He hadn’t told anyone he was coming. He was holding a paper cup of tea from the vending machine that was famous for swallowing coins.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was waiting outside the changing room afterwards. Xiaoran hung back by the vending machine, badly pretending to choose something.

“Dad.”

“You started.”

“I did.”

“You passed too early, twice.”

Yichen almost laughed. “I know.”

Mr. Zhou took an envelope out of his cardigan pocket. It was thick and soft at the corners, the kind that had been carried around for years.

He said, “Your mother found these when she was turning out my desk. I thought you should have them. I’ve been meaning to say something about them since you were fifteen, and I never found the right dinner.”

Yichen opened it. Ticket stubs. Dozens of them. Cheap paper, faded ink, school-gym tickets and city-league tickets and the invitational tournament the scouts had come to. Every game Yichen had played from the age of twelve to eighteen. On the back of each, in the same small square hand, a seat number. Always the back row.

“You said you never had time,” said Yichen. His voice had gone strange.

“I didn’t. I left early and went back to the office after. I sat at the back so you wouldn’t play for me. I thought if you knew I was there you’d play to impress me, instead of playing. I was wrong about that. I’d like to stop being wrong about it.” Mr. Zhou looked at the court.

Yichen didn’t say anything. Mr. Zhou put a hand on his shoulder, briefly, the way men in that family did everything.

“You took her to the Garden. Good. I’d have talked through the whole game,” he said.

Then he nodded across the corridor at Xiaoran, who was now holding a can of something she hadn’t meant to buy, and said, “Thank you for dinner. Next time I’ll choose the restaurant. That fish was an insult,” and walked away towards the car park with his hands in his cardigan pockets.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car park was nearly empty. Yichen put his bag in the boot. Then he turned round, took the can out of her hand and put it on the roof of the car, and backed her up against the passenger door.

“You went to dinner with my father,” he said.

“You said that already.”

“I’m still processing it.”

“You’ll have to process faster. I’m cold.”

He kissed her. Properly this time, with both hands on her face and three days of not saying anything in it, until she had to hold on to his jacket. When he finally pulled back he rested his forehead on hers, and for the first time since a plastic bag on a bench on Monday, he laughed.

“What?”

“You ate a very small fish.”

“It was a very small fish!”

He laughed again, helplessly, into her hair, and she wrapped her arms round him in the empty car park outside the Herons’ training facility, with the letter folded inside his jacket and an envelope of ticket stubs on the back seat. She thought that she’d stand in front of anyone, any time, if it meant hearing that again.

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

“Are you still turning it down?”

He lifted his head and looked at her, and at the facility behind her with its lights going off one by one, and at the stand where his father had sat in the back row.

“No, I’m going to earn it,” said Zhou Yichen.

chapters.desc: Her parents visit without telling her. Her mother inspects his fridge. Her father takes him fishing. Nobody invites her.
chapters.title: Her Parents Come to Shanghai
chapters.epigraph: “You can be their favourite child.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had always believed that introducing Zhou Yichen to her parents would be a relatively straightforward process. Her mother liked him. Her father liked him.

In fact, sometimes she suspected they liked him more than they liked her.

Still, she hadn’t expected them to become so comfortable with her boyfriend that they would eventually start making independent arrangements with him. Without telling her.

Especially not when those arrangements involved her mother’s sudden inspection of his apartment and her father’s fishing trip.

And especially not when she was the last person to find out. It started on a Thursday afternoon.

Xiaoran was sitting in the university library, struggling with a media project, when her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Are you finished with class?

Xiaoran: Not yet. Why?

Yichen: Nothing. Just checking.

Xiaoran: Suspicious.

Yichen: What did I do?

Xiaoran: You said nothing. That’s suspicious.

He sent her a laughing emoji. She put her phone down and returned to her work.

Meanwhile, across the road from her university, Zhou Yichen was standing inside his apartment, opening the door for two unexpected visitors.

“Uncle. Auntie.”

Lin Xiaoran’s mother stepped inside first. She was carrying a handbag and a small shopping bag. Her father followed, holding a paper bag of fruit.

“Yichen, we didn’t disturb you, did we?”

“No, not at all. Please come in.”

He took the bags from them. Xiaoran’s mother looked around. Then she stopped.

“Oh.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“Is something wrong?”

“No, no.”

She walked farther into the living room.

“It’s very clean.”

Yichen smiled politely.

“Thank you.”

Her father put the fruit on the kitchen counter.

“Where’s Xiaoran?”

“She has class. I think she’ll finish around five.”

“Oh, good. Then we can take our time.”

Yichen looked at him.

“Take our time?”

Her father smiled.

“Your auntie wanted to see where you live.”

Yichen turned towards Xiaoran’s mother. She was already examining the kitchen.

“It’s quite spacious. And the kitchen is clean,” she commented.

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“Do you cook?”

“Sometimes.”

“What do you usually eat?”

“Mostly simple meals.”

She opened one of the cabinets.

“Do you have enough bowls?”

Yichen blinked.

“Yes.”

“Plates?”

“Yes.”

“Rice cooker?”

He pointed towards the counter.

“Over there.”

She nodded approvingly. Then she opened the refrigerator. Yichen watched her.

He was beginning to understand why Xiaoran occasionally complained that her mother could inspect an entire household in less than ten minutes.

“Yichen.”

“Yes, Auntie?”

“Why is there so little fruit?”

He paused.

“I haven’t gone grocery shopping recently.”

Her mother looked at him, then at the refrigerator, then back at him.

“Do you know Xiaoran likes fruit?”

“I know.”

“Especially strawberries.”

“I know.”

“Then you should keep some.”

He smiled.

“I’ll remember.”

Her father laughed from the living room.

“Don’t worry about him. He’s probably better organised than our daughter.”

Xiaoran’s mother turned.

“That is exactly why I’m checking.”

Yichen lowered his head slightly, hiding a smile.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time Xiaoran finished class, her parents had been at Yichen’s apartment for most of the afternoon, and her mother had taken him to the supermarket downstairs and supervised the fruit aisle personally. She was completely unaware. She sent him a message.

Xiaoran: I’m done!

Yichen: Good. Are you hungry?

Xiaoran: A little.

Yichen: Come over later. I’ll make dinner.

Xiaoran: What are you making?

Yichen: Something you’ll eat.

Xiaoran: That’s not an answer.

Yichen: You’ll find out.

She smiled at her phone. Then she packed her things and crossed the road.

She didn’t bother calling him because she knew the door code.

When she entered the apartment, she was already speaking.

“Yichen! I’m here!”

A familiar voice answered from the living room.

“Xiaoran?”

She froze. That wasn’t Yichen’s voice. It was her father’s. She slowly turned her head. Her mother was sitting on the sofa.

Her father was beside her, holding a cup of tea. Yichen was standing near the dining table. All three looked at her. Xiaoran stared. Her father smiled.

“Hello.”

She blinked. Then she looked at her mother, then at Yichen, then back at her father.

“...What are you doing here?”

Her mother frowned.

“Visiting.”

“Visiting whom?”

Her father pointed towards Yichen.

“Your boyfriend.”

Xiaoran’s mouth opened. Closed. Opened again.

“Why didn’t anyone tell me?”

Her mother looked genuinely puzzled.

“Why? We wanted to surprise you.”

“Surprise me?”

She turned towards Yichen. He was trying hard not to smile.

“You knew?”

He nodded.

“Since this afternoon.”

Her eyes widened.

“You knew since this afternoon?”

“Your parents came over while you were in class.”

“And you didn’t tell me?”

Yichen looked at her calmly.

“Your mother asked me not to.”

Xiaoran turned towards her mother.

“Mum!”

Her mother picked up her tea.

“What?”

“You told him not to tell me?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“So we could surprise you.”

Xiaoran looked around the room. Then she pointed at Yichen.

“Why is my boyfriend cooperating with you?”

Her father laughed.

“Because he’s a sensible young man.”

Xiaoran looked betrayed.

“Dad!”

Yichen finally laughed. He walked over and gently took her bag.

“Have you eaten?”

She stared at him.

“Don’t change the subject.”

“I’m asking because you said you were hungry.”

“I’m angry.”

“Can you be angry while eating?”

Her father burst out laughing. Her mother shook her head.

“See? He knows how to handle you.”

Xiaoran was beginning to regret introducing them.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was, unfortunately, pleasant. Yichen prepared a few dishes while Xiaoran’s mother helped him in the kitchen despite his insistence that she could sit down.

Her father sat at the dining table, asking Yichen about basketball.

“How’s the professional club?”

“I’m currently training with their development group.”

“That’s good. Are they treating you well?”

“It’s going well so far.”

“Don’t overwork yourself.”

“I’ll be careful.”

Her father nodded.

Then he asked, “Do you still play university basketball?”

“Yes. When the schedule allows.”

“Good. Don’t abandon your university studies.”

“I won’t.”

Xiaoran sat beside him, quietly eating. She occasionally glanced at Yichen.

He was answering her father’s questions patiently, occasionally smiling, occasionally explaining something about the training schedule. Her father seemed pleased.

Her mother placed another serving of vegetables on Yichen’s plate.

“Eat more.”

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“Don’t be so polite. You’re practically family.”

Xiaoran nearly choked on her rice. Her father laughed.

Her mother continued eating as if she hadn’t said anything unusual. Yichen, meanwhile, simply smiled.

“Thank you.”

Xiaoran leaned closer to him.

“Practically family?”

“Is there a problem?”

“Don’t look so happy.”

His lips curved.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He leaned closer, lowering his voice.

“Would you prefer I looked unhappy?”

She immediately turned back to her food. Yichen smiled and placed a piece of fish into her bowl.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Xiaoran woke up to find a message from her father.

Dad: Yichen and I are going out today.

She stared at the screen, then sat up.

Xiaoran: Where?

Dad: Fishing.

She blinked.

Xiaoran: Fishing?

Dad: Yes.

Xiaoran: With Yichen?

Dad: Correct.

Xiaoran: What about me?

Her father replied several seconds later.

Dad: You have class, don’t you?

She stared at the message, then another arrived.

Dad: Don’t worry. We’ll bring you something.

Xiaoran put down her phone. She stared at the ceiling. Her parents had arrived in Shanghai. Her mother had inspected her boyfriend’s apartment.

Her father had apparently arranged a fishing trip with him. And nobody had invited her. She immediately called Yichen. He answered after two rings.

“Good morning.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

His voice sounded amused.

“And good morning.”

“Are you going fishing?”

“Yes.”

“With my father?”

“Yes.”

“Without me?”

He laughed.

“You have class.”

“I can skip class.”

“No.”

She frowned.

“Why not?”

“Because you have a presentation.”

She went quiet. Then she remembered.

“Oh.”

He chuckled.

“Did you forget?”

“No.”

A pause.

“Maybe.”

He laughed again. She heard movement in the background.

“Are you already with him?”

“I’m picking him up in a few minutes.”

She sighed dramatically.

“Have fun with my father.”

“I will.”

“Don’t have too much fun.”

“Why?”

“Because he’s my father.”

Yichen laughed.

“I’m aware.”

“Don’t become closer to him than I am.”

There was a brief silence.

Then he said, calmly, “I think it’s too late.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed.

“Go prepare for your presentation.”

She grumbled something unintelligible.

Before hanging up, he said, “I’ll send you pictures.”

She brightened slightly.

“Really?”

“Of course.”

“Okay. Then you can go.”

“Thank you for granting permission.”

She smiled despite herself.

“Bye.”

“Bye, Xiaoran.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The fishing trip turned out to be more successful than either man expected.

Yichen had driven her father to a quiet fishing spot outside the city. It was a place her father had visited several times during his business trips to Shanghai.

He had brought his own rods, in the boot of the car he’d driven up from home. Yichen had brought a small camera.

“You take pictures?” her father asked.

“Sometimes.”

“Of what?”

“Mostly scenery. Basketball games. Xiaoran.”

Her father looked at him, then smiled.

“Ah.”

Yichen realised what he had said. He smiled faintly.

“She’s usually the most interesting subject.”

Her father laughed.

“Good answer.”

They settled beside the water. For a while, they talked about fishing.

Her father explained the equipment, the bait, and how to recognise when a fish was biting. Yichen listened attentively. He wasn’t particularly experienced, but he was patient. Her father seemed to enjoy teaching him. Eventually, Yichen managed to catch a fish. It wasn’t particularly large. But her father looked pleased.

“Not bad!”

Yichen lifted the fishing rod slightly.

“Is this the correct size?”

Her father laughed.

“It’s your first one. You should be proud.”

Yichen took a picture of the fish. Then he took another of the water, the fishing rods, and her father sitting beside him.

“Take one of me,” her father said.

Yichen turned the camera towards him. Her father posed with the fish. Yichen took several pictures. Then he looked at the screen.

“Uncle, this one is good.”

“Let me see.”

He showed him. Her father nodded.

“Send it to me.”

“Of course.”

Yichen looked at him.

“Would you like a picture together?”

Her father smiled.

“Sure.”

Yichen placed the camera on a small stand, set the timer, and sat beside him. The first picture was slightly awkward. The second was better.

In the third, her father was laughing while Yichen looked towards him. It was probably the best one. Her father examined it.

“Good. Send me that one too.”

Yichen nodded. Then he sent the pictures to Xiaoran.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran was in the university cafeteria when the pictures arrived. She opened the first one. A fish. The second one. Her father holding the fish. The third.

Her father and Yichen sitting beside each other, smiling. She stared, then another picture arrived.

Yichen standing behind her father, holding the fishing rod while her father demonstrated something. She stared even harder. Then she called him. He answered almost immediately.

“Hello?”

“Why do you look so happy?”

He laughed.

“Good afternoon.”

“I’m serious.”

“We’re having a good time.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Where am I in these pictures?”

“Not there.”

“Exactly!”

He laughed. She heard her father in the background.

“Is that Xiaoran?”

Yichen turned slightly.

“Yes.”

“Tell her we’re having fun!”

Xiaoran heard him. Her mouth fell open.

“DAD!”

Her father laughed loudly. Yichen was laughing too. She looked betrayed.

“Why are you both laughing?”

Her father came closer to the phone.

“Xiaoran, we’re fishing.”

“I know!”

“Your boyfriend caught a fish.”

“I saw!”

“Not bad for his first time.”

She sighed.

“Dad, why did you take him fishing without me?”

Her father answered naturally.

“Because you don’t know how to fish.”

Xiaoran froze.

“Excuse me?”

Her father continued.

“And you have class.”

“I can learn!”

“Next time.”

“Next time?”

“Of course.”

She looked at Yichen. He was smiling.

“Don’t encourage him,” she warned.

Yichen nodded solemnly.

“I won’t.”

Her father spoke again.

“Yichen is very patient. He listens carefully. You should learn from him.”

Xiaoran’s eyes widened.

“Dad! I’m your daughter!”

Her father laughed.

“That’s why I’m telling you.”

She ended the call. Not because she was genuinely angry.

But because she couldn’t stand hearing the two men laugh together anymore.

✦ ✦ ✦

About twenty minutes later, her mother called. Xiaoran answered immediately.

“Mum!”

“Yes?”

“Why didn’t you tell me you were going to Yichen’s apartment?”

Her mother sounded completely unbothered.

“I told you last week we might come up.”

“You said might!”

“And then we came.”

“You didn’t tell me you were inspecting his apartment!”

“Inspecting?”

“Yes! You opened his cabinets!”

Her mother laughed.

“Of course. I wanted to see how he lived.”

“Mum!”

“What?”

“That’s my boyfriend’s house!”

“Exactly. I wanted to make sure he was taking care of himself.”

Xiaoran rubbed her forehead.

“Why?”

“Because he takes care of you.”

She stopped.

Her mother continued, “You spend so much time at his apartment. I wanted to see whether he had everything he needed.”

Xiaoran went quiet.

Then her mother added, “I made him buy strawberries. Don’t eat them all in one day.”

Xiaoran closed her eyes.

“Mum, please.”

“And vegetables. His refrigerator was almost empty before I got there.”

“He has vegetables!”

“He does now.”

“Mum.”

“And you should eat properly when you’re there.”

Xiaoran looked up at the ceiling.

“Why are you both treating him like your son?”

Her mother laughed.

“Would that be a problem?”

Xiaoran opened her mouth, then closed it. She couldn’t find a suitable answer.

Her mother continued, “He’s a good boy. We like him.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened despite herself.

Then her mother added, “Much more organised than you.”

The softness disappeared.

“Mum!”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen returned to his apartment. He had a small bag of fish her father had insisted on bringing back.

He placed it in the kitchen and called Xiaoran.

“Are you home?”

“Almost.”

“Come over.”

“Why?”

“I have something for you.”

She arrived fifteen minutes later. The moment he opened the door, she walked inside with a suspicious expression.

“What?”

He held up the bag.

“Your father caught more fish than I did. He asked me to bring some back.”

She looked inside, then looked at him.

“Are you trying to bribe me?”

He smiled.

“Is it working?”

“No.”

He placed the bag in the kitchen. Then he turned back towards her.

“How was your presentation?”

She blinked.

“You remembered?”

“Of course.”

“It went well.”

“Good.”

He bent and kissed her hairline. She looked up at him. Then she glanced towards the living room.

“Did you really have fun with my father?”

“Yes.”

“More fun than with me?”

He smiled.

“Different kind of fun.”

She crossed her arms.

“Explain.”

“He taught me how to fish.”

“I can teach you.”

“You don’t know how.”

“I can learn.”

He laughed. She stepped closer.

“And did you talk about me?”

“A little.”

Her eyes widened.

“What did you say?”

“Nothing much.”

“Yichen.”

He looked at her, amused.

“I said you’re usually the most interesting subject to photograph.”

She blinked. Then her cheeks turned pink.

“You said that?”

“Mm.”

“To my father?”

“Yes.”

She looked away.

“That’s embarrassing.”

He smiled and reached for her hand.

“Why?”

“Because.”

He gently pulled her closer.

“Your father seemed pleased.”

“Really?”

“He was. He also told me to take care of you.”

Her expression softened.

“What did you say?”

Yichen brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

“I told him I would.”

She studied him. Then leaned forward and wrapped her arms around his waist.

He held her naturally, one hand resting against her back. After a while, she mumbled into his shirt.

“I still think you betrayed me.”

He laughed.

“By going fishing?”

“By becoming friends with my father without me.”

“Would you like me to stop?”

She pulled back immediately.

“No!”

“Then what’s the problem?”

She thought about it, then sighed.

“Nothing.”

He kissed her cheek.

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The following morning, Xiaoran discovered something even worse. Her father had posted a picture on his social media.

It was the picture Yichen had taken of them together by the water. The caption read:

Good company, good weather, and a successful fishing day.

Xiaoran stared at it. Then she noticed a comment from her mother.

Yichen is considerate. Next time, bring him to dinner again.

And another comment from her aunt.

Is that Yichen? Even more handsome than at New Year.

Her father replied:

Yes. Very good young man.

Xiaoran slowly put down her phone. Then she opened Yichen’s chat.

Xiaoran: Your reputation in my family is getting out of control.

Yichen: What happened?

She sent him the screenshot.

Yichen: Your father posted the picture.

Xiaoran: YOU KNEW?

Yichen: He asked me to send it to him.

Xiaoran: AND YOU DIDN’T TELL ME?

Yichen: I thought you’d see it.

Xiaoran: I AM SEEING IT NOW.

A few seconds passed. Then he sent another message.

Yichen: Your father said we should go fishing again next month.

She stared at the screen.

Xiaoran: WE?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: What about me?

Yichen: He said you can come next time.

She narrowed her eyes.

Xiaoran: He said I CAN COME?

Yichen: His exact words.

She buried her face in her pillow. Her phone vibrated again.

Yichen: I’ll teach you how to fish.

She lifted her head.

Xiaoran: You barely know how.

Yichen: Then we’ll learn together.

She smiled, then another message arrived.

Yichen: Your mother also asked whether you have enough clothes for the changing weather.

Xiaoran froze.

Xiaoran: Why is my mother messaging you?

Yichen: She asked me to remind you to bring a jacket.

She stared at the screen. Then typed:

Xiaoran: Zhou Yichen.

Yichen: Yes?

Xiaoran: I think you’re my parents’ favourite child now.

His reply came almost immediately.

Yichen: I don’t think so.

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: Your father said I’m his favourite fishing partner.

She screamed into her pillow.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, when Yichen picked her up from the library, she was still pretending to be upset. He opened the passenger door for her. She got in without looking at him.

He closed the door, walked around, and settled into the driver’s seat.

“Still angry?”

“Very.”

He started the car.

“Should I apologise?”

She glanced at him.

“For what?”

“I’m not sure yet.”

She tried not to smile. He noticed. Of course he noticed.

At the next red light, he turned towards her.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Your father asked me to take care of you.”

She looked at him.

“And?”

“And your mother asked me to make sure you eat properly.”

She nodded.

“That’s true.”

“So I have quite a few responsibilities.”

She looked suspicious.

“What responsibilities?”

He reached over and gently squeezed her hand.

“Taking you to class when you oversleep. Making sure you eat lunch. Keeping fruit in the refrigerator. Reminding you to bring a jacket.”

“That’s a lot.”

“Apparently.”

She smiled. Then she leaned over and kissed his cheek.

“Fine.”

He glanced at her.

“Fine?”

“You can be their favourite child.”

He laughed.

“Thank you.”

“But I’m still their actual daughter.”

“Of course.”

“And I’m your girlfriend.”

He raised her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“That’s the most important part.”

She smiled, satisfied. Then, after a moment, she said:

“Next time you go fishing, I’m coming.”

He nodded.

“Of course.”

“And you’re teaching me.”

“I will.”

“And if I catch a bigger fish than you, you have to take my picture.”

He smiled.

“Several pictures.”

“Good.”

The traffic light turned green. Yichen drove forward, still holding her hand.

And Xiaoran, who had spent the past two days feeling as though her parents had adopted her boyfriend, finally decided that perhaps it wasn’t such a terrible thing. As long as she was invited next time.

And as long as nobody opened her boyfriend’s refrigerator without telling her first.

chapters.desc: Her father comes to watch Yichen play and sends her a photograph from his seat. It is in the wrong stand.
chapters.title: Her Father in the Wrong Stand
chapters.epigraph: “Even if I have to travel?”
chapters.content:
The first sign that something had gone wrong was the message, twenty minutes before tip-off.

Dad (Water Bureau): I’m here.

Xiaoran: where are you sitting?

Dad (Water Bureau): In the stands.

Xiaoran: which section??

There was a pause. Then a photograph arrived: her father, sitting comfortably among a crowd of people in the other university’s green and white.

Lin Xiaoran stared at it. She zoomed in. She checked the ticket she’d sent him that morning. She looked at the photograph again.

“Oh no.”

Zhou Yichen was on the bench beside her in the corridor outside the away changing room, tightening his laces. “What?”

“My dad’s in the wrong stand.”

He leaned over and looked at her phone. A slow smile came over his face. “He’s made friends.”

“Yichen! That’s the home end. He’s on their side.”

“I can see that.”

In the photograph Mr. Lin was wedged between two older men, one of whom seemed to be explaining something to him with a great deal of pointing. He looked perfectly happy.

She rang him. He answered on the third ring.

“Dad! Where are you?”

“In the stands. Why are you asking me that? I’m watching your boyfriend’s game.”

“You’re in the home section!”

A pause. She could hear him turning to look at the people around him. “Oh.”

“Oh?”

“They’ve been very helpful. They showed me where to sit.”

“Dad, you’re in the wrong stand!”

“I followed the signs.”

“Those are their fans!”

Another pause. “Well. The seats are very good.”

Yichen was smiling openly now. She covered the microphone with her hand. “He’s not moving.”

“Tell him to enjoy the game.”

She glared at him and went back to the phone. “Fine. Stay there. Just don’t argue with anyone.”

“Why would I argue with anyone?”

“Because you’re wearing a Huaining jacket.”

“I’m aware of that, Xiaoran. I’m here to watch basketball. Not to start a fight. Tell Yichen good luck.”

She hung up. Yichen stood and picked up his warm-up top.

“Should I be worried?”

“About what?”

“Your father changing sides,” he said, and kissed her hair, and went in to warm up before she could hit him.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was one of the last fixtures of the university season, against their rivals across the river, and the gym was louder than usual. The home end was full, and the away section had about two hundred Huaining students crammed into it with a drum and a hand-painted banner. Xiaoran sat in the front row of it with Luo Jiayi and spent most of the first quarter looking for her father on the far side of the court.

She found him eventually. He was still in the same seat. And he was talking, of all things, to the man next to him.

Xiaoran: are you cheering for OUR team?

Dad (Water Bureau): Of course.

Dad (Water Bureau): The man next to me says your boyfriend is very good.

Xiaoran: he is

Dad (Water Bureau): I know.

On the court Yichen was standing with his hands on his hips listening to the coach in a timeout, his face completely closed and calm. He had no idea that his girlfriend’s father was representing their university from behind enemy lines.

When he scored the next basket, the away end jumped up. On the far side, a single figure in a navy Huaining jacket stood up as well, among a sea of green, and clapped. Then he turned and said something to the man next to him. Probably about Yichen.

Xiaoran sat down slowly. Her father had always been interested in Yichen’s basketball, but he hardly ever asked about the game itself. He asked about everything around it. Training. Recovery. What came after. He wasn’t the kind of man who said he was proud of someone. He showed it by remembering things: whether Yichen had eaten, whether he was limping, and now by sitting through an entire game in the wrong stand, alone, rather than make a fuss about moving.

✦ ✦ ✦

With two minutes left they were three points up, and the home team called a timeout. Xiaoran was standing at the rail with her hands clasped under her chin.

Dad (Water Bureau): He’s playing well.

Xiaoran: I know

Dad (Water Bureau): His ankle looks fine today.

She looked at the court. Yichen had landed hard in the second quarter, and she’d stopped breathing, but he’d got up straight away and he was moving normally now.

Xiaoran: it’s fine. he’s been careful

Her father didn’t reply. The game restarted. Yichen got a hand on a pass at the top of the key, broke the other way, and fed the forward for the basket that made it five. The final whistle went. The away end exploded, and Jiayi grabbed Xiaoran by both shoulders and shook her and shrieked.

On the court Yichen looked up at the away end and found her straight away. She waved with both arms. He smiled. And then his eyes moved across the gym to the far side, and she saw his eyebrows go up. Among all that green, her father had raised one hand. Yichen inclined his head to him, properly, across the length of the court. Even from the rail Xiaoran could see how hard he was trying not to laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found her father by the exit afterward, still in his navy jacket, holding a paper cup of tea.

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Yes.”

“Did you make friends?”

He looked back at the two men he’d been sitting with, who were waving at him. “They were very nice.”

“You stayed there the whole game.”

“Why would I move? I could see everything.”

Yichen came out of the changing-room corridor with his bag over his shoulder and his hair still wet. “Uncle.”

“Yichen. Good game.”

“Thank you for coming.”

“How was the view from over there?” said Yichen, with a perfectly straight face.

“Very good. Although I believe I was the only person on that side cheering for you.”

“I noticed.”

“Can we please stop talking about the wrong stand?” said Xiaoran.

Her father laughed. Then his face changed a little. “How’s the ankle?”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen. He answered at once.

“Fine. No pain.”

“Any swelling after the last game?”

“No.”

“You’re seeing the physio?”

“Every week, Uncle.”

It all sounded ordinary. But Xiaoran knew that tone. Her father wasn’t asking out of politeness. He was checking. And she could see that Yichen understood that too.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat at a table in the café by the gym entrance while her mother rested at the hotel with a migraine. Xiaoran went to the counter for drinks. When she came back with three cups, the conversation at the table had changed.

“...and if the club offers you a contract,” her father was saying, “and then your ankle goes. What happens?”

She stopped a few steps away. The Herons had been talking to Yichen since February. Nothing was signed. But it was becoming real enough that people had started asking questions.

“I’m not asking because I think it will happen. I’m asking because injuries are part of the sport,” said her father.

“I understand, Uncle.”

“Have you looked at the terms?”

“Some of them. I haven’t seen the final contract.”

“And if you get injured before it’s signed?”

“Then it depends on the club and on the medical. I know what I’m risking. I know it isn’t something I can do forever. Even without an injury, there’s no guarantee.” Yichen’s voice was calm.

“And if you can’t play?”

Yichen looked down at his hands on the table. “Then I’ll find something else.”

“Such as?”

“Coaching. Management. The business side of the sport. I study business for a reason.” He looked up.

Her father almost smiled. “Good answer.”

“But I don’t want to pretend I’ve got it all worked out. I want to play. I’ve worked towards it for a long time, and I want to see how far I can get. I’ll read every page before I sign anything. The medical clauses. The insurance. What they pay if I’m hurt. The rehabilitation.”

“And if it’s not as good as you hoped?”

“Then I won’t sign it just because I’m afraid nothing else will come.”

Her father looked at him. Then he drank some tea. “That’s what I wanted to hear.”

Xiaoran was standing there holding three cups. She hadn’t meant to listen. She just hadn’t expected her father, who couldn’t laugh without crying and had once asked a waiter whether the fish was happy, to ask a question that serious.

Yichen saw her first. She came over and put the drinks down.

“What are you talking about?”

“Basketball,” said her father.

“That sounds suspicious.”

“Your father was asking about my future,” said Yichen.

“Somebody has to,” said her father.

She sat down next to Yichen, close, and leaned her shoulder against his. “Why does everyone keep asking about after university? It’s a whole year away.”

“Because it’ll come,” said her father, “whether you ask about it or not.”

Under the table Yichen found her hand and held it on her knee. His thumb moved across her knuckles once, steady, and she didn’t ask anything else.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when her father had gone to find the toilets, she turned in her chair to face him.

“Are you okay?”

“Yes.”

“That was a lot of questions.”

“Your father’s thorough.”

“He’s worried. About your ankle.”

“I know. So are you.” He looked at her.

She looked down at his leg under the table. He caught her chin gently and turned her face back up to his.

“It’s fine. And I’m being careful.”

“I know you are.”

“Then why are you looking at me like that?”

She leaned her forehead against his shoulder. “Because I love you.”

He was quiet for a second. Then he pressed his mouth to her hair. “I love you too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove them across the city to meet her mother for dinner. Xiaoran sat in the back with her father, and for a while she watched the lights go past without saying anything. Then she leaned forward.

“Dad? Why did you ask him all that? About the contract?”

Her father met her eyes in the mirror. “Because he’s at that point.”

“He’s still at university.”

“Exactly. It’s easy to think about the exciting part. The offer, the team, the games. But a career is also about what happens when things go wrong. He’s worked hard. I don’t want him to sign something without understanding what he’s agreeing to.” He looked out of the window.

She glanced at Yichen. He was listening, though he kept his eyes on the road.

“Do you think he’ll be okay?”

“Your boyfriend?”

“Yes.”

“I think he’ll be all right,” said her father.

“Because he’s clever?”

“Because he knows that being good at something doesn’t mean nothing can happen to him.”

In the mirror, Yichen’s eyes met hers for a second. She smiled at him. Her father saw, and looked out of the window, and didn’t say a word.

At dinner her father told her mother about the game. He left out the part about the wrong stand. Xiaoran didn’t.

“You sat with the other team?” Her mother put her chopsticks down.

“They were very friendly.”

“Did you cheer for them?”

“Of course not.”

“He stood up when Yichen scored. The only person on that whole side,” said Xiaoran.

“Everybody stood up,” said her father.

“Everybody on our side stood up.”

Yichen bent his head over his rice. Her mother shook hers. “Next time, check your ticket.”

“I will.”

Her father turned to Yichen.

“Next time, you tell me which section to book,” she said.

“Of course, Uncle.”

Next time. It was such a small thing for him to say. Xiaoran kept hearing it for the rest of the meal.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her home last, and parked at the kerb outside her building and turned the engine off, and she didn’t get out.

“About what my dad asked. Does it scare you?”

He thought about it. “Sometimes. Not getting hurt. That’s part of it. It’s the not knowing. You can prepare for everything and still not control anything.”

“And you still want to do it?”

“Yes,” he said, with no hesitation at all.

“Then I hope you get it.”

“Even if it means I’m busy all the time?”

“Yes.”

“Even if I have to travel?”

“Yes.”

“Even if you complain I never have time for you?”

“I don’t complain that much!”

“Of course not,” he said.

She took his hand off the gearstick and held it in both of hers. “I want you to do the thing you love. I don’t want you to look back in ten years and wonder.”

“And you? What do you want?”

“I want to work somewhere that lets me make things I’m proud of.”

“Then I hope you get that too. We’ll work out the rest.” He lifted her hand and kissed it.

She leaned across the gearstick and leaned into his shoulder and stayed there for a while, in the dark car with the engine ticking as it cooled.

“Next time I’m checking Dad’s ticket myself,” she said eventually.

“Good idea.”

“And if he ends up in the wrong stand again, I’m leaving him there.”

“He made friends, Xiaoran.”

“You’re taking his side?”

“I’m acknowledging that he had a good afternoon,” he said, and she laughed and kissed him good night and went in.

He waited at the kerb until the light went on four floors up. He had a lot to think about. The contract. The medical pages he hadn’t read yet. A year that would arrive whether he asked about it or not. But mostly he thought about what her father had said in the café, before Xiaoran came back with the drinks.

I don’t need you to promise nothing will happen. I just want you to understand what you’re choosing.

He thought that was fair. He intended to do exactly that.

chapters.desc: Five hours of silence from an away game, and Lin Xiaoran finally learns what twenty-three unread messages feel like from the other side.
chapters.title: The Night His Phone Died
chapters.epigraph: “Once was all I could manage.”
chapters.content:
The first hour, Xiaoran was patient. The second hour, she was understanding.

By the fifth hour, she was beginning to understand something she had never quite understood before. How it felt to be Zhou Yichen. It started with a perfectly ordinary message.

Yichen, 5:42 PM: Game finished. We’re heading back to the hotel. I’ll call you after dinner.

Xiaoran had been waiting for his message all afternoon. The away game was in another city, and although he had told her not to stay up waiting, she had promised she would only call if he wasn’t too tired. He’d be back on the team bus the next afternoon.

She sent him a sticker of a tiny rabbit saluting.

Xiaoran, 5:44 PM: Okay! Don’t forget to eat properly.

Yichen, 5:45 PM: I won’t.

Xiaoran, 5:45 PM: And drink water.

Yichen, 5:46 PM: Yes, coach.

She smiled at her phone. Then she put it down and went back to editing her university assignment.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 6:30, she checked her phone. Nothing. That was fine. They were probably having dinner. At seven, she checked again. Still nothing.

She opened their chat, reread his last message, and typed:

Did you eat yet?

She deleted it. He was with his teammates. She didn’t want to become the girlfriend who kept asking questions every ten minutes.

A little after seven, she sent a photograph of the dinner she had ordered.

Xiaoran, 7:18 PM: My dinner. Yours better look more nutritious than this.

No reply. She ate while watching a variety show, occasionally glancing at the screen. At eight, she checked again. A little after eight, she sent a sticker. A little before nine, she finally called. The phone rang. And rang. And eventually went to voicemail. Xiaoran stared at the screen.

“He’s probably showering.”

She said it aloud, as if hearing herself say it would make the explanation more convincing. She put her phone down. Five minutes later, she picked it up again.

She checked the team group photos posted by the university’s basketball account. There was one from the court, one of the players celebrating, and another showing the team getting onto their bus. She zoomed in on the last photograph. There he was.

Zhou Yichen, wearing his team jacket, standing near the back of the group. His hair was slightly damp, and he was looking down at something in his hand. His phone, presumably. Xiaoran frowned.

He had his phone.

She knew that was an unreasonable conclusion to draw from a photograph taken God knew when, but it didn’t stop her from looking at it again.

Just after nine, she called him a second time. No answer. A little after nine, she sent another message.

Xiaoran, 9:17 PM: Are you busy?

Then, after staring at the message for several seconds:

Call me when you’re free.

She put the phone beside her pillow. She tried to concentrate on her assignment. She really did.

But every few minutes, her eyes drifted towards the phone. She began to notice how quiet her room was. How long the evening was becoming. How she had so many small things she wanted to tell him. Her lecturer had praised her presentation.

She had seen a funny dog on the way home.

She had bought a new hair clip and wanted him to tell her whether it suited her. Nothing important. But she wanted to tell him anyway.

A little before ten, she opened their chat again.

The last thing he had said was Yes, coach. She pressed her lips together.

“Zhou Yichen.”

There was no one to hear her complaint. She sent him a sticker of a little rabbit sitting alone in the rain. Then she immediately regretted it. It looked too pitiful. She deleted it. The message remained marked as deleted.

“Ah!”

She dropped her phone onto the bed and covered her face with both hands. This was ridiculous.

He was at an away game. He was probably tired. He had a team dinner, teammates, coaches, and a bus journey. He was allowed to have a life outside their relationship. She knew all of that.

She also knew that five hours wasn’t an unreasonable amount of time to be unavailable.

But knowing something logically and feeling it were two entirely different things.

✦ ✦ ✦

And then, unexpectedly, she remembered orientation day. The first week of university. He had walked her all the way to the Media building first, because his own orientation started later and her sense of direction was a known disaster. He had told her to text him if she got lost. She hadn’t got lost.

She had got bored, wandered downstairs at the break, and stood talking to a senior called Gu Ming while her phone sat on silent at the bottom of her bag. Twenty-three unread messages.

She remembered the moment she heard her name behind her, much too calm. She remembered his face: not angry the way other people were angry. Worse. Quiet. He had already been to the orientation hall to look for her, and she hadn’t been there.

At the time, she had mostly felt guilty, and then relieved when he finally smiled.

She had never really thought about the two hours before that.

The two hours in which he had sent twenty-three messages and heard nothing back. Xiaoran looked at their chat. Then she looked at the time. 10:21 PM.

“Oh.”

For the first time, she understood exactly what he had felt that day.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little before eleven PM, Xiaoran finally decided to stop waiting.

She brushed her teeth, changed into her pyjamas, and climbed into bed. Her phone was on the bedside table.

She turned it face down, then turned it back up, then face down again. She lasted approximately four minutes.

Just before eleven, she opened their chat and typed:

I’m going to sleep. Hope you got back safely.

She hesitated. Then added:

Good night.

She pressed send. For a moment, she stared at the two grey message bubbles.

Then she put her phone back on the bedside table and settled beneath the blanket. She was almost asleep when it happened. A vibration, then another.

Then the familiar ringtone she had assigned exclusively to one person.

Xiaoran sat up so quickly that her blanket slipped to her waist.

Zhou Yichen calling…

She answered immediately.

“Hello?”

“Xiaoran?”

His voice was slightly rough, tired, and unmistakably familiar. She closed her eyes.

“You’re alive.”

There was a pause, then a quiet laugh.

“Yes. I’m alive.”

“Your phone?”

“Dead.”

She blinked.

“What?”

“My phone died on the way back. I didn’t realise until we sat down to dinner.”

Xiaoran stared at the screen.

“Your phone died?”

“Completely. Dinner, then recovery, then two hours of footage with Coach. I borrowed my roommate’s charger, but his cable wasn’t compatible. Fang Ze had the right one, and he didn’t get back to the room until half past ten.”

“Then why didn’t you borrow someone else’s phone?”

“Your number’s in mine. I don’t know it by heart. I do now. Fang Ze tested me twice. Then mine turned on and I called you.” He sounded deeply ashamed of this.

She went quiet. Yichen noticed immediately.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Xiaoran.”

She pulled the blanket closer.

“Nothing. I was just waiting.”

There was a small silence.

“How long?”

“Not that long.”

“How long, Xiaoran?”

She glanced at the clock.

“Five hours.”

He didn’t respond immediately.

Then, “I’m sorry.”

She had expected him to laugh at her, perhaps tease her for being impatient.

Instead, his apology made something in her chest loosen.

She said, “I thought you were busy. Then I thought you were eating. Then I thought you were showering. Then I thought maybe you were talking to your teammates.”

“Mhm.”

“And then I thought maybe you saw my messages but didn’t have time to answer.”

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I wasn’t ignoring you.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

She pressed her lips together.

“...I know now.”

He exhaled, the sound coming through the speaker.

“Did you worry?”

She considered lying. But she had spent the last five hours imagining all sorts of explanations. There was no point pretending she hadn’t.

“A little.”

“Only a little?”

“Don’t push it.”

He laughed. She could almost picture him sitting on the edge of the hotel bed, one hand holding his phone, his hair still damp after a shower.

“Did you eat?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Food.”

“That’s a very informative answer.”

“Rice. Chicken. Vegetables. Happy?”

“Very.”

“And you?”

“I ate with the team.”

“Properly?”

“Yes.”

“Don’t lie.”

“I’m not.”

She hummed, still not entirely satisfied. Yichen was quiet.

Then he asked, “Did you finish your assignment?”

“Almost.”

“Don’t stay up too late.”

“I was already going to sleep.”

“Good.”

Another pause. This time, Xiaoran was the one who didn’t want to end the call.

“Yichen?”

“I’m here.”

“Do you remember orientation day?”

“Twenty-three messages,” he said.

She closed her eyes.

“You counted.”

“I sent them.”

She played with the corner of her blanket.

“Was it like this?”

“What?”

“Waiting for someone to answer. Checking your phone. Wondering what they’re doing.”

Yichen didn’t answer immediately. When he did, his voice was gentle.

“Worse. At least tonight you knew I was with twelve other people and a coach.”

“And that day you didn’t know I was downstairs.”

“I didn’t know you were downstairs talking to Gu Ming.”

“You remember his name?”

“I remember everything about that day.”

She laughed into her pillow, a small, guilty laugh.

“You only said it once. That I scared you.”

“Once was all I could manage.”

Xiaoran stared at the ceiling.

“Oh.”

“Why?”

“Because I think I understand now.”

“Understand what?”

“Why you always ask me to message you when I arrive.”

He smiled on the other end.

“That wasn’t a particularly complicated mystery.”

“Don’t ruin my moment.”

“Sorry.”

“And why you ask whether I’ve eaten, even when I tell you I’m going out for only an hour.”

“That’s a different matter. You forget to eat.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed. She rolled onto her side, hugging her pillow.

“I thought you were just being fussy.”

“I am.”

“At least you admit it.”

“But I’m also allowed to worry about my girlfriend.”

She went quiet again.

Then, in a much smaller voice, “I missed you.”

His teasing disappeared.

“I missed you too.”

“You were only gone for one night.”

“I know.”

“That’s not very long.”

“No.”

“But it felt long.”

He was silent. Then she heard the faint rustle of fabric.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Next time, if my phone dies, I’ll find a way to let you know. I’ll ask Fang Ze to message you, or borrow someone else’s phone.”

She smiled.

“You don’t have to make a whole emergency communication plan.”

“I’d rather you know I’m safe.”

Her smile grew.

“Okay.”

“And you?”

“Me?”

“If you can’t reach me, don’t spend five hours imagining every possible explanation.”

She frowned.

“I didn’t imagine every possible explanation.”

“Only a few?”

“...Quite a few.”

He chuckled.

“Just send me one message. If I can answer, I will. If I can’t, I’ll get back to you when I can.”

She nodded, even though he couldn’t see her.

“Okay.”

“And don’t be afraid to tell me you’re worried.”

“I wasn’t afraid.”

“You deleted a message.”

Xiaoran froze.

“...How do you know that?”

“Because I saw the notification that you had deleted one.”

She buried her face in her pillow.

“Oh my God.”

“What did it say?”

“Nothing.”

“Was it important?”

“No.”

“Was it a picture?”

“No!”

“Then what was it?”

“Good night, Zhou Yichen.”

He laughed, a low, unhurried sound.

“All right. I’ll let you keep your secrets.”

She lifted her head.

“You’re not going to ask again?”

“I could.”

“But?”

“But I know you’ll get embarrassed.”

She narrowed her eyes at the phone. He was smiling. She could hear it.

“You’re so annoying.”

“Mhm.”

“Very annoying.”

“All right.”

“Don’t just agree with me!”

“What would you like me to say?”

She thought for a moment.

“That you missed me.”

“I already said that.”

“Say it again.”

His answer came without hesitation.

“I missed you, Xiaoran.”

Her cheeks warmed.

“Okay.”

“Anything else?”

She hesitated. Then she whispered, “I wish you were here.”

The silence that followed was different. It was the kind of quiet that came when both people were thinking the same thing.

“I’ll be back tomorrow afternoon,” he said.

“I know.”

“I’ll come straight to see you.”

“You don’t have to. You should rest.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

“Because I want to.”

She smiled into her pillow.

“Okay.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next afternoon, Xiaoran was waiting outside the university’s main entrance.

She had told herself she was only there because she happened to finish class early. It was a lie.

She had checked the time of his arrival three times, changed her outfit once, and bought two drinks from the café near the entrance because she remembered he liked the iced Americano from there.

When the team bus finally turned in at the gate, she straightened.

It stopped in front of her with a long sigh of brakes.

Yichen stepped out, wearing a dark jacket and carrying his duffel bag over one shoulder. He looked tired.

Not terribly so, but there were faint shadows beneath his eyes, and his hair was slightly dishevelled from the journey. Xiaoran walked towards him.

He barely had time to put his bag down before she wrapped both arms around his waist. Yichen’s expression softened.

He held her close, one hand settling between her shoulder blades, the other gently cradling the back of her head.

“Hello,” he murmured.

She pressed her cheek against his chest.

“Hello.”

“Waiting long?”

“No.”

He glanced at the two drinks in her hand.

“How long?”

“Not long.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Twenty minutes.”

He smiled and pressed his mouth to her hair.

“Thank you for waiting.”

She leaned back to see him.

“You’re welcome.”

His eyes moved over her face, taking in the little pout she hadn’t quite managed to hide.

“Still upset?”

“No.”

“Really?”

“Maybe a little.”

He nodded seriously.

“Then I should apologise properly.”

She blinked.

“How?”

He pressed a kiss to her temple. Then her left cheek. Then her right. Xiaoran’s pout weakened.

“That’s not enough.”

“Not enough?”

She nodded with great seriousness. Yichen’s mouth curved.

“What else does the offended party require?”

She looked at his lips, then quickly looked away.

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

“You’re tired.”

He studied her for a second, then gently touched her chin.

“I’m tired. I’m not too tired to kiss my girlfriend.”

Her face turned pink.

“Who said anything about kissing?”

“You’ve been looking at my mouth for the past ten seconds.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed and kissed her properly. It was unhurried, warm, and familiar. His hand rested lightly against her cheek, his thumb brushing once beneath her eye before he pulled away. Xiaoran looked at him, a little dazed. He smiled.

“Better?”

“Much.”

“Good.”

She handed him the iced Americano.

“I bought this for you.”

He accepted it, looking at the cup before turning back to her.

“You remembered.”

“Of course I remembered.”

“Thank you.”

She watched him take a sip. Then, as they walked towards the car park, she slipped her hand into his.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“I think I understand something now.”

He glanced at her.

“What?”

“You’re always so calm when I get lost or don’t answer quickly. But I think you’re not actually calm.”

His fingers tightened gently around hers. He considered that.

“Sometimes.”

She looked up at him.

“Then I’ll try to be more considerate.”

He smiled.

“You don’t have to change everything because of one evening.”

“I know. But I want to.”

She swung their joined hands lightly.

“And you should also be more considerate.”

“How?”

“Don’t let your phone die.”

He laughed.

“I’ll do my best.”

“Bring a power bank.”

“All right.”

“And a spare cable.”

“Anything else?”

She pretended to think.

“Maybe a satellite phone.”

“That’s a little excessive.”

“You have a girlfriend who worries.”

“I’ve noticed.”

She nudged his arm. He looked down at her, his expression quietly affectionate.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Next time, if you’re worried, just tell me. You don’t have to pretend you’re fine.”

She looked at him. For once, she didn’t have a playful answer ready. Instead, she squeezed his hand.

“Okay.”

He lifted their joined hands and kissed her knuckles.

“And I’ll do the same.”

“Good.”

They reached the car park, where his car had been sitting for two days under a layer of leaves. Yichen opened the passenger door for her, then placed his bag in the back. Before getting in, Xiaoran caught his sleeve. He turned.

“What is it?”

She watched him, then hooked a hand behind his neck and kissed his cheek.

“Welcome back.”

His expression softened in a way that made her heart flutter.

He leaned down, returning a kiss to her hair.

“I’m home.”

And somehow, that was the part that made her happiest. Those two words.

Because she had spent the previous evening learning what it felt like to wait for someone she loved.

And now she understood why, every time she walked away from him, Zhou Yichen always watched until she was safely out of sight.

chapters.desc: She wins four concert tickets for six friends who have waited weeks, and she would rather not be the one who chooses.
chapters.title: Ticket Allocation
chapters.epigraph: “Besides, I got the ticket.”
chapters.content:
The trouble began with four tickets. Not five, not six. Lin Xiaoran counted them twice.

“There’s a problem,” she said.

Zhou Yichen was on her sofa with a corporate finance textbook open on his knees. He turned a page. “What problem?”

“Four tickets.”

He looked over at the dining table, where her laptop was open on the confirmation page. “Yes.”

“Six people.”

He looked up properly.

She turned the laptop round. On the screen was the group chat: her, Tang Meilin, Chen Yuhao, Luo Jiayi and Ning. Yichen wasn’t in it, because it was called besties 4ever 🌸 and he had said, with real feeling, that he would die. They’d been talking about the concert for weeks. It was a singer Xiaoran had loved since high school, playing Shanghai for the first time, and Meilin and Yuhao had already booked trains in for the weekend. It was going to be the first time all six of them were in one city since the summer. Everyone had entered the ticket lottery, and nobody had expected anything.

Xiaoran had won. Four tickets, the most one account could buy.

“Jiayi’s cousin’s wedding is that Saturday,” he said.

“I know. So five people. Four tickets.”

“And one of the four is yours. You won them.”

“I’m not taking one just because I won them.”

“You are. So three tickets and four people,” he said.

She picked up her phone and looked at the confirmation as if the answer might be on it somewhere. “Three tickets and four people who matter.”

“Am I counted as one of the people who matter?”

“Don’t start.”

“I’m only clarifying.”

“Obviously you’re one of them. That’s the problem,” she said.

“Have you asked everyone?”

“Not yet.”

“Why not?”

“Because I don’t want anyone to feel left out.”

“Then don’t decide for them. Tell them what happened. Let them work it out,” he said.

“But someone still won’t get one.”

“That’s true.”

“You’re not helping.”

“I’m trying to.”

“You’re being too reasonable.”

“Would you rather I panicked with you?”

She thought about it. “A bit.”

He laughed and held his hand out as she walked past the sofa, and pulled her down beside him, and she curled up against his side with her phone.

“Ask them,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The chat fell apart within three minutes.

Xiaoran: important announcement. I WON THE LOTTERY

Meilin: WHAT

Yuhao: OUR GIRL

Ning: XIAORAN!!!!

Meilin: four tickets right?

Xiaoran: yes

Yuhao: perfect, four of us

Xiaoran: there are five of us without Jiayi

Yuhao: ...

Meilin: oh

Yuhao: I’ve just remembered I have an extremely important appointment that night

Meilin: you are not sacrificing yourself. don’t be dramatic

Yuhao: I was being noble

Meilin: you were being annoying

Xiaoran: nobody has to give up anything!! let’s talk about it properly on friday

Meilin: Xiaoran. breathe

Ning: nobody’s going to fight over this

Yuhao: I might

Meilin: you can fight me

Yuhao: I withdraw

She held the phone up so he could see. “They’re fighting already.”

“Yuhao and Meilin?”

“Yes.”

“That’s normal,” he said.

She tucked herself against his shoulder. “I don’t want to choose.”

“Then don’t.”

“Someone has to.”

“Not necessarily. Wait till you see them,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They met on Friday at the café by the east gate, two hours after Meilin and Yuhao’s train got in. Meilin came first, then Ning. Yuhao turned up ten minutes late with his weekend bag still on his shoulder and an iced tea in his hand, looking far too pleased with himself.

Meilin dropped into the chair opposite. “Right. Show me.”

Xiaoran passed her phone across. Meilin studied the seats.

“These are good.”

“Really?”

“You did well.”

“I didn’t do anything. I just got lucky.”

“Luck’s a skill,” said Meilin.

Yuhao leaned over. “Can I see?”

Meilin moved the phone out of his reach. “Don’t breathe on it. You’ve got bad luck.”

“Excuse me?”

“You once lost a coin toss to a vending machine.”

Ning laughed. Xiaoran took a breath.

“Okay. About the tickets—”

Meilin said, “Wait. Let’s get one thing straight first. Nobody’s going to be upset with you. You won them. One of them is yours, and that’s not up for a vote. You don’t owe us anything.”

“I know, but—”

“No, listen. We’ve all been excited. But it’s not worth you being miserable.” Meilin’s voice softened.

“She’s right,” said Ning.

Yuhao raised his iced tea. “I volunteer to give up my ticket.”

They all looked at him.

“What? I’m generous.”

“Why?” said Meilin.

“Because I can.”

“That’s not a reason.”

“I have excellent character.”

“You have a suspicious face.”

“Honestly,” Yuhao said, putting the drink down, “I like her. But I was mostly coming because all of you were. If somebody else wants it more, fine.”

“I feel the same. I want to go. But if someone wants it more, I’d sit it out,” said Ning, slowly.

“Don’t say that just to be nice,” said Meilin.

“I’m not.”

Yichen hadn’t said anything. He was next to Xiaoran with one hand on the table by hers. Meilin turned to him.

“And you?”

“What about me?”

“You’re one of the four.”

He glanced sideways. Xiaoran was already looking at him with a small crease between her eyebrows. She wanted him there. He could see it. And he could see that she wouldn’t take a ticket from one of her oldest friends because she wanted him next to her.

He found her hand under the table. “I don’t mind sitting this one out.”

“But you said you wanted to hear her live.”

“I’ll hear her down the phone. At the end of every song. Because you’ll call me,” he said.

“That’s not the same.”

“No, it isn’t. Go with your friends,” he agreed.

Meilin, watching them across the table, put her drink down. “Right. I have a proposal.”

Yuhao groaned. “That sounds dangerous.”

“Shut up. All four names in a draw. Three tickets. Whoever’s left out gets first claim on the next one. Nobody volunteers, nobody’s noble, nobody’s annoying.”

“That’s fair,” said Xiaoran.

“Finally. Democracy,” said Yuhao.

“You’re not allowed to speak,” said Meilin.

They tore a napkin into four. Ning wrote the names. Yuhao insisted on folding them. Meilin accused him of folding his own name differently so he could find it, and made Ning refold all four. Xiaoran sat with her shoulders up round her ears.

“Why are you so tense?” Yichen murmured.

“Because I don’t want to see anyone disappointed.”

He rubbed his thumb across her knuckles under the table. “Whatever happens, we’ll be fine.”

“You’re really okay with not going?”

“I’d rather you enjoyed the concert,” he said, “than spent all night worrying about me.”

Ning put the four folded squares in the middle of the table. “Ready?”

“Should we have dramatic music?” said Yuhao.

Meilin kicked him. “Pick one.”

The first one was Meilin. She grinned. “Excellent.”

The second was Ning, who let out a breath.

Two squares left. Yuhao reached for one. “Allow me.”

Meilin caught his wrist. “Don’t make it theatrical.”

“You’re ruining the moment,” he said, and opened it, and looked at it, and burst out laughing. He turned it round.

ZHOU YICHEN

Xiaoran stared at the napkin. Then at Yichen. Then at the napkin again.

“Wait. You got it.”

“So it seems.”

“You got the ticket.”

“Yes. Are you disappointed?” He was watching her face.

“No! I’m happy. I’m so happy. But—” She shook her head so hard her hair flew.

Yuhao unfolded the last square with great ceremony and laid it on the table. It said CHEN YUHAO.

“I,” he announced, “have been betrayed by probability.”

“You volunteered!” said Meilin.

“That was before probability attacked me personally.”

Xiaoran reached across the table and grabbed his wrist. “Yuhao, are you really okay?”

He waved her off. “I’m fine. I’ll be doing something much more meaningful that night.”

“Like what?”

“Watching all of you post videos and regretting my generosity. Send me everything,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the way back to her flat she was quiet. He had her bag over his shoulder and her hand in his coat pocket.

“What are you thinking about?”

“Yuhao.”

“He’s fine.”

“I know. If you hadn’t got it, I’d have wanted to give you mine.” She looked up at him.

“Would you?”

“Yes.”

“After waiting since high school to see her?”

She hesitated. “Maybe.”

He stopped on the pavement. She turned round.

“What?”

He said, “I want you to know something. I like going places with you. I like being part of the things you’re excited about. But I don’t need to be part of all of them. Some things should be yours. You should go with Meilin and Ning and scream and lose your voice and not have to check whether I’m having a good time. And I’ll still be here when you get back.”

She looked at him under the streetlamp. Then she put her arms round his middle inside his open coat and held on.

He bent his head and said into her hair, “Besides, I got the ticket.”

She laughed into his chest. “You did.”

“Very lucky.”

“Extremely.”

“Almost suspicious.”

“Don’t ruin it,” she said, and didn’t let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the night of the concert Yuhao walked them to the venue, took a photograph of the four of them outside it, reminded them loudly to enjoy themselves on his behalf, and went off to find dumplings. Inside, the hall was enormous and dark and roaring. Xiaoran stood with her phone up, taking a picture of the stage, and sent it to him out of pure habit.

Xiaoran: it’s starting!!

Yichen: I can see that.

Xiaoran: I wish you were here

Yichen: I’m right next to you.

She looked up. He was standing beside her with two drinks in one hand, looking down at her, holding the other out. She took it and wound her fingers through his.
