“Don’t spend the whole concert texting me.”

“I wasn’t!”

“You were.”

“I was updating you,” she said, and then the lights went down and the crowd screamed, and she screamed with them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning Yuhao got four photographs in the group chat. One of the stage. One of Meilin singing with her eyes shut. One of Ning laughing. And one, taken by Ning during the encore, of Xiaoran looking up at the stage with her whole face lit, and Yichen beside her with his arm round her shoulders, looking at her and not at the singer at all.

Yuhao: I see how it is

Meilin: what now

Yuhao: I gave up my ticket AND I’m excluded from the romantic photography

Xiaoran: it’s a nice picture!!

Yuhao: it’s disgusting. put him in the chat so I can tell him

Meilin: he refuses to join a chat with a flower in the name

Yuhao: a man of principle. I respect that. I still hate him

She laughed so much in the café the next morning that she had to put her phone away. Yichen, beside her with a coffee, looked over.

“Yuhao?”

“He’s still grieving.”

“Understandable.”

She leaned against his shoulder and opened the encore photograph again. “Next time we’re getting five tickets.”

“Next time?”

“Obviously. And nobody gets sacrificed.”

“Agreed. Unless Yuhao volunteers again,” he said.

“Yichen!”

He kissed her temple, entirely unrepentant, and then picked up her phone and saved the encore photograph to his own, which she pretended not to notice.

chapters.desc: A schedule planned to the minute, a cup and a fruit bowl, and a sunset that refuses to cooperate.
chapters.title: Four Years, Planned Badly
chapters.epigraph: “That one’s flexible.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had a schedule. Not a vague schedule.

Not a general idea of what she and Zhou Yichen might do on their anniversary. A schedule. Down to the minute.

She had spent three evenings preparing it, one afternoon revising it, and approximately forty minutes arguing with herself about whether the sunset was better at 4:52 or 4:55.

At the top of her notebook, written in pink ink with three little hearts, was the title:

OUR FOURTH ANNIVERSARY — A PERFECT DAY.

Below it:

08:00 — Wake up.

08:05 — Send anniversary greeting.

08:10 — Receive anniversary greeting.

08:15 — Get ready.

09:00 — Breakfast.

09:45 — First surprise.

10:30 — Activity chosen by Xiaoran.

12:00 — Lunch.

13:30 — Second surprise.

15:00 — Free time (romantic interaction encouraged).

16:50 — Sunset.

18:30 — Dinner.

20:00 — Final surprise.

21:00 — End of anniversary.

She stared at the last line, then crossed it out.

21:00 — No end.

Much better.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was admiring her work when her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Are you awake?

Xiaoran glanced at the clock. 7:56 AM. She immediately sat up. Four minutes early. He was ruining the schedule already.

Xiaoran: No.

Yichen: Then who’s replying?

Xiaoran: My assistant.

Yichen: Good morning to your assistant, then.

She giggled. Before she could reply, another message arrived.

Yichen: Happy fourth anniversary, Xiaoran.

Her smile softened. Four years. Four years since they had started dating. Four years of knowing how he took his coffee, which side of the bed he preferred, how he looked when he was concentrating, and the exact expression he made when she was about to do something ridiculous. Four years of being loved by Zhou Yichen. She typed carefully.

Xiaoran: Happy anniversary, boyfriend.

Then she added a heart, then three more, then a sticker of two little bears hugging. Her phone rang. She answered immediately.

“Hello!”

“Good morning.”

“Good morning!”

“Did you sleep well?”

“Perfectly.”

“You’re unusually energetic.”

“Because today is a very important day.”

“I know.”

There was a smile in his voice.

“Are you ready?”

Xiaoran looked at her notebook.

“More than ready.”

“Should I be worried?”

“No.”

A pause.

“That’s not reassuring.”

She laughed.

“Come pick me up at nine!”

“I’ll be there.”

“And don’t be late.”

“I won’t.”

“And wear something nice.”

“What counts as nice?”

“Something that makes me want to kiss you.”

Yichen laughed.

“That’s a rather broad requirement.”

“Then you shouldn’t have asked.”

“All right. I’ll see you soon.”

She hung up, looked at the notebook, and made her first adjustment.

08:10 — Receive anniversary greeting.

Completed.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 9:02, Zhou Yichen arrived. Xiaoran was waiting downstairs, dressed in a pretty cream-coloured dress with a small ribbon in her hair. She had a little bag over her shoulder and a notebook tucked inside it. Yichen stepped out of the car.

He wore a dark shirt with the sleeves casually folded to his forearms, tailored trousers, and a watch she had once told him looked particularly good on him. He looked at her, then smiled. He reached for her.

Xiaoran approached with a bright smile, expecting a greeting.

Instead, he took her hand, pulled her gently closer, and pressed a kiss into her hair.

“Happy anniversary.”

She beamed.

“Happy anniversary!”

His gaze lingered on her face.

“You look beautiful.”

“I know.”

He raised an eyebrow. She quickly corrected herself.

“I mean, thank you. You’re also very handsome.”

“Only also?”

“Extremely handsome.”

“Better.”

He opened the passenger door for her. Xiaoran got in, carefully arranging her dress. As he walked around to the driver’s side, she took out her notebook. Yichen noticed.

“What are you reading?”

“Nothing.”

“Your notebook?”

“It’s a private document.”

“Should I be concerned?”

“No.”

He started the car. She turned towards him.

“Before we go, I have something to say.”

“I’m listening.”

“Today, you must follow my instructions.”

“All right.”

“No complaining.”

“Understood.”

“No asking too many questions.”

“That’s going to be difficult.”

“And you have to pretend to be surprised when I surprise you.”

He glanced at her.

“How do you pretend to be surprised?”

“Like this.”

She opened her mouth, widened her eyes, and raised both hands. Yichen considered her. Then he laughed.

“Very convincing.”

“Don’t laugh! I’m demonstrating!”

“Sorry.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re already making this difficult.”

He reached over and squeezed her hand.

“All right, director. I’ll cooperate.”

✦ ✦ ✦

09:00 — Breakfast.

The first destination was the little café near campus that they had claimed as theirs the week they moved to Shanghai, the summer before first year. Xiaoran had chosen it deliberately.

The place hadn’t changed much. The wooden tables were still slightly uneven, the window seats still caught the morning light, and the owner still remembered them.

“Ah, you two! It’s been a while.” the woman greeted them warmly.

Xiaoran smiled.

“Hello, Auntie!”

The woman looked between them.

“Still together?”

Xiaoran nearly choked.

“Auntie!”

Yichen, meanwhile, looked perfectly comfortable.

“Four years today.”

“Four years! That’s wonderful. You must take good care of her.” The woman clapped her hands.

“I will.”

Xiaoran turned to him.

“Why did you answer so seriously?”

“Was I supposed to lie?”

She nudged his knee under the table. He smiled.

They ordered the same breakfast they had ordered the first morning they found the place: pancakes, eggs, and two drinks. Xiaoran had remembered the details. Yichen had remembered too.

When the food arrived, he cut a piece of pancake and placed it on her plate. She looked at it, then at him.

“You’re supposed to let me do that today.”

“Why?”

“Because I’m the planner.”

“Does that mean I can’t take care of you?”

She considered this.

“No. You can take care of me. But I should also take care of you.”

“Then we’re both doing our jobs.”

She liked that answer. After breakfast, she took out her phone.

“Wait.”

“What?”

“Photograph.”

He leaned towards her. She raised the phone, positioning them carefully. Yichen looked at the camera, but just before she pressed the shutter, he turned and kissed her cheek.

The photograph captured her surprised expression and his smile. Xiaoran stared at it.

“You’re cheating.”

“How?”

“I wasn’t ready.”

“You look happy.”

She zoomed in. Unfortunately, he was right. She looked happy. She saved it.

✦ ✦ ✦

09:45 — First surprise.

Xiaoran led him to a small photography studio. Yichen looked at the sign, then at her.

“What’s this?”

“Surprise number one.”

Inside, a photographer greeted them. Xiaoran had booked a short couple’s portrait session. Yichen looked at her.

“You arranged this?”

“Yes.”

“How long ago?”

“Two weeks.”

He glanced at the photographer, then back at her.

“Did you choose the clothes?”

“Obviously.”

She pulled a small envelope from her bag.

“Here.”

Inside were two printed photographs. The first was from their high-school days, taken when they were still young and slightly awkward about being photographed together. Yichen had one arm around her shoulders, while Xiaoran was smiling so widely that her eyes were almost closed.

The second was more recent, taken during their university years.

They stood side by side, a little more grown up, but with the same comfortable closeness. Yichen studied them.

“You kept these?”

“Of course.”

She pointed at the first photograph.

“Look at your hair.”

He looked down.

“My hair?”

“It was so flat.”

“It was raining.”

“Your expression was also so serious.”

“I was trying to take a good photograph.”

“You looked like you were attending a business meeting.”

He gave her a sidelong glance.

“Perhaps I was already practising.”

She laughed. The photographer called them over.

They took several photographs: one formal, one playful, one with Xiaoran standing on her toes to kiss his cheek, then the photographer suggested a final pose.

“Could you stand closer? Perhaps the gentleman can hold her waist.”

Yichen’s hand settled naturally at Xiaoran’s waist.

“And look at each other.”

They did. Xiaoran was prepared to smile. But Yichen was looking at her with an expression she knew very well. Quiet. Warm. A little amused.

“What?” she whispered.

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me.”

“It’s a photograph.”

“You’re supposed to look at the camera.”

“Then look at the camera.”

She tried.

He leaned closer and murmured, “You’re very pretty.”

Her cheeks warmed. The camera clicked. The photographer laughed.

“That one is lovely.”

Xiaoran didn’t need to see the result to know she would like it.

✦ ✦ ✦

10:30 — Activity chosen by Xiaoran.

This was where things began to go wrong. She had booked a pottery class. A romantic pottery class.

She had imagined them sitting side by side, making matching cups, laughing, and perhaps getting a little clay on each other’s noses.

The reality was that Xiaoran’s cup began collapsing after seven minutes.

“Why is it leaning?”

Yichen glanced at it.

“You’re pressing too hard on one side.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“Don’t criticise my cup.”

“I’m helping.”

“You’re making it worse.”

He looked at her clay, then at his own. His was perfectly symmetrical. Xiaoran stared at it.

“Why is yours so good?”

“I followed the instructor’s directions.”

“I followed the instructor’s directions!”

“You were looking at me.”

She paused.

“...That’s irrelevant.”

He smiled. The instructor came over and helped her reshape the clay.

“Don’t worry. It takes practice.”

Xiaoran nodded solemnly.

“I’ll try again.”

Ten minutes later, she accidentally pressed too hard. The cup collapsed. She stared at the clay. Yichen pressed his lips together.

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face did.”

He finally laughed. She turned towards him, scandalized.

“You’re laughing at me!”

“I’m sorry.”

“You’re not sorry.”

He leaned over and gently wiped a small streak of clay from her cheek.

“No, I’m not.”

She looked at him. His smile was so attractive that she forgot her complaint for a second. Then she remembered.

“Stop being handsome. It’s distracting.”

He laughed again. By the end of the class, Yichen had made a neat little cup.

Xiaoran had made something that resembled a bowl with an uncertain identity. The instructor placed their creations side by side.

“Very nice! A matching set.”

Xiaoran looked at the two pieces.

“His is a cup.”

She pointed at hers.

“Mine is a fruit bowl.”

Yichen considered it.

“Then we have a complete household.”

She gasped.

“You’re going to use it?”

“Of course.”

He looked at her. Her expression softened. Then she quickly looked away.

“That’s a very good answer.”

✦ ✦ ✦

12:00 — Lunch.

Xiaoran had chosen a restaurant with a view of the city.

She had also arranged a small dessert plate with a handwritten message:

Four years with you. Still my favourite person.

Yichen read it, then looked at her.

“Did you write this?”

“Yes.”

“It’s nice.”

“Just nice?”

He set the card down.

“It’s very nice.”

She waited. He didn’t elaborate. She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re supposed to say something more romantic.”

He leaned back.

“What would you like me to say?”

“Something like, ‘You’re the best thing that ever happened to me.’”

Then said, “You’re the best thing that ever happened to me.”

She blinked. He continued calmly.

“Was that what you wanted?”

“Don’t say it like you’re reading from a script!”

His mouth curved.

“Would you prefer a spontaneous version?”

“Yes.”

He found her hand on the table.

“Four years ago, I thought I was a fairly patient person.”

She looked at him.

“Then I met you.”

“Excuse me?”

He smiled.

“I learned that I could spend an entire afternoon waiting for someone to decide what to eat, change her mind three times, and still be happy about it.”

Xiaoran tried not to smile.

“That’s not romantic.”

“I also learned that I like being the person you tell everything to. Even things that don’t matter.”

She went still.

“That I look forward to seeing your name on my phone. That I remember the smallest things you say. That when something good happens, you’re the first person I want to tell.”

His thumb brushed over her knuckles.

“And that after four years, I still look at you and feel very lucky that you chose me.”

Xiaoran stared at him. Her lips parted slightly. Then she looked down at their hands.

“You’re cheating.”

He smiled.

“How?”

“You didn’t tell me you were going to say something like that.”

“I didn’t know I was going to.”

She pressed her lips together, trying to hide her smile. It didn’t work.

“Eat your lunch,” she mumbled.

He laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

13:30 — Second surprise.

This was supposed to be the most organised part of the day.

Xiaoran had booked a private room in a small gallery that hosted a rotating exhibition.

But when they arrived, the staff informed them that the room was unavailable for another thirty minutes due to a scheduling mistake. Xiaoran stared.

“Thirty minutes?”

The staff apologised. She checked her notebook. 13:30. The exact time.

She checked again, as if the numbers might change out of sympathy. Yichen stood beside her, watching.

“It’s fine.”

“But we have a schedule.”

“I noticed.”

“Everything is supposed to happen at the correct time.”

He glanced at his watch.

“We’re still together. I think we’re doing all right.”

She sighed.

“You don’t understand. I planned this.”

“I know.”

“And now we’re waiting.”

“We can wait.”

She looked at him. He was completely unbothered. It was almost offensive.

“How are you so calm?”

He looked down at her.

“Because I’m with you.”

She stared, then looked away.

“You’re doing that on purpose.”

“Doing what?”

“Saying things.”

He smiled. They spent the next thirty minutes wandering around the gallery. Xiaoran stopped at every painting, reading the descriptions aloud and occasionally inventing stories about the people depicted. Yichen followed her, listening. At one painting, she stood.

It showed two people sitting together on a balcony, their shoulders touching, looking out at the sea.

“It’s nice,” she said.

“Why?”

“Because they’re not doing anything special. They’re just sitting together.”

Yichen looked at the painting, then at her.

“That sounds familiar.”

“Maybe that’s what I want when we’re old.”

“What?”

“To sit together. Somewhere with a nice view. You can read your newspaper, and I’ll bother you.”

“You don’t need to wait until we’re old to do that.”

She turned to him.

“Really?”

“You can bother me now.”

She laughed and slipped her hand into his. When the gallery room finally opened, Xiaoran led him inside. There were photographs displayed along the walls. Their photographs.

Some were printed from old pictures she had collected. Others were candid shots from their university years: Yichen holding her bag while she tied her shoelaces, Xiaoran falling asleep on his shoulder, their hands intertwined on a café table, a blurry photograph of them laughing.

At the centre was a small table with a scrapbook. Yichen picked it up. The first page read:

FOUR YEARS OF US.

He turned the pages slowly. There were little notes beside the photographs.

The first time you walked me home.

The day you waited at the school gate because I forgot my umbrella.

The first time you watched my presentation.

The day you joined the basketball team.

The day I realised I wanted to keep choosing you.

He paused at the last one. Xiaoran was watching him.

“I wanted to make something you could keep. Not just photographs on your phone. Something physical,” she said.

He turned another page. There was a photograph of them sitting on a bench, taken from behind. Underneath, she had written:

I don’t remember what we were talking about. I just remember thinking that I could sit beside you for a long time.

Yichen closed the scrapbook gently. He said nothing. Then he looked at her.

“You made all of this?”

She nodded.

“Some of the photographs were from your phone. I stole them.”

“I noticed some were missing.”

She winced.

“Sorry.”

He smiled faintly.

“That’s all right.”

He set the scrapbook down and drew her into his arms. Xiaoran wrapped hers around his waist. He kissed her hair.

“Thank you.”

She smiled against his chest.

“You’re welcome.”

He held her for a little longer than she expected.

When he finally pulled away, his eyes were warm.

“Can I have one more photograph?”

“Of what?”

“Us.”

She immediately reached for her phone.

“Of course!”

But he shook his head.

“Not with the phone.”

He took the scrapbook, opened it to the final page, and placed it back on the table. Then he took her hand.

“Let’s make another memory.”

✦ ✦ ✦

15:00 — Free time (romantic interaction encouraged).

Xiaoran had written that part as a joke. Unfortunately, Yichen had taken it seriously.

They went to a quiet park nearby. The afternoon was cold and bright, and the plane trees had dropped nearly all their leaves on the paths.

They bought ice cream anyway, because Xiaoran said anniversaries didn’t have weather. Xiaoran chose strawberry. Yichen chose coffee.

She took one bite of his, then another, then a third. He watched her.

“Is yours not good?”

“It’s good.”

“Then why are you eating mine?”

“Because yours is also good.”

He gave her the cup. She smiled triumphantly. They found a bench and sat together.

Xiaoran leaned against his shoulder, holding the ice cream with both hands.

For a while, they simply watched people passing by. Then she remembered something.

“Oh!”

Yichen looked down.

“What?”

“I forgot something.”

He glanced at his watch.

“What’s next?”

“Nothing. I just forgot to tell you something.”

“All right.”

She sat up.

“I want to say thank you.”

He turned towards her.

“For what?”

“For these four years.”

He didn’t interrupt. She looked at her ice cream.

“I know I’m sometimes difficult.”

“Sometimes?”

She turned sharply.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He smiled.

“Continue.”

She laughed and lightly hit his arm.

“I’m serious.”

“I know.”

She took a breath.

“Thank you for being patient with me. For listening to me even when I talk too much. For remembering things I forget. For not making me feel silly when I’m excited about something small.”

Her voice softened.

“And for letting me be myself.”

Yichen watched her. She looked up.

“I know you have your own dreams and things you want to do. I don’t want you to feel like you have to make everything about me.”

“I don’t.”

“I know. But I still want you to know I see how hard you work. And I want to be someone who makes your life happier, too.”

He was quiet. Then he set his ice cream aside and turned fully towards her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“You don’t have to earn your place in my life by making it easier.”

She blinked. He reached for her hand.

“I love you when you’re organised. I love you when you forget where you put your phone. I love you when you make a schedule and get upset because the gallery is thirty minutes late.”

She laughed.

“I wasn’t upset.”

“You checked your notebook four times.”

“Because it was late!”

He smiled.

“I know.”

His fingers threaded through hers.

“And I love that you think about these things. That you remember our first dates. That you wanted to make today special.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“But you don’t have to plan every minute for me to enjoy being with you.”

She looked at him. He leaned closer.

“Some of my favourite moments with you weren’t planned at all.”

“Like what?”

“The time you got lost and called me from the wrong building.”

She groaned.

“That’s not romantic.”

“The time you fell asleep during a movie and insisted you were still watching.”

“I was listening.”

“The time you tried to teach me a dance and nearly kicked my knee.”

She covered her face.

“Why are all your memories embarrassing?”

“Because they’re memorable.”

He gently pulled her hands away from her face.

“And because I love them.”

She smiled. Then she leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“You’re my favourite person.”

He looked at her.

“You’re mine.”

✦ ✦ ✦

16:50 — Sunset.

This was the part Xiaoran had been most excited about.

She had chosen a quiet riverside spot where the city skyline looked particularly beautiful in the evening light.

She had checked the sunset time three days in advance. She had checked it again yesterday. She had even checked it that morning. Everything was supposed to be perfect. Except the weather had other plans.

Clouds gathered over the horizon, and the sunset was less golden than she had imagined. Xiaoran stood with her hands on her hips.

“Unbelievable.”

Yichen stood beside her.

“What happened?”

“The sky.”

He looked up.

“It looks fine.”

“It was supposed to be prettier.”

He studied the clouds.

“Should I call someone?”

She turned to him.

“Don’t be ridiculous.”

He smiled. They stood by the railing, watching the city lights slowly appear. Xiaoran took out her phone.

“Let’s take a photograph.”

Yichen stepped behind her and wrapped his arms around her waist. She held the phone up.

“Smile.”

He looked at the camera. She pressed the shutter. Then she looked at the photograph. It was lovely.

The sky was cloudy, the river reflected the lights, and Yichen’s chin rested lightly against her shoulder. She looked at it, then smiled.

“Actually, I like it.”

He kissed her cheek.

“Good.”

She turned in his arms.

“Even though the sunset wasn’t perfect?”

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I didn’t come here for the sunset.”

Her expression softened. He brushed a strand of hair away from her face.

“I came here with you.”

She smiled. Then she pulled his head down and kissed him. It was a gentle kiss, warm and familiar. When she pulled away, he studied her. Then he kissed her temple.

“Ready for dinner?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

18:30 — Dinner.

The restaurant was small, intimate, and beautifully lit. Xiaoran had chosen a private table near the window. She had also prepared a small gift.

It was a watch strap in a colour she knew he liked, with a tiny engraving on the underside. Yichen opened the box.

His eyes moved over the strap, then to the engraving.

For all the time we’ve spent, and all the time still waiting.

He looked at her.

“Xiaoran.”

She smiled nervously.

“Do you like it?”

He ran his thumb over the engraving.

“I love it.”

She exhaled.

“Good. I was worried you wouldn’t.”

He closed the box and set it down carefully.

Then he reached for the bag beside his chair.

“I have something for you too.”

Her eyes widened.

“You do?”

He handed her a small box. Inside was a thin silver bracelet with a tiny panda charm, no bigger than her fingernail.

She already had a star. He’d given it to her on her first birthday as his girlfriend, and she was wearing it now. He’d remembered that too. She touched it gently.

“It’s beautiful.”

“Turn it over.”

She did. There was a small engraving on the back.

My favourite place is beside you.

Her eyes lifted. Yichen was watching her. She smiled, but her eyes were already beginning to shine.

“You wrote this?”

“I chose it.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s true.”

She looked down again. Then she leaned across the table and kissed his cheek.

“Thank you.”

He smiled.

“You’re welcome.”

She touched the charm again.

“I’ll wear it every day.”

“Don’t. You’ll damage it.”

She frowned.

“Then when?”

“On days you want to.”

“But I want to every day.”

He laughed.

“Then we’ll see.”

Dinner continued with conversation, laughter, and a few photographs.

At one point, Xiaoran checked her notebook under the table. Yichen noticed.

“What’s next?”

“Final surprise.”

“At eight?”

She nodded. He glanced at his watch.

“It’s 7:56.”

She stared, then looked at her notebook, then at him.

“You’re not supposed to know the time.”

“I have a watch.”

She sighed.

“Fine. Close your eyes.”

He leaned back.

“Here?”

“Yes.”

He closed his eyes. Xiaoran stood and walked around the table.

“Don’t peek.”

“I’m not.”

She took his hand.

“Come with me.”

He followed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

20:00 — Final surprise.

The final surprise wasn’t a restaurant, an activity, or another carefully arranged event.

It was the little private room upstairs, which she had rented for the evening and planned down to the last string of lights.

There were photographs hanging on strings, warm lights around the walls, and a table in the centre with a cake. Four candles stood on top. A small card sat beside it. Yichen opened his eyes. He simply looked around. Xiaoran stood beside him, nervous.

“Surprise.”

He looked at the photographs. Some were funny. Some were sweet. Some were so ordinary that he wondered when she had taken them.

There was one of him asleep on a sofa, his hand still holding hers. Another of her laughing with her mouth full. One of them walking through the rain.

One of their hands intertwined over the gear shift of his car.

And one from that morning at the café, which Ning had printed at a shop round the corner an hour before. He turned towards her.

“You did all this?”

She nodded.

“I planned it. Jiayi and Ning hung the lights while we were at the gallery.”

“Did you ask them to keep it secret?”

“Yes. Ning said I was being dramatic. Jiayi cried.”

“Ning knows you well.”

Xiaoran glared.

“Don’t agree with her.”

He laughed. Then he walked towards the table. The cake had a simple message written on it:

FOUR YEARS. STILL NOT TIRED OF YOU.

Yichen read it, then looked at her.

“Not tired of me?”

“Not even a little.”

“That’s fortunate.”

“Why?”

“Because I don’t intend to go anywhere.”

She smiled. He looked at the candles.

“Should I make a wish?”

“Yes.”

He closed his eyes. Xiaoran watched him. She wondered what he would wish for.

More basketball victories? A successful future? A life where everything went according to plan?

He opened his eyes and blew out the candles. She clapped.

“Did you make a wish?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Can’t tell you.”

“Why?”

“Then it won’t come true.”

She pouted.

“That’s inconvenient.”

He laughed. She cut the cake, giving him the first slice. Then she took a breath.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“I have one last thing.”

He set down his fork.

“All right.”

She reached into her bag and took out a folded piece of paper. It was the schedule. He accepted it.

At the bottom, under 21:00 — No end, she had squeezed in one more line in a different pen.

Tell Zhou Yichen why I love him.

He looked at her. She took the paper back and unfolded it.

“Okay. So. I made this schedule because I wanted today to be perfect. I wanted you to have a really good anniversary, and I wanted you to know how much I love you.”

She looked down at the paper.

“But I think I made a mistake.”

He watched her.

“I spent so much time planning what we would do that I forgot the most important part.”

“You.”

His expression softened. She continued, a little shy now.

“I love you because you’re you. Because you’re patient with me, because you’re thoughtful, because you make me feel safe without making me feel small. Because you always listen, even when I talk about something that happened three hours ago and somehow need to explain it from the beginning.”

He smiled.

“I love you because you make ordinary things feel important. And because even after four years, I still get excited when I know I’m going to see you.”

Her voice grew quieter.

“I don’t know what the next four years will look like. Maybe we’ll be busy. Maybe we’ll have difficult days. Maybe some things won’t go according to plan.”

She glanced at the schedule.

“Probably a lot of things.”

He laughed.

“But I want all of it. The good days, the difficult days, the ordinary days. I want to keep choosing you.”

She folded the paper.

“Happy anniversary, Zhou Yichen.”

He didn’t move. Then he stood. Xiaoran looked up at him.

“What’s wrong?”

He came around the table and stopped in front of her.

“Nothing.”

“Then why are you looking at me like that?”

He took the paper from her hand and placed it carefully on the table. Then he reached for her waist.

“Because I’ve been listening.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

“And because I have something to say too.”

She tilted her head.

“Okay.”

“Four years ago, I started dating a girl who had a habit of making everything more complicated than it needed to be.”

Xiaoran gasped.

“Excuse me?”

“She was stubborn. She talked too much when she was excited. She got embarrassed easily, but tried very hard to hide it.”

“You’re describing me.”

“I am.”

“That’s not a very flattering anniversary speech.”

He laughed.

“But she also made me look forward to things I hadn’t thought about before. She made me want to share every ordinary part of my day. She made me understand that happiness doesn’t always have to be something extraordinary.”

His hand settled more securely at her waist.

“Sometimes it’s just having someone beside you while you eat breakfast. Someone who steals your ice cream. Someone who makes a terrible pottery bowl and insists it’s a fruit dish.”

She burst into laughter.

“You’re never going to let that go!”

“No.”

He brushed his thumb against her waist.

“And somewhere along the way, I stopped thinking about what it would be like to have a future with you.”

His eyes held hers.

“I started thinking about what I could do to make that future happen.”

Her laughter faded. He leaned closer.

“I don’t need every day to be perfect, Xiaoran. I don’t need you to plan every minute. I just want to be there when the minutes happen.”

Her eyes grew warm.

“Yichen...”

He smiled faintly.

“Four years, and you’re still the person I want to come home to. The person I want to tell everything to. The person I want beside me when something good happens, and the person I want to hold when things aren’t so good.”

He lifted a hand to her cheek.

“And if I get to choose again, I’ll choose you again.”

She looked at him, her lips trembling into a smile.

“Even if I make you do pottery?”

“Even then.”

“Even if I make a schedule?”

He glanced at the paper on the table.

“That one requires further negotiation.”

She laughed. And then he kissed her. It began gently, his palm warm against her cheek, his other arm drawing her closer.

Xiaoran pulled him down by the collar, her hands finding his shoulders. He kissed her again, slower this time, lingering. She smiled against his lips. He felt it.

“What?” he murmured.

“Nothing.”

“You’re smiling.”

“Because I’m happy.”

His expression softened. He brushed his nose lightly against hers.

“Good.”

Then he kissed her again. This time, there was no teasing smile, no playful interruption, no carefully timed moment.

He kissed her with all the affection he had been holding back throughout the day. His arm tightened around her waist, bringing her close, while his hand slid gently to the back of her head. Xiaoran’s fingers curled into his shirt.

She had kissed him thousands of times by now.

But there was something about the way he kissed her tonight that made her heart stumble.

It was warm and unhurried, but there was a depth to it that made her forget the room, the photographs, the cake, and the carefully planned schedule.

When he finally pulled away, she was still holding on to him. Her cheeks were flushed. Yichen looked at her.

“Happy?”

She nodded.

“Very.”

He kissed the corner of her mouth.

“Good.”

She looked at him, then at the schedule lying on the table.

“Wait.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“What?”

“I didn’t plan anything after that.”

He looked at the clock. It was already 9:17.

“No end. And nothing written under it,” he read off the paper.

“That was the romantic part!”

He watched her. Then calmly picked up the paper, turned it over, and wrote something on the back. She watched him.

“What are you doing?”

He handed it to her. At the bottom, in his neat handwriting, was a new line:

21:18 — Kiss Xiaoran again.

She looked up. He smiled.

“That one’s flexible.”

She laughed, her cheeks turning pink all over again.

“You’re changing my schedule!”

“Just one item.”

“That’s not how planning works.”

“Then I apologise.”

He leaned closer.

“May I?”

“Yes.”

He kissed her again. And when the kiss ended, Xiaoran decided that perhaps there was one thing she hadn’t planned badly at all. Four years ago, she had chosen Zhou Yichen. And she was still choosing him. Tomorrow, she would probably make another schedule.

But tonight, she let him hold her for as long as he wanted, with the candles burned out, the cake half-finished, and the clock entirely forgotten.

For once, she didn’t need to know what time it was.

chapters.desc: A third-year group project, one teammate who never answers messages, and a boyfriend who offers to talk to him politely.
chapters.title: Group Project From Hell
chapters.epigraph: “And I checked yours. Two of the page numbers were wrong.”
chapters.content:
By the autumn of third year, Lin Xiaoran had learned three things about group projects. The person who suggested making a group chat was never the person who did the most work. The person who said I’ll handle the research was likely to vanish for several days. And there was always, without exception, one person who didn’t answer messages until the night before the deadline.

This semester, that person was Dou Kai. He had come to the first meeting, nodded through all of it, volunteered to find the references, and disappeared. That had been on Monday. It was now Thursday evening, and Xiaoran was in the library with her laptop open, glaring at the group chat as if the force of her disappointment could make a little typing... appear under his name.

Zhou Yichen was sitting next to her with a case study for his strategy module. He’d been listening to her for fourteen minutes.

“Maybe he’s busy,” he said.

She turned her head slowly. “Don’t defend him.”

“I’m not defending him.”

“You said maybe he’s busy.”

“That was an observation.”

“He’s been busy for four days. Is he doing fieldwork in another country? Has his electricity been cut off? Is his phone at the bottom of the sea?”

“Those are all possibilities.”

She stared at him. He looked back, perfectly grave. She dropped her forehead onto his shoulder and left it there.

“I hate group projects.”

“I know. What’s he meant to be doing?” He reached over her with his free hand and moved her milk tea away from the edge of the table.

“Research and references. We split the sections on Monday. He’s supposed to find the academic sources and send them to the rest of us so we can cite them. Ning’s done her part. I’ve done mine. Our fourth person’s done his. Kai’s done nothing.”

“Has he read the messages?”

“He hasn’t even opened them.” She turned the laptop towards him without lifting her head. The last message in the chat was hers, from that afternoon.

Hi Kai, just checking how the references are going? We need to put everything together by tomorrow.

Underneath, nothing.

Yichen read it. “Would you like me to talk to him?”

She sat up and narrowed her eyes. “About what?”

“His responsibilities.”

“How?”

“Politely.”

She looked at his face. It was calm. Far too calm.

“You’re going to talk to him politely?”

“Yes.”

“Zhou Yichen, you look like you’re about to buy his company.”

“That would be easier,” he said, and she laughed so loudly that someone at the next table turned round and shushed them, and she put her face back into his shoulder to stop.

When she’d recovered she said, “No. I can handle it.”

“I know you can.”

“Really.”

“I know, Xiaoran. But you don’t have to spend your whole evening angry at someone who isn’t answering.” He tapped the edge of her laptop with one finger.

She looked at the chat. Then at him. “Will you help me write one more message?”

“Of course.”

She slid the laptop onto his half of the table. He read back through all her messages, thought, and typed.

Hi Kai. We need your section and references by 6 p.m. tomorrow so we can finish the report. If you can’t do it, please let us know tonight and we’ll divide the work between us. Thanks.

She read it over his arm. “That’s very polite.”

“Yes.”

“Very professional.”

“Yes.”

“Very frightening.”

“Good,” he said, and pressed send.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday morning Dou Kai replied.

Sorry guys been busy. Will do it tonight

Xiaoran read it sitting on the steps outside the Media building with Ning, who read it over her shoulder.

“That’s it?”

“Apparently.”

“Did he say what he was busy with?”

“No.”

“At least he’s alive,” said Ning.

Xiaoran forwarded it to Yichen.

Xiaoran: He lives.

Yichen: Good news.

Xiaoran: He says he’ll do it tonight.

Yichen: Then we’ll see if he does.

“You’re smiling,” said Ning.

“I’m not.”

“You’re texting your boyfriend.”

“I’m checking something.”

“You’re checking your boyfriend.”

“Can we please finish the slides?” said Xiaoran, and put her phone away, and got it out again thirty seconds later when it buzzed.

Yichen: 11:20 at the library steps? I have twenty minutes.

Xiaoran: You said you had a seminar.

Yichen: I have twenty minutes before the seminar.

She went. She sat on the library steps leaning against him, with her head on his shoulder, and complained about Dou Kai for nineteen of the twenty minutes, and for the last one he told her about his own group, which had a person who answered every message within thirty seconds with a long list of questions, and she decided that was worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

By midnight Kai had sent nothing. Xiaoran sent one last message — Kai, we’re still waiting, please just send whatever you’ve got — and then Ning rang, and by a quarter past they had agreed to split his section between them and write it themselves. Xiaoran had the laptop on her knees in bed, and three tabs of journal databases open, and her phone face up on the duvet.

Xiaoran: I think I need you to talk to him politely now.

Yichen: Tomorrow?

Xiaoran: Tomorrow.

Yichen: All right. Go to sleep.

She sent him a photo of the laptop screen.

Xiaoran: I can’t sleep, I’m SUFFERING

Yichen: I can see that.

Xiaoran: Do you feel sorry for me?

Yichen: Very.

Xiaoran: How sorry?

Yichen: Sorry enough to buy you breakfast tomorrow.

Xiaoran: Accepted. Call me? Just till I finish this paragraph.

He called. He didn’t say much. She could hear him turning the pages of his own reading, and once the scratch of a highlighter, and she finished the paragraph and then another one and then the whole section, and at ten to two she realised he’d gone quiet, and said, “Yichen?” and he said, “Mm. Still here,” in a voice so thick with sleep that she hung up and let him go.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday afternoon he went with her to the building where Kai’s elective finished at four. She hadn’t meant to bring him. She’d said she was going to find Kai after his class, and he’d said, “I’ll walk with you,” and picked up his bag, and that had been that.

She held his arm the whole way and got more nervous with every step.

“Don’t be harsh.”

“I won’t.”

“Really.”

“I said I’d be polite.”

“Your polite and my polite are different.”

He looked down at her. “Would you like me to smile?”

She considered it. “Maybe.”

He smiled at her. It was a perfectly pleasant smile and it made the hair on her arms stand up.

“Not like that!”

They waited by the noticeboard in the corridor. At five past four the door opened, and Dou Kai came out in a hoodie with his headphones round his neck.

“Kai.”

“Oh. Xiaoran. Hey.”

“Hi. Have you got a minute?”

“Sure.”

His eyes went to Yichen, who was standing a step behind her with his bag over one shoulder.

“And—” he said.

“Zhou Yichen,” said Yichen, with a small nod.

Kai nodded back, a little lost.

“We’ve finished the report. But your section was missing, so last night Ning and I wrote it. We couldn’t get hold of you,” Xiaoran said.

Kai rubbed the back of his neck. “Yeah. Sorry. I’ve been really busy.”

Yichen spoke for the first time. “That happens. But when you take a section in a group project, the others plan their week around you.”

His voice was level and perfectly friendly, and every word landed.

“Yeah, I know.”

“So if you can’t finish it, it helps to say so early. Then people can adjust.”

“Right.”

“Xiaoran and Ning were up past two doing your part. They didn’t have to.”

Kai looked at Xiaoran. For the first time he looked properly embarrassed. “Sorry. Really.”

“It’s okay. We just need you to answer next time.”

“Yeah. I will.”

“Good. Then that’s settled,” said Yichen, with another small nod.

It took less than three minutes. Kai walked off down the corridor looking more thoughtful than when he’d come out.

Xiaoran watched him go. Then she looked up at Yichen. “That was it?”

“Yes.”

“You didn’t threaten him?”

“No.”

“You didn’t tell him he was irresponsible?”

“I implied it. Politely,” said Yichen, and adjusted the strap of his bag.

She laughed until she had to hold onto him. “You’re unbelievable.”

“Did it help?”

“Yes.”

“Then about breakfast.”

“It’s four in the afternoon.”

“I promised breakfast.”

“Then I want something nice. And dessert.”

“Dessert isn’t breakfast.”

“It can be if you buy it,” she said, and pulled him by the hand out of the building towards the café by the east gate that did waffles all day.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the next group meeting Dou Kai arrived first.

He had a cardboard tray of four milk teas, one of them half sugar with no pearls, which meant he had asked someone, and a printed copy of his section, which was late and also, to everybody’s astonishment, good.

“I redid the references. And I checked yours. Two of the page numbers were wrong,” he said, to the table rather than to anyone.

Ning took her milk tea and looked at Xiaoran over the top of the cup.

They presented the following Friday. Kai did the first five minutes and didn’t look at his notes once. Afterward in the corridor, while the others were arguing about where to eat, he fell into step beside Xiaoran.

“Is your boyfriend in Business?”

“Yes.”

“He’s terrifying.”

“He was being polite.”

“I know. That’s what was terrifying,” said Kai, with real feeling.

They got an A minus. She sent Yichen a photograph of the mark, and he sent back a photograph of the waffle café’s menu with the desserts circled in pen, and she showed it to Ning, and Ning said, “I’m going to be sick,” and asked if she could come.

chapters.desc: One street interview, a million views, and a boyfriend who hasn’t posted anything in months.
chapters.title: The Girl on Everyone’s Feed
chapters.epigraph: “Please be kind to her.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Lin Xiaoran did wrong was answer a stranger’s question.

The second thing she did wrong was answer it so sweetly that half the internet fell in love with her.

And the third thing—though she wouldn’t discover this until much later—was forgetting that her boyfriend was also on the internet. It happened on an ordinary Thursday afternoon.

Xiaoran had just finished a group meeting at the university and was walking towards a nearby shopping street. She had her earphones in, a canvas tote bag hanging from one shoulder, and was thinking about whether she should buy milk tea before going home.

She was halfway through checking the menu on her phone when someone approached her.

“Excuse me, miss?”

She looked up. A young man stood in front of her, holding a microphone and smiling at a camera operator behind him.

“Would you mind answering a quick question for a video?”

Xiaoran pulled out one earphone.

“Me?”

“Yes. It’ll only take a minute.”

She glanced at the camera.

“Oh. Is this for a university project?”

The interviewer laughed.

“Something like that. I’m making street interview videos. Are you comfortable being filmed?”

Xiaoran hesitated, then nodded.

“Sure.”

“Great. I’m Mai Lang.”

He didn’t introduce his channel name, and Xiaoran didn’t recognise him anyway. She wasn’t particularly active on social media anymore. She used it to message friends, look at things she liked, and occasionally post photographs. She rarely watched interview videos or followed online personalities.

Mai Lang was, in fact, one of the most popular creators in the country in the category of social commentary and public knowledge. His channel had several million subscribers, and his street interviews often went viral because he asked ordinary people questions about complicated social issues. Today, the topic was financial literacy.

“Let’s start with something simple,” he said. “Do you think young people should be financially responsible for their parents once they start earning money?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Oh. That’s not simple.”

The interviewer laughed.

“Why not?”

She thought about it.

“I think they should care about their parents, but I don’t think responsibility should automatically mean paying for everything.”

Mai Lang nodded.

“Can you explain?”

Xiaoran shifted her tote bag higher on her shoulder.

“Well, parents and children are family, so naturally we should help each other. But I think it depends on the situation. Some parents are financially stable, some aren’t. Some children can afford to help, some are still struggling themselves.”

She paused, then added earnestly,

“I think it’s important to help without making either person feel like a burden.”

The interviewer looked interested.

“That’s a thoughtful answer. What if the parents sacrificed a lot to raise their children?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Then I think we should appreciate that. But I don’t think love should become a debt that has to be repaid with a fixed amount of money.”

Mai Lang’s eyebrows lifted slightly.

“Interesting. So you disagree with the idea that children owe their parents?”

“Not exactly.”

She frowned, searching for the right words.

“I think we owe them love and respect, but not necessarily a lifetime of financial repayment. Otherwise, it might make the relationship feel like a transaction.”

There was a brief pause. Then Mai Lang smiled.

“That’s actually a very good distinction.”

Xiaoran smiled back, a little shy.

“Thank you.”

He moved to the next question.

“Second question. If your partner earns significantly more than you, should they pay for more things in the relationship?”

Xiaoran laughed.

“You’re asking me difficult questions today.”

“That’s the point.”

She thought about it.

“I think it depends on what both people are comfortable with. If one person earns more, it makes sense that they might contribute more sometimes. But I wouldn’t want someone to feel that they have to pay for everything just because they can.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to be with someone, not become their financial responsibility.”

The camera operator made a small sound of amusement. Mai Lang smiled.

“And what if your partner insists?”

Xiaoran’s expression turned thoughtful.

“Then I’d probably tell him I appreciate it, but I still want to contribute in ways I can. Maybe I can’t pay for the same things, but I can still plan something, cook, remember what he likes, or do something meaningful.”

She smiled a little.

“I think being generous should be something you do because you love someone, not because you want to prove that you can afford them.”

Mai Lang nodded slowly.

“That’s a lovely answer.”

Xiaoran ducked her head.

“Thank you.”

He asked two more questions, one about online misinformation and another about whether universities should teach practical financial skills.

Xiaoran answered with the same thoughtful sincerity. She wasn’t trying to sound clever. She occasionally stumbled over her words, laughed at herself, and asked the interviewer to repeat one question because she wanted to make sure she understood it correctly. At the end, Mai Lang lowered the microphone.

“Thank you for your time. Can I ask your name?”

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“Are you a student?”

“Yes. I study Media.”

“That’s fitting.”

She laughed.

“Thank you. I was actually quite nervous.”

“You didn’t look nervous.”

“I was trying not to.”

He laughed.

“Well, thank you, Xiaoran. Have a nice day.”

“You too!”

She gave a small wave to the camera and continued walking. She didn’t think much of it.

By the time she reached the milk tea shop, she had already forgotten most of the conversation.

✦ ✦ ✦

The video was uploaded that evening. Its title was:

“Do Young People Owe Their Parents Everything? I Asked Strangers on the Street.”

Xiaoran appeared around the middle. The first few minutes showed different people giving their opinions. Some were confident, some were uncertain, and a few gave answers that sparked immediate debate, then the video reached her.

The camera showed a girl in a cream cardigan, her hair falling loosely around her shoulders. She was holding a canvas tote bag, looking slightly surprised when the microphone was offered. The interviewer asked his first question. She blinked.

“Oh. That’s not simple.”

The comments started there. And then she answered. She didn’t make a speech. She simply explained her thoughts, occasionally smiling, her expression changing as she tried to find the right words.

By the time the video reached the second question, the comment section had begun to fill.

Top comments:

- “Wait, who is this girl? She’s so pretty.”
- “Her face is so unique. Not the usual influencer pretty. I can’t explain it.”
- “She’s cute but her answers are actually so mature.”
- “The way she pauses to think before answering. I love her.”
- “Her voice is so sweet???”
- “She looks like she doesn’t even know she’s being filmed.”
- “I came for the social commentary and stayed for the girl in the cream cardigan.”
- “Can we get her full interview?”
- “The boyfriend who gets to hear her talk every day must be winning at life.”

One comment received thousands of likes:

“She has the kind of pretty that makes you want to listen to whatever she’s saying.”

Another:

“She’s not trying to sound intelligent. She’s just genuinely thoughtful. That’s even more attractive.”

The video gained traction overnight. By morning, it had been reposted across several platforms. And Lin Xiaoran had absolutely no idea.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 9:17 AM, her phone began vibrating. She was in bed, still half asleep. The first message was from Chen Yuhao.

Yuhao: XIAORAN.

Then another.

Yuhao: WAKE UP.

Then a video. She opened it. The thumbnail showed a familiar face. Her own. Xiaoran sat upright.

“...Huh?”

She watched the video, then watched it again, then opened the comment section. Her eyes widened.

“WHAT?”

She immediately called Yuhao. He answered on the first ring.

“Good morning, celebrity!”

“YUHAO!”

He burst out laughing.

“Yes, yes, I know. I know. I watched the whole thing.”

“Why am I on the internet?”

“Because you went outside.”

“That’s not funny!”

“It is a little funny.”

She scrolled through the comments.

“Why are there so many comments?”

“Because the internet has discovered you.”

She looked at the view count, then looked again. It had already crossed a million.

“Yuhao.”

“Hm?”

“Is this normal?”

“For you? No. For a viral video? Yes.”

She groaned.

“Why didn’t I know he was famous?”

Yuhao laughed until she had to move the phone away from her ear.

“Wait. You didn’t know who Mai Lang was?”

“No!”

“Xiaoran, he’s huge.”

“How was I supposed to know?”

“You’re literally a Media student!”

“That doesn’t mean I know every person on the internet!”

Yuhao was still laughing.

“Meilin is going to call you. Prepare yourself.”

As if summoned, another call appeared.

Tang Meilin calling…

Xiaoran answered.

“Meilin!”

“I’ve seen it.”

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not laughing.”

She sounded suspiciously amused.

“Meilin.”

“Okay, I’m laughing a little.”

Xiaoran flopped backward onto her pillow.

“I didn’t do anything!”

“That’s why it’s funny. You went out to buy milk tea and accidentally became a public figure.”

“I just answered questions!”

“Yes. And apparently you answered them beautifully.”

Meilin paused. Then her voice became a little more serious.

“Actually, I liked your answers. Especially the part about love not being a debt.”

Xiaoran smiled faintly.

“Really?”

“Yes. You sounded like yourself.”

That made her feel a little better. Until Meilin added:

“Also, you’re very pretty.”

Xiaoran covered her face.

“Please stop.”

“No. I’m going to enjoy this.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By lunchtime, her tagged account had become a small disaster.

Xiaoran had never been particularly active online. Her account was public, but most of her posts were ordinary photographs: campus, food, friends, trips, the occasional selfie, and a few pictures of Yichen. She had around a thousand followers.

Now the number was climbing so quickly that she stopped checking. People had found her account through the video.

They were liking old posts, commenting on photographs from months ago, and following her. Some were polite. Some were enthusiastic. Some were strange. Her direct messages were worse.

“Hi, I saw you in Mai Lang’s video. You’re really beautiful.”

“Are you single?”

“I’d love to get to know you.”

“You’re my ideal type.”

“Can I take you out for coffee?”

“I think we would get along. You seem very sweet.”

She stared at the screen, then closed the app.

Then opened it again because she wanted to see whether it had stopped. It hadn’t. She sent a screenshot to Meilin.

Xiaoran: Why are strangers asking me out?

Meilin: Because they have eyes.

Xiaoran: I don’t know them.

Meilin: They don’t know you either. That’s usually how strangers work.

Xiaoran: I’m blocking everyone.

Meilin: Good idea.

A few minutes later, another message arrived.

Meilin: By the way, don’t forget to tell your boyfriend.

Xiaoran paused. Oh. Her boyfriend. She hadn’t told Yichen yet.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen found out a little before one PM. Not from Xiaoran. From Chen Yuhao.

Yichen was in the university sports facility. He had just finished a workout and was sitting on a bench, drinking water, when Yuhao sent him the video from his own campus two provinces away.

Yuhao: Your girlfriend is famous.

Yichen opened the link. He watched the video from beginning to end. At first, he was simply amused.

There was Xiaoran, standing on a busy street, looking slightly bewildered as someone held a microphone towards her. He recognised the cardigan. He recognised the canvas bag.

He recognised the expression she made when she was thinking hard about something.

Then he heard her answer the question about financial responsibility. His mouth curved.

“That’s Xiaoran.”

His teammate glanced over. He continued watching, then came the question about relationships and money. Yichen leaned back against the bench.

He listened to her talk about wanting to contribute, about generosity, about being with someone rather than becoming their financial responsibility. His expression softened. He knew those things about her already.

He knew she disliked feeling indebted. He knew she wanted to be independent, even when he offered to help. He knew she appreciated thoughtful gestures more than expensive ones. He watched the interviewer compliment her. Then he opened the comments. The first few made him smile. The next few made him pause. And then he reached the comment section. He scrolled.

“She’s so pretty.”

“Her boyfriend must be the luckiest man alive.”

“I want to marry her.”

“Please tell me she’s single.”

“Someone find her account.”

Yichen’s thumb stopped. He looked at the screen, then at the video again, then back at the comments. Fang Ze, on the next bench, glanced over.

“What’s up?”

Yichen locked his phone.

“Nothing.”

Fang Ze narrowed his eyes.

“You don’t look like nothing.”

Yichen took another sip of water.

“My girlfriend went viral.”

Fang Ze immediately leaned over.

“Your girlfriend?”

Yichen handed him the phone. Fang Ze watched a few seconds, then whistled.

“Oh. She’s pretty.”

Yichen looked at him. Fang Ze raised both hands.

“Respectfully.”

Yichen took his phone back.

“Good.”

He stood, picked up his bag, and walked away.

Fang Ze watched him go, then looked at the phone.

“...He’s jealous.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after one PM, Xiaoran finally sent him a message.

Xiaoran: Yichen.

He was already looking at his phone.

Yichen: Hm?

Xiaoran: Have you seen something strange today?

Yichen: Define strange.

Xiaoran: I think I accidentally became famous.

He smiled.

Yichen: I noticed.

Xiaoran: YOU SAW IT?

Yichen: Yuhao sent it to me.

Xiaoran: I didn’t know that man was famous!

Yichen: I gathered that.

Xiaoran: I was just buying milk tea.

Yichen: An eventful milk tea trip.

She sent him a crying sticker, then another message.

Xiaoran: People are sending me messages.

Yichen: I saw.

Xiaoran: It’s weird.

Yichen: You can ignore them. Block anyone who makes you uncomfortable.

Xiaoran: I know. I just didn’t expect it.

Yichen: Are you all right?

She looked at the question.

Xiaoran: Yes. Just a little overwhelmed.

His reply came almost immediately.

Yichen: I’ll come see you after practice.

She smiled.

Xiaoran: Okay.

Then, because she was curious:

Xiaoran: Are you embarrassed that your girlfriend is famous?

Yichen looked at the message. He smiled slowly.

Yichen: No.

A few seconds passed.

Yichen: I’m more concerned that so many people seem to think they have a chance.

Xiaoran stared, then burst out laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

He arrived at her apartment that evening. Xiaoran opened the door wearing comfortable home clothes, her hair loosely tied up. She looked relieved when she saw him.

“Yichen!”

He stepped inside and set his bag down.

“Hello.”

She immediately wrapped her arms around his waist. He held her, kissing her hair.

“How’s the celebrity?”

“Don’t call me that.”

“All right.”

He pulled back slightly.

“How’s my girlfriend?”

“Better.”

He touched her cheek.

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“Properly?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She took his hand and led him to the sofa.

“Look.”

She showed him her account. Her follower count had increased dramatically. There were hundreds of new comments, and her inbox was still full. Yichen scrolled through a few messages. His expression remained composed. Until he reached one.

“You’re so beautiful. I wish I could be your boyfriend.”

He read it, then another.

“If you’re single, I’d love to take you on a date.”

Then another.

“Your smile is addictive. Please reply.”

He handed the phone back.

“Quite enthusiastic.”

Then, more carefully: “Are you reading the comments at night?”

She knew exactly which night he meant. Two in the morning, a screen in the dark, two weeks of skipped meals afterwards.

“No, I read them at lunch, with Ning, and Ning says something rude about each one,” she said.

His shoulders went down a fraction. “Good.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Right?”

He nodded.

“Very.”

She studied his face.

“Are you upset?”

“No.”

“Really?”

He looked at her.

“Why would I be upset?”

“Because people are sending me messages.”

“They’re allowed to find you pretty.”

She blinked.

“You’re not jealous?”

Yichen considered that.

“I’m not particularly happy about strangers asking my girlfriend out.”

Her eyes brightened.

“So you are jealous!”

He smiled faintly.

“Did you want me to be?”

“No!”

“Then I won’t.”

She laughed. He leaned back against the sofa.

“Although I do have a question.”

“What?”

“Why haven’t you told people you’re taken?”

She looked at him.

“I haven’t even had time to understand what’s happening!”

“I know.”

“And I don’t usually post relationship things.”

“I know that too.”

She tilted her head.

“Would you like me to?”

“Only if you want to.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“I don’t mind.”

She hesitated. “But I don’t want to make a big announcement. That would be embarrassing.”

“Then don’t.”

She considered him.

“You’re being very reasonable.”

“Should I not be?”

“No, but...”

She leaned closer.

“Are you sure you’re not jealous?”

He looked at her. Then he reached up and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“I’ve been your boyfriend for four years. I don’t think a few strangers in your inbox are going to change that.”

Her heart softened. He continued, quieter:

“But I’d be lying if I said I enjoyed reading those messages.”

She giggled.

“You liked hearing that.”

He gave her a small, knowing smile.

“Are you happy now?”

“Very.”

He kissed her hair.

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first post came a little before ten PM. It wasn’t a dramatic announcement. It wasn’t a long caption. It wasn’t even a photograph of their faces. Yichen posted a story. A photograph taken that evening.

Xiaoran was sitting beside him on the sofa, holding a cup of tea. Her face was turned towards him, and she was laughing at something outside the frame. The photograph was slightly candid, the lighting warm.

His hand was visible in the corner, resting on her knee. The caption was simple.

“My favourite person. Four years and counting.”

He tagged her. Xiaoran saw it a few seconds later. She looked up from her phone.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You posted me.”

“Yes.”

“On your story.”

“That’s generally where stories go.”

She laughed.

“You’re so annoying.”

“Do you want me to delete it?”

She looked at the photograph again. Her smile softened.

“No.”

“Good.”

She reposted it. With a small heart. She thought that would be the end of it. It wasn’t. Within minutes, people began replying to his story. Some were mutual friends congratulating them.

Some were surprised to learn she had a boyfriend. Others were simply curious.

But a surprising number of people continued to send Xiaoran messages. One person even replied to her repost:

“Oh, so that’s your friend? He’s handsome.”

Xiaoran stared at it, then turned towards Yichen.

“Yichen.”

He looked up.

“What?”

“People aren’t getting it.”

He glanced at her phone. He read the reply. Then his eyebrows lifted slightly.

“Apparently not.”

She showed him another message.

“You two look cute together! Is he your brother?”

Yichen looked at her. For a moment, neither of them spoke. Then he laughed. Xiaoran covered her face.

“Why would they think you’re my brother?”

He shrugged.

“Perhaps I look responsible.”

“That’s not the point!”

He took her phone gently.

“May I?”

She watched him.

“What are you doing?”

“Clarifying something.”

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after ten PM, Zhou Yichen posted on his feed for the first time in several months. The photograph was simple.

It showed the two of them standing together at the riverside during their anniversary. Xiaoran was smiling at the camera, while Yichen was looking at her instead. His arm was around her waist. Her hand rested against his chest.

The little panda bracelet he had given her that day was on the wrist against his chest. The caption read:

Four years with Lin Xiaoran.

She’s not just the girl in the interview. She’s the person I come home to, the person I want beside me, and the person I keep choosing.

Please be kind to her.

He tagged her account, then posted it. Xiaoran stared at his screen, then at him, then back at his screen.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He placed his phone down.

“Yes?”

“You posted on your feed.”

“I did.”

“You haven’t posted anything in months.”

“I know.”

“And now you posted me.”

“Yes.”

She stared at him. Then her mouth slowly curved.

“You’re claiming me.”

He looked at her. His expression was calm, but there was a small smile at the corner of his mouth.

“Is that a problem?”

She shook her head, cheeks growing warm.

“No.”

“Good.”

She leaned closer.

“You’re a little jealous.”

“A little.”

She laughed.

“Only a little?”

He considered her. Then reached for her waist and drew her closer.

“Would you like a more honest answer?”

Her smile widened.

“Yes.”

He lowered his voice.

“I don’t mind people knowing you’re beautiful. I don’t mind them appreciating your answers or finding you interesting.”

His thumb brushed lightly against her waist.

“But I don’t particularly enjoy watching strangers line up to ask whether you’re available.”

Xiaoran giggled.

“Why?”

“Because you’re not.”

Her heart gave a small, ridiculous flutter. He continued, his voice still gentle.

“And because I happen to be very happy being the man you chose.”

She looked at him. Then she leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“You’re the only one I want.”

His expression softened.

“I know.”

“You’re supposed to say you want me too.”

He smiled.

“I want you too.”

She beamed, then glanced at his post again.

“Wait. You wrote ‘the person I come home to.’”

“Mhm.”

“That’s very romantic.”

She read it again, smiling to herself. Then she looked at him.

“Can I comment?”

“Of course.”

She opened the comment section and typed.

Xiaoran: The person who steals your food and your ice cream.

Yichen laughed. He replied:

Yichen: And somehow still the person I love most.

Xiaoran’s face turned pink. She immediately locked her phone.

“Okay. Enough.”

He laughed.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re blushing.”

“I’m not.”

He leaned closer.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

He crooked a finger at her. She moved towards him willingly.

He pressed a kiss into her hair, then her cheek. She smiled.

Then, because she was feeling particularly affectionate, she wrapped her arms around his neck and kissed him.

Yichen returned it, one hand settling at her waist. When she pulled away, she was smiling.

“Happy?”

He looked at her.

“Very.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, the internet had found the post.

The comment section was full of congratulations, surprise, and people realising that the handsome man in the photograph wasn’t merely a friend.

“WAIT SHE HAS A BOYFRIEND?”

“FOUR YEARS????”

“He’s so handsome too. They’re actually such a beautiful couple.”

“The way he’s looking at her in the photo. Oh, he’s gone.”

“He posted because people weren’t getting the hint, I’m crying.”

“The caption is so boyfriend-coded.”

“She answered a street interview and accidentally gave us a love story.”

Yuhao sent the post to their group chat.

Yuhao: HAHAHAHAHAHA.

Meilin: Finally, the public has been informed.

Yuhao: Yichen really went from one story to a whole feed announcement.

Meilin: Four years of being her boyfriend. He was probably waiting for a reason.

Xiaoran: YOU TWO ARE SO ANNOYING.

Yuhao: Celebrity, please don’t forget your old friends.

Xiaoran: I’m blocking both of you.

Meilin: You won’t.

Xiaoran: I might.

Yuhao: Tell your famous boyfriend we approve.

Xiaoran laughed so much she had to put her phone down. Yichen, sitting beside her, looked over.

“What happened?”

“Yuhao and Meilin.”

“That explains it.”

She showed him the messages. He read them, then shook his head.

“They haven’t changed.”

“Never.”

She leaned against his shoulder. She asked, “Do you think this will last long?”

“The attention?”

She nodded.

“Probably not forever.”

“Will people keep recognising me?”

“Some might.”

She made a small face.

“I hope they don’t ask me difficult questions again.”

“You answered them well.”

“I was nervous.”

“I know.”

She looked up.

“Did you like my answers?”

“I liked listening to you.”

Her expression softened.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

He brushed his fingers through her hair.

“You weren’t trying to impress anyone. You were just explaining what you believed.”

She smiled.

“That’s because I didn’t know who he was.”

Yichen laughed.

“Perhaps that’s why you were so comfortable.”

She thought about it, then sighed.

“I should have asked for his channel name.”

“Why?”

“So I could have known I was being filmed by someone famous.”

He looked at her, amused.

“Would you have answered differently?”

She considered it.

“No.”

“Then it wouldn’t have made much difference.”

She smiled.

“True.”

A moment passed. Then she suddenly sat up.

“Wait.”

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

“Your post.”

“Hm?”

“You said I’m the person you come home to.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him with a suspicious little smile.

“Does that mean I can come over whenever I want?”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Xiaoran, you already do.”

“Does that mean I can keep my things at your apartment?”

“You already have things there.”

She brightened.

“More things?”

He looked at her, then smiled.

“How many things are we talking about?”

She giggled.

“Maybe a little drawer.”

“A drawer?”

“Just one.”

He nodded thoughtfully.

“All right.”

Her eyes widened.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She immediately hugged his arm.

“You’re the best!”

He kissed her temple.

“Although I suspect one drawer will eventually become three.”

She looked up innocently.

“Why would you think that?”

“Experience.”

She laughed. Then she settled against him again, perfectly content. Her phone vibrated once more. Another notification. Another stranger. Another comment.

She glanced at it, then turned the screen off and put it aside. Yichen noticed.

“Not checking?”

“No.”

“Why?”

She tucked herself closer to him.

“Because I’m already sitting next to the person I want to talk to.”

He looked down at her. His expression softened into that slow, familiar smile that always made her feel a little flustered.

“That’s a good decision.”

She smiled. Then, after a few seconds, added:

“Also, can you buy me milk tea?”

He laughed.

“Ah. Back to normal.”

“What?”

“My famous girlfriend.”

She gasped.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He kissed her temple before she could complain. And somewhere online, people were still discovering Lin Xiaoran.

But the girl herself was much more interested in stealing her boyfriend’s drink.

chapters.desc: Winter break at her parents’ house. Her mother has photographs, stories, and absolutely no mercy.
chapters.title: The Little Warrior
chapters.epigraph: “Good night, little warrior.”
chapters.content:
Yichen had always known that Lin Xiaoran was brave.

He knew it from the way she never hesitated to speak up when someone was treated unfairly. From the way she could be stubborn about the smallest things, yet surprisingly firm when something genuinely mattered. From the way she would defend her friends even when she was clearly outnumbered.

He had seen her argue with people twice her size, stand up for strangers, and get herself into trouble because she couldn’t stand watching someone being bullied.

He sometimes teased her about having a little temper. She would insist she didn’t.

But he had never really known where that part of her came from.

Until one afternoon in her hometown, while Xiaoran was upstairs looking for an old photo album, her mother told him stories about the little girl she used to be.

And Yichen discovered that his girlfriend had been a warrior long before he ever met her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened on their second day in Xiaoran’s hometown, the small town four hours from the city where she had lived until she was twelve, and where her grandparents’ house still stood at the end of a lane. Her parents had driven them down a week before New Year, before the relatives arrived, and Yichen had been given the guest room at the top of the stairs.

Her mother had been preparing fruit in the kitchen while her father was outside talking to a neighbour. Xiaoran had gone upstairs to find an old album her mother wanted to show him.

Yichen was sitting at the dining table, helping her mother arrange some fruit.

“Yichen, you can leave those there,” her mother said.

“It’s alright, Auntie. I can help.”

Her mother smiled.

“You’re always so considerate.”

He smiled politely. She sat opposite him, looking at the neatly arranged fruit.

“Actually, I wanted to show you something.”

She reached for her phone.

“Wait a moment.”

Yichen looked up.

“What is it?”

“Some pictures of Xiaoran when she was little. I had all the old albums scanned last spring, so now I can embarrass her anywhere.”

He laughed.

“I’d like to see them.”

Her mother smiled in satisfaction.

“I thought you would.”

She opened her photo gallery and began scrolling. The first picture showed a little girl with short hair, wearing a yellow dress. She was standing in front of a birthday cake, her cheeks covered in cream. Yichen immediately recognised her eyes.

“That’s Xiaoran?”

Her mother laughed.

“Yes. She was four.”

“She looks very happy.”

“She was. And very naughty.”

Yichen smiled. Her mother swiped to the next picture.

A little Xiaoran stood in a park, holding a plastic sword with both hands. Her expression was extremely serious. Yichen laughed.

“What happened here?”

“Ah. She was pretending to be a hero.” Her mother shook her head affectionately.

“Really?”

“She used to play that game all the time. She would say she was protecting everyone.”

Yichen looked at the picture again. The little girl had one hand on her waist, her chin lifted, and an expression that looked strangely familiar. He smiled.

“She’s still like that.”

Her mother laughed.

“Exactly.”

Then she continued scrolling. And the stories began.

“Xiaoran was always very protective of other children,” her mother said.

She showed him a picture of Xiaoran standing beside another little girl.

“She was in kindergarten here. This little girl was her friend.”

Yichen looked at the picture.

“What happened?”

“Her friend was being bullied by some older children.”

Her mother sighed, though there was affection in her expression.

“Xiaoran was only five or six. She saw them taking her friend’s toys and making her cry.”

Yichen listened.

“She went over and demanded that they return everything. Of course, the older children didn’t listen. They laughed at her.”

Her mother smiled.

“And then she stood in front of her friend and told them they weren’t allowed to bully her anymore.”

Yichen chuckled.

“That sounds like her.”

“She was so small. One of the boys was nearly twice her size.”

Her mother shook her head.

“I was watching from a distance. I thought she would get frightened and come back.”

Instead, Xiaoran had planted herself in front of the boy and refused to move.

“When I finally went over, she was holding her friend’s hand and telling the boys that she would call their teacher.”

Yichen smiled.

“Did she?”

“Of course. She dragged the teacher over herself.”

Her mother laughed.

“She didn’t even wait for me.”

Yichen looked at the picture again. A little girl with round cheeks and short hair.

He could almost imagine her tiny voice, probably trembling with anger, demanding that someone behave properly.

“She was very brave,” he said.

Her mother nodded.

“Yes. But sometimes she was too brave for her own good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother scrolled again. Then she stopped at a photograph.

It showed Xiaoran sitting on a low wall outside a small building. Her hair was messy, her knees were dusty, and she was holding a small ice cream. Yichen looked at the picture.

“Did she fall?”

Her mother smiled.

“She had just fought with some boys.”

Yichen raised his eyebrows.

“Fought?”

“Not exactly a fight. Well…”

She paused, reconsidering.

“Actually, it was quite a fight.”

Yichen laughed.

“What happened?”

Her mother put the phone down for a moment.

“There was a boy in the neighbourhood who liked bullying younger children. He would take their snacks, push them around, and sometimes make them cry. Xiaoran had complained about him several times.”

Yichen listened.

“One afternoon, she saw him pushing a younger boy near the playground. The little boy fell, and the boy laughed at him.”

Her mother’s expression became more serious.

“Xiaoran told him to stop. He ignored her. Then he pushed her too.”

Yichen’s smile disappeared.

“She fell?”

“Yes. She scraped her palms and knees.”

Her mother sighed.

“But she got up immediately.”

She shook her head.

“I remember it very clearly. She was crying, but she was trying so hard not to show it.”

Yichen looked at the photograph.

“What happened next?”

“She stood in front of him again. She told him that if he wanted to bully someone, he should bully someone his own size.”

Her mother laughed.

“Imagine that. A little girl with scraped knees telling a boy to find someone his own size.”

Yichen couldn’t help smiling. Then her mother continued.

“The boy laughed at her. He told her she was already hurt and should go home.”

She paused.

“But Xiaoran didn’t move.”

Yichen looked at her.

“She stayed?”

“Until the boy left.”

Her mother shook her head.

“Afterward, she took the younger boy to his home. She even told his mother what happened.”

Yichen was quiet. He could picture it too clearly.

A small girl, hurt and frightened, refusing to leave until she knew someone else was safe.

“Did you scold her?” he asked.

Her mother smiled.

“Of course. I was worried sick.”

She looked at the photograph again.

“But she didn’t understand why I was upset. She kept saying, ‘Mum, if I left, he would bully him again.’”

Yichen lowered his eyes. Something warm and unfamiliar settled in his chest.

He wasn’t surprised that Xiaoran had been like this.

But hearing it from someone who had watched her grow up made the image feel different.

He was beginning to understand that her courage wasn’t something she had developed as she grew older. It had always been there.

Even when she was too small to understand what courage meant.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then her mother found another picture. This one was different.

Xiaoran was standing outside a clinic, wearing a pink shirt and holding a small bandage.

Her mother laughed as soon as she saw it.

“Oh, this one.”

Yichen looked at the picture.

“What happened?”

Her mother shook her head.

“This girl…”

She looked at him.

“Do you know that she once tried to scare a bully while her own foot was bleeding?”

Yichen blinked.

“Her foot?”

“Yes.”

She leaned back.

“This happened when she was about eight.”

Yichen put down the fruit knife he had been holding. Her mother continued.

“There was a group of children who liked bullying a younger boy near the old playground. They would chase him away whenever he tried to play with them. Sometimes they would deliberately kick his things away.”

She shook her head.

“Xiaoran had already warned them several times. One day, she saw them surrounding him again.”

Yichen listened carefully.

“She ran over. There was a broken piece of tile near the playground, and she stepped on it while trying to get between them.”

Yichen’s eyebrows drew together.

“Did it cut her?”

“Quite badly. The sole of her foot was bleeding.”

He looked at the photograph again.

“But she didn’t tell anyone?”

Her mother laughed, although there was a hint of exasperation in it.

“No. That’s the ridiculous part.”

She explained that Xiaoran had noticed the blood almost immediately.

But the boy she was confronting had already begun laughing at her.

He told her she couldn’t even stand properly, so how could she stop him?

“And what did she do?” Yichen asked.

Her mother shook her head.
