“She lifted her foot slightly, hid the injured part behind her other leg, and stood there with the most frightening expression she could manage.”

Yichen stared at her.

“While her foot was bleeding?”

“Yes!”

Her mother laughed.

“She told him, ‘You’d better leave before I get angry.’”

Yichen lowered his head. A quiet laugh escaped him. He could almost see Xiaoran doing exactly that.

Her mother continued, “The boy hesitated because she looked so serious. She was pale, and her eyes were full of tears, but she wouldn’t let him see that she was hurt.”

“Did he leave?”

“He did. Eventually, another child ran to get an adult, and the boys scattered.”

Her mother sighed.

“When I arrived, she was still standing there. Her foot had blood on it, and she was trying to pretend nothing had happened.”

Yichen’s expression softened.

“What did you do?”

“I carried her to the clinic.”

Her mother looked at him.

“And do you know what she said?”

He shook his head.

“She asked me not to tell the younger boy she was hurt.”

Yichen looked up.

“Why?”

“Because she didn’t want him to feel guilty. She told me he had already been frightened enough.”

For a moment, neither of them spoke. Her mother smiled sadly.

“She was so little. She didn’t know how to protect herself properly, but she was always thinking about how to protect someone else.”

Yichen looked down at the photograph. A small pink-shirted girl, holding a bandage, smiling at the camera.

He wondered whether she had been smiling because the pain was gone, or because she had finally convinced everyone she was fine.

“Did she always hide her injuries?”

The question came out before Yichen realised he had asked it. Her mother looked at him.

“Quite often.”

She scrolled through more pictures.

“Once, she fell off her bicycle while trying to help another child. She scraped her elbow and didn’t tell us until we noticed blood on her sleeve.”

Another picture.

“She got bitten by a dog when she was trying to pull a smaller child away from it. Thankfully, it was a very small dog, and the injury wasn’t serious. But she was more concerned about whether the little boy had been frightened.”

Another.

“She once came home with a swollen finger because she had tried to stop two children from pulling at each other’s schoolbags.”

Yichen listened. He wasn’t smiling anymore. Her mother noticed.

“Don’t look so worried. These things happened when she was young.”

“I know.”

“She grew up. She’s much more sensible now.”

Yichen nodded. But he knew Xiaoran. He knew how she sometimes brushed off a small injury.

How she would say she was fine before anyone had even asked.

How she could be more concerned about someone else’s discomfort than her own.

He had once watched her scrape her knee and immediately stand up, insisting that it didn’t hurt.

He remembered gently cleaning the wound while she complained that he was making a big deal out of nothing. He had thought she was simply stubborn.

Her mother had told him so herself, at the top of four flights of stairs on moving day: she’ll tell you she’s fine when she isn’t. He’d thought it was a mother worrying. Then he’d watched it happen the week she got sick and tidied her studio instead of lying down, and again the fortnight she skipped meals and told him she wasn’t hungry.

Now he wondered how many times that little girl had learned to hide pain because she believed she needed to stay standing. Her mother laughed.

“Actually, there’s another story.”

Yichen looked up.

“Another one?”

“Yes. This one is funny.”

She showed him a picture of Xiaoran wearing a red cape. He smiled.

“Another hero?”

Her mother nodded.

“She organised the children in our neighbourhood.”

“Organised them?”

“She made them form a group.”

Yichen laughed.

“What kind of group?”

“She called it the Neighbourhood Protection Team.”

He laughed harder. Her mother continued, clearly enjoying herself.

“She assigned everyone roles. One person was responsible for watching the playground. Another was supposed to report anyone bullying younger children. She even made them promise not to leave their friends behind.”

Yichen shook his head, smiling.

“How old was she?”

“Maybe seven.”

He laughed again.

“And did they listen?”

“Some did. Others just wanted to play.”

Her mother smiled.

“But she took it very seriously. She made everyone line up and gave them instructions.”

She turned to Yichen. “Your girlfriend was a very strict little leader,” she said.

Yichen looked at the picture. The little Xiaoran was standing in front of several children, her hands on her hips. He could almost hear her.

You have to listen to me. Otherwise, how can we protect everyone?

He smiled.

“She’s still a leader sometimes.”

Her mother laughed.

“Yes. I can imagine.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At that moment, footsteps came down the stairs.

“Mum? Where’s the photo album?”

Xiaoran appeared in the doorway. She stopped when she saw the two of them. Her mother was holding her phone. Yichen was smiling. A particular kind of smile. She narrowed her eyes.

“What are you doing?”

Her mother looked up innocently.

“Showing Yichen your childhood pictures.”

Xiaoran froze.

“Which pictures?”

“Your childhood pictures.”

“Mum.”

Her mother smiled.

“What?”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen. He looked back at her.

His expression was calm, but his eyes were full of amusement. She immediately became suspicious.

“What did she tell you?”

“Nothing much.”

Her mother laughed.

“Nothing much? I told him everything!”

Xiaoran’s face changed.

“Mum!”

Her mother started counting on her fingers.

“I told him about the kindergarten incident, the playground, the Neighbourhood Protection Team—”

“Mum!”

“And the time you cut your foot—”

“STOP!”

Yichen laughed. Xiaoran looked at him.

“You heard that?”

“All of it.”

She covered her face.

“Oh my God.”

Her mother continued, completely unbothered.

“What’s wrong? Those were good stories.”

Xiaoran dropped her hands.

“They’re embarrassing!”

“Why? You were very brave.”

“Mum!”

Her mother laughed. Then she looked at Yichen.

“She was a little warrior.”

Yichen smiled.

“Yes. I can see that.”

Xiaoran turned towards him.

“Don’t encourage her!”

He raised both hands slightly.

“I’m not.”

“You are!”

Her mother laughed until she had to put her phone down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when her mother went to prepare dinner, Xiaoran dragged Yichen upstairs to her old bedroom, which still had glow-in-the-dark stars on the ceiling.

She shut the door most of the way, because her grandmother was downstairs, and her grandmother was her grandmother. Then she turned around.

“Tell me exactly what she said.”

He sat on the end of the bed.

“Everything.”

“Yichen.”

He looked up at her.

“She told me you used to protect other children.”

Xiaoran’s expression shifted.

“That’s all?”

“She also told me you once stood in front of a boy twice your size.”

She looked away.

“And?”

“You scraped your knees and palms. But you refused to leave until the other boy stopped bullying your friend.”

She sat beside him.

“Mum remembers everything.”

“Apparently.”

She was quiet. Then she muttered, “It wasn’t a big deal.”

Yichen turned towards her.

“Wasn’t it?”

“No.”

“You were five or six.”

She shrugged.

“Children fight.”

He looked at her. Then he said, “You also had a bleeding foot once.”

Her face immediately turned red.

“Mum told you that too?”

“Yes.”

“That’s so embarrassing.”

He smiled.

“You hid it because you wanted to scare the bully.”

She covered her face.

“Please don’t repeat that.”

He laughed. Then he reached for her hand.

“Xiaoran.”

She peeked through her fingers.

“What?”

“Why didn’t you tell anyone you were hurt?”

She lowered her hands. For a moment, she seemed to think about it. Then she shrugged.

“I don’t know. I just wanted them to leave the other children alone.”

He looked at her.

“You were hurt too.”

“I know.”

“You could have asked an adult for help.”

“I know.”

He didn’t scold her. He simply held her hand. She looked at their joined fingers. Then she smiled a little.

“It’s not like I did it because I wanted to be a hero.”

“What did you want?”

She thought about it.

“I didn’t like seeing people get picked on.”

He nodded.

“I know.”

“That’s all.”

He brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

“That’s not a small thing.”

He said, “You were little. You didn’t have to be responsible for everyone.”

She looked at him.

“But someone had to stop them.”

He was quiet. Then he smiled faintly.

“You really haven’t changed much.”

She immediately protested.

“I have!”

“Have you?”

“Yes!”

He raised an eyebrow. She thought for a second.

Then said, “I’m much more mature now.”

He smiled.

“Of course.”

“Why do you sound unconvinced?”

“I’m very convinced.”

“Liar.”

He laughed and pulled her closer.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, Yichen found himself looking at Xiaoran differently. Not because he had discovered some extraordinary secret. He already knew she was kind. He already knew she was brave.

But now, when she raised her voice at her father for stealing food from her plate, when she complained that her mother was embarrassing her, when she laughed too loudly at a joke, he found himself imagining the little girl she had once been.

The little girl who had planted her feet in front of someone bigger.

The little girl who had stood on an injured foot because she didn’t want a bully to see her weakness.

The little girl who had organised an entire neighbourhood protection team.

He wondered how many of those children still remembered her.

He wondered how many people had gone home safely because a small girl had decided she wasn’t going to walk away.

And he wondered how often she had come home, hiding her injuries until someone noticed. He looked across the dining table.

Xiaoran was laughing at something her father had said.

Her mother placed another piece of food in her bowl. She complained, but ate it anyway. She looked happy. Yichen smiled. Then her mother glanced at him.

“Yichen, what are you thinking?”

He looked up.

“Nothing, Auntie.”

Her mother smiled.

“Were you surprised by her childhood stories?”

“A little.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Why are you still talking about that?”

Her father laughed.

“Because you were very famous on this lane.”

“Dad!”

Her mother added, “Everyone knew Xiaoran would come running if someone was being bullied.”

Xiaoran lowered her head.

“Can we talk about something else?”

Yichen smiled. Her mother looked at him.

“She was always like that. Even when she was hurt, she wouldn’t tell us immediately.”

He glanced at Xiaoran. She was concentrating hard on her rice. Her father chuckled.

“That’s why her mother used to check her hands and knees whenever she came home.”

Yichen smiled faintly.

“I see. I’ll remember that.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“Remember what?”

He met her eyes.

“To check whether you’re hurt when you say you’re fine.”

She froze. Her mother laughed.

“Good! You should.”

Xiaoran stared at both of them.

“Why are you forming an alliance?”

Yichen calmly picked up his chopsticks.

“I’m just learning.”

She kicked his foot lightly under the table. He smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, after everyone else had gone to bed, Xiaoran was sitting cross-legged on the guest-room bed in her pyjamas, scrolling through her phone, with the door left open the exact width her grandmother would consider respectable.

Yichen came back from brushing his teeth and found her looking at an old photograph. He sat beside her.

“What are you looking at?”

She showed him. It was the picture of her in the red cape. Yichen smiled.

“Neighbourhood Protection Team leader.”

She groaned.

“Please forget that name.”

“Why? I think it’s impressive.”

“I was seven.”

“Very young for a leadership position.”

She laughed and pushed his shoulder. He took the phone gently. Then he looked at the photograph again.

“Can I have this?”

She blinked.

“Why?”

“I like it.”

She studied his expression.

“You really like it?”

He nodded.

“Very much.”

“Fine. I’ll send it to you.”

He returned the phone. Then he took her hand and examined her palm. She looked at him.

“What are you doing?”

“Checking.”

“Checking what?”

“Whether you have any injuries.”

She laughed.

“Yichen, that was years ago.”

“I know.”

He turned her hand over, then gently kissed her palm. She became quiet. He looked at her.

“What?”

She shook her head.

“Nothing.”

He kissed the other palm too. Then he said, “You don’t have to hide it when you’re hurt now.”

She looked at him.

He said, “You don’t have to pretend you’re not in pain just because you want to protect someone.”

Her expression softened.

“I know.”

“If something happens, tell me.”

She smiled.

“Okay.”

He watched her. Then she leaned forward and wrapped her arms around his neck.

“Are you worried about me?”

“A little.”

“Why?”

He smiled faintly.

“Because I found out my girlfriend used to challenge boys twice her size while bleeding.”

She laughed against his shoulder.

“That makes me sound ridiculous.”

“It makes you sound brave.”

She lifted her head. He brushed her hair away from her face.

“But you were still a little girl. You deserved someone looking after you too.”

Xiaoran didn’t answer. Then she hugged him again, a little tighter. Yichen held her.

He didn’t tell her that he wished he could have known her back then.

That he wished he could have been the person who carried her to the clinic, cleaned her scraped knees, and told her she didn’t need to stand on an injured foot to prove she was brave. He knew that was impossible.

He couldn’t go back and take care of the little girl she had been.

But he could take care of the woman who was still, in so many ways, that same little warrior. And he intended to.

Much later, lying beside him on top of the covers with her head on his chest and her eyes nearly closed, Xiaoran suddenly spoke.

“Yichen?”

“Hmm?”

“Did my mother tell you anything else?”

He thought about it.

“She told me you once organised children into a protection team.”

Xiaoran groaned.

“Anything else?”

“She said you were very strict.”

She buried her face in his chest.

“I’m never speaking to her again.”

He laughed.

Then, after a pause, he said, “She also told me you were the kind of child who would share your snacks with anyone who forgot theirs.”

Xiaoran lifted her head.

“Oh.”

“And that you would always save the smallest piece for yourself.”

She smiled.

“That’s because I liked the bigger pieces.”

He laughed.

“I know.”

She settled against him again. She murmured, “I wasn’t always brave, you know.”

He looked down at her.

“What do you mean?”

“I got scared too. Sometimes I cried after everything was over.”

He brushed his fingers through her hair.

“That’s alright.”

“I just didn’t want them to see me cry.”

He smiled gently.

“You know, being brave doesn’t mean you never get scared.”

She looked up. He kissed her hair.

“It just means you did what you thought was right, even when you were scared.”

She stared at him, then smiled.

“That’s a very nice thing to say.”

“It’s true.”

She tucked herself closer.

“Yichen?”

“Hmm?”

“Don’t tell anyone about the Neighbourhood Protection Team.”

He laughed.

“I won’t.”

“And don’t call me a little warrior.”

He paused.

“Alright.”

She closed her eyes, satisfied. A few seconds passed.

Then he whispered, “Good night, little warrior.”

She immediately opened her eyes.

“ZHOU YICHEN!”

He burst out laughing, and from the bottom of the stairs her grandmother called up that some people in this house were trying to sleep, and Xiaoran fled back to her own room with her face burning.

And somewhere between her indignant complaints and his quiet laughter, Yichen decided that he rather liked knowing this part of her.

The brave little girl who had grown up into the woman he loved.

The girl who had always tried to protect everyone.

Even when she was the one who needed protecting.

And perhaps, for once, she could let someone else stand beside her.

chapters.desc: The Herons send a development contract on an ordinary Tuesday, and the first person Zhou Yichen calls is the girl choosing between two steamed buns.
chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.epigraph: “Because I wanted to tell you first.”
chapters.content:
The email arrived on a Tuesday morning, in the first week of the spring semester. Zhou Yichen almost missed it.

He was sitting at his desk, reviewing a case study for his Business course, with a half-finished cup of coffee beside his laptop. His phone vibrated once. He glanced at it, expecting a message from his university basketball group. Instead, he saw an unfamiliar notification.

Shanghai Herons — Player Development

His hand stopped on the trackpad. He looked at the sender’s name. Then he opened it. The subject line was brief.

Development Contract Offer — Zhou Yichen

He read the email once, then again. The message was formal, carefully worded, and accompanied by an official document outlining the club’s offer. It confirmed that, following his previous evaluations and subsequent development sessions, the Herons were prepared to offer him a place under their development contract program.

There were details about the development squad, training commitments, performance reviews, availability, and the club’s expectations for the rest of this season and the next.

It wasn’t a first-team contract, and it didn’t promise he would ever be named for a real game. It was a formal offer to keep going, from a club that had once almost overlooked him. Yichen leaned back in his chair.

He read the document carefully, paying attention to every clause. He didn’t allow himself to become carried away by the subject line. He checked the obligations, the review process, the expected schedule, and the conditions surrounding his university commitments. He reached the final page. Then he returned to the first. His phone was beside his laptop.

There were three people he would have to tell: his university coach, his father and Lin Xiaoran. He picked up his phone.

For a few seconds, his thumb hovered over her contact. Then he pressed call.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran was in the canteen, choosing between two kinds of steamed bun, when her phone rang. She saw his name and answered immediately.

“Hello?”

“Are you busy?”

She glanced at the buns.

“Not really. I’m deciding what to eat.”

“Have you eaten?”

“Not yet.”

“Then don’t take too long.”

She smiled.

“Why? Are you hungry?”

“No.”

“Then why are you rushing me?”

“I’m not.”

She laughed, but something about his voice made her pause. It wasn’t his usual tone.

He sounded composed, as always, but there was a particular stillness to him. As if he had something on his mind and was trying to decide how to say it.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“What’s wrong?”

A brief silence.

Then he said, “I received an email this morning.”

“From whom?”

“The Herons.”

Her expression changed. She straightened in her chair.

“The Herons?”

“Yes.”

“What happened?”

“They’ve sent me an offer.”

For a second, Xiaoran didn’t respond. She was afraid she had misunderstood.

“What kind of offer?”

“A development contract.”

She stared at the table. Then her eyes widened.

“Wait.”

He heard the movement on her end, followed by the faint sound of her chair scraping against the floor.

“Yichen.”

“Yes?”

“An actual contract?”

“A development contract. They’ve offered me a place in their program,” he clarified gently.

Her hand flew to her mouth.

“Oh my God.”

He laughed. She stood up.

“Yichen!”

“I can hear you.”

“They offered you a contract?”

“Yes.”

“After the evaluations?”

“Yes.”

“After the scrimmage?”

“Yes, Xiaoran.”

She let out a breath that sounded almost like a laugh.

Then she covered her face with her free hand.

“Oh my God.”

Yichen leaned back in his chair, listening to her. He had expected her to be happy.

He hadn’t expected her to sound quite so overwhelmed.

“Are you smiling?” he asked.

She pulled her hand away.

“Of course I’m smiling!”

“I thought so.”

“Are you smiling?”

He looked down at the document. A small smile appeared.

“Yes.”

She made a tiny, excited sound.

Then, almost immediately, she asked, “Have you read everything?”

“Yes.”

“All the terms?”

“Yes.”

“Did you check the commitments? The schedule? What happens with university?”

“I did.”

“Are you sure?”

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I read the whole document.”

She went quiet. Then she laughed at herself.

“Sorry.”

“It’s fine.”

She sat down again, still holding the phone tightly.

“Yichen, I’m so happy for you.”

He didn’t answer immediately. He looked at the email on his laptop, then at the phone in his hand.

“Thank you.”

She heard something in his voice. Something quieter than excitement.

“Are you happy?”

He considered the question.

“Yes.”

“Then why do you sound so calm?”

“Because I’m talking to you.”

She blinked.

“What does that mean?”

“If I sound excited, you’ll become even more excited.”

She gasped.

“What’s wrong with that?”

“Nothing.”

“You should be excited!”

“I am.”

“Then act like it!”

He laughed. And this time, the sound was unmistakable.

She smiled so hard her cheeks began to hurt.

For a few minutes, they talked about the offer.

He explained that the club had reviewed his development sessions and the latest performance reports. The coaching staff had agreed to move him forward, and the development department was now prepared to offer him a formal place. Xiaoran listened carefully.

She asked about the next steps, whether he had to sign immediately, and whether the club expected him at training this week.

Yichen answered what he knew and admitted what he still needed to clarify.

He wasn’t going to pretend he had all the answers.

“Does it mean you’re going to play for them now?” she asked.

“Not exactly. It’s a development contract. I’ll be part of their program, with scheduled training and evaluations. It gives me a proper pathway, but I’ll still have to earn my place.”

She nodded, even though he couldn’t see her.

“Right.”

“I don’t want to treat it as if I’ve already made it.”

“I know.”

“There’s still a lot to prove.”

“Mm.”

He heard her take a breath.

Then she said, “But you got the offer.”

He smiled.

“Yes.”

“You got it, Yichen.”

“Yes.”

She laughed.

“I think I need to say that a few more times.”

“Go ahead.”

“You got the offer.”

He closed his eyes.

“I did.”

“I’m so proud of you.”

That made him quiet. He knew she was proud. She’d said it after games and evaluations and bad training days. This sounded different, as if she were holding something precious and was afraid of dropping it. He looked at the document again.

Then he said, “You’re the first person I’ve called.”

There was a pause.

“I know.”

“I haven’t called my coach.”

“Okay.”

“Or my father.”

She didn’t speak immediately. Then she asked, “You called me first?”

“Yes.”

A smile slowly spread across her face.

“Why?”

He glanced towards the window. Outside, the morning traffic continued as usual. Cars moved through the intersection, people crossed the pavement, and somewhere in the building, someone was talking loudly on the phone. An ordinary Tuesday.

And yet something in his life had just changed.

“Because I wanted to tell you first.”

Xiaoran lowered her eyes. She remembered the walk to dinner after his second evaluation, when she’d made him promise to tell her what the next stage involved. I’ll tell you when I know, he’d said.

He had known for ten minutes, and he’d called her before anyone.

“Yichen,” she said.

“Hm?”

“I’m really glad you called me.”

“I wanted to.”

She smiled.

“Then I’m glad.”

They didn’t rush to end the call. Xiaoran eventually found a quiet corner outside the canteen, away from the noise of students moving between classes. Yichen remained at his desk. She asked him to send her the document.

He told her he would send the relevant parts once he had reviewed the personal information and confirmed what he could share. She agreed, then immediately began asking questions again.

“How long is the development period?”

“We need to clarify that.”

“Will you have to travel?”

“Probably, depending on the training schedule.”

“Will it interfere with your classes?”

“That’s one of the things I need to discuss with the university.”

“Will you still be able to play for the university team?”

“Possibly, but there may be scheduling conflicts.”

She went quiet. He noticed.

“Xiaoran.”

She sighed.

“I’m thinking.”

“About?”

“Fourth year.”

He leaned back. So was he. Fourth year had always seemed far away. It was the final year of their undergraduate degrees, the year of graduation projects, internships, final examinations, and decisions about what came next. Now, it had become something more complicated.

“Let’s talk about it,” he said.

She nodded.

“Okay.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They met that evening at his apartment. Xiaoran arrived with her laptop, a notebook, and two drinks. Yichen opened the door. He looked at the notebook.

“Are we having a meeting?”

She walked past him.

“Yes.”

“Should I prepare an agenda?”

“I already have one.”

He laughed. She placed everything on the coffee table and sat down.

Yichen brought over his laptop, the contract document, and a glass of water. Xiaoran looked at the screen.

“All right. Show me.”

He sat beside her. For the next twenty minutes, they went through the offer together.

Yichen explained the structure of the development program, the club’s expectations, the evaluation process, and the commitments he would have to meet. Xiaoran listened carefully. She didn’t treat it like a fantasy.

She didn’t start planning his professional career on the assumption that everything would go perfectly. Instead, she asked practical questions.

“What happens if your training schedule overlaps with a compulsory university class?”

“We’ll need to discuss that with the faculty.”

“Would you have to travel to another city for extended periods?”

“Possibly. The club hasn’t confirmed the full schedule yet.”

“What about your final-year project?”

“I’ll have to plan it properly.”

She nodded and wrote something down. Yichen glanced at her notebook.

“You’re taking notes.”

“Of course.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to understand.”

He watched her. Then he smiled. She looked up.

“You’re doing that again.”

“What?”

“Looking at me like that.”

He leaned back against the sofa.

“I like watching you take things seriously.”

She tried not to smile.

“Well, someone has to.”

He laughed. She returned to the document. The biggest question wasn’t whether he wanted the opportunity. He did. That much was clear. The question was how to make it work.

Fourth year would already be demanding. Yichen had a Business degree to complete, final-year coursework, and a capstone project. The development contract would require regular training, performance reviews, and potentially travel.

He couldn’t assume the club would arrange everything around his university schedule.

And he didn’t want to treat his education as something he could abandon if basketball became more promising. Xiaoran understood that. She also knew how much he wanted this. She put down her pen.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“If the schedule becomes difficult, what are you most worried about?”

He considered the question.

“Not having enough time to do everything properly.”

“Meaning?”

“Training, university, recovery. I don’t want to do any of them halfway.”

She nodded.

“And what about us? I’m not asking because I’m worried you’ll forget about me.”

“I know.”

“I just want to understand what our fourth year might look like.”

He was quiet. Then he said, “We’ll have to be more deliberate.”

She nodded.

“About time?”

“Time. Travel. Plans. Everything.”

He rested his forearms on his knees.

“I might have to spend some weekends away. There may be periods when training takes priority because of the program. I don’t know how much flexibility they’ll give me yet.”

Xiaoran listened.

“I don’t want to promise you that nothing will change.”

She met his eyes.

“Yichen, things are going to change anyway.”

He smiled.

“That’s true.”

“Your basketball is becoming more serious. My final year is coming. I’ll probably have my own projects, internships, and things to deal with. We can’t expect everything to stay exactly the same.”

He turned towards her.

“But I don’t want you to feel like you have to fit yourself around my schedule.”

She turned to him.

“I don’t.”

“I mean it.”

“I know.”

He held her gaze.

“I want you to have your own year too. Your own opportunities. I don’t want you to postpone something because you think you have to be available whenever I’m free.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“That’s good.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Good?”

“Because I don’t intend to.”

He laughed. She leaned closer.

“But I also don’t want you to think that having a busy schedule means you have to handle everything alone. If you have a difficult week, tell me. If you’re tired, tell me. If you need to focus on training, tell me. I can understand that. What I don’t want is for you to decide on my behalf that I won’t understand.”

His expression softened.

“All right.”

“And I don’t want you to feel guilty every time you can’t see me.”

He was quiet.

“That’s going to be difficult.”

“I know.”

She smiled.

“We’ll figure it out.”

He reached for her hand. They began making a rough plan. Not a rigid timetable. Just a framework.

First, Yichen would speak with the club to clarify the training schedule, travel expectations, and how the program would operate during the university term.

Then he would meet with his university coach and faculty advisor to understand what academic flexibility might be available, especially for compulsory sessions and his final-year project.

He would have the university’s legal office read the contract before he signed anything.

Xiaoran would have her own final-year commitments. She was likely to be occupied with a major Media project, and she wanted to explore internship opportunities without assuming that her schedule would always align with his.

They agreed that they would keep certain things for themselves. Not as obligations, but as priorities.

One evening a week, if possible, would be theirs.

If he had to travel, they would make time for proper calls rather than relying entirely on short messages between activities.

If she had an important presentation, he would make an effort to be there whenever the schedule allowed.

And if either of them became overwhelmed, they would say so before resentment had time to build. Xiaoran wrote everything down. Then she looked at the page.

“That’s a lot.”

Yichen glanced at it. He leaned closer.

“You’re the one who made the list.”

“I know. I’m just surprised.”

He smiled. She looked at him.

“Do you think we can do it?”

He didn’t answer immediately. Then he said, “I think we’ll have to learn.”

She smiled.

“That’s not very romantic.”

“Would you prefer I promise everything will be easy?”

“No.”

He took her hand.

“I’d rather promise I’ll keep talking to you. Even when things get difficult.”

She held his gaze.

“That’s better.”

He kissed her cheek. Later, they moved to the kitchen.

Xiaoran was making tea while Yichen stood beside the counter, reading through the email again. She tilted her head.

“Are you nervous?”

“A little.”

She looked surprised.

“Really?”

“Why wouldn’t I be?”

She placed the cups on the counter.

“I thought you’d be excited.”

“I am.”

“Then?”

He put the laptop aside.

“An offer is one thing. Accepting it means committing to what comes next. I’ve spent a long time trying to get here. I know what I want, but I also know what I’ll be responsible for if I say yes.”

She looked at him thoughtfully.

“You’re allowed to be nervous.”

“Thank you.”

“You’re also allowed to be excited.”

“I know.”

She stepped closer.

“Then be both.”

He looked down at her. She reached up and adjusted the collar of his shirt.

“I know how hard you’ve worked. I know there were times when you weren’t sure the club would even give you a fair chance. And now they’ve offered you a place. You did that.”

He reached for her waist.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome. But don’t become too handsome and famous.”

He laughed.

“Is that your biggest concern?”

“Yes. I have to protect my position.”

“Your position?”

“Girlfriend. The only one.”

He looked at her with an amused expression.

“There’s no competition.”

“Good.”

He bent down and kissed her. That night, Yichen finally called his university coach.

The conversation was practical. His coach congratulated him, asked about the offer, and advised him not to rush into signing before all the academic and training arrangements were clear. Yichen agreed. He then called his father. Mr. Zhou answered after the second ring.

“Yichen.”

“Dad. The Herons sent me an offer.”

There was a pause.

“What kind?”

“A development contract.”

His father asked several questions about the program, the club’s expectations, and the terms. Yichen answered them as clearly as he could.

“Have the university’s legal office read it. Not me.”

“Because of the sponsorship.”

“Our name is on their sleeves. I won’t have anyone say I was in the room when they made you an offer.”

“I know.”

Another brief pause.

“Congratulations.”

Yichen looked towards the living room. Xiaoran was sitting on the sofa, reading something on her tablet. She glanced up when she heard his father’s voice.

“Thank you,” Yichen said.

His father continued, “This is a good opportunity. But understand what it requires. A development contract is not the same as a guaranteed first-team position.”

“I know.”

“You’ll have to earn the next step.”

“I know.”

“Good. Call your mother. She’ll want to hear it from you, not from me.”

The call ended. Yichen put his phone down. Xiaoran looked up.

“How was it?”

“Fine.”

“Your father?”

“Yes.”

“What did he say?”

“He wants the legal office to read it. Not him.”

She nodded.

“That’s sensible.”

Yichen walked towards her and sat down. She put her tablet aside.

“Have you told him you called me first?”

He glanced at her.

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Do you want me to?”

She smiled.

“No.”

He met her eyes. Then he reached over and tucked her hair behind her ear.

“I wanted to tell you before everyone else.”

She leaned into his hand.

“I know.”

It was late when Xiaoran finally prepared to leave. Yichen walked her to the door.

She put on her shoes, then turned back towards him.

“You’re really going to have a busy fourth year.”

“Probably.”

“Business final year, basketball development program, training, travel...”

“And you.”

She smiled.

“And me.”

He took her hand.

“Especially you.”

She laughed.

“Don’t say that just to make me happy.”

“I’m not. I don’t want you to become another item on my schedule. I want you to remain part of my life.”

Her expression softened.

“Then let me be part of it.”

“I will.”

She caught his collar and kissed him. When she pulled away, he kept one hand at her waist.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“I’m happy you called me first. Not because I needed to be first. Because I want to be someone you call when something important happens. Good or bad.”

His expression changed slightly. He understood what she meant.

“I know,” he said.

Then he pressed a kiss into her hair.

“And I will.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

He opened the door for her. She stepped into the corridor, then turned around one last time.

“Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“Congratulations.”

He smiled.

“Thank you.”

She lifted both hands and made a little celebratory gesture. He laughed. Then she disappeared down the corridor. After she left, Yichen returned to his desk. The email was still open.

The offer document was still waiting for his decision. He sat down and read it once more. There would be a lot to arrange.

He would need to understand how the program fitted around his final year, how much travel it meant, and what the next evaluation stage looked like.

There was no guarantee that he would make it to the first team.

There was no guarantee that the road ahead would be smooth. But there was an opportunity. A real one.

He opened his calendar and began marking the dates that needed attention. Then his phone vibrated.

Xiaoran: I just remembered something.

Yichen: What?

Xiaoran: You haven’t celebrated properly.

He smiled.

Yichen: I thought we did.

Xiaoran: No. I mean your offer.

Yichen: We can celebrate after I understand the terms.

Xiaoran: That’s not an answer.

Yichen: What would you like to do?

A few seconds passed.

Xiaoran: Something nice.

Yichen: Define nice.

Xiaoran: Food. You. No laptops. No contract documents.

He smiled.

Yichen: Sounds good.

Xiaoran: And I get to brag about you to everyone.

Yichen: You do that already.

Xiaoran: I know. I just want to.

He looked at her message, then typed.

Yichen: Then I’ll listen whenever you do.

Her reply came quickly.

Xiaoran: Goodnight, future basketball star.

He laughed.

Yichen: Goodnight, future media professional.

Xiaoran: That’s not as cool.

Yichen: I disagree.

Xiaoran: You’re biased.

Yichen: Very.

He put the phone down. Then he looked once more at the email.

The Herons had offered him a place in their development program.

It was the beginning of something he had worked towards.

But the first person he had wanted to tell wasn’t the coach who had trained him, or the father who had spent six years in the back row of his games.

It was the girl who had sat beside him through every uncertain stage, who had never mistaken his setbacks for a lack of ability, and who had always understood that his ambition was something he wanted to share—not something he needed to pursue alone.

He opened a new message to the club and began arranging a time to discuss the terms.

chapters.desc: His debut for the Herons, number eleven, with everyone who helped him get there in the stands, and his father in the front row for the first time.
chapters.title: First Real Game
chapters.epigraph: “She promised.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Xiaoran noticed when she walked into the arena was how big it was.

She had spent a lot of her life in basketball halls by now. University games, his tournaments, practice scrimmages, enough afternoons to know the smell of polished wood and rubber soles and the warm, metallic air under the lights. But today felt different. Today, Zhou Yichen wasn’t playing another game.

Today was his debut, his first official game for the Herons. Three weeks after he signed the development contract, his name had gone up on the game-day roster, and he had read it out to her over the phone twice.

She stood near the entrance, holding her ticket in one hand and her phone in the other. Row 1, it said. He’d remembered. Her eyes moved across the court, then towards the seating area. She had promised him she would cheer loudly. She intended to keep that promise.

“Xiaoran!”

She turned. Luo Jiayi was waving at her from the front row. Sun Ning stood beside her, holding a paper cup and looking as if she had already eaten something she wasn’t supposed to.

“You came early!” Jiayi called.

“I didn’t want to miss anything.”

Ning looked at the court. “You say that as if the game starts in five minutes. We still have nearly an hour.”

“That’s not the point.”

“What’s the point?”

“Today is important.”

Jiayi nodded solemnly. “Of course. The historic day when Zhou Yichen becomes a professional basketball player.”

“He’s not officially a first-team player,” Xiaoran corrected immediately.

Ning gave her a look.

“You’re very well informed.”

“Of course I am.”

Jiayi leaned towards Ning. “She’s been studying the club’s development structure again.”

“I heard that.”

“Good. I wanted you to.”

Xiaoran ignored him and walked towards their seats. She had barely sat down when her phone vibrated.

Yichen: Have you arrived?

Xiaoran: Yes!

Yichen: Where are you sitting?

She sent him a photograph of the court from her seat.

Xiaoran: Here. You can find me.

Yichen: I can see you.

She looked up immediately. Across the court, near the players’ entrance, Yichen stood with his teammates. He wore the Herons’ uniform, his number printed clearly across the front.

He was talking to one of the assistant coaches when his gaze lifted. Their eyes met. Xiaoran waved.

He gave her a smile and raised his hand. Then he returned to the conversation. She looked down at her phone.

Xiaoran: Don’t look too long. Focus on your game.

Yichen: I wasn’t looking for long.

Xiaoran: I saw you.

Yichen: Then you should focus on your seat.

She pressed her lips together, smiling. Jiayi glanced over.

“He’s texting you?”

“No.”

“Your face says otherwise.”

Xiaoran put her phone away.

“Watch the court.”

Jiayi leaned forward.

“She’s already behaving like a player’s wife.”

“Luo Jiayi.”

“What? I didn’t say anything.”

Ning laughed. The first surprise came when Xiaoran noticed Professor Xie.

He was seated a few rows behind the court, speaking with the university’s athletic director. She recognised him immediately.

“Ning.”

“Hm?”

“Look behind us.”

Ning turned.

“Professor Xie?”

“And the athletic director.”

Jiayi followed their gaze.

“Oh. They’re here.”

Xiaoran looked back towards the court. Yichen’s university coach was also present, standing near the Herons’ coaching staff. She felt a strange warmth in her chest. They had all come.

The people who had seen him during university practice, who had watched him work through the early evaluations, who had supported his request for a fair opportunity when the club’s initial selection process had been less than fair. They were here to see him play. And then she noticed someone else.

Four seats along her own row, a man in a dark jacket sat straight, his face unreadable. Mr. Zhou.

“That’s Yichen’s dad,” Xiaoran whispered.

Jiayi leaned forward to look past her. “In the front row?”

Xiaoran didn’t say anything. From the time Yichen was twelve, his father had sat in the back row of every game he played, so that his son wouldn’t play for him. Xiaoran knew about the ticket stubs. The last time she’d seen Mr. Zhou at one of Yichen’s games, the summer after first year, he had come in during the third quarter and left before the players had packed up.

Tonight the Herons’ sponsor had a box upstairs with his company’s name on the door, and he wasn’t in it. He was in the front row, where he could see the whole court. Xiaoran looked towards the players’ entrance.

Yichen was speaking to a teammate, unaware of the small discovery she had just made. She wondered whether he knew. The warm-up began.

Yichen moved onto the court with the rest of the team. Xiaoran sat forward immediately. He looked different in the Herons’ uniform.

She watched him stretch, jog, and exchange passes with his teammates. His movements were familiar: controlled, efficient, without unnecessary gestures.

He received a pass near the wing and took a shot. The ball went in. Ning nodded.

“Good.”

Jiayi glanced at her.

“You sound like a commentator.”

“I am appreciating the game.”

Xiaoran was already clapping. Yichen received another pass. This time, he drove towards the basket, changed direction, and finished with a clean layup. She clapped again.

“That’s my—”

She stopped. Jiayi turned slowly.

“Your what?”

“Nothing.”

Ning grinned.

“Go on. Finish the sentence.”

“Shut up.”

On the court, Yichen moved towards the baseline to retrieve the ball. He glanced towards the stands. Xiaoran was still watching him. He smiled. She smiled back. Then he looked away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before the game began, the teams gathered for their final instructions.

Yichen stood among his teammates, listening to the coach. His expression was focused.

He had studied the opponent’s footage. He knew their defensive tendencies, their preferred rotations, and which players were likely to force a fast transition. He knew what his role was. He also knew that a debut wasn’t the time to prove everything in one possession. He needed to play within the system. Make the right decisions. Earn his minutes.

The coach finished speaking and looked directly at him.

“Zhou.”

“Yes, Coach.”

“Don’t try to make the game bigger than it is.”

Yichen nodded.

“Understood.”

“Play the way you’ve been playing.”

“Yes, Coach.”

Kou Ran bumped his shoulder.

“Ready?”

Yichen looked towards the court.

“Ready.”

The game started quickly. The Herons opened with a strong defensive possession, forcing the opposition to take a difficult shot. The rebound was secured, and the ball moved up the court. Yichen began on the bench.

Xiaoran watched the game with both hands clasped around her drink.

She knew he wouldn’t necessarily start. The development contract didn’t guarantee him a place in the starting lineup, and she had never expected it to. Still, she wanted to see him play.

She wanted to see what he would do when the game became real.

Number seventeen was at the far end of the bench. He stayed there all night.

The first quarter passed with the Herons maintaining a narrow lead.

Then, midway through the second quarter, the coach turned towards the bench.

“Zhou. Get ready.”

Yichen stood immediately. Xiaoran’s fingers tightened around the edge of her seat. Jiayi noticed.

“He’s going in.”

“I know.”

“You’re holding your breath.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

Yichen removed his warm-up top. The navy jersey had a heron on the chest and an eleven on the back, the same number he’d worn for the university.

He listened to the assistant coach’s instructions, nodded once, and stepped towards the scorer’s table. The announcer called his name.

“Making his debut for the Herons, number eleven, Zhou Yichen!”

Xiaoran forgot how to breathe. Then she stood. And clapped. Loudly.

“YICHEN!”

Jiayi jumped up beside her, cupping her hands around her mouth.

“ZHOU YICHEN!”

Several people around them turned. Xiaoran didn’t care. She clapped harder. On the court, Yichen glanced towards the stands. He found her immediately.

She was standing, smiling so brightly that he could see it even from across the arena. He gave her a small nod. Then he stepped onto the court. His first possession was simple.

He received the ball near the perimeter, looked at the defence, and passed it to the point guard before moving into position. No unnecessary shot. No attempt to force an impressive debut.

He followed the play, set a screen, and moved towards the corner. The ball returned to him.

He took one dribble, drew the defender closer, then passed to his teammate cutting towards the basket. A clean assist. Xiaoran clapped.

“Good pass!”

Ning nodded.

“Very good.”

Jiayi smiled.

“He’s settling in.”

On the next possession, Yichen defended tightly, forcing the opposing guard to pass backward. He stayed disciplined, didn’t reach unnecessarily, and helped close the space. The opponent missed. The Herons recovered the rebound. Yichen moved into transition.

A teammate passed him the ball near the wing. He took a quick look at the basket. The defender stepped forward.

Yichen changed direction, drove past him, and finished with a layup. The ball dropped through the net. The arena reacted. Xiaoran practically jumped.

“YES!”

Jiayi caught her arm, laughing.

“Xiaoran!”

“HE SCORED!”

“I saw!”

“HE SCORED!”

Ning stood up and clapped.

“Good debut!”

Yichen jogged back on defence. His face remained composed, but the corner of his mouth lifted. He had heard her. Of course he had. The third quarter was more difficult.

The opposition adjusted their defence and began pressuring the Herons’ ball handlers. Yichen was tested.

A pass was intercepted when he tried to force a narrow opening. The opponent converted it into a fast-break score.

He didn’t argue with the referee or look towards the bench. He turned and ran back. The next possession, he made a better decision.

He held the ball, waited for the defender to commit, then passed to the open teammate on the opposite side. The Herons scored. Xiaoran clapped again. She had promised to cheer loudly.

She wasn’t going to reserve her enthusiasm only for his good moments.

When he made a mistake, she cheered for the next possession. When he defended well, she cheered.

When he made a pass that didn’t become an assist, she cheered.

And when he was substituted out for a brief rest, she clapped as he walked towards the bench.

Yichen sat down, accepted a towel, and took a drink of water. Kou Ran leaned towards him.

“Your girlfriend is loud.”

Yichen looked towards the stands. Xiaoran was talking animatedly to Ning, apparently explaining why one of his defensive rotations had been correct. He smiled.

“She promised.”

Kou Ran laughed.

“She’s keeping it.”

During the break, the camera moved across the audience.

It passed Professor Xie, who was watching with a thoughtful expression, then the athletic director, who was speaking with the university coach.

Then it moved along the front row. Mr. Zhou was watching the court. He wasn’t smiling, and he wasn’t clapping, but he was there.

Xiaoran wondered whether he was still counting mistakes, the way he had at the city-league game. Or whether, for once, he was just watching his son play. She turned back to the court.

Yichen was standing near the bench, listening to the coach.

She decided she wouldn’t spend his debut wondering what his father thought. Today belonged to Yichen.

The fourth quarter began with the score close. The Herons were ahead by two points. The coach sent Yichen back onto the court.

Xiaoran stood before she even realised she had moved. Jiayi laughed.

“You’re going to stand for the entire quarter?”

“Maybe.”

“Your legs will hurt.”

“I don’t care.”

Ning looked towards the scoreboard.

“Three minutes left. This is getting interesting.”

The game became faster. The opposition scored. The Herons responded.

Yichen defended a drive, recovered the loose ball, and moved it quickly to his teammate. Another score. The crowd grew louder.

With less than a minute remaining, the Herons were ahead by one. The opposing team called a timeout. The players gathered around their coach. Yichen listened, breathing steadily.

He wiped his face with a towel and looked towards the stands. Xiaoran was already standing. She raised both hands around her mouth.

“YICHEN! YOU’VE GOT THIS!”

He smiled. A small one. But enough. The timeout ended. The opposing team took possession.

Yichen defended the wing, forcing the player towards the sideline. His teammate closed in, and the ball was passed back towards the middle. A shot went up. It missed. The Herons secured the rebound. The ball moved quickly down the court. Yichen ran into position. A teammate passed to him. He caught it at the perimeter. The defender approached.

For a fraction of a second, he considered taking the shot. Then he saw the opening.

He drove, drew two defenders, and passed to the teammate cutting through the lane. The ball went in. The arena erupted. Xiaoran screamed, with no dignity at all.

“YICHEN!”

Jiayi was laughing beside her. Ning was clapping so hard her paper cup nearly went over the advertising boards. The Herons’ lead widened. There were seconds left. The opposition tried one final shot. It missed. The buzzer sounded. The Herons won.

Yichen stood near the free-throw line as his teammates gathered around him. A teammate grabbed his shoulders.

“Good game!”

Another bumped his chest.

“Welcome to the team!”

He smiled, breathing heavily. He had scored, assisted, defended, made mistakes, and recovered from them. He hadn’t dominated the game. He hadn’t needed to. He had played his role. And he had helped his team win.

The coach approached him and gave him a firm pat on the shoulder.

“Good work.”

“Thank you, Coach.”

“Good decisions in the final minute.”

Yichen nodded.

“I saw the cut.”

“Exactly. Keep doing that.”

Then the coach moved on. Yichen looked towards the stands. Xiaoran was still standing.

She was clapping with both hands raised, her cheeks flushed, her eyes bright. He couldn’t help smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the game, the players gathered near the court for a team photograph and media duties.

Xiaoran waited with Jiayi and Ning near the meeting area. She had sent him three messages already.

Xiaoran: YOU WERE SO GOOD.

Xiaoran: THE PASS IN THE LAST MINUTE!!!

Xiaoran: I AM STILL SO EXCITED.

Yichen glanced at his phone while waiting for the next interview. He smiled.

Yichen: I noticed.

Xiaoran: You noticed what?

Yichen: You shouting.

Xiaoran: Good. That was the plan.

Yichen: I don’t think the people in the next section needed to know my name.

Xiaoran: They should know.

He laughed under his breath, then the media coordinator called him. Professor Xie approached first.

“Yichen.”

Yichen turned.

“Professor.”

Professor Xie shook his hand.

“Congratulations. Your university coach has been telling us about your progress. It was good to see you finally make your debut.”

“Thank you for coming, Professor.”

“How did it feel?”

Yichen thought.

“Different from the scrimmages. The pace was higher, and the decisions had to be quicker.”

Professor Xie nodded.

“And?”

“I enjoyed it.”

The athletic director joined them.

“Well done, Zhou. Your university is proud to see you taking this opportunity forward.”

Yichen thanked him. His university coach came over as well, smiling.

“You looked comfortable out there.”

“Thank you, Coach.”

“Don’t get too comfortable. There’s plenty more to learn.”

“I know.”

Professor Xie laughed.

“Let him enjoy his debut first.”

Yichen smiled. The group talked about the game, his development, and how he would balance the next phase with his academic commitments.

It was a brief conversation, but it meant something to him. They had seen him before the club contract.

They had seen him when the opportunity was uncertain. And they were here now. Then he saw his father. Mr. Zhou stood a short distance away, waiting. Yichen’s expression changed almost imperceptibly.

He excused himself from the group and walked over.

“Dad.”

Mr. Zhou looked at him.

“You played.”

Yichen almost smiled at the obvious statement.

“Yes.”

His father glanced towards the court.

“Your positioning is better than in the city league.”

Yichen nodded.

“I’ve worked on it.”

“I noticed.”

Then Mr. Zhou said, “You didn’t force the final shot.”

“There was a better option.”

“Yes.”

Yichen looked at him. His father held his gaze.

“Good decision.”

It wasn’t much of a compliment. But Yichen knew his father.

He knew what it meant for Mr. Zhou to come and sit in the front row. He knew what it meant for him to stay until the final buzzer, to watch the entire game, and to speak about something other than the one mistake he could have made.

“Thank you for coming,” Yichen said.

Mr. Zhou nodded.

“I wanted to see your debut.”

Yichen looked at him for a second longer.

Then he said, “I’m glad you did.”

His father gave a small nod. They stood together for another moment before Mr. Zhou asked about the next development evaluation. The conversation moved naturally towards practical matters.

But something small had shifted, and for now that was enough.

“YICHEN!”

He turned. Xiaoran was waving from the meeting area.

She had clearly been waiting for him to finish speaking with his father. Mr. Zhou glanced towards her.

“Your girlfriend is waiting.”

Yichen smiled.

“Yes.”

“Go.”

He nodded and walked over. Xiaoran barely waited for him to reach her before she stepped forward.

“Congratulations!”

She wrapped her arms around him. He caught her easily, one hand settling against her back.

“Thank you.”

“You were so good!”

He lowered his head slightly.

“Even the turnover?”

She drew back to look at him.

“That was one mistake.”

“One?”

“One mistake that happened. Then you made better decisions.”

His eyebrows lifted.

“Very analytical.”

“I watched carefully.”

“I can tell.”

She smiled, then looked at his face.

“Are you happy?”

“Very.”

She reached up and brushed a small damp strand of hair away from his forehead.

“You did it.”

He met her eyes. She said it again, more softly.

“You made your debut.”

He smiled.

“Yes.”

“And I got to watch.”

His hand moved gently over her back.

“You were hard to miss.”

She laughed.

“Good.”

He glanced towards Jiayi and Ning, who were standing nearby.

“Did they survive?”

Jiayi raised her hand.

“Unfortunately, yes. Your girlfriend nearly destroyed my hearing.”

Xiaoran turned.

“You’re exaggerating.”

“Everyone around us knows your name now.”

“That’s a good thing.”

Ning laughed.

“She did keep her promise.”

Yichen looked down at Xiaoran.

“What promise?”

She lifted her chin.

“I told you I would cheer loudly.”

“I remember.”

“And?”

He leaned closer.

“You did.”

She smiled triumphantly.

“Exactly.”

They eventually left the arena together. The evening air was cool, and the area outside the venue was crowded with people leaving the game.

Yichen carried his sports bag over one shoulder. Xiaoran walked beside him, still talking about the final quarter.

She described his assist in great detail, including the way the defender had shifted his weight and how Yichen had noticed the open lane. He listened patiently.

When she finished, he asked, “Anything else?”

She thought.

“Your layup.”

“Anything else?”

“Your defence.”

“Anything else?”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Why? Are you testing me?”

“Just checking whether you watched the game.”

“I watched every second!”

He smiled.

“I know.”

She met his eyes. Then she asked, “Did you see your father?”

“Yes.”

“What did he say?”

“That my positioning was better.”

She nodded.

“That’s good.”

“He said the final decision was good too.”

Her smile softened.

“That’s really good.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“You’re happy?”

“Of course.”

He looked ahead.

“Me too.”

They walked a little farther before Xiaoran slipped her hand into his.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“I think today was important.”

He looked at her.

“Because of the debut?”

“Yes. And that.”

She squeezed his hand.

“But because all the people who helped you get here were there. Your coach, Professor Xie, the athletic director... And your father.”

Yichen nodded.

“I noticed.”

“I’m glad.”

He turned towards her.

“And you.”

“What about me?”

“You were there too.”

She smiled.

“Of course I was.”

He stopped walking. She turned back towards him.

“What?”

He lifted their joined hands and kissed the back of hers.

“Thank you for coming.”

She looked at him with a smile.

“Yichen, I wouldn’t miss it.”

“I know.”

“And next time, I’ll be even louder.”

He laughed.

“Should I warn the club?”

“Yes.”

“All right.”

She leaned against his arm as they continued walking.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, after he had showered and finished his recovery routine, Yichen sat on the edge of his bed with his phone. A message appeared.

Xiaoran: Are you still awake?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: I watched the recording again.

He smiled.

Yichen: Already?

Xiaoran: I wanted to see your debut again.

Yichen: Which part?

Xiaoran: All of it.

A moment later, another message arrived.

Xiaoran: Your father stayed until the end.

Yichen looked at the screen.

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: I think he was proud.

He considered that, then typed.

Yichen: Maybe.

Xiaoran: I think so.

He didn’t argue. Another message appeared.

Xiaoran: I’m proud too.

He smiled.

Yichen: You told me already.

Xiaoran: I’m telling you again.

Yichen: Then I’ll listen again.

She sent a heart. He looked at it before replying.

Yichen: I heard you from the court.

Xiaoran: Really?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: Even with everyone shouting?

Yichen: Especially you.

She didn’t reply immediately. Then:

Xiaoran: I love you.

He leaned back against the headboard.

Yichen: I love you too.

He put the phone down. For years, basketball had been something he had pursued through practice courts, university competitions, uncertain evaluations, and opportunities that hadn’t always come easily.

Today, he had stepped onto a different court wearing a different uniform. He had made his debut.

There would be more games, harder opponents, and more difficult decisions ahead. He knew better than to mistake one good night for the end of a journey.

But he would remember this one: the announcer saying his name, his coach and Professor Xie and the athletic director sitting together, his father in the front row until the buzzer, and Lin Xiaoran on her feet in the same row, as loud as she’d promised.

He picked up his phone one last time and opened the photograph she had sent him earlier. It showed the court from her seat. A little blurry. A little crooked.

At the edge of the frame, by the players’ entrance, he could see himself. He saved it. Then he turned off the light.

chapters.desc: Tang Meilin and Chen Yuhao come to Shanghai for two nights. Meilin meets Jiayi and Ning, and Yuhao and Zhou Yichen get along far too well.
chapters.title: Visitors from Home
chapters.epigraph: “You know I still like you best.”
chapters.content:
The first sign that Tang Meilin and Chen Yuhao had arrived in Shanghai was a photograph.

On a Thursday afternoon in April, Xiaoran was sitting in the university library, trying to finish a presentation slide, when her phone vibrated.

Meilin: Guess who’s here.

Attached was a photograph of Meilin standing in front of a train station sign, smiling with one hand raised. Yuhao stood behind her, holding two suitcases and looking thoroughly unimpressed.

Xiaoran: MEILIN!!!

Xiaoran: YOU’RE HERE?!

Meilin: Unfortunately, yes. Your friend has dragged me to Shanghai.

Yuhao: I changed trains in her city so I could carry the luggage. Show some gratitude.

Meilin: You packed three pairs of shoes for a weekend.

Yuhao: They serve different purposes.

Xiaoran: DON’T MOVE. I’M COMING.

Meilin: Finish your slides first. We’re not dying.

Xiaoran: I don’t care.

Yuhao: We know.

Xiaoran was already packing her things. A message arrived from Yichen.

Yichen: Leaving the library?

Xiaoran: MEILIN AND YUHAO ARE HERE.

Yichen: I see.

Xiaoran: I’M GOING TO GET THEM.

Yichen: I’ll meet you there.

She stopped.

Xiaoran: You don’t have to. I can go by myself.

Yichen: I know.

Yichen: I want to see them too.

She smiled at the screen.

Xiaoran: Okay. Hurry.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen arrived at the station before Xiaoran did. He was standing near the exit, holding his phone in one hand, when a familiar voice called out.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He looked up. Yuhao was approaching with one suitcase in each hand. Meilin walked beside him, looking around the station.

“You’re early,” Yuhao said.

“You’re late.”

“We’re exactly on time.”

Yichen glanced at the suitcases.

“How long are you staying?”

“Two nights.”

“Then why do you have enough luggage for a week?”

Yuhao looked offended.

“Some people understand the importance of preparation.”

Meilin walked up and greeted Yichen.

“Long time no see.”

“Welcome to Shanghai.”

She smiled.

“Thank you. Where’s Xiaoran?”

“On her way.”

Yuhao looked around.

“She’s probably running.”

“She is.”

“Good. I want to see her nearly trip over her own feet.”

Yichen glanced at him.

“Don’t encourage her.”

Yuhao laughed. Then, as if remembering something, he leaned closer.

“By the way, how’s your basketball?”

“Fine.”

“Fine?”

“Training’s going well.”

“Your debut was pretty impressive.”

Yichen looked at him.

“You watched?”

“On the stream. Xiaoran sent the group chat approximately seventeen messages during the game.”

Meilin corrected him.

“Forty-one.”

Yuhao nodded.

“Forty-one messages. I was kept informed of every possession.”

Yichen smiled.

“That sounds like her.”

“She also sent me a photograph of your face.”

“Which one?”

“The one where you were looking towards the stands.”

Yichen didn’t need to ask who had taken it.

“YICHEN!”

He turned just in time. Xiaoran came running towards them, her bag bouncing against her side. Meilin opened her arms.

“Slow down!”

Xiaoran ignored her and threw herself into the hug.

“You’re here!”

Meilin hugged her tightly.

“Yes, I’m here.”

“I missed you!”

“I missed you too.”

Xiaoran pulled back and looked at her face.

“You look the same.”

“Thank you?”

“Pretty.”

“That’s better.”

Then Xiaoran turned towards Yuhao. He opened his arms. She narrowed her eyes.

“Why are you standing like that?”

“Waiting for my welcome.”

“You don’t deserve one.”

“After I travelled all this way?”

“You complained about carrying the luggage.”

“Because I carried the luggage.”

She laughed and hugged him anyway. Yuhao patted her head.

“Still short.”

Xiaoran immediately stepped on his shoe.

“Ow!”

Yichen watched them with a faint smile. Some things really hadn’t changed.

Their first stop was a restaurant near the university.

Xiaoran had already made a reservation, and she had insisted on choosing somewhere with enough dishes for everyone to share. Yuhao looked at the menu.

“Why is everything here so expensive?”

Xiaoran glanced at him.

“You’re the one who said you wanted to eat somewhere nice.”

“I said somewhere nice, not somewhere that requires financial planning.”

Meilin took the menu from him.

“Stop complaining.”

Yichen sat beside Xiaoran pouring tea into her cup.

“Order what you like,” he told the others.

Yuhao looked at him.

“That’s dangerous.”

“Why?”

“Because I’ll remember this.”

Yichen smiled.

“Then remember to order reasonably.”

Meilin laughed. Xiaoran leaned towards Yichen.

“You’re being too nice to him.”

“I know.”

“He’s going to take advantage.”

“I know.”

Yuhao heard them.

“I can hear you.”

“Good,” Xiaoran replied.

The conversation quickly became noisy. Meilin asked about Xiaoran’s Media projects and university life. Yuhao wanted to know more about Yichen’s training schedule, especially whether he had been travelling frequently for the development program.

Yichen answered without making it sound more impressive than it was.

“Some weeks are busier than others. It depends on the club’s schedule.”

Yuhao nodded.

“Still balancing university?”

“Yes.”

“That’s difficult.”

“It takes planning.”

Xiaoran reached for a piece of food.

“And he has a very strict calendar.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“Who made me a strict calendar?”

“…I did.”

“Exactly.”

She smiled. Meilin watched them.

“You two are still the same.”

Xiaoran looked up.

“What do you mean?”

“Nothing. Just that it’s nice.”

Yichen smiled. Yuhao, meanwhile, was busy asking whether Yichen could teach him a few basketball moves.

“No,” Meilin said immediately.

Yuhao looked at her.

“Why?”

“Because you’ll hurt yourself.”

“I played basketball in school.”

“That was years ago.”

“I still remember.”

Yichen considered him.

“We can see.”

Yuhao looked delighted.

“Excellent.”

Meilin sighed.

“I already regret coming.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Xiaoran brought Meilin to campus. Yuhao had gone with Yichen to see the Herons’ training facility, which Xiaoran considered an unfair arrangement.

“Why does he get to go with Yichen?”

Meilin looked at her.

“Because he asked.”

“I could have asked.”

“You have classes.”

“I can skip one.”

“No.”

Xiaoran pouted. Meilin laughed and linked their arms.

“Come on. Show me your university.”

They walked through the campus, stopping at the library, the student centre, and the Media building.

Xiaoran introduced Meilin to a few classmates, then took her to the café where she often studied.

Meilin listened as Xiaoran described her projects, her professors, and the people she’d become friends with.

“You seem settled,” Meilin observed.

“I am.”

“Really?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“I was a little lost at first. But it’s nice now. I know where everything is.”

Meilin looked around.

“That’s good.”

“And I have friends here.”

“I can tell.”

Xiaoran smiled. She was happy to have Meilin here, but she also wanted her to see the life she had built in Shanghai.

They stopped outside a café where two girls were waiting.

“Xiaoran!”

Jiayi waved. Ning stood beside her, smiling. Xiaoran waved back.

“Meilin, this is Luo Jiayi, and this is Sun Ning.”

Meilin greeted them.

“Hi. I’m Tang Meilin.”

Jiayi smiled.

“We’ve heard about you.”

Meilin glanced at Xiaoran.

“Have you?”

Xiaoran immediately looked suspicious.

“What did she say?”

Ning laughed.

“Nothing bad.”

“That’s not reassuring.”

Jiayi grinned.

“She said you were her best friend from high school.”

Meilin looked at Xiaoran.

“That’s all?”

Xiaoran nodded quickly.

“Yes.”

Ning added, “She also said you were very good at knowing when she’s being unreasonable.”

Meilin smiled.

“That’s accurate.”

Xiaoran stared at her.

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I am. That’s why I know.”

The four of them sat together for coffee. Meilin found herself liking Xiaoran’s university friends almost immediately. Jiayi was loud and outspoken, while Ning had a quieter sense of humour that made her comments unexpectedly sharp.

They asked about high school, and Meilin shared a few harmless stories.

“She used to get lost even when we were going somewhere familiar,” Meilin said.

Xiaoran looked betrayed.

“That happened once.”

“Three times.”

“One of those was your fault.”

“How?”

“You walked too fast.”

Jiayi laughed. Ning leaned forward.

“Does Yichen still have to find you?”

Xiaoran hesitated. Meilin answered for her.

“Yes.”

“Meilin!”

Everyone laughed. Meilin looked at her with fondness.

“Don’t worry. She’s improved.”

Xiaoran folded her arms.

“Thank you.”

“She now gets lost with confidence.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Meanwhile, Yichen and Yuhao were getting along far too well. It began innocently enough.

Yuhao had asked about the training facility, and Yichen had offered to show him around.

Then they started talking about basketball. Then professional sports, then training methods.

Then, somehow, they were standing near the practice court discussing the differences between offensive systems.

Yuhao, it turned out, still followed the sport much more closely than he let anyone know.

“You see that?” Yichen asked, pointing towards the court.

“The spacing?”

“Yes. If the weak-side defender moves too early, the corner opens.”

Yuhao nodded.

“Unless the ball handler hesitates.”

“Exactly.”

Yuhao looked at him.

“You’re annoyingly good at explaining things.”

Yichen smiled.

“Thank you.”

“That wasn’t a compliment.”

“I’ll take it.”

They continued talking. By the time they reached the café near the facility, Yuhao had somehow convinced Yichen to join him for a game later that afternoon. Yichen agreed. Yuhao looked pleased with himself.

“Good. I want to see whether you’re actually as good as Xiaoran says.”

Yichen glanced at him.

“What does she say?”

Yuhao thought.

“That you’re handsome.”

Yichen waited.

“And?”

“Good at basketball.”

“Anything else?”

Yuhao grinned.

“That you’re very annoying when you know you’re right.”

Yichen laughed.

“That’s fair.”

Xiaoran found out about their new friendship through a photograph. It was taken by Yuhao.

Yichen stood beside him, holding two drinks, while Yuhao pointed towards the camera with a grin. The caption read:

Yuhao: Unexpected friendship of the year.

Xiaoran stared at it. Then she sent a message to Meilin.

Xiaoran: Why are they together?

Meilin: Because they went out together.

Xiaoran: I know that. Why are they smiling like that?

Meilin: Maybe they like each other.

Xiaoran: MEILIN.

Meilin: What?

Xiaoran: They’re getting along too well.

Meilin laughed at her phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon, the four of them met at a basketball court.

Yichen and Yuhao had already been playing for nearly half an hour when Xiaoran and Meilin arrived. Xiaoran stopped near the entrance. Yuhao had the ball. He attempted a shot. It hit the rim. Yichen caught the rebound.

“Your elbow.”

“What about it?”

“You’re bringing it out too far.”

Yuhao frowned.

“That’s how I shoot.”

“That’s why you missed.”

Xiaoran looked at Meilin.

“See?”

Meilin smiled.

“What?”

“They’re already arguing.”

“That’s how friendships work.”

Yuhao noticed them.

“Xiaoran! Over here.”

She pointed at herself.

“Me?”

“No, the other Lin Xiaoran.”

She walked closer.

“What?”

“Tell him I’m good.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Do you want an honest answer?”

Yuhao groaned. Xiaoran laughed.

“You’re both terrible.”

Yichen retrieved the ball and passed it to her.

“Try.”

She caught it awkwardly.

“Why?”

“Let’s see.”

“I don’t know how.”

“I’ll show you.”

Yuhao immediately stepped aside.

“Good idea. I’m tired.”

Meilin gave him a look.

“You were playing for thirty minutes.”

“Exactly.”

Yichen stood beside Xiaoran and adjusted her hand position on the ball.

“Don’t hold it too tightly.”

She looked down.

“Like this?”

“Yes. Now bend your knees slightly.”

She did.

“Look at the basket.”

She raised her eyes. Then she shot. The ball hit the backboard and bounced away. She stared at it. Yichen smiled.

“Not bad.”

“That was terrible.”

“First try.”

Yuhao retrieved the ball.

“Let me show you.”

Meilin caught his arm.

“Don’t.”

He met her eyes.

“Why?”

“Because you’ll teach her the wrong way.”

Yichen laughed. Xiaoran turned towards Meilin.

“Thank you.”

Yuhao looked deeply offended. Later, they went to a nearby restaurant for dinner.

Yuhao and Yichen sat opposite each other, still discussing basketball. Meilin and Xiaoran sat side by side. Meilin watched the two men.

“Are they going to talk about this all night?”

Xiaoran sighed.

“I think so.”

“Did you know Yuhao was this interested?”

“Not this interested.”

Meilin took a sip of water.

“Yichen seems to enjoy it.”

Xiaoran looked across the table. Yichen was listening to Yuhao explain something, occasionally correcting a detail. He looked relaxed. She smiled.

“He’s having fun.”

Meilin noticed her expression.

“You like seeing him like this.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“He’s usually quite serious about basketball. It’s nice when he can just talk about it without worrying about anything.”

Meilin smiled. Then she leaned closer.

“You’re happy here.”

Xiaoran looked at her.

“What?”

“Shanghai. Your university. Your friends. Yichen.”

She looked down at her glass.

“Yes.”

Meilin reached over and squeezed her hand.

“Good.”

Xiaoran smiled. For a while, they talked about home. Their old neighbourhood.

The school they had attended. The food they missed. The teachers they remembered.

The small things that seemed unimportant until they were far away from them. At one point, Yuhao interrupted.

“Do you remember when Xiaoran got locked outside the classroom?”

Xiaoran’s head snapped up.

“No.”

Meilin looked delighted.

“Yes.”

“Don’t.”

Yuhao continued.

“She was supposed to lock up and take the class key to the teacher’s office, but she left it inside.”

“I was fifteen!”

“You were sixteen.”

“That doesn’t make it better!”

Yichen looked at her.

“What happened?”

Meilin smiled.

“She waited outside for twenty minutes before someone found her.”

Yichen looked amused.

“Why didn’t you call someone?”

“My phone was inside too.”

Yuhao nodded.

“She was very resourceful. She sat outside and waited.”

Xiaoran pointed at him.

“You were the one who shut the door!”

“That is not relevant.”

Yichen laughed. Xiaoran looked at him.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He reached over and squeezed her hand under the table. She tried to maintain her offended expression. It didn’t last.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner, because it was their last evening, they all went back to Yichen’s apartment.

Meilin and Yuhao were staying at a hotel, but Xiaoran had insisted that they come over before leaving the next morning.

There were snacks on the coffee table, a film playing in the background, and four people occupying the living room.

Yuhao had somehow ended up sitting beside Yichen, showing him a video on his phone.

Meilin was beside Xiaoran, scrolling through photographs from the weekend. Xiaoran looked at one picture.

It showed Meilin laughing with Jiayi and Ning at the café.

“Look at this one.”

Meilin leaned closer.

“Oh, that’s nice.”

“I’ll send it to you.”

“Please do.”

Then Xiaoran swiped to another photograph. It showed Yuhao and Yichen standing beside the basketball court, both looking serious while holding drinks. She stared.

“Why do you have so many pictures together?”

Yuhao looked up.

“Because we’re friends.”

Xiaoran turned towards him.

“Since when?”

“Since this morning.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“Is that a problem?”

“No.”

He smiled.

“You’re sure?”

“Yes.”

Yuhao leaned towards Yichen.

“She’s jealous.”

Xiaoran threw a cushion at him. Yuhao caught it, laughing. Meilin shook her head.

“You’re all children.”

Yichen put the cushion back beside Xiaoran.

Then he leaned towards her and said, “You know I still like you best.”

She met his eyes.

“Obviously.”

“Obviously?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He kissed her temple. Yuhao made a loud gagging noise.

“Please. We’re in the room.”

Xiaoran turned.

“You’re the one who came to our apartment.”

“Your apartment?”

“His apartment.”

“Then I’m leaving.”

Nobody moved. Yuhao waited. Then he sighed.

“Nobody appreciates me.”

Meilin laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Xiaoran and Yichen went with them to the station. Meilin hugged Xiaoran first.

“Come home when you can.”

“I will.”

“And don’t forget to rest.”

“I won’t.”

Meilin gave her a look.

“That’s what you always say.”

Xiaoran smiled. Then Meilin hugged Yichen.

“Take care of her.”

He nodded.

“I will.”

Xiaoran immediately pulled back.

“Why are you telling him that? I can take care of myself.”

Meilin smiled.

“I know.”

Yuhao stepped forward and shook Yichen’s hand.

“Good game yesterday.”

“Thanks.”

“Next time, I’ll win.”

Yichen smiled.

“Next time, work on your shooting.”

Yuhao stared at him.

“You’re still thinking about that?”

“Yes.”

“Unbelievable.”

Xiaoran laughed. Yuhao turned to her.

“And you. Don’t get too spoiled.”

She hugged him.

“Travel safely.”

He patted her back.

“Take care, little troublemaker.”

She smiled.

“Bye.”

They watched Meilin and Yuhao disappear into the crowd. Xiaoran stood still. Yichen slipped his hand into hers.

“Miss them already?”

“A little.”

He squeezed her hand.

“They’ll come again.”

“Really?”

“Why not?”

She smiled.

“Next time, I’ll make them stay longer.”

“Then we’ll need a bigger table.”

“And more food.”

“And perhaps another basketball court.”

She laughed.

“Yuhao will demand a rematch.”

“I know.”

They began walking towards the exit. After a few steps, Xiaoran leaned against his arm.

“It was nice, wasn’t it?”

“Very.”

“Meilin liked Jiayi and Ning.”

“I noticed.”

“And Yuhao likes you.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“Is that a problem?”

She sighed dramatically.

“I don’t know. You two are becoming too close.”

He smiled.

“Should I stop talking to him?”

She thought about it, then shook her head.

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because you seemed happy.”

He looked at her. Then he lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“You’re very generous.”

She smiled.

“I know.”

They continued walking through the station, their hands joined.

Shanghai had become home in its own way: her classes, her friends, her favourite cafés, the life she had built since she left. It had still been good to have two people here who had known her before all of it, and to find out that Yuhao and Yichen could be friends, even if they were already far too pleased with themselves.

chapters.desc: The Media faculty makes a film that makes everyone cry. The Business faculty bankrupts a company. They’re both on the same stage.
chapters.title: The Last Scene Before the Credits
chapters.epigraph: “It only needed another day.”
chapters.content:
The university’s Annual Faculty Showcase was supposed to be a celebration of student talent.

Every faculty had been given a stage, a time slot, and a little freedom to show everyone what their students had been working on throughout the academic year.

Some faculties chose exhibitions. Some prepared musical performances. Others had interactive booths, demonstrations, and presentations.

The Media Faculty, naturally, decided to make a film. And not just any film.
