A twenty-minute short movie, written, directed, filmed, edited, and produced entirely by students. The title was Before the Morning Comes. Xiaoran had been involved from the beginning.

She was part of the creative team, helped develop the screenplay, participated in production planning, and eventually became the female lead after their original actress had to withdraw due to an unexpected schedule conflict. She hadn’t planned on acting.

In fact, when the director first suggested it, she had stared at him as though he’d asked her to jump off the faculty building.

“Me?”

“Yes, you.”

“But I’m behind the camera.”

“You understand the character.”

“That doesn’t mean I can act.”

“We’ve seen you cry over fictional characters during editing.”

“That’s different!”

The director had simply smiled. And somehow, two weeks later, Xiaoran was standing in front of a camera, wearing a pale blue cardigan and pretending that the person she loved was dying.

She hadn’t expected the role to affect her as much as it did.

The story was about two university students who fell in love while dealing with serious illnesses.

The male lead, played by a Media student named Chi Yuan, was diagnosed with a progressive heart condition. He knew his health was deteriorating, but he kept it from the female lead, afraid that she would spend the rest of their relationship worrying about him.

The female lead, played by Xiaoran, had her own diagnosis: a serious illness that required prolonged treatment and eventually threatened her ability to continue living the life she had imagined.

They met during a difficult period in their lives.

They fell in love in the middle of hospital appointments, late-night conversations, and small promises. The tragedy wasn’t simply that they were sick.

It was that they had so many ordinary things they wanted to do together. They wanted to graduate. They wanted to travel. They wanted to argue about what to eat. They wanted to grow old.

And they knew they might not get all of it.

The film ended with the female lead sitting beside an empty hospital bed, holding a small notebook.

The final page contained a list of things they had wanted to do together. At the bottom, she wrote:

If we had more time, I think I would still choose you.

Then the screen faded to black. No music. Just silence. It was heartbreaking. And Xiaoran had cried during the final recording.

Not because she was particularly good at acting, but because by then she had spent so much time with the character that the final scene felt strangely personal.

When the director called cut, she had remained sitting on the hospital bed, quietly wiping her eyes.

Chi Yuan, who played the male lead, had leaned over.

“Xiaoran, are you okay?”

She nodded.

“Yes. Just give me a minute.”

The director had looked at the footage and whispered to the cinematographer:

“Keep that take.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhou Yichen knew about the film. He had heard about it for weeks.

He had watched Xiaoran memorise her lines, listened to her complain about filming schedules, and occasionally received photographs of the production set.

He had even helped her rehearse a few scenes.

One evening, she had stood in front of him, holding her script.

“Okay. You’re the patient. I’m your girlfriend.”

Yichen had looked up from his laptop.

“All right.”

“You’re supposed to look sick.”

He stared at her. She frowned.

“Not like that.”

“How should I look?”

“Like you’re hiding something.”

He gave her a calm look.

“I’m always hiding something.”

“Don’t make jokes. This is serious.”

He put his laptop aside.

“All right. Continue.”

She began reading her lines.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

He answered with the line from the script.

“Because I didn’t want you to spend every day being afraid of losing me.”

Xiaoran paused, then looked at him.

“That was good.”

“Thank you.”

“Do it again, but sadder.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Are you directing me now?”

“Yes.”

He smiled. She tried to continue, but his expression was too familiar. Too much like the real Yichen, sitting in front of her, listening patiently. She suddenly felt embarrassed.

“Never mind.”

He reached for her hand.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. I just can’t act when you’re looking at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you love me.”

He smiled.

“That’s going to be difficult to change.”

She had thrown her script at him. He caught it easily.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Business Faculty, meanwhile, had chosen something entirely different.

Their showcase team had initially proposed a traditional business case competition. A panel of judges. A simulated company. A presentation. A few financial charts. It was sensible. It was also terribly boring.

Their faculty advisor had listened to the proposal, looked at the students, and asked:

“Do you want the audience to remember your presentation tomorrow?”

Nobody answered.

“Then don’t give them another presentation.”

That was how they came up with The Last Company Standing, an interactive business simulation.

The Business students created a fictional company called Northstar, a once-successful consumer technology brand facing a sudden crisis.

The audience would become the company’s shareholders and board members.

They would be given a limited budget, incomplete information, and a series of decisions to make. A product defect had been discovered. A competitor was launching a cheaper alternative. A supplier had suddenly withdrawn.

The company had to decide whether to recall its products, protect its reputation, cut costs, or invest in a new direction.

Every decision would affect the company’s simulated finances, public trust, employee morale, and long-term survival.

There would be live voting, a projected dashboard, and a final reveal showing the consequences of the audience’s choices.

Yichen was part of the Business Faculty’s organising and strategy team.

He had helped design the financial model and the decision-making structure, making sure the simulation was realistic enough to be challenging but understandable to people outside Business.

He also ended up as one of the presenters.

His role was to act as the company’s Chief Strategy Officer.

The contrast between the two faculties couldn’t have been more obvious.

Media was preparing to make an entire auditorium cry.

Business was preparing to make the same auditorium argue about whether to fire a CEO. Xiaoran found the concept hilarious.

“So you’re going to stand on stage and tell people their company is going bankrupt?”

“Not exactly.”

“What’s the difference?”

“I’ll explain why it’s going bankrupt.”

She laughed.

“That’s worse.”

“Would you like to join the board?”

“I don’t know anything about business.”

“That’s all right. Neither does the audience.”

She gasped.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed and kissed her temple.

✦ ✦ ✦

The day of the showcase arrived. The university auditorium was packed.

Every faculty had decorated its section, and students were moving around in matching shirts, carrying equipment, checking microphones, and running through last-minute rehearsals.

The Media team had a small backstage room filled with laptops, costume bags, spare props, and a suspicious amount of snacks.

Xiaoran was wearing the costume for the film’s final scene: a simple white blouse, a pale blue cardigan, and a delicate necklace.

She was sitting in front of a mirror while Luo Jiayi, who had appointed herself the film’s hair, makeup and morale department, fixed a loose strand of hair.

“You look so pretty,” Jiayi said.

Xiaoran smiled.

“Thank you.”

“Are you nervous?”

“A little.”

“You’re not even presenting.”

“I’m acting in front of everyone.”

“You’re going to be fine.”

Xiaoran nodded. She checked her phone. A message from Yichen.

Yichen: Already there?

Xiaoran: Yes. Are you ready?

Yichen: Almost.

Xiaoran: Don’t forget to eat.

Yichen: You too.

Xiaoran: I did.

Yichen: What?

She sent him a photograph of a half-eaten sandwich.

Yichen: That’s not a meal.

Xiaoran: It’s a sandwich!

Yichen: Eat the rest.

She smiled and put her phone away. Jiayi stepped back and examined her work.

“Ning’s saving us seats for the Business slot. Middle row. She says if we’re late she’s giving them to strangers.”

“She won’t.”

“She will. She enjoys it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The Media Faculty’s slot was scheduled for 4:00 PM. Before that, the Business Faculty had their performance.

Xiaoran managed to slip into the auditorium just before it began.

She found Ning in the middle row with her headphones round her neck and two coats on the seats beside her. Jiayi waved enthusiastically from the far end.

“Here! Your boyfriend is about to become a CEO!”

Xiaoran giggled and sat beside them. The lights dimmed.

The Business Faculty’s presentation began with a short video showing the fictional company Northstar’s impressive growth, followed by the sudden announcement of a product safety crisis. A projected headline appeared:

NORTHSTAR FACES MAJOR RECALL AFTER PRODUCT DEFECT DISCOVERED.

The audience immediately began whispering, then the presenters entered.

Yichen walked onto the stage wearing a dark suit, a white shirt, and a discreet name badge identifying him as the Chief Strategy Officer. Xiaoran straightened. Oh. He looked handsome.

She had seen him in formal clothes many times, but seeing him under the stage lights, speaking confidently to a full auditorium, was different. He looked entirely at ease.

“Good afternoon, shareholders.”

His voice carried clearly.

“Three days ago, Northstar discovered a defect in one of its flagship products. We have already received complaints from customers, and the media is beginning to investigate.”

The screen behind him displayed three options. Option A: Immediate full recall. Option B: Limited recall while investigating.

Option C: Continue sales while quietly resolving the issue. Yichen looked across the audience.

“You have thirty seconds to decide.”

The voting began. The room became lively almost immediately.

Students debated loudly. Some argued that a full recall would destroy the company’s finances. Others insisted that public safety had to come first.

Yichen listened to the arguments and occasionally responded to questions. One student asked:

“What if the company doesn’t have enough cash to recall everything?”

Yichen answered without hesitation.

“Then we negotiate with suppliers, secure emergency financing, and prioritise the highest-risk products. Financial difficulty doesn’t make the underlying safety issue disappear.”

Xiaoran looked at Ning.

“He’s good.”

Ning smiled.

“Very good.”

On stage, the simulation progressed. The audience chose a limited recall. The dashboard updated.

Then came another problem: a major supplier had withdrawn, a competitor had announced a cheaper product, and a leaked internal email suggested the company had known about the defect earlier.

The room became even louder. Yichen stood at the centre of it all, calmly guiding the audience through each decision.

At the final reveal, the company’s simulated valuation had fallen, but its customer trust had recovered.

The Business team concluded that the company had survived, not because it avoided losses, but because it made a difficult decision early enough to protect its long-term credibility. The audience applauded. Ning leaned towards Xiaoran.

“Your boyfriend just made bankruptcy sound attractive.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Stop.”

Jiayi looked at the stage, chin in her hand.

“He’s really good at explaining things.”

Xiaoran nodded, smiling proudly. Yichen looked towards the audience. His eyes found her. He gave her the smallest smile. She waved discreetly. He returned his attention to the stage.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 4:00 PM, the Media Faculty’s turn arrived. The host introduced the film.

“Next, we have a short film produced by the Media Faculty’s student production team. Written, directed, filmed, and edited by our students, Before the Morning Comes explores love, illness, and the things we wish we had more time to do.”

The auditorium lights dimmed. Xiaoran sat backstage, listening to the opening music through a monitor.

She had watched the film countless times during editing.

But hearing it play in the auditorium, with a full audience, made her nervous. The opening scene appeared on the screen.

Two university students met in a small campus library.

The male lead was sitting alone, looking tired. The female lead approached him with a cup of coffee.

“You’re always here.”

“Maybe I like the library.”

“Or maybe you don’t have a life.”

He smiled.

“Maybe.”

The audience laughed. The story unfolded. Their first conversation. Their growing friendship. Their first date. The quiet discovery of their illnesses. The hospital corridors. The doctor’s appointments.

The way they tried to pretend that everything was normal.

Then came the scene where the male lead finally told her the truth. Xiaoran’s voice filled the auditorium.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

He looked at her.

“Because I didn’t want you to look at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re already saying goodbye.”

The auditorium became silent. Xiaoran remembered filming that scene.

She remembered how she had held her breath after the line, how Chi Yuan had looked at her with such exhausted tenderness, and how the director had let the camera keep rolling. The story continued. The female lead’s own condition worsened.

They sat together on a hospital rooftop, sharing a packet of biscuits.

“You know what I wanted to do?” she asked.

“What?”

“Travel.”

“Where?”

“Anywhere. Somewhere with the sea.”

He smiled.

“We can still go.”

“You always say that.”

“Because I mean it.”

She smiled, but her eyes were wet. The next scene showed them making a list. Things they wanted to do together. See the sea. Eat at a restaurant without checking the time. Watch the sunrise. Graduate. Take a photograph every year. The final scene arrived. The male lead’s hospital bed was empty.

The female lead sat beside it, holding the notebook. She turned the pages. One by one. Then wrote:

If we had more time, I think I would still choose you.

The screen faded to black. Silence. For several seconds, nobody moved, then the ending music began. The credits appeared. And the auditorium erupted into applause. Xiaoran remained backstage. She was smiling, but her eyes were wet. Her director hugged her.

“We did it.”

She nodded.

“We did.”

One of her classmates was crying. Another was wiping her face with a tissue. The director laughed.

“Look at us. We made everyone miserable.”

Xiaoran laughed through her tears.

“That’s not what we were trying to do!”

“Apparently, we succeeded.”

When the lights came back on, the host invited the Media team onto the stage. Xiaoran walked out with the others. The applause continued.

She felt a little overwhelmed by the number of people looking at her.

The host introduced the production team and asked a few questions.

“Xiaoran, you played the female lead. How was the experience?”

She took the microphone.

“Honestly, it was quite difficult. I’m more comfortable working behind the camera, so acting was a little outside my comfort zone.”

The audience laughed.

“But I think the story was very meaningful. We wanted to show that illness doesn’t only affect the person who is sick. It also affects the people who love them, and sometimes the hardest part is not knowing how to help each other.”

She paused.

“And I think we wanted to remind people not to postpone the small things they want to do with the people they love.”

The host nodded.

“That’s beautiful. Thank you.”

Xiaoran returned the microphone. The applause came again. She looked towards the audience. And found Yichen.

He was standing near the aisle with his Business teammates, clapping. He was looking directly at her. His expression was proud. Not exaggerated. Not performative. Just unmistakably proud. She smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the showcase ended, the auditorium turned into a chaotic celebration.

Students were taking photographs, congratulating one another, and visiting the different faculty booths. Xiaoran was surrounded by her classmates.

“Your acting was so good!”

“That final scene!”

“I cried!”

“Everyone cried!”

She laughed, thanking them. Then Ning appeared from the sound booth. She held out a tissue.

“For the actress.”

Xiaoran took it.

“Thank you.”

Ning looked at her.

“That was really good.”

She smiled.

“Really?”

“Yes. I was trying not to cry.”

Jiayi appeared beside her, mascara everywhere.

“I wasn’t trying.”

Xiaoran burst out laughing. Jiayi hugged her.

“You did well.”

“Thank you.”

Then, from behind them, a familiar voice said:

“Congratulations.”

Xiaoran turned. Yichen was standing there, his suit jacket folded over one arm. She immediately smiled.

“Yichen!”

He opened his arms slightly. She stepped into them.

He wrapped one arm around her waist and kissed her hair.

“You did very well.”

“Did you watch the whole thing?”

“Of course.”

“Did you like it?”

“I did.”

She smiled. Then she asked, “Did you cry?”

He looked at her.

“No.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Not even a little?”

He considered it.

“I was distracted.”

“By what?”

He brushed his thumb against her cheek.

“Watching you.”

Her expression softened. Then she noticed something.

“Wait. You were watching me instead of the film?”

“I watched both.”

She laughed.

“I can’t win with you.”

He smiled. Jiayi and Ning exchanged a look. Jiayi leaned towards Ning.

“I’ve known them almost three years, and he still looks at her like that.”

Ning nodded.

“Unfortunately.”

Xiaoran heard them.

“NING!”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, the two faculties ended up sharing a table at the refreshments area. The Media team was discussing their film.

The Business team was debating the audience’s decisions during the simulation.

Yichen sat beside Xiaoran, one hand resting lightly on the back of her chair.

At some point, one of the Media students asked him:

“Yichen, what did you think of our film?”

He answered honestly.

“The story was well structured. The pacing was good, and the final scene was effective.”

The director nodded.

“Thank you.”

“Although I think the female lead could have been a little happier,” Yichen said.

Xiaoran turned towards him.

“Excuse me?”

“She spent the entire film crying.”

“Because her character was sick!”

“I know.”

“Then why are you complaining?”

He smiled.

“Personal preference.”

The table burst into laughter. The director pointed at him.

“That’s not a valid film critique.”

Yichen nodded.

“Fair enough.”

Xiaoran leaned closer.

“You’re just biased.”

“Probably.”

She smiled. Then one of Yichen’s Business teammates joined the conversation.

“Actually, we should collaborate next year.”

The Media director looked interested.

“How?”

“Business students create the crisis. Media students turn it into a documentary.”

Jiayi laughed.

“Imagine that. Northstar: The Documentary.”

Ning added, “Featuring Zhou Yichen as the CEO who refuses to admit the company is bankrupt.”

Yichen looked at her.

“I wasn’t the CEO.”

“Yet.”

Everyone laughed. Xiaoran leaned against his shoulder. For a moment, she watched the people around the table. Her classmates, his teammates, Jiayi, Ning. Two different faculties. Two different worlds.

And somehow, both of them had found a way to stand on the same stage that day.

✦ ✦ ✦

When the event finally ended, the university campus was glowing with evening lights.

Xiaoran and Yichen walked towards the parking area together.

She was carrying a small bouquet her classmates had given her, while he held her bag.

“Are you tired?” he asked.

“A little.”

“Do you want to go home?”

She nodded. They walked for a while. Then Xiaoran spoke.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Did you really like the film?”

“Yes.”

“Which part?”

He thought about it.

“The list.”

“The list?”

“Things they wanted to do together.”

She looked up at him.

“Why?”

“Because it felt real.”

She nodded.

“I liked that part too.”

“Did it make you think about anything?”

She considered the question.

“Maybe.”

“What?”

She looked ahead.

“I don’t want to wait until something bad happens to do the things I want with you.”

He slowed slightly. She continued.

“I want to travel with you. I want to graduate with you. I want to take more photographs, eat at more restaurants, see more places. I want to do ordinary things with you for a long time.”

He looked at her. Then gently took the bouquet from her hands so he could hold her hand properly.

“Then let’s do them.”

She smiled.

“All of them?”

“As many as we can.”

“What if we can’t?”

“Then we’ll find something else.”

She looked at him. He squeezed her hand.

“We don’t have to make a list of things we might lose. We can make one of things we want to experience.”

She smiled.

“That’s a very Business student answer.”

He laughed.

“Would you like me to make a spreadsheet?”

She gasped.

“Don’t you dare.”

He smiled. Then, after a moment, he stopped walking. Xiaoran turned.

“What?”

He set her bag down beside him, took her hand in both of his, and looked at her.

“You know what I was thinking during the final scene?”

She shook her head.

“I was thinking that I don’t want you to ever feel like you have to make every moment with me count.”

Her expression softened.

“I want you to have ordinary days with me. Boring days. Days when we don’t do anything special. Days when you complain about assignments and I complain about basketball practice.”

She smiled.

“Your complaints are much less interesting than mine.”

“Probably.”

He continued.

“I want to have enough ordinary days with you that we stop counting them.”

Xiaoran looked at him. The words settled somewhere deep in her chest. She stepped closer.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Can I kiss you?”

His mouth curved.

“You don’t need to ask.”

She leaned up and kissed him. It was soft at first.

Then his hand moved to her waist, drawing her closer, and he returned the kiss with more feeling.

When she pulled away, he rested his forehead against hers.

“Congratulations, actress.”

She laughed.

“Congratulations, Chief Strategy Officer.”

“Which performance was better?”

She pretended to think.

“Mine.”

“Naturally.”

“Your company nearly went bankrupt.”

“Because the shareholders made poor decisions.”

“Excuses.”

He laughed and kissed her cheek. Then her forehead.

Then, when she turned her face towards him with a small smile, he kissed her lips again. They finally reached the car.

Before getting in, Xiaoran glanced at the university building behind them.

“Today was really nice.”

Yichen opened her door.

“It was.”

“Even though my film made everyone cry?”

“Even then.”

She got into the passenger seat. He leaned down slightly before closing the door.

“Although I prefer the version of you that doesn’t have a tragic ending.”

“Me too.”

He kissed her cheek one last time, then closed the door.

As he walked around to the driver’s side, Xiaoran took out her phone and opened her notes. She created a new list.

Things I Want to Do With Yichen.

1. See the sea together.
2. Travel somewhere neither of us has been.
3. Take photographs every year.
4. Watch the sunrise.
5. Eat at a restaurant without checking the time.
6. Graduate.
7. Have more ordinary days.
8. Keep choosing each other.

She looked at the list, then added one more.

9. Make sure Zhou Yichen never gets a tragic ending.

She smiled to herself. When Yichen got into the car, he noticed.

“What are you smiling at?”

“Nothing.”

He glanced at her phone.

“Making another list?”

She hugged it to her chest.

“It’s private.”

He smiled and started the engine.

“All right.”

She reached over and took his hand before he shifted gears. He looked at her. She smiled.

“Let’s go home.”

And he did. Because unlike the film they had shown that afternoon, their story didn’t need a final scene. It only needed another day.

chapters.desc: A cracked wooden bench by the halfway vending machine becomes the place they meet between classes for most of a year.
chapters.title: Bench Days
chapters.epigraph: “Do you remember the first sign?”
chapters.content:
The bench wasn’t much to look at. It was a long wooden one under a row of old plane trees beside the halfway vending machine, at the exact spot where the path to the library split off from the path to the sports centre. One of its slats had a crack down the middle. The paint was coming off its iron legs. Whenever it rained, the seat stayed damp for a whole day after the rest of the campus had dried.

There were much nicer places to sit. Lin Xiaoran had decided anyway, in the November of first year, that it was her favourite place on campus. Not for the view, and not because it was quiet. It was because Zhou Yichen had told her, standing next to it with two strawberry milks, that it was the most inconvenient bench in the whole university: too far from everything, permanently damp, and right next to a machine that was always out of green tea. She had taken this personally.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found her there a week later, on his way back from training, sitting at one end of it and glaring at a piece of paper.

“What’s wrong?”

“Someone’s trying to take my seat.”

He looked at the empty bench around her. “Nobody’s here.”

“That’s not the point.” She held up the paper. It was a printed notice from the university’s facilities department: This bench is scheduled for maintenance. Please don’t use it from Monday.

“Where was that?”

“Taped to the back. It fell off. I picked it up.”

“So you know you’re not supposed to sit here.”

“I’m sitting here because there’s no sign now.”

“Convenient.”

“Are you saying I’m being unreasonable?”

“I’m saying you’re very committed to this bench. We can find you another one,” he said, and sat down next to her and put his arm along the back of it, behind her shoulders.

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because I like this one.”

He looked at her. “Then you should put up a sign of your own.”

“What sign?”

“Something that says it’s reserved.”

“For who?”

“For you,” he said.

He had meant it as a joke. Unfortunately, Xiaoran was good at taking jokes seriously.

Three days later there was a sheet of white paper taped to the backrest in neat black marker.

RESERVED.

Nothing else. He stopped dead on the path. At the far end of the bench, Xiaoran was pretending to read a book.

“What’s this?”

She didn’t look up. “A sign.”

“Reserved for who?”

She turned a page. “That’s confidential.”

He sat down next to her. She kept reading. He looked at the sign, and then at the side of her face, which was trying hard not to smile.

“You know they’ll take it down.”

“Let them try.”

“You’re prepared to defend it?”

“Absolutely.”

“You’re not going to tell me to take it down?”

“No, I want to see how long it lasts,” he said.

It lasted nine days. On the tenth it was gone. She discovered it at lunch and stood in front of the bench with her hands on her hips.

“Unbelievable.”

He was already sitting there, with his phone. “What?”

“They’ve taken it.”

He looked at the empty backrest. “Tragic.”

“Don’t sound so pleased.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“Shall I make you another one?”

She thought about it, and shook her head. “No. This time I’ll write something better. More mysterious.”

“I look forward to it,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second sign went up the next week. It was smaller and neater, and instead of tape she’d put it in a clear plastic sleeve held on with a bulldog clip. He found it before she did.

PLEASE DO NOT DISTURB.

He laughed under his breath, took a picture, and sent it to her.

Yichen: Your reservation’s getting serious.

Xiaoran: thank you for noticing

Yichen: Who are we not disturbing?

Xiaoran: the people sitting here

Yichen: People? Plural?

Xiaoran: don’t be difficult

When she came round the library twenty minutes later he was sitting directly underneath it with his bag on the seat beside him.

“You’re disturbing the reservation.”

He looked up. “Then I’m in the right place. Should I go?”

“Depends.”

“On what?”

“Whether you’ve brought me anything.”

He reached into his bag and took out a milk tea from the stall by the library, half sugar, no pearls. Her whole face lit up.

“You’re forgiven.”

She sat down so close to him that she was more or less on top of his bag, and leaned on him, and for twelve minutes they talked about nothing at all: the reading her lecturer had set, which was unreasonable; the teammate who’d forgotten his shoes for training; an advertisement she’d seen on the metro that she needed him to see immediately. Then his watch beeped.

“I have to go.”

“Training?”

“Yes.”

She held up the milk tea. “Thank you.”

He kissed her, briefly and got up. He’d gone a few steps when she called after him.

“Yichen.”

He turned round. She pointed at the sign. “Please do not disturb.”

He looked at her, and the bench, and her again, and a slow smile came over his face.

“I wouldn’t dream of it,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

By second year it was a habit. They never announced it as their place; they just kept coming back. Some days she got there first and put her bag on the seat beside her so nobody else would sit there. Some days he came straight from the sports centre with his hair still wet. Sometimes there was time for a proper conversation. Sometimes there was only time for a drink and a quick kiss.

The signs kept changing. PRIVATE PROPERTY. MEETING IN PROGRESS. CURRENTLY OCCUPIED. He never wrote one himself. But one afternoon, digging in his backpack for a pen, she found a black marker, a small stack of white paper, and a spare plastic sleeve.

She held them up. “What’s this?”

“Supplies.”

“For what?”

He glanced at the marker. “Your project.”

She stared at him. Then a slow smile spread across her face. “You’ve been carrying these around?”

“Not always.”

“Since when?”

“A while.”

“You’re participating.”

“Somebody has to make sure they’re legible,” he said, and took the marker out of her hand and uncapped it. “Have you got a preference?”

She leaned in, chin on his shoulder, considering the blank sheet. “Something simple. Write DO NOT MOVE.”

He wrote it.

“And underneath. WE’RE COMING BACK.”

His pen stopped for a second. She was smiling, pleased with herself, not looking at him. He bent his head and finished it.

DO NOT MOVE.
WE’RE COMING BACK.

He clipped it to the backrest. She sat back to admire it.

“Perfect.”

He looked at the sign. Then at her. “Very reassuring,” he said, and meant it more than she knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next week he had a home game. She’d meant to go, but her group’s edit had fallen behind, and she spent the whole afternoon in the Media building trying to finish before the deadline.

Xiaoran: I might not make it. I’m so sorry

Yichen: Don’t be. Finish your work.

Xiaoran: are you sure

Yichen: Yes. I’ll see you after.

Xiaoran: good luck. win

She sent a rabbit sticker. He sent one back.

They won. By the time he came out of the sports centre it was nearly seven. He was tired and hungry and his shoulder ached. He could have gone straight home across the road. He walked to the bench instead, and stopped. There was a new sign, in her handwriting.

HE WON.

And underneath, smaller:

HE SHOULD BE PROUD OF HIMSELF.

He stood looking at it. Then he took a photo.

Yichen: Someone’s updated the sign.

Xiaoran: it’s important information

Yichen: How did you know we won?

Xiaoran: the sports account. I had it open the whole time

Yichen: You were supposed to be working.

Xiaoran: I can do two things at once

Xiaoran: did you eat?

Yichen: Not yet.

Xiaoran: wait for me. I’m coming

He sat down under the sign. She came fifteen minutes later at a half run with her laptop bag banging on her hip and two takeaway boxes in a plastic bag.

“Did you see it?”

“I saw it.”

“Do you like it?”

“Very much.”

She sat down next to him, right up against him, and put one of the boxes in his lap. “I bought dinner.”

They ate on the bench in the dark with the vending machine humming beside them. After a while she put her chopsticks down and looked at him.

“You should be proud. I mean it. I watched the score go up every two minutes and I didn’t get any editing done at all.”

“We played well.”

“You played well.”

He looked at her. Then he leaned over and kissed her temple. “Thank you for checking.”

“Obviously,” she said, and let her head drop onto his shoulder and stayed there till both boxes were empty.

✦ ✦ ✦

In third year there were fewer signs. Not because they’d stopped coming. Because they didn’t need them as much. Their weeks had got complicated: her group projects and production work and the occasional paid shoot; his training and games and coursework and the team. Sometimes days went by without them sitting there together. But whenever either of them walked past, they looked. It became a reflex.

One afternoon in the spring she came round the library and found the bench empty. No sign. No Yichen.

Yichen: Where are you?

Xiaoran: bench

Yichen: Five minutes.

She sat down. The seat was dry from the sun for once, and a few leaves had collected underneath. She put her bag beside her and looked at the bare backrest, and it made her smile.

He came with two drinks and gave her one, and sat down, and she curled up against his side with her feet tucked under her. They talked about their days. Her lecturer had set an impossible assignment. A teammate had been keeping everyone late at training. Then she looked at the empty backrest.

“Yichen?”

“Mm.”

“Do you remember the first sign?”

“Reserved.”

“You remember!”

“Of course.”

“And the second?”

“Please do not disturb.”

“And the third?”

“Meeting in progress.”

“Good memory. I think we should make one more.” She looked at the backrest again.

“What should it say?”

She didn’t answer. She took a folded piece of paper out of her bag and opened it up. It was blank. She held it out, with the marker.

“Your turn.”

“Mine?”

“You’ve never made one.”

“I’ve made several.”

“You’ve written what I told you to write.”

“That’s an important distinction.”

“So now you can write whatever you want.”

He looked at the paper. He looked at her. “Anything?”

“Anything.”

He took the marker and thought about it seriously, the way he thought about everything. Then he wrote, and handed it back. His handwriting was neat, slightly slanted.

SAME TIME TOMORROW?

She looked up at him. “That’s it?”

“Three words and a question mark.”

“Are you asking me out?”

“I’m asking if you’ll be here tomorrow. At the same time.”

She looked at the sign. Then she took the marker back from him and added something underneath, and turned it round.

SAME TIME TOMORROW?
OBVIOUSLY.

He laughed. “Very confident.”

She clipped it to the backrest and leaned back against him, satisfied. “Now it’s finished.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means you’re officially part of the project.”

“After three years?”

“You’re a slow learner,” she said, and he laughed and found her hand on the bench between them.

They stayed there until the sun went down behind the library, talking about ordinary things and sometimes not talking at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next day the sign was gone. Neither of them ever found out who took it. Xiaoran was disappointed for thirty seconds, and then decided that the university had a problem with artistic expression.

“Shall we make another?” he said.

“No. We don’t need one,” she said.

The afternoon after that, when she came round the corner of the library, he was already sitting there with two drinks.

“You’re late,” he said.

She looked at her watch. “Three minutes.”

“Still late.”

“Where’s the sign?”

He glanced at the empty backrest. “Didn’t need one.”

She sat down next to him and took the drink he held out, and leaned into his shoulder.

“Same time tomorrow?”

“Obviously,” he said, and it was the last sign they ever needed.

chapters.desc: His first fan-signing as a Herons player. Someone asks him to sign her arm. Then someone familiar joins the queue.
chapters.title: The Girl at the End of the Queue
chapters.epigraph: “There’s a difference.”
chapters.content:
The first time Zhou Yichen attended a fan-signing event as a Herons player, he discovered that being recognised by strangers was a rather unusual experience. Not unpleasant. Just unusual.

He was used to people watching him on the court. He was used to the noise of the crowd, the camera flashes, the occasional chant of his name after a particularly good play. But this was different.

There were no basketballs, no opponents, no scoreboard. Just a long table, a neat row of signed jerseys, a stack of photographs, and several hundred fans waiting for their turn to speak to him.

“Smile a little,” his teammate, Kou Ran, murmured beside him.

Yichen glanced at him.

“I am smiling.”

“You look like you’re reviewing a business proposal.”

“I might be.”

Kou Ran laughed, nearly knocking over his water bottle.

The event had been organised at the end of the season to celebrate the club’s year and introduce its development players to the fans. Yichen was one of four invited to the signing session, and although he’d attended media events before, this was his first proper fan-signing.

He was dressed in the club’s navy jersey with the heron on the chest, sleeves fitted around his arms. His hair had been styled neatly, though a few strands had already fallen over his forehead. He looked composed, as usual.

Unfortunately for him, that seemed to be precisely what the fans liked.

The first few fans asked for signatures on jerseys and basketballs. Some were nervous, some excited, and some had prepared entire speeches. Yichen listened to each of them patiently.

“Thank you for supporting us.”

“I’ll keep working hard.”

“Hope to see you next season.”

He was polite, occasionally smiling, and never rushed anyone unnecessarily.

Then a girl in the queue approached him holding out her arm.

“Could you sign here?”

Yichen looked at the spot she’d pointed to.

“Your arm?”

She nodded enthusiastically. “Yes! If that’s okay.”

“Sure.”

He took the marker and carefully signed her forearm, making sure the ink wouldn’t smudge against her sleeve.

The girl looked down at his signature, practically glowing.

“Thank you! I’ll never wash this off.”

Yichen smiled faintly. “You should probably wash your hands, though.”

She laughed, thanked him again, and moved along. Kou Ran leaned towards him.

“Popular.”

Yichen capped the marker. “It’s a signature.”

“On someone’s arm.”

“Would you prefer I sign yours?”

“Absolutely not. I have standards.”

Yichen gave him a look and continued. He didn’t notice the familiar face several people behind the next fan. Not immediately, anyway. Because Lin Xiaoran was standing in the queue. And she was trying hard not to laugh.

She had arrived a little earlier with Jiayi, who had been considerably more excited about the event than Xiaoran initially admitted to being, and who had brought a sign.

She’d told herself she was only there to support him.

She’d already watched his games, attended his university tournaments, listened to him explain basketball strategies at dinner, and endured his occasional complaints about training schedules. She knew him.

She knew the way he looked when he was concentrating, the way his jaw tightened when he was frustrated, the way he rubbed the back of his neck when he was tired.

She also knew that he had absolutely no idea she was here. She’d deliberately avoided telling him. Because she wanted to surprise him.

And, perhaps more importantly, because she wanted to see what he would do when his girlfriend approached him like an ordinary fan. The queue moved forward.

Xiaoran glanced at the girl who had just received his signature. Then she looked down at her own arm. A small smile appeared.

“Oh, I have an idea,” she murmured to herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen was signing a photograph when the next fan stepped forward.

“Hello.”

He looked up.

“Hello.”

The girl smiled brightly. He looked back down at the photograph, then stopped. The marker hovered over the paper.

He simply stared at the person standing across from him. Lin Xiaoran.

She was wearing a simple cream cardigan over a white top, her hair falling loosely around her shoulders. She had a small handbag hanging from one shoulder and a innocent expression on her face. Far too innocent.

Yichen’s eyes moved from her face to the queue behind her, then back again. His expression didn’t change much.

But the corners of his mouth began to lift.

“Hello,” he said again.

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

“Hello, Mr. Zhou.”

His smile deepened.

“Mr. Zhou?”

“I’m here for an autograph.”

“Are you?”

“Yes.”

He put the photograph down.

“Where would you like it?”

She held out her arm.

“Here, please.”

Yichen looked at her arm, then at her. A quiet pause.

“You want me to sign your arm?”

“Yes.”

“Like the girl before you?”

Xiaoran blinked. She hadn’t expected him to mention that.

“...You noticed?”

“I was sitting here.”

“Oh.”

He leaned back slightly, looking at her with an expression that was becoming increasingly difficult for her to ignore.

“Is that why you joined the queue?”

“Yes.”

“Just for my autograph?”

“Of course.”

“Nothing else?”

Xiaoran nodded with great conviction. Yichen picked up the marker again.

“What’s your name?”

She stared at him. He looked perfectly serious. “Lin Xiaoran,” she answered.

He nodded slowly, as though committing this important information to memory.

“Lin Xiaoran.”

“Yes.”

“Have we met before?”

Her mouth fell open.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed. Not loudly, but enough that the staff member beside him glanced over.

It was the kind of laugh Xiaoran rarely got to see in public. His shoulders relaxed, his eyes curved, and the carefully composed expression he’d maintained throughout the event finally broke. She immediately regretted coming. Not because he had recognised her. Because he was enjoying this far too much.

“Don’t laugh,” she whispered.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I’m trying to be professional.”

“Then be professional.”

“All right.”

He straightened, picked up her arm gently, and uncapped the marker.

“Where exactly?”

Xiaoran pointed to the inside of her forearm.

“Here.”

He steadied her wrist with one hand and began writing. She watched him.

His handwriting was neat, slightly slanted. He wrote her name first, then added a small basketball beside it. When he finished, he didn’t immediately let go.

Instead, he turned her arm slightly to inspect his work.

“Anything else?”

Xiaoran considered it.

“Can you write something?”

“What?”

“Something special.”

His eyes lifted to hers.

“What would you like?”

She smiled.

“Write, ‘To my favourite fan.’”

Yichen stared at her. Then his lips curved.

“That’s a difficult request.”

“Why?”

“Because I have to be fair to the other fans.”

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“Are you saying I’m not your favourite fan?”

“I’m saying I shouldn’t announce favoritism at a public event.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He lowered his voice slightly.

“Then ask me somewhere private.”

Her cheeks warmed. She glanced at the staff member, who was politely pretending not to hear them.

“Just write it.”

Yichen looked at her for another second before adding a small line beneath her name.

To my favourite girl.

Xiaoran stared. It was worse than what she’d asked for. Much worse. Because he hadn’t written fan. He’d written girl.

And the way he looked at her while doing it made her suddenly forget the entire reason she’d planned this little performance.

“Done,” he said.

She looked down at her arm, then back at him.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

“Can I have a photo?”

“Of course.”

She stepped to the side of the table, and a staff member took her phone.

Yichen stood up slightly, leaning closer so they could fit into the frame. Xiaoran smiled brightly at the camera.

Yichen looked at it too, but just before the photo was taken, he glanced down at her. The camera caught it. His eyes were on her, not the lens. And his smile was unmistakably fond.

✦ ✦ ✦

When Xiaoran finally stepped away from the table, she could hear Kou Ran laughing.

“Was that your girlfriend?”

Yichen sat back down.

“Next.”

“Come on. Was that her?”

“Next.”

Kou Ran leaned closer, grinning.

“You wrote something different for her, didn’t you?”

Yichen picked up another photograph.

“Do you want me to sign your forehead?”

Kou Ran laughed.

“That’s a yes.”

The next fan approached, and Yichen returned to his usual polite manner.

But every now and then, his gaze drifted towards the side of the room.

Xiaoran was standing near the exit with Jiayi, looking down at her arm. She was smiling at the signature.

Then she took a picture of it, then another. Then she sent him something on her phone.

His own phone, placed face down beside his water bottle, vibrated. He couldn’t check it yet. He had a queue to finish.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was almost forty minutes before the signing ended.

By then, Yichen’s hand was slightly tired, his throat dry, and Kou Ran had already announced that he was never signing another basketball in his life.

Yichen thanked the staff, changed out of his jersey, and checked his phone. There were three messages from Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: I got my autograph!!

Xiaoran: Very handsome handwriting. 10/10.

Xiaoran: And “favourite girl” is better than what I asked for.

He smiled. He typed back.

Yichen: You weren’t a fan.

Yichen: You were distracting the player.

Her reply came almost immediately.

Xiaoran: Excuse me. I was very respectful.

Xiaoran: I even waited in the queue like everyone else.

Xiaoran: You should appreciate my professionalism.

Yichen shook his head, smiling to himself. He found her near the lobby, sitting on a bench with her legs swinging slightly. Jiayi had apparently gone to buy a drink, leaving Xiaoran alone. The moment she saw him, she stood up.

“Congratulations, Mr. Zhou. Your first fan-signing event is over.”

“Thank you.”

“How was it?”

“Good.”

“Were you nervous?”

“Not particularly.”

“Did you enjoy meeting your fans?”

“I did.”

She nodded thoughtfully.

“Did you enjoy meeting me?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Most.”

“Most?”

“By far.”

Her smile grew. He stepped closer, reaching for her hand. His gaze dropped to the signature on her arm.

“You’ve been looking at that for forty minutes.”

“It’s precious.”

“It’s my handwriting.”

“Exactly.”

He turned her arm gently, examining the ink.

“Don’t rub it too much. It’ll smudge.”

“I know.”

“And don’t use alcohol wipes.”

“I know.”

“Don’t—”

“Zhou Yichen.”

He looked up.

“I’m not going to preserve my arm in a museum.”

His mouth curved.

“Good. I was beginning to worry.”

She leaned closer, lowering her voice.

“Actually, I have a complaint.”

“Already?”

“Yes. The girl before me got a signature on her arm, and you were very gentle with her.”

Yichen raised an eyebrow.

“Was I not gentle with you?”

“You were.”

“Then?”

“You didn’t smile at her like that.”

He studied her face.

“Like what?”

“Like you were trying to make me forget what I came here to say.”

A faint smile appeared.

“Did it work?”

Xiaoran opened her mouth. Closed it, then looked away. Yichen laughed.

He lifted her signed arm and pressed a kiss just above the ink, careful not to touch the fresh writing.

“There. A special edition,” he murmured.

Her cheeks turned pink.

“That’s cheating.”

“Why?”

“Because you can’t give the other fans that.”

“No.”

He said it so naturally that she looked back at him. Yichen’s fingers slipped between hers.

“That’s the point.”

For a moment, Xiaoran forgot about the crowded lobby, the event staff, and the fact that his teammates were probably still nearby. She looked down at their joined hands. Then she tilted her head.

“Do you think people will recognise me now?”

“Why?”

“Because I’m the girl who got your special signature.”

He considered that.

“Possibly.”

“Should I post it?”

“If you want.”

She opened her camera and took another picture of her arm, making sure the words were clear. Then she looked up at him.

“Can you take one with me?”

“Of course.”

She handed him her phone and stood beside him, lifting her signed arm. Yichen took one photo, then another.

“Wait. This one looks like we’re just friends,” she said.

He glanced at the screen.

“What should I do?”

“Look like you love me.”

He looked at her. A slow, amused smile spread across his face.

“Is this not how I usually look at you?”

Xiaoran stared at him. Then she reached for her phone.

“Never mind. That’s enough.”

He laughed and handed it back. She posted the picture with a caption:

Finally met my favourite player. He was professional. Would recommend.

Yichen glanced at it.

“Very professional?”

“Extremely.”

“Is that all?”

She thought for a moment, then added another line.

Also, I think he has a favourite fan.

Yichen took her phone, read the caption, and handed it back.

“That’s inaccurate.”

Xiaoran looked offended.

“What?”

“You’re not my favourite fan.”

She gasped. He leaned down, pressing a kiss to her temple.

“You’re my girlfriend.”

And then, just as she was about to smile, he said:

“There’s a difference.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, after they returned to his apartment, Xiaoran was still talking about the event.

She had already shown him the pictures twice, recounted the moment Kou Ran had laughed, and explained that she thought the staff member had definitely recognised her. Yichen listened while changing out of his clothes.

At one point, she held up her arm again.

“Look. It’s still there.”

He glanced over.

“Good.”

“I wonder how long it’ll last.”

“Probably a day or two.”

She looked disappointed.

“Only that long?”

“You can take a picture.”

“But it’s not the same.”

He walked over and sat beside her on the sofa.

“Then I’ll sign something else.”

She brightened.

“Really?”

“Your notebook. Your phone case. A basketball. Whatever you want.”

Xiaoran considered it.

“Can you sign my forehead?”

Yichen looked at her. Then he smiled.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

“Permanent marker?”

Her eyes widened.

“Obviously not!”

He laughed, pulling her into his arms. She settled against his chest, still holding out her arm for him to inspect.

“Actually,” she said, “I think I understand why fans do that now.”

“Why?”

“It’s nice to have something that reminds you of someone you admire.”

Yichen lowered his gaze to her.

“And who do you admire?”

She looked up at him, pretending to think.

“Hmm. A basketball player. Quite handsome. A little arrogant.”

“A little?”

“Very calm. Sometimes annoying.”

“Sounds unfortunate.”

“Terrible, really.”

He brushed her hair back.

“Should I be concerned?”

“Not really. He’s also my boyfriend.”

“That’s convenient.”

“Very.”

Yichen leaned down and kissed her. It was brief at first, then lingered when she slipped her arms around his neck. When he pulled away, she was smiling.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Mm?”

“When that girl asked you to sign her arm, did you think I would do the same?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I know you.”

She frowned slightly.

“What does that mean?”

He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“You’d find some way to make it more complicated.”

Xiaoran gasped.

“I did not!”

“You asked for a special message.”

“Because I’m special.”

“I know.”

“And you wrote something different for me.”

“I did.”

She smiled, satisfied.

Then, after a moment, she asked, “What if I hadn’t joined the queue? Would you have looked for me?”

Yichen’s expression softened. He tucked her hair behind her ear.

“I was already looking for you before you came to the table.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“You saw me?”

“Not at first. But I knew you were somewhere in the room.”

“How?”

“Because Jiayi was in the queue holding a sign with my name on it in letters a foot high, and Jiayi doesn’t go anywhere without you.”

She burst into laughter.

“So you knew?”

“I suspected.”

“Then why did you ask if we’d met before?”

“You were enjoying yourself.”

He pressed a kiss into her hair.

“And I wanted to see what you’d do.”

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“You knew I was planning something?”

“I know you.”

She buried her face against his chest, laughing. Yichen wrapped both arms around her, resting his cheek lightly against her hair.

His first fan-signing had been a success, according to the club.

There had been a long queue, plenty of photographs, hundreds of signatures, and a considerable amount of attention.

But when he thought about the day later, the moment he remembered most clearly wasn’t the applause or the cameras.

It was a familiar girl standing at the end of the queue, holding out her arm with the most innocent expression he’d ever seen.

And the fact that, despite having spent the afternoon signing his name for hundreds of people, the only signature he wanted to give again was hers.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran wants to learn to drive. Zhou Yichen hands her the keys to the car he bought because of one joke.
chapters.title: The Most Expensive Driving Lesson
chapters.epigraph: “It’s a car. Not a family heirloom.”
chapters.content:
Lin Xiaoran had recently developed an interest in driving. It began rather innocently.

One afternoon, while she and Yichen were having lunch, she watched a woman effortlessly reverse her car into a narrow parking space outside the restaurant.

Xiaoran followed the car with her eyes until it disappeared.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

“Do you know how to drive?”

He looked up from his food.

“Do you think I don’t?”

“I know you do. I’m just asking.”

“Then yes.”

She nodded thoughtfully.

“Can you teach me?”

Yichen put down his chopsticks.

“Drive?”

“No, fly.”

He gave her a look. She smiled, completely unbothered.

“I want to learn. I’ve been thinking about getting a driving licence.”

“That’s good.”

“Really?”

“Why wouldn’t it be?”

“I thought you might tell me it’s dangerous.”

“Driving is dangerous if you don’t learn properly. That’s why you need lessons.”

She leaned forward.

“Will you teach me?”

Yichen considered her.

“Do you want me to teach you, or do you want to learn at a driving school?”

“Both, maybe. I think learning from someone I know would be less scary.”

He nodded.

“All right.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Really?”

“I’ll teach you.”

She returned to her lunch, apparently satisfied. Yichen, however, was already considering which car he should let her practice in.

There was his own car, the one he’d bought in first year because of one joke, which he drove to university and training every day. There were the cars at his family home, which he wouldn’t have considered for a beginner even if they hadn’t been in another city.

He decided his own would do. It was comfortable, easy to handle, and safe.

He didn’t anticipate that the biggest obstacle to Xiaoran’s first driving lesson would be the car itself.

✦ ✦ ✦

The following Saturday morning, Xiaoran arrived at his apartment wearing a loose white shirt, jeans, and sneakers. She had brought a small notebook. Yichen noticed it immediately.

“What’s that?”

“My driving notes.”

“You’ve already made notes?”

“Of course. I did some research.”

He looked at her notebook. The first page had a title written in pink:

Things I Need to Remember Before Driving.

Underneath were several bullet points.

- Adjust seat.
- Adjust mirrors.
- Seatbelt.
- Check surroundings.
- Don’t panic.
- Don’t confuse brake and accelerator.
- Don’t hit anything.

Yichen read the last line twice.

“That’s a good objective.”

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I’m pleased you’re taking this seriously.”

He took his car keys from the counter.

“Let’s go.”

Xiaoran followed him downstairs, chatting about how she had watched several beginner driving videos the night before.

She was halfway through explaining the difference between parallel parking and reverse parking when they reached the underground garage. Then she stopped. Yichen pressed the key.

His car blinked its headlights at the far end of the empty bottom level. Xiaoran stared at it. Then she turned to him.

“...You want me to drive that?”

“Yes.”

“Your car?”

He glanced at it.

“That’s generally what it means when I hand you the keys.”

She ignored his teasing and looked back at the vehicle.

She had sat in its passenger seat a hundred times. She had eaten crisps in it, cried in it, fallen asleep in it on the way home from the airport after Chengdu. She had never once looked at it from the driver’s side.

It was beautiful. Low, polished, with an elegant dark exterior and a leather interior that looked as though it belonged in a luxury showroom rather than a university student’s garage.

She knew Yichen had money. She had known for a long time.

But knowing and being reminded of it were two different things.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

“Are you teaching me in this?”

“Yes.”

She looked at the car again, then at him.

“Can we borrow a different car?”

“Whose?”

“Anyone’s. Fang Ze’s.”

“Fang Ze’s car has a dent in every door.”

“Exactly. One more wouldn’t matter.”

“Why are you so worried about this one?”

She hesitated.

“Because this one looks expensive.”

Yichen’s eyebrows lifted slightly.

“It is.”

“Then why are you letting me drive it?”

“Because you want to learn.”

“But what if I scratch it?”

“Then we’ll deal with it.”

“What if I hit the wall?”

“Hopefully, you won’t.”

“What if—”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked at him. He held the passenger-side door open.

“It’s a car. Not a family heirloom.”

“It’s an extremely expensive car.”

“And?”

“And I don’t want to be responsible for damaging it!”

Yichen smiled faintly.

“Then let’s make sure you don’t.”

He waited until she finally climbed into the driver’s seat.

She sat down carefully, almost as if she were afraid of leaving fingerprints on the leather.

Yichen walked around and got into the passenger seat. He glanced at her.

“Why are you sitting like that?”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re visiting a museum.”

“I am respecting the vehicle.”

He laughed.

“Adjust your seat first.”

✦ ✦ ✦

For the first fifteen minutes, they didn’t even start the engine.

Yichen explained the basic controls, helped her adjust the seat and mirrors, and showed her where the indicators, headlights, and wipers were. Xiaoran listened attentively. Sometimes she asked questions.

Sometimes she repeated what he said under her breath. At one point, she turned towards him.

“Why are there so many buttons?”

“Most of them are straightforward.”

“That’s easy for you to say. You’ve been driving for years.”

“Fair enough.”

He patiently explained the controls again. Then he showed her the gear selector.

“This is for changing gears. For now, just focus on the basic controls. Don’t worry about everything at once.”

She nodded.

“Okay.”

“Seatbelt.”

She fastened it.

“Mirrors?”

She checked them.

“Good.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Ready?”

Xiaoran took a deep breath.

“Yes.”

He nodded towards the empty bays of the bottom level, where nobody parked on a Saturday morning.

“Start the engine.”

She pressed the button. The engine came alive. Her eyes widened slightly.

“It’s so loud.”

“It’s normal.”

“It sounds very powerful.”

“It is.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“Are you sure this is a beginner-friendly car?”

Yichen laughed.

“It’s fine.”

“Your definition of fine is questionable.”

He settled back into his seat.

“Foot on the brake. We’ll move slowly.”

Xiaoran followed his instructions. The car began rolling forward. Very slowly. Almost comically slowly.

Yichen watched the space ahead, then glanced at her.

“Good. Keep your hands steady.”

She looked intensely focused.

“I’m doing it.”

“You are.”

“I’m actually driving.”

“Yes.”

“Yichen, I’m driving your car.”

“I’ve noticed.”

She turned her head towards him, delighted.

“I’m driving!”

“Eyes on the road, Xiaoran.”

She immediately faced forward.

“Right. Sorry.”

He smiled. It was a small thing, but he enjoyed watching her discover something new. She had a tendency to become completely absorbed in whatever interested her, and right now she was taking every instruction seriously.

She drove in a straight line, then made a gentle turn, then stopped. Yichen nodded.

“Good.”

She exhaled.

“How was that?”

“Very good for your first attempt.”

Her smile was enormous. Then she looked at the car.

“Nothing happened.”

“That’s usually the goal.”

She laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trouble began when Yichen asked her to practice turning into a parking space.

He explained the angle, the mirrors, and how to judge the distance. Xiaoran listened. She really did.

But when she started turning, she became convinced that the car was getting too close to the painted line.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

“Am I too close?”

“Not yet. Turn a little more.”

She turned the steering wheel.

“More?”

“A little.”

“Like this?”

“Good.”

Then she stopped.

“Wait.”

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

“I think I’m too close.”

“You’re fine.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

She glanced at the mirror, then the front, then the mirror again.

“Yichen, I don’t think I can do this.”

He looked at her face. Her brows were drawn together, and her hands had tightened around the steering wheel. He spoke calmly.

“Look at me for a second.”

She turned.

“Take a breath.”

She did.

“Nothing is happening. You’re moving slowly. I can see the distance, and I’ll tell you if you need to stop.”

She nodded.

“Okay.”

“Trust your eyes, not your imagination.”

Xiaoran gave him a small, embarrassed smile.

“That’s difficult.”

“I know.”

He guided her through the rest of the turn. She parked successfully. Not perfectly centred, but safely within the lines.

When she stopped the car, she looked at him.

“Did I do it?”

“You did.”

She let go of the steering wheel. Then she turned towards him.

“I’m amazing.”

Yichen laughed.

“You are.”

She looked at the car again.

“Your car is still alive.”

“Thankfully.”

She reached over and lightly hit his arm.

“Don’t make fun of me!”

He caught her hand, bringing it to his lips for a brief kiss.

“I knew you could.”

That made her smile again.

✦ ✦ ✦

After nearly an hour, they decided to take a break.

Yichen drove the car out of the garage and parked at a quiet café nearby. Xiaoran was still talking about her first successful parking attempt.

“I think I understand the steering now.”

“Good.”

“And the mirrors.”

“Good.”

“And I didn’t panic.”

“You panicked a little.”

“I did not.”

He glanced at her.

“You asked me six times whether you were too close.”

“That’s not panic. That’s checking.”

“Of course.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Are you going to be a difficult driving instructor?”

“I thought I was being patient.”

“You are. But you have a very annoying face when you’re right.”

He smiled.

“I’m afraid that’s not something I can change.”

She took a sip of her drink.

Then, after a moment, she asked, “Can I drive again next week?”

“Whenever you want.”

“Really?”

“Of course.”

She hesitated.

“Even with this car?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Would you prefer I buy another car for your lessons?”

Her eyes widened.

“No!”

He laughed.

“I was joking.”

“Don’t joke about things like that.”

“Why?”

“Because you might actually do it.”

He didn’t answer immediately. Which was, in itself, suspicious. Xiaoran put down her drink.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

“You’re not going to buy me a car just because I want to learn, are you?”

“Not today.”

“That’s not reassuring!”

He laughed, then reached across the table to brush a little foam from the corner of her mouth.

“Listen. You don’t need to worry about the price of the car every time you make a mistake. That’s why I’m here. We’ll start slowly, and when you’re ready, you’ll take lessons with a proper instructor too.”

“Why both?”

“Because I want you to learn properly. I’m your boyfriend, not a certified driving instructor.”

“Then why did you volunteer?”

“Because you asked me.”

His answer was so simple that she fell quiet.

He said, “And because I like spending time with you. Even if you spend half of it worrying about my car.”

She smiled.

“I wasn’t worrying about the car. I was worrying about your wallet.”

“That’s very considerate.”

“I’m serious!”

“I know.”

He turned her hand over and traced his thumb over her palm.

“But you don’t have to protect my wallet from yourself.”

Xiaoran looked at him for a while. Then she smiled mischievously.

“So if I accidentally scratch your car, you’ll still love me?”

“Sadly.”

“Unfortunately?”

“It’s a serious inconvenience.”

She laughed, kicking his shoe lightly under the table.

✦ ✦ ✦

The following Saturday, Xiaoran arrived with her notebook again. This time, she had added a new page.

Things I Must Not Do While Driving Yichen’s Car.

1. Panic.
2. Hit the accelerator too hard.
3. Hit the brake too hard.
4. Scratch the car.
5. Make Yichen regret teaching me.
6. Cry if I make a mistake.

Yichen read the list while standing beside her. He looked at the last item, then at her.

“Why would you cry?”

“Because I might feel bad.”

He closed the notebook.

“Let’s add something.”

“What?”

He took her pen and wrote beneath the list.

7. Remember that learning is more important than being perfect.

Xiaoran read it, then looked up at him.

“That’s a very teacher-like thing to say.”

“I’m a good teacher.”

“You’re a very handsome teacher.”

He paused.

“Is that relevant to driving?”

“Very. It helps me stay motivated.”

He laughed, opening the passenger door for her.

“Get in, student.”

She climbed into the driver’s seat, looking considerably less intimidated than the week before. Yichen settled beside her.

She adjusted the seat, checked the mirrors, and fastened her seatbelt without being reminded. He watched her with quiet approval.

“Ready?”

She nodded. Then she turned to him.

“Yichen?”

“Hmm?”

“If I become a really good driver, can I drive you somewhere?”

His expression softened.

“Where?”

“Anywhere you want.”

He considered it.

“Then take me home.”

She blinked.

“Your apartment?”

“Or somewhere else. I don’t mind.”

She smiled, placing both hands on the steering wheel.

“Okay. I’ll drive you home one day.”

Yichen leaned back, watching her start the engine.

“I’ll look forward to it.”

And he meant it. Not because he particularly needed someone else to drive him around.

But because he could already imagine it: Xiaoran sitting proudly behind the wheel, insisting she knew the way, occasionally asking him to check the navigation, and getting offended whenever he suggested a different route.

He would probably end up driving anyway. But he would let her have the keys. After all, it was only a car.

And he had never been particularly good at saying no to her.

chapters.desc: Lin Xiaoran passes her driving test first time and keeps a promise from the car park: she drives Zhou Yichen home, at twenty kilometres an hour.
chapters.title: She Passed
chapters.epigraph: “Goodnight, driver.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Lin Xiaoran did after passing her driving test was call Zhou Yichen.

The second thing she did was scream, which seemed like the correct response to passing.

“YICHEN!”

Yichen, who was in the middle of reviewing a document at his desk, immediately lifted his phone away from his ear. He waited for the sound to settle. Then he smiled.

“Nice to see you as well.”

“I passed!”

His hand stopped moving. He looked at the document in front of him. Then he leaned back in his chair.

“You passed?”

“YES!”

A laugh escaped him.

“Congratulations.”

“I passed, Yichen!”

“I heard you.”

“I really passed!”

“I know.”

She sounded breathless, as if she’d just finished running rather than completing a driving test.

He could almost picture her: eyes wide, cheeks flushed, probably holding her phone with both hands while trying hard not to jump around in public.

“How did it go?” he asked.

“At first, I was nervous.”

“Understandable.”

“But then I remembered everything my instructor taught me. I checked the mirrors, adjusted the seat, checked the blind spots, and did the parking.”

“Good.”

“And I didn’t hit anything.”

He smiled.

“That’s an important achievement.”

“Yichen!”

“I’m kidding.”

She went quiet for a second.

Then, in a much smaller voice, she said, “I passed on my first attempt.”

His expression softened.

“I know. You did well.”

There was a little pause.

Then she asked, “Are you free today?”

“Why?”

“Because...”

He waited. She lowered her voice.

“I want to drive.”

“Where?”

“Home. Yours. You told me to take you home, and I said I would,” she said.

Yichen looked at his phone. He remembered. Seven weeks ago, on the bottom level of his building’s car park, she had sat behind his steering wheel looking at the dashboard. She had been afraid of scratching his car, afraid of the accelerator, afraid of everything. And at the end of that afternoon she had asked whether, if she ever got good, she could drive him somewhere.

Then take me home, he’d said. He hadn’t forgotten.

“All right,” he said.

Her voice immediately brightened.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“Come and get me.”

He glanced at the clock.

“With what?”

“Your car.”

“So I drive to the test centre, so that you can drive me home.”

“Yes.”

“Good plan.”

“Don’t laugh!”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He was smiling too much to deny it.

✦ ✦ ✦

When Yichen pulled up outside the test centre that afternoon, Xiaoran was waiting by the gate. She walked up to the car with a different face from the one she’d worn in his car park seven weeks ago. Today she looked proud of herself. She held up her new licence.

“Look.”

Yichen took it. He glanced at the details, then looked back at her.

“Congratulations, licensed driver.”

“Thank you.”

He gave it back.

“How does it feel?”

“Very good.”

“Confident?”

“Extremely.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Extremely?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He looked at the car.

“Should I be worried?”

She immediately frowned.

“Why would you be worried?”

“Just checking.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

He laughed and opened the passenger door.

“Get in, then.”

She didn’t move. He met her eyes.

“What?”

“You’re supposed to let me drive.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you opening that door?”

He closed it again.

“Sorry, Madam Driver.”

She smiled with satisfaction.

“Better.”

He got into the passenger seat himself. Xiaoran opened the driver’s door. And then she stopped.

The familiar interior looked much more intimidating than it had when she was sitting beside him.

She had driven during her lessons. She had practised parking, turning, braking, and changing lanes. She had passed the test. But this was different. This was Yichen’s car. His expensive, beautiful, spotless car. And he was going to sit beside her. She took a breath. Yichen watched her.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re staring at the steering wheel.”

“I’m checking it.”

“It’s the same steering wheel.”

“I know.”

He waited. She finally sat down and adjusted the seat, then the mirrors, then the seat again. Yichen watched her make three small adjustments.

“Comfortable?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She put her hands on the steering wheel. He glanced at them.

“Ten and two?”

She met his eyes.

“Don’t test me.”

“Wouldn’t dare.”

The first few minutes went well. She checked her mirrors, adjusted her position, fastened her seat belt, and started the engine. Yichen remained quiet.

He didn’t reach for anything or offer unnecessary instructions.

He had learned during their first lesson that she became more nervous when he spoke too much. She looked towards him.

“Ready?”

“Whenever you are.”

She slowly released the brake. The car began moving. At approximately twenty kilometres per hour.

Yichen looked at the speedometer, then at her, then back at the road. He said nothing.

Xiaoran was concentrating so hard that her lips had pressed into a thin line. The car rolled forward. A little too slowly. A car behind them maintained a respectful distance.

She glanced at the speedometer, then at the road, then at the speedometer again. Yichen finally spoke.

“You’re allowed to go a little faster.”

“I know.”

“All right.”

She increased the speed. To twenty-one kilometres per hour. He turned his head slightly towards the window. A smile appeared. She noticed.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re smiling.”

“Am I not allowed to be happy?”

“Not like that.”

He looked at her.

“How should I smile?”

“Normally.”

“This is my normal smile.”

She gave him a suspicious look, then returned her attention to the road. At the first intersection, Xiaoran slowed down. She checked the traffic. Waited. Checked again. Yichen watched her carefully.

She finally turned the steering wheel and completed the turn. It was smooth. He nodded.

“Good.”

She smiled without looking at him.

“Thank you.”

A little farther down the road, she asked, “Was that okay?”

“Yes.”

“Did I turn too early?”

“No.”

“Too late?”

“No.”

“Then it was perfect?”

He considered.

“Very good.”

She turned to him.

“Why can’t you say perfect?”

“Because I don’t want you to become arrogant.”

She gasped.

“I’m already a licensed driver!”

“Congratulations again.”

She smiled. He reached over and gently touched her shoulder.

“You’re doing well. Keep your eyes on the road.”

She nodded. And, for the next few minutes, they drove in comfortable silence. At a red light, Xiaoran looked at him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Are you nervous?”

He turned towards her.

“About what?”

“My driving.”

He considered the question.

“Not particularly.”

“Really?”

“You’re driving safely.”

She looked pleased.

“Then you trust me?”

“Yes.”

She smiled.

“Even with your car?”

He looked at the dashboard, then back at her.

“Even with my car.”

She seemed satisfied. The light turned green. She started moving again.

A moment later, she said, “I remember the first time you taught me.”

“I remember.”

“I was so scared.”

“You were.”

“I thought I would scratch your car.”

“You were more worried about that than your own safety.”

She frowned.

“That’s because your car is expensive.”

“And now?”

She looked ahead.

“Now I’m only a little worried.”

“About the car?”

“About you judging me.”

He turned his head.

“Why would I judge you?”

“Because you’re good at driving.”

“That doesn’t mean I expect you to drive like me. You just passed your test. You’re allowed to be inexperienced.”

She nodded slowly.

“Okay.”

“And you don’t need to prove anything to me.”

Her fingers relaxed slightly on the steering wheel.

“I know.”

He smiled.

“Good.”

The journey home took longer than usual. Normally, Yichen could make the drive in a fraction of the time.

Today, they encountered every red light, every cautious turn, and every opportunity for Xiaoran to reduce her speed.

At one point, they passed the café near campus, theirs since the week they’d moved to Shanghai.

“Should I turn here?”

“That’s not our route.”

“I know. I was just asking.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted to see if you remembered.”

He turned to her.

“Remember what?”

“That it’s ours.”

“I remember.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

A few minutes later, she asked, “Do you think I’m a good driver?”

He didn’t answer immediately. She looked at him.

“Yichen?”

“You’ve passed your test.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He smiled.

“You’re a good beginner.”

She looked offended.

“A beginner?”

“An inexperienced driver.”

“That’s worse!”

He laughed.

“Would you prefer I lie?”

She thought about it.

“No.”

“Then there you go.”

She huffed. He reached over and squeezed her hand, careful not to distract her.

“You’ll get better with practice.”

She smiled again.

“I know.”

When they finally reached his residential complex, Xiaoran looked relieved. She had brought them home without hitting anything.

She slowed down as they approached the car park entrance.

Yichen gave her a few directions. She followed them, turned carefully, and took the ramp down to the bottom level, where she’d had her first lesson, then came the final challenge. Parking.

She looked at the space, then at the mirrors, then at the space again. Yichen waited.

“Take your time.”

She nodded. The first attempt was slightly crooked. She stopped. Looked at the car, then looked at him. He said nothing.

She reversed slowly, adjusted the angle, and tried again.

This time, the car settled neatly between the lines. She put the car in park. Turned off the engine. And sat completely still. Yichen looked at her.

“Done.”

She blinked. Then she turned towards him.

“I did it.”

“You did.”

“I drove your car.”

“You did.”

“All the way home.”

He smiled.

“At twenty kilometres per hour.”

She stared at him. Then her mouth fell open.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed. She hit his arm lightly.

“Don’t make fun of me!”

“I’m not making fun of you.”

“You are!”

He reached over and took her hand.

“Xiaoran.”

She stopped. He looked at her properly.

“You drove me home.”

Her expression softened. She forgot to be offended. Then she smiled.

“Yes.”

“Just like you said you would.”

She looked down at their joined hands.

“Yes.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Thank you.”

She turned towards him.

“You’re welcome.”

They didn’t get out immediately. Xiaoran remained in the driver’s seat, looking at the dashboard. Yichen watched her.

“What’s wrong now?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re staring again.”

She smiled.

“I just feel strange.”

“Why?”

“Because I finally did it.”

He nodded. She turned towards him.

“Do you remember what I said during the first lesson?”

“That you wanted to drive me somewhere?”

“Yes.”

She smiled.

“I wanted to take you home.”

He held her gaze.

“And you did.”

She nodded. Then she leaned across the centre console and wrapped her arms around him.

Yichen laughed at the sudden embrace, but his arms came around her immediately. She rested her cheek against his shoulder.

“Next time, I’ll drive faster.”

“How much faster?”

“Maybe thirty.”

He looked down at her.

“Ambitious.”

“Forty, if I’m feeling brave.”

“Let’s not get ahead of ourselves.”

She laughed against his shoulder. He kissed her temple.

“You’re doing well. There’s no need to rush.”

She pulled back.

“I know.”

He moved her hair off her cheek.

“And I like being your passenger.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She laughed.

“You’re so annoying.”

“You’re welcome.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, they ordered dinner and stayed in. Xiaoran was still talking about the drive.

She described the turns she had made, the traffic light that had made her nervous, and how she had almost forgotten to check one of her mirrors before correcting herself. Yichen listened, occasionally asking questions.

At some point, she took his phone and opened the map.

“Look.”

He glanced at the screen.

“What?”

“This was our route.”

He looked at the blue line.

“Yes.”

“It took us thirty-eight minutes.”

“Usually it takes fifteen.”

She nodded.

“Because I drove.”

“That’s right.”

She looked pleased. Then she noticed something.

“Wait.”

“Hm?”

“Why did you save the route?”

He studied her.

“Maybe I didn’t.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“Then why is it starred?”

“Because I wanted to remember the route.”

“Why?”

He leaned back against the sofa.

“Because you drove me home.”

She looked at him. Then her cheeks warmed.

“That’s so unnecessary.”

He reached for her hand.

“I disagree.”

She smiled and leaned against his shoulder. A few minutes later, her phone vibrated. A message from Meilin.

Meilin: Heard you passed your driving test. Congratulations!

Xiaoran: THANK YOU!

Meilin: Have you driven yet?

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen. Then she typed.

Xiaoran: I drove Yichen home today.

Meilin: Oh?

Xiaoran: Yes!

Meilin: How did it go?

Xiaoran smiled.

Xiaoran: Very well.

Yichen glanced at the screen.

“How fast?”

She held his gaze.

“Don’t.”

He laughed. She continued typing.

Xiaoran: I drove safely.

Meilin replied almost immediately.

Meilin: How fast?

Xiaoran stared at the message. Then, slowly, she turned towards Yichen. He was already smiling.

“Don’t you dare.”

He laughed. Later that night, when Xiaoran was ready to leave, Yichen walked her to the door.

She slipped on her shoes and turned towards him.

“Next time, I’ll drive you somewhere else.”

“Where?”

“Anywhere you want.”

He considered.

“Can I choose?”

“Yes.”
