“Then take me somewhere you like.”

She blinked.

“That’s not fair.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted you to choose.”

He smiled.

“Then I’ll choose somewhere you like.”

She shook her head, laughing.

“You’re unbelievable.”

He kissed her temple.

“Goodnight, driver.”

She smiled.

“Goodnight, passenger.”

Then she stepped into the corridor. Before the door closed, she turned around.

“Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“Next time, I’ll try to drive at thirty.”

He nodded solemnly.

“I look forward to it.”

She grinned.

“Don’t be scared.”

“I won’t.”

The door closed. He had been driven home in his own car at twenty kilometres an hour, in more than twice the usual time, and he was still smiling when he locked the door.

chapters.desc: Her father’s car, the compound gate, and Yichen in the passenger seat trying very hard to look relaxed.
chapters.title: Her First Solo Drive
chapters.epigraph: “You were driving well. I knew that.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen had never been worried about Lin Xiaoran driving. He had, however, badly underestimated what it would be like to sit in the passenger seat while she did it.

“Right,” she said, and adjusted the rear-view mirror. Then the wing mirror. Then the rear-view mirror again.

He fastened his seatbelt. His face was calm. His hands were resting neatly on his knees.

“Ready?” he said.

“Yes.”

She turned the key. The engine started. She looked at him.

“Why are you looking at me?”

“I’m not.”

“You’re making me nervous.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face is saying something.”

“Then I’ll stop using my face,” he said, and she gave him a suspicious look and turned back to the windscreen.

It was her father’s car: a twelve-year-old silver Buick that Lin Hongwei washed by hand every Sunday morning in the compound and had never once let anyone else drive. She had passed her test in Shanghai six weeks before. Since then she had driven exactly twice, both times in Yichen’s car, once round the bottom floor of his car park and once back from the test centre. On the first Saturday of the summer holiday her father had agreed, after two days of silence and one long conversation with her mother behind the bedroom door, that she could take the Buick out for one afternoon, provided she had someone sensible beside her.

She had nominated Yichen before her father finished the sentence.

“Okay. Let’s go,” she said, gripping the wheel at ten and two.

The car rolled forward. Slowly. He looked out of the windscreen. Then at the speedometer. Then at her.

“You’re doing well.”

“I know.”

“Just checking.”

At the compound gate the guard in the booth put down his newspaper to watch. She stopped, looked left, looked right, looked left again, and pulled out onto the road with enormous care.

“Good,” said Yichen.

“See?”

“See what?”

“I’m driving.”

“I noticed.”

“And you’re not doing anything.”

“I’m not doing anything,” he agreed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then they came to the first junction. She slowed. A car came from the right. She stopped. It went past. She waited a little longer than she needed to.

“Clear,” he said.

“I can see.”

“Of course.”

She turned. A little too sharply. His right hand went towards the door handle on its own. He caught it halfway, and then, after a moment’s thought, put it there anyway and left it.

Her eyes flicked sideways. “What’s that?”

“What?”

“Your hand.”

He looked down. It was holding the handle on the inside of the passenger door.

“Nothing.”

“Why are you holding it?”

“It’s a comfortable position.”

“You’re holding the door handle.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He looked straight ahead. “Just in case.”

She burst out laughing so hard that the car wobbled.

“Eyes on the road,” he said, without moving his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time they got onto the main road she’d found her rhythm. She kept to the speed limit, left a good gap to the car in front, and checked her mirrors every few seconds like the instructor had taught her. He had stopped saying anything at all. He was also still holding the door handle. Not hard, but firmly enough that she could see the tendons in the back of his hand.

She lasted three minutes.

“Are you scared?”

“No.”

“Then why are you holding on?”

“Habit.”

“What habit?”

“Passenger habit.”

“You weren’t like this when I drove you back from the test.”

“That was a straight road. And it was my car,” he said.

She gasped. “So you trust me less in my dad’s car?”

“I trust you completely. I don’t trust your father’s opinion of me if it comes back with a scratch.”

“That’s not the same thing!”

“No?”

“No!”

“All right,” he said, and looked out of the side window, and the corner of his mouth was doing something.

“You’re laughing at me.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The second incident was a motorbike. It cut across from the next lane without signaling, and she did everything right: came off the accelerator, held her distance, let it go. Nothing happened at all. But out of the corner of her eye she saw his fingers tighten round the handle.

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

“Are you okay?”

“Perfectly.”

“Your hand.”

He looked down at it. He loosened it, one finger at a time. “Sorry.”

“You’re nervous.”

“A bit,” he said.

She glanced at him, surprised. He didn’t often admit to that, and never about something so ordinary.

“Really?”

“Would you rather I lied?”

“No. But why?”

He was quiet. “Because I know how careful you are. I also know you’ve only been doing this six weeks. And it’s you.”

“So you’re worried about me.”

“I’m sitting right next to you.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

“Yes, I’m worried about you,” he said.

She kept her eyes on the road, but she smiled, and her shoulders came down. “Don’t worry. I’ll look after you,” she said.

He laughed out loud. “Thank you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The café was twenty minutes away. She’d picked it because the route was mostly straight and the car park was big, and she’d been there with Meilin and knew where the entrance was. She’d even looked at it on the map the night before. What she hadn’t planned for was that on a Saturday afternoon in July, the car park would be full. She crawled along the rows.

“There’s one,” he said.

“I see it.”

She put the indicator on. Then she stopped. The space was between a black SUV and a white van. It was just narrow enough to worry about.

She looked at it. He waited. She edged forward, stopped, turned the wheel, stopped again.

“Do you think I’ll fit?”

He looked at the space, then at her. “Yes.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

She looked at the SUV. She looked at the van. His hand went back to the door handle. She turned her head slowly.

“Yichen.”

“Yes?”

“You’re doing it again.”

He looked at his hand. He let go.

“Sorry.”

She reversed in. She checked her mirrors. She went back out and came in again. The second time, the car slid in between the lines and stopped, almost perfectly straight.

She put it in park. Neither of them said anything. She looked at the lines. She looked at him. She looked at the lines again, and a slow, enormous smile came over her face.

“I did it.”

He leaned over and looked out of her window at the gap. “Perfectly.”

“Really?”

“Really.”

She undid her seatbelt and leaned across the handbrake and kissed his cheek. “Good boy.”

His eyebrows went up. “Good boy?”

“For letting go of the handle.”

He caught her wrist before she could sit back and kissed her properly, over the gearstick, in her father’s car.

“Well done, driver. I’ll be submitting my passenger feedback later,” he said.

“Don’t you dare.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The drive back was easier. She was relaxed now, and he had stopped holding the door handle, mostly. At a crossing the light went amber and she slowed and stopped well before the line.

“Did you see that?”

“What?”

“I stopped. Correctly.”

“I saw.”

“You’re supposed to praise me.”

“Excellent braking.”

“That’s not romantic.”

He thought about it. “Very attractive braking technique.”

“That’s worse!”

The light changed. She pulled away smoothly, and after a while she said, “Were you holding the door handle the whole time?”

He took a moment. “Most of it.”

“Why didn’t you just say you were nervous?”

“Because you were enjoying yourself. I didn’t want you to think you were doing badly. You were driving well. I knew that.” He turned his head to look at her.

“Then why?”

“Knowing you can do something,” he said, “and being comfortable while you’re doing it at sixty kilometres an hour are two different things.”

She reached over at the next red light and put her hand on his arm and left it there until the light changed.

“Next time I’m driving again.”

“All right.”

“And you’re not holding the handle.”

“I’ll try.”

“Yichen.”

“I’ll try very hard,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

When they turned into the compound, her father was standing by the guard’s booth with his hands behind his back, as if he had happened to be passing at exactly that moment and for no reason. He watched her park in the space by the bicycle shed. He watched her get out.

“How was it?”

“Good!”

“Any problems?”

“None.”

Yichen got out of the passenger side and shut the door gently. Her father looked at him.

“How was she?”

“Very good, Uncle.”

“See?” said Xiaoran.

Her father nodded slowly. “You can take it out again.”

“Really?”

“Be careful. And you. Was the ride comfortable?” He looked at Yichen again.

Xiaoran turned to look at Yichen. Her eyes went wide. Yichen looked at her, and then back at her father.

“Very comfortable, Uncle.”

“Good.”

Her father walked once round the car, slowly, bending to look at the front bumper, and then at the back bumper, and then, satisfied, went inside without another word.

She waited until the building door had shut behind him. “Very comfortable?”

“Yes.”

“You held that handle like your life depended on it!”

“I was being polite.”

“Polite?”

“I didn’t want to frighten the driver,” he said, and she laughed and held on to him in the middle of the courtyard and leaned on him.

“Next time I’m driving you somewhere far.”

“All right.”

“And you won’t be scared.”

“I promise to be a very polite passenger.”

She kissed him, quick, by the bicycle shed, and he kissed her hair and then looked over her head at the Buick.

“Xiaoran?”

“Mm?”

“Next time, maybe we practice parking somewhere with fewer witnesses.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

She hit his arm and walked off towards the building door, complaining about his lack of faith in her, and he followed a step behind. His right hand, he noticed, still remembered exactly the shape of that handle.

chapters.desc: He arrives with a printed packing list of thirty-two items. Hers has three, and the third is him.
chapters.title: Packing List
chapters.epigraph: “Your hairbrush was under a pillow.”
chapters.content:
The trouble started when Zhou Yichen showed her his packing list.

They were sitting on the floor of her old bedroom at her parents’ flat, surrounded by an open suitcase, folded clothes, and several small heaps of things Xiaoran hadn’t decided about yet. On Friday they were taking the coach to her grandparents’ house in the town for five days, because at New Year her grandfather had said in front of the whole family, bring the boy in summer, I’ll teach him to fish properly, and in her family that counted as a summons.

Yichen had arrived at ten with his own suitcase already packed and a sheet of A4 in a plastic sleeve.

She took it out of the sleeve. She looked at it. She looked at him.

“Thirty-two items?”

“Yes.”

“Thirty-two?”

“That’s the current list.”

“Why does it say current?”

“Because I might add something.”

“Yichen. Are we moving?”

“No.”

“Are you going somewhere for six months?”

“No.”

“Then why do you have thirty-two items?”

“Because I don’t want to forget anything,” he said, as if this were obvious, and she started reading it out loud just to make him suffer.

“Clothing. One, shirts. Two, trousers. Three, shorts. Four, socks—”

“Those are necessary.”

“I know they’re necessary! Eight, basketball shoes. Nine, casual shoes. Ten, sandals. Three pairs of shoes? For a village with one road?” She lowered the paper.

“There’s a basketball court at the primary school. Your grandmother told me.”

“When did my grandmother tell you that?”

“At New Year. I asked.”

“You asked my grandmother where the basketball court was.”

“It seemed like useful information.”

She went back to the list. “Sixteen, portable charger. Seventeen, charging cable. Eighteen, backup charging cable.”

“In case the first one stops working.”

“You’re a menace.”

“Have you made yours?”

“Of course I have.”

“Can I see it?”

She got her phone out, opened her notes, and turned the screen round with a flourish.

Xiaoran’s Packing List

1. Clothes.
2. Toiletries.
3. Yichen.

He read it. He read it again. Then he looked at her over the top of the phone.

“Three items.”

“Yes.”

“That’s the whole list?”

“That’s the complete list.”

“Number three.”

“You’re important. You’re the most important item. I put you last so I’d remember,” she said.

“Am I being packed?”

“Obviously. Here. You go here.” She patted the floor beside the suitcase.

“That’s not how packing works.”

“Then you should be grateful I’m making an exception,” she said, and leaned sideways until her head was on his shoulder, and stayed there, which made it hard for either of them to pack anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

His mistake, he said afterward, was asking whether she’d packed everything else. She hadn’t. He found this out when he looked properly into her suitcase and saw three tops, one pair of trousers, two dresses, a small washbag, and a novel.

“Where are your other clothes?”

“Those are my clothes.”

“For how long?”

“Until we get back.”

“Xiaoran. It’s five days.”

“I know how long it is.”

“You’ve packed three tops.”

“I’m planning to wear them more than once.”

“In July. In the countryside. Next to a pond.”

She considered this. “Maybe four tops.”

“Where’s your phone charger?”

“In my bag.”

“Toothbrush?”

“Washbag.”

“Hairbrush?”

A pause.

“Somewhere.”

“Your ID card?”

“In my wallet.”

“And your wallet?”

She pointed in the general direction of her desk. He looked. The wallet was on top of a stack of old exam papers, under a hair clip and half a packet of biscuits. He shut his eyes.

“Don’t,” she said.

“I’m not saying anything.”

“You’re thinking something.”

“I’m thinking we should go through your bag together.”

“See? This is why you’re on the list.” She beamed at him.

“Only as number three.”

“Number three is the important one!”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother put her head round the door at that point, holding a basket of laundry on her hip, and stopped.

“What’s that?”

“His packing list. Thirty-two items. With a backup charging cable,” said Xiaoran.

Mrs. Lin put the basket down. She held out her hand for the list and read it from top to bottom, twice, without any expression at all, the way she read the electricity bill, and handed it back to Yichen.

“Backup charging cable,” she said.

“In case the first one stops working, Auntie.”

“Good.” She turned to her daughter. “And yours?”

Xiaoran held up her phone. Her mother read all three lines. She looked at the third one for a little longer than the other two.

“Well, at least you’ve written down the important thing,” she said.

“Mum!”

Mrs. Lin took the pen off the floor, wrote Grandma’s tea (in the hall, DO NOT FORGET) at the bottom of Yichen’s printed list, because Yichen was so clearly the one who would read it, picked up her laundry, and left. From the hall they heard her say to Xiaoran’s father, “He has a backup cable,” and her father say, “Of course he does.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next half hour was packing. Yichen refolded her clothes so they took up half the space. She told him she didn’t need everything arranged by size. He arranged them by size anyway. She moved his washbag into a different pocket of his suitcase for no reason at all, and he moved it back without a word, and she moved it again, and he gave up and left it there.

She clipped a small plush capybara to the zip of her case.

“Is that on the list?”

“It’s emotionally important.”

“All right,” he said, and wrote capybara on the list in pencil, and that was the end of the argument.

At some point she noticed he had added three more lines in pencil at the bottom.

“What’s thirty-three?”

“Spare notebook.”

“Thirty-four?”

“Spare pen.”

“Thirty-five?”

“Small first-aid kit.”

“Are you planning an expedition?”

“Your grandfather has fishhooks.”

She took the pen from him and wrote underneath, in her own big handwriting, 36. Xiaoran’s patience.

“That’s not an item.”

“It is. You need it. Mostly when you travel with me.”

He took the pen back and wrote under that, 37. Xiaoran’s hairbrush.

“Why are you adding things to my list?”

“Because you’ve forgotten it.”

“I haven’t forgotten it. I was going to pack it.”

“Where is it?”

She looked around the room. Her eyes went from the desk to the windowsill to the bed, and she pointed, without any confidence at all, at the bed. He leaned over and lifted the pillow. The hairbrush was underneath.

He put it in her washbag and zipped the washbag up. “Of course you were.”

Her father appeared in the doorway a few minutes later with something behind his back. Lin Hongwei didn’t, as a rule, come into his daughter’s room when Yichen was in it. He stood on the threshold.

“Dad? What is it?”

“For the pond,” he said, and held it out to Yichen. It was a cotton fishing hat, faded from navy to something like grey, with a little brass ring on the side where a hook had once been kept.

Yichen got up off the floor to take it. “Uncle. This is yours.”

“It was my father’s before it was mine. He gave it to me when I was twenty and I never caught anything in it either. He’ll want to see it. Wear it the first morning. Don’t wear it the second, or he’ll think you’re showing off.” Mr. Lin looked at the hat, not at Yichen.

“The first morning. Not the second.”

“And don’t talk while the float’s in the water. He hates that.”

“I won’t talk.”

“And when he catches something, say it’s a good size, even if it isn’t.”

“Dad,” said Xiaoran, “are you coaching him?”

“I’m giving him a hat,” said her father, with dignity, and went back to the living room, and they heard the television go on loud.

Yichen sat down on the floor again with the hat in both hands and looked at it.

“He’s never given me anything before,” he said.

“He gave you a fishing trip in Shanghai.”

“That was a test.”

“So’s this,” said Xiaoran, and put the hat on his head, where it sat a little too small, and laughed so much she had to lie down on the carpet. He let her. He didn’t take it off. He wrote 38. hat (first morning only) at the bottom of his list in pencil, neatly, and underlined first.

✦ ✦ ✦

When they’d finished, his suitcase was arranged like a shop window, with the list folded in the front pocket, and hers was zipped shut and standing up on its own, which she regarded as a personal triumph.

“See? Three items,” she said, with her hands on her hips.

“Your list has grown.”

“Only because you interfered.”

“Your hairbrush was under a pillow.”

“That’s irrelevant.”

She opened the note on her phone again to admire it. He held his hand out for the phone, and she gave it to him, curious, and he typed something under the third line and handed it back.

3. Yichen. (Already packed. Don’t need to bring him.)

“What does that mean?”

“It means I’m coming anyway. You don’t need to remember me. I’ll be there.”

She looked at it for a while. Then she turned the phone over on the carpet and climbed into his lap, suitcase or no suitcase, and put her arms round his neck.

“That’s a very long way of saying you’re coming with me.”

“It’s four words.”

“It’s a long four words,” she said, and kissed him, and the door was open and her mother was in the kitchen, so it was quick.

He leaned back to look at her. “Did you pack your charger?”

“Zhou Yichen.”

“I’m only asking.”

She threw a pair of socks at him. They were his.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday morning her father drove them to the coach station. At the door Yichen took the list out of the front pocket of his suitcase and went down it with a pencil, ticking. He ticked the shirts and all three pairs of shoes and both charging cables and the first-aid kit, and at the bottom he ticked the tea, which was still in the hall, where Xiaoran had walked past it twice.

“Tea,” he said, and handed it to her.

“I was going to take it.”

“I know you were.”

Her mother, putting her shoes on, watched this happen and didn’t say a word. But at the lift she held Yichen’s elbow for a second, which she had never done before, and said, “Thirty-eight items. Bring them all back.”

“Yes, Auntie.”

“Including her.”

“Especially her,” said Yichen, and Mrs. Lin let go of his elbow and pushed the lift button and looked at the ceiling.

Xiaoran ticked her own list in the back of the car on the way to the station. It took her four seconds. She showed him the third tick, holding the phone up close to his face, and he looked out of the window, and her father, driving, pretended hard not to have heard any of it.

chapters.desc: The last summer before their final year, at her grandparents’ house, where her grandfather has promised to teach him to fish properly.
chapters.title: Last Summer in the Hometown
chapters.epigraph: “Besides, I think your grandfather likes me.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen had been to her grandparents’ house twice before, both times at New Year, when the house was so full of relatives that her grandfather had been too busy pouring drinks for Uncle Deng to do more than look at him across the table. This was the first time in summer. It was also the first time her grandfather was standing at the end of the lane holding a bamboo fishing rod when they came up from the bus stop, which, Xiaoran said later, should have been the warning.

“So, the fisherman,” said her grandfather. He was a lean, brown man with a face like a walnut and the sort of look that made Xiaoran stand up straighter without meaning to.

“Hello, Grandpa.”

“Her father says you can fish.”

“Her father took me once. In Shanghai. I caught nothing,” Yichen said carefully.

“He said you caught nothing very politely. Have you eaten?” Her grandfather took the gift bag, looked inside, and nodded at the tea.

“Yes, thank you.”

In the doorway behind him, her grandmother was drying her hands on her apron and beaming. “Have you been eating breakfast?” she called, exactly the way she had once asked it every night at nine down a phone line, one summer years ago.

“Every day, Grandma.”

“Good boy. Ranran. Come here. You’re thin. Why are you thin?” She held her arms out.

“I’m not thin, Grandma, I’m exactly the same.”

“You’re thin,” said her grandmother, holding her by both arms and looking at her, and then she looked past her at Yichen. “Is she eating?”

“Mostly,” said Yichen.

“Mostly,” said Xiaoran. “Whose side are you on?”

“Yours. That’s why I said mostly.”

Her grandfather cleared his throat. “Your grandmother’s made too much food again. Go and help her.”

“I just got here.”

“And now you’re going to help.”

She turned to Yichen with a look of deep betrayal. He looked back at her, perfectly composed.

“Go on. I’ll be fine,” he said.

“You won’t.”

“I’ll be fine,” he said again, and squeezed her hand once before he let it go, and she went into the kitchen, but slowly, and looking back over her shoulder the whole way.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twenty minutes later she was laying out dishes on the table under the window when she saw two figures walking down the path towards the pond behind the house. Her grandfather was carrying two rods. Yichen was carrying a bucket and a stool. She put down the plate she was holding.

“Grandma. Where are they going?”

“Fishing.”

“Oh no.”

Her grandmother came and looked out of the window too, wiping her hands. “What’s ‘oh no’?”

“Grandpa’s testing him.”

“Your grandfather wants someone to fish with. Your father hasn’t sat still long enough for him since 1998.”

“He’s going to fail.”

“Then he’ll fail. Put the fish dish in the middle. Not there. The middle,” said her grandmother comfortably.

He failed within twelve minutes. Xiaoran knew this precisely, because at minute eleven she went down to the pond with two bottles of water as an excuse.

Yichen was sitting on the low wooden stool at the edge of the water, holding the rod with the concentration he normally kept for free throws in the last minute of a close game. Her grandfather sat beside him on an upturned crate, looking at him the way you look at a dog that has tried to climb a tree.

“Too much movement,” her grandfather was saying.

Yichen adjusted his grip. “Like this?”

“Don’t ask me. Watch the water.”

“I brought water,” said Xiaoran.

Both men looked up at her. Her grandfather looked at the bottles, then at her, then at the house, where everyone could see that the table was already laid.

“Very thoughtful,” he said.

She sat down on the grass next to Yichen’s stool, close enough that her shoulder touched his knee, and looked at the bucket. It was empty.

“How’s it going?”

“Fine.”

“He’s been sitting there for ten minutes,” said her grandfather, “and the fish are laughing at him.”

“Grandpa!”

“Look. They can see you. You’re holding that rod like you’re trying to catch a thief.” Her grandfather pointed at the pond with his chin.

Xiaoran lost the battle and laughed. Yichen turned and gave her a long, pleading look.

“Don’t.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I’m supporting you,” she said, and leaned her head against his leg, and laughed into his knee.

“Basketball. He’s used to chasing things,” her grandfather said to her, as if that explained everything about the fish.

“I’ll stop chasing,” said Yichen.

“You can’t stop by saying it. You have to stop.”

“Yes, Grandpa.”

He stopped. Xiaoran watched it happen: the slight hunch came out of his shoulders, his hands loosened on the rod, and he went still the way he did on the free-throw line, when the whole gym was shouting and he didn’t seem to hear any of it. Her grandfather watched it too, sideways, without comment.

He still didn’t catch anything. But her grandfather stopped telling him what he was doing wrong, which, Xiaoran knew from long experience, was much better.

✦ ✦ ✦

By lunch her grandfather had caught two fish and Yichen had caught none, and the difference was important enough that her grandfather mentioned it three times on the walk back up to the house.

“Two,” he said, holding up the bucket.

“That’s very impressive, Grandpa.”

“It’s not difficult. If you know what you’re doing.”

Xiaoran walked between them with her arm through Yichen’s and her head turned up to him. “How was your first fishing lesson?”

“Educational.”

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Very much.”

“Did you catch anything?”

“I’m only asking,” she said.

“Your grandfather caught two.”

“I know. He told me.”

“He told me as well. Twice. On the way up he told the neighbour,” said Yichen.

She laughed, and then she noticed the wet patch all down one sleeve of his shirt and brushed at it with her free hand. “How did you get wet?”

“There was an incident with the bucket.”

“You’re terrible at fishing.”

“I’ve gathered that.”

“It’s all right. You’re good at other things.” She leaned her head against his arm as they walked.

“Such as?”

“Basketball.”

“Thank you.”

“Studying.”

“Mm.”

“And being my boyfriend,” she said, and looked up at him to see what he’d do with that, and he looked straight ahead at the house with the tips of his ears going red.

“That one I’m going to keep practising.”

“Yichen! Come and help me with these fish,” her grandfather called from the courtyard.

“Coming, Grandpa.”

He went. She let go of his arm and then caught up and took it again, and walked him the last ten metres to the courtyard like that, so that her grandfather looked round and saw them and looked away again with an expression she couldn’t read.

✦ ✦ ✦

The real test came after dinner. Her grandfather sat on the veranda with a cup of tea. Yichen was rinsing the rods under the yard tap and hanging them up on the nails where they lived, in the order her grandfather told him. Xiaoran sat on the steps peeling an orange and pretending not to listen.

“You’re not very good at fishing,” said her grandfather.

“Not yet.”

“Not yet?”

“I can learn.”

Her grandfather drank some tea. “That’s a better answer than most. A lot of young people don’t like being bad at something. They try once and they say it’s boring.”

“I was bad at basketball for a long time. I missed every shot for a whole year. My coach used to make me stay behind,” said Yichen.

Xiaoran looked up. He had never put it like that to her.

“Fishing’s like that. You have to sit there when nothing’s happening,” said her grandfather.

“I’m beginning to understand that.”

Her grandfather looked across at Xiaoran. “She’s not patient either.”

“Grandpa!”

“She couldn’t sit still long enough to finish a meal when she was small. Your grandmother used to chase her round the courtyard with a spoon.”

“That isn’t true!”

“Round and round that tree,” said her grandfather, pointing with his cup at the persimmon tree, “with a spoon of egg.”

Yichen bent his head over the tap so she wouldn’t see his face, which only made it worse.

“Don’t let her get away with everything,” her grandfather told him.

“I’ll try.”

“You’re supposed to defend me,” said Xiaoran.

“I think your grandfather has a point.”

She gasped, genuinely outraged, and threw a piece of orange peel at him, and her grandfather laughed out loud, a short, dry bark of a laugh. It was the first time that day.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later she walked him to the little guest room at the end of the corridor, still complaining.

“You betrayed me.”

“I didn’t.”

“You agreed with Grandpa.”

“He wasn’t wrong. You do get bored.”

“I’m not bored now.”

“Because you’re arguing with me.”

She stopped him in the corridor with a hand flat on his chest. “You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I am on your side. That’s why I agreed with him. He wanted to know if I’d say yes to everything you say. I wouldn’t. He liked that.” He tucked a piece of hair behind her ear.

“How do you know he liked it?”

“Because he laughed. And because he’s asked me to go fishing again at six tomorrow.”

“Six?”

“Six.”

“In the morning?”

“Fish don’t get up late, apparently. Besides, I think your grandfather likes me.” He looked down at her, entirely untroubled.

“He made you sit by a pond for an hour and watched you fail.”

“That might be how he shows it.”

She put her arms around his waist and her face against his chest, and stood there in the narrow corridor with the moths knocking against the light.

“I’ll come at six.”

“You’ll be asleep.”

“I’ll come. I’ll bring the water. I’ll sit on the grass. I won’t laugh,” she said into his shirt.

“You’ll laugh.”

“I’ll laugh a bit,” she admitted, and he laughed too, and kissed her hair, and then her grandmother’s voice came down the corridor asking whether anyone wanted the last of the soup, and she let go of him fast.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the kitchen for water before bed and found her grandparents still at the table, the tea gone cold between them.

“He’s a good boy,” her grandfather was saying.

Xiaoran stopped in the doorway.

“Yes, I told you he was. Years ago, I told you,” said her grandmother.

“You said he was a good study group.”

“I knew what I meant.”

Her grandfather turned his cup round on the table. “Not very good at fishing.”

“Grandpa!”

He didn’t look round. “What? It’s true. Bring him again next summer.”

“I will.”

She took her glass of water back to bed and didn’t drink any of it. Through the thin wall she could hear them still talking, low, about the persimmon tree and the price of bait and the boy, and once her grandmother laughed, and once her grandfather said, “Hopeless,” in a voice so fond that she knew exactly who he meant.

At ten to six her alarm went off. She went down to the pond in a cardigan over her pyjamas with two bottles of water, and found him already there in her father’s old grey hat, and her grandfather looking at the hat with an expression she had never seen on him before. She sat on the wet grass beside his stool, and leaned against his knee, and fell asleep again within five minutes with her head on him while he and her grandfather watched the water. He caught his first fish at twenty past six. It was small. Her grandfather said it counted.

chapters.desc: Mai Lang invites them onto his channel for a how-well-do-you-know-your-partner quiz. Somebody is going to be exposed.
chapters.title: The Couple Quiz Went Live
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t need a reason to want something.”
chapters.content:
The invitation came on a Tuesday evening. Xiaoran was lying on Yichen’s sofa, scrolling through her phone while he sat beside her reviewing some documents from his Business faculty. She suddenly made a small noise.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

“Do you remember Mai Lang?”

Yichen didn’t look up immediately.

“The man who made you famous on a milk tea run.”

“Yes. He does celebrities and athletes now. Those challenge videos.”

“I’ve seen a few videos.”

Xiaoran sat up.

“He invited us.”

That made Yichen look at her.

“Us?”

She turned her phone towards him. On the screen was a message from Mai Lang’s production team.

They were preparing a couples’ special for his channel, featuring a How Well Do You Know Your Partner? challenge. The concept was simple: each couple would answer a series of preference questions separately, then compare their answers to see how well they knew each other. They wanted Yichen and Xiaoran to participate. Yichen read the message. Then he looked at her.

“Do you want to go?”

Xiaoran’s eyes were already sparkling.

“Of course!”

“All right.”

She blinked.

“That’s it?”

“What else?”

“You didn’t even ask what the questions would be.”

“It’s a preference quiz. I know your preferences.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“That’s a very confident statement.”

He returned to his documents.

“Should I be worried?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I’m going to expose you.”

Yichen smiled without looking up.

“I look forward to it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The filming took place on Saturday afternoon at Mai Lang’s studio.

It was a bright, comfortable set with a large sofa, two individual answer boards, and a small table displaying several props. There were cameras positioned around the room, and a production assistant was checking the microphones. Mai Lang greeted them enthusiastically.

“Finally! The couple everyone’s been asking me to invite.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Really?”

“Of course. I’ve seen your clips. Especially the basketball ones.”

Yichen shook his hand.

“Thank you for having us.”

Mai Lang looked between them.

“Four years together, right?”

“Four and a half,” Xiaoran corrected him.

“And you’re both confident you know each other well?”

Xiaoran immediately nodded.

“Very.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“She’s confident.”

She turned towards him.

“Why did you say it like that?”

Mai Lang burst out laughing.

“Interesting. We’re not even filming properly yet, and there’s already tension.”

Yichen smiled politely.

“She’s competitive.”

“I’m not!”

“You’re already arguing.”

“Because you’re provoking me!”

Mai Lang clapped his hands.

“Excellent. This is going to be fun.”

The rules were straightforward. For every question, Xiaoran and Yichen would write down their own answers on separate boards. Then, before revealing them, they would each guess what the other person had written.

The goal wasn’t to answer correctly according to some official standard. It was to match their partner’s actual preference. There were ten questions.

Mai Lang explained that the questions would cover everyday preferences, habits, food, dates, and little things people might or might not notice about their partners.

“Remember,” he said, looking directly into the camera, “you are not answering what you think your partner should like. You’re answering what they actually like.”

Xiaoran nodded seriously. Yichen picked up his marker. Mai Lang grinned.

“Let’s see whether four and a half years of dating has made you two experts.”

Round 1: Favourite Drink

Mai Lang held up the first card.

“What’s your partner’s favourite drink?”

Xiaoran immediately started writing. Yichen wrote just as quickly.

“Okay! First, what does Xiaoran think Yichen’s favourite drink is?”

She revealed her board.

Black coffee.

Yichen nodded.

“Correct.”

Xiaoran looked pleased.

“See?”

Mai Lang turned to Yichen.

“What does Yichen think Xiaoran’s favourite drink is?”

He revealed his answer.

Milk tea. Half sugar. No pearls.

Xiaoran stared at him.

“Why did you write the whole order?”

“Because you have a very specific order.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“That’s not just knowing her favourite drink. That’s knowing her entire milk tea personality.”

Xiaoran pointed at Yichen’s board.

“Actually, sometimes I want less ice.”

“I know.”

“And sometimes I want pudding in it.”

“Mm.”

Mai Lang raised an eyebrow.

“Should we give him extra points?”

“No. Don’t encourage him,” Xiaoran said immediately.

Yichen looked amused.

Score: 1–1.

Round 2: Ideal Weekend

“What is your partner’s ideal way to spend a free weekend?”

Xiaoran thought for a moment. Then she wrote her guess for him.

Stay home, watch something, eat good food, and do absolutely nothing.

Yichen turned over his own answer. It was almost identical.

A quiet day at home. Good food, a movie or a series, and no schedule.

Xiaoran pointed at it.

“See? He’s the lazy one.”

“I’m very enthusiastic about doing nothing.”

“That’s called being lazy.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“Yichen, what’s Xiaoran’s ideal weekend?”

Yichen revealed his guess.

Going somewhere new, preferably with me. Exploring, taking pictures, trying food, and having no strict itinerary.

Xiaoran’s mouth opened. Then she turned over her own answer.

A little trip somewhere. Cute cafés, shopping, taking photos, and spending the whole day together.

She pointed at him.

“That’s basically the same!”

“Basically.”

Mai Lang leaned towards the camera.

“Notice how both of them included spending time together without explicitly saying it.”

“She likes having somewhere to go, but she doesn’t like feeling rushed,” Yichen said.

She looked at him. It was such a small detail. But he was right.

Score: 2–2.

Round 3: Favourite Food

Mai Lang looked excited.

“This one can be dangerous. What is your partner’s favourite food?”

Xiaoran wrote quickly. Yichen took a little longer. Mai Lang turned to Xiaoran.

“What do you think Yichen wrote?”

She revealed:

Japanese food. Especially a good sushi or sashimi restaurant.

Yichen turned his board around.

Japanese food. Sushi, sashimi, and good grilled dishes.

“Correct!” Mai Lang announced.

Xiaoran smiled triumphantly.

“I know his taste.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“You do.”

“Okay, your turn.”

Yichen revealed his guess.

Hotpot.

Xiaoran blinked.

“That’s not my favourite food!”

“It’s one of your favourites.”

“Yes, but not the favourite.”

He looked at her.

“Then what is?”

She considered it.

“Maybe pasta?”

Yichen nodded slowly.

“Then I should have written pasta.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“Wait, you don’t know her favourite food?”

Yichen looked at Xiaoran.

“I know what she likes to eat. I’m not sure she has one fixed favourite.”

Xiaoran paused. That was actually true. She liked pasta, hotpot, Japanese food, noodles, desserts, and a long list of other things. Mai Lang looked at her.

“Is that acceptable?”

Xiaoran nodded.

“He’s right. I change my mind all the time.”

“That’s a very diplomatic way to avoid losing points,” Mai Lang teased.

Score: 3–2.

Round 4: Preferred Date

“What kind of date does your partner enjoy most?”

Xiaoran wrote first. Yichen looked at her board, then at his own. Mai Lang turned to Yichen.

“Your guess?”

He revealed:

Something thoughtful. Doesn’t have to be expensive. She likes when there’s something new to experience, but she also loves ordinary dates with me.

Xiaoran stared at the answer. She smiled, a little softer.

“That’s right.”

Mai Lang nodded.

“Very detailed. Xiaoran?”

She revealed her guess for Yichen.

An activity he genuinely enjoys. Basketball, exploring a new place, or something he can get interested in. He likes sharing his interests with me.

Yichen looked at her board, then nodded.

“That’s right.”

Mai Lang looked between them.

“So both of you understand that the other person doesn’t necessarily need an elaborate date.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Yichen doesn’t really care whether we’re going somewhere expensive. He just likes doing things properly.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“And she likes it when I plan something, but she also likes deciding things spontaneously.”

“Because sometimes your plans are too detailed.”

“I thought you liked that.”

“I do. But sometimes I want to wander around!”

Mai Lang laughed.

“Four years together, and they’re still negotiating their itinerary.”

Score: 4–3.

Round 5: Favourite Type of Weather

Mai Lang held up the next card.

“This sounds simple, but let’s see. What is your partner’s favourite weather?”

Xiaoran wrote. Yichen wrote. They revealed their guesses. Xiaoran guessed Yichen preferred cool, sunny weather, the kind that made it comfortable to go outside without being too cold.

Yichen guessed Xiaoran preferred rainy weather when she could stay indoors, curled up with a blanket, a warm drink, and something to watch. Both were correct. Xiaoran pointed at him.

“Because I love rainy days.”

“You love rainy days when you don’t have to go anywhere.”

“Exactly.”

“If you have a morning class, suddenly you don’t like the rain.”

She gasped.

“That’s irrelevant!”

Mai Lang was laughing.

“Yichen, you know the conditions attached to her preferences.”

“Yes.”

Xiaoran hit his arm lightly. He caught her hand and held it before letting go. The cameras caught it. Mai Lang noticed.

“Very casual. Very natural. The cameras are right here, by the way.”

Yichen smiled.

“Sorry.”

He didn’t look particularly sorry.

Score: 5–4.

Round 6: Shopping Preference

“Does your partner prefer shopping online or in person?”

Xiaoran wrote online for Yichen. Yichen wrote in person for Xiaoran. They revealed their answers. Both correct. Mai Lang looked at Xiaoran.

“Why online for Yichen?”

“He doesn’t like wasting time going through shops. If he knows what he wants, he’ll research it, compare things, and order it.”

Yichen nodded.

“Efficient.”

Mai Lang turned to him.

“Why in person for Xiaoran?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Because she likes seeing things properly before deciding. Especially clothes. She’ll say she’s just looking, then try on six things.”

Xiaoran frowned.

“That’s not true.”

“Seven, last time.”

She paused.

“Those were different styles.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“I’m learning so much about this relationship.”

Score: 6–5.

Round 7: What Makes Your Partner Happiest?

The next question appeared.

What small thing makes your partner happiest?

Xiaoran’s expression softened. She thought for a little longer before writing. Yichen also took his time. Mai Lang turned to Xiaoran.

“What did you write for Yichen?”

She revealed:

When someone remembers the little things he mentions and makes an effort without him asking.

Yichen looked at her. He didn’t speak immediately. Then he nodded.

“That’s true.”

Mai Lang smiled.

“That’s a very thoughtful answer.”

Xiaoran shrugged a little.

“He doesn’t always say what he wants, but he notices when people pay attention.”

Yichen looked down at his board before revealing his answer for her.

When I give her my full attention. Especially when she’s telling me something she’s excited about.

Xiaoran stared. Then she looked at him.

“That’s...”

Mai Lang waited.

“That’s very accurate,” she admitted.

Yichen smiled.

“She doesn’t always need me to solve something. Sometimes she just wants to tell me about it.”

Xiaoran lowered her eyes, smiling. Mai Lang looked directly at the camera.

“Ladies and gentlemen, this is what happens when a couple actually listens to each other.”

Score: 7–6.

Round 8: Favourite Gift

“What kind of gift does your partner appreciate most?”

Xiaoran wrote something quickly. Yichen looked at his board, then wrote. Mai Lang turned to Yichen first.

“What do you think Xiaoran likes?”

He revealed:

Something personal. Something that shows the person remembers what she likes or something she mentioned wanting.

Xiaoran nodded.

“Correct.”

“Not necessarily expensive,” he said.

“Correct.”

“Although she does appreciate pretty things.”

She turned towards him.

“Of course I do.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“Now, Xiaoran. What kind of gift does Yichen appreciate?”

She revealed:

Something related to his interests, but with thought behind it. Something he wouldn’t necessarily buy for himself.

Yichen nodded.

“That’s right.”

Mai Lang raised a finger.

“Can you give us an example?”

Xiaoran smiled.

“I once got him two tickets to a game at the Garden in New York for his birthday.”

Mai Lang’s eyes widened.

“Madison Square Garden?”

Yichen nodded.

“It was the one place I’d always wanted to go.”

Xiaoran said, “He only said it once, one weekend morning, watching a game on his sofa. I remembered. He was very happy.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“I was.”

Mai Lang leaned back.

“Okay, that’s a difficult standard for the rest of us.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“You don’t have to buy someone a trip. It can be anything.”

Yichen said, “She once bought me a small thing related to something I’d mentioned casually. I liked that just as much.”

He didn’t elaborate, but Xiaoran knew exactly what he meant.

The miniature basketball keychain she’d given him before his first club trial. She smiled at him.

Score: 8–7.

Round 9: Biggest Pet Peeve

Mai Lang looked delighted.

“Now we’re getting dangerous. What is your partner’s biggest pet peeve?”

Xiaoran immediately started writing. Yichen looked at her and smiled.

“Already?”

“I know this one.”

She revealed:

People being inconsiderate. Especially when they waste other people’s time or don’t respect boundaries.

Yichen nodded.

“Correct.”

Mai Lang turned to him.

“What about Xiaoran?”

Yichen revealed:

People being dismissive when she’s explaining something she’s genuinely interested in. Also, being rushed when she’s making a decision.

Xiaoran’s eyebrows lifted.

“That’s right.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“Interesting. So Yichen dislikes inconsideration, and Xiaoran dislikes being dismissed.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“I don’t mind if someone disagrees with me. But I don’t like when people make me feel silly for caring about something.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“That’s fair. And she doesn’t like when someone makes a decision for her because they think it’s easier.”

Xiaoran looked at him. He had remembered that too.

Score: 9–8.

Round 10: The Little Luxury

Mai Lang picked up the final card.

“Last question. What is your partner’s favourite little luxury?”

Xiaoran immediately looked at Yichen. He looked back at her. Both started writing. Mai Lang grinned.

“Final question. This could decide everything.”

He turned to Xiaoran.

“What does Yichen consider a little luxury?”

She revealed:

A really good meal, a comfortable hotel, and a quiet place where he doesn’t have to think about anything.

Yichen laughed.

“That’s accurate.”

Mai Lang nodded.

“Very reasonable.”

Then Yichen revealed his guess for Xiaoran.

Milk tea, pretty little things, and buying something she has been thinking about for a while.

Xiaoran stared.

“That’s not wrong.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Not wrong?”

She laughed.

“It’s correct!”

Mai Lang looked between them.

“So, final score...”

He checked the boards.

“Ten to nine! Xiaoran wins by one!”

Xiaoran jumped slightly.

“Really?”

“The only miss of the day: her favourite food!”

Yichen smiled. Xiaoran turned towards him triumphantly.

“See? I told you I’d expose you.”

“You did.”

“On camera!”

“On camera,” he agreed.

Mai Lang clapped.

“Congratulations! Four years together and only one secret, and it’s pasta.”

Xiaoran immediately shook her head.

“No, no. We have secrets.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“Do we?”

“Yes. You don’t know everything about me.”

“Like what?”

She looked thoughtful, then smiled mischievously.

“I’m not telling you.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“That’s a terrible way to end a nearly perfect score!”

✦ ✦ ✦

The official filming ended, but Mai Lang asked them to stay for a few extra minutes to record a short closing segment. He sat opposite them.

“Before we finish, I want to ask one final question. Not part of the quiz.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“Okay.”

Mai Lang looked at Yichen.

“After four years together, do you think knowing someone’s preferences becomes easier?”

Yichen considered the question.

“Some things become easier because you spend enough time together. You start noticing patterns. You know what they like, what they avoid, what makes them comfortable.”

He glanced at Xiaoran.

“But I don’t think you should assume you know everything just because you’ve been together for a long time.”

Mai Lang nodded.

“Why?”

“People change. Their preferences change. Sometimes they don’t even realise it themselves until they try something new.”

Yichen said, “I think it’s important to keep asking.”

Mai Lang turned to Xiaoran.

“What do you think?”

She looked down at her hands briefly.

“I think knowing someone’s preferences is nice, but I don’t think that’s the most important part.”

“What is?”

“Remembering that they’re still a person outside the relationship. They have their own interests, their own things they want to try, and their own opinions. I like that Yichen doesn’t always assume I’ll like something just because I liked it before.”

She smiled.

“He still asks me.”

Yichen looked at her.

“And she still surprises me.”

Mai Lang smiled.

“That’s a good answer. But I have to ask. Who do you think knows the other person better?”

Xiaoran pointed at herself.

“Me.”

Yichen didn’t even hesitate.

“Her.”

She turned towards him.

“Wait. You agree?”

“Yes.”

Mai Lang laughed.

“Yichen surrendered very quickly!”

Yichen looked at Xiaoran.

“She pays attention to details I don’t even notice about myself.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened. Then she smiled proudly.

“That’s because I’m observant.”

“I know.”

Mai Lang looked into the camera.

“That’s it for today’s episode. Apparently, these two know each other a little too well. Ten to nine, four years together, and still looking at each other like they’re on a first date.”

Xiaoran burst out laughing. Yichen simply smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

The video went live the following week. Xiaoran watched it with Yichen at his apartment.

She had already watched the first few minutes twice, mostly because she thought her own expressions were funny.

“Look at your face here,” she said, pointing at the screen.

Yichen glanced over.

“What about it?”

“You looked so confident.”

“I was confident.”

“Too confident.”

He leaned back against the sofa.

“Did I get anything wrong?”

“That’s not the point.”

“What is the point?”

She paused.

“Your attitude.”

He smiled.

“My attitude?”

“Yes. You acted like you knew everything.”

“I knew most things.”

She turned towards him.

“Don’t be arrogant.”

He laughed. She continued watching, then reached the part where he’d answered the question about what made her happiest.

When he said that she liked having his full attention, she went quiet. Yichen noticed. He looked at her.

“You’ve been staring at the screen without blinking.”

She turned away.

“I just think it’s sweet.”

He reached over and tucked a strand of hair behind her ear.

“It’s true.”

She smiled. Then the video reached the final question, where she’d guessed his favourite little luxury. Xiaoran suddenly sat upright.

“Wait!”

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

“I forgot something.”

“What?”

She picked up her phone and opened the comments. There were already thousands.

People were praising their chemistry, laughing at the little exchanges, and pointing out how naturally Yichen watched Xiaoran whenever she spoke. One comment caught her attention:

The way he doesn’t just know her favourite things, but understands WHY she likes them. That’s the real green flag.

She read it aloud. Yichen glanced at the screen.

“That’s nice.”

Xiaoran scrolled further. Another comment said:

Four years together and he still looks at her like he’s learning something new about her.

She stopped. Then she turned towards him.

“Yichen.”

“Hmm?”

“Do you really think you still have things to learn about me?”

He studied her.

“Of course.”

“Like what?”

He put his phone aside.

“What’s something you’ve wanted to try recently but haven’t told me?”

Xiaoran blinked. She hadn’t expected him to turn the question around.

“That’s not fair.”

“Why?”

“Because now I have to think.”

He waited. She looked up at the ceiling, thinking. Then her eyes brightened.

“I want to learn ice skating.”

Yichen nodded.

“Ice skating?”

“Yes. I saw a video of a couple skating backwards holding hands. I want to try.”

“Then we can go.”

She smiled.

“Really?”

“Find a place you like.”

She leaned against his shoulder.

“And I want to try making pasta from scratch.”

“All right.”

“And maybe learn how to play tennis.”

He glanced down at her.

“Anything else?”

She thought for a moment.

“Actually, I want to go somewhere we’ve never been. Not a big trip. Just somewhere neither of us knows.”

Yichen nodded.

“Then we’ll do that too.”

She looked up at him.

“You’re making a list now?”

“I’m listening.”

Xiaoran smiled and wrapped her arms around his waist.

“You know, I think that’s my favourite thing about you.”

“What?”

“You never make me feel silly for wanting to try something.”

His expression softened. He lowered his head and kissed her cheek.

“You don’t need a reason to want something.”

She looked at him. She laughed and settled against him again.

On the television, the video continued playing, the credits rolling beneath a final shot of them laughing together. Mai Lang’s title card appeared:

HOW WELL DO YOU KNOW YOUR PARTNER? — ZHOU YICHEN & LIN XIAORAN

They had scored ten to nine, and she was never going to let him forget the pasta.

But as Xiaoran rested her head against his chest, she thought that perhaps the best part wasn’t knowing each other’s favourite drinks, ideal weekends, or preferred gifts.

It was knowing that even after four years, there were still new things to discover.

And Yichen, who had quietly begun searching for ice rinks on his phone, seemed to agree.

chapters.desc: A full contract arrives on a Tuesday in his final year, and his father asks a question he has never asked before: what does Zhou Yichen want?
chapters.title: The Herons Want an Answer
chapters.epigraph: “Who did you want to tell first?”
chapters.content:
The email arrived at 9:17 on a Tuesday morning, in the second week of his final year.

Zhou Yichen was halfway through reviewing a case study when his phone vibrated beside his laptop. He glanced at the screen, expecting a message from Xiaoran or perhaps a reminder from his coach.

Instead, he saw Jiao Rui’s name, from the Herons’ recruitment department. He opened it.

The first paragraph was formal. The second was familiar. By the third, he had stopped reading the words as words and started understanding what they meant.

The Herons were offering him a full professional contract.

It wasn’t another evaluation, or another year in the development program. A contract.

His eyes moved down the page: a place on the first-team roster from November, his university timetable to be arranged between the club and the sports office, and an answer by Friday.

He read it once, then again. A quiet breath left him. His phone vibrated a second time.

Xiaoran: Are you busy?

He looked at the email again, then typed.

Yichen: Just received something.

Xiaoran: Is it bad?

Yichen: I haven’t decided.

Three dots appeared almost immediately.

Xiaoran: That sounds suspicious.

Xiaoran: What happened?

He considered telling her over text. Then he closed the email and picked up his phone.

Yichen: Can you come over tonight?

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: I want to tell you in person.

A pause.

Xiaoran: Okay.

Then, a few seconds later:

Xiaoran: Should I bring food?

That got a smile out of him.

Yichen: You can.

Xiaoran: That’s not an answer. Should I bring food because you’re upset or because you’re hungry?

Yichen: Both are possible.

Xiaoran: Zhou Yichen.

Yichen: Something good happened. I think.

Her reply came quickly.

Xiaoran: I’M COMING.

He put his phone down. For a while, he didn’t return to his case study.

He had spent years imagining what this moment might feel like. When the scout first approached him, when he entered the development program, when he played his first game for the Herons, he had told himself not to think too far ahead. One step at a time.

He had repeated it so often that it had become instinct.

Now the next step was sitting in front of him, written in a formal email with a deadline. And it was bigger than the last one.

Xiaoran arrived at his apartment with a paper bag in one hand and her handbag slipping off her shoulder.

She had bought two portions of food from a place near campus, along with a small dessert she insisted was an emergency provision.

Yichen opened the door before she could knock a second time. She looked at his face immediately.

“Okay. First, are you happy?”

He stepped aside to let her in.

“Lovely to see you too.”

“Hello. Are you happy?” She walked past him, then turned around.

He closed the door.

“I think so.”

“That’s not very convincing.”

“I’m still processing it.”

She put the food on the kitchen counter and turned to face him properly.

“Tell me.”

Yichen took his phone out, opened the email, and handed it to her. She read the subject line. Then she read it again. Her eyes widened.

“Wait.”

He watched her.

“Wait, wait.”

“Take your time.”

“Is this—”

“Yes.”

She met his eyes.

“They’re offering you a full contract?”

“That’s what it says.”

“Not a development contract?”

“No.”

“Not another evaluation?”

“No.”

“A full contract?”

He nodded. For one second, she stared at him. Then she made a small sound that was somewhere between a laugh and a gasp.

“Yichen!”

She threw her arms around him. He caught her easily, one hand at her back, the other keeping his phone from being crushed between them.

She hugged him tightly, her cheek pressed against his chest.

“You did it.”

His expression softened.

“We’re not celebrating yet.”

“Why not?”

“Because I haven’t signed anything.”

“That’s a technicality.”

“It’s a fairly important technicality.”

She leaned back just enough to look at him.

“Don’t ruin my excitement with technicalities.”

“All right.”

She looked at him for another moment, then hugged him again. This time, he held her longer.

There was something about hearing her say it that made the news feel more real. He had been careful with his expectations for so long that he hadn’t allowed himself to fully enjoy the possibility.

But Xiaoran was already enjoying it for both of them.

She pulled away eventually, though her hands remained around his waist.

“Are you happy?” she asked again, more.

Yichen looked down at her.

“Yes.”

Her smile softened.

“Good.”

Then she pointed towards the phone.

“Now show me the details.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You want to inspect the contract?”

“Obviously. I need to know what they’re offering my boyfriend.”

“Your boyfriend?”

“Yes. He’s quite promising.”

“Quite?”

“Don’t get arrogant.”

He laughed under his breath and brought her to the sofa. They read through the email together.

Xiaoran was attentive, asking questions about the reporting date, training commitments, the duration of the contract, and what it would mean for his university schedule. She didn’t pretend to understand every technical detail, but she was interested in all of it.

When she reached the section about the club’s expectations, she stopped.

“They’re serious about you.”

“They wouldn’t offer it otherwise.”

“I know. But look at this. They’re not just asking you to play. They want you to be part of the team properly.” She pointed to the paragraph.

“That’s usually the point of a contract.”

She gave him a look.

“Can you let me be sentimental for five minutes?”

“Of course.”

She continued reading, but he noticed her smile returning. A little later, she put the phone down.

“Have you told your father?”

“No.”

“Your coach?”

“Not yet.”

“Your university?”

“The club will coordinate with them once I respond.”

She nodded.

Then, after a pause, she asked, “Who did you want to tell first?”

Yichen looked at her.

“You.”

Her expression changed. It wasn’t a dramatic change. Her lips parted a little, and the smile she had been wearing became something quieter.

“Oh.”

He reached over and brushed a loose strand of hair away from her cheek.

“Why?”

“Nothing.”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked down at the phone.

“I just like being the first person you tell.”

“I know.”

“And you didn’t even tell me over text.”

“I wanted to see your face.”

She looked up again.

“Was it worth it?”

“Very.”

She tried to suppress her smile and failed. Then she leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“Congratulations, Zhou Yichen.”

He turned his face slightly.

“That’s all?”

“What?”

“That’s all I’m getting?”

She stared at him, then laughed.

“You’re so shameless.”

“Only asking.”

She leaned in and kissed him properly. He let her pull away first, though his hand remained at her waist.

“Better?” she asked.

“Considerably.”

She rolled her eyes and settled against his shoulder.

For the rest of the evening, they talked about the contract in between eating dinner and arguing over which film to watch. Xiaoran tried to make him celebrate with a proper dessert, and he pointed out that she had already brought one.

“That one was emergency dessert.”

“And what is this?”

“Congratulations dessert.”

“How is it different?”

“Emotionally.”

He accepted this explanation without comment. But when she was choosing a film, his gaze drifted back to the email on his phone. The offer was real. And so was the decision waiting behind it. His father called the following afternoon.

Yichen was leaving the training facility when the call came in. He answered while walking towards the car park.

“Hello.”

“Are you free tonight?”

His father’s voice was as measured as ever.

“After training, yes.”

“Come home for dinner.”

Yichen paused.

“Is something happening?”

“No. I want to talk.”

“All right.”

The call ended shortly after. Yichen stood with his phone in his hand.

His father had always been capable of making a simple sentence sound like an appointment with a board of directors.

He wasn’t surprised by the invitation. The club would have contacted the university, and there was little chance the news hadn’t reached his father through one channel or another.

Still, he wondered what exactly his father wanted to discuss. He drove to the family home that evening.

Dinner was already on the table when he arrived. His mother greeted him warmly, asked whether the club fed him properly, and complained that he looked thinner. Yichen assured her that he was fine.

His father was in the dining room, reading something on his tablet. He looked up.

“You’re here.”

“Yes.”

They ate first. His mother asked about Xiaoran, and Yichen told her that she was busy with her final-year preparations. She asked when Xiaoran was coming for dinner again, and he promised a date before the month was out. His father listened without interrupting.

After dinner, his mother went to the living room to take a call. The two men remained at the dining table. His father set his tablet aside.

“The Herons sent an offer.”

Yichen nodded.

“Yes.”

“A full contract.”

“That’s right.”

His father looked at him.

“Congratulations.”

The word was simple. Yichen inclined his head.

“Thank you.”

His father poured himself a little tea. He didn’t immediately continue, and Yichen waited.

Then his father asked, “Have you decided?”

“Not yet.”

“Why?”

Yichen considered the question.

“Because I want to understand what I’m agreeing to.”

His father nodded once.

“That’s reasonable.”

He took a sip of tea.

“How long do they expect an answer?”

“By the end of the week.”

“And what do you think?”

Yichen leaned back slightly.

“I think it’s a good offer.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

His eyes lifted. His father was looking directly at him now.

For years, their conversations about basketball had been built around performance. His training, his studies, his prospects, his decisions. Even when his father attended a game, he tended to speak about what had happened on the court rather than what it had meant to him.

The one sentence after the city-league game had stayed with Yichen.

You passed too early.

He remembered it. He also remembered the words after his debut.

You didn’t force the final shot.

Neither had been a warm expression of affection, but both had meant something.

Now his father was asking him a different question.

“What do you want?” his father asked.

Yichen didn’t answer immediately. His father waited.

“Not what the club wants,” he said. “Not what your university thinks is best. Not what I think. What do you want?”

For a moment, Yichen found himself looking at the tea in front of him.

It was a question he had asked himself many times. He wanted to play. That part was simple.

He wanted to know how far he could go if he gave basketball the seriousness it deserved. He wanted to test himself against players who were better, faster, more experienced. He wanted to find out whether the work he had put in over the last few years could become something more than a promising university career. But he also wanted to finish his degree.

He wanted the knowledge he had worked for. He wanted the business world to remain a possibility, not a path he had abandoned because he was afraid of choosing.

And he wanted to make the decision without having to spend the rest of his life wondering whether he had been allowed to make it for himself.

“I want to play,” he said at last.

His father didn’t move.

“I want to know how far I can go. I don’t want to stop now just because there’s another option waiting for me.”

“And business?”

“I don’t intend to abandon it.”

“Basketball will take time.”

“I know.”

“Your studies will be affected.”

“I’ve considered that.”

“Your schedule will become more difficult.”

“Mm.”

His father studied him.

“You seem very certain about the difficulties.”

“I’ve been dealing with them already.”

A small silence followed.

Then his father asked, “And if it doesn’t work out?”

Yichen met his gaze.

“Then I’ll know I tried.”

His father looked down at his tea. It wasn’t the answer he might have expected from a son who had grown up surrounded by the security of a family business. It wasn’t a promise of success, or a declaration that he would become the best player in the league. It was an answer.

“I see,” his father said.

Yichen waited. His father leaned back in his chair.

“When you were younger, I thought you were choosing basketball because you disliked the direction I had planned for you.”

Yichen’s expression remained calm, though something in his eyes sharpened.

“I never said that.”

“No. You didn’t.”

His father paused.

“I may have assumed too much.”

It was a small admission. From him, it wasn’t small at all. Yichen looked at his father.

“I don’t dislike the company.”

“I know.”

“I’ve always understood why you wanted me to learn the business.”

His father nodded.

“But I don’t want to enter it simply because it’s there.”

His father looked at him again.

“Then don’t.”

Yichen was quiet.

His father continued, “If you join the company one day, I want you to know why you’re there. I don’t want you sitting in a meeting wondering whether you could have been somewhere else.”

There was no dramatic shift in his voice. No sudden warmth, no attempt to turn the conversation into something it had never been. But Yichen heard him.

For the first time, his father wasn’t asking him to prove that basketball could become a career.

He was asking him to choose a life he could accept.

“Thank you,” Yichen said.

His father gave a small nod.

“Don’t thank me yet. You still have to make a decision.”

Yichen almost smiled.

“Of course.”

“And don’t sign anything before you’ve read every clause.”

“I’ve read it.”

“Read it again.”

“I will.”

His father picked up his tablet, but before Yichen stood, he spoke once more.

“Your first game with the Herons was good.”

Yichen looked at him. His father kept his eyes on the tablet.

“You played with discipline. You didn’t rush to prove anything.”

“Thank you.”

“Keep doing that.”

It wasn’t a long conversation. But when Yichen left the dining room, he felt as if something that had been left unfinished for years had finally been given a place to rest.

Xiaoran was waiting for him when he returned to his apartment.

She was sitting on the sofa with her legs tucked underneath her, laptop open and a half-finished drink beside her. She had apparently been working, though the film paused on her screen suggested she had become distracted. She looked up when he entered.

“You’re back.”

“Mm.”

“How was dinner?”

“Fine.”

She squinted at him.

“That was suspiciously short.”

He put his keys down.

“My father wanted to talk about the contract.”

She closed her laptop.

“Oh.”

Yichen took off his jacket and hung it up.

“He asked what I wanted.”

Xiaoran watched him.

“And?”

“I told him.”

She didn’t immediately ask what he had said. Instead, she waited until he came over and sat beside her.

“What did you tell him?”

“That I want to play.”

Her face softened.

“And what did he say?”

“He asked me to read the contract again.”

She blinked.

“That’s it?”

“He also said I shouldn’t join the company just because it’s there.”

Xiaoran looked at him. Then she smiled.

“That’s actually quite a lot.”

“Yes.”

She moved closer, resting her head against his shoulder.

“How did it feel?”

Yichen looked down at her.

“Strange.”

“Strange?”

“I’m not used to him asking.”

She understood. There were things about Yichen’s relationship with his father that she had learned gradually. Not through dramatic stories or long confessions, but through the small pauses in his conversations, the way he sometimes chose his words carefully, and the things he remembered even when he claimed they didn’t matter. She knew that he respected his father.

She also knew that being respected and being understood weren’t always the same thing.

“Did you feel better after talking to him?” she asked.

“Yes.”

She nodded.

“Good.”

He met her eyes.

“You’re not going to ask what I’m going to choose?”

“I think I know what you want.”

“Do you?”

She lifted her head.

“You want to play.”

“That’s one part.”

“And you don’t want to give up business completely.”

“That’s another.”

She thought about it.

“Then I think you should find a way to have both, if that’s what you really want.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Very straightforward.”

“Well, I didn’t say it would be easy.”

“No?”

“No. I think you’ll be extremely busy. I think you’ll complain about having to study after training. I think you’ll come home tired and fall asleep before dinner sometimes.”

“That sounds unpleasant.”

“It does.”

She touched his arm.

“But I also think you’ll regret it if you don’t try.”

Yichen watched her. She wasn’t telling him to choose basketball because she wanted to watch him play. She wasn’t telling him to choose business because it would be safer. She wasn’t treating his future like a decision that had to be made around her. She was looking at him.

“Would it bother you?” he asked.

“What?”

“If I had to spend more time away.”

Her expression changed slightly. She knew what he meant.

A full contract would mean a different schedule. More training, more travel, more pressure. The comfortable routine they had built around university life would change.

She would have her own final-year projects, and he would have a professional season to navigate. There would be days when they couldn’t meet.

There would be weekends when one of them had to leave before the other woke up. It wasn’t an imaginary concern. Xiaoran considered her answer carefully.

“Of course I’d miss you.”

“But that doesn’t mean I want you to give it up.”

He glanced at her.

“I don’t want you to say that just because you think it’s what I need to hear.”

She straightened.

“I’m not.”

She placed both hands on his shoulders, making sure he was looking at her.

“Yichen, I want you to have things that belong to you. I want you to have your basketball career. I want you to have your business degree. I want you to be proud of what you do.”

“And I want you to come back to me when you’re done. Preferably with enough energy to eat dinner,” she said.

A quiet laugh escaped him.

“That’s your condition?”

“Yes. I’m very reasonable.”

“Very.”

“And you have to call me.”

“I can do that.”

“And send me pictures.”

“Of what?”

“Anything. The training facility. The hotel. Your food. Your shoes. Your face.”

“My face?”

“Your face too.”

He smiled.

“Understood.”

She seemed satisfied, then leaned forward and wrapped her arms around his neck. Yichen drew her closer. For a while, neither of them spoke.

He rested his cheek against her hair, one hand moving slowly along her back. She held him with the quiet certainty of someone who didn’t need to convince him to stay.

Eventually, she murmured, “You did it.”

He closed his eyes.

“Thank you.”

“Even if you haven’t signed yet.”

“I’ll remember that.”

“And when you do sign, I’m going to be even more annoying.”

“That sounds inevitable.”

“I’ll wear your jersey everywhere.”

He leaned back to look at her.

“Please don’t.”

She gasped.

“Why?”

“You’ll distract everyone.”

“Good. They should know.”

“Know what?”

“That I’m dating a professional basketball player.”

He gave her a slow, amused smile.

“Not yet.”

She looked at him, then pointed a finger at his chest.

“Don’t you dare become modest now. It’s too late.”

He caught her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“All right.”

She watched him, then her expression turned thoughtful.

“Do you know what I think?”

“What?”

“I think your father was waiting for you to say it.”

Yichen’s thumb brushed over her knuckles.

“Maybe.”

“Maybe?”

“He might have wanted to hear it for a long time.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Then I’m glad you told him.”

He held her gaze.

“So am I.”

Three days later, Yichen sat at his desk with the contract open in front of him. He had read it twice.

Then a third time with the university’s sports office reviewing the academic arrangements. He had spoken with the Herons’ recruitment director, clarified the training schedule, and asked about the club’s expectations for his first season. There were still details to consider. But the question had changed.

It was no longer whether he wanted the opportunity. He did.

The question was how to take it without losing sight of the rest of his life. His phone lit up.

Xiaoran: Have you decided?

He looked at the message.

Yichen: Almost.

Xiaoran: That’s not a real answer.

Yichen: It is.

Xiaoran: Are you being difficult on purpose?

Yichen: A little.

Xiaoran: Zhou Yichen!

His mouth curved.

Yichen: I’ll call you tonight.

Xiaoran: Okay.

A moment later:

Xiaoran: Whatever you choose, I’m on your side.

He read it twice. Then he looked back at the contract.

Outside, the afternoon light was beginning to fade. His basketball shoes sat beside the door, still carrying the faint smell of the training court. His Business textbooks were stacked neatly on the other side of the desk.

Those two things had seemed like separate versions of his future.

Now, for the first time, he could imagine building a life in which neither had to disappear. He picked up his pen. Not to sign yet.

Just to mark the final page, where the acceptance instructions waited.

Then he took out his phone and called Xiaoran. She answered on the second ring.

“Hello?”

“Are you busy?”

“Not anymore.”

He heard the soft rustle of paper on her end.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Then why are you calling?”

He leaned back in his chair, looking at the contract.

“I wanted to tell you something.”

There was a small pause.

“Okay.”

“I’m going to accept.”

Silence.

Then, “Really?”

“Yes.”

A delighted laugh came through the phone.

“Yichen!”

That got a smile out of him.

“I’ll still finish my degree. We’ll work out the schedule with the university and the club. I’ll have to travel more, and there’ll be a lot of things to adjust.”

“I know.”

“But I want to do it.”

She was quiet for a second. Then she said, “I’m happy for you.”

He heard the smile in her voice.

“Thank you.”

“Are you nervous?”

“A little.”

“That’s okay.”

He looked down at the page.

“Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“When I sign it, will you come with me?”

There was no hesitation.

“Of course.”

He smiled.

“Good.”

She made a small pleased sound.

“Wait. Does this mean I get to see you sign a real professional contract?”

“Yes.”

“Can I take pictures?”

“Within reason.”

“Can I bring flowers?”

“You’re not required to.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He laughed.

“Bring flowers if you want.”

“I do.”

He could picture her already: choosing something bright, probably asking the florist too many questions, then arriving with a bouquet almost as large as her enthusiasm.

“Then I’ll bring flowers,” she declared.

“All right.”

“And after that, dinner.”

“Of course.”

“My treat.”

He raised an eyebrow, though she couldn’t see him.

“Your treat?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because my boyfriend got a full contract.”

He laughed under his breath.

“That’s a good reason.”

“And I’m paying.”

“All right.”

She sounded pleased with herself.

“See? I’m supporting your career.”

“Very generously.”

“Don’t tease me.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He let her hear the smile in his voice.

“Maybe.”

She laughed. For the first time since the email arrived, the future no longer felt like a list of conditions and deadlines. It felt like something he was choosing.

When he imagined the difficult days ahead—the long training sessions, the away games, the exams, the uncertainty—he could still picture the end of them. A familiar apartment. Two portions of dinner.

A girl who would ask him whether he had eaten, complain when he forgot to send pictures, and fall asleep against his shoulder while insisting she wasn’t tired. He wanted the court. He wanted the degree.

He wanted the life he would build after both. And he wanted her in it.

“Xiaoran?”

“Yes?”

“I’ll see you tonight.”

“You’re coming over?”

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll order food.”

He glanced at the clock.

“Don’t order too much.”

“Why?”

“Because you always order too much.”

“That’s because you eat half of mine.”

His mouth curved.

“Then order enough for two.”

“Obviously.”

The call ended a few minutes later. Yichen looked once more at the contract.

Then he closed the laptop, put the printed copy in the drawer with the bundle of ticket stubs his father had given him the year before, and went to find his car keys.

chapters.desc: Her media module wants a documentary about ordinary intimacy. Lin Xiaoran chooses her subject in thirty seconds, then moves in with him for two weeks to observe it.
chapters.title: The Assignment Was to Study Love
chapters.epigraph: “Maybe that’s the problem with studying someone you love.”
chapters.content:
The first sign that something was wrong was Xiaoran’s expression when she let herself into his apartment on a Wednesday night.

She didn’t look tired, or annoyed, or even hungry. She looked suspicious.

Yichen, who was sitting on the sofa with his laptop open, glanced up from the business report he was reading. He had been home for nearly an hour, showered after training, and was halfway through reviewing a presentation for the following morning.

Xiaoran stood in the entrance, holding her tote bag against her chest. He met her eyes.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s convincing.”
