She narrowed her eyes at him. “Why do you always assume something is wrong?”

“Because you’ve been standing there for thirty seconds, staring at me like I’ve committed a crime.”

“I haven’t decided whether you have.”

Yichen closed his laptop.

“All right. What happened?”

Xiaoran walked over, dropped her bag beside the sofa, and sat down next to him. She looked at the coffee table, then at him, then back at the coffee table.

“I have a weird assignment.”

“How weird?”

“Very.”

“Is it illegal?”

“Zhou Yichen!”

“I’m asking.”

She slapped his arm lightly. He smiled, then waited.

Xiaoran took out her laptop and opened the university portal.

“Our lecturer gave us a project. It’s for this module about media, human behaviour, and storytelling. We’re supposed to document something ordinary that people usually overlook, then turn it into a short-form documentary.”

“That doesn’t sound particularly weird.”

“Wait.”

She scrolled down.

“The assignment is called An Unusual Study of Ordinary Intimacy.”

Yichen read the title. His expression remained neutral. Xiaoran watched him carefully.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face.”

“My face is normal.”

“You’re already thinking something.”

He looked at the screen again. “What exactly are you supposed to do?”

She sighed dramatically.

“We have to observe a person in their natural environment. Study their habits, routines, small behaviours, and interactions. Then create a documentary about something that reveals their personality without relying on interviews or direct explanations.”

“Interesting.”

“That’s not the weird part.”

“All right.”

“We have to choose someone we know well.”

Yichen nodded.

“And the subject has to be someone whose ordinary behaviour we might have stopped noticing because we’re too familiar with them.”

He turned to her. She looked back. There was a pause.

Then Yichen asked, calmly, “You’ve chosen me?”

Xiaoran’s mouth fell open.

“How did you know?”

“Because you’ve been staring at me for thirty seconds.”

“That’s not fair. I haven’t even told you the most embarrassing part.”

“Go on.”

She turned her laptop towards him. There was a list of possible observation categories.

1. Repeated habits and unconscious gestures.
2. Behaviour around a familiar person.
3. Unspoken communication.
4. Emotional responses to ordinary situations.
5. The difference between what a person says and what they actually do. Yichen read through them. Then he leaned back.

“So I’m your research subject.”

“Temporarily.”

“How long?”

“Two weeks.”

“Two weeks?”

“Yes.”

“You’re at your own place from Sunday to Thursday.”

“Not for the next two weeks. The subject has to be observed in his natural environment.”

“My natural environment is the training court.”

“Your other one.”

He considered this.

“Do I get paid?”

“You’re my boyfriend.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

She hit his shoulder with the back of her hand. Yichen laughed.

“Fine. I’ll cooperate.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Really?”

“Would you prefer I refuse?”

“No, but I thought you’d make fun of me.”

“I can do both.”

She gave him a suspicious look. He reached over and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear.

“What’s the first thing you need to observe?”

Xiaoran hesitated. Then she looked at him with the seriousness of a researcher preparing to conduct an important experiment.

“Your morning routine.”

Yichen’s eyebrows lifted.

“My morning routine?”

“Yes.”

“What about it?”

“I need to know what you do when you wake up.”

“I get up.”

“That’s not detailed enough.”

“I brush my teeth.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

Something in his face eased.

“All right, researcher. Ask your questions.”

The following morning, Xiaoran woke up earlier than usual.

She had no early class and no deadline. She had decided that the best way to conduct her research was to observe Yichen before he knew he was being observed. Unfortunately, Yichen woke up before she could begin.

He opened his eyes and found her staring at him. He blinked once.

“Good morning.”

Xiaoran didn’t answer. Instead, she reached for her phone. Yichen watched her unlock it.

“What are you doing?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re recording?”

“No.”

“Then why is your camera open?”

She quickly turned the screen off.

“You’re too observant.”

He smiled sleepily and reached for her waist, drawing her closer.

“You’re not very good at being inconspicuous.”

“Don’t interfere with my research.”

“I’m not.”

“You are. You’re changing your natural behaviour because you know I’m watching.”

Yichen looked at her. Then he deliberately closed his eyes again.

“Is this better?”

“No.”

He opened one eye.

“Then what would you like me to do?”

“Act normal.”

“I was sleeping.”

“Exactly. Continue.”

He stared at her. Then, without another word, he pulled the blanket over both of them and rested his chin against her head. Xiaoran tried to remain serious. She really did. But after a few seconds, she began laughing. Yichen opened his eyes.

“What’s funny?”

“Nothing.”

“Your research is going well.”

“Shut up.”

He kissed her hair.

“Go back to sleep, researcher.”

She wrote in her notes later:

Subject appears to be unusually affectionate in the morning. Frequently initiates physical contact. Doesn’t seem to distinguish between being awake and being asleep when maintaining physical proximity.

She stared at the sentence. Then added:

Possibly a habit rather than a conscious decision.

By the third day, Xiaoran had become a little too enthusiastic. She had a small notebook now.

Yichen had discovered it beside her laptop, and although he hadn’t read the contents, he had noticed the increasingly serious way she observed him.

At breakfast, she watched him make coffee. At lunch, she watched him arrange the groceries.

At night, she watched him review his training schedule. Sometimes he would catch her staring.

Sometimes he would deliberately do something unusual just to see whether she would write it down.

On Thursday evening, he was sitting at the dining table with his laptop when Xiaoran appeared from the kitchen carrying two cups of tea. She placed one beside him.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

She sat opposite him. Yichen took a sip. Xiaoran watched. He took another. She watched again. Finally, he put the cup down.

“Is there something on my face?”

“No.”

“Do I have something in my teeth?”

“No.”

“Then why are you looking at me like that?”

She opened her notebook.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Why do you always put my cup on the right side?”

He glanced at the cup, then at her.

“Because you’re right-handed. How do you know?”

“You hold your spoon with your right hand. You use your right hand to pick up your phone. When you’re carrying things, you usually leave your right hand free.”

Xiaoran stared at him. Yichen returned to his laptop. She slowly wrote something down.

“What’s that?” he asked.

“Nothing.”

“Read it.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because it’s private research.”

He leaned back in his chair.

“You’re studying me, but I don’t get to see the results?”

“Correct.”

“Sounds unfair.”

“Research ethics.”

He laughed. She looked at him again.

“Wait. Another question.”

“Hm?”

“Why do you always move my things when I’m not looking?”

“I don’t.”

“You do.”

“Give me an example.”

“My phone. When I leave it somewhere, you always put it beside me.”

“Because you forget where you put it.”

“My hair clip?”

“You leave it on the dining table.”

“My water bottle?”

“You forget to drink water.”

“My bag?”

“You once left it outside the bathroom.”

“That was one time.”

“Twice.”

She blinked at him. Yichen smiled.

“Do you want me to stop?”

Xiaoran was quiet.

“No.”

He nodded, as if that settled the matter. Then he returned to work. Xiaoran looked down at her notebook.

Subject displays an unusual tendency to notice and correct small inconveniences in another person’s environment. He doesn’t seem to regard these actions as acts of care.

She paused. Then wrote:

He appears to consider them ordinary.

The strangest part of the assignment came on Saturday.

Xiaoran had arranged a short observation session in the living room.

She placed her camera on a small tripod, adjusted the angle, and checked the lighting.

Yichen came out of the bedroom wearing a black T-shirt and grey sweatpants. He stopped when he saw the equipment.

“What is this?”

“Filming.”

“Of me?”

“Yes.”

“What am I supposed to do?”

“Nothing.”

He looked at the camera, then at her.

“That’s a difficult instruction.”

“Just behave naturally.”

“You’re making that sound like a test.”

“It is.”

He sat on the sofa. Xiaoran pressed record, then went to sit beside him with her laptop. For the first few minutes, nothing happened. Yichen read an article on his phone. Xiaoran edited some footage.

He occasionally shifted his position, crossed his legs, or rubbed the back of his neck.

Then Xiaoran got up to retrieve something from the bedroom. Yichen didn’t look up. A minute later, she returned. She had forgotten her water bottle.

She picked it up from the table and sat down again.

Yichen moved his phone slightly to make space for her bottle. She noticed. She said nothing.

A few minutes later, she leaned forward to look at something on his screen.

He tilted the phone towards her without being asked.

Then, when she sat back, he placed his hand on the back of the sofa behind her. Not quite touching. Just there. Xiaoran continued reading. Eventually, she leaned against his arm.

Yichen adjusted his position to make her more comfortable, then continued reading. The camera kept recording. Neither of them paid attention to it. After twenty minutes, Xiaoran looked at the footage. She watched the whole thing twice. There was no dramatic moment. No interesting action.

Just Yichen making space for her, tilting his phone, moving her water bottle, and adjusting his arm when she leaned against him. She frowned. This was supposed to be a documentary. How could something so ordinary be interesting? She rewound the footage, then watched it again. Yichen noticed her expression.

“What’s wrong?”

“I think my footage is boring.”

He glanced at the screen.

“What were you expecting?”

“I don’t know. Something more obvious.”

“Like what?”

“Like you doing something.”

“I was doing something.”

“Reading.”

“And?”

“Moving my phone.”

He held her gaze.

“Would you prefer I juggle?”

She laughed despite herself.

“Honestly.”

Yichen closed his phone.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Maybe you’re looking for something that isn’t supposed to be obvious.”

She met his eyes. He nodded towards the camera.

“You said the assignment was about things people stop noticing because they’re familiar with them.”

She went quiet.

“Maybe that’s why you think it’s boring.”

She looked at the footage again. Yichen didn’t add anything.

He reached for her hand and began absentmindedly rubbing his thumb over her knuckles. On Sunday, Xiaoran decided to interview him. Not formally.

She sat opposite him at the dining table, with her phone recording audio. Yichen had just finished lunch.

“Okay. Question one.”

“Go ahead.”

“What’s something you do every day without thinking about it?”

He considered the question.

“Check my training schedule.”

“That’s boring.”

“You asked.”

She frowned.

“Something else.”

“Check whether you’ve eaten.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“That’s not something you do.”

“It is.”

“Why?”

“Because you forget.”

“I do not.”

He gave her a look. She lowered her eyes.

“Okay, sometimes. Sometimes I check whether you’ve got your keys before we leave.”

She looked at him.

“And whether your laptop is charged if you have a presentation.”

“How do you know that?”

“Because you complain when it isn’t.”

She looked down at her notes.

“Next question. What’s something you notice about me that I don’t realise you notice?”

Yichen didn’t answer immediately. He looked at her, seemingly considering how to phrase it.

“You press your lips together when you’re concentrating.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“You do it when you’re editing something, too. And when you’re reading instructions.”

She instinctively pressed her lips together. Yichen smiled.

“Like that.”

She immediately relaxed her mouth. He continued.

“You also move your feet when you’re excited. Not very much. Just a little.”

Xiaoran looked down at her feet.

“Really?”

“And when you’re nervous, you start asking questions you already know the answers to.”

She looked up.

“That’s not true.”

“You’re doing it now.”

She closed her mouth. He laughed. She was beginning to suspect that the assignment was becoming dangerous.

“One more question,” she said.

“All right.”

“What’s something you do for me that you don’t think counts as affection?”

Yichen’s expression softened slightly. He looked at her.

“Probably a lot of things.”

“Like?”

“Making sure your side of the bed isn’t too cold when you get in. Keeping the snacks you like in the kitchen. Remembering which food you don’t like. Waiting for you to finish talking even when I’m in a hurry.”

She stopped writing. He noticed.

“Why?”

“Nothing.”

“Xiaoran.”

She turned to him.

“You’re making my assignment difficult.”

“How?”

“Because I don’t know how to write all that without making it sound like I’m writing a love letter.”

Yichen smiled.

“Maybe you are.”

She gave him a look. He reached across the table and gently tapped the end of her pen.

“Don’t make it complicated.”

“Easy for you to say.”

“Just write what happened.”

She held his gaze. Then she slowly nodded. The night before the submission, Xiaoran sat on the floor in front of the television, surrounded by footage, photographs, notes, and an increasingly concerning number of sticky notes.

Yichen had finished training and showered. He came out of the bedroom to find her staring at her laptop with a deeply troubled expression. He sat beside her.

“Still editing?”

“Yes.”

“How much is left?”

“Everything.”

He looked at the screen. The documentary was currently titled The Ordinary Behaviour of Zhou Yichen. He raised an eyebrow.

“Very flattering.”

“Don’t start.”

He watched her scroll through the footage. There were clips of him making coffee, checking her laptop charger, moving her water bottle, holding the door, waiting for her to finish tying her shoelaces, and putting a blanket over her when she fell asleep on the sofa.

There was also a clip of him standing in the kitchen watching her explain a new recipe. He had been listening with an expression of such patient concentration that Xiaoran had included the entire thirty-second clip. Yichen watched it. Then he looked at her.

“Why did you record that?”

“Because you looked like you were attending a very important business meeting.”

“I was learning how to make your pasta.”

“Exactly.”

He laughed. She leaned back against the sofa.

“I think I know what the documentary is about now.”

“What?”

She looked at the screen.

“It’s about how people show affection without actually saying anything.”

Yichen nodded.

“That sounds reasonable.”

“But I don’t want it to be too romantic. It’s an academic assignment.”

“Then don’t make it romantic.”

She looked at him.

“How?”

“Just be honest.”

She considered that. Then she turned back to her laptop.

The final documentary was six minutes and forty seconds long. She titled it Things We Stop Noticing.

The opening showed Yichen making two cups of coffee in the morning. One black. One with milk.

Then a shot of him moving her water bottle closer to her laptop.

Then a clip of his hand reaching back to find hers while they walked. The narration was Xiaoran’s voice.

When we become familiar with someone, we stop noticing the small things they do. They become part of the background of our daily lives. We stop asking why someone remembers our preferences, why they make room for us, or why they seem to know what we need before we ask.

The footage continued. Yichen opening the car door. Yichen waiting while she took photographs of a dessert. Yichen looking up from his laptop when she called his name. Yichen placing a cushion behind her back.

These actions aren’t necessarily extraordinary. They are often too small to be remembered individually. But perhaps that is what makes them meaningful. They are repeated without expectation. They happen so naturally that the person doing them may not even consider them worth mentioning.

The final clip was from the living room. Xiaoran had been sitting beside Yichen, editing something on her laptop. He was reading an article. Without looking away from the screen, he had reached over and tucked her hair behind her ear. Then he had continued reading. She had continued working. Nothing else happened. The narration ended.

I thought this assignment would require me to discover something unusual about someone I knew well. Instead, I realised that I had been surrounded by things I had stopped noticing.

The screen faded to black.

A single line came up in white: Sometimes the closeness isn’t in the moments we remember. It’s in the ones we stop recording.

Yichen watched the finished video in silence. When it ended, Xiaoran turned towards him.

“Well?”

He didn’t answer immediately. She began to worry.

“Is it bad?”

“No.”

“Then?”

He looked at the black screen.

“It’s good.”

“Just good?”

He turned towards her.

“It’s very good.”

She eyed him.

“You’re only saying that because I’m your girlfriend.”

“I’m saying that because it’s good.”

“You’re biased.”

“Probably.”

She groaned and let her head drop onto his shoulder. Yichen smiled and kissed her hair.

He said, “You know what I found interesting?”

“What?”

“You filmed me for two weeks, but most of the footage was actually about you.”

She lifted her head.

“What?”

“Look at it again.”

He pointed at the screen.

“You filmed me moving your things closer. You filmed me waiting for you. You filmed me making room for you. But the interesting part is how naturally you fit into all those moments.”

Xiaoran stared at him.

He said, “You didn’t have to ask me to make space. You didn’t have to ask me to wait. You just assumed I would.”

Her expression softened. Yichen brushed his thumb across her cheek.

“That’s probably what familiarity looks like.”

She didn’t say anything. Then she asked, “Does it bother you?”

“What?”

“That I take all those things for granted?”

Yichen considered her question.

“No.”

“Really?”

“I don’t do them so you’ll notice every time.”

He leaned forward and pressed a kiss into her hair.

“But I like that you notice them eventually.”

Xiaoran smiled. Then, as if remembering something, she quickly reached for her notebook. Yichen watched her.

“What are you writing?”

“An additional observation.”

“About?”

She wrote something, then turned the notebook towards him.

Subject claims that his actions aren’t intended to be noticed. However, he appears pleased when they are.

Yichen read it. Then he looked at her.

“That’s your conclusion?”

“Yes.”

“Interesting.”

“Thank you.”

He took the notebook from her hand and placed it on the coffee table. Then he drew her into his arms.

“You’re welcome.”

She settled against his chest, smiling. After a few seconds, she looked up.

“Wait. I have another question.”

“Of course you do.”

“If you could give my documentary a title, what would you call it?”

Yichen looked at her. Then his lips curved.

“Living With Lin Xiaoran.”

She blinked.

“That’s not the assignment.”

“I know.”

“Why that?”

“Because you’ve been living here for two weeks, and most of the things you filmed only happen when you’re around.”

She stared at him, then slowly began to smile.

“That’s cheating.”

“How?”

“You’re supposed to be the subject.”

“I was.”

“But you made it about me.”

Yichen lowered his head and kissed her cheek.

“Maybe that’s the problem with studying someone you love.”

Xiaoran tilted her head.

“What problem?”

“You eventually realise you aren’t observing them from the outside anymore.”

He kissed her other cheek.

“You’re part of the footage.”

She looked at him, her expression growing soft. Then she wrapped her arms around his neck and kissed him.

Yichen smiled against her lips, one hand settling at her waist.

When she pulled back, she looked pleased with herself.

“Good answer.”

“Will that be included in your report?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I need to maintain academic objectivity.”

He laughed. She tucked herself against his chest again. A few seconds passed.

Then she mumbled, “Actually, I think I need to do a follow-up assignment.”

Yichen closed his eyes.

“What’s the topic this time?”

“How living together changes people’s behaviour.”

He opened his eyes.

“How long?”

“Maybe a month.”

“Do I get paid this time?”

She looked up innocently.

“I’ll give you kisses.”

Yichen considered that.

“That’s not a particularly competitive offer.”

Xiaoran gasped.

“Excuse me?”

He smiled, slow and entirely too pleased with himself.

“Perhaps I should negotiate.”

She immediately understood the expression on his face. Her cheeks warmed.

“You’re not allowed to flirt with the researcher.”

“I’m not flirting.”

“You are.”

“Then perhaps you should document it.”

Xiaoran stared at him before burying her face in his chest.

Yichen laughed, wrapped both arms around her, and pressed his mouth to her hair.

chapters.desc: She follows him to Saturday training in secret. He knows by the first drill, and has water and crackers left at her end of the corridor.
chapters.title: The Girl Who Couldn’t Keep Up
chapters.epigraph: “You’re not very good at surprising me.”
chapters.content:
Yichen’s training schedule wasn’t a secret. At least, not from Xiaoran.

She knew his usual routine almost as well as he did. On training days, he left the apartment early, arrived at the facility before the team briefing, completed his individual warm-up, and then spent several hours on court. Depending on the day’s program, he would finish with conditioning, strength training, or recovery work. He was disciplined about it. Almost annoyingly so.

And Xiaoran had recently developed a particular interest in seeing him train.

Matches didn’t count, and neither did the open practices when he knew she was coming. She wanted to see him during his ordinary training. The unremarkable parts. The moments when he wasn’t performing for anyone.

She wanted to watch him run, shoot, practice footwork, listen to his coach, and concentrate on something he loved. But there was one problem. She didn’t want to disturb him.

Yichen had his routine. She knew how much he valued it, and she didn’t want him to feel obligated to entertain her or adjust his training just because she had decided to appear.

So, naturally, Xiaoran came up with a brilliant plan. She would follow him. Secretly. And observe him from a distance. It was a good plan. In theory.

On Saturday morning, Yichen left the apartment at his usual time. The Herons trained on Saturdays, and she slept at his on Fridays. The plan practically wrote itself.

Xiaoran was still in bed when he kissed her hair.

“Going now.”

She made a sleepy noise.

“Mm.”

“Sleep a little longer.”

“Okay.”

He pulled the blanket up over her shoulder and left. Five minutes later, Xiaoran opened one eye. Ten minutes later, she was out of bed.

She had already prepared her clothes the night before: comfortable leggings, a loose athletic top, a light jacket, and a pair of trainers she hadn’t worn in a while.

She tied her hair into a ponytail, packed a small bag with her phone, water bottle, and some snacks, then checked the time. Perfect.

She wasn’t going to interfere. She wasn’t even going to speak to him.

She would go to the facility, find somewhere to sit, and watch. Easy. Xiaoran looked at herself in the mirror.

“Operation: Observe Zhou Yichen.”

She nodded.

“Very professional.”

Yichen was already on court when she arrived. The training facility was familiar to her. She had visited enough times to know the entrance, the reception area, and the route to the viewing section. She also knew which side of the court offered a clear view without being too close to the players.

She found a seat near the upper side of the court. Then she spotted him.

He was wearing his training kit, basketball in hand, listening to one of the assistant coaches. His hair was slightly damp already, and his expression was focused.

Xiaoran’s eyes followed him as he stepped onto the court. She had seen him play countless times.

But there was something different about watching him train.

There were no crowds cheering. No scoreboard to distract her. No dramatic moment that made everyone stand up.

Just the repeated sound of basketballs hitting the floor. The squeak of shoes. The coach’s instructions. And Yichen.

He moved through the warm-up with practised efficiency, his body seemingly familiar with every movement. He listened carefully, asked a question, then demonstrated the footwork again. Xiaoran leaned forward. He was handsome. That was her first observation.

Her second observation was that he looked even more attractive when he was concentrating.

She quickly took out her phone and opened her notes.

Observation 1: Zhou Yichen looks serious during training.

She paused. Then added:

Unfortunately, this makes him more handsome.

She smiled to herself. The training began in earnest.

Yichen moved between shooting drills, defensive footwork, and short bursts of sprinting. His movements were controlled, economical, and precise. Even when he missed a shot, he didn’t react dramatically. He retrieved the ball, adjusted his position, and tried again. Xiaoran watched him for nearly twenty minutes. Then she began to feel slightly restless. Not because she was bored. Because sitting still seemed insufficient.

She wanted to see the court from another angle.

And perhaps, if she was being honest, she wanted to feel a little closer to what he was doing. She stood up.

There was a quieter corridor along the side of the facility, with a glass partition overlooking part of the training area. She walked over and found a place where she could watch without getting in anyone’s way. From there, she could see him even better. She couldn’t help smiling. Perfect.

Yichen was halfway through a conditioning drill when he noticed her. It wasn’t that he had become distracted.

His focus remained on the court. He completed the sprint, changed direction, received the ball, and finished the sequence.

But between repetitions, his eyes moved towards the glass partition. A familiar figure. A ponytail. A light-coloured jacket.

And a girl who was trying hard to look as if she wasn’t watching him. Yichen’s mouth curved. Just slightly. He turned back towards the court. The next repetition began. He didn’t call her name. Didn’t wave. Didn’t approach. Instead, he continued his drill.

He knew Xiaoran well enough to understand what she was doing.

She hadn’t come to interrupt him. She was trying to give him space while satisfying her curiosity.

And, judging by the way she was standing with her phone held against her chest, she probably thought she was being discreet. Yichen found that amusing. He also noticed something else.

She was standing a little too close to the glass, shifting her weight from one foot to the other.

He glanced at the clock, then at the water station. He made a mental note.

A few minutes later, during a break, he approached his teammate.

“Can you pass me the spare bottle?”

His teammate handed it over. Yichen took a drink, then casually asked one of the facility staff to leave a bottle of water at the small table near the viewing corridor. He didn’t explain why. He returned to the court.

Xiaoran was beginning to realise that watching someone train was much more physically demanding than she had expected. Not because she was exercising. But because she had been standing.

She shifted her feet, then leaned against the wall, then straightened again when someone walked past. She looked at the court.

Yichen was now practising a series of movements involving quick changes of direction. His shoes squeaked against the floor as he moved between markers. Xiaoran watched, fascinated. He made it look so easy. She knew it wasn’t.

She had seen the bruises he sometimes came home with, the tiredness after demanding training sessions, and the way he occasionally sat after a game, letting his body recover.

But seeing the repetition made her understand it differently. He did the same movement again. And again. And again. Not because he hadn’t done it correctly. Because he wanted to do it better. She looked down at her own trainers. A thought occurred to her. Perhaps she should try some of the movements. Not now, obviously. But maybe later. She could ask him to teach her. Just a little.

She smiled at the idea. Then her eyes caught sight of something on the small table nearby. A bottle of water.

Beside it was a packet of her favourite crackers. Xiaoran blinked. She looked around. Nobody seemed to be paying attention. She approached the table and examined the items. There was no note. But she recognised the water bottle.

It was the brand Yichen usually bought for her. Her eyes slowly narrowed. She looked back towards the court.

Yichen was facing the other direction, listening to his coach. Xiaoran stared at him. Then she smiled.

He knows.

She was almost certain. The next thirty minutes were where Xiaoran’s plan began to fall apart.

She had originally intended to watch the entire training session. But she had underestimated two things.

First, how long a professional athlete could train without seeming to lose his energy.

Second, how little stamina she herself possessed when required to stand around in an unfamiliar environment for an extended period. She drank the water.

Ate the crackers, then found a nearby bench and sat down. From there, she could still see the court. Yichen was now doing repeated sprint drills.

Xiaoran watched the first few, then the next few. Then she checked the time. He was still going.

He was running as if he had somewhere urgent to be. She frowned.

“How does he do that?”

A staff member passing by smiled.

“Long training history.”

Xiaoran nodded politely.

“Right.”

She looked down at her legs. She had been sitting for approximately seven minutes.

And she was already considering whether she should take a nap. She wasn’t proud of this.

But she was beginning to suspect that her boyfriend had been built differently. Yichen noticed her sitting down.

He was in the middle of a shooting drill when his eyes moved towards the bench.

Xiaoran had her legs stretched out slightly, one hand resting on her knee. She was watching him. Then she caught him looking. Her eyes widened.

She immediately pretended to be interested in the wall. Yichen nearly laughed.

He turned back to the basket, received the ball, and made the shot. His teammate caught the rebound.

“You’re in a good mood today.”

Yichen wiped his forehead with a towel.

“Am I not allowed to?”

His teammate gave him a knowing look. Yichen took another drink.

“Focus on your own shooting.”

“Right.”

The teammate glanced towards the viewing area, then back at him.

“Oh.”

Yichen didn’t respond. His teammate grinned.

“Understood.”

The final straw came during the conditioning session. Xiaoran had decided to stand again.

She wanted to get a better view of the court, and the bench was slightly obstructed by a pillar.

She moved to the side, stood near the wall, and watched Yichen complete another series of sprints. One. Two. Three. Four. She was impressed.

Then she became concerned. Then impressed again, then concerned.

By the time he finished, she was already feeling tired on his behalf. She leaned her shoulder against the wall. And, without thinking, she copied his stance. Feet apart. Knees slightly bent. Arms relaxed.

She tried to imitate the way he positioned himself before a sprint. It looked easy.

She bent her knees a little more, then straightened, then tried again.

Unfortunately, she had forgotten that she was wearing shoes with little grip. Her foot slipped slightly. She caught herself against the wall. A soft gasp escaped her. On court, Yichen turned his head. He saw it. His expression changed immediately. Not alarmed exactly, but attentive.

He watched her straighten herself, check her shoe, and look around to make sure nobody had noticed. Then she glanced towards him. Their eyes met. Neither moved. Yichen’s lips curved. A slow, knowing smile. Xiaoran’s cheeks warmed. She looked away.

He shook his head slightly, amused, and turned back to his coach. He still didn’t approach her.

But a few minutes later, when the coach called for a short recovery break, Yichen walked towards the water station. He didn’t go directly to Xiaoran.

Instead, he stopped near the side entrance and spoke with a staff member.

Then he took a towel, wiped his face, and returned to the court. Xiaoran watched him. Her eyes narrowed. He was definitely doing that on purpose. The session ended almost twenty minutes later.

Yichen completed his final shooting drill, exchanged a few words with his coach, and gathered his belongings.

Only then did he walk towards the viewing corridor. Xiaoran immediately sat up straighter.

She had been pretending to look at her phone. Convincingly. Yichen stopped in front of her.

“Good morning.”

“Good morning.”

He glanced at the water bottle beside her.

“Did you drink?”

“Yes.”

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He looked at her for another moment. Then his mouth curved.

“Enjoying the training?”

Xiaoran tried to maintain a neutral expression.

“Yes.”

“Really?”

“Very much.”

“How long have you been here?”

She hesitated.

“Not long.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Xiaoran.”

“Okay, a while.”

“How long?”

“Since you started.”

He met her eyes. She looked back. Then she smiled sheepishly.

“Surprise.”

Yichen laughed.

“You’re not very good at surprising me.”

“I was trying!”

“I noticed.”

Her eyes widened.

“You knew?”

“From the beginning.”

“How?”

He leaned slightly towards her.

“Because I know what you look like when you’re trying not to be noticed.”

She frowned.

“What’s that supposed to mean?”

“You keep looking at me, then pretending to look somewhere else whenever I turn around.”

She gasped.

“You’re making that up.”

“All right.”

She studied his face.

“Wait. When did you first notice?”

“During the conditioning drill.”

“That’s so early!”

“Not really.”

“Then why didn’t you come over?”

Yichen took a moment to answer.

“Because you came here to watch me train, not to make me stop training.”

He said, “I figured you wanted to see my usual routine. So I let you.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened. She looked down at her hands.

“I didn’t want to disturb you.”

“I know.”

“And I didn’t want you to change your schedule just because I came.”

“I didn’t.”

He reached over and gently straightened the strap of her bag.

“But I did make sure you had water.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“And crackers.”

“And crackers.”

That made her grin.

“You’re very considerate.”

“Someone has to be.”

She pinched his arm. He laughed. Then his gaze moved down towards her legs.

“How are you feeling?”

“I’m fine.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

He waited. She sighed.

“My legs are a little tired.”

Yichen’s smile widened.

“A little?”

She gave him a warning look.

“Don’t.”

“Did you do some training yourself?”

“No.”

He glanced at her trainers.

“Then why are you tired?”

“I stood for a long time.”

He nodded solemnly.

“Very demanding.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

He laughed and reached for her hand.

“Come on. Let’s go.”

Where the glass ended and nobody from the team could see, he bent and kissed her, quickly, still warm from the court.

They were halfway down the corridor when Xiaoran stopped.

“Wait.”

Yichen turned.

“What?”

She looked at the court through the glass.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“How long were you training today?”

He told her. She blinked.

“That’s so long.”

“It’s normal.”

“For you.”

He smiled.

“Yes.”

She looked at his legs, then at her own, then back at him.

“Can you teach me?”

Yichen studied her.

“Teach you what?”

“Some of the things you did today.”

“Basketball?”

“Not necessarily. The footwork. The running. Maybe the warm-up.”

Then asked, “Why?”

She shrugged.

“I want to try.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“All right.”

Her face brightened.

“Really?”

“Of course.”

“But not during your usual training. I don’t want to interrupt.”

“We can do it on a day when I’m not training.”

She nodded enthusiastically.

“And you have to teach me properly.”

“I will.”

“And don’t laugh if I’m bad.”

Yichen looked at her.

“I won’t.”

“You’re thinking about laughing.”

“I’m thinking about how to keep you from falling over.”

She gasped.

“I can run!”

“I know.”

“I can!”

Something in his face eased.

“Then show me.”

She looked at him, then looked towards the exit.

“...Not today.”

Yichen laughed. On the way home, Xiaoran was unusually quiet. Yichen glanced at her from the driver’s seat.

“Tired?”

“A little.”

“Want to sleep?”

“No.”

A few seconds passed. Then she turned towards him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Do you mind if I come again?”

He held her gaze.

“Why would I mind?”

“Because I don’t want you to feel like you’re being watched all the time.”

He smiled.

“I play in front of a few thousand people most weeks. I think I can handle one girl watching me.”

She pouted.

“That’s different.”

“How?”

“Because those people don’t know you.”

He studied her. She was looking out the window now, her fingers playing with the strap of her bag.

“I like seeing you when you’re doing your own things. I don’t always get to see this side of you,” she said.

His expression softened.

“What side?”

“The serious one.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“I’m serious with you.”

She laughed.

“No, you’re not. You’re always teasing me.”

“That’s also a side of me.”

“Unfortunately.”

He reached over and squeezed her hand.

“You can come whenever you want, Xiaoran. You don’t have to sneak around.”

“I know.”

“And if you want to watch, just tell me.”

“I don’t want you to feel like you need to pay attention to me.”

“I won’t.”

She looked at him. He continued, calm and certain.

“I’ll train. You can watch. If I have a break, I’ll come find you. That’s all.”

She smiled more brightly.

“Okay.”

A moment later, she said, “But I think I should improve my stamina.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Why?”

“So I can stay longer.”

That got a smile out of him.

“You can sit down whenever you want.”

“No. I want to be able to walk around with you.”

He considered that, then nodded.

“All right. We’ll start slowly.”

She looked pleased. She leaned back against the seat.

Then, after a moment, she turned towards him again.

“By the way.”

“Hm?”

“Your training outfit today was very nice.”

Yichen glanced at her.

“What did you like about it?”

She looked at him innocently.

“Everything.”

His lips curved.

“Is that part of your observation?”

“Yes.”

“What did you observe?”

That made her grin.

“That my boyfriend is very handsome.”

He laughed.

“That’s a biased conclusion.”

“I don’t care.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles at a red light.

“Noted.”

The following week, Xiaoran returned to the training facility. This time, she didn’t sneak in. She told Yichen beforehand.

She arrived a little after his warm-up had started, carrying her own water bottle and a small bag of snacks. She found her usual seat and settled down. Yichen noticed her almost immediately. He didn’t stop. He didn’t wave.

He glanced towards her, and when their eyes met, his lips curved into that familiar, teasing smile. Xiaoran smiled back. Then she opened her notebook.

Observation 2: Subject has become aware of the researcher’s presence and appears mildly pleased.

She watched him return to his drill. A few minutes later, Yichen glanced over again. She lifted her water bottle. He nodded and went back to the drill.

Xiaoran sat down on the end of the bench, still breathing hard, and drank half his water.

chapters.desc: His first-team Herons jersey arrives, number eleven, with an extra O in his name.
chapters.title: Eleven, Misspelled
chapters.epigraph: “Actually, I liked the first one.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Lin Xiaoran noticed was that his name was wrong. The second was that he hadn’t noticed.

He was standing in front of his new locker at the Herons training centre, the first-team one with a brass plate on the door, halfway into his training kit, when she came to the changing-room doorway with two drinks and a paper bag. Partners were allowed in the corridor on Thursdays. She had checked.

“Yichen.”

He looked round. “You’re early.”

“My meeting finished early. I brought you something.” She held up the drinks.

He came over and took the bottle and bent down to kiss her forehead. “Thank you.”

She looked past him at the open locker. His first-team kit was hanging inside, still creased from the packet: the navy jersey, number eleven, with his surname printed across the shoulders above it. Except it wasn’t quite his surname. She stopped smiling. She leaned closer. Then closer.

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

“Your name.”

He glanced at the jersey. “What about it?”

She pointed. He looked. There was a short silence.

ZHOOU

“That’s unfortunate,” he said.

She made a strangled noise. “Unfortunate?”

“An extra letter.”

“Your name has grown.”

He took the jersey off its hanger and examined the print with the seriousness of a man reading the small print on a contract. “So it has.”

She put the drinks down on the bench and covered her mouth, and her shoulders shook.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“I’m sorry.”

“You’re not.”

“No,” she said. “I’m not. How did they do that?”

“Maybe they thought I needed more.”

“An upgraded Zhou. Zhoou Yichen. Deluxe.” She took the jersey out of his hands and held it up against him.

“Perhaps I’ll keep it.”

“You’re not going to wear it?”

“Why not? It’s still my number.”

“Yichen! That letter was not invited.”

He bent his head and lowered his voice. “Are you jealous?”

“Of what?”

“There’s another O between us now.”

She stared at him. Then at the jersey. “That’s terrible.”

“I thought so too.”

“Never say that again.”

He laughed and kissed her cheek, and she got her phone out.

“What are you doing?”

“Documenting a historical event. I’m sending it to Meilin.” She took four photographs, making sure the extra O was perfectly lit.

“Please don’t.”

Xiaoran: URGENT. HIS NAME HAS BEEN REPLACED

Meilin: HAHAHAHAHAHA

Meilin: ZHOOU

Meilin: welcome to the new and improved zhou family

She held the screen up for him. “Meilin says welcome.”

“Your friends are very supportive.”

“She’s my friend.”

“That explains it. I’ll tell the kit manager after training,” he said, and hung the jersey back in the locker.

“Good.”

“I wouldn’t want the wrong man getting credit for my rebounds.”

She laughed all over again, and he went off to training with her laughter following him down the corridor.

✦ ✦ ✦

The correction took three days. For all three days she refused to call him anything but Zhoou.

She did it over messages. She did it in the twelve minutes they still sometimes managed between her final-year seminar and his training. She did it once in front of Fang Ze, who still played for the university and came to watch Herons sessions whenever he could get through the door, and who adopted it instantly and with enormous joy.

On the first evening they were in the café by her studio when she went up to the counter for napkins. His phone was on the table. He sent her a message from where he sat, You forgot your straw, purely to see what would happen, and her phone lit up on the table beside his.

Zhoou (Deluxe Edition): You forgot your straw.

When she came back he was looking at it.

“You renamed me.”

“I updated you. You’re the new model. More letters. Same great taste.” She picked up her phone and admired it.

“Change it back.”

“When the correction comes.”

On the second morning Fang Ze sent him a photograph from the university changing room: a paper cup on which someone had written ZHOOU in thick black marker and drawn a small crown. The caption said only the people have spoken. Eleven of his old teammates had reacted with crowns.

He put up with it, mostly, until lunch on the second day, when he opened his own contacts and made a change.

That evening she was lying at the other end of his sofa with her feet on his knees, too comfortable to say anything out loud, so she messaged him instead to ask whether he wanted noodles. His phone lit up on the cushion between them. She glanced at it without meaning to, and froze.

Linn Xiaoran: noodles?

She looked at the screen. She looked at him.

“What is that.”

“An update.”

“I’m spelled correctly!”

“So was I, until Thursday.”

“Nobody has two Ns. Nobody.”

“You’re the new model. More letters,” he said, without looking up from his laptop.

She sat up, picked up her own phone, opened his contact, typed for a while, and held it up so he could see.

Zhoou (Deluxe Edition, Do Not Return)

He laughed until he had to put the laptop down, and she crawled down the sofa and lay on top of him, laptop and all, and held the phone in front of his face until he admitted defeat.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third day the kit manager, a small, grey, apologetic man everyone called Old Gu, found Yichen in the corridor and apologised for nearly a full minute. It had been the printer, he said. A new printer. The printer had been spoken to. He was sorry. And he wondered, if Zhou didn’t mind, whether he might keep the wrong one for the wall in the kit room, where there was already a ZHANGG from 2019 and a jersey with the number printed upside down.

Yichen said he would think about it. He didn’t tell Xiaoran about the wall until much later. If she had known it existed, she would have wanted to go and see it, and she’d have taken pictures, and Old Gu would never have recovered.

On the fourth day the new jersey arrived, and she was there when he opened the packet.

ZHOU

“Much better,” she said.

“Thank you for your approval.”

He turned it round to check the number. Then he looked at her. “Disappointed?”

“About what?”

“No extra O.”

“Very funny. Actually, I liked the first one.” She leaned against the locker beside his and watched him fold it into his bag.

“Why?”

“Because it was funny.”

“Only because it wasn’t your name.”

She thought about it. “Maybe. And because it was the first one. It’s the first one with your name on it at all. Even if they got your name wrong.”

He looked at her. Then he shut the locker and kissed her temple.

“Thank you for the drinks.”

“You’re welcome, Zhoou.”

He sighed. She grinned and took his arm, and walked him to the door of the gym, and let go only when the coach looked over.

✦ ✦ ✦

That Saturday was a home game. She sat in row F with Fang Ze, who’d come straight from his own training with his hair still wet, and when the announcer read the starting five and said, “Number eleven, Zhou Yichen,” with exactly the right number of letters, Fang Ze leaned over and whispered “Zhoou” under his breath. She elbowed him. Then she said it herself.

Yichen played twenty-two minutes. He scored nine points, which she knew because she counted every one, and threw one bad pass, which she knew because the man behind her said so loudly. She turned round in her seat and defended it to the man at some length, until Fang Ze bought him a drink to make her stop.

Afterward, in the corridor where partners were allowed on match nights too, Yichen came out with his bag over his shoulder and his hair damp and found her waiting by the wall.

“Nine,” she said.

“Eight. I missed a free throw.”

“Nine,” she said, and took hold of his arm with both hands, and held up her phone with the other. She had changed his contact again.

Zhou Yichen (Original)

He looked at it for a while. Then he took out his own phone, changed hers back to one N, and showed her, and she laughed and leaned her whole weight against him all the way down the corridor, past the kit room and its wall, to the car park.

The misspelled jersey went into the back of his wardrobe. He never wore it again, and he never threw it away either. When they moved in together a year later, it came with them in the box marked KEEP, folded so the extra O was on top.

chapters.desc: For one Sunday, the clingy one is Zhou Yichen.
chapters.title: Not Letting You Go Today
chapters.epigraph: “Today I don’t want to let you go.”
chapters.content:
There was something wrong with Zhou Yichen. Xiaoran realised this at 9:23 on a Sunday morning, when she tried to get out of bed for the third time and he pulled her back without saying a word.

The first time, she had only wanted to get her phone from the bedside table. The second time, she had remembered that she hadn’t brushed her teeth.

The third time, she had announced that she was getting breakfast.

And every single time, Yichen had found a reason to keep her where she was.

Now she was lying on her back, staring at the ceiling, while he rested his cheek against her shoulder and held her around the waist.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“I need to get up.”

“Why?”

She turned her head.

“Because it’s morning?”

“That isn’t a reason.”

She blinked.

“Since when?”

He didn’t answer. Instead, his arm tightened slightly around her waist, and he pressed a lazy kiss against her shoulder. Xiaoran stared at him. Usually, she was the one who did this.

She was the one who followed him from the bedroom to the kitchen, who leaned against him while he made coffee, who appeared beside his desk with absolutely no purpose except to occupy his attention. Yichen had always indulged her, sometimes teasing her about being unable to stay away for more than ten minutes. But this? This was different.

He had been following her around since she woke up.

And now he was actively preventing her from leaving the bed.

“Are you sleepy?” she asked.

“No.”

“Then why are you holding me?”

“Because I want to.”

She considered that answer.

“Okay...”

She tried to sit up. His hand settled against her stomach.

“Where are you going?”

“Bathroom.”

“All right.”

He didn’t move. She looked down at his arm.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You’re coming with me?”

He finally lifted his head. A faint smile appeared.

“Would you like me to?”

“NO.”

He laughed, released her, and let her get out of bed.

Xiaoran walked towards the bathroom, glancing over her shoulder once. He was still lying there. Good. She had won.

Except when she came out five minutes later, he was standing outside the bathroom door, waiting. She stopped.

“...What?”

“Nothing.”

“Why are you standing here?”

“Waiting.”

“For what?”

He met her eyes.

“For you.”

She stared at him. Then she narrowed her eyes.

“You’re being weird.”

His smile widened. He reached out, gently tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear, and kissed her, briefly.

“Come on. Breakfast.”

By ten, Xiaoran had identified the problem. Yichen wanted her attention.

Not in his usual quiet way, where he would occasionally pull her closer while reading or place a hand on her knee under the table. No.

Today, he wanted her attention with an almost unreasonable level of determination.

When she sat on the kitchen counter while he prepared breakfast, he stood between her knees. When she reached for her phone, he asked what she was looking at. When she got down to help him, he moved the cutting board away from her and told her to sit.

When she finally finished eating and opened her laptop, he came over and stood behind her chair. She looked up.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Then why are you standing there?”

He rested his hands on the back of her chair.

“Can’t I?”

“You can. But you’re blocking the light.”

He moved half a step. She returned to her laptop. A few seconds passed.

Then she felt his hand brush over her hair. Another few seconds. His fingers touched her shoulder. Then he leaned down and kissed her temple. Xiaoran slowly stopped typing.

“Yichen.”

“Yes?”

“Are you bored?”

“No.”

“Are you lonely?”

He thought about it.

“A little.”

She turned around.

“But I’m right here.”

“I know.”

“Then?”

He looked at her, his expression calm.

“That’s why.”

She stared. It took her a second to understand what he meant. Then her cheeks warmed.

“...You want to be with me?”

“I am with you.”

“No, I mean—”

“I know what you mean.”

He smiled, and she immediately looked away.

That smile again: the one that made her forget what she had been trying to say.

She cleared her throat.

“Well, you can sit down.”

He pulled out the chair beside hers. Then, instead of sitting normally, he dragged it closer until their knees touched.

Xiaoran looked at the gap between the chairs, then at him.

“You’re ridiculous.”

He opened his laptop.

“Get back to work.”

At eleven-thirty, Xiaoran received a message from Jiayi. They had planned to meet at a café that afternoon to discuss a Media project. Xiaoran had already told her she would be there. She glanced at the message and began typing.

Jiayi: Are we still meeting at two?

Xiaoran: Yes! I’ll be there.

Before she could send it, Yichen’s voice came from beside her.

“Where are you going?”

She looked up.

“To meet Jiayi.”

“When?”

“Two.”

He glanced at the time.

“Today?”

She laughed.

“Yes, today.”

He nodded. Then he looked back at his laptop. Xiaoran waited. That was it? She looked at him suspiciously.

“Why?”

“Nothing.”

“Yichen.”

He turned his head.

“What?”

“Do you have something planned?”

“No.”

“Then why are you asking?”

“I was checking.”

She studied his expression. It was perfectly normal. Too normal. She sent the message. Then she put her phone down. Yichen’s hand found hers beneath the table. He began rubbing his thumb over her knuckles. Xiaoran looked at their joined hands.

“You’re doing it again. Being clingy.”

He turned to her.

“Does it bother you?”

She hesitated.

“No...”

His thumb continued moving gently over her hand.

“Then it’s fine.”

Xiaoran stared at him. He was impossible. At twelve-fifteen, she decided to test something. She stood up.

“I’m going to get my bag.”

Yichen looked up immediately.

“Why?”

“Because I need to check something.”

He stood too.

“I’ll get it.”

“No. I can get it.”

He paused. Then he sat back down. Xiaoran walked towards the bedroom.

She reached the wardrobe, took out her bag, and checked its contents.

When she turned around, Yichen was standing in the doorway. She froze. She looked at him.

“...What?”

“Nothing.”

“Why are you here?”

He leaned against the doorframe.

“You were taking a while.”

“I was checking my bag.”

“I see.”

She eyed him.

“Did you follow me?”

“Yes.”

He said it so casually that she almost laughed.

“Why?”

He didn’t answer immediately. Instead, he walked towards her, stopped close, and looked down at the bag in her hands.

“Do you have everything?”

“Yes.”

“Your charger?”

“Yes.”

“Notebook?”

“Yes.”

“Keys?”

She lifted them. He nodded.

“Good.”

She blinked at him. Then she put the bag down. She opened her arms. He raised an eyebrow but stepped closer. She reached up and cupped his face.

“What’s going on with you today?”

He looked at her, his expression softening.

“Nothing’s going on.”

“Then why are you following me everywhere?”

He was quiet. Then he lowered his head slightly, resting his forehead against hers.

“Because I like having you around.”

Her expression softened.

“You always have me around.”

“Not always.”

She blinked. He continued, his voice low and unhurried.

“Sometimes you’re busy. Sometimes I’m busy. Sometimes we spend the whole day together and still barely get a chance to sit down.”

Xiaoran listened.

“And today?”

“Today I don’t want to let you go.”

She looked at him. Then she laughed.

“You’re saying that as if I’m moving to another country.”

“I know you’re not.”

“Then?”

He gave her that small, almost helpless smile.

“I just want you here.”

Something warm spread through her chest. She tugged him down and kissed his cheek.

“Okay.”

He held her gaze.

“Okay?”

“Yes. You can be clingy today.”

His eyes softened.

“Thank you.”

She laughed.

“But don’t follow me into the bathroom.”

He laughed.

“I’ll try.”

At one-thirty, Xiaoran was getting ready to leave. Yichen sat down on the bed, watching her put on her earrings. She glanced at him through the mirror.

“Why are you looking at me?”

“Can’t I?”

“You can. But you’re making me nervous.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Why?”

“Because you’re staring.”

“You’re pretty.”

Her fingers stopped. She looked at him through the mirror. Then she quickly returned to adjusting her earrings.

“That’s not relevant.”

“Isn’t it?”

“No.”

He stood and walked over. She expected him to kiss her cheek.

Instead, he stood behind her and rested his chin lightly on her shoulder, his arms slipping around her waist. Xiaoran looked at their reflection.

He was taller, his face relaxed, his eyes fixed on hers in the mirror. She placed her hands over his.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“I’m really going.”

“I know.”

“You’re not going to stop me?”

He was quiet. Then he pressed a kiss against her cheek.

“No.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Good.”

She turned around and kissed him properly. It was supposed to be a quick goodbye kiss.

But when she tried to pull away, he followed her, stealing another.

Then another, softer one near the corner of her mouth. She laughed against his lips.

“You’re doing it again.”

He smiled.

“One more.”

“That’s what you said last time.”

“Then this is the last one.”

She let him kiss her. When he finally released her, she picked up her bag.

“Bye.”

He walked her to the door. She put on her shoes.

He handed her the keys she had forgotten on the counter.

“Thank you.”

Then he kissed her temple.

“Text me when you arrive.”

“I will.”

She opened the door. And just before she stepped out, she turned back. He was still standing there. She smiled.

“Yichen?”

“Yes?”

She reached for him. He walked over. She held his face and kissed him once more.

“Don’t miss me too much.”

He looked at her with a faint smile.

“Too late.”

She laughed all the way down the corridor. The café meeting lasted longer than expected.

Jiayi and Ning were discussing the project’s visual direction, and Xiaoran had become so involved in the conversation that she barely checked her phone.

When she finally looked down, she found four messages.

Yichen: Arrived?

Yichen: Lunch?

Yichen: What are you doing?

Yichen: Are you busy?

Her mouth tipped up.

Xiaoran: Yes, I arrived.

Xiaoran: I ate.

Xiaoran: We’re discussing the project.

His reply came almost immediately.

Yichen: All right.

A few seconds later:

Yichen: Miss you.

Xiaoran stared at the message. Then she covered her mouth. Jiayi noticed. Ning glanced over.

“Yichen?”

Xiaoran looked up.

“How did you know?”

Jiayi laughed.

“Your face.”

Xiaoran looked down again. She typed.

Xiaoran: We only separated an hour ago.

Yichen: I know.

Xiaoran: You’re very clingy today.

Yichen: Yes.

She blinked. He wasn’t even denying it.

Xiaoran: Are you okay?

Yichen: Perfectly fine.

Xiaoran: Then why?

Yichen: No particular reason.

A moment later, another message appeared.

Yichen: I want to see you.

She pressed her lips together. This was unfair. She had spent years being the one who said things like that.

Now he was doing it with such calm sincerity that she didn’t know how to respond.

Xiaoran: I’ll come back after we’re done.

Yichen: I’ll be here.

She smiled at the screen. Jiayi leaned forward.

“You’re smiling again.”

Xiaoran put her phone away.

“Can we work?”

Ning laughed.

“Sure.”

When Xiaoran returned, it was nearly five. She unlocked the apartment door and stepped inside.

“Yichen?”

“I’m here.”

His voice came from the living room. She put down her bag and walked over.

He was sitting on the sofa with his laptop open. The moment he saw her, he closed it. Xiaoran stopped.

“...Were you waiting for me?”

“Yes.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What did you have?”

“Something.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“That’s not an answer.”

He held out his hand. He held out his hand. She walked towards him.

He caught her hand and gently pulled her down onto the sofa beside him.

Then he wrapped both arms around her and drew her against his chest. Xiaoran laughed.

“Yichen!”

He buried his face against her shoulder. She blinked. He wasn’t even teasing. He was holding her. She slowly relaxed against him.

“Did you miss me?”

“Yes.”

She smiled.

“How much?”

He lifted his head.

“Do you want an accurate answer?”

She nodded. He considered it.

“Enough that I checked the time several times.”

She laughed.

“That’s not a measurement.”

“Then I don’t have one.”

She reached up and touched his cheek.

“You’re really clingy today.”

He caught her hand and kissed her palm.

“You’ve mentioned that.”

“Because it’s true.”

“Does it bother you?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

He studied her.

“Good.”

She leaned closer.

“Actually, I think it’s cute.”

His eyebrows lifted.

“Cute?”

“Yes.”

He gave her a look. She grinned.

“Very cute.”

“Careful.”

“Why?”

“You might encourage me.”

She laughed.

“Maybe I want to.”

He looked at her. Then he leaned forward and kissed her.

It was warm and unhurried, his hand resting against her cheek. When he pulled away, he stayed close enough that their noses almost touched.

“Then I’ll take advantage of that.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“You’re already taking advantage.”

“Of what?”

“My kindness.”

He laughed. Later, they ordered dinner. Xiaoran sat cross-legged on the sofa, leaning against Yichen while they waited for the delivery.

He had one arm around her and was absentmindedly playing with her fingers. She looked down at their hands. Then she looked at him.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Why today?”

He stopped moving his thumb.

“What do you mean?”

“You’re usually affectionate. You like being around me. But today you’re... Extra.” She searched for the right word.

His mouth curved.

“Extra?”

“Unbearably extra.”

He laughed. She waited. He looked towards the window.

“Maybe because I’ve been thinking about the next few months.”

“The Herons?”

“Partly. Training, university, everything.”

She nodded. His schedule had become more demanding since he’d signed the full contract. There were more sessions, more expectations, and more decisions to make about his future.

“Have you been stressed?”

“Not particularly.”

“Then?”

He considered his answer.

“Sometimes I get so focused on what I need to do next that I forget to enjoy what’s already here.”

He said, “Today I had the time. So I wanted to spend it with you.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Then why didn’t you just say that?”

“I did.”

“You said you didn’t want to let me go.”

“That’s what I meant.”

She laughed and leaned into his shoulder.

“You’re so strange.”

“I know.”

She lifted her head.

“Are you secretly enjoying this?”

“Very much.”

She gasped.

“So you know how it feels!”

That got a smile out of him.

“Of course.”

“Then you understand how difficult it is when you keep walking away to do your own things.”

He turned towards her.

“Do you?”

“Sometimes.”

He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“Then I’ll make sure you don’t have to wonder whether I want you around.”

Her expression softened. She leaned forward and kissed him. The food arrived.

They ate on the sofa, sharing dishes and occasionally arguing over who had taken the last piece.

After dinner, Xiaoran tried to get up to wash the dishes. Yichen caught her hand.

“I’ll do it.”

She met his eyes.

“You’re going to do everything today?”

“Would you like to?”

She thought about it.

“No.”

“Then sit.”

She laughed.

“You’re spoiling me.”

He stood, gathered the plates, and carried them to the kitchen. Xiaoran followed him. He glanced over his shoulder.

“Where are you going?”

“Nowhere.”

He smiled. She leaned against the kitchen counter while he washed the dishes.

She walked over and wrapped her arms around his waist from behind. Yichen paused. Then his smile appeared.

“What’s this?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re following me.”

“Yes.”

He laughed. She rested her cheek against his back.

“How does it feel?”

“Good.”

She tightened her arms.

“Really?”

“Very.”

That made her grin.

“Then maybe I’ll be clingy today too.”

He turned off the tap, dried his hands, and turned around inside her embrace.

“Is that so?”

“Yes.”

He bent down and kissed her temple.

“Then I won’t complain.”

She turned to him.

“Even if I follow you everywhere?”

“Even then.”

“Even if I keep asking what you’re doing?”

“Yes.”

He laughed under his breath. Xiaoran laughed.

“You’re unbelievable.”

He wrapped his arms around her.

“And you’re not?”

She considered it. Then she nodded.

“Fair.”

By the time they went to bed, Yichen had returned to his usual level of composure. Mostly.

Xiaoran was lying on her side, scrolling through her phone, when she felt his arm settle around her waist. She smiled without looking up.

“Again?”

“Hm?”

“You’re holding me.”

“Is that a problem?”

She put her phone down and turned towards him.

“No.”

He drew her closer. She tucked herself against his chest, resting one hand over his shirt.

“Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“Tomorrow, I might have to go out again.”

“I know.”

“And the day after that, I have a meeting.”

“All right.”

“And next week you’ll probably be busy with training.”

“Yes.”

She looked up.

“So you can’t keep me all to yourself.”

His mouth curved.

“I know.”

She touched his cheek.

“But you can ask me to stay when you miss me.”

His expression softened.

“I will.”

“And you can tell me when you want attention.”

He gave her an amused look.

“I think I’ve made that quite clear today.”

She laughed.

“Very clear.”

He kissed her hair.

Then, after a moment, he said, “Xiaoran?”

“Hm?”

“Stay a little longer.”

She smiled.

“Yichen, we’re going to sleep.”

“I know.”

“So I’ll be here tomorrow morning.”

He looked at her.

“Good.”

She settled against him again. A few seconds passed.

Then she felt him press another kiss to her hair. She smiled into his chest.

Usually, she was the one who wanted just five more minutes, one more hug, one more kiss before letting him go.

Yichen had always been affectionate in a way that made her feel wanted without ever making her feel held back.

But every so often, even someone as composed as him wanted to be selfish with the person he loved.

And today, he had decided that he was going to be. She slipped her arms around him.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Tomorrow, I’ll be the clingy one again.”

He laughed.

“All right.”

“Don’t complain.”

“I won’t.”

“And don’t get used to being the one who gets chased.”

He lowered his head, his smile brushing against her forehead.

“Too late.”

She giggled. Then he kissed her once more, and she finally closed her eyes.

chapters.desc: His birthday falls on an away game. She takes the train down with Ning, and the cake arrives as crumbs.
chapters.title: Birthday, Away
chapters.epigraph: “I wanted to be here today.”
chapters.content:
The cake arrived as crumbs. Not metaphorically, and not slightly squashed. Crumbs.

Lin Xiaoran and Ning sat in the back of the taxi and looked into the open box. For several seconds neither of them said anything.

“I think,” said Ning carefully, “we have a situation.”

Xiaoran closed the lid. “Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You were going to.”

Ning lifted the lid a centimetre and looked in again. “It’s not a cake anymore.”

“It’s still a cake.”

“It’s a collection of cake-related materials.”

It had been a small chocolate cake with HAPPY BIRTHDAY, YICHEN piped across the top in white. They’d ordered it from a bakery near the hotel where the Herons were staying and picked it up themselves to save the delivery fee, which had been the mistake, because the taxi driver took the big roundabout by the station at a speed the cake hadn’t agreed to. Now one side had slid into the other, and most of the message was underneath a collapsed bank of cream.

“What do we do?” said Ning.

Xiaoran took a breath. “We fix it.”

“With what?”

She looked into the box. At the little bag of candles. At the plastic knife.

“Optimism,” she said, and Ning laughed so much the driver looked at them in the mirror.

✦ ✦ ✦

His birthday fell on an away weekend, his third with the first team. Training on Friday, the game on Saturday, his birthday, and the team train home on Sunday morning. His teammates had already planned something at the team hotel, where wives and girlfriends weren’t allowed past the lobby. But Xiaoran wanted to do something of her own. So she and Ning had taken the train down after Ning’s last seminar on Friday and booked a twin room in a cheaper hotel across the road.

“A small cake. Some candles. Something quiet after the game. That’s all,” she had said on the train, ticking it off on her fingers.

Now she was sitting on a hotel bed with a ruined cake on the desk, a packet of napkins, and Ning trying to push the cream back into shape with a teaspoon from the kettle tray.

“We could make it a trifle,” said Ning.

“It’s not a birthday trifle. It’s a birthday cake.”

“It’s dessert.”

“It’s supposed to say happy birthday.”

Ning bent over it. “Technically it still does.”

Xiaoran leaned in. Where the cream had slid, the message now read HAPPY BIR... YICH... She shut her eyes. Ning started laughing again.

“Stop laughing!”

“I’m sorry!”

“You’re not!”

“I’m trying!”

Xiaoran sighed, and took the teaspoon out of Ning’s hand. “Give me that.”

It took forty minutes, a second trip to the bakery for a tube of icing, and most of Ning’s patience. Then they put the box on the desk, washed the cream off their hands, and took a taxi to the arena, round the same roundabout so slowly that the driver asked them if they were all right.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat in the away end, twelve rows up, with about forty Herons fans who’d made the trip and one loud drum. Nobody around them knew whose birthday it was. Xiaoran found this unbearable. She lasted until halfway through the first quarter, when she told the woman next to her, who told her husband, who told the drum.

By the third quarter the whole away end was singing happy birthday every time Yichen touched the ball. He heard it. She knew he heard it, because the second time, running back on defence, he looked straight up at row twelve with an expression of total betrayal, and Ning had to sit down.

He scored eleven. The drum did a special roll for every basket. Ning filmed all of it as evidence and sent it to Meilin, who replied from four hundred kilometres away with nothing but a row of drum emojis.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Herons won. He had forty minutes before the team curfew, and Ning had tactfully gone down to the lobby with her laptop, and at a quarter to eleven there was a knock on the door.

He was in his team tracksuit with his hair still wet from the shower. She opened the door and put her arms round his neck before he’d got all the way through it.

“Happy birthday.”

“Thank you. The drum, Xiaoran.” He held on to her with the door still open behind him.

“That wasn’t me.”

“It was entirely you.”

“It was the woman next to me. And her husband. And the drum. How’s your ankle?” She leaned back to look at him.

“Fine.”

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“Properly?”

“Yes, Xiaoran.”

“Good.” She pulled him in and shut the door, and he looked past her at the desk, where there was a cake box with a towel over it.

“What’s that?”

“Your birthday cake.”

He looked at her. Then at the box. “Should I be worried?”

“No,” she said, and took the towel off, and lifted the lid.

He looked down. The cake was no longer exactly round. The cream had been pushed back where it belonged, the chocolate curls had been redistributed, and the message had been piped again on top in a steady, slightly crooked hand: HAPPY BIRTHDAY, YICHEN. One candle leaned to the left. Another had sunk into the cream almost to its wick.

He looked at the cake. He looked at her. She folded her arms.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re thinking something.”

“I’m thinking it looks very good.”

“You’re lying.”

“A little,” he said, and she gasped, and he laughed and pulled her in by the waist and held her against him.

“Thank you.”

“You haven’t even tried it.”

“Thank you anyway,” he said, and kissed her, and when he let her go she was smiling again. She lit the candle that was still standing up.

“Make a wish.”

He shut his eyes for a second longer than she expected. Then he blew it out.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat on the end of the bed and ate it straight out of the box with the teaspoon and a plastic fork. It was messy. It was good.

“Did the bakery make this?”

“The bakery made it. Ning and I repaired it.”

“How long did that take?”

“Long enough.”

He looked at the piping. “I can tell.”

She hit his arm. “You’re supposed to be grateful.”

“I am. You could have done this when I got home tomorrow.” He put the fork down and turned towards her, and his voice went quieter.

“I know.”

“You came all this way. On a Friday. You missed your seminar.”

“I wanted to be here today.”

He was quiet. Then he brushed a smear of cream off the corner of her mouth with his thumb.

“That’s enough. That’s more than enough,” he said.

She tucked herself against his shoulder. They ate the rest of it slowly, talking about the game and the drum and the man in front of them who had shouted at the referee for the entire second half. Then he looked down into the box.

“Did you take a picture before you fixed it?”

She went still.

“Xiaoran.”

“Yes.”

“Show me.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because it’s embarrassing.”

“For who?”

“For everyone.”

He held out his hand. She looked at it for a while. Then she gave him her phone.

He opened the photograph. The cake was almost completely flat, the message was partly upside down, and one of the chocolate curls had ended up stuck to the inside of the lid. He looked at it for three seconds and then laughed, properly, the helpless kind, with his head back.

She put her face in her hands. “I knew you would!”

“It’s wonderful.”

“It’s horrible.”

“It’s the best birthday cake I’ve ever had. I’ll remember this one,” he said, still laughing, and pulled her hands away from her face.

“Unfortunately.”

“Fortunately,” he said, and kissed her on the temple.

✦ ✦ ✦

With eleven minutes left before curfew, and Xiaoran half asleep against his shoulder, he took a photograph of what was left in the box and sent it to the group chat that Ning had made for the weekend.

Yichen: Thank you for the cake.

Ning: you’re welcome. I did most of the repairs

Xiaoran: LIES

Ning: I was emotionally supportive

Yichen: An important contribution.

Ning: thank you. at least someone appreciates me

Xiaoran lifted her head. “What are you doing?”

“Thanking everybody.”

“Don’t encourage her. She laughed at me.”

“She helped. Both can be true,” he said.

She gave him a look of deep offence. He kissed her hair. Then he looked at his watch, and she looked at it too, and she made a small, unhappy sound and wrapped both arms round his middle.

“Eight minutes.”

“Eight minutes,” he agreed, and didn’t move. Neither did she.

At two minutes to curfew he kissed her one last time at the door, and went back across the road, and was in his room on the stroke of eleven. There was cream on his sleeve. Kou Ran, his roommate on away trips, pointed it out at breakfast in front of the entire team, and Yichen looked at it, and didn’t wipe it off.

chapters.desc: Seven days to their fifth anniversary, the lift still broken, and a pact of one surprise each that neither of them keeps very well.
chapters.title: The Week Before
chapters.epigraph: “I get one surprise. That’s fair.”
chapters.content:
There were seven days left until their fifth anniversary, and Lin Xiaoran wasn’t counting.

She happened to know it was seven days away because she had checked the calendar that morning, again at lunch, and once more on the fourth-floor landing outside her studio while getting her breath back. The lift was still broken. It had been broken for four years. She had come to think of the stairs as a kind of personal trainer who didn’t charge.

Five years since a boy with an umbrella had walked her home in the rain. She thought that deserved something special.

She had already decided on the general idea: a nice dinner, somewhere warm, with pretty lighting and food they both liked. Nothing grand. She wanted somewhere that felt like them, the kind of place where he’d take his jacket off and lean his elbows on the table. And she had found it.

A small restaurant on a quiet lane off Wukang Road, eight tables, a wooden door with no sign, and a menu that changed every week depending on what the owner had found at the market. She had saved a photograph of its window three weeks ago, a picture of a table with two glasses and a candle in a jar, and then spent most of an evening reading every review on the internet.

There was one problem. The anniversary itself was on Sunday, the sixth of December, and the restaurant was closed on Sundays.

So it would be Saturday. The night before. She found she liked that even better: an anniversary eve, like a festival.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday evening she sat cross-legged on her bed with the reservation page open. Saturday at seven had two tables left. She took one, and in the box marked Special requests she typed, after some thought:

Anniversary dinner (five years) for my boyfriend, Zhou Yichen. Please don’t mention it if he calls you for anything. A small bouquet on the table, pale pink and white, nothing big.

She pressed confirm. Then she took a screenshot and sent it to Meilin, four hundred kilometres away, who was supposed to be writing her own thesis.

Xiaoran: I booked it.

Meilin: The secret restaurant?

Xiaoran: Yes!

Meilin: Does he know?

Xiaoran: No. It’s a surprise.

Meilin: Lin Xiaoran, you have never once surprised that man.

Xiaoran: This time is different.

Meilin: That’s what you said about his birthday.

She put her phone away, satisfied, and didn’t think about his birthday.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the road and up eleven floors, Yichen was looking at the same restaurant’s confirmation email. Saturday. Seven o’clock. Two guests.

He had seen the photograph three weeks ago over her shoulder, a window with a candle in a jar, and had watched her save it, and say nothing about it, and look at it twice more that week when she thought he was reading. He had booked a table the same night. In the box marked Special requests he had typed:

Anniversary dinner (five years) for my girlfriend, Lin Xiaoran. Flowers on the table, small. A card, which I’ll bring.

He didn’t know she had done the same. Not yet.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday afternoon the restaurant called him.

“Mr. Zhou? This is Ms. Pei, from the restaurant on Saturday. I’m so sorry to bother you. We’re a very small place, and I read all the booking notes myself, and I have two tables at seven on Saturday that both say anniversary dinner, five years. One of them is for a Lin Xiaoran. The other one is from a Lin Xiaoran, and it’s for a Zhou Yichen.” The owner had a voice like someone trying not to laugh in church.

Yichen was in the university library. He put his pen down carefully.

“I see.”

“I didn’t want to seat you at two separate tables. It seemed sad,” Ms. Pei said.

He laughed then, into his hand, in the silent study area, and a girl at the next desk looked up and then away.

“Could you cancel mine,” he said, “and put my requests on her table? The card is mine. The flowers too, if that doesn’t cause trouble.”

“She’s also asked for flowers.”

“Then one bouquet. Whichever she asked for.”

“And I’m not to tell her?”

He thought about Xiaoran saving the photograph, and her face when she finally got to say surprise, and how rarely she ever got to say it to him.

“Please don’t,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦
