Unfortunately, Ms. Pei was a scrupulously honest woman, and on Thursday she sent Xiaoran a message asking whether Miss Lin would like her pale pink bouquet to include the white ranunculus Mr. Zhou mentioned, or keep it as it is.

Xiaoran read it in the library, sitting next to Luo Jiayi, who was supposed to be helping her with subtitles and was instead reading over her shoulder.

“Mr. Zhou mentioned?” Jiayi said.

Xiaoran read it again. Then she opened their chat.

Xiaoran: Yichen.

Yichen: Hm?

Xiaoran: Did you book a restaurant for Saturday?

The typing dots appeared, stopped, and appeared again.

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: Which one?

Yichen: The one you booked.

Xiaoran put her phone down on the desk and her forehead down beside it. Jiayi laughed until a librarian came over.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang her that evening. She was lying on her bed staring at the ceiling, and he sounded calm and unmistakably amused.

“So.”

“So. Meilin said I’d never surprised you once.” She turned on her side.

“You surprised me on Wednesday. The owner rang. I nearly fell off my chair.”

“You didn’t.”

“I put my pen down very carefully. I cancelled mine. You were first. It’s your dinner.”

“I wasn’t first. You saw me save the photograph.”

“I did.”

“That’s cheating.”

“It’s paying attention,” he said, and she couldn’t argue with that, so she complained instead about Ms. Pei’s honesty for a while, and he listened, and at the end he said, “Did you ask for a card?”

“No. Did you?”

“Yes.”

“What does it say?”

“It’s a surprise.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

“You get one surprise. I get one surprise. That’s fair,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday, Xiaoran changed her outfit twice. Jiayi, who had come over to supervise, rejected the first one before Xiaoran had finished putting it on, approved the second, and stood back with her arms folded like a tailor.

“Good. Now don’t fall down the stairs.”

Four flights later, Xiaoran came out of the building door slightly out of breath. Yichen was leaning against his car at the kerb. He looked at her without saying anything, which she had learned was worse, or better, than anything he could say, and then he opened the passenger door.

“You look beautiful.”

“I took the stairs in these.”

“I know. I could hear you from here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The restaurant was warm and lit, and smelled of butter and something with ginger in it. Ms. Pei herself showed them to the table by the window, the one from the photograph, with a candle in a jar. There was one small bouquet, pale pink with a few white ranunculus, and beside it a little envelope.

Ms. Pei put the menus down and said, to nobody in particular, “Five years. Congratulations. I only had to cancel one table,” and went away.

Xiaoran picked up the envelope. Yichen watched her open it.

Five years. I’d still choose you, every time, even the rectangle.

She read it twice. The rectangle was the long way home, the second time he had walked her home, past the same peaches twice. She hadn’t known he remembered.

“You wrote this?”

“It’s very short.”

“Too short?”

She shook her head and put it in her bag, carefully, in the inside pocket.

Then she took out her own envelope and slid it across the table. Inside was a photograph from their first winter, the two of them outside the school gate in their winter uniforms, both looking at the camera with the expressions of people who hadn’t yet learned how to stand next to each other in a picture. On the back she had written:

Five years ago I didn’t know the boy beside me would become my favourite person. I suspected.

He looked at it.

“You kept this.”

“Meilin took it. I stole it from her phone.”

He turned it over and read the back again and didn’t say anything, and she let him not say anything, because she knew what it looked like when Zhou Yichen was moved and trying to hide it, and she had decided long ago to let him have that.

They ordered whatever Ms. Pei said was good, which was everything. They talked about their theses, and Meilin’s thesis, and the Herons, who still wanted an answer, and the small things that had happened that week, which were mostly about restaurants. At some point Xiaoran reached across the table and took his hand.

“Tomorrow,” she said, “is the real one.”

“I know.”

“What are we doing?”

“It’s a surprise.”

“You said one surprise each.”

“That was for Saturday. Sunday has its own rules,” he said.

She narrowed her eyes. He ran his thumb over her knuckles and didn’t explain, and she found, to her own surprise, that she didn’t want him to.

When they left, Ms. Pei was standing at the door with her coat on, and she said, “Next year, one booking,” in the voice of a woman who had been through something.

“Mine,” said Xiaoran.

“Mine,” said Yichen, at the same time.

Ms. Pei closed the door on both of them.

chapters.desc: Their fifth anniversary falls on a Sunday. He remembers what she blurted out behind the library at graduation, and brings a ring that is not a proposal.
chapters.title: Five Years, on a Sunday
chapters.epigraph: “I want to marry you one day.”
chapters.content:
Sunday mornings had always been Xiaoran’s favourite kind of morning.

There was no rush to get to campus, no lecture to catch, no presentation waiting to be delivered. No one needed her to make a decision before noon. She could wake up slowly, steal half of Yichen’s blanket, and pretend she hadn’t heard him asking whether she wanted breakfast.

Today, however, was the sixth of December, and she had a plan. An important plan.

She had been thinking about their fifth anniversary for weeks, and she had decided that five years deserved something more memorable than their usual routine. Not that she disliked their usual routine. Their usual routine was excellent. But five years was five years.

She was currently sitting cross-legged on Yichen’s bed, scrolling through the photos she had taken of them over the years, when he came out of the bathroom.

“You’re awake.”

She looked up. “I’ve been awake.”

“How long?”

“Long enough.”

It wasn’t an answer, and they both knew it.

“Why do you always need exact information?”

He walked over, wearing a loose T-shirt and sweatpants, his hair still slightly damp. He bent and kissed her hairline before looking at her phone.

“What are you looking at?”

“Nothing.”

He glanced at the screen. It was a photo of them from their first year together. Xiaoran had been making a silly face at the camera while Yichen looked at her instead of the lens.

“Nothing?” he repeated.

“Private archival material.”

“Should I be concerned?”

“Very.”

He sat beside her, and she immediately leaned against his arm.

“Happy five years,” she said.

His expression softened.

“Happy five years.”

She smiled, then lifted her phone again.

“Look. We were so young.”

“That was four years ago.”

“Exactly. So young.”

“You say that as if we’re old now.”

“We’re practically historical.”

He laughed. She swiped to another picture. Then another. There were photographs from high school, university orientation, their first campus date, Chengdu in the rain, New York in the snow, basketball games, birthdays, and countless ordinary moments that neither of them had thought important when they happened. Yichen looked at them with her.

“You kept all of these?”

“Of course.”

“Why?”

“Because I like them.”

She stopped at one photograph. It was taken during their graduation from high school. Xiaoran was holding a bouquet, smiling brightly at the camera. Yichen stood beside her in his graduation clothes, one arm around her shoulders. She stared at it, then laughed.

“What?” he asked.

“Do you remember what I said that day?”

“Which part?”

She turned to him with an exaggeratedly innocent expression.

“I proposed to you.”

He met her eyes.

“By the fence behind the library. Then you said you meant someday. Maybe. In theory.”

“That was a very clear clarification.”

“It clarified nothing.”

“And then you told Yuhao!”

“He asked.”

She burst out laughing.

“And you said you’d probably say yes.”

“If you asked seriously later.”

“Zhou Yichen!”

He smiled, looking entirely too pleased with himself. She pushed his shoulder.

“Three and a half years, and I still haven’t had a real answer.”

“Have I not?”

“No.”

He looked at her for another second, then reached for her hand.

“Happy anniversary, Xiaoran.”

“You’re changing the subject.”

He kissed the back of her hand.

“Then I’ll answer you later.”

She blinked.

“Later?”

“Mm.”

She studied his face, but he had already stood up.

“Come on. Let’s get breakfast.”

She watched him walk towards the bedroom door. Something about his expression made her suspicious. But she decided not to investigate. Not yet. They spent the morning doing little.

Yichen made breakfast while Xiaoran sat on the kitchen counter, supposedly helping by keeping him company. She stole pieces of fruit from the chopping board, complained that he was taking too long, and asked whether he had considered opening a restaurant.

“I have a contract with the Herons,” he reminded her.

“You can have two careers.”

“That’s ambitious.”

“You’re good at basketball and cooking. It’s a waste not to explore your options.”

He set a plate in front of her.

“Eat.”

She looked down.

“That was quick.”

“Because I didn’t listen to your business proposal.”

She laughed and picked up her fork. After breakfast, they went out.

Yichen had suggested taking her somewhere, but he refused to tell her where. Xiaoran had tried asking him three different ways, and all three attempts had failed.

“Is it a restaurant?”

“No.”

“A shopping mall?”

“No.”

“A basketball court?”

He turned to her.

“Why would I take you to a basketball court for our anniversary?”

“Because you’re a basketball player now. Maybe you’ve forgotten how normal people celebrate.”

“Is that what you think?”

“Yes.”

He smiled. She gave him a suspicious look.

“You’re doing that thing again.”

“What thing?”

“Smiling without telling me anything.”

“Would you prefer I looked unhappy?”

“No. I prefer you to be transparent.”

“Noted.”

He took her hand as they walked. The afternoon was cold but bright, the kind of winter day that made the city look clear. They wandered through a quieter part of Shanghai, stopping at a small bookstore and then a café where Xiaoran insisted they share a pastry. Yichen let her choose.

He always let her choose when she was excited about something.

At one point, she stopped in front of a display of little decorative objects.

“Look.”

He followed her gaze. There were small ceramic houses, miniature trees, and tiny figures arranged in a winter village.

“That’s cute,” she said.

“Do you want one?”

She considered it.

“No. We don’t need it.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes. I just like looking.”

He didn’t insist. They continued walking. A few minutes later, she slipped her hand into his coat pocket because hers were cold. Yichen looked down.

“Cold?”

“Very.”

“You should have brought gloves.”

“I brought you.”

He turned his head. She smiled proudly, as if she had delivered a clever answer.

“That’s convenient,” he said.

“Very. You’re warm.”

He squeezed her hand inside his pocket. They returned to his apartment before dinner.

Xiaoran had spent the entire journey home trying to guess whether he had arranged something else. She suspected he had bought her a gift, but she couldn’t tell from his behaviour. He was acting normal. Almost too normal.

He put their coats away, brought her a glass of water, and asked whether she wanted to rest before dinner.

She sat on the sofa, watching him move around the apartment.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Are you hiding something?”

He turned.

“What makes you think that?”

“You’re being suspiciously calm.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Would you like me to panic?”

“No, but—”

He walked over and sat beside her. He opened his arms. She moved closer, and he took her hand. He didn’t say anything. Then he looked at her.

“Do you remember what you said at graduation?”

She blinked.

“The proposal?”

“Mm.”

“Of course. You were very difficult.”

Something in his face eased.

“You said someday, maybe, in theory.”

“I said it more romantically than that.”

“You said it into your hands.”

“Well, my memory is more reliable.”

He gave a quiet laugh. She looked at him more carefully.

“Why are you asking?”

Yichen released her hand and reached into the pocket of his trousers.

When he placed the small box in her palm, she stopped speaking. It was a simple, dark-coloured box. She looked down at it, then at him.

“What’s this?”

“Open it.”

Her fingers moved slowly over the lid. Inside was a ring.

A delicate band, understated and elegant, with a small stone set into it. It wasn’t extravagant. It wasn’t designed to attract attention from across a room.

It looked like something she could wear every day. Something that belonged on her hand. Xiaoran stared at it. For several seconds, she didn’t move. Yichen watched her.

He said, “I thought about getting something more elaborate. But I didn’t think you’d want something you had to be careful with every time you washed your hands or cooked.”

She looked up.

“You chose it?”

“Yes.”

“By yourself?”

“Yes.”

She looked back at the ring.

“It’s beautiful.”

“I’m glad.”

Her thumb brushed the edge of the box.

“Is this…?”

“A promise ring.”

She raised her eyes again. He took a breath, though his voice remained steady.

“It’s not a proposal.”

She nodded slowly.

“I know.”

“I don’t want to ask you to marry me before we’re ready. I want us to finish our degrees, find our footing, and have jobs that we’ve chosen for ourselves. I don’t want you to feel that you have to make a decision about your future just because I have. But I remember what you said that day.”

Her eyes had begun to shine.

“You were joking,” he said, “but I wasn’t sure I wanted to treat it as a joke.”

She met his eyes.

“Yichen…”

“I want to marry you one day.”

The words were simple. He didn’t dress them up. He didn’t make them sound like a grand declaration. He said them with the same calm certainty with which he told her he would pick her up after class. And somehow, that made them even more overwhelming.

He said, “But I want to ask you properly. When we’ve both started working. When we’re ready to make that decision as adults who have built their own lives.” He looked at the ring in her hand.

“Until then, I want this to be a promise. Not a deadline. Not an obligation. Just something that reminds us where we’re going.”

Xiaoran pressed her lips together. She was trying hard not to cry. Yichen noticed. His expression softened.

“Hey.”

She shook her head.

“I’m fine.”

“I know.”

“I’m just—”

She laughed, but her voice trembled.

“You can’t say things like that so casually.”

He reached up and brushed his thumb beneath her eye.

“I wasn’t being casual.”

She turned to him.

“I know.”

A tear slipped down her cheek anyway. He wiped it away. She looked down at the ring again.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Anything.”

“Why now?”

He considered the question.

“Because today is five years.”

She gave him a watery smile.

“That’s very obvious.”

“And because I wanted you to know that I remember.”

Her smile faltered slightly.

“Remember what?”

“That day. What you said. The way you looked at me when I didn’t give you a proper answer.”

She laughed.

“I was very offended.”

“I remember.”

“You said probably.”

“I was eighteen and Yuhao was screaming.”

“You were already annoying.”

He laughed under his breath.

“Probably.”

She looked at the ring again.

“And now?”

“Now I know.”

He reached for her hand.

“May I?”

She nodded. He lifted the ring from its box and slipped it onto her finger. It fit. Xiaoran stared at her hand.

Then she turned it slightly, watching the small stone catch the light. Yichen waited. She finally looked up.

“So…”

“Mm?”

“Does this mean you’re accepting my proposal?”

He looked at her, then that slow, familiar smile appeared.

“The one you made behind the library?”

“Yes.”

“I thought I was supposed to ask properly.”

“You can still ask properly later.”

“Then I suppose I should be careful not to waste my opportunity.”

She laughed. He leaned forward and kissed her hair.

“Happy five years.”

She wrapped her arms around him. He held her close, one hand resting against the back of her head. For a while, she didn’t say anything.

Then, against his shoulder, she whispered, “I want to marry you too.”

His hand paused. She pulled back.

“One day. When we’re ready.”

He held her gaze.

“All right.”

“And I want a proper proposal.”

“I know.”

“With flowers.”

“Of course.”

“And I want to wear a pretty dress.”

“Naturally.”

“And you have to look handsome.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“That’s a requirement?”

“A very important one.”

He laughed and kissed her.

“Then I’ll do my best.”

She leaned her forehead against his.

“You’re going to have to do better than your best.”

“How demanding.”

“You’re marrying me.”

“Not yet.”

She gasped.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed, catching her before she could pull away.

“One day. I’m promising you one day,” he said, pressing a kiss to her cheek.

Dinner was later than planned. Not because either of them had forgotten to eat, but because Xiaoran kept looking at her hand.

She looked at it while Yichen ordered food. She looked at it while they waited.

She looked at it again when he handed her a glass of water. Eventually, he noticed.

“Do you like it?”

She looked up.

“What?”

“The ring.”

She held her hand up.

“Obviously.”

“You’ve been looking at it for twenty minutes.”

“It’s new.”

“I understand.”

“And it’s from you.”

“I understand that too.”

She smiled and reached across the table.

“Do you know what I was thinking?”

“What?”

“That behind the library, I really thought you’d laugh at me.”

He studied her.

“I wanted to say yes properly.”

“Then why didn’t you?”

He took a moment before answering.

“Because I knew you were joking, and I didn’t want to turn something playful into a promise neither of us understood yet.”

He said, “I wanted to be able to give you an answer that I could stand behind.”

Her expression softened.

“That’s very you.”

“Is that good?”

“Very good.”

He reached for her hand.

“Besides, Yuhao was screaming.”

She laughed.

“He was so loud.”

“The birds left.”

He considered her. Then he smiled.

“I think I got the better deal anyway.”

She immediately looked pleased.

“Correct.”

He rubbed his thumb over her ring.

“Though I should warn you.”

“What?”

“You’ll have to keep me for a long time.”

She stared at him. Then her expression turned mischievous.

“Is that a threat?”

“A promise.”

She smiled, and he lifted her hand to kiss her knuckles.

That night, Xiaoran took a photograph of the ring.

She didn’t post a picture of the box or write a long caption. She took a photo of her hand resting on Yichen’s, their fingers intertwined, and added the date.

6 December 2026.

Then she showed him.

“Do you think it’s okay?”

He looked at the picture.

“Yes.”

“Should I post it?”

“If you want to.”

She thought about it, then uploaded it. Her caption was short.

Five years. And he still hasn’t officially accepted my proposal.

Yichen read it over her shoulder. He laughed.

“That’s what you’re going with?”

“Yes.”

“You’re making me look difficult.”

“You are difficult.”

He took out his phone. A moment later, he posted a picture too.

It was the same photograph, but he added his own caption.

Five years with my favourite person. I haven’t forgotten what she asked me at graduation. I’ll ask her properly when the time comes.

Xiaoran read it. Then she read it again. Her smile grew.

“That’s so sweet.”

He put his phone down.

“Good.”

She leaned into him, resting her cheek against his chest.

“Yichen?”

“Mm?”

“Do you think we’ll be different in another five years?”

He looked down at her.

“Probably.”

“How?”

“We’ll have jobs. Different schedules. More responsibilities.”

“Maybe a home.”

“Maybe.”

“Maybe a kitchen where you cook and I supervise.”

“That part seems likely.”

She laughed.

“And maybe we’ll have a proper dining table.”

“You’re very invested in furniture.”

“Because your sofa is not a dining table.”

“You seem to enjoy eating on it.”

“That’s beside the point.”

He smiled and drew her closer. She looked down at her ring once more.

“Do you think we’ll remember today?”

“Yes.”

She considered that. Then she lifted her head.

“Promise?”

Yichen looked at her. He had promised her many things over five years. Some were small: to pick her up, to call when he arrived, to bring her favourite dessert. Others had been more difficult: to keep choosing each other through university, distance, uncertainty, and all the changes that came with growing up.

This one pointed towards something they hadn’t reached yet. He took her hand and kissed the ring.

“Promise.”

Xiaoran smiled. Then she curled closer against him, her fingers resting between his.

Outside, the Sunday evening settled over the city. Xiaoran kept turning the ring with her thumb, and he let her.

chapters.desc: Mrs. Zhou has been making her mother’s braised beef wrong for twenty years. She would like Xiaoran’s help, as long as her son never finds out.
chapters.title: His Mother’s Kitchen, Without Him
chapters.epigraph: “I know you love her. I can see it.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Zhou Yichen’s mother told Xiaoran was that she wasn’t allowed to tell her son. The second was that the recipe was wrong.

“For twenty years. I have been making it wrong for twenty years,” said Mrs. Zhou, standing at the counter with a wooden spoon.

Xiaoran looked down at the handwritten recipe on the counter between them, and then up at her. “Twenty years?”

“At least.”

“How did you find out?”

Mrs. Zhou sighed. “Your boyfriend.”

It was a Saturday afternoon in February, at the Zhous’ house. Yichen had gone off to Herons training after lunch, promising to be back before dinner, and his mother had asked Xiaoran to stay and keep her company in the kitchen, because she needed an extra pair of hands. Xiaoran had assumed it was an ordinary family dinner. She hadn’t expected an investigation.

“Read it,” said Mrs. Zhou, and pushed the paper towards her.

It was old and soft, yellow at the edges, in neat faded handwriting with corrections squeezed into the margins. Braised beef with preserved mustard greens.

“His grandmother’s. My husband’s mother. She made it every New Year. When Yichen was small he’d eat three bowls and fall asleep at the table,” said Mrs. Zhou.

“It sounds wonderful.”

“It is wonderful. Or it was. Last month he ate it here, and he put down his chopsticks, and he said, ‘It’s good, Mum.’ Just like that. It’s good.” Mrs. Zhou lowered her voice, although there was nobody else in the house.

Xiaoran waited.

“He’s said ‘It’s delicious, Mum’ about that dish since he was four years old. Last month it was only good,” said Mrs. Zhou darkly.

Xiaoran pressed her lips together hard.

“His grandmother’s back from Hainan in March. It’s her eightieth. I’m making this for the dinner. I want it right, and I don’t want either of them to know I couldn’t work it out on my own. Taste.” She handed Xiaoran a little bowl and a spoon.

Xiaoran tasted. It was rich and savory and a little sweet.

“It’s good,” she said.

Mrs. Zhou looked at her with deep disappointment. “That’s not helpful.”

“I’m sorry!”

“Don’t be sorry. I know it’s good. I’ve been making it for twenty years.”

“Maybe that’s the problem,” said Xiaoran, before she could stop herself.

Mrs. Zhou stared at her. Xiaoran froze. Then, slowly, Mrs. Zhou began to laugh.

“You’re just like him. Always saying something when I don’t expect it. Come on. We’ll start again from the beginning.” She turned back to the stove.

✦ ✦ ✦

They spent forty minutes getting everything ready. Xiaoran rinsed the mustard greens three times while Mrs. Zhou cut the beef. It was easy, being with her. She didn’t treat Xiaoran like a guest who had to be entertained. She gave her jobs, and topped up her tea without asking, and twice reached over and tucked Xiaoran’s hair back behind her ear so it wouldn’t fall near the flame, the way Xiaoran’s own mother did.

When Xiaoran reached for the sugar, Mrs. Zhou put a hand on her wrist. “Not so much.”

“It says two spoons.”

“I always use one and a half.”

“Why?”

“Because Yichen doesn’t like things too sweet. When he was little he used to pick out anything sweet and line it up on the edge of the bowl. His grandmother said he was the fussiest child in the province.”

“He still is a bit fussy.”

“Don’t tell him I said so.”

“I won’t. He lines his carrots up on the side of the plate too,” said Xiaoran.

“Still?”

“In size order.”

Mrs. Zhou put her knife down and laughed until she had to wipe her eyes on her wrist.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran was looking at the recipe again while the beef browned, and something near the bottom caught her eye. She leaned in closer.

“Auntie? What’s this?”

Mrs. Zhou came and looked over her shoulder. Xiaoran pointed at a line of faded characters.

“Is that vinegar?”

“That’s what I’ve always thought.”

“How much do you put in?”

“One spoon.”

Xiaoran tilted the paper towards the window. “It might say two. And there’s something next to it. Really small. Last. A little.” She squinted.

“Add at the end. Only a little,” Mrs. Zhou read slowly.

She went quiet. Then she turned and looked at the pot, where the vinegar had gone in ten minutes ago with the soy sauce, at the start, the way it had gone in every New Year for twenty years.

“Oh,” said Mrs. Zhou.

Xiaoran pressed her lips together.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I’m trying not to.”

Mrs. Zhou put her hand over her eyes. “Twenty years. His grandmother will never let me forget this. She’ll tell the neighbours. She’ll tell the temple.” And then she started laughing too, helplessly, with her hand on the counter, and Xiaoran gave up and laughed with her.

They started a second pot. This time the vinegar waited in a little dish beside the stove.

✦ ✦ ✦

While it simmered Xiaoran wiped down the counter, and Mrs. Zhou dried her hands and said, “Xiaoran. Can I ask you something?”

“Of course, Auntie.”

“Have you and Yichen talked about what happens after you graduate?”

It was asked gently. But it landed differently from everything else they’d said all afternoon.

“A little.”

“A little?”

“About jobs. Where we’d like to work. Things like that.”

“He’s staying in Shanghai. With the Herons.”

“I know.”

“And you?”

“I’m looking too. There are a few studios I’d love to work for. Some in Shanghai. Some not.”

Mrs. Zhou nodded, and didn’t ask which ones. She pulled out a chair at the kitchen table and sat, and after a moment Xiaoran sat down opposite her.

“I don’t want to make you uncomfortable. But I wondered whether you’ve talked about what you’ll do if your plans don’t line up perfectly,” said Mrs. Zhou.

Xiaoran looked down at her hands. She understood what the question was. Not whether she loved him; his parents had watched that grow since they were sixteen. It was the part nobody could predict.

“We have. Not every detail. But we’ve talked,” she said eventually.

“And?”

“We’re still working it out.”

“Does that worry you?”

Xiaoran thought about it, and was surprised how easily the answer came, here in the warm kitchen with nobody else listening.

“A bit. Sometimes I think, what if I get something somewhere else? Or he does? I don’t want either of us to give something up before we’ve even tried. I love him. But I want to build my own life too. And I think he wants the same thing for me.” She turned her teacup round on the table.

“He does,” said Mrs. Zhou at once.

“I know. He’s never once asked me to choose between him and my work.”

“That sounds like my son. He’s very stubborn, though.” Mrs. Zhou smiled.

“Very.”

“And he thinks he can solve everything by being quiet and sensible.”

“Yes.”

“Does he do that with you?”

“Sometimes. But I tell him when he’s being annoying.”

Mrs said, “Good. Then I’ll only say one thing. Whatever happens when you graduate, I hope you won’t make yourself smaller to fit into his life. He’s always known what he wants. Even as a little boy. But that doesn’t mean the people he loves should arrange their lives around him.” Zhou, and reached across the table and put her hand over Xiaoran’s.

Xiaoran’s throat went tight. “Thank you, Auntie.”

“And don’t think that because you’ve been together so long, everyone expects you to have it all decided.”

“I think I’m more frightened of disappointing myself than anyone else,” Xiaoran said, low.

Mrs. Zhou looked at her with an understanding that made her eyes sting. “Then don’t disappoint yourself. There’s plenty of time,” she said, and squeezed her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past five the sauce had thickened and the beef was coming apart at the touch of a spoon. Mrs. Zhou tipped in the vinegar, a little, right at the end, and stirred it once, and tasted. Then she handed Xiaoran the spoon without a word. Xiaoran tasted it. She stopped.

It was still rich, but brighter now. The vinegar sat on top of the flavour instead of sinking into it, and the sweetness didn’t linger the way it had before.

“Oh.”

“Different?”

“Very different.”

“Better?”

“So much better.”

Mrs. Zhou looked enormously pleased. She took a pen out of the drawer and crossed out her own old note in the margin and wrote the correction beside it, neatly. Then, underneath, smaller: Corrected after twenty years. And under that: With Xiaoran.

“Auntie. You don’t have to write my name.”

“I know. I want to.” She put the pen down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen came home at six with his hair blown about by the wind.

“Mum?”

“Kitchen!”

His eyes found Xiaoran first. “You’ve been here all afternoon?”

“Yes.”

He came over and kissed her cheek, right in front of his mother, who looked away at the ceiling and smiled. “Have you eaten?”

“Not yet. Your mother’s been making something.”

He looked at the stove. “What?”

His mother turned round with a smile that was a little too pleased. “Something you’ve been complaining about.”

“I haven’t complained about anything.”

“You said it was good.”

He looked at her blankly. Then at the pot. Then at the recipe on the counter. Xiaoran watched him see the correction in the margin, and his face changed.

“You add the vinegar at the end.”

His mother lifted her chin. “Yes.”

He took a clean spoon from the drawer and tasted it. He didn’t say anything. Xiaoran and his mother both watched him in total silence. He tasted it again.

“It’s delicious,” he said.

His mother looked at Xiaoran. Xiaoran looked at the floor and bit the inside of her cheek.

“Did you help?” he asked her.

“Your mother was very patient with me.”

“She usually is.”

“Excuse me. Go and wash your hands,” said his mother.

He went. On his way past Xiaoran he ran his fingers along the back of her hand on the counter, a small, familiar touch, and she turned her hand over and caught his for a second before he was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was long and warm. His father came down from his study, and the conversation went from the Herons to her final-year project to the grandmother’s eightieth in March and who would sit where. Yichen ate two bowls of the beef without comment. His mother watched him across the table the whole time.

Eventually she said, “Well?”

“Well what?”

“Does it taste right?”

He nodded. “Yes.”

“Good.”

He looked at the dish, and then at her. “Why did you change it?”

“Because I wanted to,” said his mother, and lifted her teacup.

He glanced at Xiaoran, who was smiling down at her rice. His eyes narrowed. “What did you two do this afternoon?”

“Nothing,” said Xiaoran.

“She helped me fix your grandmother’s recipe. And we talked about graduation,” said his mother.

Xiaoran nearly dropped her chopsticks. Yichen looked at his mother. His mother looked perfectly innocent. He looked at Xiaoran, and she gave him a small, helpless smile, and he understood. Not the details. Enough. He didn’t ask in front of his parents. He just put his hand under the table and found hers on her knee, and held it for the rest of the meal.

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her to the gate afterward, and helped her into her coat in the hall, and tucked the end of her scarf in properly at the front.

“What did you and Mum talk about?”

“Cooking.”

He waited.

“Your grandmother’s recipe.”

“Xiaoran.”

“Fine. Graduation.”

His face softened. “What about it?”

“She asked if we’d talked about our plans. I said we had. I said we were still working it out.”

“Good.”

“You’re not upset?”

“Why would I be?”

“Because we haven’t decided everything.”

“We’re allowed not to have everything decided. I’ve been thinking about it too. About after. I want to stay in Shanghai, if it works out with the Herons. You’ve got your own plans. I don’t want to assume you’ll pick the same place as me just because I’m there. I don’t want you to choose something smaller because it’s easier for me. And I don’t want to choose something just because I’m scared of being far away from you.” He kept his hands on her scarf. He looked at her.

“So what do we do?”

“We keep talking.”

“That’s your solution?”

“For now.”

“Very practical.”

“I study business,” he said.

She laughed and slid her arms round him inside his open jacket.

“I want a future with you. That part isn’t uncertain. I just don’t think we have to decide its whole shape before we’ve graduated,” he said into her hair.

She nodded against his chest.

“And when you get an offer somewhere,” he said, “I want to hear about it before you start worrying whether it fits round me.”

“You’re making it very hard to be dramatic.”

“Would you like me to argue?”

“No,” she said, and held on.

After a while she lifted her head. “Your mother wrote my name on the recipe.”

“Did she?”

“In the margin. With Xiaoran.”

He smiled. “Then you’re part of the recipe now.”

“That’s a terrible line.”

“I thought it was good.”

“It’s terrible,” she said, and kissed him, and let go only when the taxi he’d called turned into the road. With the door half open she turned round.

“Yichen. Your mother said it’s been wrong for twenty years.”

“I know.”

“How do you know?”

“Grandma told me. When I was about ten.”

She stared at him. “Then why didn’t you ever say?”

He thought about it, standing at the gate in the cold. “Because Mum liked making it for us. And it was still good.”

“But last month you only said good. Not delicious.”

He went still. “Is that what she told you?”

“That’s how she knew.”

“I’d had a bad game. I wasn’t paying attention to the beef,” he said slowly.

Xiaoran looked at him for one long second. Then she put both hands over her mouth and was laughing too much and had to sit down in the taxi with the door still open, and the driver asked if she was all right, and she couldn’t answer.

“You’re not to tell her,” she managed at last.

“I wasn’t going to,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Back in the kitchen his mother was putting the leftovers away. He picked up the recipe off the counter and looked at the new line in the margin.

“Mum. You wrote her name.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

She looked at him as if the answer were obvious. “Because she helped.”

He nodded and put the paper down.

“She’s a good girl. She has her own plans, you know,” said his mother.

“I know.”

“Don’t make the mistake of thinking that loving someone means they’ll fit into your plans.”

“I won’t.”

She touched his arm. “I know you love her. I can see it. When you graduate there’ll be a lot of decisions. Let her make hers. And make yours honestly.”

“I will.”

She studied him. Then she smiled. “And when are you bringing her back to cook with me?”

“Why?”

“Because she’s got better eyes than me, and now I’ve got someone who can read your grandmother’s handwriting.”

He laughed. Then he folded the recipe carefully, so the crease didn’t run through Xiaoran’s name, and put it back in the drawer where it lived, between the rice cooker manual and a takeaway menu from 2009.

chapters.desc: A small studio in Shanghai and the Beijing company from her internship both want her. He tells her not to choose a smaller future to make their schedule easier.
chapters.title: Job Fair
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t want my worry to become your limitation.”
chapters.content:
The spring job fair was in the second week of March, and Xiaoran had prepared for it as if she were going to war.

There were three copies of her résumé in a folder, a digital portfolio saved on her laptop and phone, a notebook containing questions she had researched the night before, and a carefully selected outfit that had taken her nearly forty minutes to decide on.

She had even practised introducing herself in front of the mirror. Twice.

The third attempt had been interrupted by Yichen walking into the bedroom and asking whether she was auditioning for a television program. She had thrown a cushion at him.

Now, standing in front of the university’s employment fair, she was beginning to regret not bringing a fourth copy of her résumé.

“Relax,” Yichen said.

She turned to him.

“Don’t tell me to relax.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You just did.”

“I said relax.”

“Exactly.”

He looked at the folder in her hands.

“You’ve checked everything?”

“Yes.”

“Portfolio?”

“Yes.”

“Résumé?”

“Yes.”

“Phone charged?”

She paused. He raised an eyebrow. Xiaoran immediately took out her phone.

“Eighty-two percent.”

“Good.”

She put it away and looked at him suspiciously.

“Why are you so calm?”

“Because I’m not the one looking for a job.”

She blinked at him.

“That’s not supportive.”

He smiled and adjusted the strap of her handbag where it had slipped down her shoulder.

“You’re prepared. You know what you’ve done. Just talk to them.”

She met his eyes. Then she nodded.

“Okay.”

He lowered his head slightly.

“And don’t forget to enjoy it.”

“Enjoy a job fair?”

“You’re meeting people who might want to work with you.”

She considered that. Then her expression brightened a little.

“That’s actually a nice way to think about it.”

“I know.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“Don’t look so pleased.”

He smiled.

“Go on. I’ll be around.”

She turned towards the entrance, took three steps, then came back. Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

She held out her hand. He glanced at it.

“What’s this?”

“Luck.”

He took her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Good luck.”

That made her grin. Then, as she walked away, he called after her.

“Xiaoran.”

She turned.

“Yes?”

“Your folder.”

She looked down. She had nearly left it on the bench. He held it out. Her face went blank. Then she hurried back and took it.

“Don’t tell anyone.”

“I won’t.”

“Especially not Meilin.”

“I wouldn’t dare.”

She gave him a warning look and disappeared into the crowd. Yichen watched her go, smiling to himself. The fair was busier than Xiaoran had expected.

There were companies from different industries, recruitment teams standing behind booths, students moving between them with résumés, and a steady stream of conversations that made the entire hall sound like one enormous interview.

She started with the companies she was less interested in. It was a strategy.

She wanted to warm up before approaching the studios and media companies she had actually researched.

The first conversation went well. The second was a little awkward. By the third, she had found her rhythm.

She explained her eight weeks in Beijing the summer after second year, the campaign proposal her supervisor had sent back three times, and the noodle-shop campaign she had rewritten four times before anyone saw it.

When one recruiter asked about a challenge she had faced, she described the noodle shop: an owner who wanted students, and students who only wanted it cheap.

She explained what she had learned about audience research and how she would approach the campaign differently now. The recruiter nodded, taking notes.

“That’s a thoughtful reflection. A lot of candidates focus only on what they achieved.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“I think understanding what could have been done better is also important.”

“Absolutely.”

By the time she moved to the next section, she was feeling more confident. Then she saw the booth.

Morrow Studio, Shanghai.

A creative production studio specialising in branded films, digital campaigns, and short-form storytelling. She had researched them the previous evening.

Their work was visually distinctive, and several of their campaigns had caught her attention because they combined commercial objectives with strong narrative concepts. She approached the booth. A woman in her early thirties greeted her.

“Hello. Are you interested in our creative team?”

“Yes. I’m studying Media, and I’m particularly interested in content strategy and creative production.”

“Great. Do you have a portfolio?”

Xiaoran handed over her folder and opened the digital version on her laptop.

The recruiter, whose name tag read Lin Qian, began looking through it.

“Tell me about this project.”

Xiaoran leaned slightly closer.

“That’s Before the Morning Comes. I directed it with my partner, Chi Yuan, for the faculty showcase last May.”

Lin Qian spent a few moments reviewing the opening and reading the accompanying description.

“Interesting. What was your main responsibility?”

Xiaoran explained the development process, how she had worked through the initial concept, coordinated with her team, and made decisions about pacing and visual language.

She also discussed the difficulties of maintaining a consistent creative direction when different people had different interpretations of the story. Lin Qian listened carefully.

“Did you enjoy directing?”

“Yes. Although I also enjoy the strategy behind a project. I like understanding why a particular story should be told, who we’re telling it to, and what we want the audience to take away.”

“So you don’t want to limit yourself to production?”

“Not necessarily. I would like to understand the entire process.”

Lin Qian smiled.

“That’s good. We’re looking for people who can think creatively but also understand the objectives behind the work.”

She asked Xiaoran a few more questions about her previous experience and the kind of projects she wanted to work on. Then she closed the folder.

“I’d like our creative director to look at your portfolio. Would you be available for a formal interview next week?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Yes. Absolutely.”

Lin Qian handed her a card.

“Send me your updated portfolio and résumé. I’ll arrange something.”

Xiaoran accepted it with both hands.

“Thank you so much.”

“Thank you. I enjoyed speaking with you.”

She stepped away from the booth, looking down at the card. Then she looked at it again. A formal interview. She hadn’t expected that to happen so quickly. Her phone vibrated.

Yichen: How’s it going?

She took a photograph of the card and sent it.

Xiaoran: LOOK.

He replied almost immediately.

Yichen: Interview?

Xiaoran: Next week.

Yichen: Congratulations.

Xiaoran: I haven’t even interviewed yet.

Yichen: They wouldn’t invite you if they weren’t interested.

Her mouth tipped up.

Xiaoran: I’m going to pretend to be calm.

Yichen: How’s that going?

Xiaoran: Terribly.

He sent a laughing emoji. She put her phone away and continued walking. There was another booth she wanted to visit.

The booth from Beijing was larger, and she knew the logo before she could read the name: the company where she had spent eight weeks the summer after second year.

Their recruitment team was speaking with several students, and a digital display showed photographs of their office, production facilities, and recent campaigns.

Lanshan Media Group, Beijing.

At the end of the internship, one of the senior staff had asked whether she’d come back. She had laughed and said she had two more years of university. In January, her old supervisor had sent a two-line message: the graduate program was open, and she should apply.

She had. She hadn’t expected much. The program took few people. She approached the booth. A recruiter looked up.

“Hello. Are you here for our graduate program?”

“Yes.”

“Have you applied online?”

“Yes. I’m Lin Xiaoran.”

The recruiter checked her tablet. Her expression changed slightly.

“Ah. Your supervisor from the summer program put a note on your file.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Really?”

“And your portfolio went straight to our content strategy team.”

She tried not to look too surprised.

“Thank you.”

The recruiter introduced herself as Zhang Wen and asked Xiaoran to sit down. They spoke for nearly twenty minutes.

Unlike the conversation at Morrow Studio, which had focused heavily on creative production, this one explored Xiaoran’s ability to think across different business functions.

Zhang Wen asked about her campaign experience, her understanding of digital audiences, and how she would approach a project with limited resources.

Xiaoran spoke about the summer campaign in Beijing: a reading app that had to win over teenagers and the parents who paid for it.

She described the balance between something a fifteen-year-old would open and something a parent would trust. Zhang Wen listened.

“What would you do differently if you had the opportunity to run that campaign again?”

“I would gather more insights from parents and students earlier in the planning stage. We had a good understanding of the platform’s objectives, but I think we could have made some creative decisions more effective if we had tested our assumptions earlier.”

Zhang Wen nodded.

“That’s sensible.”

She looked at Xiaoran’s portfolio again.

“And your showcase film is quite different from the campaign work.”

“Yes.”

“Do you prefer one?”

Xiaoran thought about it.

“I like different parts of both. With film, I enjoy developing an idea and translating it into something people can experience. With marketing, I enjoy understanding the audience and figuring out how to communicate something effectively.”

“So you’re interested in both creative development and strategy.”

“Yes. I don’t think they’re necessarily separate.”

Zhang Wen smiled.

“That’s a good answer.”

She closed the portfolio.

“Our Beijing office has a graduate position in the content and brand strategy team. It’s a structured program, and successful candidates will have the opportunity to work across several projects.”

Xiaoran listened carefully.

“We’d like to invite you to the next round of interviews. The team would be interested in meeting you.”

Xiaoran didn’t respond. Then she smiled.

“Thank you. I’d be very happy to.”

Zhang Wen handed her another card.

“One thing I should mention: the position is based in Beijing. The team expects successful candidates to relocate.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“I understand.”

“Would that be something you’d consider?”

She hesitated. Not because she had never considered living in Beijing. She had.

But it was different when someone asked her to make it a practical decision.

“Yes, I’d consider it,” she said.

Zhang Wen nodded.

“Good. We’ll be in touch about the next stage.”

Xiaoran thanked her and stepped away. She walked several metres before stopping.

Then she looked down at the two cards in her hand. One Shanghai. One Beijing. Two interviews. Two different opportunities. She stared at them. Then she whispered to herself:

“Oh.”

Yichen found her near the café area. She was sitting at a small table with her laptop open, two business cards placed neatly beside her notebook. He approached from behind.

“Finished?”

“Yichen!”

He sat down opposite her.

“How was it?”

She didn’t answer immediately. Instead, she pushed the two cards towards him. He looked at them. Then he looked at her.

“Both?”

She nodded.

“Both.”

He picked up the first card.

“Morrow Studio.”

“They want to interview me next week.”

He picked up the second.

“Lanshan.”

“They also want me for the next round.”

He set the cards down.

“That’s good.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“That’s all?”

“What else?”

“Can you be a little more excited?”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Congratulations.”

She waited. He leaned forward.

“Look at you.”

Her expression softened.

“Thank you.”

He glanced at the cards again.

“How different are the positions?”

She immediately became more animated.

“Very different. Morrow is more creative production. They work on branded films, campaigns, short-form content. I think I would get to be involved in the development process and maybe eventually work with directors and production teams.”

“And Beijing?”

“More structured. It’s a graduate program in content and brand strategy. I’d get to work across different projects and teams.”

“Which one do you prefer?”

She looked down at the cards.

“I don’t know.”

He didn’t rush to fill the silence.

She said, “I like Morrow’s work. Their creative direction is really interesting. I can imagine myself learning a lot there.”

“And Lanshan?”

“I think the program would give me broader experience. More exposure to strategy and different parts of the business.”

She leaned back.

“They’re both good.”

“Then that’s a good problem to have.”

She turned to him.

“No.”

“Then yes.”

She laughed. He reached for her hand.

“Don’t make yourself choose before you’ve even interviewed.”

“I know.”

“Talk to both teams. Find out what the actual work looks like. Ask about the people, the responsibilities, the opportunities to grow.”

She nodded.

“And think about where you want to be.”

She looked at the Beijing card.

“That’s the difficult part.”

Yichen followed her gaze.

“Because of the city?”

She nodded.

“Beijing is far.”

“Yes.”

“And you’re here.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him. He was still holding her hand.

“Would you mind?”

He tilted his head slightly.

“Would I mind what?”

“If I moved to Beijing.”

He didn’t answer immediately. Not because he didn’t know what he wanted, but because he wanted to answer the question she was actually asking.

“Would I miss you?” he said.

She nodded.

“Of course.”

He rubbed his thumb over her knuckles.

“Would it be difficult? Yes.”

She looked down.

“But would I want you to reject a good opportunity just because I’m in Shanghai?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Then you already know my answer.”

She looked up again. Something in his face eased.

“I want you to have a career you’re excited about, Xiaoran. I don’t want you to choose a smaller future just because it makes our schedule easier.”

Her eyes softened.

“But I don’t want to be far away from you.”

“I know.”

“And I don’t want you to feel like you have to support me if I leave.”

“Xiaoran.”

She stopped. He leaned closer.

“I’m not supporting you because I have to. I’m supporting you because I want to.”

She held his gaze. Then she smiled.

“You’re being very reasonable.”

“Should I be less reasonable?”

“No.”

He smiled. She picked up the two cards again.

“I think I’ll go to both interviews.”

“Good.”

“And then I’ll decide.”

“Good.”

She studied him.

“You’re not worried?”

“About what?”

“That I’ll go to Beijing.”

He met her eyes.

“I’d rather miss you than watch you turn down something you really want because you’re afraid of missing me.”

She was quiet. Then she reached across the table and touched his cheek.

“You’re really good at saying things that make me like you more.”

He caught her hand and kissed her palm.

“That’s fortunate.”

She laughed. The first interview was at Morrow Studio.

It took place the following Wednesday in a bright office with large windows and an open production area. Xiaoran arrived fifteen minutes early.

She had prepared for the interview carefully. She knew the studio’s recent campaigns, had reviewed the job description, and had prepared questions about the role.

Lin Qian greeted her and introduced her to the creative director, a man named Gao Yan. The interview was detailed.

They discussed her portfolio, her final film, and her previous marketing experience. Gao Yan asked how she handled creative disagreement and what she would do if a client rejected an idea she believed in. Xiaoran answered thoughtfully.

She explained that she would first try to understand the client’s concern rather than immediately defend her idea. She believed creative work had to serve a purpose, and if the purpose wasn’t being communicated clearly, she needed to reconsider how she presented it. Gao Yan seemed interested. At the end, he closed her portfolio.

“I think you’d fit well with the team.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Thank you.”

“We’re still speaking with other candidates, but I’d like to move you forward.”

She nodded.

“Of course.”

“One question. If we made you an offer, would you be comfortable starting in Shanghai?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

That got a smile out of him.

“I think we can give you quite a bit of room to grow here. You’ll be involved in real projects from the beginning, not just supporting work.”

Xiaoran listened carefully. It sounded exciting. It also sounded like the kind of environment where she would have to learn quickly. She left the office feeling optimistic.

But she didn’t know yet whether it was the right place.

The Lanshan interview took place two days later, online.

The interviewers were from the Beijing office: one from recruitment and another from the content strategy team. It was more structured than the Morrow interview.

They asked about her experience, her analytical approach, and how she would respond to a campaign that was performing below expectations.

Xiaoran described how she would review audience behaviour, examine the campaign’s performance against its objectives, and identify whether the problem was with the content, targeting, distribution, or the underlying strategy. The content strategy manager nodded.

“Good. And what would you do if the creative team disagreed with your recommendation?”

“I’d want to understand their reasoning. I wouldn’t assume that the data automatically tells us what creative decision to make. It helps us identify a problem, but we still need judgement to decide how to solve it.”

The manager smiled.

“That’s a balanced answer.”

They discussed the graduate program, the expected workload, and the possibility of moving between teams. Then the recruiter asked:

“Are you comfortable relocating to Beijing?”

Xiaoran took a breath.

“Yes. I’d be open to it.”

“Do you have any concerns?”

She thought about the question.

“I’d want to understand the relocation support and the working arrangements. But professionally, I’m comfortable with the opportunity.”

“That’s reasonable.”

The interview ended on a positive note. When she closed her laptop, she sat. Two interviews. Two teams. Two different possibilities.

She didn’t feel the same excitement she had felt at the job fair.

Instead, she felt the weight of a decision approaching. That evening, she went to Yichen’s apartment.

He was reviewing footage from his latest game when she arrived. He looked up as she entered.

“How was it?”

She put her bag down.

“Good.”

“Good?”

“Very good, actually.”

He closed the laptop. He reached for her. She walked over, and he pulled her into a hug. She rested her cheek against his shoulder.

“I think they liked me.”

“I know.”

She leaned back.

“How do you know?”

“Because they invited you to interview.”

“That’s not the same.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“All right. Tell me.”

She sat beside him and explained the interview. She told him about the creative director’s questions, the team structure, and how much responsibility the role might offer. Then she told him about Lanshan.

When she finished, he asked, “Which one made you more excited?”

She thought about it.

“Morrow.”

“Which one made you think more?”

“Lanshan.”

“Why?”

“Because it feels like a bigger decision. It’s a graduate program. A structured path. I might learn more about strategy and business.”

“And Morrow?”

“I’d get to work on projects I genuinely like.”

He turned to her.

“Those aren’t mutually exclusive.”

“I know.”

She leaned back against the sofa.

“That’s why it’s difficult.”

Yichen reached for her hand.

“Have you thought about what you want your first job to give you?”

She considered it.

“Experience. Good people to learn from. The chance to work on projects that matter.”

“Anything else?”

She tilted her head.

“I want to feel like I’m becoming good at something.”

He nodded.

“Then ask them how they’ll help you do that.”

“You’re making this sound very simple.”

“It’s not simple. But you don’t have to decide based on the company name or how impressive the program sounds.”

She looked down at their hands.

“I think I’m afraid of choosing wrong.”

He was quiet. Then he said, “You might.”

She looked up.

He said, “Not because you’re careless. Sometimes you make the best decision you can with what you know, and later you learn something you couldn’t have known at the time.”

She listened.

“That doesn’t mean you chose badly.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“You’re making me feel better.”

“Good.”

She leaned against him.

“Do you ever feel like everyone else knows what they’re doing?”

“Yes.”

She turned her head.

“Really?”

“Of course.”

“But you always seem so sure.”

“That’s because I don’t usually announce every time I’m uncertain.”

She laughed. He kissed her.

“You’re allowed to figure things out.”

She closed her eyes.

“Okay.”

The offers came the following week. Morrow called first.

Lin Qian explained that the creative director had been impressed with Xiaoran’s portfolio and interview. They wanted to offer her a junior creative producer position, with opportunities to work across branded films and digital campaigns.

The offer included a starting salary, a clear reporting structure, and a six-month review.

Xiaoran thanked her and asked for the written offer.

She was still processing it when her phone rang again. Lanshan.

Zhang Wen told her that the content strategy team wanted to move forward with her application.

They were offering her a place in the graduate program.

The program included rotations across content strategy, campaign planning, and brand development. The position was based in Beijing, with a planned start date after graduation.

Xiaoran thanked her and asked for the written details. Then she sat at her desk. Two offers. Not just interviews anymore. Two companies wanted her. She stared at the emails. A smile slowly appeared on her face.

Then she picked up her phone and called Yichen. He answered while leaving the training facility.

“Hello?”

She didn’t say anything. He paused.

“Xiaoran?”

“Yichen.”

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Then?”

She took a breath.

“I got both.”

There was a short silence. Then he smiled.

“Both offers?”

“Yes.”

“Congratulations.”

She laughed.

“I got both!”

“I heard you.”

“They both want me.”

“I know.”

She could hear the smile in his voice.

“Yichen.”

“Yes?”

“I’m really happy.”

“I’m happy for you.”

She sat back in her chair.

“Morrow offered me the creative producer position. And Lanshan offered me the graduate program.”

“That’s excellent.”

“One in Shanghai. One in Beijing.”

“I remember.”

She laughed. Then she became quiet.

“What do I do?”

He didn’t answer immediately.

“Have you read both offers?”

“Yes.”

“All the details?”

“Mostly.”

“Then let’s read them properly tonight.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Together?”

“Of course.”

She looked at the emails again.

“Okay.”

“And Xiaoran?”

“Mm?”

“Don’t forget that you earned both of them.”

Her smile softened.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

She laughed.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He opened the car door.

“I’ll come over after training tomorrow. We’ll look through everything.”

She nodded, then remembered he couldn’t see her.

“Okay.”

“Congratulations, filmmaker.”

She smiled.

“Thank you, basketball player.”

They spent the following evening at his apartment, comparing the offers. Yichen had made tea. Xiaoran had brought her laptop and a notebook.

They sat at the dining table, with the two offer letters open side by side. She had created a comparison sheet. Yichen looked at it.

“You made a table.”

“Yes.”

“Of course you did.”

She pointed at the screen.

“Don’t underestimate the power of a table.”

“I’m not.”

“Good.”

They went through the details one by one. Morrow offered a more direct creative role. She would work closely with the production team and gain practical experience in content development and branded storytelling.

Lanshan offered a structured graduate program, broader exposure, and the opportunity to build a foundation in content and brand strategy. The salaries were different. The benefits were different. The working environments were different. And the cities were different. Xiaoran rested her chin on her hand.

“Which one would you choose?”

Yichen looked at her.

“I’m not you.”

“I know. I’m asking what you think.”

He considered the two documents.

“I think both are good opportunities. But I wouldn’t choose Lanshan just because the program sounds more prestigious, and I wouldn’t choose Morrow just because it’s in Shanghai.”

“That’s what I was thinking.”

“Which job would you want to wake up for?”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“That’s a difficult question.”

“Then think about it.”

She looked at the Morrow offer.

“I can imagine myself working there.”

Then she looked at Lanshan.

“I can also imagine myself there.”

Yichen leaned back.

“Then maybe you need more information.”

She looked at him.

“Such as?”

“Ask to speak with someone who would work with you directly. Ask about the projects you’ll actually handle. Ask what success looks like after six months.”

She nodded slowly. That made her grin.

“You sound like you’ve become very experienced.”

“I’ve learned a few things.”

“From basketball?”

“From working with people.”

She studied his face. Then she closed her laptop.

“I think I want to sleep on it.”

“Good.”

She stood and walked around the table. Yichen looked up as she came to stand beside him. She leaned down and kissed his cheek.

“Thank you.”

He caught her hand.

“For what?”

“For not telling me to stay.”

He held her gaze.

“Would you have stayed?”

She thought about it.

“I don’t know.”

“Then I’m glad I didn’t.”

She rested her forehead against his.

“You’re not worried?”

“I am.”

She blinked.

“Really?”

“Of course. If you move to Beijing, I’ll miss you.”

Her expression softened.

“But?”

“But I don’t want my worry to become your limitation.”

She looked at him. Then she kissed him, slowly, with both offer letters still open on the screen behind her. He held her.

And for a while, neither of them said anything.

Later that night, Xiaoran sat at the edge of his bed, looking at the two offer letters on her laptop. Yichen was in the bathroom. She glanced at the ring on her finger. Five years together. A promise made in December.

A future they had begun to imagine, but not yet built. She opened a blank document. At the top, she typed:

What do I want from my first job?

Then she began writing. She wrote about the work she wanted to do, the skills she wanted to develop, the kind of people she wanted to learn from, and the person she wanted to become.

When Yichen came out, he found her still typing.

“Still thinking?”

She nodded.

“Just organising my thoughts.”

He came over and sat beside her.

“Anything interesting?”

She turned the laptop slightly. He read the heading. Then he looked at her.

“Good question.”

She smiled.

“I think I need to answer it before I choose.”

He nodded. She closed the laptop.

“Not tonight, though.”

“Not tonight.”

She leaned against his shoulder.

“Can we just have a normal evening?”

He put his arm around her.

“Of course.”

“No job talk.”

“All right.”

“No contract talk.”

“All right.”

“No basketball. That’s becoming difficult.”

She laughed.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He smiled and kissed her temple.

“Fine.”

She settled against him. After a few minutes, she spoke again.

“Actually, one thing.”

He looked down.

“What?”

“When I become successful, you have to be proud of me.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Only when?”

That made her grin.

“Well, I’m not successful yet.”

He took her hand and kissed the ring.

“I’m proud of you now.”

Her expression softened.

“Good.”

He studied her.

“And when you become successful, I’ll be proud of you then too.”

She smiled and rested her head against his chest.

Two offers sat in her inbox, and she fell asleep before she had chosen either.

chapters.desc: Beijing has made her an offer. Everyone wants to know why not, and she wants to be the one who answers.
chapters.title: Why Not Beijing
chapters.epigraph: “I understand that you want the job.”
chapters.content:
It started over dinner, with a question about her laptop.

It was a Sunday evening in March. They were both home for the weekend, and Zhou Yichen had come round to the Lins’ for dinner, the way he did most weekends they were home now. Lin Xiaoran had her laptop open on the dining table beside a half-finished bowl of soup. Her mother was cutting fruit in the kitchen. Her father came out of the study, glanced at the screen as he sat down, and said, “What’s that?”

“Oh. It’s an offer.”

“What offer?”

She hesitated, only for half a second. Not because she meant to hide it. Because she knew the conversation wasn’t going to be short.

“From Lanshan. In Beijing. The company I interned with, the summer after second year. They were at the spring job fair. My old supervisor had put a note on my file. I interviewed last week, and they sent me the details yesterday.”

“Another internship?”

“No. A real job. Junior creative producer.”

Her father pulled the laptop towards him and read it. She watched his face. It didn’t move.

“Where’s the office?”

She showed him.

“Where would you live?”

“They’ve sent some recommendations. I’ve looked at flats near the office as well.”

“And the salary?”

She told him.

“Is that enough to live on in Beijing?”

“I’ve worked it out. Rent, transport, food. It’s enough.”

He read to the bottom. Then he pushed the laptop lid halfway down.

“No.”

She stared at him. She hadn’t expected him to be pleased. She hadn’t expected that.

“Dad, you haven’t even—”

“I’ve read enough.”

“Enough to know what?”

“That it’s in Beijing.”

Her mother came out with the plate of fruit and stopped, looking from one to the other. “What’s wrong?”

“Your daughter wants to go to Beijing.”

Her mother put the plate down. “For work? Is this the one you mentioned last week?”

“Yes.”

Her father sat back. “Why does it have to be Beijing?”

It was said. But it wasn’t really a question.

Xiaoran put her spoon down. “Because that’s where the job is.”

“There are companies here. Shanghai has plenty of studios.”

“I know, Dad.”

“Then why go so far?”

“Because I want to try. Somewhere new. A bigger team. Being responsible for myself. It’s exactly the kind of work I want to do.”

“You can find that here.”

“Maybe. But this is the offer I’ve got.”

“You’re about to graduate. You should think carefully about what kind of life you want. Not just take a job because somebody offered it to you in another city.”

“I’m not just taking it.”

“Then what are you basing it on?”

“The role. The people. The work.”

“And the distance?”

Her fingers tightened round the spoon. “What about it?”

“You’ll be on your own. You won’t know anyone.”

“I’ll make friends.”

“That’s not the point.”

“Then what is the point?”

He didn’t answer. Her mother sat down next to him and put her hand on his arm.

“Let her explain.”

“I’m listening,” said her father. But his face said he had already decided.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen hadn’t said a word. He wasn’t absent; he’d listened to every sentence, his eyes moving between her and her father. He knew all about the job. He knew how her voice had gone when she told him about the interview, and how many evenings she’d spent reading about the company’s old campaigns, curled up against him on his sofa with her laptop on her knees. He knew she hadn’t said yes. She’d wanted to talk to her parents first.

He didn’t say Beijing was a good idea. He didn’t tell her father she was perfectly capable of living on her own. He didn’t offer to visit every weekend or say that the distance wouldn’t matter. She hadn’t asked him to defend her, and her father hadn’t asked for his opinion. So he kept quiet. Then her father turned to him.

“Yichen.”

“Yes, Uncle?”

“What do you think?”

Xiaoran looked at him too. He put his glass down.

“About the job?”

“About her going to Beijing.”

“I think the job’s worth considering.”

“Why?”

“Because it fits what she’s studied. And she wants it.”

“That’s all?”

“That’s what I know.”

Her father looked at him. “Would you be comfortable with her going?”

He didn’t look at Xiaoran. “Yes.”

“Just like that?”

“Uncle,” he said, “I don’t think my comfort should decide whether she takes a job.”

The table went quiet. Xiaoran looked down at her bowl. Under the table, she found his knee with her hand and held on to it.

“You’re together. It’s not unreasonable to think about how it affects both of you,” said her father.

“I agree. If she wants to talk about how we’d manage the distance, I’ll talk about it with her. But I don’t think she should turn something down just because I’m in another city.”

“And if it affects your plans?”

“Then we’ll talk about our plans.”

“And if you don’t agree?”

“Then we’ll find out why.”

Her father seemed to be waiting for something more. A promise, perhaps. Some sign that Yichen would ask her to stay, or take the decision off her hands. But Yichen only picked up his glass again and drank, and put his other hand under the table, over hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner she went to her room to find her phone charger. When she came back, her father was on the sofa and Yichen was standing by the bookshelf, looking at the photograph of her on her first day at the city school, in the uniform that was too big for her.

“Are you two talking about me?”

“Should we not?” said her father.

“You can talk about me when I’m here.”

“Your father was asking about my plans. After graduation,” said Yichen.

“Since everybody’s making plans,” said her father.

Xiaoran sat down on the arm of the sofa. “Dad. I’m not asking you to be happy I’m going away. I’m asking you to understand why.”

“I understand that you want the job.”

“But not why I want Beijing.”

“Why not something closer?”

“Because I don’t want to choose a city before I choose the work. I’ve done four years of this. I’ve built my portfolio. I’ve taken every chance I could find. I know I’m inexperienced. But I want to start somewhere that’ll push me.” She heard her own voice shake and kept going.

“Beijing isn’t the only place that can do that.”

“No. But they’re offering me a chance now. Something better might come along somewhere else. Or it might not. I can’t keep saying no to something real in case.”

Her father looked away. She thought he might understand. Instead he said, “You don’t know what it’s like, living on your own in a city like that.”

She swallowed. “Then I’ll learn.”

“You think it’s that simple?”

“No. I think it’ll be hard. I think I’ll miss home. I’ll get lost. I’ll have days when I don’t know what I’m doing. That’s part of growing up, isn’t it?” She looked at him.

He didn’t answer. He got up and went into the study and shut the door, not hard.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother sat down beside her on the sofa. Xiaoran had started rearranging the slices of pear on the plate without noticing.

“Are you upset?”

“A bit.”

“Your father’s frightened.”

“I know.”

“He doesn’t think you can’t do it.”

“Then why does he keep talking as if I can’t?”

Her mother sighed. “Because knowing someone can do something doesn’t make it any easier to let them. That doesn’t mean he gets to decide.” She put her hand over Xiaoran’s on the plate.

“You’re on my side?”

“I’m on your side. I’m also on your father’s side.”

“That’s very convenient.”

Her mother laughed, a little tiredly, and got up. “Yichen. You must be exhausted. Sitting through our family arguments.”

“It’s all right, Auntie.”

“Thank you for coming.”

“Thank you for dinner.”

She went to bed. Xiaoran sat where she was for a while. Then she slid off the arm of the sofa and sat right next to Yichen, against him, and pulled his arm round her shoulders herself.

“You didn’t say much.”

“You didn’t need me to.”

“I know. I didn’t want you to. I just wanted you here.”

“I’m here,” he said, and pressed his mouth to her hair.

She leaned into him. “Did you think I was being unreasonable?”

“No.”

“Not even a bit?”

“No.”

“You’re not just agreeing with me?”

He thought about it properly. “I think you need to decide with everything in front of you. The job. Where you’d live. The money. What you want the first few years to look like. And I think you’re allowed to want something that takes you away from home. But I won’t tell you Beijing’s the right answer just because you want it. You still have to decide whether it’s right.” He tucked her hair behind her ear.

“That’s fair.”

“You can be excited about it and still be careful,” he said, and for the first time that evening she felt her shoulders come down.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday morning her father found the printed offer on the dining table. There were notes in the margins in her handwriting: questions about the probation period, the housing allowance, the hours, the insurance, what happened to new graduates in their first year. He picked it up.

She came out of her room and stopped when she saw him reading it.

“Morning.”

“Morning.”

She poured herself a glass of water. “That’s the offer I was telling you about.”

“I can see that. Have you seen the accommodation yourself?” He turned the page.

“I’ve talked to their housing person. And I’ve looked at other places.”

“The commute?”

“I’ve checked.”

“Have you talked to anyone who works there now?”

“Two people. One’s a junior producer. I asked her about the hours, and the team, and what the first six months are really like.”

He looked up at her. Then back at the paper. She didn’t ask whether he’d changed his mind. She didn’t want to spend another morning trying to persuade him. She sat down and ate her breakfast.

After a while he said, “When do they need an answer?”

“The end of the month.”

“Don’t rush.”

“I’m not.”

He folded the paper and put it back on the table. “Send me the accommodation details.”

She looked up. “Okay.”

It wasn’t a yes. But it wasn’t the same no as the night before. For now, she could work with that.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xiaoran: my dad’s asked for the accommodation details

Yichen: That’s good.

Xiaoran: he still doesn’t agree

Yichen: He doesn’t have to agree today.

Xiaoran: you’re very calm

Yichen: Would you rather I panicked?

Xiaoran: a bit. so I’m not the only one being dramatic

Yichen: You’re doing enough for both of us.

She sent him an angry rabbit. Then, after a minute:

Xiaoran: do you really not mind

He typed, deleted it, and typed again.

Yichen: I won’t pretend I wouldn’t miss you.

Yichen: But missing you isn’t a reason to ask you to stay somewhere you don’t want to be.

She read it twice. Then she rang him.

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

“You’re supposed to be my boyfriend.”

“I am.”

“You’re supposed to be selfish sometimes.”

He laughed. “I can be selfish.”

“Then why aren’t you?”

He was quiet. “Because I love you. And I want you to have a life you’re proud of. I want to be part of it, Xiaoran. I don’t want to be the reason you make it smaller.”

She pressed her lips together hard. “You’re making me cry.”

“Are you crying?”

“No.”

“All right. Shall I come over?”

“Yes, now,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came at seven. She was sitting on the floor of her bedroom with all the papers spread out round her, and he sat down on the floor next to her, so close their knees touched, and read every page. He found a clause about relocation costs she hadn’t noticed. He asked whether they’d told her what happened at the end of the probation period. She wrote it all down.

Then she looked at him. “You’re allowed to have an opinion, you know.”

“I have several.”

“About Beijing.”

He thought about it. “I think you’d do well there.”

“Thank you.”

“I also think the first few months would be hard.”

“That’s not very encouraging.”

“It’s not meant to be discouraging. New job. New city. Doing everything on your own. Some days would be exhausting. But I think you’d manage.” He looked at her.

She looked down at the papers. “Would you visit?”

“Yes.”

“Even when you’re busy?”

“Yes.”

“Would you complain about the train tickets?”

“Probably.”

“Yichen!”

“I’m being honest.”

She let her head drop onto his shoulder. “Would you miss me?”

“Every day. And I’d still want you to go, if that’s what you decide,” he said.

They sat on the floor among the papers, with her head on his shoulder and his arm round her, not knowing where either of them would be in six months. She knew one thing. The decision would be hers.

She made it three weeks later, on her own, for reasons that turned out to have nothing to do with anyone’s comfort. Including his.

chapters.desc: Mr. Zhou invites her to lunch at his office, alone, because there is something he would like to say before she decides.
chapters.title: Lunch at Zhou Logistics
chapters.epigraph: “He asked what I think of you.”
chapters.content:
The invitation came on a Wednesday morning in March, and it wasn’t for Zhou Yichen. It was for her.

Lin Xiaoran was in the library going through her final-project notes when her phone lit up.

Uncle Zhou (Logistics): Xiaoran, are you free for lunch this Friday?

She read it twice. Yichen’s father messaged her now and then, usually to ask whether she was coming for dinner or to remind her to take some of his wife’s soup home. He had asked her to a meal on her own exactly once before, in third year, the week the Herons nearly hadn’t picked his son, and she still remembered every word of that dinner.

Xiaoran: Hello Uncle! I should be free. Is something happening on Friday?

Uncle Zhou (Logistics): Nothing special. I’d like to have lunch with you. I’ll send the address.

The location came through. Zhou Logistics. The company he had built over twenty-five years, which she had heard about at a hundred dinners and had never once been inside. She opened her chat with Yichen.

Xiaoran: your father has invited me to lunch

Yichen: That’s nice.

Xiaoran: alone

Yichen: I see.

Xiaoran: at his OFFICE

Yichen: Have you said yes?

Xiaoran: yes

Yichen: Then enjoy it.

Xiaoran: that’s all??

Yichen: Would you like me to come?

Xiaoran: NO. he asked me alone

Yichen: Then I won’t interfere.

Xiaoran: aren’t you curious

Yichen: A little.

Xiaoran: A LITTLE?

Yichen: I trust my father.

She put the phone down on the library desk and glared at it. That was the problem with Zhou Yichen. He could give a perfectly reasonable answer and make it sound like he was hiding something.

That evening she went across the road and up to his flat with her laptop and lay on his sofa with her head in his lap, and interrogated him for half an hour, and got nothing at all.

“What does he want to talk about?”

“I don’t know.”

“You must have some idea.”

“I genuinely don’t.”

“Is it about Beijing?”

“Maybe. Whatever it is, he’s not going to be unkind to you. He doesn’t know how.” He ran his fingers through her hair.

“That’s not comforting.”

“It’s true, though,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday she arrived fifteen minutes early. She had changed twice that morning: the first blouse was too casual, the second looked like a job interview. In the end she wore a pale blue one and dark trousers, and checked her reflection in the lobby glass, and checked the time, and checked his message again.

“Miss Lin? Mr. Zhou’s expecting you. Please come up.” A receptionist had come over.

The office was bigger than she’d imagined, but not frightening. Glass walls, a long open floor of desks, people walking fast with folders, phones ringing. The company logo on the wall by the lifts. It gave her a strange feeling to realise that here, Yichen’s father wasn’t anyone’s father. He was the person in charge.
