The receptionist showed her into a small private dining room with a round table and framed photographs on one wall: a warehouse opening, a ribbon-cutting, a group of men in hard hats in front of a row of trucks. In one of them, Mr. Zhou was twenty years younger and much thinner, squinting into the sun, with a small boy on his shoulders.

She was looking at that one when the door opened.

“Xiaoran.”

She turned round. “Uncle.”

“Sorry to keep you waiting.”

“It’s okay. I was early.”

“I know. My assistant told me. You must be wondering why I asked you here.” He smiled and pulled out a chair for her.

“A bit,” she admitted.

He laughed. “Good. At least you’re honest.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They started with ordinary things. He asked about her final project and her applications. She told him about Morrow Studio and the Beijing offer and the portfolio she’d rebuilt three times. He listened the way his son listened, all the way to the end.

“Do you enjoy it? The work?”

“Very much.”

“Which part?”

She thought about it. “There’s always something to solve. Sometimes it’s a creative problem. Sometimes it’s people. Sometimes it’s just working out how to make an idea happen with no money and three days.”

“That sounds familiar. Yichen says you’ve been working very hard,” he said dryly.

“He does?”

“Occasionally.”

“He never tells me what he says about me.”

“That’s probably wise. He also says you’re thinking about Beijing.” He poured her tea.

“Yes.”

“Have you decided?”

“Not yet. I’m looking at the role, and the people, and how it would work.”

“Good. Don’t decide it lightly.”

“I’m not going to.”

“I know you’re not,” he said, and there was nothing in it of a test. He said it as if he believed it.

Then he put down his chopsticks. “Xiaoran. May I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“What do you think of Yichen?”

She blinked. It was such a sudden turn that she forgot how to talk.

“Yichen?”

“My son. Yes,” he said, smiling.

“That’s a very big question.”

“Then take your time.”

She looked down at her tea. She knew Yichen in ways that were hard to explain to anyone who hadn’t spent years next to him: his silences, how he went quiet when he was tired, how his mouth moved when he was trying not to laugh at her. But saying it to his father was different.

“He’s very dependable. He doesn’t say a lot, but he notices everything. He remembers things. He takes his responsibilities seriously. Sometimes too seriously,” she said slowly.

His father laughed. “That sounds like him.”

“He’s stubborn, too.”

“Also like him.”

“And he thinks he’s very good at hiding it when he’s worried.”

“Is he not?”

“Not from me.”

His father looked at her. “That’s good,” he said.

He turned his cup on the table. “He was always a quiet child. He never told us what was on his mind. We had to work it out. He always wanted to do everything properly, the first time. Sometimes I wonder whether he gives himself any room to get things wrong.”

“He’s still young,” she said.

“He doesn’t always remember that.”

“Then you should remind him.”

“I’ve tried. He listens to you more,” said Mr. Zhou.

✦ ✦ ✦

While they waited for dessert, he looked at her again, and she sat up straighter without meaning to. He noticed.

“Don’t look so nervous. This isn’t an interview.”

“Sorry.”

“I wanted to say thank you.”

“For what?”

“For being with him. I’ve watched you both grow up. You’ll both graduate this summer, and the next few years will be very different. He may get offers that take him away. You may get offers that take you somewhere else. Some of the decisions won’t be easy.” He said it.

He said, “I don’t want you to arrange your life around his. That’s what I wanted to tell you, before you decide about Beijing. He has his ambitions. You have yours. Take yours seriously. Don’t give up something that matters to you because you think it’ll make things easier for him. And don’t let him give up something for you, either. Talk to each other. Decide together when it’s both of you. That’s all.”

She looked at her hands. She thought of the nights on his sofa talking about Beijing, and how he had listened without once trying to decide for her. I want to be part of your future, he’d said, not the reason you make it smaller.

“He said nearly the same thing,” she said.

“Did he?”

“In January.”

“Then perhaps I taught him something. Although he was stubborn long before he met you.” Mr. Zhou looked pleased, and then less pleased.

She laughed, and the dessert came, and it was mango pudding, and she wondered whether that was a coincidence and decided it wasn’t.

At the lift he said, “Come again sometime.”

“I will.”

The doors opened. Before she stepped in, he said, “Xiaoran. Don’t worry too much about what Yichen will think of your decision. He thinks the world of you.”

“I know,” she said.

“Good,” said his father, and the doors closed, and only when she was alone did she let out the breath she’d been holding since the lobby.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was Friday, so she went to his flat. He was on the sofa with his laptop, and he shut it the moment the door opened.

“How was lunch?”

“Your father is very nice.”

“I know.”

“He asked about my project. And my applications.”

“That sounds like him. Anything else?”

She dropped her bag by the door and came and stood in front of him. “He asked what I think of you.”

Something crossed his face. “What did you say?”

“That you’re dependable.”

“Accurate.”

“Stubborn.”

“Also accurate.”

“And that you think you’re good at hiding it when you’re worried.”

“Not very accurate, apparently,” she said, and climbed into his lap, one knee on either side of him, and put her arms round his neck.

“What else?”

“That you take your responsibilities too seriously.”

“Did he agree?”

“Very much.”

He sighed. “Wonderful.”

She laughed and put her forehead against his. “He also told me not to arrange my life around you.”

He was quiet. “That’s good advice.”

“Did you know he was going to say it?”

“No.”

“Really?”

“Really. I think he wanted to say it to you without me there to answer for him.” His hands were on her waist.

“Would you have answered for him?”

“Probably.”

She kissed him on the nose. “Your father likes me.”

“I know.”

“How?”

“He took you to lunch alone. He’s never done that for anyone. He likes you very much, Xiaoran.” He looked at her.

“Did he tell you to say that?”

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Quite sure.”

She settled against his chest with her head on his shoulder. He let her stay there. After a while he said, into her hair, “Did you tell him about the shopping mall?”

She went still. “What shopping mall?”

“When I was six. When I got lost and the security guard announced my name over the speakers.”

She lifted her head slowly. “No.”

“Good.”

“Why? Are you embarrassed?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

“Because he already knows. My mother told you at New Year. And my mother tells him everything. So he knows you know.” He looked at her.

She burst out laughing, and put her face back in his neck, and didn’t move again until it got dark.

chapters.desc: The first-round interview with a Shanghai studio is online, and from the waist up she looks entirely professional.
chapters.title: Interview Outfit
chapters.epigraph: “I think I represented myself well.”
chapters.content:
At eighteen minutes to ten, Lin Xiaoran stood in front of the mirror in her studio and inspected herself.

White blouse. Navy blazer, borrowed from Luo Jiayi and taken in at the waist with two safety pins. Hair tied back, with two loose strands at the front. Small pearl earrings her mother had given her for the gaokao. She looked professional. She looked like someone who knew exactly what she was doing.

She looked down. Pink pyjama shorts, with tiny yellow ducks all over them.

“Perfect,” she said to the mirror.

It was the first-round interview for Morrow Studio, the one in Shanghai, the one she hadn’t told anyone she wanted more than Beijing. Her laptop was on the desk, propped on two textbooks so the camera caught her face and not her chin. Behind her she had arranged the bookshelf, a small plant, and a framed photograph which she had moved twice because it looked too personal and then moved back because without it the shelf looked like a hotel.

She checked the camera. The microphone. The connection. The time. Her phone buzzed.

Yichen: Good luck today.

Xiaoran: thank you!!

Yichen: Don’t forget to breathe.

Xiaoran: I know how to breathe

Yichen: You forgot during your thesis pitch.

Xiaoran: that was different

Yichen: Of course. Send me the blazer. I want to see it before they do.

She took a careful picture from the waist up and sent it.

Yichen: Very professional. They’re lucky.

Xiaoran: you can’t see the bottom half

Yichen: I can imagine the bottom half.

Xiaoran: DON’T

Yichen: Ducks?

She put the phone down on the desk without answering and sat down and smoothed the blazer, which was answer enough, and the phone buzzed once more under her hand, and she didn’t look.

✦ ✦ ✦

At five to ten she opened the link. Just before ten the doorbell rang.

She looked at the clock. She looked at the door. The doorbell rang again.

“Oh, no.”

She had ordered lunch for twelve. Apparently it was coming now. She ran to the door with the blazer flapping and opened it a crack.

A delivery driver in a yellow jacket was standing on the landing, slightly out of breath from the four flights, holding a paper bag.

“Miss Lin?”

“Yes! Sorry! Could you just leave it there? On the floor? Thank you so much.”

“Sure. Miss, are you going to a meeting?” He put it down. Then he looked at her: the blazer, the earrings, the hair.

“Ah. Yes. An interview.”

He smiled at her. His eyes dropped, and came back up. “Good luck!”

“Thank you!”

She shut the door and stood with her back against it for a second. Then she looked down. The ducks looked back.

“Never mind,” she told them, and ran to the desk.

The panel was already there: a woman with short grey hair and a younger man with a notebook. “Good morning, Xiaoran. Can you hear us?”

“Good morning. Yes, perfectly.”

“Wonderful. Shall we start?”

For the next twenty-five minutes she was flawless. She talked about her final-year film and the noodle-shop campaign she’d shot with Chi Yuan, and the freelance work she’d been doing since second year, the first of which had paid for a lens. She talked about what had gone wrong on a group project and what she’d done about it. She asked them two questions of her own that she had rehearsed in the shower, and one she hadn’t. She made the grey-haired woman laugh, once.

Nothing on the screen suggested that she was sitting in her bedroom in duck shorts with a cold lunch on the landing.

When the call ended she shut the laptop and sat completely still for five seconds.

Then she put her face in her hands. “Oh my God.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She rang him before she’d even taken the blazer off. He picked up straight away.

“How did it go?”

“I think it went well.”

“Good.”

“Really well, actually.”

“Even better.”

“Except—”

He heard her voice change. “Except?”

“The delivery man saw me.”

“What?”

“The delivery man. My lunch came early. He came to the door. I was in the blazer and the—” She stopped.

There was a pause on the line. Then a low sound she knew well.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not laughing.”

“You are.”

“I’m listening.”

“Zhou Yichen.”

He laughed properly then, and she dropped her forehead onto the closed laptop with a groan.

“I looked so professional. And then he looked down.”

“Did he say anything?”

“He asked if I was going to a meeting. I said yes. He said good luck.”

“I think that’s sweet.”

“He saw my shorts.”

“Then maybe he was wishing the ducks good luck too.”

“I regret telling you.”

“No, you don’t.”

She was quiet for a second, and then smiled at the laptop despite herself. “No.”

“Forget the delivery man,” he said. “How do you feel?”

She looked at the laptop. At the bookshelf. At the photograph she’d moved twice.

“I think I represented myself well.”

“Then that’s what matters.”

“Yes.”

“Good,” he said, and then, in a different voice, “Well done. I know what that one means to you.”

“I haven’t told you what it means to me.”

“You didn’t have to. You’ve had their website open on your phone since February.”

She pulled her knees up onto the chair, the phone pressed to her ear. “Are you coming later?”

“Training till six. I’ll come after.”

“Okay.”

“And Xiaoran?”

“Mm?”

“Next time, wear trousers.”

“You’re supposed to be on my side!”

“I am. I’m also on the side of trousers,” he said, and she hung up on him.

Thirty seconds later:

Yichen: Ducks and all. Well done.

She went and got her lunch off the landing. It had gone cold. She ate it sitting on the floor in the blazer and the shorts, with the safety pins digging into her waist.

✦ ✦ ✦

At one, her mother messaged.

Mum (Accounts Dept.): Did you have the interview?

Xiaoran: Yes! It went well

Mum (Accounts Dept.): Which company?

Xiaoran: A studio in Shanghai. First round

Mum (Accounts Dept.): Not the Beijing one.

Xiaoran: Beijing is later

There was a pause, the kind her mother used to leave at the dinner table when a report card had come home.

Mum (Accounts Dept.): Your father says good luck. He also says wear proper shoes next time.

Xiaoran: it was ONLINE

Mum (Accounts Dept.): He knows. He says the shoes know.

She looked down at her bare feet and the ducks and decided her father had been a fortune-teller in a previous life and had never mentioned it.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he came round that evening she was waiting for him at the bottom of the stairs, changed into jeans and a sweatshirt, and she glared at him as he came through the door.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face.”

“What about it?”

“You’re smiling.”

He made his face carefully, deliberately blank. “Better?”

“No. That’s worse.” She took his arm with both hands and started up the stairs with him.

“How was the rest of the day?”

“Fine. I ate. I sent the panel a thank-you email. I took the safety pins out. I looked at the email three times to check for typos and found one after I’d sent it.”

“What was it?”

“I wrote best regrads.”

“They’ll think you’re relaxed.”

“They’ll think I’m an idiot.”

On the second-floor landing he stopped, and turned round on the step above her, so that for once their faces were level.

“You didn’t look ridiculous. Your interview outfit was entirely appropriate. From the waist up,” he said. He let her relax.

She hit him. He caught her hand and pulled her up onto his step and kissed her.

“You did well.”

“Even with the ducks?”

“Ducks included.”

She laughed at last, and put her arms round him on the narrow landing, and leaned her whole weight against him until he said “We’re going to fall down the stairs,” and she said “Then we’ll fall,” and didn’t move.

He had the sense not to mention the ducks for the rest of the evening. Right up until they were sitting on her sofa with their dinner on their knees, and he said, casually, “Do you think the delivery man will recognise you next time?”

She threw a tissue at him. He caught it, folded it into a neat square, and put it in his pocket, which she found far more annoying than if he’d thrown it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The email came on Thursday, while she was in the library pretending to edit subtitles.

Second round. In person. Tuesday, 10:00. Please bring your portfolio.

She sent him the screenshot with her hands shaking.

Xiaoran: IN PERSON

Yichen: Congratulations.

Xiaoran: I have to wear trousers

Yichen: I’ll clear Saturday. We’ll practice.

Xiaoran: practice what?

Yichen: Everything they could ask. Bring your notes. I’ll bring questions.

She looked at that with the feeling, which she would come to know well over the next five days, of someone who has asked for a little help and is about to get a great deal more of it than she bargained for. Then she typed thank you and sent it with eleven hearts, and put her phone down, and picked it up again to add one more.

chapters.desc: A weekend at her grandparents’ house, a promise ring, and by noon half the town believes she is engaged.
chapters.title: The Ring at Grandma’s
chapters.epigraph: “Does he treat you well?”
chapters.content:
By eleven in the morning Lin Xiaoran was accidentally engaged. By noon, half the town knew. By two, her grandmother was discussing dates.

It had all started with the ring, and the ring wasn’t even new. That was the most important detail, and she would spend the whole afternoon wishing she’d said it sooner.

Zhou Yichen had given it to her on their fifth anniversary in December: a thin plain band she wore on her right hand, so simple that nobody noticed it unless they were looking. She hardly ever took it off. He had never asked her to wear it, or attached any conditions to it. It was a promise they had made to each other, long before graduation was something they could see coming.

They weren’t engaged. They were still students, still talking about where they’d work and what kind of lives they wanted. He had told her that when the time came he wanted to ask her properly: flowers, a dress she loved, and a moment she wouldn’t have to share with a dozen relatives asking whether she’d eaten enough. She had told him she expected all three. He had said he knew.

So when she took the Friday evening bus up to her grandparents’ house in the town for the weekend, it didn’t occur to her for one second that the ring might cause trouble.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came out to the kitchen at half past seven on Saturday morning. Her grandmother was supervising a pot of congee with a tea towel over her shoulder.

“You’re up. Why didn’t you get up earlier?”

“It’s half past seven, Grandma.”

“Half past seven isn’t early.”

Xiaoran laughed and hugged her from behind, and her grandmother patted her arm and then turned round and held her at arm’s length.

“You’re thinner.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“I ate breakfast on the bus.”

“That means nothing. Sit.” She put a bowl in front of her. “How are your classes? When do you graduate? Have you found work? Are you sleeping?” And, inevitably: “Where’s Yichen?”

“In Shanghai. He’s got training, and a meeting with the club at noon.”

“Still playing?”

“Of course.”

“That boy is always busy. Does he still look after you?” Her grandmother ladled congee.

“Grandma.”

“What?”

“Why do you ask that every single time?”

“Because I want to know.”

“He does.”

“Good,” said her grandmother, and went back to the stove, and Xiaoran thought that was the end of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first person to notice was Auntie Fan from next door. She arrived just before eleven with a jar of home-made pickles and the boundless interest in other people’s lives that Xiaoran had always found slightly frightening.

“Ah, Xiaoran! You’re back! Look at you. All grown up.”

“Hello, Auntie Fan.”

Auntie Fan took both her hands to look at her properly. Then she stopped. Her fingers had found the ring.

“Oh?”

Xiaoran looked down. “Oh. That’s—”

Auntie Fan’s eyes went wide. She didn’t finish her own sentence. She didn’t need to. Xiaoran understood exactly what she was thinking about one second too late.

“No, it isn’t—”

But Auntie Fan had already turned towards the kitchen. “Your granddaughter is engaged!”

From the kitchen: “What?”

“I’m not!” Xiaoran called.

Too late. Her grandmother appeared in the doorway drying her hands on her apron.

“What did you say?”

“Look! A ring!” Auntie Fan held up Xiaoran’s hand like a prize.

Her grandmother looked at the ring. Then at Xiaoran. Then at the ring. For a few seconds she said nothing.

Then, calmly: “When?”

Xiaoran nearly choked. “Grandma, I’m not engaged!”

“But the ring—” said Auntie Fan.

“It’s a promise ring.”

There was a short silence.

“A promise?” said her grandmother.

“Yes.”

“From Yichen?”

“Yes.”

Her grandmother’s whole face softened. “Oh.”

Xiaoran let her breath out. “So it’s not—”

“Then he’s promised to marry you.”

“Grandma!”

Auntie Fan put her hand over her mouth. Her grandmother, however, appeared to have arrived at a perfectly reasonable conclusion.

“Well. That’s good.”

“It’s not an engagement!”

“Did I say it was?”

“You said when!”

“I meant when did he give it to you,” said her grandmother serenely, and Xiaoran opened her mouth, then closed it and looked at Auntie Fan, who was already smiling in a way that gave Xiaoran a terrible feeling.

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past eleven her grandmother had rung her aunt. By twenty to twelve her aunt had rung her uncle. By ten to, someone had mentioned it to the woman who ran the fruit stall. And at noon Xiaoran’s phone started to buzz.

Cousin Lele (Breaking News): CONGRATULATIONS!!!!

Xiaoran: for what

Cousin Lele (Breaking News): grandma says you’re getting MARRIED

Xiaoran: I’M NOT

Cousin Lele (Breaking News): she says yichen gave you a ring

Xiaoran: it’s a PROMISE ring

Cousin Lele (Breaking News): that’s what engaged means before the wedding

She turned the phone over on the table. Across from her, her grandmother was talking to Auntie Fan again in a low voice, and Xiaoran could make out the words Yichen, graduation, and young people these days. She lowered her forehead slowly onto the table.

“Don’t put your head there. It’s not clean,” said her grandmother.

“Grandma. Please stop telling people I’m engaged.”

“I’m not telling people that.”

“Then what are you telling them?”

“That Yichen gave you a ring.”

“That’s the same thing to everyone in this town!”

Her grandmother considered this. “Well. You should have explained earlier.”

“I did!”

“You were too fast. I couldn’t hear properly,” said her grandmother, and went back to her soup.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen found out at a quarter past twelve, sitting on a bench at the Herons training centre while the physio wrapped an ice pack round his ankle.

Xiaoran: I need you to know something

Yichen: What happened?

The dots appeared. Disappeared. Appeared.

Xiaoran: apparently we’re engaged

He looked at that.

Yichen: Apparently?

Xiaoran: don’t laugh

Yichen: I’m not laughing.

Xiaoran: you are. I can FEEL it

“You look happy,” said the physio. “Was it the ice?”

Yichen: How did this happen?

Xiaoran: my RING. auntie fan saw it. grandma thinks you’ve promised to marry me. the whole town knows

He leaned his head back against the wall.

Yichen: Your grandmother isn’t wrong.

There was a long pause.

Xiaoran: YICHEN

Yichen: What?

Xiaoran: you’re supposed to HELP

Yichen: I am helping.

Xiaoran: HOW

Yichen: By not denying that I intend to marry you.

Her phone rang ten seconds later. He picked up before it finished the first ring.

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Lin Xiaoran,” he said, calm and amused.

“Don’t use that voice.”

“What voice?”

“That voice.”

He laughed. “Are you embarrassed?”

“I’m being publicly married without my consent.”

“That’s a serious accusation.”

“You’re enjoying this.”

“A little,” he said, and let her complain for a full minute. Then: “What else did your grandmother say?”

“She asked when we’re getting married. I said we’re still at university. She said that doesn’t matter, people can plan early.”

“That’s also reasonable.”

“You’re not helping!”

He laughed again. Then his voice changed. “Xiaoran. Did it upset you?”

The question caught her off guard. He wasn’t teasing now.

“No. Not really. It’s just embarrassing. Everyone keeps looking at my hand,” she admitted.

“Then take it off, if you’d rather.”

She looked down at it. She turned it with her thumb. “No. I like wearing it.”

“I know.”

“I just don’t want everyone thinking we’re getting married tomorrow.”

“We’re not getting married tomorrow. And when I ask you properly, I won’t leave you to explain it to Auntie Fan,” he said.

She smiled at the wall. “Good.”

“I’ll tell her myself.”

“Please don’t. She’ll start planning the wedding before you’ve finished asking.”

“Then I’ll be quick,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He hadn’t planned to come. But she’d mentioned that her grandmother wanted to see him, and his meeting finished at one, and the drive up was four hours if the expressway behaved. At ten to six there was a knock on the gate, and when her grandmother opened it he was standing there with a box of pastries.

“Yichen!”

“Grandma.”

“You came!”

“Xiaoran said you wanted to see me.”

“Of course I want to see you. Come in, come in.”

Xiaoran appeared in the courtyard. The moment she saw him she narrowed her eyes, even though her whole face had lit up.

“You.”

“Me.”

“You’re here.”

“I am.”

She glanced at her grandmother, and then crossed the courtyard in three steps and wrapped her arms round him and pressed her face into his chest, pastries and all, and said into his jacket, “Don’t say anything.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Good.”

“Why are you two standing in the gate?” said her grandmother.

He took his shoes off. Her grandmother asked whether he’d eaten. He said yes. She asked whether he wanted fruit. He said he would. She asked about his classes and his training and the drive. And then, inevitably:

“Yichen. That ring you gave Xiaoran is very pretty.”

Xiaoran shut her eyes.

“Thank you, Grandma.”

“She likes it very much. She wears it every day.”

“I’ve noticed.”

“Young people should have something to look forward to,” said her grandmother.

“Yes, Grandma,” said Yichen, and Xiaoran opened her eyes and turned to him.

“You’re not supposed to agree with everything.”

He bent his head towards her. “Would you rather I argued with your grandmother?”

She glared at him. Her grandmother, who had heard every word, laughed until she had to sit down.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner her grandfather took Yichen off to the storeroom to carry things, and Xiaoran sat with her grandmother on the sofa while she sorted through a biscuit tin of old photographs. Her grandmother picked one out: Xiaoran and Yichen at the New Year dinner four years ago, younger, standing side by side and not quite sure how to stand.

“You’ve been together a long time.”

“Yes.”

“Since school.”

“Mm.”

Her grandmother put the photograph down. “Does he treat you well?”

“He does.”

“Do you treat him well?”

Xiaoran laughed. “I think so.”

Her grandmother took her hand and held it in her lap. The ring caught the lamplight. “I know you’re not engaged.”

Xiaoran looked up. “You know?”

“Of course I know. You told me five times. I just thought it was nice.” She rubbed her thumb over the back of Xiaoran’s hand.

“What was?”

“That he gave you something you want to wear every day. You don’t have to hurry. You’re young. Finish your studies. Find your work. Make your own life. But it’s good to know someone is serious about you.” Her grandmother looked at the ring.

“He’s serious.”

“I can see that. Just don’t let everyone else’s excitement make you feel you have to rush.” She patted Xiaoran’s hand.

Xiaoran looked at her. Under all the teasing and the phone calls and Auntie Fan, her grandmother had understood the important thing all along. She wasn’t asking her to marry anyone. She was happy, that was all, that her granddaughter had found someone who loved her.

“Okay,” said Xiaoran.

“Now go and see whether your boyfriend needs help.”

“He’s carrying boxes, Grandma. He’s fine.”

“Then go and keep him company,” said her grandmother, and pushed her off the sofa.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came out of the storeroom with his sleeves rolled up and dust on one shoulder. She brushed it off.

“Did you survive?”

“Your grandfather is very efficient. When I’d finished the first two things he gave me three more.”

“That’s how he is. Grandma knows we’re not engaged. She said we don’t have to hurry.” She took his arm with both hands and leaned on it.

“She’s right.”

She held up her hand between them. “Do you regret giving me this? Now the whole town thinks we’re getting married?”

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“No. I gave it to you because I wanted you to have it. What anybody else thinks doesn’t change that. Although I should get ready for your grandmother asking me about dates next time.” He took her hand and turned it over and ran his thumb along the band. The corner of his mouth went up.

“She’ll ask you directly.”

“I’ll answer.”

“What will you say?”

He looked at her. “That I’ll ask when I can do it properly.”

“And when’s that?”

“Not today. But I know what I want. Come on. Your grandmother’s waiting,” he said, and she made a face, and he lifted her hand and kissed the ring.

They stayed the night, Yichen in the little guest room under her grandfather’s fishing rods. On Sunday morning her grandmother packed enough food for six people into the boot of his car, reminded him three times to drive carefully, and told Xiaoran to bring him back next month. Auntie Fan came out of her gate to wave them off, and waved at Xiaoran’s right hand in particular.

The rumour never got completely corrected. Xiaoran found she didn’t mind as much as she’d expected. The ring was still on her finger. And for four hours on the expressway, with the town getting smaller behind them, every time they slowed for a toll gate he reached across and held hers.

chapters.desc: The second round is in person, so he clears his Saturday, puts on a dark shirt, and becomes the most difficult interviewer she has ever met.
chapters.title: Mock Interview
chapters.epigraph: “Why should we hire you?”
chapters.content:
“Good morning. Thank you for coming in today.”

Lin Xiaoran looked up from her notes. Zhou Yichen was sitting opposite her at his dining table with his laptop open and a glass of water at his elbow. He had put on a dark shirt and combed his hair, and his face was so serious that she nearly laughed. She sat up straighter instead.

“Good morning. Thank you for having me.”

“Please introduce yourself.”

She took a breath. “My name is Lin Xiaoran. I’m a final-year Media student, and I’m particularly interested in creative production, digital storytelling and brand communication. During my time at university I’ve worked on several projects involving—”

“Stop.”

“What?”

“You’re reading.”

She looked down. Her notebook was open on the table in front of her. “I was referring to it.”

“You’ve been looking at it for twenty seconds.”

“Because it’s there.”

“The panel won’t be sitting across from you to admire your notes. Again. Look at me.” He leaned back.

“You’re supposed to be supportive.”

“I am.”

“You’re being mean.”

“I’m being accurate.”

She pointed her pen at him. “You’re enjoying this.”

The corner of his mouth moved, slightly. “Continue.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The second round at Morrow Studio was on Tuesday, in person, in trousers. She had done everything right: she’d read about every project on their website, rebuilt her portfolio, written out answers to every question she could think of. She knew she could do the work. What frightened her was the room. When she was nervous she talked too fast, explained too much, or knew exactly what she meant and couldn’t find the first sentence.

He had cleared his Saturday. She hadn’t expected him to be this convincing.

“Tell me about a project you’re proud of.”

She told him about the noodle-shop campaign: the brief, the research, the three days of shooting in a kitchen at forty degrees, what the owner had said when he saw the final cut. He didn’t interrupt once. When she stopped, he looked at his notes.

“What exactly was your part?”

She told him.

“What would you do differently?”

“Probably spend more time testing the concept before we went into production. We had a few assumptions about the audience that turned out to be wrong, and it cost us a week.”

“Why didn’t you test them earlier?”

“Because we didn’t have time.”

“That’s a constraint. Not a reason,” he said.

She looked at him. He looked back, calm and patient and absolutely relentless.

She drank some water. “We trusted our first idea of who the audience was. We could have shown a rough cut to a small group before committing to the full shoot. We didn’t, because we were excited, and we didn’t want anyone to tell us it was wrong.”

“What did you learn?”

“That being excited about an idea isn’t the same as knowing it works.”

Something in his face eased. “That’s a good answer.”

She smiled. He turned a page.

“Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate.”

The smile vanished. “Oh, no.”

“What?”

“I hate that question.”

“It’s a very common question.”

“I know. That’s why I hate it. I don’t want to sound like I’m blaming someone.”

“Then don’t blame someone.”

She stared at him. He waited. Eventually she told him about Dou Kai: the missing section, the silent group chat, the messages, the conversation in the corridor. She left out the part where her boyfriend had done most of the talking.

“And if he’d still refused to cooperate?”

“I’d have gone to the lecturer.”

“After how long?”

“After trying to sort it out directly.”

“How many times?”

“Why do you want a number?”

“Because ‘after trying’ can mean anything.”

She looked at him. Then she laughed. “You’re a terrible boyfriend.”

“Shall I go easier on you?”

“Don’t you dare.”

“Then answer the question,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

After forty minutes she put her pen down. “Can we have a break?”

He looked at the clock. “Five minutes.”

“Ten.”

“Seven.”

“You’re negotiating my break?”

“Yes.”

“Fine.”

He closed the laptop halfway and pushed her water glass towards her. “Drink.”

She drank. He watched her.

“You’re doing well.”

“Really? You’re not just saying that because I’m your girlfriend?”

“No. Your answers are good. You understand what you’ve done and you can explain why. You just keep treating every question as if there’s one correct answer hidden somewhere and you have to guess it.”

“I know.”

“Do you? You’ve written whole paragraphs for every question.” He reached over and turned her notebook round so he could see it. Every page was full.

“That’s preparation.”

“These are speeches.”

“They help me.”

“Then keep them. Just don’t learn them by heart. You don’t need to sound like someone else,” he said. He turned the notebook back towards her and put his hand over hers on top of it.

“That’s easy for you to say. You’re good at interviews.”

“Who told you that?”

“You always sound calm.”

“That’s not the same as being good.”

She looked at him. “Are you ever nervous? About your own stuff?”

He was quiet. “Sometimes.”

“About the contract?”

“Among other things.”

She turned her hand over under his and held on. “You’re allowed to be nervous too.”

“I know,” he said.

She got up, came round the table, and sat sideways on his lap with her arms round his neck, which wasn’t something interviewers generally allowed. He let her.

“This is very unprofessional,” he said.

“It’s my break.”

“You’ve got two minutes left.”

“Then I’m spending them here,” she said, and leaned into his shoulder, and he leaned his cheek against her hair and didn’t say anything until the two minutes were up and some way beyond.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second half was worse. He moved on from questions about the past to questions about things that hadn’t happened.

“You’re given a brief with an impossible deadline. What do you do?”

“Clarify the scope.”

“Then?”

“Work out the priorities.”

“Then?”

“Talk to the team about the timeline.”

“The client refuses to extend the deadline.”

“Then I look at what we can realistically deliver in the time.”

“The client insists on everything.”

“I explain the trade-offs.”

“They don’t accept them.”

“Yichen.”

“Yes?”

“Do you want me to get this job or not?”

“Very much.”

“Then stop trying to make me fail!”

“I’m trying to prepare you for someone who won’t make it easy. I’m on your side. That’s why I’m asking,” he said, and he wasn’t smiling now.

She stopped. She looked at him across the table. He meant it. He wanted her to walk into that room on Tuesday and not be surprised by anything.

“Fine, ask me again,” she said.

He asked her again. This time she took her time. She talked about finding out what the client actually needed, which wasn’t always what they’d asked for; about being honest early instead of late; about offering two alternatives instead of saying no. He listened all the way through.

“Good.”

“Thank you.”

“Last one.”

She groaned. “You said that twenty minutes ago.”

“I mean it this time. Why should we hire you?” He looked down at his notes, and then up.

She opened her mouth. Nothing came out. He waited.

“I think,” she said. Stopped. Looked at her notebook. There was a whole page on this one. She didn’t look at it.

“I think I’m a good fit because I care about the work. I don’t just want to deliver the brief. I want to understand what it’s for, and who it’s for, and whether it will mean anything to them when it’s done. I know I’ve still got a lot to learn. But I’m curious, and I’ll work hard, and I can take feedback without losing hold of what the idea was in the first place. And I think I can bring something new, but I know when to listen. I want to be somewhere that makes me better than I am.” Her voice was steadier now.

The room was quiet. He shut the laptop.

“Thank you.”

“How was it?”

He looked at her. “Good.”

She waited.

“Very good,” he said.

She let out a long breath and put her face in her hands. “Oh, thank God.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterward she moved round to his side of the table and sat in the chair next to him, as close as the chair arms allowed.

“Was I really okay?”

“Yes.”

“Which answer was the best?”

“The last one.”

“Why?”

“Because you stopped trying to say what you thought they wanted. You said what you think,” he said.

She leaned against his shoulder. “Would you hire me?”

He considered it. “Yes.”

“Really?”

“Although I’d want to discuss your habit of negotiating breaks.”

She hit his arm. “You’re not funny.”

“I’m a very fair interviewer.”

“You’re a terrible interviewer.”

“Would you like to give me feedback?”

She sat up straight. “Yes, actually. One, you were too serious. Two, you asked too many follow-up questions. Three, you didn’t smile once.”

“Would you like me to smile?”

“Yes. It would be less frightening.”

He turned to her and let a slow smile come over his face. “Like this?”

She went quiet. She looked at his face. Then she looked hard at the table.

“Is that better?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because that isn’t an interview smile,” she said, and picked up her notebook and hid behind it, and he laughed and took it gently out of her hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed at his flat on Monday night, because it was twenty minutes closer to the studio and because she’d asked. On Tuesday morning she came out of the bedroom in her blouse and blazer, trousers this time, and turned round once in front of him.

“Too formal?”

“No.”

“Too plain?”

“No.”

“Should I wear the other earrings?”

He got up from the table and came over. He straightened the collar of her blazer and tucked a piece of hair behind her ear.

“You’re ready.”

“Don’t learn speeches,” she said.

“Good.”

“Answer honestly.”

“Good.”

“Don’t treat every question like there’s one right answer.”

“Exactly.”

She reached for his hand. “And if I get nervous?”

“Take a breath. You don’t have to rush. Go.” He kissed her temple.

When she came back at one, he was at the table. It was his recovery day, and as far as she could tell he had spent all of it in that chair. He looked up the moment the door opened.

“How was it?”

She put her bag down. She came and stood in front of him.

“I think it went well,” she said.

She told him all of it, standing up, then sitting on the edge of the table, then in his lap: the question she hadn’t expected, the twenty minutes they’d spent on the noodle-shop film, the moment the grey-haired woman had put her pen down and just listened. He didn’t interrupt once.

“You went in and said what you meant,” he said at the end.

“Even if I don’t get it?”

“Even then.”

She put her arms round him and her face in his neck.

“You know what? You should charge people for mock interviews.”

“Would you recommend me?”

“No. Too frightening. One star.”

“Out of five?”

“Out of one,” she said, and kissed him, and for once he didn’t have a follow-up question.

chapters.desc: The camera was supposed to be off. She comes back to find forty minutes of him talking to it.
chapters.title: The Footage She Didn’t Use
chapters.epigraph: “Come back soon. I miss you.”
chapters.content:
The camera was supposed to be off. That was the first mistake. The second was leaving Zhou Yichen alone with it.

Lin Xiaoran’s final-year portfolio piece was a short documentary about the routines people build around the things they love: the repetitions nobody notices, the small habits that make a life feel like yours. She had thought about filming athletes she didn’t know. Then musicians. Then she’d decided she couldn’t face another week of arranging interviews with strangers who cancelled the night before.

“Film me,” Yichen had said, from the other end of her sofa.

“You hate being filmed.”

“I do. But I’ll turn up.”

So on his one free afternoon of the week he gave her the university court, where the Herons let him shoot on his days off, and stood where she told him to stand, and did his shooting routine over and over while she followed him round with the camera. It was going well. The only problem was that Xiaoran had a habit of forgetting to stop recording. And Yichen had a habit of noticing when she was distracted.

✦ ✦ ✦

She set the camera on the tripod by the bench to check a wide shot. The red light was on. She wasn’t looking at it.

“Can you stand there a second?”

“Here?”

“A bit to the left.”

He moved.

“Your other left.”

He met her eyes.

“Sorry. Your right.”

He moved again.

“Good. Now look at the basket. Not like you’re posing.”

“I’m not posing.”

“You look like you’re posing.”

“What should I do, then?”

“Just stand.”

He stood. She watched the little screen.

“Perfect. Stay there. I left the lavalier mic in the editing room, I’ll be two minutes.”

She ran off. He stayed exactly where he was for a while, looking at the basket. Then he looked over at the camera. The red light was still on.

“Is this still recording?”

No answer. The door at the far end of the court had swung shut behind her. He looked at the lens. Then he came over and sat down on the bench beside the tripod.

“You’re not here. Obviously. You’re looking for the microphone. It’s not in the editing room. You put it in the side pocket of your tote bag. The one you never use because you say things vanish in there,” he said to it.

He leaned forward with his elbows on his knees.

“You’re very organised for someone who loses everything.”

At the other end of the court a ball bounced; two of the university second-years had come in to shoot around. He glanced over and back.

“Do you know what I think? I think you won’t use this. You’ll watch it tonight and decide the light’s wrong and delete the whole thing. Or you’ll say I don’t look natural. Which is unfair, because I think I’m being very natural.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came back after forty minutes with her water bottle and her notebook and the microphone, which had been in the side pocket of her tote bag.

“Sorry! I couldn’t find the—”

She stopped. Yichen was on the bench beside the tripod, looking directly into the lens. He turned his head.

“Found it?”

“It was in my bag. The whole time.”

“Good,” he said, without the faintest trace of surprise.

She went to the camera to set up the next shot and saw the red light. “Oh. I forgot to stop it.”

“I noticed.”

She pressed the button and looked at the counter. “Forty minutes?”

“Is that how long?”

“What did you do?”

“Talked to your camera.”

“Did it answer?”

“No.”

“Rude,” she said, laughing, and packed up the tripod, and didn’t think about it again until she opened the files that night.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first few minutes were ordinary. Yichen standing where she’d put him. Yichen shifting his weight. Then the moment he realised she’d gone.

She smiled at the screen. He talked about the microphone. Then her tote bag. Then her habit of losing things. She laughed out loud on her own in her studio.

“You’re so annoying.”

At around fifteen minutes he started talking about her project. He described exactly how she had explained it to him the night before, sitting cross-legged on her bed with the laptop on her knees. He used her own words. He remembered that she’d changed the title three times.

Her smile changed. He wasn’t talking to an audience. He wasn’t giving an interview or trying to sound interesting. He was talking to a camera she’d forgotten about in the same easy voice he used when she was right next to him.

At twenty-three minutes he started talking about the first week of university, when she’d tried to find him at the sports centre and got lost. She had rung him from outside the wrong building. He’d walked all the way across campus to find her, and discovered that she was standing in front of the right building after all, only at the back.

Xiaoran put her hand over her mouth. She remembered. She’d been mortified. He had never mentioned it once, in four years.

At twenty-eight minutes he looked straight into the lens.

“She’s going to complain about this later. She doesn’t like being filmed when she’s not ready. She’ll say she looked strange, or she wasn’t prepared, or I should have told her. But I think she looks nicest when she forgets the camera’s there. She talks to herself when she’s concentrating. Sometimes she reads things out loud. Sometimes she pulls a face at her laptop like it’s insulted her. She thinks nobody notices. I notice.” The corner of his mouth went up.

Xiaoran felt her face go hot. She tipped the laptop screen down a little, as if someone might come in and catch her watching. Then she put it back up.

✦ ✦ ✦

The last twelve minutes were different. He had moved off the bench and was sitting on the floor with his back against the wall, and the court behind him was empty; the second-years had gone. He didn’t say anything. Then:

“You’re taking a long time. Which means you’ve lost something else. I don’t mind waiting. Actually, I mind a bit. I’m hungry.”

She laughed out loud again.

He looked back at the camera. “Do you remember what you said about this project? That you wanted to film ordinary things, because people think the important moments are the big ones. I think that’s true. Most days I don’t remember what I did. I remember that you were there. Or that you sent me a picture of something ridiculous. Or that you were annoyed because I finished your drink.” He tilted his head.

He looked down at his hands.

“I don’t think you know how much of my day is little things with you in them. I don’t know if that’s any use for your project. Probably not. But I thought I’d tell you anyway.”

A few seconds passed. Then, almost casually, to the empty court:

“Come back soon. I miss you.”

The recording ran on for another minute. He didn’t say anything else. He just sat there by the wall, waiting for her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She watched it twice. The second time she paused it on I miss you and sat looking at the frozen picture of him on the floor with his arms round his knees.

There was nothing dramatic in it. No big confession, no speech. Nothing that would have made a stranger understand everything. It was just Yichen talking to a camera because he thought she might be nearby, remembering things she’d forgotten and noticing things she hadn’t known anyone noticed. And waiting.

The documentary was nearly finished. She had all the footage she needed: the ball on the floor, the squeak of shoes, his breathing between free throws, the empty court at the end. The forty minutes didn’t belong in it. It wasn’t the story she was telling. And she wasn’t going to put something that private into a university submission just because it was beautiful.

She made a new folder and called it Unused. She dragged the file in. She renamed it Yichen – 40 min. She looked at that for a while. Then she deleted the name and typed a new one.

For Xiaoran.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came round the next afternoon, up the four flights, with a paper bag from the bakery she liked, and found her at her desk with two cups of tea already poured.

“Working?”

“Nearly finished.”

He put the bag beside her laptop and bent down to kiss her forehead. “How’s the edit?”

“Good.”

“Can I see?”

“Not yet. When it’s finished.”

“All right,” he said, and sat down in the chair beside hers and picked up his tea.

She turned the laptop slightly away from him. “Yichen. The other day. When I left the camera running.”

“Yes.”

“You talked to it.”

“I did.”

“For forty minutes.”

“Forty? That’s longer than I thought.” He drank some tea.

She narrowed her eyes. “You knew it was recording.”

“Not at first.”

“And then?”

“Then I worked it out.”

“Why didn’t you stop?”

He thought about it. “You weren’t there.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“I thought you might find it later.”

“What if I’d deleted it?”

“Then you’d have deleted it. It’s your camera,” he said.

Something warm and heavy settled in her chest. “Did you mean it? All of it?”

His face changed. Not surprised. Just softer. “You watched it?”

“All forty minutes.”

“That’s a lot of listening. Which part?” She nudged his arm, and he looked at her.

She looked away, shy all at once. “The part about noticing things.”

He reached over and tucked her hair behind her ear. “Yes.”

“And the part about missing me?”

“That part most,” he said.

She didn’t say anything. She got up out of her chair and into his lap, tea and all, and put her arms round his neck and kissed him. He kissed her back with one hand on her cheek, and when she pulled away he brushed his thumb under her eye, although she wasn’t crying.

“Why?”

“Nothing. I just like you,” she said.

“That’s fortunate.”

“Very,” she said, and put her face in his neck, and stayed there while his tea went cold on the desk.

✦ ✦ ✦

A week later she submitted it. She got a good mark and a comment from her supervisor about the honesty of the footage and the patience of the final sequence. Yichen asked to see it, and she showed him on her laptop, and he watched the whole thing without saying a word.

When it ended he said, “I liked what you did with the sound. And the end.”

“Which bit?”

“The empty court. It felt familiar.” He was quiet for a second.

“That was my favourite part too.”

He shut the laptop. Then he looked at her. “Where’s the footage you didn’t use?”

“What footage?”

“The forty minutes.”

She tried hard to look innocent. Then she gave up and opened the laptop again and the folder, and he read the filename.

For Xiaoran.

“You kept it.”

“Of course I kept it.”

“Why?”

“Because I liked it. It’s not for the project. It’s just for me.” She was embarrassed now.

He looked at the little thumbnail: him on the bench, looking amused. “Then keep it.”

“I will.”

“Although next time you should tell me when you’re recording.”

“Why?”

“So I can prepare something more interesting.”

“You talked for forty minutes without preparing anything.”

“I knew what I wanted to say.”

“About my tote bag?”

“It was an important subject,” he said. “Would you like another forty minutes?”

“No.”

“Thirty?”

“Yichen.”

“Twenty?”

She laughed and pushed his shoulder, and he caught her hand and kissed her knuckles. Then, in a different voice: “I meant it, though.”

“Which part?”

“That I don’t mind waiting. And that I miss you when you’re not there.”

“I know,” she said, and leaned against him with their hands linked on the desk.

She never put the forty minutes in anything. She never showed it to her supervisor or to Meilin or to anyone. She backed it up to three separate drives.

chapters.desc: Her portfolio documentary is due tomorrow afternoon, and the render has been stuck at 98% for forty minutes.
chapters.title: Render Queue
chapters.epigraph: “I like that it’s quiet.”
chapters.content:
At a quarter to midnight Zhou Yichen was brushing his teeth when his phone lit up on the edge of the sink.

Xiaoran: it’s stuck

He finished, rinsed, and dried his hands.

Yichen: What’s stuck?

Xiaoran: the render

Xiaoran: it says 98%

Yichen: For how long?

Xiaoran: forty minutes

He looked at that. Then he video-called her. She answered with the face of someone who had been personally betrayed by a machine.

“Hello.”

“Have you tried leaving it alone?”

“Yes. For forty minutes.”

“Have you tried restarting it?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because it’s at ninety-eight percent.”

He shut his eyes. “Xiaoran. If it’s been at ninety-eight for forty minutes, it’s probably not going to finish on its own.”

“Don’t say that. It’s due at two tomorrow. Today. It’s due at two today.” She pulled her knees up on the chair. Behind her, the whole studio was dark except for the laptop and the desk lamp.

“I’m coming over,” he said.

“You don’t have to—”

“I know,” he said, and hung up, and put his shoes on.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was her final-year portfolio documentary. She had spent five weeks on it: cutting, colour grading, fixing the sound, making a hundred small changes nobody else would ever notice. She’d exported a test version, checked the subtitles, and sent a rough cut to her supervisor the week before. This was meant to be the last render. It had been going beautifully. Until it hadn’t.

He came across the road and up four flights in seven minutes, with two bottles of tea and a bag from the all-night shop. She was sitting cross-legged on her desk chair, staring at the progress bar as if she could push it with her eyes.

“You’re still watching it?”

“Look.”

He put the bag down and crouched beside her chair. 98%.

“What format are you exporting?”

She told him.

“Resolution?”

She told him.

“Frame rate?”

She told him. He nodded. “Can you fix it?” she said.

“Maybe.”

“That’s not reassuring.”

“I haven’t looked at it yet,” he said, and she slid off the chair to give it to him and then sat on the floor right next to it with her head against his knee.

He opened the task manager. “It hasn’t crashed. It’s still working.”

“Then why isn’t it moving?”

“Maybe it’s stuck on a heavy bit. Have you got a lot of effects near the end?”

“Colour grading. Some overlays. A few transitions.”

“How many?”

She told him. He looked down at her.

“That’s quite a lot.”

“It’s a documentary.”

“I know. Have you saved a copy of the project?” He scrolled to the end of her timeline.

“Yes.”

“Good. Let’s not touch the original. We’ll export just the last two minutes at low resolution and see if it gets through.”

He didn’t take over. He didn’t pretend to know the software better than she did, because he didn’t. He sat in her chair and asked questions, and she leaned over his arm and did the clicking. The test export ran. It finished in a minute and a half.

She let out a breath. “Oh.”

“So the timeline’s probably fine. It’s something in the full export. Memory, maybe, or one of the effects. We’ll narrow it down.”

“You sound like you’re fixing a business problem.”

“Is that an insult?”

“It’s a description,” she said, and he kissed her temple.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took an hour. They worked backward through the last sequence, a section at a time. She found one overlay she didn’t really need and took it off. She changed two settings he pointed at, and one he didn’t. Then she started the full render again. It reached twenty-four percent.

While it crawled, he made her drink half a bottle of tea, and she made him watch the opening. It was her grandmother’s hands shelling peas in the courtyard in the town, shot the summer before, with the persimmon tree’s shadow moving over them. Nobody had seen it but her grandmother.

He watched it all the way through and didn’t say anything at all. She had known he wouldn’t. It was the right thing to say.

“She didn’t know I was filming her hands. She thought I was filming the tree,” she said.

“Did you tell her?”

“I showed her last month. She said, ‘Why would anyone want to look at an old woman’s hands?’ And then she watched it four times.”

The bar moved to fifty-one. Then seventy-six. At eighty-nine she grabbed his wrist.

“What’s wrong?”

“Don’t move.”

“Why not?”

“You’ll jinx it.”

He looked at her, and then slowly sat back in the chair and kept absolutely still.

At ninety-four she stopped breathing. At ninety-seven she leaned so close to the screen her nose nearly touched it. At ninety-nine she whispered, “Please.”

100%. Export complete.

She stared at it. Then she turned round and threw both arms round his neck so hard the chair rolled backward.

“It finished!”

He caught her, laughing. “Congratulations.”

“We did it!”

“You did it.”

“You helped!”

“I mostly sat here.”

“You were emotionally supportive,” she said, and he said that sounded like an important contribution, and she said not to make fun of her, and he said he wasn’t, and she kissed him on the cheek and then the mouth and then turned back to the laptop to check the file.

✦ ✦ ✦

It played. The sound was there. The picture was clean. The subtitles lined up. She skipped through it chapter by chapter until she got to the last sequence: a long, still shot of the university basketball court after training, with the lights half off, and Yichen walking away from the camera towards the doors with his bag over his shoulder.

She smiled at the screen. “Look.”

He leaned in. “That’s good.”

“You like it?”

“Yes.”

“I nearly cut it. I thought it was too long.”

He watched it play out: the court, the half-light, him at the far end pushing the door open and the door swinging shut behind him, and the ball someone had left rolling slowly across the floor until it stopped by the baseline.

He watched it to the end. “I like that it’s quiet.”

“Me too.”

At twenty past one she finally shut the editing program and stretched her arms over her head until her back cracked. He handed her the shop bag.

“Eat something.”

“What did you get?”

“What you eat when you’re working late.”

She looked in. Two egg sandwiches and a little plastic tub of cut pineapple. She smiled.

“You remembered.”

“You’ve had that every deadline night since second year.”

She sat on the floor and ate a sandwich with her back against his legs while he looked at the file on the screen.

“Have you backed it up?”

She stopped chewing.

“Xiaoran.”

“Yes.”

“Where?”

“External drive.”

“And?”

“The cloud.”

“Good.”

“You’re very thorough.”

“Somebody has to be.”

She put her head back against his knee. “Thank you for coming.”

“You sounded like you were about to fight your laptop.”

“I was.”

“I could tell. Do you think it’s good enough?” He ran his hand over her hair.

“That’s my question.”

“Then I’ll answer it. I think it’s five weeks of work. And I think tomorrow you’ll watch it again and want to change things. But tonight it’s finished.” She groaned.

“Tonight it’s finished,” she repeated.

“Come on. Bed.”

“Can we watch the last bit once more?”

He looked at the clock. “Once.”

They watched the empty court, the half-light, the door swinging shut, the ball rolling to a stop by the line. When the screen went black she closed the laptop, and he stood up and held out his hand, and she took it and didn’t let go of it, even when she was lying down, even when she was asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

She slept four and a half hours. When she woke the studio smelled of coffee, which was wrong, because she didn’t own anything that made coffee. His side of the bed was empty and cool. On the desk, next to the shut laptop, there was a paper cup from the shop downstairs, still warm, and a note in his slanted handwriting.

Training at 9. Backed it up a fourth time, to your blue drive. Don’t watch it again before you submit. (You will.)

She watched it again before she submitted. Twice. The second time she didn’t change anything at all, which she decided counted as personal growth.

At two minutes to two she uploaded it. The submission page thought about it for an alarming length of time, long enough for her to stand up, sit down, and seriously consider a career in accounting. Then it showed a green tick and a line of small grey text: Submission received. She took a screenshot, because she wasn’t a fool, and then a second one, in case.

Xiaoran: submitted

Yichen: At what percent?

Xiaoran: very funny. 100

Yichen: Then it’s finished.

Xiaoran: you said that last night

Yichen: It was true last night too.

At four her supervisor replied to the submission with a single line, which was more than he usually gave anyone: Received. The ending is good.

She read it six times. Then she sent him a screenshot of that too.

Yichen: I told you. I liked that it’s quiet.

Xiaoran: you did

Xiaoran: come over after training? I want to watch it with you on a proper screen. once. I promise

Yichen: Once.

He came at seven. They watched it on her wall with the projector she’d borrowed from the department, sitting on the floor with her leaning against his chest and his arms round her, and when the ball rolled to a stop by the baseline she didn’t say anything, and neither did he. She was asleep by nine, in daylight, with nothing left in the queue.

chapters.desc: Their mothers have started a group chat about flowers. Their fathers have still exchanged nothing but a nod.
chapters.title: The Mothers’ Group Chat
chapters.epigraph: “Your father fishes. Mine golfs.”
chapters.content:
The first bouquet arrived on a Tuesday morning in April. Lin Xiaoran didn’t think much of it when her mother sent her a photograph between lectures.

Mum (Accounts Dept.): Look what came.

It was a beautiful arrangement on the dining table at home: pale pink tulips, white roses, a few sprigs of green, wrapped in cream paper with a pink ribbon.

Xiaoran: so pretty!! who from?

Mum (Accounts Dept.): Yichen’s mother.

Mum (Accounts Dept.): The card says she saw them and thought of me.

Xiaoran looked at the picture. It was simple and pretty and exactly right, the way everything Mrs. Zhou chose was exactly right.

Xiaoran: that’s so sweet of her

Twenty minutes later another photograph arrived. Yellow freesias and white lisianthus, in brown paper.

Mum (Accounts Dept.): I’ve sent her these back.

Xiaoran: ALREADY??

Mum (Accounts Dept.): I can’t be the only one getting flowers.

She put her phone down, smiling. It seemed like a small thing. It wasn’t, as it turned out. The next morning at 9:12 she got a message from Yichen’s mother.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): Good morning Xiaoran. Have you eaten?

Xiaoran: good morning Auntie! yes! have you?

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): Yes. Your mother sent me some lovely flowers yesterday.

Xiaoran: I saw! they’re beautiful

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): She has very good taste. I hope she liked mine. I couldn’t decide whether she’d like pink or white.

Xiaoran: she likes both!

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): Then I’ll remember.

She put the phone down. Then picked it up again and read the conversation back. She had the odd, warm feeling of watching two people become friends in front of her, through flowers.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Thursday it was a regular thing. Her mother sent a photo of the tulips opening. Mrs. Zhou sent a photo of an arrangement she’d made herself. Her mother sent back a photo of the tulips moved to a different vase, with better light. In the middle of her afternoon seminar, Xiaoran’s phone buzzed.

Yichen: Do you know why my mother is asking me whether your mother likes hydrangeas?

Xiaoran: because they’re becoming friends

Yichen: I see.

Yichen: She wants to know blue or white.

Xiaoran: ask HER

Yichen: I asked your mother. On my own phone. She said both, depending on the season.

Yichen: I think I’m being used as a flower information service.

Xiaoran: it’s a very important job

Yichen: I’ll put it on my CV.

That evening she rang him on her walk back from the library, and he answered on the first ring.

“Your mother messaged me again. She asked if you’d like flowers for your flat,” she said.

“Why would I want flowers?”

“I told her you like flowers as long as you don’t have to look after them.”

“That’s accurate.”

“She says she’ll choose something you can’t kill.”

“That’s optimistic,” he said, and she laughed so loudly on the path that a cyclist swerved.

✦ ✦ ✦

The real surprise came at the weekend. Xiaoran had gone home on the Friday train, and on Saturday morning her mother called her into the living room and held out her phone without a word.

A new group chat was open. The Flower Corner. Three members.

“Who’s in this?”

“Me. Yichen’s mother. You.”

“Why am I in it?”

“She asked me to add you,” said her mother, as if that settled it, and went back to peeling a pear.

Xiaoran scrolled up. It had started without her.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): I’ve found a lovely florist near the old market.

Mum (Accounts Dept.): Oh, please send me the address.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): I’ll send it when I’m home.

Mum (Accounts Dept.): Thank you!

“Mum. You’ve been talking to her every day.”

“Not every day.”

“Mum.”

“Most days,” her mother admitted, and put a slice of pear in Xiaoran’s mouth so she would stop talking.

✦ ✦ ✦

The fathers had made no progress at all.

They had met precisely once, if it counted: in the dark at the end of the gaokao, two men shaking hands over the bonnet of a car, perhaps a dozen words between them, which neither of them had ever mentioned to their children. Since then, nothing. When the mothers’ messages arrived at all hours, her father read them over her mother’s shoulder, said “Hm,” and went back to the news. According to Yichen, across the city his father did exactly the same thing in a different chair.

“They’re the same man,” Xiaoran said on the phone that night, lying on her childhood bed.

“They’re not the same man. Your father fishes. Mine golfs,” said Yichen.

“Badly?”

“Very badly.”

“Then they’re the same man.”

“Your father once told me that golf was for people who were afraid of fish.”

“He did not.”

“He did. At New Year. While he was gutting a carp.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday the Flower Corner had a new message.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): I made these this afternoon. Which do you think your mother would like better?

It was a picture of two small bouquets side by side, one soft pink, one white and pale yellow. Xiaoran turned the phone round to her mother across the dinner table.

“Pink. But the yellow’s lovely too. Tell her I’ve found a flower market by the river. We should go together. Next Saturday,” said her mother at once.

Xiaoran typed it in.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): Wonderful. Let’s go.

Auntie Zhou (Flower Committee): The fathers can come too.

Xiaoran looked at the screen. Then at her father, who was eating his rice and hadn’t seen. She took a screenshot and sent it to Yichen.

Xiaoran: your mother has invited our fathers to the flower market

Yichen: Interesting.

Xiaoran: do you think they’ll talk

Yichen: I wonder how long they’ll last.

✦ ✦ ✦

The mothers had never actually stood in the same place. They had exchanged forty photographs of hydrangeas, a florist’s address, two recipes, and a long voice message about a neighbour, but they had never once met in person. Xiaoran, who heard about it afterward from both sides, gathered that the first five minutes at the market gate had been extremely polite.

Then Mrs. Zhou had said, “Your daughter told me you don’t like roses when they’re too open,” and Xiaoran’s mother had said, “Your son told me you think lilies smell like a hospital,” and they had looked at each other and burst out laughing, and from then on it was fine.

They bought peonies for themselves. They bought, together, after twenty minutes of argument, a small bunch of white ranunculus for a graduation two months away and a girl who wasn’t supposed to know about it. They drank tea standing up at a stall and talked about their children in a way that would have mortified both of them. The fathers came to carry things.

A little after ten Xiaoran, back in Shanghai, got a photograph in the Flower Corner. Her mother and Yichen’s mother, standing in front of a stall, each holding a bunch of peonies, smiling at whoever was taking it. Behind them, at opposite ends of the same stall, stood the two fathers. Each was holding a paper bag. Each was looking, with tremendous concentration, at a bucket of tulips.

She sent it to Yichen with no message at all. He was in the library two floors above her, and a minute later he came down the stairs and sat next to her and looked at it over her shoulder.

“They’re not talking,” he whispered.

“Do you think they will?”

“Not before the parking runs out.”

Her phone buzzed.

Mum (Accounts Dept.): Your father bought flowers for the house.

“Dad bought flowers?” she said out loud, and the girl across the table glared at her.

Yichen’s phone buzzed in his hand.

Mum (Flower Committee): Your father bought flowers too. He said they looked nice.

“Progress,” he murmured.

Then his phone buzzed again. A message from his father.

Dad (Logistics): Your girlfriend’s father nodded at me. I nodded back.

Yichen looked at it. He turned the screen so she could read it. She clapped both hands over her mouth.

Dad (Logistics): Tell him hello next time. From me.

She hid her face in her arms on the library table and laughed into her arms until her shoulders shook, and he put his hand on her back and left it there, and the girl across the table gave up and moved.

“At least they’re consistent,” she said, when she could breathe.

“Hello is a good start,” he said.

Two months later, at the graduation, in two black gowns, she would turn round and find the two men standing together behind her, talking about the practical arrangements for the months ahead. And as far as she knew, until that afternoon, they had never exchanged more than a nod.

chapters.desc: A water town an hour and a half from Shanghai, a pale blue hanfu, and a boyfriend who rates the outfit before she can ask.
chapters.title: The Day Zhou Yichen Fell in Love with Hanfu
chapters.epigraph: “You were winding up to it.”
chapters.content:
The idea had started with Xiaoran sending Yichen a photograph.

It was a picture of an old Chinese street, its traditional wooden buildings lining a narrow stone-paved road. Red lanterns hung beneath the eaves, delicate bridges crossed a small canal, and the afternoon sunlight fell across the rooftops in a warm golden haze.

Xiaoran: I want to go here.

Yichen had been in the middle of reviewing a training schedule when the message arrived.

He looked at the photograph, then at her message.

Yichen: When?

Xiaoran: This weekend?

Yichen: All right.

Xiaoran: Can we dress up? Hanfu!

He glanced at the photograph again.

Yichen: You want to wear hanfu?

Xiaoran: YES.

Yichen: Then we’ll go.

He hadn’t thought much more about it. Until Saturday morning.

The water town was an hour and a half’s drive from Shanghai, an old canal district that had been carefully preserved and developed into a cultural destination. It wasn’t entirely untouched by modern tourism—there were souvenir shops, cafés, and plenty of visitors—but the old architecture, stone bridges, narrow waterways, and traditional courtyards gave it an atmosphere that made Xiaoran feel as if she’d stepped into another period of time.

They arrived shortly before ten. Xiaoran was already excited before they even entered the main street.

“Yichen, look!”

“I see.”

“There’s a little bridge!”

“Yes.”

“And a boat!”

“I see that too.”

She turned to him.

“You’re not excited?”

“I am.”

“You don’t look excited.”

He met her eyes.

“Would you prefer me to jump up and down?”

She laughed.

“No. That would be strange.”

“Then I’m expressing my excitement appropriately.”

She nudged his arm. They walked past several shops before reaching the hanfu rental studio Xiaoran had bookmarked. It occupied the second floor of an old building, with wooden windows overlooking the street below. Inside, there were rows of garments in different colours and styles, accessories displayed in glass cabinets, and several makeup stations arranged along the wall. Xiaoran’s eyes practically sparkled.

“Oh, my God.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Found something?”

“Everything.”

She moved towards a rack of garments, carefully touching the fabric of a pale blue robe.

The shop assistant greeted them and explained the rental packages. Xiaoran listened carefully, asking about the different styles, hair arrangements, makeup options, and photography packages. Yichen stood beside her, listening.

“Would you like to try a more elaborate hairstyle? We have several options depending on the style of hanfu,” the assistant asked.

Xiaoran nodded enthusiastically.

“Yes, please.”

She looked at Yichen.

“Which colour do you think I should choose?”

He looked over the racks. There were soft pinks, pale greens, cream, lavender, and several shades of blue.

“Which one do you like?”

“That’s not helpful.”

“It’s your outfit.”

“But I want your opinion.”

He considered her.

“Light blue.”

She looked at the pale blue garment she’d been admiring earlier.

“Why?”

“I think it’ll suit you.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Okay. I’ll try that one.”

The assistant then turned towards Yichen.

“And would your boyfriend like to rent one as well? We have matching couple sets.”

Xiaoran immediately turned around.

“Matching?”

Yichen looked at her.

“Would you like that?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll rent one.”

The assistant brought out a dark blue set with understated embroidery, paired with a black belt and a matching outer robe. Xiaoran looked at it, then at him.

“You’re going to look like a young master.”

Yichen raised an eyebrow.

“Is that good?”

“Very good.”

“Then I suppose I’ll trust your judgement.”

The styling process took longer than Xiaoran expected. She was seated in front of a mirror while the stylist arranged her hair, carefully dividing it into sections and pinning it into an elegant half-up style. Delicate ornaments were added, including a small floral hairpin and dangling pearls that framed the sides of her face. Her makeup was soft and delicate.

The stylist applied a light base, added a gentle flush to her cheeks, and carefully defined her eyes. A little colour was added to her lips, making them look naturally rosy. Xiaoran watched the transformation in the mirror.

“Do I look strange?”

The stylist smiled.

“Not at all. You look lovely.”

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen through the mirror. He was sitting on a sofa nearby, looking through his phone.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Come and see.”

He put his phone away and walked over. He stopped behind her. He didn’t answer. His gaze rested on her reflection.

The pale blue hanfu was layered delicately, with long flowing sleeves and subtle embroidery along the collar. Her hair was arranged beautifully, and the ornaments gave her an appearance that was softer and more refined than her usual everyday style. But it was still unmistakably Xiaoran. Her expressive eyes.

The little crease between her eyebrows when she was uncertain.

The way she was currently looking at him through the mirror, waiting for his opinion. His mouth curved.

“You look beautiful.”

Her expression brightened. She turned slightly in her chair.

“The pins aren’t too much?”

He lowered his head, adjusting a small ornament that had become slightly loose near her temple.

“Does it feel uncomfortable?”

“No.”

“Then don’t worry about it.”

He looked at her reflection again.

“I like it.”

She smiled. The stylist watched them with an amused expression.

“Your boyfriend looks very pleased.”

Xiaoran immediately became shy. Yichen, however, smiled.

“He has good taste,” he said.

She met his eyes.

“Who?”

He met her eyes in the mirror.

“Me.”

She laughed. When Yichen went to change, Xiaoran was still having the finishing touches done.

She was given a small fan, delicate enough to fit comfortably in her hand, and a little fabric pouch to complete the outfit.

She practised holding the fan in front of the mirror.

The stylist showed her how to position her hands, how to turn slightly, and how to let the long sleeves fall naturally. Xiaoran tried, then tried again.

“Like this?”

“Very good.”

Her mouth tipped up. She was beginning to feel like she was playing a character in a historical drama, then the assistant called her attention.

“Your boyfriend is ready.”

Xiaoran turned. And stopped. Yichen stood near the doorway.

His outfit was dark blue, with a structured inner robe and a flowing outer layer. The embroidery was subtle, the sleeves neat, and his hair had been styled with a traditional hairpiece that kept it away from his forehead. He looked different.

Not dramatically different, but enough that Xiaoran needed a moment to process it.

He looked like someone who belonged in the courtyard of an old Chinese residence, perhaps a young scholar or the son of a distinguished family.

His usual composed expression somehow suited the outfit even more. He noticed her staring.

“What?”

Xiaoran blinked, then smiled.

“Oh.”

He approached.

“Oh?”

“You look...”

She searched for a word.

“Very handsome.”

His lips curved.

“Only very?”

“Extremely handsome.”

“Better.”

She laughed. Then she looked at him again.

“Wait. Stand there.”

He stopped. She took out her phone.

“Don’t move.”

“All right.”

She took a photograph, then another. Then she looked at the screen.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You look like the male lead.”

“Of what?”

“A historical drama.”

He looked at her.

“And what are you?”

She lifted her chin.

“The female lead, obviously.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Naturally.”

She approached him and adjusted the collar of his robe.

“Now we match.”

He looked down at her hands.

“Do we?”

“Yes.”

She stepped back to admire them together. Then, said:

“We look like a couple who would have a very beautiful love story.”

Yichen looked at her. Then he reached for her hand.

“I think we already do.”

The first photography session took place in the courtyard behind the studio.

The photographer had prepared several traditional props and suggested a series of poses. At first, Xiaoran was a little awkward.

She knew how to pose for ordinary photographs, but traditional hanfu photography required a different kind of elegance.

“Could you turn slightly? Yes, like that. Hold the fan a little higher.” the photographer instructed.

Xiaoran followed. Yichen stood a short distance away, watching.

“Very good. Now look towards the camera.”

Click.

“Beautiful.”

The photographer checked the screen, then asked Yichen to join her.

“Could you stand beside her? Perhaps hold her hand.”

Yichen moved closer. Xiaoran instinctively looked up at him.

“Where?”

“Here.”

He took her hand. The photographer smiled.

“Look at each other.”

They did. Xiaoran tried to maintain a graceful expression. Yichen looked at her calmly.

Then, just as the photographer was about to take the picture, he leaned slightly closer.

“You’re very serious.”

She whispered back, “I’m trying to look elegant.”

“You already do.”

“Don’t distract me.”

His mouth curved. Click. The photographer lowered the camera.

“That one was lovely.”

Xiaoran looked at the preview. It was a beautiful photograph.

She stood in her pale blue hanfu, her fan held delicately in one hand. Yichen stood beside her in dark blue, his hand wrapped around hers. Their eyes were on each other rather than the camera. She looked at the picture for a while.

“Can we keep that one?”

The photographer laughed.

“Of course. It’s one of my favourites.”

Yichen glanced at the screen.

“So is mine.”

They spent the next hour walking through the old district. Xiaoran was having the time of her life.

She wanted photographs on every bridge, beside every wooden doorway, near every lantern, and in front of every pretty building. Yichen accompanied her without complaint.

He carried her phone, held her little pouch, and occasionally helped arrange the long sleeves of her hanfu when they became tangled.

At one point, she stopped beside a stone bridge.

“Yichen, can you take a picture of me here?”

He took her phone.

“How?”

“Like this.”
