“Very. I was a bit sad when you drove away this morning.” She held on.

“You told me to.”

“I know.”

“So I followed instructions.”

“You’re very obedient.”

“Only when the instructions are clear. You’re done now. You did it.” He turned round inside her arms and put his own round her.

She looked up at him. “Thank you for waiting. Both times.”

“I said I would. And I wanted to.” He tucked her hair behind her ear.

She kissed him, a long, slow kiss in the middle of his kitchen with the fridge door still open behind him, and when she pulled back he leaned his forehead against hers.

“Tomorrow,” he said, “do you want me to drop you at the door?”

She thought about it. “No. Round the corner.”

“All right.”

“But you can wait until I get inside.”

“I can do that.”

“And maybe on Friday you can walk me to the door.”

“Why Friday?”

“Because by Friday I’ll know everyone, and I won’t be nervous.”

“Then Friday.”

“And you can kiss me goodbye.”

“Only on Friday?”

“Don’t push your luck,” she said, and put her face back against his chest, and he shut the fridge with his foot.

At ten he walked her across the road and up the four flights to her studio, carrying her bag, and waited on the landing while she hunted for her keys, which turned out to be in the side pocket she never used. She found them and turned round in the doorway.

“Same corner tomorrow.”

“Same corner,” he said, and stayed on the landing until her door was shut and he heard the chain go on.

chapters.desc: Her first salary, checked seventeen times by lunch, and the first dinner she pays for.
chapters.title: First Pay Slip
chapters.epigraph: “Not because I owe you. Because I want to.”
chapters.content:
Her first salary arrived on the last Friday of July, and by lunchtime Xiaoran had checked her bank account seventeen times. Yichen knew because he had counted.

The first time had been when she woke up. The second was while brushing her teeth. The third was during breakfast.

By the time they met for lunch, she had checked it another six times.

And now, sitting across from him in a café near her office, she was looking at her banking app again. Yichen lowered his cup.

“Did the number change?”

Xiaoran looked up.

“No.”

“Then why are you checking?”

She turned her phone towards him.

“Look.”

He glanced at the screen. Her first salary had arrived that morning.

The amount was displayed beneath her account balance, accompanied by a small transaction description from her employer. Yichen looked at it, then back at her.

“Congratulations.”

Her mouth tipped up. It wasn’t a large smile at first. More like she was trying to contain something that had been building inside her since she saw the notification. Then it grew.

“I got paid.”

“I can see that.”

“My first salary.”

“I know.”

“From my job.”

He nodded solemnly.

“Yes, Xiaoran. That’s generally how salaries work.”

She kicked his shoe beneath the table. He laughed. She looked down at her phone again.

“I can’t believe it.”

He watched her. It was a small thing, really. A salary notification. A number appearing in an account. But he knew what it meant to her.

She had spent months working towards this. Her first days at Morrow Studio had been filled with unfamiliar names, unfamiliar expectations, and the pressure of proving that she deserved to be there. She had come home tired, sometimes frustrated, sometimes excited enough to talk about a project for an hour.

She had learned how to communicate with clients, defend creative decisions, manage production schedules, and work with people who had entirely different ideas about what a project should become.

And now, for the first time, she had been paid for work that she had done as a professional. He reached across the table. He held out his hand.

She put her phone down and gave him her hand. He kissed her knuckles.

“I knew you could.”

“Thank you.”

Then she picked up her phone again. Yichen looked at her.

“Again?”

“I’m just looking.”

“At the same number?”

“It’s a very nice number.”

He laughed. The idea came to her that afternoon.

They were walking towards the car when Xiaoran stopped.

“Yichen.”

He turned.

“Mm?”

“I want to take you to dinner.”

He met her eyes.

“We’re having dinner tonight.”

“I know.”

“Where?”

She smiled.

“Somewhere nice.”

He waited.

“And I’m paying.”

He turned to her. Then his expression softened.

“All right.”

She blinked.

“That’s it?”

“What else?”

“You didn’t even pretend to argue.”

“Would you like me to?”

She thought about it.

“No.”

“Then I’ll save us both the trouble.”

She laughed and took his arm.

“I’ve been thinking about it since this morning.”

“About dinner?”

“Yes. I want to use my first salary to buy you a meal.”

He glanced at her.

“You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

“I’m serious.”

“So am I.”

She met his eyes.

“You’ve taken me to so many places. You’ve paid for so many dinners. You’ve bought me things, driven me around, planned trips, and made sure I never had to worry about anything when we’re together.”

He smiled.

“That’s not a list of things you owe me for.”

“Mm.”

She stopped walking and turned towards him.

“That’s why I want to do this. Not because I owe you. Because I want to.”

He held her gaze. Then he nodded.

“All right.”

Her face brightened. She immediately opened her phone.

“Let me choose the restaurant.”

He glanced at the screen.

“Take your time.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“You’re not going to secretly book somewhere else?”

“No.”

“Or call the restaurant and tell them you’re paying?”

“No.”

“Or give them your card?”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Do you think I would do that?”

“Sometimes.”

He laughed.

“Then you’ll have to watch me carefully.”

Choosing the restaurant turned out to be harder than Xiaoran expected.

She had initially wanted somewhere elegant, but the prices made her hesitate.

Then she found a place with a beautiful interior, but the menu looked too small.

Another restaurant had excellent reviews, but she wasn’t sure whether Yichen would enjoy the food. She spent nearly an hour comparing options.

Yichen, who had been sitting beside her on the sofa, eventually asked:

“Are you choosing a restaurant or negotiating a business acquisition?”

“Both require careful consideration.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Of course.”

She showed him her shortlist.

“Which one?”

He studied the options.

“Where do you want to go?”

“That’s not helpful.”

“It’s your dinner.”

She looked at the screen again. Then she pointed to one.

“This one.”

“Then let’s go there.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Okay.”

He looked at her.

“Are you sure?”

“I checked the menu. It’s within my budget.”

He didn’t comment on the budget. He said, “Then it’s settled.”

She booked a table. Then she put her phone down and leaned against him.

“Do you know what I want?”

“What?”

“I want to be able to do this more often.”

He looked down at her.

“Take me to dinner?”

“Yes. Pay for things. Buy you something without you noticing the price first.”

He laughed.

“That last part might be difficult.”

She lifted her head.

“Why?”

“Because I usually notice.”

She groaned.

“You’re the worst.”

He kissed her hair.

“I’ll try to be less observant.”

The restaurant was lovely. It had warm lighting, dark wooden furniture, and large windows overlooking the evening traffic.

Xiaoran had arrived a little early and checked the reservation twice.

When Yichen walked in, she was already sitting at the table, looking at the menu.

He approached and pulled out the chair opposite her.

“Waiting long?”

“No.”

He sat down. She immediately handed him the menu.

“I’ve already looked.”

“I assumed.”

“There’s a dish I think you’ll like.”

He glanced at the menu.

“Which one?”

She pointed.

“This.”

He read the description.

“Looks good.”

“I thought so.”

He studied her.

“You’ve researched the entire menu, haven’t you?”

She smiled proudly.

“Yes.”

“Of course.”

They ordered. Xiaoran chose a dish she had been wanting to try, while Yichen ordered the one she had recommended. She also insisted on ordering dessert before they had even finished their main courses.

“Why are you ordering dessert now?” he asked.

“Because if we wait, I’ll forget.”

“You won’t.”

“I might.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“All right.”

She looked pleased. Dinner was easy. They talked about her first month at work, the people she had met, and the projects she was beginning to handle more independently.

She told him about a client who had changed their mind three times about the same visual concept.

Yichen listened with the patient attention he always gave her.

“Did you agree with the final direction?” he asked.

“Not entirely.”

“Then?”

“I explained why I thought the earlier version was stronger. But they had a different objective, so we adjusted it.”

“Good.”

She turned to him.

“You’re not going to tell me I should have fought harder?”

“Do you think you should have?”

She considered it.

“No. I think I explained my reasoning properly.”

“Then you did your job.”

That made her grin. Sometimes, she liked that he didn’t automatically tell her she was right.

He took her work seriously enough to ask her to think about it. After a while, the food arrived. Xiaoran watched him take the first bite.

“Well?”

“Good.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She looked pleased.

“I chose well.”

“You did.”

She rested her chin on her hand.

“Do you know why I chose this restaurant?”

“Because you liked the menu?”

“Partly.”

He waited. She smiled.

“Because I wanted somewhere that felt special, but not somewhere I would be uncomfortable paying.”

He considered her.

“That’s sensible.”

“I know.”

She picked up her glass.

“I wanted to take you somewhere nice with my first salary. I didn’t want to spend more than I could comfortably afford just to prove something.”

Yichen nodded.

“That’s a good way to think about it.”

That made her grin.

“I think I’m becoming a responsible adult.”

“Are you?”

She kicked his shoe again. He laughed. After dinner, they ordered dessert.

Xiaoran had chosen a small chocolate cake to share, but when it arrived, she immediately took the first bite. Yichen watched her.

“How is it?”

She nodded enthusiastically.

“Very good.”

“Then I’m glad we ordered it.”

She pushed the plate towards him.

“Try.”

He took a bite. She watched him.

“Well?”

“Good.”

“Only good?”

“Very good.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“That’s better.”

They finished the dessert slowly. When the waiter brought the bill, Xiaoran reached for it before Yichen could move. He noticed. But he didn’t interfere. She took the bill folder and opened it. She looked at the total. Then she took out her card. Yichen watched her. She handed the folder to the waiter.

“Thank you.”

When the waiter left, she sat back. Her expression was strangely serious. Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

She shook her head.

“Nothing.”

He waited. She looked down at the table.

“I paid.”

He smiled.

“Yes.”

“With my salary.”

“I know.”

She held his gaze.

“You’re not going to say anything?”

He leaned back slightly.

“What would you like me to say?”

She thought about it. Then her smile slowly appeared.

“That I did well.”

He took her hand across the table.

“You did very well.”

Her eyes softened.

He said, “Not because you paid for dinner. Because you worked for that salary, and you wanted to use a part of it to make someone you love happy.”

She looked down. Then she squeezed his hand.

“You’re making it sound very emotional.”

“Isn’t it?”

She laughed.

“A little.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her fingers.

“Thank you for dinner.”

“You’re welcome. Next time, I’ll buy you something too.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You’re already planning the next one?”

“Of course.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Very.”

He laughed. They walked out of the restaurant together.

The night air was cool, and the street was quieter than it had been when they arrived. Xiaoran slipped her hand into his.

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Very much.”

Her mouth tipped up. Then she looked down at her hand. The promise ring caught the light. She turned it slightly.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Do you think I’ll get used to receiving my salary?”

“Probably.”

“Will it always feel this exciting?”

He thought about it.

“Maybe not in the same way.”

“That’s sad.”

“Not necessarily. The first time is special because it’s the first. Later, it might feel normal. That’s not a bad thing.”

She nodded.

“I suppose.”

He looked at her.

“But I hope you keep remembering what you worked for.”

“I will.”

He opened the passenger door for her. Before getting in, she turned around.

“Wait.”

He glanced at her. She stepped closer and wrapped her arms around his waist. He returned the hug.

“Thank you for letting me pay.”

He smiled against her hair.

“You’re welcome.”

“And thank you for not making it awkward.”

“Was I supposed to?”

“No. But you sometimes try to pay before I can.”

He laughed.

“I’ll be more careful next time.”

She leaned back and looked at him.

“Good.”

Then she caught his face in both hands and kissed him.

“Thank you for coming to dinner, Mr. Zhou.”

He met her eyes.

“Thank you for having me, Ms. Lin.”

She climbed into the car, smiling. Later, back at his apartment, Xiaoran opened her banking app again.

Yichen was changing out of his shirt when he saw her sitting on the bed.

“Checking your salary again?”

“No.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“I’m checking my remaining balance.”

“Ah.”

She turned the phone towards him.

“Look. I still have enough.”

His mouth curved.

“That’s good.”

“And I didn’t spend too much.”

“I know.”

She put the phone down and looked at him.

“Today was nice.”

He came over and sat beside her.

“It was.”

“I liked paying for you.”

“I liked being taken out.”

She smiled. She leaned against him.

“Then I’ll do it again.”

He put an arm around her shoulders.

“I’ll look forward to it.”

She looked up. She laughed. Then she became quiet.

She said, “I think I understand something now.”

“What?”

“Why you like paying for things sometimes.”

She said, “It’s not always about the money. Sometimes it’s just nice to be able to do something for someone you care about.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Yes.”

She rested her head against his chest.

“I used to think I had to wait until I could afford something expensive to give you something meaningful.”

He brushed her hair away from her face.

“You don’t.”

“I know that now.”

She lifted her hand and looked at the ring.

“Today was meaningful.”

He kissed her hair.

“It was.”

She smiled and settled against him. Her first salary had been deposited that morning.

By evening, a part of it had become dinner, dessert, and a memory she would probably remember long after the exact amount had faded from her mind.

It was the first time she had looked across a restaurant table, handed over her own card, and felt that she was giving him something from a life she was beginning to build for herself.

And Yichen, who had spent years taking care of her in ways both large and small, understood exactly why she had wanted to do it. He held her a little closer.

“Congratulations on your first salary, Xiaoran.”

She smiled against his chest.

“Thank you. Next month, I’m buying you breakfast too.”

He laughed.

“All right.”

She closed her eyes, satisfied.

chapters.desc: His first full preseason with the Herons, and a fridge full of labelled containers he didn’t ask for.
chapters.title: Preseason Meal Prep
chapters.epigraph: “Because I know you’ll want something comforting after a difficult day.”
chapters.content:
Zhou Yichen’s first mistake was saying he could manage his own meals. His second was saying it while Lin Xiaoran was standing in his kitchen.

She looked up from her laptop on the counter. “Sorry?”

He was getting a bottle of water out of the fridge. “What?”

“What did you just say?”

“I said I can manage my own meals.”

She closed the laptop. “During preseason.”

“Yes.”

“With double sessions.”

“Yes.”

“Three meals a day.”

“That’s generally how meals work.”

“Don’t be clever.”

“I’m not,” he said, and drank his water.

She looked at him. Then she said, “Fine,” and opened the fridge and started taking things out.

“What are you doing?”

“Helping you manage your meals.”

“I didn’t ask you to.”

“I know. I’m doing it anyway.” She put three carrots and a cabbage on the counter.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Herons’ preseason had started at the beginning of August: double sessions, strength work, conditioning, two hours of game film every afternoon. It was his first full one with the first team, and he’d come home every night that week at half past eight with his hair wet and his eyes half shut. He wasn’t bad at looking after himself. He knew what his body needed. But he was also exactly the kind of person who would get in late, look at the fridge, decide that an egg and some toast was enough, and fall asleep on the sofa before he’d finished the toast.

She’d noticed. She didn’t want to watch what he ate or turn food into one more job for him. She wanted to make the long days a bit shorter.

On Wednesday she’d suggested cooking some meals ahead for the week. He’d said that sounded like a good idea. He hadn’t expected her to treat it like a production.

On Saturday morning she arrived at his door with a notebook.

“What’s that?”

“The plan.”

She opened it on the counter. She had asked the Herons’ nutritionist, through Fang Ze, through Kou Ran, what the team was meant to be eating, and had checked his fridge on Wednesday while he was in the shower, and the result was two pages of columns ruled in pencil, the way her mother ruled the household accounts.

He looked at it. “You’ve made a spreadsheet.”

“I haven’t.”

“That’s a spreadsheet.”

“It’s handwritten.”

“That doesn’t make it not a spreadsheet. There’s a column called backup.” He turned the page.

“In case you don’t like something.”

“I like everything.”

“You don’t like aubergine.”

He was quiet. “How do you know that?”

“Because you push it to the side of your bowl and cover it with rice so your mother won’t see. You’re helping,” she said, and handed him an apron.

“I assumed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The kitchen got busy fast. She did the vegetables. He did the chicken and the beef. She’d tied her hair up and was cutting carrots into exactly even pieces with a look of total concentration, and after a while he stopped what he was doing to watch.

“Those are very precise.”

“They need to cook evenly.”

“You’re cutting them into identical pieces.”

“Then why are you watching?”

“Because you’re very serious about it.”

She pointed the knife at him. “Cooking is serious.”

He went back to the chicken, smiling. They worked side by side in the narrow kitchen, reaching past each other, bumping shoulders, checking the rice in turns. At one point he reached for a glass bowl and she moved it out of his way.

“Not that one.”

“Why?”

“That’s for the vegetables.”

He took a different one. A minute later he reached for a container.

“Not that one.”

“Xiaoran. Am I allowed to use anything in my own kitchen?”

“Yes. Just follow the system.”

“Your system has more rules than my training schedule.”

“Your training schedule doesn’t involve containers.”

“Thankfully,” he said, and she bumped him with her hip, and he bumped her back, and she nearly dropped a carrot and called him a menace.

✦ ✦ ✦

By noon the counter was covered. They packed everything into boxes, matched to the days he’d need them, and she checked each one off in the notebook while he read the labels she’d written on masking tape.

“Monday. Tuesday. Wednesday. Why does this one say eat first?” He picked one up.

“Because it won’t keep as long.”

He picked up another one. It had a note on the lid in her round handwriting. For the day training is terrible.

“What’s this?”

She glanced over from the sink. “Oh. That one’s for when you’re really tired.”

“What’s in it?”

“Something you like.”

He lifted the corner of the lid. It was dan dan noodles, the kind from the stall by the university’s east gate that he’d eaten twice a week for four years, which she had made from scratch from a recipe she’d found online and tested on Ning twice.

“You made this as well?”

“Just one portion.”

“Why?”

“Because I know you’ll want something comforting after a difficult day.”

He put the box down on the counter. He didn’t say anything. Then he came round to her side, turned off the tap she was using, and put his arms round her from behind and his chin on her hair.

“Thank you.”

“It’s only noodles.”

“I know,” he said, and didn’t let go, and she leaned back against him with her wet hands held out in front of her so she wouldn’t drip on his arms.

✦ ✦ ✦

The real problem was getting everything into the fridge. There were too many boxes. She took out one shelf and moved it. Then another. Then she found a bottle of juice at the back.

“Where did this come from?”

“Your mother gave it to me.”

“When?”

“Last month.”

She turned round with the bottle in her hand. “Yichen. Why is it still here?”

“I haven’t finished it.”

“Drink it today.”

“Yes, ma’am.”

She gave him a look. He laughed and took the bottle from her and drank a third of it right there, standing in front of the open fridge, to make a point, and then helped her rearrange the shelves until everything fitted.

She stepped back. “Done.”

“Impressive.”

“Now you don’t have to think about what to eat after training.”

“I still have to think about taking it out.”

“That’s not difficult.”

She shut the fridge and leaned back against it and looked at him. He was looking at her.

“Tell me.”

He reached over and picked a scrap of cabbage off her sleeve. “I like that you think about these things.”

“It’s not a big thing.”

“I know. You do it anyway. You do it every time.” He took her hand.

“You’re my boyfriend. I’m allowed to look after you,” she said.

He kissed her then, against the fridge door, with the timer for the second batch of rice going off behind them, and neither of them moved to turn it off until it had beeped for a full minute.

✦ ✦ ✦

Three days later, at lunch at the studio, she got a photograph of an empty box.

Yichen: Finished.

Xiaoran: which one?

Yichen: The chicken.

Xiaoran: did you like it?

Yichen: Yes.

On Thursday evening another photograph came. It was the box with the note on the lid. For the day training is terrible. It was empty.

Xiaoran: oh no. was it bad?

Yichen: Coach had us do suicides for forty minutes because Kou Ran was late.

Yichen: This one was very good.

Xiaoran: I knew it would be

Yichen: Can I request another one?

Xiaoran: you can request. I can’t promise

Yichen: Understood.

Yichen: Thank you, Xiaoran.

Yichen: I miss you.

Xiaoran: I miss you too

Yichen: And the noodles.

She stared at her phone for a second and then laughed so loudly that Gao Yan looked up from the next desk.

Xiaoran: ZHOU YICHEN

Yichen: Both can be true.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she went across the road to his flat after work, because she’d heard it in the messages: he was tired. He came in from training at nine. He didn’t say hello first. He went straight to the kitchen and opened the fridge and stood looking at the boxes, and took one out, and only then came over to the sofa where she was sitting with her laptop and kissed her hair.

“Thank you for all this.”

“You’re welcome. You okay?” She looked up at him.

“I am now. Although I think we need more boxes.” He glanced back at the fridge.

“Already?”

“Already. Next time I’m making the noodles.” He sat down next to her and leaned into her, which he almost never did, his head heavy on her shoulder.

“Why?”

“Because you made them this time. I should make something for you.”

“You can’t cook noodles.”

“I’ll learn.”

“Okay,” she said, and put her hand in his damp hair, and felt him breathe out.

They ate at his little table. She told him about the tea campaign and the client who wanted the leaves to look “more spiritual,” talking with her hands, and halfway through he reached across and touched her fingers, and she stopped.

“You’re looking at me.”

“I know.”

“Why?”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles. “Just because.”

She went straight back to the spiritual tea leaves as if he hadn’t done anything at all. But she held on to his hand for the rest of dinner, and ate left-handed, and spilled rice on the table, and didn’t let go.

chapters.desc: She is moving in with Yichen in November. Her mother approved in September. Her father was fishing.
chapters.title: Telling, Not Asking
chapters.epigraph: “I liked that your door only had one name on it.”
chapters.content:
The decision had been made for eleven days.

Lin Xiaoran had worked it out the way she worked out everything: the rent he already paid and the half she would now pay, the twenty-minute walk to Morrow instead of five minutes across the road, the day her studio lease ran out, the four flights of stairs she wouldn’t miss. She had made a spreadsheet. Her mother would have approved of the spreadsheet.

She and Zhou Yichen had been talking about it since the summer. They had looked at three flats and disliked all three, gone over the money more than once, and in September, on his sofa, decided on his. He had given her a key on a plain ring that he had obviously been carrying around in his pocket for a week. He knew which weekend in November the van was booked, and he had cleared two shelves and half his wardrobe without once asking whether that would be enough.

Her mother had been told on the phone. She had asked one question about the rent and one about whose name would be on the lease, and approved of both answers. That left her father.

She had put it off twice. Not because she was going to change her mind. Because she kept waiting for the right moment, which was becoming ridiculous, because there was no right moment to tell your father you were moving in with someone.

On the second afternoon of the National Day holiday, home on the train for three days, she found him in the little storeroom off the kitchen, trying to fix the handle on an old cabinet.

“Dad.”

He looked round. “What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Then why are you standing there like that?”

She leaned on the doorframe. “Can I talk to you?”

He put the screwdriver down. “Of course.”

She had prepared a speech. It was quite a good speech. It covered the lease, the rent, the walk to work, the fact that she had thought about the money. When he looked at her, she forgot all of it.

“I’m moving in with Yichen.”

He didn’t say anything straight away. He straightened up slowly, with one hand on the cabinet.

“When?”

“November. The second weekend.”

“Your mother knows?”

“Since September.”

He took that in. “So I’m last.”

“You were fishing.”

He nodded once, as if that were fair.

She said, “I wanted to tell you properly. Not on the phone. I’ve thought about it. I’ve done the rent and the lease and the walk to work. I know you’ll think it’s soon. I know you’ll worry. But I’ve decided. I’m not asking, Dad. I’m telling you.”

He looked at her. There was no sharp question, no reminder that she was twenty-two.

“Is your name going on the lease?”

She blinked. “Yes. They’re adding me in November.”

“Have you read it?”

“Twice.”

“Read it a third time before you sign. And keep your own copy. Not on his computer. Yours.”

“I know.”

“Do you, though?”

“Yes, Dad.”

He looked at her a second longer. Then he picked the screwdriver up again and turned back to the cabinet.

“All right.”

She didn’t move. “All right?”

“Do you need me to say it twice?”

She let out a breath that was almost a laugh. “I thought you’d be angry.”

“I’m not angry. I worried when you went to Shanghai on your own. I worried when you took a flat up four flights of stairs with a lift that’s never worked. I’ll worry about this as well. You’re my daughter. I’ll worry whether you’re twenty-two or forty.” He turned a screw a quarter turn and stopped.

“Dad—”

“But you didn’t decide this yesterday. You’ve thought about it. And if I tell you to wait because I’m worried, what am I asking? For you to give something up so I feel better? I don’t want that.” He looked at the cabinet handle, not at her.

Her eyes had started to sting. “It doesn’t mean I’ll come home less.”

“I know.”

“I’ll still visit.”

“I know.”

“And I’ll call.”

“I know, Xiaoran. You’re moving across a road. Not to another planet.” He looked at her at last.

She laughed, and it wobbled. “That’s not what it feels like.”

“It’ll feel smaller once you’ve unpacked,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He saw her wipe under one eye. He didn’t say anything about it. Instead he bent down, opened the bottom drawer of the cabinet, and lifted out a metal toolbox. It was old and scratched, with a faded label on the lid and a handle that had been mended with black tape. He set it on the floor between them.

“What’s that?”

“A toolbox.”

“I can see it’s a toolbox.”

“Then why did you ask?”

She gave him a look. He opened it. Screwdrivers, a measuring tape, pliers, a small hammer, a craft knife, a little packet of screws, and several things she couldn’t name.

“A flat with two people in it comes loose twice as fast. Handles. Shelves. Hinges,” he said, taking things out one at a time and looking at them.

“Dad, it’s his flat. He has tools.”

“Does he?”

She thought about it. “He has a screwdriver.”

“One screwdriver.”

“Yes.”

“Exactly. Some of these are old. I’ll replace them before November,” said her father, and tested the edge of a chisel with his thumb.

“You’re giving me this?”

“Yes.”

“But it’s yours.”

“I’ve got another one.”

She looked at the taped handle, at the places inside where the metal had worn smooth from thirty years of hands. “Dad, you don’t have to.”

“I know. Which way do you turn it to tighten?” He held up a screwdriver.

“Clockwise.”

“And to loosen?”

“Counterclockwise.”

“Good. At least you won’t wreck the furniture.”

“Dad!”

He laughed, a short surprised sound. Then he took out the measuring tape and showed her how to lock it. “Don’t let it go all the way out. It snaps back and takes the skin off your knuckles.” He showed her how to hold the hammer near the end of the handle and not the middle, and which screwdriver head went with which screw, and how to use the pliers without pinching herself. It was such an ordinary thing to be taught. Almost absurdly ordinary, after what they had just said.

“Dad,” she said. “Are you really okay with it?”

His hands stopped. He looked up at her.

“I liked that your door only had one name on it.”

She nodded slowly. “It’ll have two now.”

“I know. I’m okay with it. You don’t need my permission to grow up.” He shut the toolbox.

Her eyes filled up properly then. Her father looked deeply uncomfortable.

“Oh, don’t start crying.”

“I’m not.”

“Your eyes say otherwise.”

She stepped over the toolbox and hugged him. He stood there for a second with a screwdriver still in his hand, and then put it down on the cabinet and held her properly, one hand on the back of her head the way he used to when she was small and had fallen off something.

“You can come home whenever you want.”

“I know.”

“If anything goes wrong, you call me.”

“I will.”

“Even if it’s late. Even if you think it’s small.”

“Okay,” she said into his shoulder.

He held her a bit longer. Then he let go and cleared his throat and picked up the toolbox. “Come on. Let’s see if it fits.”

“Fits where?”

“In your suitcase.”

“Dad, it’s a toolbox.”

“Then we’ll find another bag,” he said, and walked out of the storeroom with it, and she heard him in the hall asking her mother where the big canvas bag had gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yichen was home for exactly one night before the Herons left for twenty-six days on the road. He came round after dinner and found her sitting on the living room floor with the toolbox open beside her and small metal objects spread across the rug.

He stopped in the doorway. “What happened?”

“My father gave me a toolbox.”

He looked at the tools. “I see.”

“He taught me how to use everything. He asked if I knew which way to turn a screwdriver.”

He looked at her with great interest and said nothing at all.

“Don’t start.”

He came over and sat down on the rug beside her, close, and picked up a screwdriver and turned it over in his fingers. “This is a good set.”

“He’s had it for thirty years.”

He understood straight away that it wasn’t a box of tools. He put the screwdriver down carefully, back in its place.

“You told him.”

“The lease, the rent, the second weekend in November.”

“And?”

She picked up the measuring tape and ran her thumb along the worn plastic. “He said I don’t need his permission to grow up.”

Yichen was quiet. “That’s a good answer.”

She leaned sideways against him until her head was on his shoulder. “He’s going to replace the old tools before November. And he says I have to keep my own copy of the lease. Not on your computer.”

“That’s also good advice.”

“You’re both very annoying.”

He laughed and put his arm round her. In the kitchen her parents were washing up, and her father was talking, which he didn’t usually do while washing up, and her mother laughed at something.

“Shall I clear a third shelf?” he said.

“For the toolbox.”

“For the toolbox.”

“And not under the sink, where I’ll never find it.”

“Not under the sink.”

She turned and kissed him, quick, because the kitchen door was open. He followed her when she pulled back and touched his nose to hers.

“What was that for?”

“For being sensible.”

“I’ll try not to make a habit of it,” he said.

She stayed leaning against him with the toolbox open between their knees, full of things that had fixed a hundred small problems in this flat. In November it would go across the road with her and up eleven floors, onto a third shelf, and Yichen would put his one screwdriver beside it, out of respect.

chapters.desc: Twenty-six days, four cities, a missed call and an argument about dinner. They nearly make themselves lonely being considerate.
chapters.title: Away Season
chapters.epigraph: “Send each other one ordinary thing every day.”
chapters.content:
The first time Yichen told Xiaoran he would be away for three weeks in October, she said it was fine. The second time he mentioned that the schedule might extend by another week, she said it was still fine.

The third time, when he explained that the Herons would be travelling between cities for a series of away games, she looked at him.

Then she asked, “How many cities?”

“Four.”

“How many days?”

“Probably twenty-six.”

She nodded.

“Okay.”

Yichen watched her.

“That’s all?”

“What else should I say?”

“I don’t know.”

She smiled and reached for his hand.

“Go play basketball.”

He met her eyes. She squeezed his fingers.

“I know it’s part of the season. I know you can’t just come back whenever you want. I’ll be busy too.”

“Your studio has a major project coming up.”

“Exactly. We’ll both be busy.”

He studied her expression. She was smiling, but he knew her well enough to notice the little things: the way she was turning the ring on her finger, the way her thumb kept moving over the same spot on his hand.

“Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“If it’s difficult, tell me.”

She looked up.

“I will.”

He nodded. Then she leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“Besides, I’ll get to watch my boyfriend play away games. That’s quite impressive.”

He smiled.

“You already do.”

“I know. I’m just reminding people.”

He laughed and pulled her closer. Neither of them knew yet how long twenty-six days could feel. The first week was easy. Almost suspiciously easy.

Yichen left on a Monday morning. Xiaoran accompanied him to the station, carrying his small travel bag while he handled the larger luggage.

He was dressed casually, with a cap pulled low over his forehead. She stood beside him, checking the departure time.

“Do you have everything?”

“Yes.”

“Charger?”

“Yes.”

“Training shoes?”

He turned to her.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I packed them.”

“Okay. I’m just checking.”

He smiled and took the bag from her. The announcement for boarding came shortly afterward. She looked at him.

“Call me when you arrive.”

“I will.”

“And when you reach the hotel.”

“All right.”

“And after training.”

“Yes.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“Don’t just say yes to everything.”

He laughed.

“What would you like me to say?”

“That you’ll miss me.”

He lowered his head and kissed her, briefly.

“I’ll miss you.”

“Good.”

Then she wrapped her arms around him. He held her for a little longer than usual.

When they finally separated, he brushed her hair away from her face.

“Go home safely.”

“You too.”

He picked up his luggage. She watched him walk towards the platform.

Before disappearing into the crowd, he turned around once. She waved. He laughed under his breath. Then he was gone.

That evening, Xiaoran received a photograph of his hotel room.

It showed a large bed, a desk, a window overlooking the city, and his suitcase placed neatly beside the wardrobe.

Yichen: Arrived.

Xiaoran: The room looks nice.

Yichen: It is.

Xiaoran: Have you eaten?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: What?

He sent her a photograph of his dinner. She zoomed in.

Xiaoran: That’s not enough vegetables.

Yichen: There are vegetables.

Xiaoran: Three pieces of broccoli.

Yichen: Four.

She laughed.

Xiaoran: I’m reporting you to your nutritionist.

Yichen: Please don’t.

They called later that night. Xiaoran was already in bed, her laptop open beside her. Yichen was sitting against the hotel headboard, his hair still slightly damp from his shower.

“How was training?” she asked.

“Good. We had a light session after travelling.”

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Then sleep early.”

He held her gaze.

“You’re still working?”

“Just reviewing something.”

“What time is your meeting tomorrow?”

“Nine.”

“Then you should sleep too.”

She closed her laptop halfway.

“Look at us. We’re both telling each other to sleep.”

“Someone has to.”

That made her grin. For a while, they talked about their day. Nothing important.

A colleague who had misunderstood her instructions. A teammate who had made an amusing mistake during practice. The restaurant near the hotel. The weather.

When they finally said goodnight, Xiaoran felt that the distance wasn’t too bad. They had their routines. They had their calls. They were fine.

By the second week, their schedules began to collide.

Yichen’s games were usually in the evening, but training and team meetings occupied much of the day. Travel between cities made his schedule unpredictable.

Xiaoran’s studio, meanwhile, had entered the final stages of a major campaign.

She was working on a branded short film, coordinating with the production team and helping prepare the final presentation for the client. The project was important. It was also becoming increasingly exhausting.

On Wednesday, she sent Yichen a photograph of her desk.

There were two empty coffee cups, a notebook, a half-eaten sandwich, and her laptop displaying a timeline.

Xiaoran: My office has become my second home.

Yichen: Have you eaten properly?

Xiaoran: Yes.

Yichen: That’s not an answer.

Xiaoran: I had a sandwich.

Yichen: When?

She looked at the time. It had been four hours.

Xiaoran: Earlier.

Yichen: Xiaoran.

Xiaoran: Don’t start.

Yichen: I’m not starting. Order something.

She sighed and put her phone down. A few minutes later, a delivery notification appeared. Yichen had ordered dinner to her office. She stared at the notification. Then she called him. He answered after the second ring.

“Hello?”

“Why did you order food?”

“Because you haven’t eaten.”

“I could have ordered something myself.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

He was quiet.

“Because I wanted to.”

She leaned back in her chair.

“You’re not here, so you can’t keep sending food every time I forget to eat.”

“I know.”

“Yichen.”

“Xiaoran.”

He continued, gently, “You don’t have to make it difficult for me to take care of you just because I’m away.”

Her expression softened.

“I know.”

“Good. Eat before it gets cold.”

She smiled.

“Okay.”

After the call, she opened the delivery bag. There was a handwritten note attached to the container.

Eat properly. I’ll call after the game.

She took a photograph and sent it to him.

Xiaoran: You’re very annoying.

Yichen: I know.

Xiaoran: Thank you.

Yichen: You’re welcome.

The first missed call happened on a Friday. Xiaoran had been waiting for him to finish training.

He had told her he would call around eight. At eight fifteen, she sent a message.

Xiaoran: Done?

No reply. At eight forty, she tried calling. It rang until the call ended. She assumed he was still occupied. At nine, she received a message.

Yichen: Sorry. Team meeting ran late. Heading to dinner now.

She looked at it. Then typed:

Xiaoran: It’s okay. Eat first.

He replied with a heart. She put her phone down and returned to her work. At ten thirty, he called.

She was in the middle of editing a presentation.

“Hello?”

“Still working?”

“Yes.”

“Can you take a break?”

“Just five minutes.”

He heard the clicking of her keyboard.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You’re not taking a break.”

That made her grin.

“You’re not here. You can’t see me.”

“I can hear you.”

She laughed. He asked about her day, and she told him about the client meeting.

But after a few minutes, she realised she was answering him without really thinking. Her eyes kept moving towards the screen. Yichen noticed.

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Then let’s talk tomorrow.”

She met his eyes.

“But you called.”

“And you’re working.”

She hesitated.

“I wanted to talk to you.”

“I know.”

He looked at her through the screen.

“Finish what you need to finish. I’ll be here tomorrow.”

“Okay.”

They said goodnight. After the call ended, she stared at the dark screen. She had wanted to talk to him.

But she had also wanted to finish her work.

She hadn’t realised how difficult it could be to want two things at once. The following week was worse.

The Herons had two away games in four days. Yichen’s team won the first.

He sent her a photograph from the locker room, still wearing his jersey, his hair damp with sweat.

Yichen: Won.

Xiaoran smiled at the photograph.

Xiaoran: I watched the last quarter!

Yichen: I saw your messages.

Xiaoran: You played well.

Yichen: Thank you.

Xiaoran: Especially that assist near the end.

Yichen: You noticed?

Xiaoran: Obviously. I’m a very knowledgeable basketball girlfriend.

He laughed when he read it. He wanted to call her, but the team was heading to a post-game meeting. He sent a voice message instead.

“Thank you for watching. I’ll call you when I get back.”

She listened to it twice. Then she went back to work. The second game ended differently. The Herons lost by a narrow margin.

Yichen played well, but the team had struggled to maintain their lead in the final minutes. He was disappointed.

Not visibly, perhaps. He answered the post-game questions, spoke to his teammates, and reviewed the game footage.

But by the time he returned to the hotel, he was exhausted. He called Xiaoran. She didn’t answer. He tried again. Nothing. He sent a message.

Yichen: Finished the game. Are you still awake?

There was no reply. He waited. At midnight, he finally put his phone down. The next morning, he received a message.

Xiaoran: Sorry. I fell asleep while waiting for a file to export.

He stared at it.

Yichen: It’s okay. How’s the project?

Xiaoran: Still alive.

Yichen: That’s reassuring.

Xiaoran: How was the game?

He hesitated. Then replied:

Yichen: We lost.

She answered immediately.

Xiaoran: I’m sorry. Are you okay?

He looked at the screen. He wanted to tell her that he was disappointed. That he had been thinking about one particular play all night. That he was tired of replaying it in his head. Instead, he typed:

Yichen: I’m fine. We’ll review it and prepare for the next one.

She sent a heart. He put the phone away.

It wasn’t that he didn’t want to tell her.

He didn’t want to make her carry another thing when she was already struggling with her own deadline.

He didn’t realise she was doing exactly the same thing.

The first real argument happened over a missed call. It was a Tuesday night.

Xiaoran had just finished a long day at the studio. The client had requested a major revision, and the team needed to present a new version the following morning. She was exhausted.

Yichen had finished training earlier than expected and called her. She was in the middle of a meeting. She declined the call and sent a message.

Xiaoran: In a meeting. I’ll call you after.

Yichen replied:

Yichen: Okay.

An hour passed, then another. She finished the meeting, went back to her desk, and began revising the presentation. At ten, Yichen called again. She answered, but her attention was divided.

“Hello?”

“Are you still at the studio?”

“Yes.”

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What did you have?”

She closed her eyes.

“Yichen, can we not do this right now? Do what?”

“Ask me if I’ve eaten every time you call.”

He was quiet. Then he said, “I was just asking.”

“I know. But I’m working.”

“I can hear that.”

She rubbed her forehead.

“Then why did you call?”

The question came out sharper than she intended. There was a brief silence.

“I wanted to talk to you.”

Her expression changed. She looked at the laptop, then at the clock.

“I know, but I can’t always stop everything.”

“I didn’t ask you to.”

“Then what do you want me to do?”

He leaned back in his hotel chair.

“Nothing.”

She exhaled.

“Yichen—”

“It’s fine. Finish your work.”

He ended the call gently. But the silence afterward felt worse than an argument. Xiaoran stared at her phone. She wanted to call him back. She also wanted to finish the presentation.

And she was angry that she couldn’t do both. She put her phone down.

Across the city, Yichen sat on the edge of his hotel bed, looking at the screen. He knew she was under pressure. He knew the timing was bad.

But he also knew he had been waiting all day to hear her voice. And now he felt foolish for wanting it. They didn’t speak properly the next day. There were messages. Good morning. Have you eaten? Good luck with the presentation. How was training? Nothing was wrong with any of them. But something was missing. Xiaoran’s presentation went well.

The client approved the revised direction, and her manager congratulated the team. She should have felt happy.

Instead, the first thing she wanted to do was tell Yichen. She opened their chat. Then she stopped. He was probably training. She didn’t want to interrupt. A few minutes later, her phone vibrated.

Yichen: How was the presentation?

Her mouth tipped up.

Xiaoran: Approved.

Yichen: Congratulations.

Xiaoran: Thank you.

She waited. He didn’t say anything else. She stared at the screen. Then she typed:

Xiaoran: Are you free tonight?

Yichen: We have a team dinner. I’ll be back late.

Xiaoran: Okay.

She put her phone down. It was ridiculous. They were both trying not to inconvenience each other. And somehow, they were becoming strangers for it. That evening, Yichen called from his hotel room. Xiaoran answered immediately.

“Hello.”

“Hi.”

She was sitting on her sofa, still wearing her office clothes. He looked tired. She studied his face.

“Are you okay?”

“Yes.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“That’s not an answer.”

His mouth curved.

“Where have I heard that before?”

She didn’t smile.

“Yichen.”

“Are you upset?”

She hesitated, then nodded.

“A little.”

“About yesterday?”

“Yes.”

He waited. She looked down at her hands.

“I know you wanted to talk. I wanted to talk too. But I was so tired, and the presentation was due, and I couldn’t think about anything else.”

“I know.”

“And then when you called, I felt like I was failing at something.”

He frowned slightly.

“Failing?”

“At being your girlfriend.”

His expression changed.

“Xiaoran.”

She continued before he could interrupt.

“I know that sounds stupid. But I keep thinking that I should be more available. I should watch your games, answer your calls, ask about training, and still finish my work. And when I can’t, I feel bad.”

He was quiet. Then he said, “I don’t expect you to do all that.”

“I know you don’t.”

“Then why are you putting that pressure on yourself?”

She turned to him.

“Because I miss you.”

The words came out smaller than she expected. Yichen’s expression softened.

She said, “I miss being able to tell you something the moment it happens. I miss eating dinner with you. I miss complaining about my day while you’re sitting beside me. I miss being able to hug you without scheduling it.”

He studied her. Then he said, “I miss you too.”

She nodded.

“I know.”

He leaned forward slightly.

“Can I tell you something?”

“Yes.”

“I’ve been doing the same thing.”

She blinked.

“What?”

“I keep telling myself not to bother you because you’re busy. I don’t call when I want to because I assume you’re working. When we do talk, I try not to mention the difficult parts of my day because I don’t want to add to yours.”

She blinked at him.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

He gave her a smile.

“Because I thought I was being considerate.”

She let out a quiet laugh.

“That’s exactly what I thought I was doing.”

He nodded.

“Apparently, we’re both very considerate.”

“Very stupid.”

He laughed. She smiled for the first time that evening. Then her expression softened again.

“I don’t want us to become people who only exchange schedules.”

“Neither do I.”

She looked at him.

“How do we fix it?”

He thought.

“Maybe we stop treating every call like it has to fit into the perfect schedule.”

She listened.

“If you’re working, tell me. I’ll understand. If I’m at training, I’ll tell you. But we don’t have to wait until we’re both completely free to talk.”

She smiled.

“And if one of us misses the call?”

“We call back when we can.”

“And no pretending we’re fine when we’re not?”

He nodded.

“No pretending.”

She held his gaze.

“Promise?”

“Promise. Also, I want you to tell me when you miss me.”

She blinked.

“I do.”

“Sometimes you say you’re fine.”

She looked away. He smiled gently.

“You don’t have to be fine all the time.”

She was quiet. Then she said, “I miss you.”

His expression softened.

“I miss you too.”

She leaned closer to the screen, as if that would make the distance smaller.

“Very much.”

“Very much?”

“Don’t make me repeat it.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“You’re smiling.”

“I like hearing it.”

She laughed. He considered her.

Then said, “I wish I could hold you right now.”

Her smile faded into something softer.

“Me too.”

They changed their routine after that. Not dramatically. They didn’t create an elaborate schedule or promise to speak for hours every night. They became more honest.

Sometimes Yichen sent a voice message from the bus after a game. Sometimes Xiaoran called him while walking home from the studio, telling him about something that had happened before she forgot the details. Sometimes they spoke for only three minutes.

Sometimes they stayed on the phone for an hour.

If one of them was busy, they said so.

If one of them was disappointed, they said that too.

And if they missed each other, they stopped pretending that they didn’t.

One night, Xiaoran was reviewing a rough cut at home when Yichen called. She answered with her laptop still open.

“Hello.”

“Busy?”

“Very.”

Something in his face eased.

“Should I call later?”

She thought about it, then shook her head.

“No. Talk to me while I work.”

“About what?”

“Anything.”

He settled back in his hotel chair.

“All right.”

She returned to the timeline. For a while, neither said anything.

Then Yichen began telling her about a teammate who had accidentally worn two different shoes to the team meeting. Xiaoran burst out laughing.

“How does that even happen?”

“He said he was tired.”

“That’s not an excuse.”

“He seemed to think it was.”

She shook her head, still laughing. Then she went back to editing. Yichen watched her through the screen.

“How’s the film?”

“Better. I’m adjusting the sound.”

“Is that the part you were worried about?”

“Yes.”

“Do you want me to watch?”

She looked up.

“Now?”

“If you want.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Okay. But don’t judge me if it’s unfinished.”

“I won’t.”

She shared her screen. He watched as the footage played.

When it ended, he said, “The transition feels smoother now.”

She looked pleased.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“You’re not just saying that?”

“No.”

She smiled and returned to the timeline. Yichen remained on the call. He didn’t need to say anything. Neither did she. It was enough to hear each other there.

The final away game of the trip was in Chengdu. The Herons won.

Yichen played well, and the team had a good performance overall.

After the game, he sent Xiaoran a photograph from the court.

Yichen: Last away game. Won.

She was still at the studio, waiting for a final export.

Xiaoran: I knew you would.

Yichen: You watched?

Xiaoran: The second half. I was eating dinner at the same time.

Yichen: What did you eat?

She couldn’t help smiling.

Xiaoran: Proper food. Vegetables included.

Yichen: Good.

Then he sent a voice message.

“Last game is done. I’ll be back tomorrow evening. Don’t stay up waiting for me. You have work.”

She listened to it, then replied with her own voice message.

“Okay. But I’m still going to miss you until tomorrow. Also, I have something to show you when you come back.”

He replied almost immediately.

“What?”

“Secret.”

Yichen returned on Saturday evening. Xiaoran had finished work early and gone to his apartment.

She had bought groceries, tidied the living room, and put a small vase of flowers on the dining table. Nothing extravagant. Just a familiar space waiting for him.

When the door opened, she was sitting on the sofa with her laptop. Yichen stepped inside, pulling his luggage behind him. She looked up. Neither moved. Then she closed her laptop and stood.

He barely had time to put his bag down before she crossed the room and wrapped her arms around him. He laughed, catching her around the waist.

“Hello.”

She pressed her face into his chest.

“Hello.”

“Missed me?”

She nodded.

“Very much.”

He pressed his mouth to her hair.

“I missed you too.”

She tightened her arms.

“You’re home.”

“I’m home.”

He held her for a while. Then he leaned back to look at her.

“What’s the surprise?”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Come.”

She took his hand and led him towards the dining table. There was a small envelope beside the vase. He picked it up. Inside was a printed photograph.

It showed the two of them at the university on graduation day, standing beneath the Media faculty sign. Xiaoran was looking at him, and he was looking back at her. On the back, she had written:

For the days when we can’t be in the same city.

He looked at it, then at her.

“You printed this?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

She shrugged.

“Because I wanted you to have something that wasn’t on your phone.”

She said, “You can put it in your suitcase. Or your room. Or wherever you want.”

He turned the photograph over again. Then he placed it carefully back in the envelope.

“Thank you.”

That made her grin.

“Do you like it?”

“I love it.”

He set it down and pulled her close again. Then he noticed the laptop on the sofa.

“How’s your deadline?”

Xiaoran made a face.

“Don’t ask.”

He laughed.

“That bad?”

“Almost finished. I just need to send the final version on Monday.”

He brushed her hair away from her face.

“Then let’s have dinner.”

She nodded.

“Together.”

“Together.”

Dinner was simple. They cooked something easy, ate at the dining table, and talked about the trip.

Yichen told her about the away games, the different arenas, and the long bus rides.

Xiaoran told him about the campaign, the client presentation, and the final changes she had made to the film. They interrupted each other sometimes. They laughed. They asked questions. And neither of them looked at the clock. After dinner, they settled on the sofa.

Xiaoran curled against his side, her legs tucked beneath her. Yichen rested his arm around her shoulders.

“Are you tired?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Want to sleep?”

“In a while.”

He kissed her cheek. She looked up at him.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Next time you’re away, can we do something?”

“What?”

“Send each other one ordinary thing every day.”

He glanced at her.

“An ordinary thing?”

“Yes. Not just match results or work updates. Something small. What you ate. Something funny you saw. A photograph of the sky. Anything.”

He considered it.

“That sounds nice.”

“And no pressure to make it interesting.”

“All right.”

She smiled.

“Even if it’s just a picture of your breakfast.”

“I’ll try to make it presentable.”

She laughed. Then she rested her head against him. He looked down at her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“I don’t want you to think you have to make yourself available every time I’m away.”

She looked up.

“And I don’t want you to think you have to hide things from me because I’m away.”

“Deal.”

She held out her little finger. He looked at it.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

He hooked his finger around hers.

“Deal.”

She smiled, satisfied. Then she leaned up and kissed him.

It was a soft kiss, followed by another, and then a longer one when he cupped her cheek and drew her closer.

When she finally pulled away, she rested her forehead against his.

“Welcome home.”

He smiled.

“I’m glad to be home.”

Later that night, Yichen placed the photograph in the drawer beside his bed. Not because he didn’t want to display it. He wanted to find a proper frame first.

Xiaoran was already asleep beside him, one hand resting near his.

The away season had been difficult in ways he hadn’t expected.

They were both building lives that wanted their time, and sometimes their absence.

He had wanted to protect her from the difficult parts of his days, and she had wanted to protect him from hers. They had nearly made themselves lonely being considerate. His phone vibrated on the bedside table.

A message from the Herons’ team manager confirming the next training schedule.

He read it, replied, and put the phone away. Then Xiaoran shifted closer in her sleep.

He smiled and drew the blanket over her shoulder.

Tomorrow there would be another deadline and another session. He set the photograph by the lamp, where he’d remember to pack it.

chapters.desc: Packing up the fourth-floor studio, her parents bring her every note her father ever left her.
chapters.title: Boxes
chapters.epigraph: “Did you know I kept all of them?”
chapters.content:
The first box was books. The second was clothes she wouldn’t need before spring. The third was meant to be miscellaneous, and Lin Xiaoran had already filled it with a camera strap, two notebooks, a little lamp, and three mugs she said she couldn’t possibly leave behind.

The lease on the studio had ended on Wednesday. The landlord, who in four years had never once fixed the lift, agreed she could keep the key until Saturday, which was the most generous thing he had ever done. Her parents came up to Shanghai on the Friday train for the move, with one suitcase of their own and a second full of things from home that her mother had decided the new flat needed. By the time her mother had climbed the four flights and got her breath back, Xiaoran was sitting in the middle of the floor surrounded by cardboard.

“How many boxes do you need?”

“I don’t know.”

“How many have you packed?”

“Four.”

Her mother looked round the room. There were six.

“Well, four are properly packed,” said Xiaoran.

“You’re making a mess. It’s only one room.”

“I’m organising.”

“You’re spreading things across the floor.”

“That’s part of organising,” said Xiaoran, and her mother sighed and picked up a flat box and started folding it into shape.

“Your father’s gone to buy more tape.”

“He already bought three rolls.”

“He doesn’t trust the tape we’ve got.”

“Of course he doesn’t.”

Her mother put the box down beside her. Then she reached into her handbag and took out a bundle of paper held together with a rubber band. “What do you want to do with these?”

Xiaoran looked at it. Old notes. Folded scraps, some yellow at the edges, some written on the backs of envelopes, some torn out of notebooks. All in her father’s square handwriting.

“Where did you find those?”

“In the drawer of your old desk at home. And in your schoolbooks. There were dozens. I thought you might want them in the new place.” Her mother put them on the floor between them.

Xiaoran slid the rubber band off. The first note was on a page of lined paper.

Dinner is in the rice cooker. Don’t forget to eat.

The second was on the back of a supermarket receipt.

Your umbrella is by the door. It will rain today.

The third: I’ve left the spare key with Auntie Qiu downstairs. Call me if you need it. There was a date in the corner. She’d been fourteen. She remembered that day: she had forgotten her key and sat on the steps outside the building for two hours rather than ring the neighbour’s bell.

“You didn’t go to Auntie Qiu,” said her mother, reading over her shoulder.

“I was embarrassed.”

“He was so cross. Not with you. With himself, for not saying it to your face.”

There were more. Some were practical. Some were so short they were nearly ridiculous. Milk is finished. The parcel is with the security guard. Don’t leave wet shoes in the cupboard. And one, written fast, the pen pressed hard:

I know you’re upset. We’ll talk when you’re ready.

She stopped on that one. She’d been fifteen, and had argued with both of them about something she couldn’t even remember now, and shut herself in her room and refused to come out for dinner. Her father hadn’t knocked. He had pushed this under the door.

“He used to leave them everywhere. Sometimes I thought he said more to you on paper than he did out loud,” said her mother.

“He was always busy.”

“He was always shy,” said her mother. She picked one out of the pile and held it up. “Do you remember this?”

Your school project is on the dining table. I didn’t touch it. I only moved the fruit bowl.

Xiaoran laughed. “He was so scared of touching my things.”

“He was scared you’d say he’d ruined it.”

“I probably would have.”

They kept going. There were notes from middle school and high school, from the first year after they moved to the city, from every university holiday she’d come home for. Fewer as she got older, but they never stopped. One from the winter of her first year at university: There’s food in the fridge. Your mother says you’re studying late. Don’t come home hungry. One from the day she’d come home with a bad mark: One result doesn’t decide everything. Come home and eat first. And one from the morning she left for orientation, with her camera bag by the door:

Camera battery is charged. I’ve put the spare next to your bag.

She looked at that one.

“What is it?” said her mother.

“I didn’t know he’d charged it. I didn’t even know he’d touched the bag.”

“Your father notices more than he says.”

The last one was inside an old university textbook, folded into a narrow strip between two pages.

You don’t have to be good at everything immediately.

And underneath, smaller:

And you don’t have to pretend you’re not tired.

The date said the summer after her second year. She remembered that summer: too many assignments, a student film she’d agreed to help with from three hundred kilometres away, a boyfriend she called every night at nine. She’d told her parents she was fine.

“He left that after you fell asleep at the dining table. He carried your laptop into your room and put that next to your books,” said her mother.

“Why didn’t he just wake me up?”

“Because you’d have said you had to finish something.”

Xiaoran couldn’t argue with that.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father came back up the four flights an hour later with two more rolls of tape, slightly out of breath, and stopped in the doorway at the sight of the two of them sitting in a sea of paper.

“What’s all this?”

Xiaoran held one up. “Your handwriting.”

He looked at it, and at her. “Why are you reading those?”

“Mum found them.”

He put the tape down. “Those are old.”

“Very old.”

“Then why keep them?”

“You kept them.”

“I didn’t keep them. You did.”

She looked at her mother. Her mother looked innocently at the ceiling.

“Some were in your books. Some were in your drawer. I only collected them,” her mother said.

Her father looked mildly betrayed.

“Do you remember this one?” Xiaoran held up the umbrella note.

“That was a rainy day.”

“I know it was a rainy day.”

“You always forgot your umbrella.”

“I was thirteen!”

“Still, that one’s from university,” he said, and his eyes went to the one she’d put on its own, apart from the pile. You don’t have to pretend you’re not tired. Something moved in his face.

“I remember.”

He sat down on the floor on the other side of the paper, which he never did, with his knees up, and picked up a note and looked at it without reading it.

“I used to leave these because I left early. I thought it was easier than waking you.”

“You left them when you were home too.”

“Sometimes.”

“You once left me a note telling me not to forget a parcel when you were sitting right next to me.”

Her mother laughed out loud.

“It was important,” said her father, with dignity.

“It was a box of printer paper.”

“Your project needed it.”

She laughed, and then stopped, and said, more quietly, “Did you know I kept all of them?”

He looked at her. “No.”

“I did. I didn’t even know I was doing it. I just never threw one away.”

He looked down at the pile for a while. Then he cleared his throat.

“Well. You don’t need to take every bit of paper across the road.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“Good.”

She started gathering them up. Then she stopped. “Actually, I think I’ll take them. All of them.”

“They’re just reminders.”

“I know.”

He nodded, as if he did understand. Then he reached for the nearest box, moved two heavy books out of it, and made a space at the top. “Put them in here. Don’t fold them any smaller.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, after her parents had gone back to their hotel, Yichen came across the road to help with the last boxes. He found her at her desk, sliding the notes one by one into a big brown envelope.

“What’s that?”

“Every note my father ever left me.”

He came and stood behind her chair. “Every one?”

“Nearly.” She handed him three without looking round.

He read them over her shoulder. The rice cooker. The umbrella. Good luck. Don’t rush when you speak.

“Your father has a very practical writing style.”

“He’s a practical person.”

He picked up another. “One result doesn’t decide everything. Come home and eat first.”

“I’d got sixty-one in a chemistry test. He didn’t ask what happened until after dinner.”

“That sounds like him. You’re taking them with you.” He put it down.

“You’re not going to tell me I’m being sentimental?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because you are. There’s nothing wrong with keeping something that made you feel loved,” he said, and she turned round in the chair to give him an offended look, and he bent down and put his hand on her cheek.

She didn’t say anything. She stood up and slid her arms round him and her face against his chest, and stayed there for a while in the middle of the half-packed room.

“I’m going to put them in the drawer on my side of the bed. So when I forget something I can pretend he’s still leaving me reminders,” she said into his shirt.

“He probably will. I’d be surprised if he doesn’t start messaging you about umbrellas.”

“And asking if I’ve eaten.”

“Definitely.”

He took the envelope and put it in the box on top of the books, and folded the flaps down without taping them.

“We’ll do this one last. So nothing heavy goes on it,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven the next morning, the day of the move, her father climbed the four flights one more time and put a small piece of paper on her desk.

She looked up from the box she was taping. “What’s that?”

“Nothing.”

She picked it up. His handwriting, unmistakable.

When you get there, call home.

And underneath:

And don’t forget your umbrella.

She laughed. “Dad, it’s across the road.”

“Call anyway.”

She got up and hugged him. He patted her back and looked over her shoulder at the bare room.

“Put it somewhere you can find it.”

“I will.”

She slid it into the envelope with the others. He watched her do it and didn’t say anything. Then he took the roll of tape from her hand, bent over the last box, pressed the flaps down gently around the envelope, and sealed it, running his thumb along the tape to make sure it held.

“All right. This one’s ready,” he said.

For once she didn’t tell him she could do it herself. She held the box steady while he taped it, and when he’d finished she carried it down the four flights in her own arms, and wouldn’t let Yichen take it.

chapters.desc: She moves into his apartment. Both sets of parents come to help, and within fifteen minutes she has lost control of her own kitchen.
chapters.title: Moving Day, Again
chapters.epigraph: “Now yours can stop pretending it’s visiting.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Lin Xiaoran learned about moving in together was that Zhou Yichen owned too many things. The second thing she learned was that he had somehow managed to make all of them fit into his apartment without her noticing.

The third thing was that her own belongings, which she had always considered perfectly reasonable in quantity, looked less reasonable once they were placed beside his.

She stood in the middle of his living room, holding a cardboard box against her hip.

“Yichen.”

He was crouching beside another box, checking its contents.

“Mm?”

“How many jackets do you own?”

He met her eyes.

“Why?”

“Because I found another one.”

“Where?”

“In the wardrobe.”

“That’s where jackets usually are.”

She looked at him.

“Don’t be clever.”

He smiled and returned to the box. It was Saturday morning. Their move had officially begun at eight, although Xiaoran had arrived at seven thirty because she had been too excited to sleep.

Her lease had ended the previous week. After months of discussing the practicalities—rent, expenses, commuting distances, work schedules, and the amount of closet space they would need—they had finally decided to move into Yichen’s apartment. It wasn’t a spontaneous decision.

They had visited several places together. They had discussed whether to rent somewhere new or use his existing apartment. They had gone through the expenses more than once, and Xiaoran had insisted on contributing a fair share rather than letting him cover everything because he could.

In the end, they chose to stay in his apartment for now.

It was spacious enough for two people, close enough to both their workplaces, and, most importantly, they both liked it.

Still, knowing something was the right decision and actually watching your belongings enter another person’s home were two different experiences. Xiaoran looked around.

Her books were stacked beside his. Her desk lamp was on the dining table. Two boxes of skincare products had somehow occupied an entire corner of the kitchen counter. And her boyfriend was apparently still hiding jackets.

“How many?” she repeated.

Yichen stood up.

“Enough.”

“That’s not a number.”

“Do you want to count them?”

She considered it.

“Actually, yes.”

He laughed and took the box from her arms.

“Go check your own boxes first.”

“My boxes are perfectly organised.”

“I know.”

“Then why did you say that?”

“Because you put your hair dryer in a box labelled ‘miscellaneous’.”

She opened her mouth, then closed it.

“That’s because I didn’t know what else to call it.”

“Hair appliances?”

“That’s too specific.”

He looked at her for a second. Then his mouth curved.

“Of course.”

She squinted at him.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“A little.”

She turned away, pretending to be offended. He caught her hand before she could walk off and kissed her knuckles, his thumb brushing over the promise ring on her finger.

“Come on. Let’s finish before everyone arrives.”

“Everyone?”

He turned to her. She looked back.

“Yichen.”

“Yes?”

“You said our parents would come later.”

“They are coming.”

“All of them?”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Yes.”

She slowly put her hands on her hips.

“Why did you say that as if it’s a normal thing?”

“Because it is.”

“Four parents. In one apartment. On moving day.”

“Six, counting us.”

She stared at him. He bent and kissed her hairline.

“Don’t worry. They’ll help.”

That, Xiaoran thought, was precisely what she was worried about.

By ten thirty, the apartment had become a small family operation. Yichen’s parents arrived first.

His mother came carrying two bags of groceries and a container of homemade food. His father followed with a toolbox, a folded step ladder, and the expression of a man who had already decided there were several things in the apartment that needed fixing.

“Xiaoran!”

Yichen’s mother greeted her warmly.

“Have you eaten? I brought breakfast.”

Xiaoran looked at the bags.

“Auntie, you didn’t have to bring so much.”

“It’s moving day. Of course I had to.”

She turned towards Yichen.

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes, Mum.”

“Properly?”

He paused. Xiaoran immediately answered for him.

“Not really.”

Yichen looked at her. His mother gave him a disapproving look.

“Then eat first.”

He glanced at Xiaoran again. She smiled sweetly. He understood, then, that he had been betrayed.

“You’re enjoying this,” he murmured as his mother carried the food towards the kitchen.

“A little.”

His father was already examining a bookshelf.

“This needs to be moved.”

Yichen looked over.

“Why?”

“It’s too close to the window.”

“It has been there for four years.”

“And now there are two people living here.”

Xiaoran blinked. Mr. Zhou turned towards her.

“Do you think it should be moved?”

She looked at the bookshelf, then at the window.

“Maybe a little?”

His father nodded, satisfied.

“Good. We’ll move it.”

Yichen stared at both of them.

“All right.”

His mother laughed.

“Don’t look so unhappy. Your father is helping.”

“I know.”

“Then go help him.”

Xiaoran covered her mouth. Yichen looked at her.

“You’re enjoying this considerably more than I expected.”

She whispered, “Your father asked for my opinion.”

“And?”

“I’m influential.”

He laughed under his breath and went to move the bookshelf. Xiaoran’s parents arrived shortly before eleven.

Her mother came in carrying a large box, which she insisted was light despite Xiaoran immediately reaching out to take it.

“Mum, give it to me.”

“It’s fine.”

“You’re holding it with both hands.”

“Because it’s a box.”

Her father walked in behind her, carrying another two boxes. He looked around the apartment, then at Yichen.

“Busy day?”

Yichen stepped forward to greet him.

“Uncle. I’ll take those.”

“No need. I can carry them.”

Yichen took them anyway. Xiaoran’s mother looked towards the kitchen, where Yichen’s mother was arranging food. The two women greeted each other warmly.

Within five minutes, they were standing together discussing the kitchen storage. Within ten minutes, they had decided that the current arrangement was inefficient.

Within fifteen minutes, Xiaoran had lost control of her own kitchen.

“Should we put the bowls here?” her mother asked.

Yichen’s mother considered it.

“Maybe the upper cabinet. The lower one is easier for plates.”

“That’s true. And the glasses?”

“Near the refrigerator.”

Xiaoran stood between them.

“Actually, I was thinking—”

“Xiaoran, where are your tea cups?” her mother asked.

“That box.”

“Good. We’ll unpack those.”

Yichen appeared beside her, carrying a box of books.

He looked at the three women, then at her.

“Need help?”

She turned to him with an expression of quiet desperation. He lowered his voice.

“What’s wrong?”

“They’ve taken over.”

He glanced towards the kitchen, then back at her.

“Should I rescue you?”

“Please.”

He nodded solemnly.

“All right.”

He walked into the kitchen.

“Mum, Auntie, Dad needs help with the bookshelf.”

His father, who was standing nowhere near the bookshelf, looked up. Yichen continued smoothly.

“He said he needs two people.”

Both women looked towards the living room.

“Again?”

“Yes.”

They exchanged a glance, then began walking out. Xiaoran stared at Yichen. He picked up a tea cup.

“You’re welcome.”

She whispered, “You’re very good at this.”

“I’ve had years of practice.”

She smiled and took the cup from him.

“Your father is going to know you made that up.”

“He already knows.”

From the living room, Mr. Zhou called, “Yichen, are you coming?”

Yichen sighed.

“See?”

Xiaoran laughed. By early afternoon, most of the boxes had been unpacked. The living room looked noticeably different.

There was a new rug beneath the coffee table, chosen by Xiaoran after three weeks of sending Yichen photographs and asking him to compare shades of beige. Her books occupied two shelves.

His basketball trophies and framed photographs had been moved to the study, making room for her small collection of cameras and film equipment.

The dining table now had two chairs that didn’t match. Xiaoran liked them that way.

Her father had assembled a new storage cabinet. Yichen’s father had fixed a loose hinge and adjusted the bookshelf. Their mothers had reorganised the kitchen twice, though they insisted the second arrangement was much better.

At one point, Xiaoran walked into the kitchen and found both mothers standing in front of the refrigerator.

“What are you doing?”

“Making space,” her mother answered.

“For what?”

“Your food.”

Yichen’s mother smiled.

“And his.”

Xiaoran looked at the refrigerator. There were containers on the shelves, fresh fruit in the drawer, and a row of drinks arranged neatly in the door. That made her grin.

“Thank you.”

Her mother turned towards her.

“Don’t just thank us. You two need to keep the kitchen organised.”

“We will.”

“And don’t rely on takeout every day.”

“We won’t.”

Yichen walked in at that moment. His mother pointed at him.

“And you. Don’t let her do all the cooking.”

He nodded.

“I won’t.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Why are you looking at me?”

“Because your mother is talking about you.”

“Your mother is talking about you too.”

Something in his face eased.

“Then we’re both in trouble.”

Her mother laughed.

“Good. At least you know.”

The only real disagreement of the day happened over the bedroom. It wasn’t a serious one.

But it was the first time they discovered that moving in together involved more than deciding where to put furniture.

Xiaoran had brought a small bedside table from her old apartment. It was light wood, with one drawer and a little open shelf underneath.

She wanted to put it beside her side of the bed.

Yichen thought it would look better beside the window.

“It’s too close to the wardrobe here,” he said, moving it slightly.

“But I want it here.”

“Then the drawer won’t open properly.”

“It will.”

He crouched and pulled the drawer. It opened halfway before hitting the edge of the wardrobe. Xiaoran looked at it, then at him.

“That’s because you moved it too far.”

He shifted it back. The drawer opened, but the table now obstructed the walkway. Neither spoke.

Finally, Yichen said, “We can put it on the other side.”

“But that’s your side.”

“I don’t mind.”

She looked at him. Then she shook her head.

“No. I want it here.”

He considered the space.

“All right. Let’s move the wardrobe slightly.”

“You’ll move the wardrobe?”

“Why not?”

“Because it’s heavy.”

“That’s manageable.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“You’re very indulgent.”

He stood and brushed his hands together.

“Only about furniture?”

She laughed.

“Don’t push your luck.”

He leaned down and kissed her cheek.

“Never.”

From the doorway, her mother watched them. She smiled and walked away without interrupting. By five, everyone was tired.
