chapters.desc: The skirt has waited in the wardrobe since her birthday. Tonight she wears it, and he takes the pictures.
chapters.title: The Skirt Meilin Bought Her
chapters.epigraph: “Because you weren’t posing.”
chapters.content:
The skirt had been hanging in Xiaoran’s half of the wardrobe since her birthday. Not because she didn’t like it. Quite the opposite.

She liked it so much that she had been waiting for the right occasion to wear it.

It was a black mini skirt, slightly tailored, with a flattering high waist and a subtle pleated detail. It wasn’t extravagant, but it had a certain style to it. Meilin had picked it out for Xiaoran’s birthday, insisting that she needed something a little different from her usual collection of comfortable skirts and jeans. At the time, Xiaoran had been delighted.

She had tried it on immediately, sent Meilin several pictures, and received a voice message that consisted mostly of Meilin saying, “Finally. Something that makes you look like you know you’re pretty.”

Xiaoran had laughed and promised to wear it soon. Months later, it was still hanging there. Until Friday evening.

She stood in front of the open wardrobe, holding the skirt against herself.

Then she looked at the mirror, then at the skirt again.

“Okay.”

She nodded.

“Today.”

From the bathroom, Yichen’s voice came.

“What’s today?”

Xiaoran turned around.

“Nothing!”

A pause.

“All right.”

She heard the shower running again. She looked at the skirt, then smiled. Tonight, she was finally going to wear it.

Yichen noticed something unusual when he came out of the bathroom.

Xiaoran was standing in front of the mirror, carefully adjusting the hem of her skirt.

She was wearing a simple fitted top, the black mini skirt, and a pair of shoes that made her legs look lovely. Her hair was down, with a slight curl at the ends, and she had put on a little more effort with her makeup than usual. Yichen stopped by the bedroom door. He didn’t say anything immediately.

Xiaoran noticed his reflection in the mirror and turned.

He walked over and stood behind her, his hands settling lightly at her waist, and looked at the two of them in the glass for a while before he said anything.

“You look beautiful.”

Xiaoran’s smile arrived before she could stop it. He kissed her cheek.

“New?”

“Meilin gave it to me for my birthday.”

Yichen glanced at the skirt again.

“Ah.”

“I’ve wanted to wear it for a while, but somehow I never found the right occasion.”

“And tonight is the occasion?”

She nodded.

“We’re going out, aren’t we?”

“Yes.”

“Then I thought I should finally wear it.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Good decision.”

She looked at herself in the mirror again.

“I don’t usually wear skirts this short.”

“I know. You’ve been holding it up against yourself in front of this mirror since your birthday.”

She gasped.

“You saw that?”

“Every time.”

Yichen reached for his watch.

“Ready?”

“Almost!”

She hurried back to the mirror to check her hair. Yichen watched her amused.

He had a feeling Meilin would be receiving a thank-you message tonight.

They were going to a restaurant for dinner, followed by a walk around the shopping district. Nothing elaborate.

Yichen had made the reservation earlier that afternoon, and Xiaoran had been looking forward to it since he told her. When they reached the elevator, she stopped. Yichen turned.

“What happened?”

She looked down.

“My skirt.”

He met her eyes.

“What about it?”

“Do I need to keep pulling it down?”

He looked at the hem.

“No.”

“But when I walk, it moves.”

“That’s what skirts do.”

She gave him an unimpressed look.

“You’re not helping.”

He smiled and stepped closer, lowering his voice.

“You’re comfortable?”

“Then don’t worry about it.”

He offered his hand.

“And if you need to adjust it, just do so. There’s no need to spend the entire evening worrying about your clothes.”

She took his hand.

“Okay.”

The elevator doors opened. As they walked towards the parking area, Yichen noticed her glancing down occasionally. He didn’t comment. Instead, he adjusted his pace to match hers.

The restaurant was busy, but their table was in a quieter corner. Xiaoran was in a good mood.

She had been telling Yichen about something that happened at work when the waiter came to serve their drinks.

She thanked him, took a sip, and then noticed Yichen looking at her.

“You’re looking at me.”

“Am I not allowed?”

That made her grin.

“You’re allowed.”

He leaned back slightly.

“Enjoying your birthday present?”

She immediately understood.

“Yes!”

She looked down at her skirt.

“I should have worn it earlier.”

“Why didn’t you?”

“I don’t know. I kept saving it.”

“For what?”

She thought about it.

“Maybe I thought I needed a special occasion.”

Yichen nodded.

“And now?”

“Now I think I should just wear things I like.”

“Good.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Meilin would be very happy if she knew.”

“Tell her.”

“I will.”

She took another sip of her drink, then looked at him.

“Do you think she chose it because she knew I’d like it?”

“Probably.”

“She usually buys me things that are a little different from what I normally choose.”

“Maybe she wants you to try new things.”

Xiaoran nodded.

“She said I always buy the same type of clothes.”

Yichen smiled.

“She’s not entirely wrong.”

She gasped.

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I am.”

“Then defend me.”

He considered this.

“Your wardrobe has a very consistent theme.”

“What theme?”

“Comfortable.”

She stared at him, then laughed.

“That’s because I have good taste.”

“Of course.”

She reached across the table and stole a piece of food from his plate. Yichen watched her.

“Is that also good taste?”

“Yes.”

He pushed the plate closer to her. After dinner, they walked around the shopping district.

The evening was cool, and the streets were illuminated by shop windows and decorative lights. Xiaoran walked beside Yichen, occasionally stopping to look at something.

At one point, she found a display of hair accessories. She leaned closer to the window.

“Look.”

Yichen followed her gaze.

“Pretty?”

“Very.”

She pointed at a small black ribbon.

“That would look nice with this skirt.”

He looked at her hair.

“It would.”

She turned towards him.

“Should I buy it?”

“If you like it.”

She thought about it, then shook her head.

“Maybe next time.”

They continued walking. A little further ahead, they passed a shop window with a full-length mirror. Xiaoran stopped. Yichen noticed and stopped beside her. She looked at their reflection.

He was wearing dark trousers and a neat shirt, his jacket draped over one arm. She stood beside him in her skirt, holding his hand. She smiled.

“Wait.”

She took out her phone.

“Let’s take a picture.”

Yichen moved closer. She held the phone up, adjusted the angle, and took a few pictures. Then she examined them.

“Look!”

He looked.

“Good.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She zoomed in.

“Your expression is too serious.”

“I’m standing.”

“You can smile.”

He turned to her, then smiled. She took another picture.

“Much better.”

She was about to put her phone away when Yichen reached for it.

“Let me.”

He took a photograph of her standing beside the window. Xiaoran blinked.

“Why?”

“Because I like this outfit.”

She looked at him. He took another picture. This time, she wasn’t looking at the camera. She was laughing at something he had said, her head slightly turned towards him. He checked the result.

“Good.”

She leaned closer to see.

“Oh.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Send that to me.”

“I will.”

She met his eyes.

“You’re going to keep it?”

“Of course.”

Her expression softened. Then she slipped her hand back into his.

On the way home, Xiaoran was busy sending Meilin the photographs.

Xiaoran: Finally wore your birthday present!

Meilin: FINALLY???

Meilin: Show me.

Xiaoran sent the picture Yichen had taken. A few seconds later, Meilin called. Xiaoran answered.

“Hello?”

“YOU WORE IT!”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Yes!”

“How does it feel? Isn’t it cute?”

“It’s really cute. I love it.”

“Why did you take so long?”

“I was waiting for the right occasion.”

“Xiaoran, it’s a skirt, not a wedding dress.”

Yichen glanced at her from the driver’s seat, clearly hearing the conversation. Xiaoran covered the microphone.

“She’s being mean.”

“Sounds familiar.”

She gave him a look before returning to the call.

“Anyway, thank you. I really like it.”

Meilin’s voice softened.

“You’re welcome. You look pretty.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Really?”

“Obviously. Also, your boyfriend better appreciate my excellent taste.”

Xiaoran looked at Yichen. He raised an eyebrow. She turned back to the phone.

“He does.”

“Good. Tell him I expect a commission.”

Xiaoran laughed. After they hung up, she placed her phone in her lap. Yichen glanced at her.

“Good.”

She turned towards him.

“Meilin said you better appreciate her taste.”

“I do.”

“She expects a commission.”

He laughed.

“Tell her I’ll consider it.”

Xiaoran grinned. When they arrived home, Xiaoran went straight to the bedroom to change.

Yichen followed a few minutes later and found her carefully hanging the skirt back in the wardrobe. He leaned against the doorframe.

“Putting it away already?”

She turned to him.

“Of course. I don’t want it to get wrinkled.”

He watched her smooth the fabric.

“Are you going to wear it again?”

She nodded.

“Definitely.”

“Good.”

She closed the wardrobe and turned around. Then she looked at him with a slightly mischievous expression.

“What?”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me.”

His mouth curved.

“You’re very pleased with yourself tonight.”

“Because I finally wore my skirt.”

“That must be it.”

She walked towards him and wrapped her arms around his waist.

“I’m keeping the pictures, by the way,” he said.

She grinned.

“Already?”

“Already saved.”

“Where?”

“On my phone.”

She looked delighted. Then, after a moment, she tilted her head.

“Which one is your favourite?”

“The one where you’re laughing.”

She blinked.

“Why?”

“Because you weren’t posing.”

He brushed a strand of hair behind her ear.

“You looked happy.”

Her smile softened. Then she kissed him before he could say anything else.

“Thank you for taking me out.”

“You’re welcome.”

“And thank you for liking my skirt.”

He laughed.

“You’re welcome.”

She started to pull away, but he caught her hand and drew her back.

“Although...”

She looked up.

“What?”

“I have one request.”

Her eyes narrowed playfully.

“What request?”

“Don’t leave it in the wardrobe until your next birthday.”

She burst out laughing.

“I won’t!”

“Good.”

He kissed her temple.

“Because I think Meilin chose well.”

Xiaoran smiled against his chest. Later that night she sent Meilin one final message.

Xiaoran: He took pictures of me in it.

Meilin: I know. I have excellent taste.

Xiaoran laughed so loudly that Yichen looked up from his book.

“What?”

“Meilin.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Of course.”

She put her phone down, climbed onto the bed beside him, and tucked herself against his shoulder.

The skirt hung on the outside of the wardrobe door now, where she could see it.

chapters.desc: She is on the 3:40 train. He is supposed to be on the team train at 6:15, and isn’t.
chapters.title: The Train Back
chapters.epigraph: “I just want to stay with you.”
chapters.content:
The plan was simple. Xiaoran would get back on Sunday afternoon and Zhou Yichen would get back on Sunday evening.

She had spent the weekend at her parents’ for her mother’s birthday. He’d been in Hangzhou with the Herons for an away game on Saturday night, and the team train came back on Sunday when it always did, which was too late for dinner and too early for anything else.

They’d swapped times on Friday, lying on opposite ends of their sofa with their phones.

“Mine gets in at three-forty,” she said.

“Mine’s six-fifteen.”

“That’s so late.”

“It’s not that late.”

“I’ll be home before you. I’ll be home for hours before you.”

“Save me some dinner.”

“Depends whether you’re nice to me.”

“I’m always nice to you,” he said, and she put her feet in his lap, and that was the end of the conversation.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her train got in at 3:40 exactly. By a quarter past four she was back in the flat with her suitcase open on the bedroom floor and a bag of her mother’s sesame pastries on the kitchen counter, and the flat had that particular silence it only had when one of them was away.

Yichen: Home?

Xiaoran: yes. you?

Yichen: On the train.

She looked at the clock. She looked at the sofa, with nobody on it. She sent him a crying cat and went to unpack, slowly, because there was no point doing anything quickly when there were two hours to fill.

What she didn’t know was that his train had got in a little after four, and it wasn’t the team train.

The team train would leave Hangzhou at 4:40 and get in at 6:15 as usual, with twelve tall men asleep on each other’s shoulders and Fang Ze eating everybody’s crisps. At breakfast that morning Yichen had gone to the coach’s table and asked whether he could travel back on his own, for a personal reason. The coach had looked at him over his coffee.

“Is the personal reason about a metre sixty tall?”

Yichen hadn’t said anything.

“Go,” said the coach.

He didn’t message her from the platform. He got a taxi from the station, and he spent most of the ride smiling at the back of the driver’s headrest.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was on her knees in front of the suitcase, sorting socks, when she heard the front door.

She went still. There was a rustle, and the familiar double click of the lock.

“Xiaoran?”

She was in an old university T-shirt with her hair knotted on her hair and a cardigan thrown over the back of the sofa and her suitcase exploded over half the bedroom floor. She hadn’t expected him for another two hours.

“Yichen?”

He came to the bedroom doorway with his bag still over his shoulder and his hair flat from the headrest. He looked a bit tired. He was smiling.

She stared at him. She looked at the clock on the bedside table. She looked back at him.

“You’re early.”

“The train was early.”

“Trains aren’t two hours early.”

“This one was,” he said, with a perfectly straight face.

She got up off the floor, stepping on a sock, and crossed the room in two strides, and he barely had time to drop his bag before she walked straight into him and wrapped both arms round his waist and held on as hard as she could.

He caught her. One arm round her back, his other hand coming up to the back of her head.

“Hello.”

“Hello,” she said into his chest.

“Did you miss me?”

She nodded against him without letting go.

“Me too,” he said.

She leaned back just far enough to look up. “Did you eat?”

“I had something on the train.”

“What?”

“A sandwich.”

“That’s not a meal.”

“I was travelling.”

“Still.”

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Rice.”

“With what?”

She narrowed her eyes. “You sound like my mother.”

“Your mother’s usually right,” he said, and she laughed and put her face back against him and stayed there. He didn’t try to move. He stood in the doorway with his arms round her and his chin on her hair until his phone buzzed in his pocket and they both ignored it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They unpacked together, which mostly meant that she unpacked and talked and he picked things up off the floor and put them in the right drawer.

“How was the game?”

“We won by four.”

“Only four?”

“You’re supposed to tell me we won by thirty.”

“Would you like me to lie?”

“Just a little. I brought something,” she said, and then she dug in the side pocket of her suitcase and came out with a small paper bag.

“Food.”

“Why do you always guess food?”

“Because it’s usually food.”

“That’s not true.”

“It’s not always true. They’re from the shop near Mum and Dad’s. The walnut ones. You liked them at New Year,” she said, and opened the bag.

He looked at the pastries, and then at her. “You remembered.”

“Of course I remembered. You ate four.”

He took one and broke it in half and gave her the bigger piece, and they sat at the foot of the bed eating them over the open suitcase, getting crumbs on her clothes.

“Can we stay in today?” she said.

“We can.”

“No going out?”

“Not unless you want to.”

“No seeing anyone?”

“I haven’t made any plans.”

“Good.”

“What’s the occasion?”

“Nothing. I just want to stay with you.” She leaned sideways against his arm.

He put his arm round her, and they sat there not unpacking for a while.

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past five they were on the sofa. She was lying along it with her legs across his lap, and he was scrolling through the team chat on his phone with one hand and holding her ankle with the other. His phone buzzed. A message from Fang Ze lit up the screen, right where she could see it.

Fang Ze: Coach says next time you have a “personal reason” bring the personal reason to the station so he can check she exists

She read it. She read it again. Then she sat up and looked at him.

“Personal reason?”

He looked at the ceiling.

“The train wasn’t early.”

“No.”

“You changed your ticket.”

“At breakfast.”

“You left the team?”

“I asked the coach. He said yes. He also said something about your height.” He turned the phone off, far too late.

“Why?”

He looked at her, and she saw him decide not to make a joke of it.

He said, “Because you were going to be home at four, and I wasn’t going to be home till after six, and I didn’t want you to be in the flat on your own for two hours on a Sunday.”

“That’s ridiculous. It’s two hours.”

“I know.”

“I’ve been on my own for longer than that.”

“I know. That’s why.” He ran his thumb along the bone of her ankle.

She didn’t have an answer. So she climbed along the sofa and kissed him on the jaw, and then on the mouth, and then, because she was who she was, she picked up his phone and replied to Fang Ze herself.

Yichen: She exists. This is her. Tell the coach thank you

Fang Ze: HAHAHAHAHA hello personal reason

Fang Ze: he says you’re welcome. he also says the personal reason is taller than he thought

✦ ✦ ✦

They ordered dinner and ate it on the sofa, and watched half an episode of a drama neither of them cared about, and argued about whether the male lead was being unreasonable. She said yes. He said the female lead hadn’t told him anything, so what was he meant to do. She said that wasn’t the point. He asked what the point was. She said the point was that he should have known.

“How?”

“The way you knew about the train.”

“That wasn’t knowing. That was looking at your ticket,” he said.

At some point she stopped arguing. He noticed when her answers started coming later and later and then didn’t come at all.

“Xiaoran?”

Nothing. Her eyes were shut. Her hand was lying over his on his knee.

He turned the television down. He reached over her carefully and moved the empty containers off the edge of the coffee table, and pulled the blanket down off the back of the sofa. She stirred when he tucked it round her.

“Mm.”

“Go to sleep.”

She opened her eyes halfway. “You’re still here?”

“Where else would I be?”

“Good,” she said, and found his hand again, and held it, and shut her eyes.

He looked down at her. That afternoon they had been on two different trains coming from two different directions, and one of them had been on the wrong train on purpose. Now she was asleep on him with her suitcase still half unpacked in the next room and the pastry bag on the kitchen counter.

He bent and kissed her. “Welcome home.”

She mumbled something without opening her eyes.

“What?”

“Welcome home too,” she said, and was asleep again before he could answer.

At a quarter past six, across the city, the team train pulled into the station without him. Fang Ze sent a photograph of the empty seat beside his, with a crisp packet on it. Yichen saw it an hour later and didn’t reply, because his phone was on the other side of the sofa and his hand was busy.

chapters.desc: One fan comments on every post he makes. Xiaoran is not jealous; she is conducting research. The next evening, he posts a photo of his own.
chapters.title: A Jealous Girlfriend’s Investigation
chapters.epigraph: “You’re very cute when you’re investigating.”
chapters.content:
Xiaoran had a perfectly reasonable explanation for what she was doing. She wasn’t stalking anyone. She was conducting research. There was a difference. An important difference.

At least, that was what she had been telling herself for the past twenty minutes. It started innocently enough.

Yichen had posted a photograph on his social media account that afternoon. Nothing unusual: a picture from training, taken by one of the team photographers. He was standing near the court in his Herons jersey, one hand holding a basketball, his expression relaxed, hair slightly damp from practice. The caption was brief.

Back to work.

Within an hour, the post had collected thousands of likes and hundreds of comments.

Xiaoran had liked it, naturally. She had even saved the photograph because she thought he looked handsome. Then she noticed a comment.

@momo_w: You look especially good today. Hope to see you at the next game! ❤️

Nothing strange. Except the same account had commented on his previous three posts. And the three before those.

And apparently, she had also replied to several of his team’s official posts. Xiaoran scrolled upward. One comment. Two. Three. She stopped.

“Interesting.”

She tapped the profile. The account belonged to a young woman. Her profile picture showed her smiling in front of a café window. There were photographs of flowers, restaurants, concerts, and several basketball-related posts. Xiaoran looked at the screen, then at Yichen.

He was sitting on the other side of the living room sofa, watching a game replay on his tablet. She looked back at the phone.

Hope you recover quickly, Yichen.

Your performance was amazing today!

No. 11 is my favourite.

Xiaoran’s lips pressed together. She scrolled farther. There was a photograph of the woman holding a Herons ticket, then another from the arena.

Then a picture of Yichen on the court, taken from the stands. Xiaoran stared at it. The photograph was actually quite good. She enlarged it.

Then immediately felt annoyed with herself for thinking that.

“What’s wrong?”

Yichen’s voice came from beside her. She almost dropped her phone.

“Nothing.”

He met her eyes.

“You’re making a face.”

“I’m not.”

“All right.”

He returned to his tablet. Xiaoran glanced at him, then back at the profile. She wasn’t jealous.

She was curious about the frequency of this particular person’s engagement. That was all. Ten minutes later, Yichen noticed something.

Xiaoran had stopped watching the drama playing on the television.

She was holding her phone at an unusual angle, her eyebrows drawn together, occasionally tapping the screen with a seriousness usually reserved for her work assignments, then at the television. Then back at her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“What are you looking at?”

“Nothing.”

He smiled.

“Nothing seems interesting.”

She glanced up.

“Are you watching me?”

“You’re sitting beside me.”

“That doesn’t mean you have to watch me.”

“I wasn’t aware I needed permission.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“You’re distracting.”

Yichen put his tablet down.

“Then I should probably stop.”

He shifted closer. Xiaoran immediately moved her phone away. That was when he became interested. His eyes followed the movement.

“What’s that?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re hiding something.”

“I’m not.”

He held out his hand. She looked at it, then at him.

“What?”

“Let me see.”

“No.”

His eyebrows lifted.

“Now I’m curious.”

“You don’t need to be.”

Yichen smiled. It was a particular smile. The kind that suggested he had already worked something out but was waiting to see how long she intended to maintain her story. Xiaoran knew that smile. She disliked that smile.

Mostly because she found it ridiculously attractive, which was deeply inconvenient when she was trying to be annoyed with him.

“You’re investigating someone,” he said.

She froze. Yichen’s smile grew.

“Am I right?”

“No.”

“Then show me.”

“Why?”

“To prove me wrong.”

She looked at him suspiciously. Then, after a moment, she turned her phone towards him.

“Fine.”

Yichen glanced at the screen. A woman’s profile. Several comments beneath his photographs.

He looked at the screen for a few seconds. Then he looked at Xiaoran. Understanding settled over his expression.

“Ah.”

Xiaoran immediately became defensive.

“Don’t say ‘ah’ like that.”

He leaned back against the sofa.

“You’re looking at my fan’s account.”

“I’m not looking at your fan’s account.”

He glanced at the phone again.

“Whose account is this?”

She hesitated.

“...A person.”

Yichen laughed. Xiaoran frowned.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not laughing at you.”

“You are.”

He took her phone gently and returned it to her.

“You’re jealous.”

“I’m not.”

“All right.”

She met his eyes.

“Why do you always do that?”

“Do what?”

“Agree with me when you clearly don’t believe me.”

“Would you prefer I disagree?”

“Yes.”

He considered it.

“You’re jealous.”

She grabbed a cushion and hugged it against her chest.

“You’re unbearable.”

Yichen smiled and rested his arm along the back of the sofa.

“What’s bothering you?”

“Nothing is bothering me.”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked away. He waited. That was one of the things about Yichen. He rarely pushed when he knew she was still deciding whether she wanted to say something. Eventually, she sighed.

“She’s commented on almost every post you’ve made recently.”

He nodded.

“Okay.”

“And she always says something about how handsome you are.”

“Does she?”

“Yes.”

He seemed to consider that. Then he said, quite calmly, “I haven’t noticed.”

Xiaoran turned towards him.

“You don’t read your comments?”

“Sometimes. Not all of them.”

She looked down at her phone.

“She also goes to your games.”

“Many people do.”

“I know.”

Yichen watched her expression. She wasn’t angry, exactly. She looked a little troubled, a little embarrassed, and annoyed that he had caught her investigating. He reached over and touched her chin lightly. He crooked a finger at her.

She leaned closer, though she tried to maintain a displeased expression.

“Do you want me to stop posting photographs?”

Her eyes widened.

“No!”

“Do you want me to stop playing basketball?”

“Yichen!”

He laughed.

“I’m asking.”

“Obviously not.”

“Then what would you like me to do?”

She looked at him. She seemed genuinely unsure.

“I don’t know.”

He brushed his thumb along her cheek.

“Then you don’t have to decide right now.”

She lowered her gaze.

“I know you’re not doing anything wrong.”

“I know.”

“And I know fans will comment. That’s normal.”

“Yes.”

She was quiet. Then she muttered, “But she comments a lot.”

Yichen’s mouth curved.

“That’s what you found after twenty minutes of research?”

Xiaoran immediately looked up.

“How did you know it was twenty minutes?”

He laughed.

“Because I’ve been watching you.”

She blinked at him. Then she pushed his shoulder.

“Stop watching me!”

He caught her hand.

“You’re very cute when you’re investigating.”

“I’m not cute.”

“You’re right. Very intimidating.”

She tried to pull her hand away. He didn’t let go.

“Especially when you enlarge the photographs.”

Xiaoran’s eyes widened.

“You saw that?”

“I saw you zooming in.”

“That was because I wanted to see the picture properly!”

“Of course.”

“Yichen!”

He laughed again and pulled her closer, kissing her forehead.

“All right. I’ll stop.”

She remained suspicious.

“You’re enjoying this.”

“A little.”

The next morning, Xiaoran woke up before Yichen. She was still half-asleep when she reached for her phone. A notification appeared. Yichen had posted a story.

It was a photograph of his breakfast: eggs, toast, fruit, and a glass of milk.

The caption read:

Breakfast before training.

Xiaoran smiled. Then she noticed another notification. The same woman had replied to his story.

@momo_w: You always eat so well. Good luck today! ❤️

Xiaoran stared. She blinked. Then she slowly turned her head towards Yichen. He was still asleep.

She looked at the phone again, then back at him.

She considered waking him. She considered not waking him.

She considered whether it was reasonable to send him a screenshot. Finally, she placed her phone down.

She wasn’t going to investigate again. She had dignity. She was a mature adult. She was a working professional. She had a campaign presentation later that morning.

She wouldn’t spend her time looking at another woman’s social media account. Five minutes passed. She picked up her phone. She opened the account.

“Just checking,” she whispered.

Yichen woke up to find his girlfriend sitting against the headboard, wearing an expression of intense concentration. He blinked.

“Good morning.”

“Morning.”

He glanced at her phone, then at her face.

“Back to work?”

She froze.

“What?”

“Your investigation.”

Xiaoran immediately locked her screen.

“There’s no investigation.”

He smiled sleepily.

“Of course.”

“Go back to sleep.”

He reached for her waist and pulled her closer.

“Five more minutes.”

She allowed herself to be drawn into his arms, her phone still in her hand. Yichen kissed her temple.

“Did you find anything?”

“No.”

“Nothing at all?”

She hesitated.

Then mumbled, “She replied to your breakfast story.”

He laughed.

“Did she?”

“Yes.”

“Should I be worried?”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“Don’t make fun of me.”

His smile softened.

“I’m not.”

She studied his face. He was still sleepy, his hair messy, one arm wrapped around her waist.

He looked so comfortable that her annoyance began to dissolve.

“I know it’s silly,” she said.

“It’s not.”

She looked up.

“Really?”

He brushed her hair back.

“You’re allowed to be jealous.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened.

“But I don’t want to become the kind of girlfriend who checks every woman who comments on your posts.”

“Then don’t.”

She blinked. Yichen smiled.

“If something bothers you, tell me. It’s faster than twenty minutes of research.”

She nodded slowly.

“Okay.”

He kissed her hair.

“And for the record, I don’t know that woman.”

“Have you ever met her?”

“Not that I remember.”

She looked relieved. Yichen noticed. Then his expression turned amused.

“Although I have to say, she’s received a lot of attention from you.”

Xiaoran groaned.

“Please forget this happened.”

“I don’t think I can.”

“Yichen!”

He laughed and kissed her cheek. That evening, after training, Yichen came home earlier than expected.

Xiaoran was in the kitchen preparing dinner. She had tied her hair up and was wearing one of his old shirts.

He walked up behind her, placed his hands at her waist, and kissed her cheek.

“Smells good.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“You’re early.”

“Training ended sooner.”

“Did you eat anything afterward?”

“Not yet.”

She pointed at the counter.

“There’s fruit. Eat some while you wait.”

He obediently reached for a piece of apple. Xiaoran glanced at him, then smiled.

“Good.”

He turned to her.

“Am I being evaluated?”

“Yes.”

“How am I doing?”

“Acceptable.”

He laughed. She returned to stirring the food. A moment later, Yichen spoke.

“By the way.”

“Hm?”

“I posted something.”

She turned.

“What?”

“Check your phone.”

Xiaoran looked at him suspiciously.

“Why?”

“Just look.”

She wiped her hands and picked up her phone.

He had posted a photograph on his social media. It was a picture taken that morning. Not of his breakfast. Of Xiaoran.

She was sitting at the kitchen counter in his shirt, hair tied up, looking down at a bowl of fruit. The photograph was slightly candid, with sunlight falling across her face. She hadn’t known he had taken it. The caption was simple.

Someone makes sure I eat properly.

Xiaoran stared at the screen, then at him.

“Yichen.”

He looked perfectly innocent.

“What?”

“You posted me?”

“Yes.”

“Without telling me?”

“You look nice.”

She looked back at the photograph. It was actually a good picture. Then she noticed the comments. Fang Ze had already replied.

@fangze: Manager Lin reporting for duty.

Another teammate commented:

@herons_17: Finally, the person in charge has been officially introduced.

Xiaoran burst out laughing. She turned towards Yichen.

“You did this on purpose!”

“Did what?”

“You know exactly what!”

He stepped closer, his hands returning to her waist.

“I thought people should know who’s responsible for my breakfast.”

She laughed and pushed his chest.

“I’m not responsible for your breakfast!”

“Then who is?”

“You’re an adult!”

“An adult who needs to eat.”

She looked at him. Then, slowly, her expression became suspicious again.

“Wait.”

“What?”

“Did you post this because of yesterday?”

Yichen looked at her. A faint smile appeared.

“Perhaps.”

“You’re teasing me.”

“A little.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“You’re enjoying this too much.”

He leaned closer.

“Would you prefer I post the investigation instead?”

Her mouth fell open.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed, catching her before she could push him away. Then he kissed her. Once on the cheek. Then her forehead.

And finally, when she tilted her face up, on her lips.

She forgot what she had been about to complain about. For a moment. Then she pulled back.

“You’re still not allowed to laugh at me.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise?”

He nodded.

“Promise.”

She studied him.

“Even if I investigate again?”

His smile returned.

“That depends on how thorough your investigation is.”

She groaned and buried her face against his chest. Yichen laughed, wrapping both arms around her.

After a while, she murmured, “I really wasn’t that jealous.”

“Of course not.”

“I was just curious.”

“Naturally.”

“And I only checked because she kept commenting.”

“I understand.”

She lifted her head.

“You’re not listening.”

“I am.”

“What did I just say?”

“You’re curious, not jealous.”

She smiled triumphantly.

“Exactly.”

Yichen looked at her. Then he gently tucked her hair behind her ear.

“All right, my curious girl.”

She smiled. And when he kissed her again, she didn’t object.

Later that night, Xiaoran checked his post one last time. The woman had commented again.

@momo_w: She’s so pretty! You two look happy together. ❤️

Xiaoran stared at it. Then she looked at Yichen, who was sitting beside her on the sofa. He glanced at her phone.

“Everything all right?”

“Yes.”

A pause. Then she leaned against his shoulder.

“Actually, she has good taste.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“Does she?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

Xiaoran smiled, slipped her hand into his, and gave it a little squeeze.

“Because she thinks you’re handsome.”

He laughed.

“And?”

She turned to him.

“And she thinks we’re happy together.”

His expression softened. He raised her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“She’s right about that.”

Xiaoran smiled, satisfied. Then she put her phone away. Investigation concluded. At least for tonight.

chapters.desc: Their first Spring Festival living together: a drive up from Shanghai, lunch at one house, dinner at the other, and a trunk full of food.
chapters.title: Spring Festival, Two Houses
chapters.epigraph: “Do you know what I liked most today?”
chapters.content:
The first Spring Festival since they’d moved in together was supposed to be simple. Two meals. Two houses, twenty minutes apart across the same city, and three and a half hours of expressway between that city and Shanghai. Lunch at the Zhous’. Dinner at the Lins’. Back to Shanghai that night, because the Herons had given Zhou Yichen exactly one day off.

It sounded perfectly manageable. Then Lin Xiaoran realised that this would be the first time she arrived at either house as someone who didn’t, technically, live at either.

She was still her parents’ daughter, with a room at home and a mother who’d ask whether she’d eaten. But now she lived eleven floors up in Shanghai with Zhou Yichen, and her name was on the lease next to his. They had their own fridge and their own washing and their own routines. She knew which side of the bed he liked. He knew she always left her phone charging on the wrong end of the sofa. They had become a small household. And somehow that made going home feel different.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re bringing too much,” he said, standing over the open suitcase at seven in the morning.

“This one’s for your parents.”

“There are already two bags for my parents.”

“This one’s different. Tea. For your father.” She held it up.

“He does like it.”

“And this is for your mother.”

He looked in the next bag. “Face cream?”

“She mentioned it at the housewarming. She wanted to try it.”

“And that?”

“Snacks.”

“For who?”

“Everyone.”

“Xiaoran. It’s one day.”

“Exactly. One very long day.”

He picked the suitcase up and nearly put his back out. He looked at her.

“What’s in here?”

“Clothes.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“And snacks.”

“Some snacks?”

She smiled at him innocently, and he laughed and zipped it shut, and carried it down to the car.

They left in the dark, and she slept with her head against the window for the first hour, and woke up with the sun coming up over the fields and his hand on her knee.

✦ ✦ ✦

They got to the Zhous’ just before noon. His mother was already at the gate.

“You’re here!”

“Happy Spring Festival, Auntie!”

Mrs. Zhou hugged her. “Happy Spring Festival. Come in, come in. It’s freezing.”

His father came out behind her. “You’re late.”

“We’re ten minutes early,” said Yichen.

His father looked at his watch. “Your mother’s been waiting since eleven.”

“I have not been waiting. I’ve been making lunch,” said Mrs. Zhou.

“She’s been making lunch at the window,” said Mr. Zhou, and Xiaoran laughed.

Mrs. Zhou took one of the gift bags and looked inside. “You’ve brought so much.”

“Just a few things.”

“You’re always bringing things.”

“I can’t come empty-handed, Auntie.”

“Of course you can. You’re family,” said Mrs. Zhou.

She said it lightly, almost in passing, and turned to go in. But Xiaoran felt it land somewhere warm in her chest, and stay. She looked round for Yichen. He was setting the suitcase down by the stairs, and he caught her looking and smiled at her, and she smiled back and went over and took his arm before they went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunch was loud. Mrs. Zhou had made far too much, and Mr. Zhou had brought out a tin of tea he’d been saving all year. He asked about Morrow, and whether Gao Yan had let her lead a shoot yet.

“Twice. Once badly.”

“Only once badly? Good.” He nodded, as if this were an excellent ratio.

“And the kitchen? Is it still the way we left it?” said Mrs. Zhou.

Xiaoran looked at Yichen. He was already smiling into his bowl.

“Mostly, there were a few disagreements,” she said.

“Your mother and I have different opinions.”

“Very different.”

“Did you keep the rice cooker where I put it?”

Xiaoran hesitated. Yichen bent his head lower.

“Actually—”

Mrs. Zhou laughed. “She moved it back.”

“It works better there!”

“Of course it does. It’s your kitchen.”

“She’s very protective of it,” said Yichen, and Xiaoran kicked him gently under the table.

“Good. She should be,” said his father.

“A home should be arranged for the people who live in it,” said his mother.

Xiaoran looked down at her bowl. She didn’t quite know why that sentence got to her so much. Maybe because she was still getting used to it: that the flat was theirs, that she had somewhere to go back to that wasn’t her childhood bedroom. While she was thinking about it, Yichen put a piece of fish in her bowl without a word, the way he always did.

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch his mother insisted they stay for tea. Yichen went to help his father with the fruit, and Xiaoran sat on the sofa with Mrs. Zhou.

“Will you come back often, the two of you?”

“As much as we can. His season makes it hard.”

“I know. But you should both have your own plans, too. Don’t arrange everything round each other’s schedule.”

“Uncle said something like that. When he took me to lunch.”

Mrs. Zhou laughed. “That sounds like him. He’s always been very independent. Too independent, sometimes. But he holds on very tightly to the people he loves.” She looked across at the dining room, where Yichen was listening to his father with his arms folded.

“I know,” said Xiaoran.

“And you? Are you happy? Living together?”

She thought about it properly. About their mornings. The shared fridge. Arguing about dinner. Coming home after a long day and finding him already there, or waking up with his hand lying over hers.

“Yes,” she said.

“Good. Keep talking to each other. And ask for help when you need it.” Mrs. Zhou patted her hand.

Xiaoran was starting to understand that the older women in both families had their own ways of giving advice. Some did it with questions. Some did it with food. And some did it by rearranging your kitchen cupboards.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four Yichen looked at the time. “We should go soon.”

“Already?”

“We’ve got another dinner.”

“I know you have.” His mother got up and started putting food into boxes.

“Auntie, you don’t have to—”

“Take it.”

“But we’re eating at my parents’.”

“Then eat it tomorrow.”

“Your mother has cooked for three households,” said Mr. Zhou.

Mrs. Zhou ignored him. She gave Xiaoran two boxes and Yichen a whole bag, and then she fixed Xiaoran’s scarf at the front.

“Drive carefully. Ring when you get there. And don’t let him drive too fast.”

“I’ll watch him,” said Xiaoran.

“You’re supposed to be on my side,” said Yichen.

She smiled at him sweetly. “Happy Spring Festival.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was twenty minutes across a city hung with red lanterns, with fireworks already going off over the river although it was barely five. She sat in the passenger seat with a box of food on her lap because the boot was full, and it was still warm through the lid.

“Are you nervous?” she said.

“About what?”

“Going to my parents’.”

“No.”

“Not even a bit?”

“Why would I be?”

“Because it’s the first Spring Festival since we moved in together. We’re arriving together.”

“I know. It does feel a bit different.” He was quiet, changing lanes.

“How?”

“Before, we went to see our families and then went back to wherever we were staying. Now we’re going back to our place.”

Their place. Two words that still made her unreasonably happy. He reached over at the next red light and put his hand over hers on the warm box.

“Is that a problem?”

“No,” she said, and looked out of the window so he wouldn’t see her face, and he saw it anyway in the glass.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother had the door open before they’d finished unloading the car.

“You’re here!”

“Mum!”

Her mother hugged her and immediately turned to Yichen. “Happy Spring Festival.”

“Happy Spring Festival, Auntie.”

Her father came out behind. “Come in. It’s cold.”

Her mother looked at the boxes. “What’s all this?”

“Food from Auntie Zhou.”

“She’s sent food again? Good. Kitchen,” said her mother, delighted.

“How was the drive up?” said her father.

“Good, Uncle. Three and a half hours.”

“Did you stop?”

“Once.”

“Good. You’ve brought too much.” He looked at the bags.

“That’s what I told him,” said Yichen, and Xiaoran stared at him in outrage.

Dinner was louder than lunch. Her mother had made all of Xiaoran’s favourites. Her father had brought out the good tea. And her mother kept putting food in Yichen’s bowl.

“Eat more.”

“Thank you, Auntie.”

“And some of this.”

“All right.”

“You don’t have to keep feeding him,” said Xiaoran.

“Why not?”

“Because he’s already had lunch.”

“Did you eat properly at the Zhous’?” her father asked him.

“Yes, Uncle.”

“Good. Then you can eat properly here too.”

“Dad.”

“What?”

“You’re both doing it.”

“He’s our guest,” said her mother.

Xiaoran looked at Yichen. He was eating steadily and clearly enjoying every second of it. Traitor, she mouthed at him. He looked back at her with perfect innocence and took another dumpling.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner her father fetched the biscuit tin of old photographs.

“Oh no.”

“What?” said her mother.

“Why are you bringing that out?”

“Because it’s Spring Festival.”

“That’s not a reason!”

Her father opened it anyway. Yichen leaned in. She gave him a look.

“Don’t.”

“Don’t what?”

“Don’t look so interested.”

“I am interested.”

Her mother picked one out. It was Xiaoran at eight, at her grandparents’ house, standing next to a little table with a cake on it, her hair in two lopsided bunches, pulling a face at whoever held the camera.

“That’s cute,” said Yichen.

“Please.”

Her father found another. “Her first day at the new school. The September we moved to the city.”

Xiaoran at twelve, with a backpack nearly as big as she was, looking serious and holding her mother’s hand tightly.

“She cried that morning,” said her mother.

“I did not.”

“You did.”

“Only a little.”

“That’s adorable,” said Yichen.

“Don’t.”

Then her father found one from their first year at university: the two of them at a campus event, her with a drink, looking at the camera; him looking at her. He put it on the table and looked at it for a while.

“This one’s nice. You both look happy.”

“We were. We are,” said Yichen.

Her father nodded. He put it back in the tin. Then he looked at Yichen. “Look after each other.”

“We will, Uncle.”

Xiaoran didn’t say anything. She put her hand on Yichen’s knee under the table. Her father already knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight they started trying to leave. Her mother packed another bag of food.

“Mum, we’ve already got food from the Zhous’.”

“Then you’ll have food for tomorrow.”

“We can’t eat all this.”

“Freeze some.”

Her father was standing by the door with a box. “And these.”

“What’s that?”

“New Year snacks.”

“Dad! You’re both sending us home with food.”

“You’re going home,” said her mother.

The words made Xiaoran stop with one shoe on. Her mother saw it, and smiled, and corrected herself. “Well. You’re going back to your flat.”

“Yes,” said Xiaoran.

Her father gave Yichen the box. “Drive carefully. Ring when you get there.”

“I will, Uncle.”

Her mother hugged her at the door. “Don’t work too hard. Ring us.”

Then she turned to Yichen.

“Make sure you both eat,” she said.

“I will, Auntie.”

“You’re taking responsibility for both of us now?” said Xiaoran.

“Apparently,” said Yichen.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were alone in the car at 8:26. The back seat was full: two bags from his mother, a box from her father, a bag of oranges from her mother. Xiaoran let her head fall back against the seat.

“That was a lot.”

“Yes.”

“Your mother gave us food. My mother gave us food. We’ve got enough food for a week.”

“Probably.”

“We’re going to have to rearrange the fridge.”

“Again?”

“Again,” she said, and he laughed and took her hand.

“Happy Spring Festival.”

“Happy Spring Festival.”

The city fell away behind them, and the expressway was dark and nearly empty. After a while she said, “Do you think they see us differently now?”

“Who?”

“Our parents.”

“Probably.”

“Because we live together?”

“Probably.”

She looked out of the window. “I felt it today. Your mother said I was family. My mother said we were going home. Both our dads told you to look after us. And they all sent us off with food.”

She turned to him. “They weren’t treating us like two people going out together. They were sending us home together,” she said.

“I noticed.”

“Does it feel strange?”

“No, it feels right,” he said.

She leaned her head against the window, and then against his shoulder, which was awkward with the seatbelt, and stayed there anyway.

“Next year we should invite them all to ours.”

“That’ll be interesting.”

“Why?”

“Your mother and mine in our kitchen again.”

She thought about it. Then she started laughing. “Oh no. They’ll rearrange everything.”

“Probably.”

“And our dads will sit in the living room pretending not to notice.”

“Definitely,” he said, and she laughed until she had to wipe her eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

They got home just before midnight. The flat was quiet and dark and exactly as they’d left it: her books on the shelves, his shoes next to hers by the door, two mugs from that morning still by the sink. They carried everything up in three trips and put it all on the kitchen counter.

She opened the fridge. “There’s no room.”

He came and stood behind her and looked in over her head. “Move the drinks into the door.”

“It’s already full.”

“Then some can wait till tomorrow.”

They did it together: boxes on shelves, oranges in the bowl, snacks in the cupboard. When everything was put away she leaned back against the counter. He leaned next to her. The clock on the oven said 12:08.

“Happy Spring Festival,” she said again.

“Happy Spring Festival.”

She took his hand. “Our first one. Living together.”

“Not bad.”

“Not bad?”

“Quite good,” he said, and she laughed and turned and put her arms round him, and he held her with his cheek on her hair in the dark kitchen.

She tipped her head back to look at him. “Do you know what I liked most today?”

“What?”

“Both our mothers kept telling us to look after each other.”

“They’re not wrong.”

“No. But I think they still see us as children.”

“To them we always will be,” he said, and kissed her.

On the counter beside the stacked boxes, just before she switched off the light, she saw two red envelopes, one from each family. Neither of them had seen anyone put them in a bag.

chapters.desc: Looking for batteries, he finds her emergency snack drawer, and quietly starts restocking it.
chapters.title: The Secret Snack Drawer
chapters.epigraph: “It’s not just snacks.”
chapters.content:
Yichen discovered the secret snack drawer on a Thursday evening. He wasn’t looking for anything interesting. He was looking for batteries.

The television remote had stopped working, and Xiaoran had casually mentioned that she thought there might be spare batteries somewhere in the living room. Yichen opened the first drawer of the cabinet, found a few instruction manuals, two charging cables, and a collection of things neither of them remembered buying. The second drawer contained stationery. The third drawer was unexpectedly difficult to open. He pulled it once. Nothing.

He pulled it again. Something shifted inside. Yichen frowned slightly and tried a different angle. The drawer slid open. He looked down, then paused. Inside was an assortment of snacks. Not a small assortment.

There were chocolate bars, individually wrapped biscuits, gummy candies, crackers, dried fruit, little packets of potato chips, and several bags of snacks he recognised from the convenience store near their apartment. Everything was arranged in neat little sections.

Some packages were stacked horizontally. Others were placed upright in small organisers. There was even a tiny basket containing sweets. Yichen stared at it. Then he picked up a small chocolate bar. There was a handwritten label on the basket.

Emergency.

He looked at it for another moment. Then he smiled.

“Interesting.”

Xiaoran was in the bathroom when he discovered her secret.

When she came out, she found Yichen sitting on the sofa with a chocolate bar in his hand. She stopped walking.

Her eyes moved to the chocolate, then to him. Then, slowly, towards the living room cabinet. Yichen noticed the direction of her gaze.

“Good evening.”

She squinted at him.

“Why are you holding that?”

He looked at the chocolate.

“Is it yours?”

She didn’t answer. His mouth curved.

“Ah.”

“Yichen.”

“Yes?”

“Where did you get that?”

He glanced towards the cabinet.

“From a drawer.”

Her expression changed. He watched her face. Then he laughed.

“Is that your secret?”

Xiaoran walked over immediately.

“Don’t touch it.”

He raised his eyebrows.

“Why?”

“Because that’s mine.”

“I gathered.”

She reached for the chocolate. He held it just out of reach.

“What’s all this, then?”

“Nothing.”

He looked towards the cabinet.

“An entire drawer of nothing?”

She folded her arms.

“It’s an emergency supply.”

Yichen looked at the chocolate in his hand.

“Emergency?”

“Yes.”

“What kind of emergency requires seventeen varieties of snacks?”

“Different emergencies require different solutions.”

He laughed. She looked at him with complete seriousness.

“Don’t laugh. It’s important.”

“All right. Explain.”

Xiaoran sat beside him, apparently deciding that if her secret had been discovered, she might as well defend it properly.

“Sometimes I get hungry at night.”

“Mm.”

“Sometimes I’m working and suddenly want something sweet.”

“Mm.”

“Sometimes I want something salty, but I don’t want to go downstairs.”

“Reasonable.”

“And sometimes I’m watching a drama and I need snacks.”

Yichen nodded slowly.

“That sounds like a very demanding emergency schedule.”

“It is.”

His mouth curved.

“Understood.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“You’re not allowed to eat everything.”

“I haven’t.”

“You already took chocolate.”

“I found it.”

“That’s still taking it.”

He glanced at the wrapper.

“May I have this one?”

She considered it, then sighed.

“Fine. But only one.”

Yichen smiled and unwrapped it.

“Thank you, Manager Lin.”

She immediately reached for the cushion beside her and hit his arm with it.

After that evening, the drawer became a recurring subject of conversation. Mostly because Yichen found it increasingly amusing.

The next morning, Xiaoran was looking for a particular packet of crackers when she discovered that someone had rearranged the drawer. Not dramatically. Just enough to make her suspicious.

The chocolate bars were stacked more neatly. The biscuit packets had been grouped by type. The gummy candies were no longer scattered across the bottom.

She stood in front of the open drawer, then called out.

“Yichen?”

He was in the kitchen.

“Yes?”

“Did you touch my drawer?”

He looked over his shoulder.

“Which drawer?”

She gave him a look. He smiled.

“What happened?”

“You reorganised it.”

“Was it a problem?”

She examined the arrangement.

“No.”

“Then?”

She picked up a packet of chocolate biscuits.

“Why did you put these here?”

“So they’re easier to reach.”

She met his eyes, then at the drawer, then back at him.

“...Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

She closed the drawer. A few seconds later, she opened it again. Yichen watched from the kitchen. She was smiling. The real surprise came on Saturday.

Yichen had a morning training session, while Xiaoran had decided to spend the day working on a presentation from home.

By late afternoon, she was sitting at the dining table, staring at her laptop with an expression of deep dissatisfaction. She had been working for almost three hours.

Her shoulders were tense, and she had rewritten the same paragraph several times. Eventually, she pushed her chair back.

“I need a break.”

Yichen, who had returned from training and was sitting on the sofa reviewing footage, looked up.

“Good idea.”

She walked towards the living room cabinet. Opened the drawer. And stopped. There were new snacks. Several of them. A packet of her favourite seaweed crackers. Two chocolate bars.

A small box of strawberry-flavoured biscuits she hadn’t bought recently.

And a bag of the particular gummy candies she always searched for at the convenience store but frequently found sold out. She blinked, then reached into the drawer.

There was a small handwritten note tucked underneath the basket.

For emergencies.

Xiaoran stared at it, then turned around. Yichen was still on the sofa, apparently concentrating on his tablet. She held up the note.

“Yichen.”

He glanced over.

“Hm?”

“What’s this?”

He looked at the drawer.

“Your emergency supply.”

She looked at the snacks again.

“Did you buy these?”

“Some of them.”

“Some?”

He put his tablet down.

“All right. Most of them.”

She looked at the drawer, then at him.

“Why?”

He shrugged.

“You were running low.”

She stared.

“How did you know?”

“I saw the drawer.”

“When?”

“A few days ago.”

She looked down at the snacks again. He had remembered which ones she liked. Not just the general categories, either. He had bought the exact flavours. She picked up the seaweed crackers.

“These were sold out last time.”

“I know.”

Her eyes lifted.

“You went to the convenience store?”

“On my way back from training.”

She looked at him for another moment, then a smile slowly appeared.

“You replenished my emergency supply.”

“Yes.”

“Without telling me.”

“That was the idea.”

She laughed. Then she walked over to him, holding the packet of crackers against her chest.

“Why are you so nice?”

Yichen looked up.

“Because you’re easy to bribe.”

She laughed.

“With snacks?”

“Apparently.”

She leaned down and kissed his cheek.

“Thank you.”

He caught her hand before she could walk away.

“You’re welcome.”

Then he looked at the packet in her other hand.

“Are you going to share?”

She immediately pulled it closer to her chest.

“That’s an emergency supply.”

Yichen laughed.

“Of course.”

The drawer gradually became a shared project. Not officially.

There was no announcement, no agreement, and certainly no formal division of responsibilities.

But Yichen began adding things whenever he noticed something was running low.

Sometimes he brought home a few packets from the supermarket.

Sometimes he added a new flavour he thought she might like.

Once, he bought a snack Xiaoran had mentioned wanting to try after seeing it in a short video.

She discovered it the following morning and sent him a message while he was at training.

Xiaoran: Did you buy this?

Yichen: Yes.

Xiaoran: Why?

Yichen: Thought you might like it.

Xiaoran: You remembered?

Yichen: You mentioned it twice.

Xiaoran: I did not.

Yichen: Three times, actually.

Xiaoran: You’re exaggerating.

Yichen: Enjoy your snack.

She sent him a heart, then another. Then a photograph of the empty packet an hour later.

Xiaoran: Very good. Approved.

Yichen replied with a single smiling emoji. One evening, Yichen came home to find Xiaoran sitting on the living room floor. The cabinet was open.

The snack drawer was completely emptied onto the floor. He stopped.

“What’s happening?”

“Inventory.”

He glanced at the collection.

“Inventory?”

“Yes.”

She held up a small notebook.

“I think we need a system.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Do we?”

“Of course. We’re running low on chocolate.”

He glanced at the chocolate section. There were still six bars.

“How many do you need?”

“At least ten.”

“Why ten?”

“For emergencies.”

He crouched beside her.

“What kind of emergency?”

She turned to him.

“Yichen, please don’t question the system.”

Something in his face eased.

“All right.”

She continued writing.

“Also, we’re almost out of strawberry biscuits.”

“I bought those yesterday.”

“Yes, but they’re very good.”

“Should I buy more?”

She nodded immediately.

“Please.”

He laughed. She wrote something else, then looked at him.

“Do you want to add anything?”

He thought about it.

“Maybe some nuts.”

She frowned.

“That’s not a snack.”

“It is.”

“Not an emergency snack.”

“Why not?”

“Because emergency snacks need to be exciting.”

Yichen stared at her. Then he laughed until she started laughing too.

“Fine. No nuts,” he said.

She nodded, satisfied. A few weeks later, Yichen discovered something else. The emergency supply had expanded. There were now two drawers. The original one contained Xiaoran’s favourite snacks.

The second contained things she had apparently decided were suitable for shared consumption: nuts, dried fruit, protein bars, and a few snacks Yichen liked.

He stood in front of the cabinet, then called out.

“Xiaoran?”

She came out of the bedroom.

“What?”

He pointed at the drawers.

“What’s this?”

She looked, then smiled proudly.

“Expansion.”

“Expansion?”

“Yes. The original drawer was becoming crowded.”

He opened the second drawer.

“What’s the difference?”

She pointed.

“That’s yours.”

He looked at the contents, then at her.

“You made me a snack drawer?”

“Well, technically, it’s a shared drawer.”

“How generous.”

She nodded.

“I know.”

He picked up a protein bar.

“Thank you.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“You’re welcome.”

He looked at the first drawer again.

“And this one?”

She immediately stepped forward.

“Mine.”

Yichen laughed.

“Understood.”

He closed both drawers. Then he reached for her waist and pulled her closer.

“One question.”

“What?”

“If I eat something from your drawer, is it still an emergency?”

She considered it.

“Depends.”

“On what?”

“Whether you replace it.”

He laughed under his breath.

“Of course.”

She looked pleased with the arrangement. Then he pressed a kiss into her hair.

That night, Xiaoran was sitting beside him on the sofa, eating strawberry biscuits while Yichen watched a basketball game replay. She held one towards him.

“Want one?”

He looked at it.

“From your emergency supply?”

“Yes.”

He took it.

“Thank you.”

She ate another, then leaned against his shoulder. After a while, she glanced towards the cabinet.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“I think the drawer is one of my favourite things in this apartment.”

He looked at her.

“Really?”

“It’s silly, isn’t it?”

“No.”

“It’s just snacks.”

He brushed his thumb over her shoulder.

“It’s not just snacks.”

She turned towards him. He smiled.

“It’s you making room for little things you enjoy. And me making sure you have them.”

She held his gaze. Then her expression softened.

“You’re making it sound very romantic.”

“Is it not?”

She laughed.

“Maybe.”

He kissed her. She let her head drop onto his shoulder again. A few minutes passed before she spoke.

“By the way.”

“Hm?”

“I think we should add another category.”

Yichen looked down.

“What category?”

“Bad-day snacks.”

He nodded seriously.

“All right.”

“Different from emergency snacks.”

“What’s the difference?”

“Emergency snacks are for when I’m hungry. Bad-day snacks are for when I’m sad.”

Yichen considered that.

“Understood.”

“And they should be chocolate.”

“Only chocolate?”

“Mostly.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Anything else?”

She thought.

“Maybe those strawberry biscuits.”

“I’ll remember.”

She tilted her head.

“Really?”

He kissed her temple.

“Of course.”

And the following morning, when Xiaoran opened the drawer, she found a small new basket tucked neatly beside the chocolate.

Inside were her favourite strawberry biscuits and two chocolate bars. There was another handwritten note.

For bad days. Hopefully, you won’t need them often.

Xiaoran stood in front of the cabinet without moving.

Then she took a photograph and sent it to Yichen, who was already at training.

Xiaoran: You’re spoiling my emergency system.

Yichen: Is that a complaint?

Xiaoran: No.

Yichen: Good.

Xiaoran: I love you.

His reply came a few seconds later.

Yichen: Love you too. Don’t forget to eat lunch.

She smiled at her phone. Then opened the drawer, took one strawberry biscuit, and closed it again. The emergency supply was fully stocked.

chapters.desc: In the kitchen, at the mirror, in a crowded aisle: she notices where his hand always goes, and then she starts putting it back.
chapters.title: A Hand at Her Waist
chapters.epigraph: “Because whenever I move my hand away, you find a reason to stand closer.”
chapters.content:
Xiaoran had recently discovered that Zhou Yichen had a habit. A unfair habit, actually. He liked holding her waist.

And he did it so naturally that she sometimes didn’t notice until she was already standing closer to him than she’d intended. It happened in the kitchen first.

Xiaoran was standing in front of the refrigerator, deciding what she wanted to eat. She had opened the door several times, taken out a bottle of milk, put it back, and finally stood there staring at the shelves as if the answer might reveal itself. Behind her, Yichen walked in.

“Still deciding?”

“There’s nothing to eat.”

He glanced at the refrigerator.

“There’s quite a lot.”

“Nothing I want.”

“Then what do you want?”

She turned her head.

“I don’t know.”

Something in his face eased.

“Very helpful.”

She was about to close the refrigerator when he stepped behind her. His hand settled at her waist, gently guiding her a little to the side so he could reach past her for a container.

“Excuse me.”

Xiaoran looked down. His hand was still there. She met his eyes.

“Why are you holding me?”

Yichen retrieved the container.

“Because you’re standing in front of what I need.”

“You could have asked me to move.”

“I could have.”

“But you didn’t.”

He looked at her, his expression perfectly composed.

“Would you prefer that?”

She considered it, then shook her head.

“No.”

His mouth curved.

“Then we’re fine.”

He kissed her cheek before walking away. Xiaoran remained in front of the refrigerator for another moment. She had forgotten what she wanted to eat.

The second time happened while they were getting ready to leave.

Xiaoran was standing in front of the bedroom mirror, fastening an earring. She had already put on her shoes, but she was still pushing at her hair.

Yichen was adjusting his watch. He looked at her through the mirror, then came up behind her. His hands settled at her waist. Xiaoran stopped moving.

He looked at her reflection, then gently adjusted a strand of hair that had fallen against her cheek.

“Your hair is fine.”

She smiled at the mirror.

“Okay.”

He didn’t move away. Instead, he remained behind her, his hands resting comfortably at her waist, his chin almost touching her hair. Xiaoran looked at their reflection.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Are we going somewhere or not?”

“In a moment.”

“Why?”

He met her eyes in the mirror.

“Because you’re standing here.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“You’re pretty.”

Her expression softened immediately. Then she turned around in his arms.

“You could have said that earlier.”

“I’m saying it now.”

He laughed and leaned down to kiss her. When he pulled away, his hands were still at her waist.

She looked down at them, then back at him.

“You’re doing it again. Nothing.”

That got a smile out of him.

“All right.”

By the afternoon, Xiaoran had started noticing. They were at a department store, browsing through a homeware section. She had become interested in a set of mugs with a blue floral pattern. Yichen stood beside her.

“Do you like them?”

“They’re cute.”

“Do you want them?”

She turned one over.

“Maybe. We already have mugs.”

“Not ones that match.”

She turned to him.

“That’s actually a good point.”

“I know.”

She laughed and placed it in the shopping basket. Then she moved towards another display. Yichen followed.

There was a narrow aisle between two shelves. Xiaoran was looking at a set of glasses when someone passed behind her with a trolley. Yichen’s hand found her waist.

He gently drew her closer to him, making room for the trolley to pass. It was quick, almost absent-minded. But Xiaoran noticed. The trolley passed. He let his hand fall. He looked back.

“What?”

That made her grin.

“Nothing.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You’re smiling.”

“Am I not allowed?”

“You’re allowed.”

She moved closer to him. Then, deliberately, took his hand and placed it back at her waist. Yichen looked down, then at her. Xiaoran smiled sweetly.

“There.”

His expression changed. Only slightly. But she saw it.

“What’s this?” he asked.

She tilted her head.

“You seemed to like it.”

He stared at her before a slow smile appeared.

“You’re learning.”

She laughed. That evening, they went out for dinner.

The restaurant was busy, and the host led them through a narrow passage towards their table.

Yichen walked behind Xiaoran, his hand resting lightly at her waist as they moved through the crowd.

When they reached the table, he pulled out her chair.

She sat down, looking at him with a smile.

“What?”

He looked at her.

“Nothing.”

“You’re very gentlemanly today.”

“Today?”

She giggled. He took his seat opposite her. For a while, they discussed ordinary things: her upcoming project, his training schedule, a funny message Meilin had sent, and whether they should go somewhere on their next day off.

Then Xiaoran reached across the table to take his hand.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Why do you always hold my waist?”

He met her eyes.

“Always?”

“Recently, yes.”

He considered the question.

“Do you dislike it?”

She shook her head quickly.

“No.”

“Then what’s the problem?”

“There’s no problem. I’m curious.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile.

“Because I like holding you.”

She waited.

“That’s it?”

“Would you like a more complicated explanation?”

She laughed.

“Maybe.”

He leaned back slightly.

“It’s comfortable. You’re close to me. And I like knowing you’re there.”

She held his gaze. Then her expression became a little softer.

“Oh.”

Yichen squeezed her hand.

“Does that answer your question?”

She nodded, and after a moment she said, “I like it too.”

His smile deepened.

“I know.”

She frowned.

“How?”

“Because whenever I move my hand away, you find a reason to stand closer.”

Xiaoran opened her mouth, then closed it. He was right. She looked away.

“That’s not true.”

“All right.”

“Really.”

“Of course.”

He was smiling again. She knew that smile. She didn’t like how easily he could make her feel caught.

Later, when they returned home, Xiaoran went to the bedroom to change.

She came out in comfortable clothes, her hair loosely tied up, and found Yichen standing by the kitchen counter, drinking water. He looked at her.

“Finished?”

“Yes.”

She walked over and stood in front of him. He put his glass down.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

She wrapped her arms around his waist. He smiled and rested his hands at her back. She held him.

Then she pulled away just enough to look at him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Hold my waist.”

He blinked, then laughed.

“You’re giving me instructions now?”

“Yes.”

He obliged, placing both hands at her waist and drawing her closer. Xiaoran smiled.

“Like that.”

He looked down at her. His thumbs moved lightly against her sides.

“Anything else?”

She thought about it, then shook her head.

“No.”

He bent and kissed her hairline. She looked up.

“Actually...”

“What now?”

“Can you hold me like that when we’re walking too?”

“Of course.”

“And when we’re standing?”

“Yes.”

“And when we’re at home?”

He laughed.

“Xiaoran, I already do.”

She grinned.

“Just checking.”

He shook his head, then leaned down to kiss her.

She kissed him back, her hands resting against his chest. When they separated, she remained close, looking pleased. Yichen brushed his thumb along her waist.

“Are you satisfied?”

She nodded.

“Very.”

“Good.”

He kissed her cheek. Then, just as she started to turn away, he gently drew her back.

“Where are you going?”

“To get water.”

“There’s water here.”

She looked at the glass on the counter.

“Oh.”

“Anything else you need?”

She thought, then wrapped her arms around his neck.

“No.”

Yichen laughed and held her, one hand at her waist, exactly where she had told him to put it.

chapters.desc: She shrinks his favourite charcoal shirt, then spends a weekend with conditioner and tutorials trying to rescue it.
chapters.title: The Laundry Incident
chapters.epigraph: “Because it has a story now.”
chapters.content:
The problem began with a shirt. Not an ordinary shirt, apparently.

It was a dark charcoal-grey button-down, made from a soft fabric, with a relaxed cut and sleeves Yichen usually rolled up to his elbows. Xiaoran had seen him wear it to business meetings, casual dinners, and occasionally around the apartment when he wanted to look presentable without making much effort. She liked that shirt. She also liked how Yichen looked in it. Unfortunately, she had just ruined it.

Or, at least, she thought she had. It was a Saturday morning. Yichen had gone to the training facility early, leaving Xiaoran with the laundry basket and an ambitious plan to get their apartment properly organised.

She had separated the clothes, checked the labels, and started the washing machine. Everything had gone smoothly. Until she took out the charcoal shirt.

She held it up, then frowned, then held it up again. Something was wrong. The shirt looked smaller.

Not dramatically smaller, but enough that the shoulders seemed narrower and the sleeves shorter. The fabric had also lost some of its original softness.

Xiaoran checked the washing machine settings, then the care label, then the machine again. Her expression gradually changed.

“Oh, no.”

She checked the label a second time.

“Oh, no, no, no.”

She had washed it at the wrong temperature. And she had put it in the dryer.

She stood in the laundry area, holding the shirt in both hands, looking as if she had just received terrible news. Yichen had other shirts. Many other shirts.

His wardrobe was larger than hers, and some of his clothes cost more than she wanted to think about. He could replace this shirt without even noticing the expense. That wasn’t the point. He liked this one.

She had seen him reach for it repeatedly. She knew it was one of his favourites, even though he had never specifically told her. And she had ruined it. Xiaoran looked at the shirt again. Then she took out her phone. She searched:

How to fix clothes that shrink after washing.

The results weren’t encouraging. She tried another search.

Can you restore a shirt after accidentally putting it in the dryer?

Then another.

How to stretch cotton blend fabric.

She stared at the screen.

“Please work.”

Yichen came home shortly after noon. He found Xiaoran in the bedroom, sitting cross-legged on the floor beside an open laundry basket.

There were several of his shirts folded neatly beside her. She looked up when he entered.

“You’re back!”

“Mm. What are you doing?” He put his gym bag down.

“Nothing.”

He looked at the clothes.

“Nothing?”

“Organising.”

His gaze moved to her face. She was smiling. A little too brightly.

“Everything all right?”

“Of course.”

He pressed a kiss to her hair.

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Food.”

He met her eyes. She smiled.

“Rice. Chicken. Vegetables. A very balanced meal.”

“Good.”

He changed out of his training clothes, showered, and returned to the bedroom. Xiaoran had already gathered the remaining laundry.

He noticed the charcoal shirt folded separately on the far end of the bed.

“Is that mine?”

She froze.

“Yes.”

“Why is it over there?”

“Because...”

She looked at the shirt, then at him, then back at the shirt.

“I made a mistake.”

Yichen’s expression changed slightly.

“What happened?”

She picked up the shirt and held it out.

“I washed it.”

He looked at it, then at her.

“All right.”

“I used the wrong temperature.”

He examined the fabric, running his fingers over the material.

“And?”

“I put it in the dryer.”

He looked at the shirt again. Then he understood.

“It shrank?”

Xiaoran nodded. Her mouth pressed into a small line.

“I think so.”

Yichen held it up against himself, examining the shoulders.

“It did.”

Her expression fell.

“I’m sorry.”

He turned to her.

“Xiaoran.”

“I checked the label. I really did. I thought it was okay because the other shirts were fine, but I must have missed the temperature instructions, and then I put everything in the dryer because I thought it would be faster.”

He listened.

“I tried searching for ways to fix it, but I’m not sure if any of them work. I haven’t done anything else to it because I didn’t want to make it worse.”

She took a breath.

“I’m sorry. I know you like this shirt.”

Yichen looked at her. Then he placed the shirt on the bed. He held out his hand. She hesitated.

“Why?”

“Humour me.”

She stepped closer. He put his hands around her waist.

“Are you upset?”

“Of course I’m upset. I ruined your shirt.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

She blinked. Yichen brushed his thumb over her side.

“Have you been worrying about this all morning?”

She hesitated.

“...A little.”

“How little?”

She looked away. That got a smile out of him.

“Xiaoran.”

“Quite a lot.”

He let out a quiet breath, then kissed her temple.

“It’s a shirt.”

“I know.”

“I can buy another one.”

“I know.”

“I can buy ten.”

She gave him a small, unwilling smile.

“That’s not helping.”

“Why?”

“Because I know you can buy another one. But it won’t be the same shirt.”

Yichen looked at her. That, he understood. It wasn’t about the money. It wasn’t about replacing something expensive.

She knew he could afford to replace it. She was upset because she had damaged something he liked, something she had wanted to take care of. He gently lifted her chin.

“Look at me.”

She did.

“I’m not angry.”

Her expression softened a little. He kissed her cheek.

“And I’m more concerned that you’ve been sitting here looking miserable over a shirt.”

She let out a small laugh.

“I don’t look miserable.”

“You do.”

“You’re exaggerating.”

“Your eyebrows have been doing this all morning.”

He lightly touched the space between her brows. She immediately frowned again. He smiled.

“That.”

She pushed his hand away.

“Stop.”

He caught her hand and kissed her knuckles.

“Don’t worry about it anymore.”

“But—”

“We’ll see if it can be fixed. If it can’t, I’ll keep it or replace it. That’s all.”

She met his eyes.

“You’re really not upset?”

“Xiaoran, I own more shirts than I can reasonably wear.”

She laughed.

“That’s true.”

“And I have a girlfriend who apparently takes laundry very seriously.”

She gave him a look.

“Don’t make fun of me.”

“I’m not.”

He kissed her, briefly again.

“Come on. Let’s have lunch.”

Yichen thought the matter was settled. Xiaoran, however, had other plans.

For the rest of that day and the next, he noticed several unusual things.

First, the charcoal shirt had disappeared from the bedroom.

Second, Xiaoran became strangely protective of the laundry area.

Third, whenever he entered the room while she was holding her phone, she would immediately switch applications. He noticed. He didn’t say anything.

On Sunday afternoon, he came home from a short training session and found the bedroom door slightly open. Xiaoran was sitting at the dressing table. In front of her was the charcoal shirt.

There was also a bowl of water, a towel, a bottle of hair conditioner, and her laptop. Yichen stopped at the doorway. He watched her carefully stretch one sleeve. She leaned closer to examine the fabric. Then she consulted something on her laptop. Then she stretched it again. Yichen stood there for several seconds. Finally, he spoke.

“What’s happening?”

Xiaoran startled. The sleeve slipped from her hands. She turned around.

“Yichen!”

He looked at the arrangement on the desk, then at her.

“Is this a science experiment?”

She immediately reached for the towel.

“No.”

He walked closer.

“Then what are you doing?”

“Nothing.”

He looked at the shirt.

“You’re trying to fix it.”

She didn’t answer. He glanced at the laptop. The search page was still open.

How to safely stretch a shrunken shirt without damaging the fabric.

Below it were several tabs. One was a video tutorial. Another was an article about fabric composition. A third was a discussion forum. Yichen looked back at her.

“Xiaoran.”

She lowered her eyes.

“I was just trying something.”

He sat down on the end of the bed beside her.

“For how long?”

She shrugged.

“Not long.”

He looked at the open tabs.

“How long?”

She hesitated.

“Since yesterday.”

He blinked.

“Yesterday?”

“I thought maybe I could restore some of the original shape.”

He looked at the shirt.

“Did it work?”

She made a small face.

“Not really.”

Yichen pressed his lips together, trying not to smile. She noticed.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I’m looking at you.”

“You’re smiling while looking at me.”

He finally laughed. Not loudly, but enough that she became increasingly embarrassed.

“Yichen!”

He reached for her hand.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

She looked down.

“Because you already said it was fine.”

“And?”

“I thought I could fix it.”

He watched her. Then he glanced at the shirt again.

“Did you spend all yesterday researching this?”

“Not all day.”

“Xiaoran.”

“...A few hours.”

He leaned back slightly.

“How many?”

She held up two fingers.

“Two?”

She hesitated.
