“That one has a different personality.”

Yichen looked at her. A faint smile appeared at the corner of his mouth.

“Of course.”

Xiaoran grinned and continued scrolling. She was apparently not finished.

For the next ten minutes, she showed him a series of things she had saved: a funny video, a café with beautiful desserts, a dress she liked, a cat that looked like it had committed tax fraud, and a short clip of a couple trying to assemble furniture. Yichen listened to every explanation. He answered her questions.

He even watched the entire furniture video when she insisted the man’s expression at the end was worth seeing.

But somewhere between the third ceramic animal and the fourth video, he noticed something. Xiaoran hadn’t once considered sitting down.

She kept leaning over him, her upper body resting increasingly close against his shoulder, sometimes bracing a hand on the sofa, sometimes placing it on his chest without thinking.

Every time she wanted him to see something, she moved closer.

And every time she moved closer, he became a little less interested in whatever was on her phone. He had been trying to be patient. He really had.

But when she leaned across him again, bringing her face almost level with his, Yichen finally reached out. His hand caught her waist. Xiaoran stopped mid-sentence.

“Eh?”

He gently drew her towards him. Not enough to startle her, just enough to make her straighten up and look at him. Yichen’s hand remained at her waist.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Do you realise how distracting you are?”

She blinked. Then she glanced at the tablet.

“Am I blocking the screen?”

He met her eyes.

“No.”

“Then what?”

His eyes moved over her face before returning to hers.

“You’re standing very close.”

She looked down. Indeed, she was close. Her hip was almost against his knee, his hand was still around her waist, and their faces were only a short distance apart. But she didn’t see the problem.

“We live together.”

“I know.”

“And?”

“And you’ve been leaning over me for the last twenty minutes.”

She thought about it. Then she smiled.

“Did you notice?”

Yichen gave her a look.

“How could I not?”

Her smile grew.

“Oh.”

She looked at him for another second, then asked with exaggerated innocence, “Was I disturbing your work?”

“Not exactly.”

“Then?”

He leaned back against the sofa, his hand still resting at her waist.

“Here.”

Xiaoran’s eyes brightened.

“Why?”

“Because I want to see whether you can stay still for five minutes.”

She laughed.

“That’s easy.”

She put her phone on the coffee table and moved around the sofa, intending to sit beside him. But Yichen caught her hand.

“Where are you going?”

“To sit.”

“Here.”

He gave her waist a gentle tug, and she ended up settling sideways on his lap.

Xiaoran looked at him, then at the sofa beside them.

“There’s a perfectly good seat.”

“I know.”

“Then why am I here?”

“Because you keep coming close enough to distract me. I thought I’d save you the trouble.”

She laughed, placing her hands on his shoulders.

“You’re blaming me?”

“Am I wrong?”

“Yes.”

Yichen raised an eyebrow.

“Then explain.”

She considered her answer.

“I was showing you things.”

“For twenty minutes.”

“Because there were many things.”

“Clearly.”

“And you were supposed to look at them.”

“I did.”

“Then why are you complaining?”

He turned to her. Then he smiled. Slowly. Xiaoran’s expression faltered.

It was that particular smile again: the one that began at the corners of his mouth, his eyes remaining steady on hers, as if he had already thought of something amusing and was waiting for her to realise it.

She knew that smile. She also knew she was usually the one who lost her composure first.

“You’re doing that on purpose,” she murmured.

“Doing what?”

“That face.”

“What face?”

She pressed her lips together. Yichen’s thumb moved lightly against her waist.

“You were very talkative a moment ago.”

“I’m still talkative.”

“Then keep going.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“About what?”

“Whatever you wanted to show me.”

Xiaoran glanced at her phone on the table, then back at him.

She had completely forgotten what she had been showing him. Yichen noticed. His smile deepened.

“Forgot?”

“No.”

“What was it?”

She looked towards the table again.

“...The duck.”

“Which duck?”

“The one with the hat.”

“Ah.”

He nodded, pretending to consider it.

“Very important.”

“It is!”

“Tell me more.”

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“You’re making fun of me.”

“A little.”

She tried to look offended, but his hand was warm at her waist, and he was looking at her with such quiet amusement that it was difficult to maintain the expression. Instead, she reached up and touched his cheek.

“You’re not very interested in my things today.”

“I’ve been listening to you all evening.”

“Not properly.”

“Not properly?”

She nodded. Yichen tilted his head slightly.

“Then what should I do?”

She leaned closer, as if sharing a secret.

“Pay more attention.”

His eyes softened.

“All right.”

He lifted one hand to her cheek and kissed her.

It was a gentle kiss, but he didn’t immediately pull away. Xiaoran’s fingers slipped into his hair, and she returned it with a smile. When they separated, she remained close. Yichen brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“Is that better?”

“Much.”

“Good.”

She was quiet. Then she looked at him again.

“Actually...”

“Hm?”

“I have another video.”

He closed his eyes. Xiaoran burst out laughing.

“Wait! This one is really funny.”

“I believe you.”

“It’s only fifteen seconds.”

“That’s what you said about the furniture video.”

“That one was different.”

“How?”

“It was twenty seconds.”

He looked at her. She grinned. Then, instead of reaching for her phone, she leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“Please?”

Yichen gave a quiet laugh.

“Show me.”

She reached across the coffee table to retrieve her phone, but before she could move too far, his arm tightened gently around her waist.

“Careful.”

“I can reach.”

“I know.”

She retrieved the phone and settled back against him. This time, she didn’t lean over his shoulder.

She sat on his lap, her back against his chest, holding the phone between them. Yichen rested his chin lightly against her shoulder.

“Is this the video?”

“Yes.”

She pressed play. A tiny dog appeared on the screen, attempting to climb onto a sofa and failing spectacularly. Xiaoran snorted into his shoulder. Yichen watched the video. Then he watched her laughing. When it ended, she turned her head.

“Funny, right?”

“Very.”

“You didn’t laugh.”

“I was watching.”

“Watching what?”

He kissed her cheek.

“You.”

Her smile softened. Then she turned back to her phone, trying to hide how pleased she was.

“You’re distracting me now.”

Yichen’s eyebrows lifted.

“Should I stop?”

She pretended to think. Then she leaned back more comfortably against him.

“No.”

His arm settled around her waist again.

“All right.”

A few minutes later, Xiaoran put her phone down and began telling him about something that had happened at work. Yichen listened, occasionally asking questions, his fingers tracing small, absent-minded patterns against her side.

She was halfway through explaining a colleague’s strange presentation when she stopped.

“Wait.”

“What?”

She turned around in his arms.

“Did you finish watching your basketball footage?”

“No.”

“Why?”

He glanced at the tablet on the sofa.

“Because someone kept showing me ceramic cats.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“You’re never going to let me forget that, are you?”

“Probably not.”

She leaned forward and kissed him once, then again, on the other cheek.

“Sorry.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Are you?”

She nodded solemnly.

“Very.”

He gave her a knowing smile.

“Then you can make it up to me.”

“How?”

“Stay here.”

She looked down at his arms around her waist, then back at him.

“That’s it?”

“For now.”

Xiaoran smiled and settled against his chest.

“Okay.”

Yichen picked up his tablet with one hand, keeping the other around her. He returned to the footage. Xiaoran remained quiet for almost a minute. Then she lifted her head.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Do you think the duck with the hat would look better on the shelf or the coffee table?”

He stared at the screen. A small smile appeared.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Show me the duck again.”

She beamed. And Yichen, who had planned a peaceful evening of game footage, spent the next fifteen minutes comparing the decorative merits of two ceramic ducks while Professor Quack watched from her key ring on the table.

chapters.desc: At her studio’s networking evening, a brand representative keeps finding reasons to stand next to her. Yichen stays calm all night, and doesn’t let go of her waist at home.
chapters.title: A Little Too Friendly
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t think you can be stolen.”
chapters.content:
Yichen noticed him before Xiaoran did. It wasn’t difficult.

The man had been standing beside Xiaoran for the better part of fifteen minutes, holding a glass of wine he barely seemed to drink. He was one of the brand partnership representatives invited to Morrow Studio’s annual networking event. Yichen had heard his name earlier during introductions, though he couldn’t remember it now.

What he did remember was how often the man laughed at Xiaoran’s jokes.

And how he kept finding reasons to stand closer.

Yichen stood a few metres away, speaking with one of the event organisers. He wasn’t deliberately watching them. At least, that was what he told himself.

He happened to notice when the man leaned closer to hear Xiaoran over the music.

Then again when he touched her elbow while making a point, then when he complimented her dress.

Xiaoran was wearing a simple black dress to her studio’s event, elegant without being flashy. Her hair was pinned loosely behind her ears, revealing the little flower earrings she often wore. She had spent nearly half an hour deciding whether to wear this dress or another one, eventually asking Yichen which looked better. He had chosen this one.

He was beginning to think he had made an excellent decision for entirely inconvenient reasons.

“Mr. Zhou?”

Yichen turned his attention back to the person speaking to him.

“Yes?”

The conversation continued. He remained polite, attentive, and perfectly engaged. He didn’t interrupt Xiaoran’s conversation or approach them because another man seemed interested in her. He knew his girlfriend.

Xiaoran was friendly. She was expressive, enjoyed talking to people, and could become animated when discussing something she cared about. She was also perfectly capable of handling herself. He trusted her.

That didn’t mean he had to enjoy watching someone else discover how charming she was.

Across the room, Xiaoran laughed at something the man said. Yichen took a sip of his drink.

The organiser beside him continued talking about next quarter’s partnership opportunities. Yichen listened. Mostly.

A little later, Xiaoran finally excused herself and walked towards the refreshment table. She spotted Yichen almost immediately. Her face brightened.

“Yichen!”

He turned.

“Finished networking?”

“Almost. My feet are tired.” She reached for a glass of water.

He glanced down at her shoes.

“Those?”

She nodded.

“I thought they were comfortable.”

“They were comfortable when I tried them at home.”

His mouth curved.

“That’s different from wearing them for three hours.”

“Exactly. I need to file a complaint with the shoe company.”

Yichen took her empty glass and placed it on the table.

“Want to sit?”

“Not yet. I should probably talk to a few more people.”

He nodded. She studied his face.

“Are you tired?”

“No.”

“You’re quiet.”

“I’m listening.”

“To what?”

He met her eyes.

“To you.”

She smiled, then reached up to straighten the edge of his collar.

“You’re very handsome tonight.”

“Thank you.”

“Very serious, too.”

Yichen laughed.

“I don’t.”

“I know. But you look like you could.”

She gave his chest a light pat before turning towards a colleague who had called her name.

“I’ll come back later!”

“All right.”

He watched her leave. Then he finished his drink. He wasn’t angry. That was the important distinction.

There was nothing Xiaoran had done that warranted an argument, and he wasn’t going to turn an ordinary professional event into something uncomfortable for her.

Still, when the evening finally ended, he found himself looking forward to having her to himself.

And judging by the way she slipped her hand into his as they walked towards the car, she was ready to leave too.

“Finally,” she sighed as he opened the passenger door.

Yichen smiled.

“That bad?”

“No. It was actually quite fun. But I think I’ve talked enough for one evening.” She settled into the seat and began removing one of her earrings.

He leaned over to help her with the seat belt.

“Did you have a good time?”

“Yes. I met a few people from other agencies, and one of the brand managers was interested in our next campaign.”

“That’s good.”

She met his eyes.

“How about you?”

“Productive.”

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Enough.”

She narrowed her eyes.

“That’s not a very enthusiastic answer.”

He smiled and closed her door. During the drive home, Xiaoran told him about the event.

She talked about a potential collaboration, a colleague who had accidentally spilled sparkling water on his own trousers, and the dessert table that had been disappointingly small. Yichen listened, occasionally asking questions. He didn’t mention the man. Not yet.

When they arrived home, Xiaoran kicked off her shoes near the entrance and sighed with relief.

“Freedom.”

Yichen placed their keys in the bowl.

“Your feet?”

“Never making that mistake again.”

He looked at her.

“Want me to get you something comfortable?”

“Can you get my slippers?”

He brought them over. She slipped them on, then immediately walked towards him and wrapped her arms around his waist.

“Thank you.”

Yichen’s hands settled at her back.

“You’re welcome.”

She leaned against him before pulling away.

“I need to remove my makeup.”

“Go ahead.”

She took a few steps towards the bedroom, then turned back.

“Are you coming?”

“In a minute.”

“Okay.”

She disappeared into the bathroom. Yichen remained in the living room, loosening his watch.

He was still thinking about the evening when she returned, now wearing a comfortable top and shorts, her face clean and her hair tied loosely.

She looked much more like the Xiaoran who belonged to their home.

“Better,” she announced, stretching her arms.

Yichen looked at her.

“Much better.”

She walked towards the sofa and sat down, patting the space beside her. She patted the space beside her. He joined her.

She immediately leaned against his shoulder, reaching for his hand. For a while, they sat. Then Yichen’s arm moved around her waist.

He drew her closer, his palm resting against her side. It was a familiar gesture. Except tonight, his hand stayed there. A little longer than usual.

His thumb moved slowly against her waist, occasionally brushing the fabric of her shirt. Xiaoran noticed after a while. She looked down, then up at him. She tilted her head.

“You’re holding me.”

“Yes.”

“You usually do.”

“Yes.”

She studied him.

“You’re holding me differently.”

Yichen glanced at her. He didn’t answer immediately. Instead, he adjusted his arm, drawing her closer until her shoulder rested more comfortably against his chest.

Xiaoran looked at him again, then a smile appeared.

“Are you jealous?”

Yichen’s eyes shifted towards her. There was a brief pause.

“Would that surprise you?”

Her smile widened.

“A little.”

“Why?”

“Because you looked so calm the entire evening.”

“I was calm.”

“Then?”

He turned to her.

“Being calm doesn’t mean I didn’t notice.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Notice what?”

Yichen’s expression remained composed.

“The man who spent most of the evening finding reasons to talk to you.”

She blinked at him. Then her mouth slowly curved.

“Oh.”

He held her gaze.

“Something amusing?”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

She giggled.

“Nothing! I just didn’t realise you noticed.”

“Was it difficult to notice?”

She thought about it, then laughed again.

“Maybe not.”

Yichen’s hand moved slightly higher along her waist.

“He seemed particularly interested in what you had to say.”

“He works with one of the brands we’re trying to collaborate with. He was asking about our campaign.”

“I see.”

“And he was quite friendly.”

“Very.”

She turned towards him.

“So you are jealous.”

“I don’t like making assumptions about people’s intentions.”

“That’s a very diplomatic answer.”

“I’m trying to be fair.”

She smiled, then rested her chin against his chest.

“Well, he was friendly, but I wasn’t particularly interested in talking to him for that long.”

Yichen’s eyebrows lifted slightly.

“Why?”

“Because he kept asking questions that weren’t about work.”

He waited. Xiaoran continued, counting on her fingers.

“He asked whether I lived nearby. Then whether I came to these events often. Then whether I usually came alone.”

Yichen’s expression didn’t change, but his hand became still against her waist.

“And what did you say?”

“I told him I lived on the other side of the river, that I came when work required it, and that I usually came with my boyfriend.”

Yichen looked at her. She couldn’t help smiling.

“Actually, I think I mentioned you twice.”

“Twice?”

“Maybe three times.”

His mouth curved.

“Very thorough.”

“I was being polite.”

“I know.”

She watched his expression. Then she asked, “Did you want to come over?”

Yichen considered the question.

“At one point.”

“Why didn’t you?”

He brushed his thumb over her side.

“Because you were having a conversation. I didn’t see a reason to interrupt.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened.

“You could have.”

“I could have.”

“I wouldn’t mind.”

“I know.”

She played with the cuff of his sleeve.

“Next time, you can just come stand beside me.”

Yichen looked down at her.

“Would you like that?”

“Of course. I like introducing you to people.”

That got a smile out of him.

“All right.”

She leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

Then, with a little mischievousness, she asked, “Were you worried he’d steal me?”

Yichen laughed.

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

He turned slightly, his hand settling more securely around her waist.

“I don’t think you can be stolen. You make your own decisions, and I trust you.”

Her teasing expression softened. Yichen looked at her for another moment.

“But I can still dislike someone being overly familiar with my girlfriend.”

She smiled.

“Your girlfriend?”

“Yes.”

“Very possessive.”

“Is that a complaint?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

He leaned closer, his forehead almost touching hers.

“Good.”

Xiaoran smiled. Then she seemed to remember something.

“Oh, wait.”

“What?”

“That man asked whether I had a boyfriend.”

Yichen’s eyes narrowed just slightly.

“And?”

“I told him yes.”

“Good.”

“Then he asked what you did.”

Yichen waited.

“I said you’re a professional basketball player.”

He nodded.

“And then?”

She grinned.

“I showed him a picture of you.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Which picture?”

“The one from our anniversary dinner.”

“The one in the black shirt?”

“Yes!”

He gave a small nod.

“All right.”

Xiaoran’s smile became wider.

“He said you were handsome.”

Yichen looked at her.

“And what did you say?”

She raised her chin.

“I said I knew.”

He laughed.

“Very modest.”

“I’m just telling the truth.”

His hand moved to the small of her back.

“And did you tell him anything else?”

She pretended to think.

“Maybe that you’re very busy, that you train a lot, and that you don’t like people disturbing you.”

“That’s an interesting description.”

“And that you’re very affectionate at home.”

Yichen’s eyebrows rose. Xiaoran giggled.

“You look amused.”

“I’m wondering how much of our private life you shared.”

“Not much!”

“How much is not much?”

She leaned closer and whispered, “I told him you always hold my waist.”

Yichen looked at her. Then at his own hand, which was currently doing exactly that. A quiet smile appeared.

“Did you?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“Then I suppose I should be consistent.”

Before she could ask what he meant, he drew her closer and kissed her.

He tasted of the event’s terrible sparkling wine, and his hand was steady at her back. Xiaoran’s arms slipped around his neck, and she smiled when he kissed her again, just a little longer this time. When they parted, she stayed close.

“You’re still jealous.”

Yichen brushed her hair back.

“Perhaps.”

“I think it’s cute.”

“Do you?”

“Mm-hm.”

He gave her a quiet look.

“Don’t encourage me.”

“Why?”

“Because I might start asking you to come stand beside me at every event.”

Xiaoran laughed.

“You can. I like standing beside you.”

His expression softened. He kissed her hair.

“Then I will.”

She settled against him again, and his arm remained around her waist.

After a few minutes, Xiaoran reached for the television remote.

“Should we watch something?”

“Sure.”

She turned on the television and began browsing. Yichen stayed close, his hand still resting at her waist. Eventually, she glanced down at it.

“You’re still holding me.”

“Yes.”

“Your hand hasn’t moved.”

“Do you want me to move it?”

She considered that. Then she placed her own hand over his.

“No.”

Yichen smiled, and his hand didn’t move for the rest of the episode.

chapters.desc: He promised to teach her to swim. She spends most of the lesson studying something other than technique.
chapters.title: A Very Serious Swimming Lesson
chapters.epigraph: “Because you’re mine.”
chapters.content:
Xiaoran had agreed to go swimming for one simple reason.

Yichen had promised to teach her how to swim properly. That was it.

She hadn’t agreed because he mentioned the private swimming pool at a hotel he occasionally visited. She hadn’t agreed because he said the water was heated and the facilities were excellent. And she certainly hadn’t agreed because he casually mentioned that he usually swam a few laps after training. No.

She was going because she wanted to improve her swimming.

At least, that was what she told herself when she packed her swimsuit the night before.

“Have you brought everything?”

Yichen stood beside the open wardrobe, watching her check her swimming bag for the third time.

“Yes.”

“Towel?”

“Yes.”

“Change of clothes?”

“Yes.”

“Swimming cap?”

She paused, then looked at him.

“Do I need one?”

“Not necessarily.”

“Then why are you asking?”

He smiled. “Just checking.”

She zipped the bag.

“You’re treating me like I’m going on a school trip.”

“You’re the one who packed three different snacks.”

“Swimming makes people hungry.”

“Before swimming?”

“Preparation.”

Yichen laughed and took the bag from her.

“Come on, then.”

The swimming facility was quieter than Xiaoran expected. It was a private indoor pool with floor-to-ceiling windows, soft natural lighting, and a few people swimming in separate lanes. The water was a beautiful shade of blue, and the entire place smelled of chlorine.

She had zipped her promise ring into the inside pocket of her bag, because chlorine and small stones didn’t mix, and checked the zip twice.

Yichen had already changed when Xiaoran came out of the changing room.

He was standing near the pool, checking something on his phone. He wore simple black swimming trunks. His upper body was bare. Xiaoran stopped. Yichen looked up. And saw her. He didn’t say anything immediately.

His eyes moved over her face, then his lips curved.

“What?”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Nothing.”

He put his phone down.

“Why are you standing there?”

“I’m looking.”

“At what?”

She met his eyes, then at the pool, then back at him.

“The facilities.”

Yichen glanced around.

“Good facilities?”

“Very good.”

He smiled. He opened his arms. She walked towards him, trying hard to behave normally. It wasn’t easy.

Because, although Xiaoran knew her boyfriend was athletic, she wasn’t accustomed to seeing him like this outside the context of a basketball game.

His shoulders were broad, his arms defined from years of training, and his abdomen— She looked away, then looked again. Unfortunately, Yichen noticed. Of course he did.

He had been dating her for more than six years.

He knew exactly what her face looked like when she was trying to pretend she hadn’t noticed something.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Are you ready?”

“Yes.”

“Then let’s get in.”

She nodded. But before following him, she glanced down once more. Yichen’s smile deepened.

“Something interesting?”

She immediately looked up.

“No.”

“All right.”

He picked up her towel.

“Let’s go, researcher.”

The first fifteen minutes were dedicated to warming up. Yichen was surprisingly patient.

He stood in the shallow end, showing her how to move her arms, how to control her breathing, and how to relax her legs instead of kicking frantically. Xiaoran listened attentively. Mostly.

“Don’t hold your breath.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“How do you know?”

“Your cheeks are puffed up.”

She exhaled. Yichen laughed.

“Again.”

She tried once more. This time, she managed to float with his support.

“See? You’re doing well.”

Xiaoran smiled. She was pleased. Then she looked at him.

“Can you let go?”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

He slowly loosened his hold. Xiaoran managed to stay afloat for a few seconds before immediately grabbing his arm.

“Wait!”

He caught her.

“Got you.”

She clung to his shoulders, laughing.

“That was scary.”

“You were doing fine.”

“I know, but you let go!”

“That’s usually how learning to swim works.”

She frowned.

“You’re supposed to be supportive.”

“I am.”

He adjusted his hand beneath her arm.

“Try again. I’ll stay beside you.”

She nodded. This time, she lasted longer. When she finally reached the edge, she looked extremely proud of herself.

Yichen rested his arms on the poolside beside her.

“Good job.”

She grinned.

“Did you see?”

“I was right here.”

“I did it!”

He leaned over and kissed her wet forehead.

“Yes, you did.”

She smiled so brightly that he couldn’t help smiling back. For a while, swimming was going very well. Then Yichen decided to demonstrate something.

“Watch.”

He moved away from the shallow end and positioned himself at the beginning of a lane. Xiaoran held onto the pool edge.

“What are you doing?”

“Swimming.”

“I can see that.”

He laughed under his breath.

“Then watch.”

He pushed off. His movements changed completely once he started swimming.

There was no hesitation, no unnecessary movement. His strokes were smooth and controlled, his breathing steady. He moved through the water with the kind of ease that came from years of physical conditioning.

Xiaoran watched him reach the other end, then turn, then swim back.

When he reached her, he surfaced and pushed his wet hair away from his forehead.

“How was that?”

She stared. Yichen blinked. He rested his forearms on the edge.

“You’re very quiet.”

“I’m observing.”

“Observing what?”

“Your swimming technique.”

His mouth curved.

“Of course.”

She nodded solemnly.

“Very professional.”

He laughed. Then he noticed her eyes drifting down again.

This time, he didn’t bother pretending not to notice.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up.

“Yes?”

“Would you like to ask me something?”

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

He tilted his head.

“Then why are you staring?”

She was quiet for two seconds. Then said, seriously:

“Do you have to be so muscular?”

Yichen stopped. Then he laughed. A genuine, low laugh that made Xiaoran’s cheeks turn pink.

“What?”

She looked defensive.

“I’m asking a question.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re swimming.”

He glanced down at himself, then back at her.

“I should probably stop, then.”

“No!”

He raised an eyebrow. She immediately realised what she’d said.

“...I mean, you can continue. It’s good exercise.”

Yichen’s smile became more amused.

“Understood.”

The next few minutes were difficult for Xiaoran. Not because the swimming was difficult. Because Yichen had become aware of her attention. And he was enjoying it.

He continued demonstrating different strokes, occasionally swimming a length before returning to her. Every time he surfaced, he pushed his hair back and looked at her with an expression that was becoming increasingly suspicious.

Xiaoran eventually decided she needed to regain control of the situation. She moved closer.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

She held out her hand. He approached. She reached out and placed both hands on his shoulders. He looked down at her.

“What is it?”

She studied him. Then, with the utmost seriousness, asked:

“How many people have seen you like this?”

Yichen blinked.

“Like what?”

“Like this.”

He looked around the pool.

“People at the swimming facility?”

“Yes.”

“Quite a few, probably.”

She frowned.

“How many?”

“I haven’t counted.”

She gave him a suspicious look.

“Do they look at you?”

Yichen stared at her. Then his lips slowly curved.

“Sometimes.”

Xiaoran’s expression changed.

“Sometimes?”

He was clearly trying not to laugh.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Are you jealous?”

“No.”

“All right.”

He nodded. She continued holding his shoulders.

“I’m just asking.”

“Of course.”

“Because you’re very noticeable.”

He smiled.

“That’s unfortunate.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“Why?”

“Because I only came here to swim with you.”

She paused. Then her expression softened. Yichen lowered his head slightly.

“Does that help?”

She tried to maintain her serious expression.

“A little.”

He laughed.

“But you should probably stay near me.”

His eyebrows lifted.

“Should I?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

She looked him directly in the eyes.

“Because you’re mine.”

Yichen went still for half a second. Then he smiled. Not his usual teasing smile. Something warmer.

“Am I?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He leaned closer.

“Then I suppose I’d better stay where I belong.”

He kissed her, briefly. Xiaoran smiled, pleased with herself. Unfortunately, he wasn’t finished.

“And should I wear a sign?”

She blinked.

“What?”

“Something that says, ‘Reserved for Lin Xiaoran’?”

She looked at him, then splashed water at his chest.

“Don’t be ridiculous!”

He laughed and caught her hand. A little later, Yichen suggested they swim together.

He showed her how to coordinate her breathing and movements, staying beside her as she attempted a short distance. She was getting better. Not fast, but better.

When she reached the end, she held onto the edge and looked at him proudly.

“How was that?”

“Good.”

That made her grin.

“Am I talented?”

“Very.”

“Are you just saying that?”

“You’re making progress.”

She nodded, satisfied. Then Yichen pushed himself up slightly, resting his arms on the pool edge. Xiaoran looked at him.

Water ran down his shoulders and chest. His hair was wet and falling slightly over his forehead. She stared.

Then said, “I think I have another problem.”

He turned his head.

“What problem?”

She looked down at the water.

“I can’t concentrate.”

Yichen smiled.

“Why?”

She pointed vaguely at him.

“You.”

He laughed.

“Me?”

“Yes.”

“What am I doing?”

“Existing.”

His smile widened.

“That’s difficult to avoid.”

She sighed dramatically.

“I came here to learn swimming.”

“And you are learning.”

“But you’re distracting.”

“Would you like me to put a shirt on?”

She turned to him, then looked away.

“No.”

Yichen laughed and had to lower his head. She immediately splashed him again.

After swimming, they sat beside the pool for a while.

Xiaoran was wrapped in a large towel, her hair damp and slightly messy. Yichen sat beside her, drinking water. She had been unusually quiet. He glanced at her.

“Tired?”

“A little.”

“Want to rest before showering?”

She nodded. He placed his bottle down and reached for her hand. She leaned against his shoulder. They watched the water. Then Xiaoran spoke.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Can I tell you something?”

“Of course.”

“I think I understand why you like swimming.”

He met her eyes.

“Why?”

“It’s peaceful.”

He nodded.

“And?”

“And you look very good doing it.”

He laughed.

“I see.”

She tilted her head to look at him.

“Don’t you agree?”

“About what?”

“That you look good.”

He pretended to consider.

“I haven’t really examined myself.”

She gave him an incredulous look.

“You’re ridiculous.”

He smiled and kissed her temple.

“Thank you.”

She returned her attention to the pool. Then, after a moment, she said:

“Next time, can we come again?”

“Of course.”

“And maybe you can teach me more.”

“Certainly.”

Then added, “But I have one condition.”

Yichen looked at her.

“What?”

She reached over and took his hand.

“You have to stay close to me.”

Something in his face eased.

“I thought that was already the plan.”

“Good.”

She looked satisfied. Then she glanced down at his abdomen again. Yichen noticed. He leaned closer.

“Anything else?”

She looked up innocently.

“No.”

“Nothing?”

“No.”

He smiled slowly.

“You’re staring again.”

Xiaoran’s cheeks turned pink.

“You’re imagining things.”

He leaned back, looking entirely too pleased with himself.

“All right, sweetheart.”

She squinted at him.

“Stop smiling like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you know something.”

He took another sip of water.

“I do know something.”

“What?”

He turned to her.

“You like my abs.”

Xiaoran froze, then immediately pulled the towel higher around herself.

“Zhou Yichen!”

He laughed. She turned away, pretending to be offended.

But he could see the little smile she was trying to hide.

In the car park he took the ring out of her bag before she could ask and slid it back onto her finger.

On the way home, Xiaoran was scrolling through the pictures they had taken.

There were several photographs of the pool, a few selfies, and one picture of Yichen standing beside the water. She stopped at that one, then zoomed in. Yichen glanced over from the driver’s seat.

“What are you looking at?”

“Nothing.”

He looked at the screen.

“That’s a good picture.”

“Yes.”

A moment passed. Then she opened her messaging app. Yichen recognised Meilin’s name. He raised an eyebrow.

“Who are you sending it to?”

“Meilin.”

“Why?”

“She asked what I was doing today.”

He laughed under his breath.

“All right.”

Xiaoran typed something, then sent the picture. A few seconds later, Meilin replied.

Meilin: HELLO????

Meilin: IS THAT YICHEN???

Xiaoran grinned.

Xiaoran: Yes.

Meilin: WHY DOES HE LOOK LIKE THAT?

Xiaoran glanced at Yichen. Then typed:

Xiaoran: I know. Very distracting.

Meilin sent a string of laughing emojis.

Meilin: KEEP YOUR MAN.

Xiaoran laughed out loud. Yichen glanced at her.

“What?”

She turned the phone towards him. He read the messages, then looked at her.

“Keep my man?”

“Yes.”

He smiled.

“Should I be worried?”

“No.”

“Good.”

He reached over at a red light and squeezed her hand.

“Because I’m not planning on going anywhere.”

That made her grin. Then, after a moment, she said:

“Actually, Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Next time, I want to learn how to swim properly.”

“We’ll practice.”

“And I want to get stronger.”

“That’s a good goal.”

She nodded. Then looked at him with a small, mischievous smile.

“But I also want to come swimming with you because...”

She paused. He glanced at her.

“Because?”

She leaned closer.

“You’re very nice to look at.”

Yichen laughed.

“Is that the real reason?”

“One of the reasons.”

He shook his head, smiling.

“At least you’re honest.”

She settled back into her seat, pleased with herself.

And when they arrived home, she made one final declaration while unpacking her swimming bag.

“Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“I think we should swim every week.”

He held her gaze.

“Every week?”

“Yes.”

“That’s quite a commitment.”

She nodded seriously.

“For my health.”

“Of course.”

She put her towel away, then turned around.

“And for your abs.”

Yichen burst out laughing. Xiaoran grinned, completely unashamed.

chapters.desc: A night market, a row of game stalls, and a professional basketball player who misses three shots in a row.
chapters.title: The Plush Toy He Couldn’t Win for Her
chapters.epigraph: “Then I’ll teach you.”
chapters.content:
The night market had been Xiaoran’s idea. Naturally. Yichen had suggested a quiet dinner after his afternoon training, perhaps somewhere near the river. Xiaoran had agreed enthusiastically, only to send him a message twenty minutes later.

Xiaoran: Change of plan.

Yichen: What happened?

Xiaoran: There’s a night market nearby.

Yichen: All right.

Xiaoran: And there are games.

Yichen: I see.

Xiaoran: And prizes.

Yichen: Understood.

Xiaoran: I think we should go.

Yichen had looked at the messages, smiled, and replied.

Yichen: I’ll pick you up at seven.

Forty minutes later, he was standing beside her beneath a row of glowing red lanterns, holding two drinks while Xiaoran examined a stall filled with stuffed animals.

The night market was lively. Food stalls lined both sides of the street, filling the air with the smell of grilled meat, fried dumplings, sweet pancakes, and freshly made milk tea. Music played from a small stage farther down the road, while groups of friends and families wandered between stalls. Xiaoran was delighted.

She had already bought grilled squid, a little paper bag of candied fruit, and a cup of strawberry milk tea. Yichen had bought her everything she pointed at.

He was beginning to suspect that the evening would be expensive, although not in any way that concerned him.

“Yichen.”

He looked down.

“Hm?”

She pointed towards a game stall.

“Look.”

The stall had a row of colourful balloons attached to a board. Players were given darts and had to pop a certain number of balloons to win a prize. Yichen glanced at the display.

“Do you want to play?”

“Yes.”

“All right.”

She looked at the prizes. There were several small plush toys, keychains, and one large white rabbit sitting on the top shelf. Xiaoran pointed at it.

“That one.”

Yichen followed her finger.

“The rabbit?”

She nodded.

“It’s cute.”

“Do you want it?”

“Yes.”

He took out his wallet.

“Let’s try.”

She immediately caught his wrist.

“Wait.”

He met her eyes.

“We should compete.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Compete?”

“Yes. Whoever wins gets to choose what we do next.”

He considered this.

“And the loser?”

She smiled mischievously.

“Has to buy the winner a snack.”

Yichen laughed.

“All right.”

She held out her hand.

“Deal.”

He shook it.

“Deal.”

Xiaoran looked at him with great confidence. She had absolutely no idea what she was getting herself into. The first game was balloon darts. Xiaoran went first. She stood behind the line, holding three darts. The stall owner explained the rules.

“Pop at least five balloons to win the medium prize. Seven for the large one.”

Xiaoran nodded seriously.

“Understood.”

She raised her first dart. Threw. Missed. She blinked, then tried again. Missed.

Yichen stood beside her, holding her drink and watching. Xiaoran turned towards him.

“Don’t look at me.”

Something in his face eased.

“I’m not doing anything.”

“Your presence is distracting.”

He laughed. She took her final dart. Focused. Threw.

The dart hit the board, bounced off, and landed on the ground. Silence. Xiaoran stared. The stall owner gave her an encouraging smile.

“Would you like another round?”

She looked at Yichen. He was pressing his lips together.

“Don’t.”

He raised his free hand.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face did.”

He laughed.

“Would you like me to try?”

She handed him the darts.

“Fine. Show me.”

Yichen stepped behind the line. He examined the board, adjusted his grip, and threw. Pop. The first balloon burst. Xiaoran blinked. He threw again. Pop, then another. Pop. His fourth dart hit. His fifth dart hit.

By the seventh throw, he had won the large prize.

The stall owner smiled and handed him a small plush bear. Yichen accepted it, then looked at Xiaoran. She stared at him.

“...What?”

He held out the bear.

“Your prize.”

She looked at the toy, then at him.

“How did you do that?”

He shrugged.

“Just aim.”

She took the bear.

“That’s not an explanation.”

“Would you like me to teach you?”

“No.”

“All right.”

She hugged the bear against her chest, then looked towards the large white rabbit.

“That one is still cuter.”

Yichen followed her gaze.

“Then let’s try again.”

The second game was ring toss. Xiaoran was determined to win this one herself.

She stood in front of the counter, studying the bottles.

The rings were small, and the bottles were arranged at different distances. Yichen stood beside her.

“Which one do you want?”

She pointed to a little pink cat.

“That one.”

He nodded.

“All right.”

She took the rings. The first landed on the counter. The second bounced off a bottle. The third rolled away.

Xiaoran looked at the rings, then at the bottles, then at Yichen.

“These rings are defective.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Are they?”

“Yes.”

She handed them back to the stall owner.

“Can I try again?”

The owner laughed and gave her another set. Yichen watched her take a deep breath. She threw. Missed. She threw again. Missed.

Her final ring landed around the neck of a bottle, wobbled, and slipped off. Xiaoran stared at it. Yichen looked at the bottle, then at her.

“Almost.”

She turned towards him.

“Don’t say almost.”

He laughed.

“All right.”

He took the rings. Xiaoran folded her arms.

“Let’s see.”

Yichen tried once. The ring landed perfectly around the bottle. The stall owner looked impressed.

“Very good!”

Yichen tried again. Another ring landed. He won the little pink cat. Xiaoran stared at him in disbelief.

“Again?”

He turned towards her.

“What?”

“You’re good at everything!”

He laughed.

“Not everything.”

“Name one thing.”

He considered it.

“Winning you a pink cat, apparently.”

She took the toy from him.

“That’s not what I meant.”

“Then you’ll have to be more specific.”

She looked at the pink cat in her hands, then at him. A smile slowly appeared.

“Actually, you’re quite useful.”

“Thank you.”

She tucked the toy under her arm beside the bear. Yichen looked at the growing collection.

“Are we starting a zoo?”

“Maybe.”

By the third game, Xiaoran had become suspicious. The game involved throwing small beanbags into holes on a wooden board. Each hole had a different score, and the highest score won the largest prize. She studied the board, then turned to Yichen.

“You’re not allowed to play.”

He looked amused.

“Why?”

“Because you’re too good.”

He laughed.

“You haven’t even tried.”

“I’ve seen enough.”

She paid for her turn. Yichen stepped aside, still holding their drinks. Xiaoran threw the first beanbag. It landed in a low-scoring hole. She threw the second. It missed. The third bounced off the board.

She stared at the result, then took a breath.

“Fine.”

She threw the fourth. It landed in the highest-scoring hole. Her face brightened.

“YES!”

Yichen smiled.

“Good shot.”

She turned towards him, delighted.

“Did you see?”

“I did.”

“I got it!”

“Very impressive.”

She threw the fifth. Missed. The sixth. Missed. Her final throw landed in a middle-scoring hole.

She didn’t win the top prize, but the stall owner gave her a small yellow duck. Xiaoran accepted it proudly.

“Thank you.”

She turned to Yichen.

“See? I can win.”

He nodded solemnly.

“Of course.”

She held up the duck.

“Look at him.”

Yichen examined it.

“He’s cute.”

“His name is Dean.”

“Dean?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because he outranks Professor Quack.”

Yichen looked at the duck’s slightly crooked eyes, then at Xiaoran.

“Very intelligent.”

She smiled and tucked it into her bag. They continued walking.

Yichen bought grilled corn while Xiaoran inspected a stall selling handmade hair accessories.

She tried on a small white flower-shaped clip and turned towards him.

“Pretty,” he said.

Her mouth tipped up.

“Then I’ll buy it.”

He reached for his wallet. She stopped him.

“I can pay for this one.”

He turned to her.

“All right.”

She paid, then carefully placed the clip in her bag.

They walked a little farther until they reached another game stall. This one had a row of basketball hoops. Xiaoran stopped. Yichen glanced at the display, then at her.

“No.”

She turned.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You were looking at the basketballs.”

She smiled.

“You’re a basketball player.”

“Yes.”

“So you should win something.”

He laughed.

“That’s not how it works.”

She pointed at a large plush shark hanging above the counter.

“That one.”

Yichen looked at it, then at her.

“Do you want it?”

“Very much.”

He paid for a round. The stall owner handed him three basketballs. Xiaoran stood beside the counter, looking extremely confident.

“Easy.”

Yichen glanced at her. He smiled. He took the first ball. Shot. It bounced off the rim. Xiaoran blinked.

Yichen looked at the hoop, then at the ball. He picked up the second. Shot. It hit the backboard and rolled out. Xiaoran’s mouth slowly opened. Yichen took the third. Shot. The ball hit the rim and bounced away. There was a brief silence. Then Xiaoran burst out laughing. She bent forward, holding her stomach. Yichen looked at her.

“Enjoying yourself?”

She could barely speak.

“You’re... you’re a professional basketball player!”

He laughed.

“I noticed.”

“How did you miss all three?”

“The hoop is smaller than it looks.”

She laughed harder. Yichen took the balls back to the stall owner.

“Another round.”

Xiaoran immediately straightened.

“Wait. You’re trying again?”

He looked at her.

“Don’t you want the shark?”

She looked at the plush toy, then at him.

“...Yes.”

He paid again. This time, he adjusted his stance. He took the first ball. Shot. The ball went cleanly through the hoop. Xiaoran clapped.

“Yes!”

The second shot landed too. The third bounced off the rim, but he managed to win a medium prize.

The stall owner handed him a small blue shark. Xiaoran took it. She looked at the shark, then at Yichen.

“Not the big one.”

“Not the big one.”

She hugged the shark. Then looked up at him with a determined expression.

“We’re coming back.”

He laughed.

“Of course.”

The night market grew busier as the evening progressed.

They stopped for food, sharing a plate of dumplings and a bowl of noodles. Xiaoran had begun arranging her prizes on the table. The bear sat beside her drink. The pink cat was next to it. Dean the duck occupied the centre. The blue shark leaned against her bag. Yichen looked at the collection.

“You’re carrying quite a lot.”

“Yes.”

“Happy?”

She looked at the toys, then at him.

“Very.”

His mouth curved.

“Good.”

She picked up Dean.

“Although...”

He held her gaze.

“What?”

She turned the duck around.

“Dean is lonely.”

Yichen raised an eyebrow.

“Is he?”

“He needs a friend.”

Yichen glanced at the collection.

“Doesn’t he have four?”

“Those are acquaintances.”

He laughed.

“Of course.”

She put the duck down and looked towards the game stalls again. Her gaze stopped at the large white rabbit. It was still sitting on the top shelf.

Its ears were long, its fur looked incredibly soft, and it wore a tiny blue ribbon around its neck. Xiaoran stared at it. Yichen followed her gaze.

“Still that one?”

She nodded. He looked at the rabbit.

“Let’s go.”

She turned towards him.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She smiled and immediately stood up. The final game was a claw machine.

It stood at the edge of the market, beneath a row of colourful lights.

Inside were several plush toys, including the white rabbit.

Xiaoran approached the machine as if she had found her life’s purpose. Yichen stood beside her.

“Is this the one?”

“Yes.”

He examined the machine.

“Have you played before?”

“Of course.”

“Are you good?”

She met his eyes.

“Don’t ask unnecessary questions.”

He laughed. She inserted a coin. The claw moved. She adjusted the joystick.

“Left... a little more... no, too much.”

Yichen watched her concentrate. She pressed the button. The claw descended. It grabbed the rabbit by one ear. Xiaoran held her breath. The claw lifted. The rabbit slipped. It fell. She stared at the machine.

“No.”

Yichen smiled.

“Unlucky.”

She inserted another coin. This time, the claw caught the rabbit around its middle. It lifted. Moved towards the opening, then dropped it. Xiaoran closed her eyes.

“Why?”

Yichen looked at the machine.

“Perhaps the claw strength is low.”

She turned towards him.

“Don’t defend it.”

He laughed. She tried again. And again. And again.

The rabbit seemed to have developed a personal grudge against her. Every time she almost won, it slipped away. Yichen watched her expression become increasingly serious.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Maybe we should—”

“No.”

He stopped. She inserted another coin. That got a smile out of him.

“All right.”

Twenty minutes later, Yichen had bought them two more drinks. Xiaoran was still at the machine. Her brows were drawn together. Her lips were pressed into a thin line.

The white rabbit had moved slightly closer to the opening, but not enough. Yichen stood behind her, looking at the machine.

“How many attempts?”

She didn’t answer.

“Xiaoran?”

“Don’t count.”

He laughed. She pressed the button. The claw descended. It caught the rabbit. Lifted it. Moved. Dropped it. Xiaoran stared, then slowly turned towards him.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“I think this machine is cheating.”

He nodded.

“Possibly.”

“Do you think I should report it?”

He laughed.

“To whom?”

“Someone.”

He looked at her, then gently touched her shoulder.

“Do you really want that rabbit?”

“Yes.”

He smiled.

“Then let me try.”

She hesitated.

“Are you good at claw machines?”

“No.”

“Then—”

“Trust me.”

She turned to him. He took the joystick. He didn’t rush.

He studied the position of the rabbit, the shape of the claw, and the opening at the bottom. Xiaoran stood beside him, watching with intense concentration.

“More to the left.”

He adjusted it.

“Not too much.”

He adjusted it again.

“Yichen, I think—”

“One moment.”

He pressed the button. The claw descended. Caught the rabbit around its body. Lifted it. Xiaoran held her breath. The rabbit swayed slightly.

The claw moved towards the opening, then dropped it. The plush toy landed inside. Neither moved. Then Xiaoran let out a loud gasp.

“OH!”

She grabbed Yichen’s arm.

“YICHEN!”

He laughed as she rushed towards the prize opening. She reached inside and pulled out the rabbit.

The white rabbit was even softer than she had expected. She hugged it tightly, then turned around. Her eyes were shining.

“YOU GOT IT!”

Yichen laughed.

“I did.”

She ran towards him and threw her arms around his waist.

He caught her naturally, laughing as she hugged him.

“You got it! You got it!”

He wrapped his arms around her.

“Yes, I know.”

She leaned back to see him.

“You’re amazing!”

“Thank you.”

She held up the rabbit between them.

“Look!”

He examined it.

“Very cute.”

She nodded enthusiastically.

“Very!”

Then she looked at him again.

“How did you do that?”

He shrugged.

“Positioning.”

She stared.

“That’s your answer?”

“Yes.”

She squinted at him.

“You’re not allowed to be good at everything.”

He laughed. They eventually left the night market with more prizes than they had planned to carry. Yichen carried the food bags. Xiaoran carried the plush toys. Or at least, she tried.

The rabbit was quite large, and the other toys kept slipping from her arms.

Yichen watched her struggle, then held out his hand.

“Give me some.”

“No.”

“Xiaoran.”

“I can carry them.”

His mouth curved.

“You’re going to drop Dean.”

She looked down. Dean was indeed slipping. She immediately handed him the duck.

“Okay. Just Dean.”

Yichen took it. A few steps later, she handed him the pink cat, then the blue shark, then the bear.

Eventually, she was carrying only the large white rabbit. Yichen looked at the collection in his arms.

“Interesting.”

She smiled innocently.

“You’re stronger.”

He laughed.

“Convenient.”

She slipped her arm through his free one.

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

They walked towards the car, the night market lights glowing behind them. After a while, Xiaoran looked up.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Which prize is your favourite?”

He looked at the toys.

“Probably the rabbit.”

She brightened.

“Really?”

“Because you wanted it so badly.”

Her mouth tipped up, then hugged the rabbit closer.

“I like it too.”

He studied her.

“What’s its name?”

She thought about it.

“Maybe...”

She looked at the rabbit’s blue ribbon.

“Little Master.”

Yichen laughed.

“Little Master?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because he looks like he comes from a rich family.”

He looked at the rabbit, then at her.

“Interesting.”

“And Dean is his advisor.”

Yichen laughed again.

“What about the others?”

“The pink cat is his younger sister. The shark is his bodyguard. The bear is... His friend.”

Yichen looked at her.

“Quite a complicated family.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Very.”

When they reached home, Xiaoran arranged the toys on the sofa. Little Master sat in the middle. Dean was placed beside him.

The pink cat and bear were arranged on either side, while the blue shark was positioned slightly behind them. Yichen stood in the doorway, watching her work. She stepped back.

Examined the arrangement, then moved Dean a little to the left.

“Better.”

Yichen smiled.

“Are they settled?”

“Yes.”

He walked towards her and slipped his arms around her waist.

“Did you have fun?”

She leaned back against him.

“Very much.”

“Even though you lost most of the games?”

She turned her head.

“I did not lose most of the games.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“You didn’t?”

“I won Dean.”

“Yes.”

“And I nearly beat the ring toss.”

“Yes.”

“And I got the rabbit.”

“With my help.”

She turned around in his arms.

“That still counts.”

“Of course.”

She looked at him, then reached up and kissed his cheek.

“Thank you for tonight.”

He brushed his thumb against her waist.

“You’re welcome.”

She glanced at the toys.

“Actually, I think we should go to another night market next time.”

Yichen laughed.

“Another one?”

“Yes.”

“More games?”

“Yes.”

“More prizes?”

She nodded. Something in his face eased.

“All right.”

She looked pleased. “Next time, I want to win something myself,” she said, completely serious.

He lowered his head slightly.

“Then I’ll teach you.”

She considered that.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“Even if I take a long time?”

He laughed under his breath.

“We have time.”

Her expression softened. Then she reached up and kissed him properly. When she pulled away, he was smiling.

“Is that my reward?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

“For helping you win the rabbit?”

“For being my teammate.”

He considered her. Then glanced at the little collection on the sofa.

“Then I suppose we make a good team.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“The best.”

Yichen kissed her. And just before they went to bed, Xiaoran returned to the living room to adjust Little Master’s blue ribbon. Yichen watched her from the hallway.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up.

“What?”

“He’s already wearing it correctly.”

She frowned.

“I know. I just wanted to make sure.”

Yichen smiled.

“Goodnight, Manager Lin.”

She grinned.

“Goodnight.”

He turned towards the bedroom, then heard her voice again.

“Yichen?”

He looked back.

“Yes?”

“Do you think Little Master needs a girlfriend?”

Yichen stared at her, then laughed.

“Let’s discuss that tomorrow.”

chapters.desc: She has been stealing his shirts since December. Tonight it is the new dark blue one, and he reads the same paragraph four times.
chapters.title: His Shirt, Again
chapters.epigraph: “You look like you’re at home.”
chapters.content:
The first time Xiaoran wore one of Yichen’s shirts around the apartment, he hadn’t thought much of it. Well, that wasn’t entirely true. He had noticed.

It was his white shirt, off the back of the bedroom chair, on the December afternoon they never made it to the convenience store. She had kept it.

Then she had discovered that his other shirts were comfortable too, and three months later she took them whenever she pleased. Tonight was no different.

Yichen was in the living room, reviewing a document on his tablet after dinner. He heard the bedroom door open, followed by the familiar sound of Xiaoran walking across the wooden floor.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Do you know where my hair clip is?”

He looked up. And stopped. She was wearing his dark blue shirt.

This wasn’t the white one, or any of the older shirts he had already given up to her unofficial wardrobe. It was a relatively new shirt, one he had worn only twice. The sleeves were too long for her, so she had folded them twice. The collar sat loosely around her neck, and the first few buttons were undone because she had apparently decided that fastening them properly was unnecessary.

Her hair was still slightly damp, falling over one shoulder. She was looking at him expectantly. Yichen didn’t answer immediately. Xiaoran glanced down at herself.

“What?”

He blinked once.

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He set his tablet down.

“You’re wearing my shirt.”

She looked down again, as if this were new information.

“Oh. This one?”

“Yes.”

“It’s comfortable.”

“I see.”

She walked closer, still searching through the little basket of hair accessories she had brought from the bedroom.

“Have you seen my hair clip?”

“What colour?”

“White. The little flower one.”

He watched her search through the basket.

“On the dressing table.”

“I already looked there.”

“Then beside the mirror.”

She turned. Found it.

“Oh!”

She picked it up triumphantly, then turned back towards him.

“Thank you!”

Yichen nodded. She clipped her hair back, seemingly satisfied, and wandered towards the kitchen. He watched her go. Then he looked down at his tablet. He read the same sentence three times. It was becoming a problem.

Not because he disliked seeing her in his clothes. Quite the opposite. He liked it far more than he had any intention of admitting.

There was something about seeing Xiaoran in an ordinary piece of his wardrobe that affected him in a way he found difficult to explain. The shirt looked good on her, but it was the casualness of it that got him. The fact that she wore it without thinking.

She wasn’t dressing up for him. She wasn’t trying to get his attention.

She was wandering around their home, wearing his shirt, looking for her hair clip. And somehow that was worse.

A few minutes later, she returned with a glass of water.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Can you help me with something?”

He looked up.

“What is it?”

She held out her phone.

“Look at this dress. Do you think I should buy it?”

He took the phone. The dress was pale yellow, with a delicate neckline and a slightly fitted waist.

“It’s pretty.”

“Right? But I’m not sure about the colour.”

“I think it would suit you.”

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She leaned over his shoulder to look at the picture again.

“Maybe I should get it in blue instead.”

Yichen glanced at the screen, then at her. She was standing close enough that her shoulder brushed his. The loose collar of his shirt shifted slightly as she leaned forward, and a few strands of damp hair slipped against his arm. He looked back at the dress.

“Either colour.”

Xiaoran frowned.

“That’s not helpful.”

She took her phone back and scrolled through the other colours.

“What about this one?”

He looked.

“Pretty.”

“And this?”

“Also pretty.”

She lowered her phone.

“You’re not paying attention.”

Yichen looked at her.

“I am.”

“Then tell me which one you like best.”

He held her gaze. Then he said, calmly, “The one you’re wearing.”

Xiaoran blinked. She looked down at her shirt, then back at him.

“This?”

“Yes.”

“It’s not even mine.”

“I know.”

She smiled, amused.

“You’re so strange.”

He reached for her hand. He reached for her. She stepped closer.

Yichen drew her gently between his knees, where he was sitting on the sofa. His hands settled at her waist, and he looked up at her. Xiaoran’s smile became curious.

“You’re doing that again. Looking at me like you have something to say.”

He considered her. Then he asked, “Do you know why I keep looking at you?”

She smiled.

“Because I stole your shirt?”

“That’s one reason.”

Her eyebrows lifted.

“One?”

“Would you like the full explanation?”

Xiaoran laughed.

“Yes. Please enlighten me.”

Yichen’s thumbs moved lightly against her waist.

“First, that’s my shirt.”

“I know.”

“You’ve rolled the sleeves unevenly.”

She looked at her arms.

“They’re fine.”

“The left one is higher.”

“Nobody cares.”

“I do.”

She laughed and tried to pull her arm away, but he kept her close.

“Second,” he said, “you’ve left three buttons undone.”

Xiaoran glanced down.

“Because it’s more comfortable.”

“I know.”

“And?”

“And I find it distracting.”

Her laughter softened. Yichen’s expression was calm, but there was something unmistakably different in his eyes now. He wasn’t making an exaggerated effort to tease her. He was telling her something he had apparently been keeping to himself. She tilted her head.

“How distracting?”

He looked at her for a second.

“Enough that I’ve read the same paragraph four times.”

Xiaoran’s lips parted, then a smile slowly spread across her face.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She looked towards his tablet.

“Because of me?”

“Who else?”

She giggled.

“You’re exaggerating.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re a professional basketball player. You can concentrate under pressure.”

“On a basketball court.”

“So?”

“So this is a different situation.”

She laughed harder. Yichen watched her, his expression softening.

He liked that laugh. He liked how quickly her amusement appeared, how her eyes narrowed slightly when she was trying not to laugh too much, and how she sometimes looked at him.

He lifted one hand and tucked her hair behind her ear.

“Third,” he said.

Xiaoran immediately looked at him.

“There’s a third?”

“Yes.”

“What is it?”

He paused. Then his gaze moved over her face, lingering before returning to her eyes.

“You look comfortable.”

She blinked. Yichen’s voice was quieter now.

“You wear my clothes like you’ve always belonged in them. You walk around the apartment, make yourself a drink, complain about work, ask me where your things are. You don’t even think about it.”

Xiaoran’s smile gradually faded into something gentler. He brushed his thumb along her side.

“I like seeing you like that.”

She didn’t say anything. Then she looked down at the shirt again.

“I didn’t know you liked it so much.”

“I thought that was obvious.”

“No, it wasn’t.”

“I’ve been looking at you all evening.”

“Maybe I thought you were looking at my hair.”

“Your hair?”

She nodded.

“Because it’s wet.”

Yichen stared at her. Then he laughed.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“How did you arrive at that conclusion?”

She giggled embarrassed.

“I don’t know!”

He gently pulled her closer.

“Over here.”

“I’m already here.”

“Closer.”

She leaned forward, placing her hands on his shoulders.

Yichen looked up at her, and the corner of his mouth lifted.

“Do you know what else?”

She shook her head.

“I think you should stop borrowing my shirts.”

Her eyes widened.

“What?”

“They’re becoming difficult to keep in the wardrobe,” he said, once he’d let her react.

Xiaoran’s expression immediately changed. She looked offended.

“Why?”

“Because you keep taking them.”

“That’s not a reason!”

“I have fewer shirts than I used to.”

“You have so many!”

“Apparently not enough.”

She folded her arms.

“Fine. I’ll stop.”

Yichen’s eyebrows lifted.

“Will you?”

“Yes.”

“All right.”

He released her waist. Xiaoran stared at him. He picked up his tablet again. She waited. He returned to his document. Her eyes narrowed. That wasn’t how this was supposed to go.

“Zhou Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You really want me to stop?”

He looked up. A faint smile appeared.

“Do you want me to say no?”

She pressed her lips together. He put the tablet aside again.

“Xiaoran, you can wear whatever you like. My shirts included.”

“Then why did you say that?”

“Because I thought you might want to know what happens when you wear them.”

She blinked at him.

“What happens?”

He reached out, catching her hand and drawing her closer again.

“I lose a considerable amount of concentration.”

She laughed, her cheeks turning pink.

“That’s your problem.”

“Apparently.”

“You should learn to control yourself.”

“I’ve been trying.”

His answer was so immediate that she stopped laughing. Yichen looked at her. Then his smile turned a little more pronounced.

“Would you like me to demonstrate?”

Xiaoran’s eyes widened.

“Demonstrate what?”

“How much concentration I have left.”

She gave a small, suspicious laugh.

“You’re not going to do anything.”

“Am I?”

He gently drew her down until she was standing close against him, her hands resting on his shoulders. Then he kissed her.

It began, his hand resting at her waist while hers slipped into his hair. Xiaoran had expected a quick kiss, perhaps followed by another teasing remark, but Yichen lingered. He kissed her again when she smiled against his lips, and she found herself forgetting the dress on her phone and the hair clip she had spent several minutes searching for.

When he finally pulled back, she was still leaning towards him. He brushed his thumb against her cheek.

“Still think I’m exaggerating?”

Xiaoran looked at him. Her cheeks were warm.

“...Maybe a little.”

Yichen smiled.

“All right.”

She remained between his knees, looking down at him. Then she grinned.

“Actually, I think I understand now.”

“Understand what?”

“Why you like me wearing your shirts.”

She leaned down and whispered, “Because I look like your girlfriend.”

Yichen’s expression softened.

“That’s not quite it.”

“Then what?”

He looked at her before answering.

“You look like you’re at home.”

Her smile became smaller. More genuine. Yichen reached up and kissed her cheek.

“And I like that.”

Xiaoran stood there for another moment, then bent down to wrap her arms around his neck.

He held her, his cheek resting against her shoulder.

After a while, she murmured, “Can I keep this one?”

He glanced at the dark blue shirt she was wearing.

“You’ve already claimed it.”

“So that’s a yes?”

“Yes.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Good. I like this one.”

“I noticed.”

She pulled back slightly.

“Should I wear another one tomorrow?”

Yichen looked at her. He could have said no.

He could have reminded her that he had work to do, training footage to review, and a perfectly reasonable intention to spend the evening concentrating.

Instead, he brushed his fingers along the loose collar of the shirt.

“That’s up to you.”

Xiaoran narrowed her eyes.

“You’re hoping I will.”

He gave her that slow, unmistakably amused smile.

“I wouldn’t complain.”

She laughed, then kissed his cheek.

“Then I’ll borrow another one.”

“Of course.”

“And maybe the white one.”

“All right.”

“The grey one too.”

He met her eyes.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“At this rate, I’ll have to start borrowing your clothes.”

She burst into laughter.

“You’re too big for my clothes!”

“Then I suppose I’ll have to buy more.”

She kissed him again, delighted. Yichen let her, his hand settling at her waist.

A few minutes later, she finally wandered towards the bedroom to put her phone away. Yichen picked up his tablet.

He looked at the document, then at the bedroom doorway.

He could still hear her humming as she moved around, completely unaware that she had just ruined his plans for a productive evening.

He smiled to himself and added two shirts to the basket on his phone, both in his size.

chapters.desc: A weekend in Suzhou, an umbrella he holds too far towards her, and every puddle in the old town.
chapters.title: A Rainy Night in Suzhou
chapters.epigraph: “Then we’ll come again when it rains.”
chapters.content:
The rain began just as they reached the old town, on the first evening of their weekend in Suzhou.

Xiaoran stood beneath the entrance of a small riverside street, looking at the sudden curtain of water falling from the sky.

A moment ago, the weather had been perfectly pleasant. The sky was cloudy, but nothing concerning. They had even debated whether to bring an umbrella when leaving the hotel. Yichen had brought one. Xiaoran had said it was unnecessary.

Now, she was looking at the rain with the expression of someone who had just been personally betrayed by the weather.

“Well.”

Yichen opened the umbrella.

“Well?”

She turned towards him.

“I think the weather forecast lied.”

He glanced at the rain.

“It said there would be showers.”

“Yes, but I thought it meant small showers. Like a little drizzle. Something romantic.”

He looked at the heavy rain hitting the stone pavement.

“Very romantic.”

“Don’t be sarcastic.”

He smiled and held the umbrella over her.

“Come on.”

They stepped onto the narrow stone walkway. Suzhou looked different in the rain.

The white walls and dark tiled roofs seemed softer beneath the grey sky. Water streamed from the curved edges of traditional rooftops, while red lanterns glowed warmly along the narrow streets. The canals reflected the lights of restaurants and old buildings, their surfaces constantly disturbed by raindrops. There were fewer people outside now.

The occasional passerby hurried beneath umbrellas, and the smell of rain mixed with the fragrance of freshly cooked food drifting from nearby restaurants. Xiaoran loved it. She walked slowly, looking at everything.

“Yichen, look.”

He followed her gaze. A small wooden boat was moving along the canal.

“Pretty.”

“Very pretty.”

She looked at the reflections in the water, then at the old bridge ahead.

“Can we go there?”

“Of course.”

She took his hand. And then, without warning, stepped directly into a puddle. Splash. Yichen looked down. Xiaoran looked down too. Neither spoke. Then she lifted her foot.

“...Oh.”

He glanced at her shoes.

“Careful.”

“I didn’t see it.”

“Apparently.”

She met his eyes.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

His expression suggested otherwise. She continued walking. Three minutes later, she stepped into another puddle.

This time, Yichen stopped before she could take the next step.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Look down.”

She looked. There was a puddle directly in front of her. She stepped around it.

“See? I can do it.”

“Excellent.”

She gave him a satisfied smile. Then she stepped into a third puddle. Yichen closed his eyes. Xiaoran burst out laughing. The umbrella wasn’t small.

It wasn’t designed to accommodate Xiaoran’s habit of walking wherever she wanted while Yichen tried to keep both of them dry.

She wandered towards the edge of the walkway to look at a shop window. Then she stopped to admire a lantern.

Then she moved closer to the canal to watch the boats. Every time she moved, Yichen adjusted the umbrella. At first, he managed. Eventually, the rain began reaching his shoulder.

Xiaoran noticed when they passed beneath a row of old buildings.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Your shoulder is wet.”

He glanced down.

“A little.”

She frowned.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“You were looking at the shops.”

She looked at the umbrella, then at him.

“You’re holding it too far towards me.”

He raised an eyebrow. She reached up and tried to adjust his hand. The umbrella shifted. A few drops landed on her hair. She gasped. Yichen laughed.

“Careful.”

“You’re making it worse!”

He took her hand away from the umbrella handle.

“Let me.”

She looked at his shoulder again.

“You’re going to get wet.”

“I’m fine.”

“That’s not fair.”

He looked down at her.

“What’s not fair?”

“You always do this.”

“Do what?”

“Give me all the dry space.”

He smiled.

“You’re smaller.”

“That doesn’t mean I don’t get wet.”

He glanced at her damp hair.

“You’re already getting wet.”

She looked offended.

“That’s because of the rain.”

“I see.”

She folded her arms. He laughed, then moved the umbrella closer to the middle.

“There. Better?”

She looked up.

“Yes.”

He held out his free hand. He crooked a finger at her. She stepped closer.

He placed his arm around her shoulders, drawing her against his side. The umbrella seemed much more effective. Xiaoran looked up at him.

“Oh.”

“Comfortable?”

“Very.”

They stopped at a small shop selling traditional Suzhou pastries. Xiaoran immediately became interested.

The shop was warm and brightly lit, with glass displays filled with delicate pastries, small cakes, and local sweets.

She stood in front of the counter, examining everything.

“What’s that one?”

Yichen followed her gaze.

“Which?”

“That little white one.”

He looked at the display.

“Do you want to try it?”

She nodded.

“And that one.”

“All right.”

“And maybe the green one.”

He met her eyes.

“Are you hungry?”

She considered the question.

“Not particularly.”

Something in his face eased.

“Then why are we buying three?”

“Because we’re in Suzhou.”

“Reasonable.”

She turned towards him with a pleased expression. He ordered several pastries, and they found a small table near the window. Outside, the rain continued.

Xiaoran took a bite of one pastry and immediately looked delighted.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“This is good.”

He took a bite from the piece she offered.

“Not bad.”

“Not bad?”

“Very good.”

“Better.”

She broke off another small piece and held it towards him. He leaned forward and took it.

Then she noticed a little bit of pastry filling near the corner of his mouth.

“Wait.”

He paused. She reached over and brushed it away with her thumb.

“You’re messy.”

He turned to her. She wiped her thumb with a napkin. Yichen watched her. Then he leaned closer and kissed her cheek. She blinked.

“What was that for?”

“Thank you.”

“For cleaning your face?”

“Yes.”

She laughed.

“You’re welcome.”

By the time they left the pastry shop, the rain had become heavier.

The street lamps had come on, and the old town was glowing against the darkening sky. They walked along the canal, sharing the umbrella. Xiaoran had become unusually quiet. Yichen glanced down.

“Tired?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Cold?”

“A little.”

He tightened his arm around her shoulders.

“Better?”

She nodded. They walked past a small bridge where several red lanterns hung above the canal. Xiaoran stopped.

“Can we take a picture?”

Yichen looked at the bridge.

“Here?”

She nodded. He passed the umbrella to her and took out his phone.

“Stand there.”

She moved beneath the lanterns. The rain was falling behind her, the warm lights reflecting in the water. Her hair had become slightly damp, and she was holding the umbrella with both hands. Yichen raised his phone.

“Look here.”

That made her grin. He took a photograph, then another.

“One more.”

She tilted her head.

“Like this?”

“Yes.”

He took another. She immediately walked towards him.

“Let me see.”

He showed her the photographs. Her eyes brightened.

“Oh, I love this one!”

She pointed at the second picture. Yichen looked at it.

She was smiling naturally, with the lanterns behind her and the canal reflected in the background.

“Good.”

“Can you send it to me?”

“I’ll send all of them.”

She turned to him.

“You’re so useful.”

He laughed.

“Thank you.”

She took his phone and held it up.

“Now one of you.”

He stood beside her. She adjusted the angle, making sure the lanterns were visible.

“Come closer.”

He moved closer.

“Closer.”

He put his arm around her waist. She smiled.

“Good.”

Just before she took the photograph, Yichen turned his face towards her. She looked at him instead of the camera.

The picture captured both of them smiling at each other beneath the umbrella. Xiaoran looked at it. Then her expression softened.

“I like this one more.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re looking at me.”

He glanced at the picture, then at her.

“Then keep it.”

They continued walking until they reached a quieter stretch of the canal.

The shops were beginning to close, and the sound of rain had become more noticeable.

Xiaoran was still looking around when Yichen felt her hand slip slightly in his. He looked down.

She was walking with her attention fixed on a small wooden boat passing beneath the bridge.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“Watch your step.”

She looked down. There was another puddle. She stepped around it carefully. Yichen smiled.

“Progress.”

She gave him a proud look.

“I’ve learned.”

Then she turned to look at a shop on the opposite side of the street and stepped directly into the edge of a much larger puddle. Splash. She stopped.

Yichen looked at her shoes, then at her face. She slowly turned towards him.

“...Don’t.”

He pressed his lips together. She narrowed her eyes.

“Don’t you dare.”

His shoulders moved. He was laughing.

“Yichen!”

“I’m sorry.”

“You’re not sorry!”

He laughed harder. She turned away dramatically.

“Fine. I’ll walk by myself.”

He caught her hand before she could take another step. He held out his hand. She looked back.

He lifted his arm slightly, opening the space beside him.

“Under here.”

She hesitated for half a second, then moved closer.

He wrapped his arm around her shoulders, pulling her snugly against his side.

“Now stay here.”

She looked up at him.

“Why?”

“Because apparently, you can’t walk without finding every puddle in Suzhou.”

She laughed.

“I don’t do it on purpose!”

“I know.”

He adjusted the umbrella above them.

“And because it’s raining.”

She slipped her arm around his waist.

“Then you should hold me tighter.”

He looked down.

“Like this?”

He drew her closer until her cheek rested against his shoulder. That made her grin.

“Yes.”

They continued along the canal like that. The umbrella was now almost unnecessary between them. His arm sheltered her from the rain, while she stayed tucked against his side, occasionally looking up at the old buildings and lanterns. After a while, she spoke.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Do you like Suzhou?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He looked ahead.

“It’s peaceful.”

“Me too.”

A few steps later, she said, “I think I like rainy Suzhou more.”

He glanced down at her. She laughed.

“Interesting.”

She lifted her face.

“Because I get to walk like this.”

He held her gaze. Then his expression softened. He bent his head and kissed her hair.

“Then we’ll come again when it rains.”

Her mouth tipped up. When they finally returned to the hotel, Xiaoran’s shoes were damp, the ends of her hair were slightly wet, and Yichen’s right shoulder was noticeably darker from the rain. She noticed immediately.

“Look at your shirt.”

He glanced down.

“It’s fine.”

“No, it’s wet.”

“A little.”

She looked guilty.

“Because of me.”

He took the umbrella from her and closed it.

“Because of the rain.”

“But—”

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up. He reached over and gently tucked a damp strand of hair behind her ear.

“I had a good evening.”

She blinked.

“Really?”

“Very good.”

She smiled. Then she looked down at their shoes.

“Although I think I should stop stepping into puddles.”

Yichen laughed.

“That would be a good start.”

She hit his arm lightly. He caught her hand and brought it to his lips.

“Come on. Let’s get you warm.”

Later, after showering and changing into comfortable clothes, they sat together near the hotel window. The rain was still falling outside.

Xiaoran was wearing Yichen’s shirt, her legs tucked beneath a blanket. Yichen sat beside her with one arm along the back of the sofa.

She was scrolling through the photographs from the evening.

“Look at this one.”

He leaned closer. It was the photograph beneath the lanterns. She enlarged it.

“Look at your shoulder. It’s completely wet.”

He glanced at the photograph.

“Yes.”

“And my hair.”

“A little.”

She held his gaze.

“You should have told me earlier.”

“You would have worried.”

“Of course I would.”

“I know.”

She leaned into his shoulder. She showed him the photograph of them looking at each other.

“This is my favourite.”

He looked at it.

“Mine too.”

Her mouth tipped up. Then she opened the camera and took a photograph of their hands resting together beneath the blanket. She posted it with a simple caption.

Rainy evening in Suzhou. Slightly wet shoes, too many puddles, and the best company.

Yichen read it over her shoulder.
