“Too many puddles?”

“Many.”

He smiled and kissed her temple.

“Next time, I’ll bring a bigger umbrella.”

She looked up.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

She thought about it, then shook her head.

“No.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“No?”

She nestled closer against him.

“This one is fine.”

He looked down at her. She couldn’t help smiling.

“I like having to stand close.”

“Is that so?”

She nodded. He leaned down, his voice quiet.

“Then perhaps I should keep bringing the small one.”

Xiaoran immediately blushed.

“You’re doing that on purpose again. Being smug.”

He laughed and pulled her closer, and outside the rain kept falling on the lake.

chapters.desc: The morning after the rain, she wakes before him and has breakfast set out on the balcony over the lake.
chapters.title: The Hotel Breakfast Date
chapters.epigraph: “I wanted to have breakfast with you without needing to go anywhere afterward.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Xiaoran noticed when she woke up was that the bed was too comfortable.

The second thing was that Yichen’s arm was heavy across her waist. She opened her eyes slowly.

The hotel room was still dim, curtains drawn almost completely, with only a thin line of morning light slipping through the gap. The city outside was beginning to wake, but the room remained quiet, cool, and wonderfully peaceful. Yichen was sleeping beside her.

He was lying on his back, one arm resting above his head, the other draped over her. His hair was slightly messy, and the blanket had slipped down to his waist. Xiaoran watched him.

He looked different when he was asleep. Not dramatically different, but softer. The usual alertness in his eyes was gone, his expression relaxed, his breathing slow and even. She smiled. Then she remembered something. Breakfast.

Her eyes moved towards the bedside clock. It wasn’t even seven.

She had specifically asked the hotel concierge the previous evening about private in-room breakfast arrangements. She had even spent fifteen minutes looking through the breakfast menu, comparing dishes and deciding what Yichen might like. She had wanted to surprise him. Carefully, she lifted his arm from her waist. He stirred.

“Where are you going?”

Xiaoran froze. His eyes were still closed.

“Nowhere.”

His hand found her waist again.

“Mm.”

She waited. A few seconds later, his breathing settled. She gently removed his arm once more. This time, she succeeded.

She slipped out of bed, collected her phone and the hotel room-service menu, and tiptoed towards the balcony. Before closing the bedroom door, she looked back. Yichen hadn’t moved. She smiled to herself. Operation breakfast was officially underway.

Their room was a corner suite above the lake on the modern side of Suzhou.

The bedroom opened into a spacious living area, and beyond that was a private balcony with a small dining table. From there, the skyline stretched across the horizon, with the lake reflecting the pale morning light.

Xiaoran had noticed it immediately when they checked in the afternoon before, while the sky was still dry.

She had even told Yichen that the balcony was her favourite part of the room.

He had replied that he thought the view was nice too.

She suspected he hadn’t understood how much she liked it.

Now, she was determined to make use of it. She called room service.

“Good morning. I’d like to order breakfast for two, please.”

The staff member greeted her warmly and asked what she would like. Xiaoran opened the menu.

“Could I have the eggs Benedict, a fruit platter, and the French toast? And the smoked salmon platter. Actually, could I have the pancakes too?”

The staff member confirmed.

“And coffee?”

“One black coffee, please. And one iced latte.”

She glanced towards the bedroom.

“Could you make the latte less sweet?”

After confirming the order, she added one final request.

“Would it be possible to arrange everything on the balcony? The weather looks nice this morning.”

The staff member assured her they could. Xiaoran thanked them and ended the call. Then she looked at the order summary. It was quite a lot of food. She considered it, then decided it was fine. They were on holiday.

There was no reason to be sensible about breakfast.

When Yichen finally woke up, the first thing he noticed was the empty space beside him. He opened his eyes. It was past seven.

He sat up, ran a hand through his hair, and looked towards the bathroom. Empty.

Then he noticed the bedroom door was slightly open.

He could hear a faint sound from the living area. A voice. His girlfriend was talking to someone.

He got out of bed, pulled on the hotel robe, and walked towards the sound. When he reached the living area, he stopped.

Xiaoran was standing near the balcony, arranging something on the table.

She had changed into a soft cream-coloured dress, her hair loosely tied back. There were two glasses on the table, a small vase of flowers, and a few plates already being arranged by the hotel staff.

She was speaking to one of the staff members.

“Thank you so much. It looks lovely.”

The staff member smiled and left. Xiaoran turned around. And saw him. Her face brightened.

“You’re awake!”

Yichen leaned against the doorway.

“Apparently.”

She looked him up and down.

“Why are you wearing the robe?”

He raised an eyebrow.

“I was sleeping.”

“Right.”

He glanced at the balcony, then at the table, then back at her.

“What’s all this?”

She clasped her hands behind her back.

“Breakfast.”

“I can see that.”

“Surprise.”

He looked at the arrangement again. The table was set for two, with breakfast dishes, fresh juice, coffee, and a little vase of flowers in the middle. The balcony doors were open, letting in the cool morning air.

Beyond it, the city was bathed in soft golden light. Yichen’s expression softened.

“You arranged all this?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“Earlier.”

“What time?”

“Not important.”

He looked at the clock.

“Xiaoran.”

“Six something.”

“You woke up at six?”

“Six thirty.”

He gave her a look.

“Why?”

She shrugged.

“I wanted to.”

He walked towards her. He opened his arms. She stepped closer.

He placed one hand at her waist and kissed her, briefly.

“Good morning.”

That made her grin.

“Good morning.”

Then he kissed her cheek.

“Thank you.”

She looked pleased.

“Do you like it?”

He glanced at the table, then at the view, then back at her.

“I do.”

“Really?”

“Very much.”

She grinned.

“Good. Because I ordered too much food.”

He laughed. They sat down to breakfast. Xiaoran had chosen the seat facing the city, while Yichen sat opposite her. For a while, neither spoke much. The morning was beautiful.

The city was still relatively quiet, the sunlight gradually brightening the buildings in the distance. A few boats moved across the lake, and the breeze carried the faint sounds of traffic from far below. Xiaoran poured coffee into his cup.

“Here.”

“Thank you.”

She passed him the eggs Benedict. He looked at the spread.

“How many people are we feeding?”

“Two.”

“Are you sure?”

She nodded.

“We can finish it.”

He looked at the French toast, pancakes, fruit, salmon, and eggs.

“Very confident.”

She picked up a strawberry.

“We’re on holiday.”

“That’s your justification?”

“Yes.”

He smiled and took a sip of coffee. It was exactly how he liked it. Black, no sugar. He met her eyes.

“You remembered.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Of course.”

He didn’t say anything more, but his eyes stayed on her. She noticed.

“Why are you looking at me?”

“Can’t I?”

She smiled.

“You can.”

He reached across the table and brushed his thumb over her knuckles.

“Thank you for arranging this.”

She tilted her head.

“It’s just breakfast.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you thanking me so seriously?”

“Because you woke up early to do it.”

She smiled a little shy.

“I wanted to surprise you.”

“You did.”

She looked satisfied. Then she pointed at his plate.

“Eat your eggs before they get cold.”

He laughed.

“Yes, Manager Lin.”

After breakfast, Xiaoran decided that they should take photographs. Naturally.

She took several pictures of the table, the flowers, the view, and her coffee. Then she took a photograph of Yichen.

He was leaning back in his chair, one hand around his coffee cup, looking towards the skyline. The morning light fell across his face. She took the picture, then another. Yichen turned his head.

“How many are you taking?”

“Not many.”

He looked at her phone.

“That’s at least six.”

“You’re handsome.”

He laughed.

“Is that the reason?”

“Yes.”

She looked at the photographs, then smiled.

“I like this one.”

He held out his hand.

“Let me see.”

She passed him the phone. He looked at the picture.

It was a candid photograph. He hadn’t been looking at the camera, and his expression was relaxed. He turned to her.

“Not bad.”

“Not bad?”

“Good.”

She eyed him.

“You’re supposed to say it’s beautiful.”

He looked at the photograph again, then back at her.

“It’s beautiful.”

That made her grin.

“Better.”

He handed her the phone.

“Take one with me.”

She stood up immediately.

“Okay!”

Yichen pulled out the chair beside him.

“Sit here.”

She walked around the table and sat beside him.

He slipped an arm around her waist, drawing her closer. She raised the phone.

“Look at the camera.”

He did. Her mouth tipped up.

“Again.”

“Why?”

“This one isn’t good.”

He glanced at the screen.

“You look fine.”

“I want another.”

He leaned closer, pressing his cheek against hers.

“Like this?”

She smiled.

“Yes.”

She took the photograph. Then, just as she lowered the phone, Yichen turned and kissed her cheek. She laughed.

“Wait!”

He kissed the other cheek.

“Yichen!”

“What?”

“I’m trying to take pictures!”

“Then take another.”

She looked at him. He was smiling. That particular slow, amused smile that always made her forget what she had been trying to say. She gave him a suspicious look.

“You’re doing it on purpose. That face.”

He leaned closer.

“Which face?”

She looked away.

“Never mind.”

His smile deepened.

“All right.”

She immediately turned back.

“Don’t smile like that!”

He laughed and pressed a kiss into her hair. They didn’t leave the balcony immediately. Instead, they moved their chairs closer together.

Xiaoran tucked herself against his shoulder, holding a glass of juice while Yichen looked through the photographs on her phone. He paused at one particular picture. It was a photograph of her.

She was sitting across the table, looking towards the city, with one hand resting beside her coffee cup. She hadn’t noticed him taking it. He looked at it for a while.

“What’s this?”

She glanced at the screen.

“Oh.”

He tilted the phone slightly.

“When did you take it?”

“When you were looking at the view.”

He looked at the photograph again.

“You look happy.”

“I was.”

“Good.”

She watched him.

Then asked, “Do you want to know why I planned this?”

He put the phone down.

“Tell me.”

She played with the edge of her glass.

“Because we always have breakfast together, but usually it’s just before work. Sometimes we’re rushing. Sometimes you’re checking your training schedule, and I’m checking my emails.”

Yichen listened.

“And even when we’re having breakfast at home, one of us usually has something to do afterward.”

She looked towards the skyline.

“I wanted to have breakfast with you without needing to go anywhere afterward.”

He was quiet. Then his hand found hers.

“That’s a good reason.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“I thought so.”

He brought her hand to his lips and kissed her knuckles.

“Then let’s stay here a little longer.”

She turned towards him.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

“But don’t you want to go sightseeing?”

“We can go later.”

“Or shopping?”

“Later.”

“Or explore the hotel?”

That got a smile out of him.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“I’m sitting with you. I’m not in a hurry.”

She met his eyes. Then her smile softened.

“Okay.”

Eventually, the breakfast dishes were cleared. The flowers remained on the table.

Xiaoran was reluctant to leave the balcony, so Yichen suggested they take a walk around the hotel grounds before going out.

She agreed, but only after insisting that they take one more photograph.

This time, she stood in front of the balcony doors while Yichen held the phone.

She was still adjusting her dress when he took the first one. She walked towards him.

“Give me the phone.”

He raised it slightly. He reached for her. She stopped in front of him. He took one last photograph. Then he lowered the phone.

“Beautiful.”

She smiled.

“Thank you.”

He put the phone down and drew her closer by the waist.

“Although I think I prefer this.”

“Which?”

He kissed her. She smiled against his lips. When he pulled away, she looked at him with a little surprise.

“What was that for?”

“For breakfast.”

She laughed.

“That’s a very generous tip.”

“I thought so.”

Later that afternoon, Xiaoran posted three photographs. The first was the breakfast spread overlooking the city. The second was Yichen holding a coffee cup, looking out at the skyline.

The third was a photograph of them together, her cheek pressed against his. Her caption was simple.

An early morning, a slow breakfast, and my favourite view.

Yichen saw the post while they were waiting for the elevator. He looked at her phone.

“Your favourite view?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He looked towards the elevator doors, then back at her.

“Which one?”

She gave him an innocent look.

“The city, obviously.”

“Obviously.”

The elevator doors opened. She walked inside, still smiling.

Just before the doors closed, Yichen caught her hand and pulled her gently towards him.

“Although,” he said, lowering his voice, “I think I know which view you meant.”

Xiaoran looked up. His expression was calm, but the corner of his mouth had lifted. She immediately blushed.

“Zhou Yichen.”

He laughed and kissed her temple.

“What?”

“You’re getting too confident.”

He slipped his hand into hers.

“Come on. Let’s go.”

Xiaoran was already planning the next breakfast before the elevator reached the lobby.

chapters.desc: The rain has gone. On their second day in Suzhou the gardens open early, and she has her camera.
chapters.title: Suzhou, the Second Day
chapters.epigraph: “But I like seeing what you remember.”
chapters.content:
The rain had gone by the time they came down from breakfast. Overnight it had rinsed the whole of Suzhou and left, and what it left behind was real spring sunshine, wide and warm, lying across the hotel lobby in gold patches and turning the wet pavement outside into glass.

Lin Xiaoran stopped at the revolving door. “Is it actually sunny?”

Zhou Yichen, who had checked the forecast at six while she slept and again over coffee while she photographed the coffee, held the door for her. “Look.”

Upstairs, over the last of breakfast on the balcony, she had announced that she intended to spend the whole morning in bed. He’d said that was fine. Then he’d looked out at the sky and mentioned, to nobody in particular, that the gardens opened at half past seven and would be quiet until ten.

“You knew,” she said on the steps.

“I knew.”

He was still carrying last night’s umbrella, out of habit. She looked at it, and up at the sky, and started laughing, and he folded it under his arm without a word and held out his other hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the time they got to the gardens the morning had become almost unreasonably pretty. The paths were still empty, the trees were bright with new leaves, and the sunlight came through the branches and moved over the stone in shifting patterns. She stopped just inside the gate. He stopped next to her. Neither of them said anything. Then she got her camera out.

“Oh, this is lovely.”

“It is.”

It was all details. The curved eaves of a pavilion. A white wall upside down in the pond. A stone bridge arching over clear water, a crab apple in flower by a narrow path. She photographed everything. He stood a little way behind her and let her take as long as she liked.

After a while she turned round. “Stand there. On that bit.”

She pointed at a stretch of path where the sun fell across the stones.

“Here?”

“Yes. Look this way. No, not at me. Over there.”

He turned his head. She took a picture. Then another. Then she lowered the camera and looked at him.

“What?” he said.

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me.”

“Because I’m taking pictures.”

“You’re very obedient today,” she said.

This time he was looking out at the water instead of the camera, his hands in his coat pockets, the light catching the side of his face. She checked the screen. It was beautiful. “Don’t move.”

He didn’t move. She took one more.

“Okay.”

He came back to her. “Can I see?”

She showed him. He looked for a while. “Not bad.”

“Not bad?”

“Very good,” he corrected, and handed the camera back, and took her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t follow a route. She liked that. Nobody had to rush from one famous view to the next or keep looking at the time. They could stop whenever something caught her eye, or walk slowly by the water, or sit on a bench because the sun felt nice.

By one pond she crouched down. Fish were moving under the surface, their shadows sliding over the pale stones.

“Look. That one’s enormous.”

He looked. “Not particularly.”

“Look at it.”

“I am.”

“Compared to the others!”

He studied the fish. “All right. It’s bigger.”

“Thank you,” she said, satisfied, and took a photograph. Then she noticed his reflection in the water behind her own, and turned the camera slightly. He was standing behind her with one hand in his pocket, watching her with that quiet look of his. She took it.

“Was that me?”

“No.”

“Maybe,” she said.

He bent down to see the screen. She pulled it away.

“Don’t. It’s a candid.”

“I know.”

“Then don’t look. You’re ruining my artistic process.”

“Sorry,” he said, laughing, and held out his hand to pull her up, and she kept hold of it afterward.

✦ ✦ ✦

By midday the gardens were fuller and the sun was warm. They sat in a little pavilion over the water while he went to buy drinks from a stall. When he came back she was scrolling through her camera.

“How many have you taken?”

“Don’t ask.”

“That many?”

“There’s no such thing as too many photographs.”

He sat down beside her. “How many will you keep?”

“Most of them.”

“Most?”

“Some are blurry.”

She showed him: a flower, a bridge, the pond. He didn’t pretend to know anything about photography. He asked questions, and now and then pointed at something she hadn’t noticed herself. At one picture of a tree he stopped.

“Why this one?”

“Because the light’s pretty.”

“That’s all?”

“That’s enough.”

He looked at it again, and then at her. “You’re right.”

She leaned against his shoulder. A young couple came past and stopped on the bridge to take a picture of themselves. Xiaoran watched them, and then looked up at him.

“Should we take one?”

“Together?”

“Yes.”

He held out his hand for her phone, and stood up and held it out at arm’s length. She slid her arm round his waist and moved in close.

“Wait.”

“What?”

She reached up and fixed his collar, which had folded under. He stood patiently and let her.

“Okay.”

He took it. It was a simple picture: the garden behind them, the sun on their faces, her cheek against his shoulder. He looked relaxed. She was smiling.

“I like this one. Take another.”

He took another. And another. By the fourth she was laughing, because he’d started deliberately making his face more and more serious.

“Stop. That’s your passport face.”

“Should I smile?”

“Yes.”

He bent his head towards her a little. “Like this?”

She looked up at him. It was a smile, warm and familiar. She forgot to answer.

“Yes,” she said eventually, and he took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch they found a quieter path where the trees grew close together and the light came through in scattered pieces, and the air smelled of wet stone. She walked a little ahead of him, stopping every few steps. She’d been quiet for a while. He noticed.

“What are you thinking about?”

“Nothing.”

“Really. I was thinking I like travelling with you,” she said, and then came back down the path to him.

“Why?”

“Because you never rush me. Some people would get impatient. They’d want to see everything, take the main picture, go on to the next place.”

“And I don’t?”

“No. You let me look at things.”

“I like watching you look at things,” he said.

“That’s strange. I’m not doing anything.”

“You’re doing a lot. You get excited about small things. You stop walking when you see a flower you like. You take three pictures of the same bridge because you can’t decide which angle’s better. You tell me about things I’d have walked straight past. I don’t mind waiting.” He took her hand. He shrugged.

“You’re very patient.”

“With you.”

She looked up at him. “That sounded very romantic.”

“It was meant to,” he said, and she laughed and put her arm through his and leaned on him the rest of the way along the path.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the afternoon they found a tea shop near the garden gate and sat by the window to rest. He ordered tea and a plate of osmanthus cakes. When he came back with the tray she was going through her photographs again.

“Still choosing?”

“Just my favourites.”

“How many?”

“Twenty-three.”

“That’s a lot of favourites.”

“Don’t judge me. Look at this one.” She turned the camera round.

It was him crossing the stone bridge. He hadn’t known she was taking it. His head was turned slightly and the sun had caught the edge of his hair. Then another: his hand holding hers on the path. Then their two reflections in the pond, side by side, wobbling.

“You’re keeping these?”

“Of course.”

“All of them?”

“Yes.”

“Then I’ll have to remember this trip properly. So I recognise everything when you show me later,” he said.

“You were here. You’re supposed to remember it yourself.”

“I will. But I like seeing what you remember.” He reached across the table and turned her hand palm up and ran his thumb over her fingers.

She didn’t say anything. She turned her hand over and held his. Then she picked up an osmanthus cake with her other hand and held it out to him.

“Eat.”

He leaned across and took a bite out of her fingers.

“Good?”

“Yes.”

She ate the rest herself, and didn’t let go of his hand once.

✦ ✦ ✦

They left when the sun began to soften. On the way out she went quiet again, but this time because she was tired, and he noticed her steps getting slower.

“Do you want to sit down?”

“Not yet.”

“Do your feet hurt?”

“A bit.”

He looked down at her shoes. “Why did you wear those?”

“They’re comfortable.”

“They’re clearly not.”

“They were comfortable this morning.”

“That’s not the same thing. Sit,” he said, and stopped her by a low stone wall.

She sat on the wall. He crouched down in front of her and looked at the strap on her shoe, which had worked loose and was rubbing her ankle, and fixed it, and stood up.

At the gate she turned round for one last look. The gardens were still bright, but the shadows were long. Somebody nearby was laughing. She took one last picture, and then held the camera out to him.

“Will you take one of me?”

He took it. She walked a few steps away and stood where the sun fell across the path, and he took one, and another, and a third.

“That’s enough!”

She came back. The first was too posed. The second had caught her looking at the trees. The third had her laughing at something out of frame.

“That one’s my favourite,” she said.

“Mine too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the hotel she put the photographs on her laptop. He was on the sofa with his book. Every so often she turned the screen round.

“Look.”

“Nice.”

“Look at this one.”

“Very nice.”

“And this?”

“Also nice.”

She turned all the way round in her chair. “You’re not even looking.”

He closed the book and patted the cushion beside him.

She came. He moved his legs so she could sit, and she climbed onto the sofa beside him with the laptop and curled up under his arm, and this time he looked properly at every single one. The garden, the flowers, the bridges, the pond, the tea shop. The two of them.

He stopped at one she didn’t remember taking: herself, by the water, looking down at the camera in her hands, with the sun on her cheek and the loose hair by her face, completely absorbed.

“Keep this one.”

“I’m not looking at the camera.”

“I know.”

“You always pick the ones where I’m not looking.”

“You’re more interesting when you forget I’m watching.”

“That’s a very strange compliment.”

“It’s still a compliment,” he said, and she let her head drop onto his shoulder.

After a while she said, “I think today was my favourite day.”

“More than yesterday?”

“Yesterday was nice. But today was sunny.”

“So it’s the sun that makes the difference?”

“Obviously.”

“I liked today too,” he said.

“Even though I stopped every five minutes?”

“Yes.”

“And took too many pictures?”

“Yes.”

“And made you stand in the same place three times?”

He looked at her. “That part was difficult.”

“Yichen!”

He laughed and pulled her closer. “I’m joking.”

“You’re on very thin ice.”

“I know,” he said, and pressed his mouth to her hair.

Outside, the evening was fading over the rooftops. She saved the pictures into a folder and named it Suzhou – Day Two. Then, after a moment, she made another folder underneath it and called it Us, and dragged the one by the water into it, and the one on the bridge, and the fourth one from the pavilion, where he was smiling at her and not the camera. He saw. He didn’t say anything. He went back to his book with his arm still round her, and she kept sorting, leaning against him, until it was dark.

chapters.desc: She borrows his phone to check a menu and finds herself on his lock screen, in a picture she never knew he took.
chapters.title: A Photo He Keeps to Himself
chapters.epigraph: “Because I can’t take the same photograph twice.”
chapters.content:
Yichen had taken hundreds of photographs of Xiaoran. Some were intentional.

Birthday pictures, holiday photographs, pictures of her standing beneath pretty lanterns during their trip to the water town, and the occasional selfie she insisted they take together because she thought they hadn’t taken enough lately. Others were accidental.

Her sleeping against the car window. Her hand reaching across the dining table to steal food from his plate. Her reflection in a café window, unaware that he had lifted his phone to capture it.

He had a habit of photographing her when she wasn’t looking. Xiaoran knew this.

She occasionally complained about it, when he showed her a picture in which she was chewing, blinking, or making an expression she considered unsuitable for public viewing. Yichen usually kept those pictures anyway.

But there was one photograph he had never shown her.

It had been taken on a Sunday afternoon, several weeks earlier.

They had gone out for lunch and spent the rest of the day wandering around an old shopping district. Nothing special. Xiaoran had wanted to look at a stationery shop, then a small bookstore, and finally a dessert café she’d saved on her phone.

It was a warm afternoon, with sunlight filtering through the trees along the street.

She had been standing outside the café, waiting for him to finish paying.

Yichen had stepped out a moment later and found her looking through the glass window at the desserts inside.

She was wearing a cream-coloured dress, a light cardigan over her shoulders, and the little flower-shaped earrings she had bought herself during their shopping trip.

The sunlight had caught the side of her face.

Her hair moved slightly in the breeze, and she was smiling at something she had seen inside the café.

It was a small, unguarded smile, the kind she never made for a camera. She looked happy. And, to him, unbearably beautiful.

He had taken out his phone and captured the moment. Xiaoran hadn’t noticed.

When she finally turned around, she immediately asked whether he was ready. He had put his phone away.

“Ready?”

“Yes. Let’s go.”

She had taken his hand and continued walking. He hadn’t thought much about the photograph afterward, except that he had looked at it several times that evening.

Then he had set it as his phone wallpaper. He didn’t tell her. And, for several weeks, she didn’t notice. Until one ordinary evening. They were at home, preparing to order dinner.

Xiaoran was sitting on the living room sofa with her legs tucked beneath her, scrolling through a delivery app. Yichen had just finished showering and was sitting beside her, his phone in one hand.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Do you want noodles or rice?”

“Either.”

She met his eyes.

“That’s not an answer.”

“Then noodles.”

“Which noodles?”

He glanced at her screen.

“The one you want.”

Xiaoran sighed.

“You’re not helping.”

She continued scrolling, then remembered something.

“Oh, I need your phone.”

Yichen looked up.

“For what?”

“I want to check the restaurant’s menu. Mine isn’t loading properly.”

He handed it to her without hesitation. Xiaoran unlocked the phone. And stopped. She stared at the screen. Then she blinked. Then she looked again. It was a photograph of her. She had never seen it before.

She was standing outside the dessert café, her head slightly turned towards the window, sunlight falling across her cheek. Her expression was soft and happy.

The photograph was beautiful because she looked so naturally herself. She tilted the phone slightly. Then she looked at Yichen.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“What’s this?”

He glanced at the screen. His eyes landed on the photograph. For a brief moment, he said nothing. Then he looked back at her.

“My wallpaper.”

“I can see that.”

She looked down again.

“Since when?”

“A while.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

He leaned back against the sofa.

“You didn’t ask.”

Xiaoran turned towards him.

“How can I ask when I don’t even know you changed it?”

“That’s true.”

She looked at the photograph again.

“Where was this taken?”

“Outside the dessert café.”

She frowned.

“When?”

“That Sunday we went to the old shopping district.”

Her eyes widened.

“Wait. You took this?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“While you were looking inside the café.”

She looked at him.

“I didn’t even notice.”

“I know.”

“Why didn’t you show me?”

Yichen looked at her. Then he answered.

“Because I liked it.”

She blinked.

“Isn’t that why you show me pictures?”

“Usually.”

“Then why not this one?”

He reached for his glass of water on the coffee table, took a sip, and put it down.

“I wanted to keep this one.”

Xiaoran went quiet. She looked at the picture again. There was something unexpectedly intimate about it.

She had seen plenty of photographs of herself. She knew what she looked like when she smiled at a camera, when she posed for a picture, when she tried to look pretty. But this one was different.

She hadn’t known he was looking. She hadn’t been trying to look beautiful. She had been enjoying her afternoon. And Yichen had thought to keep that moment.

“Do you really like it that much?” she asked.

He turned his head towards her.

“Yes.”

“More than the pictures from our trip?”

“Different.”

“More than our anniversary photos?”

“Different.”

“More than the one where I’m wearing hanfu?”

That got a smile out of him.

“That one is very beautiful.”

“But?”

“But this one is my favourite.”

She turned to him.

“Why?”

Yichen was quiet. Then he shifted slightly towards her. She lowered the phone.

“Because you didn’t know I was taking it. You weren’t looking at me. You weren’t waiting for me to take a picture. You weren’t asking whether your hair looked right or whether the lighting was good.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“I do that?”

“Quite often.”

“That’s because you take terrible pictures sometimes.”

“I’ve been told.”

She laughed. Yichen reached over and gently tucked her hair behind her ear.

“You were just standing there, looking at something you liked. You looked happy.”

His thumb brushed her cheek.

“I liked seeing you like that.”

Xiaoran looked down at the phone again. The photograph seemed even more precious.

She hadn’t realised that he had noticed such a small moment. She hadn’t realised that he had kept it.

“Can you send it to me?” she asked.

Yichen looked at her.

“Of course.”

She couldn’t help smiling.

“Without the wallpaper crop. I want the original.”

“All right.”

“And don’t delete it.”

“I won’t.”

She looked at him with a playful expression.

“Actually, I think you should put a picture of us together as your wallpaper. Then everyone will know you’re taken.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“Does my current wallpaper suggest otherwise?”

She looked at the screen, then back at him.

“...No.”

“Good.”

“But it’s only me.”

“Is that a problem?”

She shook her head, smiling.

“No.”

Yichen held out his hand.

“Give it back.”

She placed the phone in his palm, but before he could take it, she leaned closer.

“Wait.”

“Hm?”

“Can I see it again?”

He unlocked the screen and showed her. She looked at the photograph for a few seconds. Then she glanced at him.

“You really look at me like that?”

Yichen’s expression softened.

“Like what?”

“Like I’m something worth keeping.”

He didn’t answer immediately. Instead, he put his phone down and reached for her hand.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up.

“I have six years of photographs of you.”

She laughed.

“That’s a lot.”

“And I still take more.”

“I know. You take pictures of me eating.”

“Those are important records.”

“Yichen!”

He smiled, then brought her hand to his lips.

“But this one... I like having it where I can see it.” He paused, his gaze returning to hers.

She felt her cheeks warm.

“Why?”

“Sometimes I look at it before training. Sometimes when I’m travelling. Sometimes when I have a few minutes between things.”

His voice was as calm as ever.

“It reminds me of home.”

Xiaoran’s expression softened. She hadn’t expected that. She had thought he liked the photograph because she looked pretty in it. That alone would have made her happy.

But knowing he kept it for those moments when they weren’t together made something warm settle in her chest.

She moved closer and wrapped her arms around his waist. Yichen’s arm came around her immediately.

“You’re making me emotional,” she murmured against his shoulder.

“Sorry.”

“Don’t apologise.”

He kissed her temple. For a while, they stayed like that. Then Xiaoran pulled back.

“Actually...”

Yichen looked down at her.

“What?”

“Can I take a picture of you?”

He blinked.

“Now?”

“Yes.”

She reached for her own phone. Yichen glanced down at his casual clothes, then at her.

“Why?”

“Because I want a wallpaper too.”

She moved a little farther away, holding her phone up.

“Don’t pose.”

He gave her a faint smile.

“All right.”

“Don’t smile too much either.”

“Understood.”

“Just look at me.”

He did. Xiaoran lifted her phone. But before she could take the picture, Yichen’s expression changed slightly.

His eyes softened, and the smile that came was quieter than the teasing one, and meant for her. She pressed the shutter. Then she looked at the result.

“Oh.”

Yichen glanced at her screen.

“Good?”

“Very.”

She sat beside him again and showed him the picture. He studied it.

“Not bad.”

“Not bad?”

“Very good.”

She smiled proudly. Then she opened her wallpaper settings.

Yichen watched her select the photograph, adjust the crop, and save it.

A moment later, she turned the screen towards him. His face filled her wallpaper. That made her grin.

“Now we’re even.”

He looked at her phone, then at her.

“Are we?”

“Yes.”

“Then I suppose I should take another picture of you.”

She laughed.

“You already have hundreds!”

“Not enough.”

He reached for his phone again, and Xiaoran immediately leaned towards him.

“Wait. Are you going to change your wallpaper?”

“No.”

She blinked.

“Why not?”

“I like this one.”

She smiled. Then she reached up and kissed his cheek.

“Okay. Keep it.”

Yichen turned his head slightly.

“Thank you.”

She kissed his other cheek.

“You’re welcome.”

He caught her hand before she could pull away and pressed a kiss to her palm.

“Besides,” he said, “I don’t think you’ll be able to replace it easily.”

Xiaoran tilted her head.

“Why?”

He met her eyes.

“Because I can’t take the same photograph twice.”

She considered that. Then she smiled.

“Then you should keep taking new ones.”

Yichen’s eyes softened.

“I intend to.”

Then he lifted his phone, and she was laughing too hard to stop him.

chapters.desc: One evening the promise ring is gone from her finger. They search the whole apartment before he finds it behind the soap dispenser.
chapters.title: The Ring on the Sink
chapters.epigraph: “The promise isn’t inside the ring, Xiaoran.”
chapters.content:
The first sign that something was wrong was that Lin Xiaoran stopped talking. Zhou Yichen noticed it immediately.

He was sitting at the dining table with his laptop open, reviewing footage from the Herons’ previous game. The television was off, the apartment was quiet except for the soft sound of the kitchen exhaust fan. Usually, when Xiaoran cooked, she narrated everything.

She talked about the recipe, complained about the vegetables, asked him whether he preferred more sauce, and occasionally announced that she was doing something dangerous with a knife even though she was only cutting a tomato.

Tonight, she had been unusually quiet for almost ten minutes. Yichen looked towards the kitchen.

She was standing at the counter, concentrating on something in the pan. He watched her.

“Xiaoran.”

“Mm?”

“Everything okay?”

“Yes.”

He returned his attention to the laptop.

A few seconds later, she said, “Yichen?”

“Yes?”

“Can you come here?”

He closed his laptop.

“What’s wrong?”

She didn’t answer immediately. Instead, she looked at the stove, then at the counter, then at her left hand. Yichen walked over.

“What happened?”

“I think...”

She stopped. He waited.

“I think I lost something.”

His expression changed.

“What?”

She lifted her left hand. The ring finger was bare. Yichen looked at it, then at her face. Neither spoke.

“Your ring?” he asked.

She nodded. The promise ring had been on her finger for well over a year.

It was delicate, understated, and easy to wear every day. A thin band with a small, subtle stone that caught the light when she moved her hand. It wasn’t an engagement ring. They had both been clear about that.

It was Yichen’s promise that when they were ready, when they had established their own lives and careers, he would ask her properly.

With flowers, a pretty dress, and everything she had once jokingly demanded.

She had tried hard not to cry when he first gave it to her, and failed. Since then, she had rarely taken it off. Now her finger was empty. Yichen looked at her carefully.

“When did you last see it?”

“This afternoon.”

“Are you sure?”

She nodded.

“I remember washing my hands before cooking. It was still there.”

“All right.”

She looked increasingly distressed.

“I was washing the vegetables, then I prepared the meat, and I washed my hands again. I didn’t notice anything.”

“Did you take it off?”

“No.”

“Then let’s look.”

She turned towards the sink.

“I already checked.”

“Where?”

“Here. The counter, the sink, the floor.”

He nodded.

“Okay. We’ll check again.”

She swallowed.

“I don’t understand. It doesn’t just fall off.”

Yichen glanced at her finger.

“Has it felt loose recently?”

She hesitated.

“A little.”

He met her eyes.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I didn’t think it was that loose.”

He didn’t scold her. He nodded.

“All right. Let’s find it first.”

They began with the kitchen. Yichen switched off the stove and moved the pan to a safe spot. Xiaoran stood beside him, watching as he carefully checked the counter.

He moved the chopping board, lifted the kitchen towel, and looked beneath the small appliances. Nothing.

“Maybe it fell into the sink,” Xiaoran said.

Yichen looked at the drain.

“Don’t turn the water on.”

“I haven’t.”

He checked the sink basin first, then the drain strainer. Nothing. Xiaoran’s breathing became a little uneven.

“What if it went down?”

“Let’s not assume that yet.”

“But the drain—”

“I’ll check.”

He crouched and examined the area beneath the sink. There was no obvious sign of it.

He opened the cabinet, looked around the pipes, then checked the floor again. Still nothing. Xiaoran rubbed her bare ring finger.

“I should have taken it off.”

Yichen stood.

“Maybe.”

He continued gently, “But we don’t know where it is yet. Don’t start blaming yourself.”

She nodded, but her eyes were already turning glossy. He noticed. He reached for her hand. He crooked a finger at her. She stepped closer. He held her hand between both of his.

“We’ll look properly. Don’t panic.”

She tried to smile.

“I’m not panicking.”

He looked at her. She exhaled.

“Okay. Maybe a little.”

He kissed her hair.

“That’s allowed.”

They searched the kitchen again. This time, Yichen checked the area around the stove while Xiaoran looked through the rubbish bin.

She carefully separated the paper towels and packaging from the vegetable scraps.

“Nothing,” she said.

“Check the food waste container too.”

She opened it. A few vegetable peels, a piece of onion skin, and the remains of the ingredients she had prepared. She stared at them.

“I don’t want to throw anything away.”

“Then don’t. I’ll check.”

He put on a pair of disposable gloves and carefully searched through the contents. No ring.

He washed his hands and returned to the counter.

“Let’s check the living room.”

She followed him. They looked beneath the sofa, around the dining table, and between the cushions.

Yichen checked the pockets of the cardigan she had worn earlier. Nothing. Xiaoran was becoming quieter.

At one point, she sat down on the sofa and stared at her hand. Yichen returned from the bedroom.

“Not there either.”

She nodded. He sat beside her.

“Xiaoran.”

She looked up.

“Do you remember the last time you took it off?”

She thought.

“Not recently. Maybe when we went swimming?”

“When was that?”

“Last month.”

“Did you put it back on?”

“Yes. I remember because you helped me.”

He nodded.

“All right.”

She looked down again.

“It’s stupid.”

“What is?”

“I’m so upset over a ring.”

Yichen turned towards her.

“It’s not stupid.”

She pressed her lips together.

“It’s not even an engagement ring.”

“I know.”

“And I know what it means. You don’t have to give me a ring to know you love me.”

“But I liked wearing it. It reminded me of that day. And what you said,” she whispered.

Her eyes finally filled.

“I don’t want to lose it.”

Yichen’s expression softened. He took her hand and kissed the bare finger.

“I know.”

She turned to him.

“We’ll keep looking.”

It was nearly ten when they returned to the kitchen.

Yichen had checked the bedroom, the bathroom, and even the laundry basket. Xiaoran had retraced her movements from the afternoon. Nothing.

She stood beside the sink, looking at the counter.

“I washed the vegetables here.”

She pointed towards the basin.

“Then I put the meat here. I remember because I moved the cutting board.”

Yichen followed her movements with his eyes.

“All right.”

“And then I washed my hands again.”

She turned on the tap slightly, demonstrating where she had stood. Yichen watched her left hand.

“Wait.”

She stopped.

“What?”

“Do that again.”

She blinked.

“What?”

“Show me how you washed your hands.”

She looked confused but did as he asked. She turned towards the sink, reached for the soap, and rubbed her palms together. Then she moved her hands beneath the tap. Yichen’s gaze shifted towards the sink.

“Did you use the soap dispenser?”

“Yes.”

“Which hand?”

“My right.”

He looked at the counter.

“Can you move?”

She stepped aside. Yichen examined the narrow space between the soap dispenser and the faucet. There was a small gap.

He reached behind the dispenser, then felt along the edge of the sink. His fingers stopped. He didn’t move. Then he leaned closer.

“Xiaoran.”

Her heart seemed to stop.

“What?”

He held out his hand. She rushed towards him.

He was looking at the narrow space between the sink and the wall.

Something small was caught there, partially hidden beneath the edge of the soap dispenser. A thin metallic glint. Yichen carefully reached for it. Then he lifted his hand. The ring rested between his fingers. For a second, Xiaoran didn’t move. She stared.

Then she let out a breath that sounded almost like a laugh.

“Oh my god.”

Yichen smiled.

“Found it.”

She covered her mouth.

“That’s my ring.”

“I know.”

“That’s really my ring.”

He laughed.

“Yes, Xiaoran.”

She reached for it, but stopped before touching it, as if she needed to confirm it was real. Yichen brought it closer. The small stone caught the kitchen light.

There was a faint trace of water on the band.

“It must have slipped off when you washed your hands. It got caught behind the dispenser,” he said.

She stared at it, then looked at him, then back at the ring. And she started crying. Not loudly.

Just a few tears slipping down her cheeks as the tension finally left her. Yichen’s smile softened.

“Hey.”

She laughed through the tears.

“I thought I lost it.”

“I know.”

“I looked everywhere.”

“I saw.”

She reached for him instead of the ring and kissed him, wet hands and all.

He wrapped an arm around her and held her close. For a while, she stood against his chest. Then she pulled back.

“Can I have it?”

He smiled.

“Of course.”

He placed it in her palm. She held it carefully, turning it between her fingers. Then she looked at him.

“Can you put it back on?”

His expression changed.

“Your finger?”

She nodded. He took the ring from her hand.

But before putting it on, he examined the band.

“It’s loose.”

She looked away.

“I know.”

“How long?”

“A little while.”

He turned to her. She made a small face.

“Don’t lecture me.”

“I’m not.”

“You have that expression.”

“What expression?”

“The one where you’re about to say something sensible.”

He laughed.

“Then I’ll save it for tomorrow.”

That made her grin. He took her left hand and slipped the ring onto her finger.

It settled there, slightly looser than it should have.

He turned her hand gently, checking that it sat comfortably.

“There.”

She looked at it, then at him.

“Thank you.”

He kissed her knuckles.

“You’re welcome.”

They didn’t go back to cooking immediately. Yichen made tea while Xiaoran sat at the dining table, turning the ring on her finger. She looked at it several times. He noticed.

“Still checking?”

“Just making sure.”

He placed a cup in front of her.

“It’s not going anywhere.”

“Don’t say that. It might.”

He smiled and sat opposite her.

“Then we’ll get it resized.”

She looked down.

“Can we?”

“Of course.”

“Will it look different?”

“Not if we have it done properly.”

She considered this.

Then asked, “Do you remember why you chose this one?”

Yichen leaned back slightly.

“Yes.”

“Tell me.”

He held her gaze.

“You want me to tell you again?”

She nodded. He laughed under his breath.

“I wanted something you could wear every day. Something that wouldn’t get in the way of your work, or feel too formal.”

She listened.

“And I didn’t want you to feel like you had to keep it safe in a box. I wanted it to be part of your life.”

She looked at the ring.

He said, “I knew you would probably wear it all the time.”

Her mouth tipped up.

“Because I like it.”

“I know.”

“And now I have to take it off to cook.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“I didn’t plan for the soap dispenser.”

She smiled. He reached across the table and touched her hand.

“Do you remember what I told you when I gave it to you?”

She nodded.

“You said it wasn’t a proposal.”

“Correct.”

“And that you’d ask me properly when we’re ready.”

“Yes.”

She held his gaze.

“And you said you weren’t going to rush me.”

“I meant it.”

“I know.”

She turned the ring once more.

Then said, “I think I was scared because it felt like losing that promise.”

She said, “I know a ring is just an object. But this one is something we chose together. It reminds me that we’re building towards something.”

He reached for her hand.

“The promise isn’t inside the ring, Xiaoran.”

She looked up.

“It’s between us.”

She was quiet. He rubbed his thumb over her knuckles.

“The ring is something you can wear. Something that reminds you of it. But if you lose it, the promise doesn’t disappear.”

Her eyes softened.

“I know.”

“Good. Although I’d prefer you not to test that theory again.”

She laughed.

“Okay.”

The next morning, Yichen took her to have the ring checked.

They found a jeweller who could adjust the size without changing the design. Xiaoran watched carefully as the jeweller examined it.

“Can you make it a little smaller?”

The jeweller nodded.

“Of course. It should fit more securely after adjustment.”

Yichen stood beside her.

“Could you also check the setting?”

“Certainly.”

Xiaoran looked at him.

“You don’t have to worry so much.”

“I’m not worried.”

She raised an eyebrow. He smiled.

“All right. A little.”

She laughed. When the jeweller finished checking the ring, they were told it would be ready later that afternoon.

Xiaoran left the shop with an empty ring finger. She kept looking at it. Yichen noticed.

“Do you want to hold it until it’s ready?”

She shook her head.

“No. It’s safer here.”

He studied her.

“You’re learning.”

She laughed.

“Don’t tease me.”

He took her hand.

“Come on.”

That evening, they returned home. The ring was back on her finger. It fit properly now.

Xiaoran held her hand beneath the kitchen light, admiring how it sat against her skin. Yichen was unpacking the groceries. She tilted her head.

“Yichen.”

“Mm?”

“Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“If, one day, I actually lose it...”

She said, “Would you be upset?”

He considered the question.

“Would you be upset?”

She thought.

“Yes.”

“Then I’d probably be upset too.”

She frowned.

“That’s not comforting.”

He smiled and came closer.

“But I’d help you look for it.”

She looked up.

“And if we couldn’t find it?”

“Then we’d figure out what to do.”

She stared at him. He touched the ring lightly.

“We could replace it. Or keep the memory of the original. Or choose something else together.”

“Even if it wasn’t the same?”

“Even then.”

He bent and kissed her hairline.

“Xiaoran, I didn’t give you this ring because I wanted you to spend the rest of your life worrying about losing it.”

“I gave it to you because I wanted you to enjoy wearing it.”

Her smile softened.

“Okay.”

He kissed her cheek.

“Now, can you help me with dinner?”

She nodded.

“Yes.”

He returned to the groceries. She watched him, then glanced at the sink.

The soap dispenser had been moved slightly away from the wall. She smiled.

“Yichen?”

He looked over.

“Yes?”

“Do you think we should put the ring somewhere safe when I cook?”

He considered it.

“That might be a good idea.”

“Maybe a little dish.”

“All right.”

“Beside the sink?”

He considered her. She immediately corrected herself.

“No. Not beside the sink. Somewhere farther away.”

He laughed.

“Good decision.”

She smiled proudly, then walked over and kissed his cheek.

A few days later, Yichen came home from training and found a small ceramic dish on the bedroom dresser.

It was cream-coloured, with a tiny blue flower painted in the middle, the same as the cup their toothbrushes lived in. Beside it was a handwritten note.

For my ring, when I need to take it off.

He picked it up and smiled. Xiaoran appeared from the bathroom, drying her hands.

“Do you like it?”

He looked at the dish.

“Yes.”

“I thought it would be safer here.”

“Much safer.”

She walked over and looked at it with him. Then she lifted her left hand. The ring was still there. Yichen glanced at her.

“You’re wearing it.”

“Yes.”

“Then what is the dish for?”

“For when I need to take it off.”

He nodded.

“Very practical.”

“Thank you.”

He put the dish back on the dresser. Then he took her hand and kissed the ring. She watched him.

“Yichen?”

“Mm?”

“Do you think when you propose properly, I’ll still wear this?”

He glanced at her.

“You can wear whatever you want.”

She tilted her head.

“What if I wear both?”

Something in his face eased.

“Then I’ll have to find a ring that sits beside it.”

She laughed.

“You’re already planning?”

“I’ve had a little time to think about it.”

Her expression softened. He brushed his thumb over her cheek.

“But not yet.”

“I know.”

“After we’ve built the life we want.”

She nodded.

“After we’re ready.”

He kissed her temple.

“Exactly.”

She leaned into him, smiling. The promise ring caught the light between them. Tomorrow it would go in the ceramic dish before she cooked, and he would check anyway.

chapters.desc: She books a professional couple shoot. He poses as if he were at a board meeting, until the photographer asks them to forget the camera.
chapters.title: The Way He Looks at Her
chapters.epigraph: “Who else would I look at like that?”
chapters.content:
Xiaoran had booked the photoshoot three weeks in advance.

She had researched photographers, compared portfolios, saved references, and created an entire album on her phone titled Couple Photoshoot Ideas.

There were photographs taken in studios, gardens, old streets, and beautiful apartments. Some were elegant and romantic. Others were playful, with couples laughing, running, or stealing kisses when the photographer wasn’t looking. She had shown Yichen the album one evening. He had scrolled through it carefully.

“How many photographs do you want?”

Xiaoran had looked at him.

“That’s your first question?”

“I’m trying to understand the scale of the operation.”

She had laughed.

“I just want some nice photographs of us.”

“We have plenty.”

“Those are mostly selfies.”

“What’s wrong with selfies?”

“Nothing. But I want professional ones. The kind we can frame.”

He had looked at her, then nodded.

“All right. Let’s do it.”

And that was how Zhou Yichen found himself standing in a photography studio on a Saturday morning, wearing a carefully selected dark charcoal suit while his girlfriend stood in front of a mirror, adjusting the collar of her cream-coloured dress for the fourth time. He had to admit, she looked beautiful.

Her hair fell in soft waves over her shoulders, and the dress suited her perfectly. She had chosen delicate earrings and a pair of heels, and her promise ring caught the light whenever she moved her hand.

He watched her adjust one loose strand of hair.

“Xiaoran.”

“Hm?”

“You’re ready.”

“You look beautiful,” he said.

Her expression brightened, and she walked towards him, smoothing the front of his suit.

“You’re handsome too.”

“Thank you.”

She looked at him for another moment.

“Although you look a little too serious.”

He raised an eyebrow. He laughed under his breath.

“I’ll try to remember.”

She laughed and took his hand. The photographer, a woman named Anqi, greeted them warmly.

She was experienced, friendly, and immediately seemed to understand that Xiaoran was the enthusiastic half of the couple.

“You’re Lin Xiaoran, right? We spoke about the mood board.”

“Yes! Thank you for accommodating the references.”

“Of course. I loved your ideas. And Zhou Yichen?”

He shook her hand.

“Hello.”

Anqi glanced between them.

“Lovely. You two look great together.”

Xiaoran smiled. Yichen gave a polite nod. The first setup was a simple studio backdrop in warm beige, with soft natural lighting and a few pieces of furniture. Anqi explained the process.

“We’ll start with some classic portraits. Nothing too complicated. Just stand together, look at the camera, and we’ll adjust as we go.”

Xiaoran nodded enthusiastically. Yichen listened attentively. The first few photographs went smoothly.

Yichen stood beside Xiaoran with one hand resting at her waist. His posture was straight, his expression composed. Xiaoran smiled at the camera, occasionally turning her face towards him. Anqi checked the monitor.

“Beautiful. Let’s try one with you looking at each other.”

Xiaoran turned towards Yichen. That made her grin. He smiled back, although subtly. The shutter clicked. Anqi checked the image.

“Very nice. Maybe a little closer?”

Yichen moved closer.

“Good. Zhou Yichen, could you relax your shoulders a little?”

He did.

“Perfect. And Lin Xiaoran, perhaps place your hand on his chest.”

She did so immediately. Anqi raised her camera.

“Lovely. Now look at each other.”

They did.

“Good. A little smile, please.”

Xiaoran smiled. Yichen’s expression softened slightly. Click. Anqi looked at the monitor. Then she smiled.

“You’re both very photogenic. But I have a feeling we’re going to get something even better once you stop thinking about the camera.”

Xiaoran looked curious.

“What do you mean?”

“Let’s take a short break from posing. Just talk to each other. Forget I’m here.”

Yichen nodded.

“All right.”

Anqi lowered her camera.

“Tell him something you like about him.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Right now?”

“Yes.”

She turned towards Yichen. He looked at her expectantly. For some reason, she became shy.

“Um...”

Yichen’s mouth curved.

“Go on.”

She glanced at the photographer, then back at him.

“I like that you’re patient.”

He tilted his head.

“Only that?”

She laughed.

“No. I like that you’re thoughtful. And that you always remember little things.”

His expression softened. She continued, more comfortably now.

“And I like that you’re very handsome.”

He laughed. Anqi raised her camera. Click. Xiaoran didn’t notice. Yichen did.

He looked towards the photographer for a second before returning his attention to Xiaoran.

“Anything else?”

She smiled.

“I like that you always let me have the last piece of dessert.”

“Not always.”

“Most of the time.”

“That’s because you take it before I can.”

She laughed. Anqi took another photograph. The next setup was outdoors.

The studio had a small garden with a stone pathway, flowering plants, and a wooden bench beneath a tree. The afternoon light was soft, filtering through the leaves. Xiaoran loved it immediately.

“It’s so pretty.”

Yichen stood beside her.

“Do you like this one?”

“Very much.”

Anqi suggested they begin with a few photographs sitting together on the bench. Xiaoran sat first.

Yichen sat beside her, leaving a small space between them. Anqi looked through the camera.

“Could you move a little closer?”

Yichen shifted.

“Closer still.”

He moved again. Xiaoran glanced at him.

“You’re being very cooperative.”

He met her eyes.

“Am I not usually?”

“You are. But you’re behaving like a very well-trained model.”

He smiled.

“Would you prefer otherwise?”

She thought about it.

“Maybe.”

Anqi lowered her camera.

“Actually, let’s try something different. Zhou Yichen, could you put your arm around her and let her lean against you?”

He did. Xiaoran settled against his side.

“Good. Now, Lin Xiaoran, look at him.”

She turned. Yichen was already looking at her.

“Lovely. And Zhou Yichen, perhaps kiss her forehead,” Anqi said.

He lowered his head and pressed a kiss to her hair. Click. Xiaoran smiled. Anqi checked the photograph.

“Beautiful.”

Then she looked at them again.

“Could you stay like that for a moment?”

Yichen didn’t move. His arm remained around Xiaoran, his fingers resting gently against her upper arm. Xiaoran looked up.

“What?”

He brushed his thumb over her skin.

“Nothing.”

“Why are you looking at me?”

“Because you’re here.”

That made her grin.

“That’s a very strange answer.”

“Is it?”

She shook her head, laughing. Anqi took another photograph, then another.

The camera captured the small smile on Xiaoran’s face and the way Yichen’s attention never seemed to leave her.

By the third setup, Xiaoran had become increasingly comfortable. She was beginning to enjoy the process.

Yichen, meanwhile, had become noticeably less concerned about the camera. It happened when Anqi suggested a playful series.

“I’d like you two to walk towards me. Hold hands, talk to each other, and don’t worry about posing.”

Xiaoran immediately stood.

“Can we walk together?”

Yichen looked at her.

“We’re supposed to.”

She laughed. They began walking along the garden path.

Xiaoran held his hand, swinging their joined hands slightly.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Do you think the photographs will turn out well?”

“Yes.”

“How do you know?”

“Because you’re in them.”

She looked up, then narrowed her eyes.

“You’re trying to make me happy.”

“Is it working?”

“Maybe.”

He didn’t bother hiding the smile. She continued walking.

“Actually, I want one where I’m looking at you and you’re looking at the camera.”

“Why?”

“Because I want people to see how handsome you are.”

He turned to her.

“Then why would you be looking at me?”

“Because I’m admiring you.”

He laughed. Anqi was already taking photographs.

“That’s wonderful! Keep talking!”

Xiaoran became more animated.

“And I want one where you carry me.”

Yichen looked down.

“Carry you?”

“Yes.”

“Here?”

“Yes.”

He glanced at the photographer. Anqi smiled.

“If you’re comfortable, let’s try.”

Yichen looked at Xiaoran again.

“Are you sure?”

She nodded. He stopped walking, placed one arm behind her back and the other beneath her knees, then lifted her effortlessly. Xiaoran let out a surprised laugh.

“Yichen!”

“What?”

“You actually did it!”

“You asked.”

She instinctively wrapped her arms around his shoulders. Anqi began taking photographs.

“Perfect! Stay like that!”

Xiaoran was laughing now, her face turned towards him. Yichen looked down at her. His expression had changed completely.

He wasn’t thinking about his posture or where to place his hands. He was looking at the girl in his arms, smiling at her as if the photographer and the camera had disappeared. Click. Click. Click. Anqi lowered the camera slightly.

“That was wonderful.”

Yichen carefully put Xiaoran down. She was still smiling.

“That was fun.”

He brushed a loose strand of hair away from her face.

“Did I hurt you?”

She shook her head.

“No.”

“Good.”

Then, almost absentmindedly, he kissed her. Anqi captured it.

During the next break, Xiaoran went to look at the photographs on the monitor. She stood beside Anqi, looking through the previews.

“Oh!”

She pointed at one.

“This one!”

It was the photograph of Yichen carrying her. She looked delighted.

“Look at his expression!”

Anqi smiled.

“He’s very affectionate.”

Xiaoran glanced towards him. Yichen was standing a little distance away, speaking with one of the assistants.

“He’s usually quite composed,” Xiaoran said.

“Not when he’s looking at you, apparently.”

Xiaoran smiled. Then she looked at another photograph. It showed Yichen kissing her forehead while she closed her eyes. She stared at it for a little longer.

“I like this one too.”

Anqi nodded.

“It’s one of my favourites. You look very comfortable with him.”

Xiaoran’s smile softened.

“I am.”

The final setup was in a quiet indoor room with a large window.

The afternoon light came through the sheer curtains, creating a soft glow across the room. There was a cream-coloured sofa, a small table, and a few books arranged on a shelf. Anqi suggested a more relaxed concept.

“Let’s make this one feel like an ordinary afternoon at home.”

Xiaoran immediately liked the idea.

“Can we sit together?”

“Of course.”

Yichen sat on the sofa first. Xiaoran sat beside him, then shifted closer until her shoulder touched his. Anqi watched them.

“Actually, I have a suggestion.”

She looked at Yichen.

“Could you forget the camera completely? Just interact with her the way you normally would.”

Yichen nodded.

“All right.”

“And Lin Xiaoran, you don’t need to look at the camera either. Just do whatever you would usually do when you’re together.”

Xiaoran smiled.

“Okay.”

Anqi lifted her camera.

“Let’s begin.”

For the first few seconds, Xiaoran wasn’t sure what to do. Then she noticed Yichen’s watch. She reached for his wrist.

“Your watch.”

He looked down.

“What about it?”

“Let me see.”

He held out his hand. She examined it, turning his wrist slightly.

“Is this the one you wore last week?”

“Yes.”

“I like this one.”

Something in his face eased.

“You said that yesterday.”

“Because I still like it.”

She released his wrist, then leaned against him. Yichen slipped his arm around her.

“Comfortable?”

“Mm.”

She adjusted herself, placing her head against his shoulder. Anqi continued taking photographs. Yichen lowered his head.

“Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Want to rest?”

She shook her head.

“No. I’m enjoying this.”

“Good.”

She lifted her face.

“Do you think we should get one of these photographs framed?”

“Which one?”

“The one where you’re carrying me.”

“Why that one?”

“Because I look happy.”

He looked at her.

“You look happy in all of them.”

“Then maybe the one where you’re kissing my forehead.”

“All right.”

She considered it.

“Actually, I want several.”

He laughed.

“How many?”

“At least five.”

“Very reasonable.”

She rested her chin against his chest.

“You’re not complaining?”

“Why would I?”

“Because you said we already have plenty of photographs.”

He held her gaze.

“Those are mostly selfies.”

She stared, then burst out laughing.

“You remembered!”

That got a smile out of him.

“Of course.”

She lifted herself slightly and kissed his cheek.

“You’re so cute.”

Yichen turned his face towards her.

“Am I?”

She nodded.

“Sometimes.”

He gave her a slow, amused smile. It was the smile that always made her forget what she had been saying. Yichen noticed.

“What?”

She looked away.

“Nothing.”

He leaned closer.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“You’re staring.”

She pressed her lips together.

“I’m not.”

“All right.”

Then he gently caught her chin and kissed her. It was supposed to be a quick kiss.

But when she smiled against his lips, he kissed her again.

His hand moved to the back of her head, fingers slipping into her hair. Xiaoran leaned closer, one hand resting against his chest. Anqi continued shooting. Neither of them noticed.

When they finally separated, Xiaoran was smiling, her cheeks slightly pink. Yichen brushed his thumb along her cheek.

“What’s that expression?”

She laughed.

“You know.”

“Maybe.”

From behind the camera, Anqi spoke.

“That was perfect.”

They both turned towards her. She lowered the camera, looking thoroughly pleased.

“I think we have it.”

Xiaoran blinked.

“Really?”

“Yes. The last few photographs are exactly what I wanted.”

Yichen glanced at the camera.

“What did you capture?”

Anqi smiled.

“You two.”

The photoshoot ended a little after four. Xiaoran was still excited as they collected their belongings.

She thanked Anqi several times and promised to leave a review once the photographs were delivered. Yichen stood beside her, holding her bag.

When they finally stepped outside, she immediately reached for his hand.

“That was so much fun.”

He studied her.

“Did you enjoy it?”

“Very much.”

“Good.”

She swung their hands.

“You were good.”

“Thank you.”

“Especially towards the end.”

His mouth curved.

“What happened towards the end?”

She looked up at him.

“You became very affectionate.”

She looked at him suspiciously.

“You were so serious at the beginning.”

“I was listening to the photographer.”

“You looked like you were attending a meeting.”

He laughed.

“Was I that bad?”

“Not bad. Just... very professional.”

He nodded thoughtfully.

“Understood.”

She squeezed his hand.

“But I liked the last part best.”

“Why?”

“Because you forgot about the camera.”

He looked down at her. She smiled.

“You weren’t trying to look handsome. You weren’t trying to pose. You were just being yourself.”

He was quiet. Then he lifted their joined hands and kissed the back of hers.

“That’s because I was looking at you.”

She looked up. He continued walking, his expression perfectly calm. Xiaoran stared at him. Then her cheeks slowly turned pink.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“You’re very good at saying things like that.”

That got a smile out of him.

“Like what?”

“Things that make me embarrassed.”

He considered her.

“Should I stop?”

She thought, then shook her head.

“No.”

He laughed. The photographs arrived a week later. Xiaoran opened the gallery while they were sitting together on the sofa.

Yichen was reviewing something on his tablet when she made a small sound.

“Oh!”

He looked over.

“What?”

“They’re here.”

She immediately moved closer.

“Look!”

She opened the gallery. The first few were the formal portraits. They were beautiful.

Yichen looked composed and handsome, while Xiaoran looked elegant and radiant. They stood close together, hands at each other’s waists, smiling gently towards the camera, then came the photographs from the garden.

The walking shots. The one where he carried her. The one where she was laughing. And finally, the indoor photographs. Xiaoran stopped scrolling. She stared at one.

It showed her sitting against Yichen’s chest, her head tilted up towards him. He was looking down at her with an expression so gentle and unguarded that she almost didn’t recognise it as something he would allow a camera to capture. His hand was resting against her cheek. She was smiling. Not at the camera. At him. Yichen looked at the screen.

“That’s nice.”

Xiaoran nodded. She moved to the next photograph. It was the moment after their kiss.

Her eyes were slightly lowered, her cheeks pink. Yichen was smiling at her, his thumb still resting against her cheek. She stared at it.

“Yichen.”

“Hm?”

“Look at your face.”

He leaned closer.

“What about it?”

“You look so...”

She paused, searching for the word. He waited.

“Fond.”

He looked at the photograph again, then smiled.

“Do I?”

She nodded.

“Very.”

He took the phone from her and scrolled back to the photograph. He studied it.

Then he said, “I suppose I was.”

Xiaoran turned towards him.

“You were?”

He looked at her.

“Xiaoran.”

“What?”

“Who else would I look at like that?”

She went quiet. Her fingers curled slightly around his sleeve. Then she leaned forward and kissed his cheek.

“Me, I hope.”

Yichen smiled.

“Always.”

She let her head drop onto his shoulder. She looked at the gallery again.

“I want to frame this one.”

“Which?”

“The one where you’re looking at me.”

He nodded.

“Let’s frame it.”

“And the one where you’re carrying me.”

“All right.”

“And the one where we’re kissing.”

He glanced at her.

“Three frames?”

She considered it.

“Maybe four.”

He laughed.

“Of course.”

She smiled and opened the gallery again. Yichen slipped his arm around her waist, pulling her closer as she began selecting photographs.

A few minutes later, she paused at the first formal portrait.

“Actually, this one should go in the living room.”

“Why?”

“Because it looks elegant.”

He nodded.

“And the others?”

“Our bedroom.”

He smiled.

“Then we should choose carefully.”

Xiaoran leaned against him, scrolling through the photographs one by one, then looked up from the phone.

“Yichen?”

“Hm?”

“Can we do this again next year?”

He looked down at her.

“Another photoshoot?”

“Yes. Maybe every year.”

“All right.”

She grinned.

“Then we’ll have photographs from every year.”

“Sounds good.”

She looked at the photograph on the screen one last time.

Then she turned and wrapped both arms around him. Yichen laughed, his hand settling at her back.

“What is this for?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing?”

She shook her head against his chest.

“I just want to hug you.”

He kissed her hair.

“Then hug me.”

And when Xiaoran eventually uploaded one photograph to her social media, she chose the one where she was looking at him and he was looking at her. Her caption was short.

Somehow, my favourite photographs are always the ones where he forgets the camera exists.

Yichen saw it later. He liked the post, then left a comment.

Hard to remember there’s a camera when you’re standing in front of me.

Xiaoran read it while sitting beside him. She turned her head slowly. He was looking at his phone, perfectly composed.

She stared, then covered her face with both hands. Yichen glanced at her.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

His mouth curved.

“All right.”

She peeked at him between her fingers.

“You’re doing it again. Making me fall in love with you all over again.”

His expression softened. He put his phone down, pulled her into his arms, and kissed her temple.

“Good, I was hoping you would,” he murmured.

chapters.desc: At her parents’ table on May Day, her grandfather asks Yichen when he plans to marry his granddaughter.
chapters.title: Her Grandfather’s Question
chapters.epigraph: “I intend to marry you, Lin Xiaoran.”
chapters.content:
The question came on the second night of the May Day holiday, at her parents’ table, between the second helping of fish and the arrival of the fruit. Lin Xiaoran decided afterward that this was an extremely unfair moment to ask it.

Her grandparents had come up from the town for the holiday, four hours on the bus with a box of eggs on her grandmother’s knees the whole way. Xiaoran had been eating happily. Her grandfather, who had lived round the corner from her until she was twelve and considered this a lifelong qualification for opinions about her, had been telling Zhou Yichen a story about an old neighbour who’d once tried to keep chickens on his balcony. Her mother was laughing. Her father was pretending not to. Yichen was listening with the grave attention he always gave old people.

It was all perfectly ordinary. Until her grandfather put his chopsticks down, looked at Yichen, and said:

“So. When are you going to marry my granddaughter?”

Xiaoran stopped chewing. Her mother looked up. Her father put his teacup down slowly. Yichen, who had just reached for the teapot, stopped with his hand on it. It was a remarkably quiet three seconds.

“Grandpa,” said Xiaoran.

“What?”

“That’s very sudden.”

“I’ve been thinking about it for a long time.”

“That’s worse.”

Her grandfather ignored her. “I’m asking him.”

Yichen took his hand off the teapot. “I understand, Grandpa.”

Xiaoran turned to look at him. She knew that face. He wasn’t startled anymore. It had settled into the calm, attentive look he got when he was taking something seriously, and that was exactly what made her nervous.

“You’ve been together for years. You’ve graduated. You live together. Both families know each other. I don’t think it’s an unreasonable question,” said her grandfather.

“No, it isn’t. I do intend to marry her,” Yichen agreed.

Her grandfather nodded, as if this were the answer he’d expected. “Then what’s stopping you?”

This time Yichen didn’t answer straight away. He glanced at Xiaoran. She was looking at him with her face somewhere between mortified and curious. He turned back to her grandfather.

“Nothing’s stopping me from wanting to. But I don’t want to do it just because we’ve reached a certain age, or because we’ve been together a long time. I want us both to be ready. Not just happy to say yes. Ready for what comes after.”

Xiaoran looked down at her bowl. Her face was burning.

Her grandfather considered this for a while. “That’s a reasonable answer. But don’t take another ten years about it.”

“Grandpa!”

He laughed. Yichen smiled. “I’ll remember that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The conversation moved on, eventually. Her mother asked whether anyone wanted more soup. Her father went for another dish. Her grandfather started telling the story of his own wedding, which involved a long account of how hard it had been to find a car in 1971.

Xiaoran listened, but she kept looking sideways at Yichen. He was perfectly normal. He ate. He listened. He laughed at one of her grandfather’s jokes. How could he be so calm? He had just told her entire family that he intended to marry her.

Not that she didn’t know. She knew about the ring. She knew he’d said he would ask properly, when it was time. She knew he wasn’t someone who said things lightly. But hearing it in front of her grandfather made it feel much closer. It wasn’t a vague someday anymore. It had come into the dining room and been served up with the fish.

When the meal was over she helped her mother clear. Her mother watched her stack plates in the sink.

“You’re quiet.”

“I’m not.”

“You’ve been quiet since Grandpa asked him.”

“Because he asked in front of everyone.”

“Would you rather he’d asked you privately?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because now everyone knows I have to think about it.”

Her mother laughed. “Darling. You’ve been thinking about it for years.”

Xiaoran nearly dropped a plate. “Mum.”

“What?”

“Don’t.”

Her mother dried her hands. “There’s nothing wrong with the question. And nothing wrong if the answer isn’t today. Just remember it’s not a finish line. You don’t have to get there because everyone else thinks it’s time. And you get to say what you want too. Don’t just wait for him to decide.” She leaned against the counter.

“I know.”

“And I think your grandfather likes him a great deal, or he wouldn’t have asked.”

Xiaoran smiled despite herself. “Grandpa likes anyone who listens to his stories.”

“He likes Yichen because Yichen doesn’t interrupt.”

“That’s also a very good quality,” said her mother.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she came out of the kitchen, Yichen and her grandfather were on the sofa with the old photo album open between them, and her grandfather was saying, “She’s always been stubborn.”

“I know,” said Yichen.

“She won’t admit when she’s tired.”

“I know.”

“And when she wants something, she pretends she doesn’t care until somebody notices.”

Yichen smiled. “I’ve noticed.”

Xiaoran stopped dead in the doorway. Excuse her?

Her grandfather turned a page. “She’s a good child.”

Something in Yichen’s face went soft. “She is.”

“Don’t let her work too hard.”

“I’ll remind her to rest.”

“And don’t spoil her too much.”

Yichen looked up from the album. “That might be difficult.”

Her grandfather laughed his short dry laugh. Xiaoran came into the room.

“What are you two talking about?”

“Nothing,” said her grandfather.

“Your childhood,” said Yichen.

She came round the sofa at once. “Grandpa, don’t show him the embarrassing ones.”

“He’s already seen them.”

“Which ones?”

“The one where you wouldn’t take your rain boots off indoors. For a week,” said Yichen.

“How do you know about that?”

“Your mother told me. At the housewarming.”

She sat down next to him and tried to close the album. He caught the edge of it. “Wait. I haven’t seen the next page.”

“You’re not supposed to.”

“Good, you two can look at the rest together. Think about what I asked,” said her grandfather, getting up. As he passed, he put his hand on Yichen’s shoulder.

“I will, Grandpa.”

Her grandfather gave Xiaoran a long look with something in it she couldn’t quite name, and went off to the kitchen to find her grandmother.

Xiaoran waited until he’d gone. “You’re both very suspicious.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re having private conversations about me.”

“We were talking about your rain boots.”

“That wasn’t all.”

“No,” he admitted.

“What else did he say?”

“That you’re stubborn. That you don’t admit when you’re tired.”

“That’s not true.”

He looked at her. She looked back. Then she sighed. “Fine.”

“And that you’re a good child. He thinks you hung the moon, Xiaoran,” he said.

She looked down at her hands. “I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They left after tea for the long drive back to Shanghai; he had training on the fourth. Her father walked them down to the car carrying the bag of food her mother had insisted on.

“Drive carefully.”

“We will, Uncle.”

“Ring when you get in.” Then, to Yichen: “About what Grandpa asked.”

Xiaoran shut her eyes. Not again.

“Don’t mind him too much. He likes to ask questions before people are ready to answer them. But it’s good that you’re thinking about it,” said her father.

“Dad. Can we go?”

He laughed and stepped back. Yichen opened the passenger door for her. Just as she was getting in, her father said, “And Xiaoran.”

She turned round.

“Don’t let him do all the thinking. It’s your life too.”

“I know, Dad.”
