“Good,” said her father, and stood by the gate with his hands in his pockets until they’d turned the corner.

✦ ✦ ✦

They drove for nearly fifteen minutes before either of them said anything. She sat with her hands folded over her bag, watching the shops go by.

“You were very calm,” she said at last.

“Should I have looked frightened?”

“Maybe a bit.”

“Would that have made you feel better?”

“Possibly.”

He laughed. “I didn’t know he was going to ask. I was surprised.”

“You didn’t look surprised.”

“I don’t think I reacted very much.”

“That’s the problem with you. You always look like you’ve already thought about everything.”

“Not everything,” he said.

She looked down at her left hand. The ring was there, where it had been since she moved it over. She turned it with her thumb.

“Yichen. When you said you intend to marry me. Did you mean soon?”

He didn’t answer straight away. Not because he was avoiding it; because he was choosing the words.

“I mean it’s not some distant possibility anymore. We’ve graduated. We’ve started building our lives. We know what living together is like. We’ve seen each other when things are easy and when they’re not.”

“Mostly when they’re not.”

“Those count double,” he said.

“So you have thought about it.”

“Xiaoran. I gave you a ring. I didn’t give it to you as a nice gesture and leave the meaning vague. I want to marry you. That isn’t the uncertain part.” He reached over and put his hand on hers on the console.

“Then what is?”

“When. How. What we want our lives to look like when we do. I don’t want you to fit your work round a wedding. And I don’t want to rush through everything we’re still building just because we already know we want to be together.”

She nodded slowly. That was so exactly like him. When Lanshan had offered her Beijing the spring before graduation, he had never once asked her to say no. He had only asked what she wanted, and waited until she knew. He would never ask her to give something up to make marriage easier.

“Would you want to get married while we’re still young?” she said.

“How young?”

“Don’t be annoying.”

“I’m asking.”

“Before we’re thirty.”

He thought about it. “Yes.”

“That’s very specific.”

“You asked,” he said, and she smiled at the window.

Then, in a smaller voice: “Do you ever worry? About whether we’d be good at it?”

“Of course.”

“You do?”

“I don’t worry about loving you. I worry about whether we’ll keep doing the work. Whether we’ll talk when we’re tired. Whether we’ll make room when each other’s plans change. Whether we’ll remember we’re on the same side when we disagree. I think marriage needs more than being sure we love each other. It needs us to keep choosing each other when it’s inconvenient,” he said, with no hesitation at all. He squeezed her hand.

She was quiet. “That’s a very Yichen answer.”

“Is that good?”

“Yes. I worry about those things too. But I don’t worry about whether I want to be with you. That’s not the uncertain part for me either.” She turned her hand over under his.

He looked at her for a second at the red light, and didn’t say anything, and didn’t need to.

“Have you thought about how you’d ask?” she said, as the light changed.

“Yes.”

She sat bolt upright. “You have?”

“Some things.”

“What things?”

“I’m not telling you.”

“Why not?”

“Because then it wouldn’t be a surprise.”

“That’s unfair.”

“You asked if I’d thought about it. I answered.”

“That’s not enough information!”

“It’s all you’re getting,” he said, and she folded her arms and stared at the road and was silent for almost a full minute.

“I still want flowers,” she said.

“I remember.”

“And a dress I love.”

“I remember that too.”

“And you’re not allowed to ask me when I’m in an old T-shirt.”

“Noted.”

“Or when I’m eating.”

“That’s a very specific restriction.”

“Because you know me. And don’t make me wait too long,” she said, and he laughed.

The laugh went out of his face, and something gentler came into it. “I won’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At home she changed and he put away the food. He found her sitting on the bed, looking at her hand. He leaned on the doorframe.

“Thinking?”

“About everything.”

He came and sat down next to her. She held her left hand out between them.

“Do you remember when you gave me this?”

“Of course.”

“You were so calm.”

“I was terrified.”

“You were not.”

“I checked my pocket every ten minutes for a whole day.”

She looked delighted. “Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because you were already nervous enough for both of us.”

She laughed, and then looked at the ring again. “I remember thinking it was a promise, but I didn’t know exactly what you were promising. And now I think I do. It wasn’t a promise that everything would happen right away. It was a promise that you knew where you wanted us to go.”

He took her hand. “That’s right.”

“I like that,” she said, and he lifted her hand and kissed the ring.

She leaned into his shoulder. The bedroom was quiet; outside, somewhere far below, a car door slammed.

“Can I tell you something?” she said.

“Anything.”

“I don’t want to get married just because our families are asking. And I don’t want to wait just because we’re supposed to be young and enjoy ourselves first. I want to marry you when we’re ready. But I don’t want us to pretend we don’t know what we want.”

“We don’t have to pretend.”

“So we’re agreed? We’re getting married. Some day.”

He gave her a look. “Xiaoran. I thought we’d established that.”

“I want to hear it again.”

He turned her hand over in his and ran his thumb across her palm.

“I intend to marry you, Lin Xiaoran. Not because your grandfather asked. Not because we’ve been together six years. Not because it’s the next thing people expect. Because I want to build a life with you. The ordinary parts and the hard parts. All of it.” He said it without looking away from her.

She felt her eyes sting. “Okay, I want that too,” she said.

He kissed her, slowly, without any hurry at all. When he pulled back she stayed where she was, her forehead against his.

“But I’m still expecting flowers,” she whispered.

He laughed against her cheek. “I know.”

“And I want you to look nervous.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to know you’re nervous.”

“That’s a difficult request.”

“Try.”

“I’ll do my best,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Two days later her phone buzzed while she was making tea.

Grandpa (Chief Egg Officer): Did you talk to Yichen?

Xiaoran: yes

Grandpa (Chief Egg Officer): And?

She looked across the flat. Yichen was at the dining table with his laptop. He glanced up when he saw her smiling.

Xiaoran: we talked

Grandpa (Chief Egg Officer): Good.

Grandpa (Chief Egg Officer): Don’t rush. But don’t be afraid to be happy either.

She read it twice. Then she put the phone down on the counter, left the tea, and went over and stood beside his chair.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. Grandpa says we shouldn’t rush.” She held out her hand, and he took it.

“He’s right.”

“He also says we shouldn’t be afraid to be happy.”

“He’s right about that too,” said Yichen.

She bent down and kissed his cheek, and then put her chin on his shoulder and stayed there, reading his screen without taking in a word of it. He put his free arm round her waist.

“Are you going to stand there?”

“Yes.”

“All right,” he said, and went on working, and she stayed exactly where she was until the kettle, forgotten on the counter, clicked itself off.

chapters.desc: Four hours beside a fishing pond, two fathers, no fish, and a great deal of conversation.
chapters.title: The Fathers Have Dinner
chapters.epigraph: “I think they have grown up.”
chapters.content:
The fishing pond outside the city had been Lin Hongwei’s idea, on the Saturday of the Dragon Boat weekend, when both families were home and both mothers had decided, independently and then together, that their husbands needed to be got out of the house.

It was quiet. It was said to be peaceful. It was supposed to be full of fish.

Zhou Mingyuan had agreed to go because he had never fished in his life and had recently been beaten at golf by two clients and a nephew. Neither man had expected to spend four hours beside a pond without catching a single fish. Neither had expected to talk quite so much.

“Are you sure this is the place?” said Mr. Zhou, standing by the car and looking at the hand-painted sign over the gate.

Mr. Lin checked his phone. “I’ve been here before.”

“When?”

“A few years ago.”

“Recently?”

“Not especially.”

Mr. Zhou laughed. “Then let’s see whether your memory’s better than your fishing.”

“Don’t worry. I know where the good spots are,” said Mr. Lin.

That confidence lasted about seven minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

They hired two rods, bought bait from the man in the hut, and found a shaded spot under a willow on the far bank. Mr. Lin set everything up with the ease of long practice. Mr. Zhou watched him.

“You do this a lot?”

“Not as much as I used to. Work. Family. You golf.” Mr. Lin threaded the bait.

“Badly, I’m told.”

“Your son told my daughter, who told her mother, who told me.”

Mr. Zhou sighed. “Then it’s true.”

They cast. The lines vanished into the brown water. They sat in their folding chairs and for a while nobody said anything at all.

Then Mr. Lin said, “How’s Yichen doing? Really?”

“Busy. Training. Always too much going on. He’s always been like that. When he was small, if he decided he wanted something, he wouldn’t stop until he had it.” Mr. Zhou turned his tea flask round in his hands.

“That sounds familiar.”

A ripple moved on the water. Both men watched it. Nothing happened.

“Our children are quite alike in that way,” said Mr. Lin.

Mr. Zhou laughed. “That’s true.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first hour was mostly about fishing. The second was mostly about work. By the start of the third they had covered their children, their marriages, how much the city had changed, the price of flats, and the impossibility of finding an honest mechanic. They hadn’t caught a single fish.

Mr. Lin reeled in and looked at his hook. “Nothing.”

“Maybe it’s the bait.”

“I used this last time.”

“Perhaps the fish have changed their preferences.”

Mr. Lin looked at him. “Fish don’t change their preferences.”

“People do.”

“Fish aren’t people.”

“Fair enough,” said Mr. Zhou, laughing, and they changed the bait anyway, and cast again, and the pond went on ignoring them.

At some point, without either of them deciding to, they got on to the children. Mr. Zhou was telling a story about Yichen’s first university season when Mr. Lin said, “She rang home in her first month in Shanghai. In that studio. Because a cupboard hinge had come loose.”

“She rang you?”

“She rang her mother first. Her mother rang me. I told her the boy across the road probably had a screwdriver.”

“Did he?”

“One.”

Mr. Zhou laughed out loud. “Did she fix it?”

“In the end. She sent me a photograph afterward. The hinge was fixed. And she’d put a scratch right across the door. She’s always been independent. Too independent, sometimes. She doesn’t like asking for help.” Mr. Lin smiled at the water.

“Yichen’s the same. He’ll sort something out himself even when somebody could help him in two minutes.”

The two men looked at each other. Then both laughed.

“Those two,” said Mr. Lin.

“Exactly.”

They were quiet for a while. A dragonfly landed on the end of Mr. Lin’s rod and took off again.

“I’m glad they’ve got each other,” said Mr. Zhou.

“So am I,” Mr. Lin said.

It was a simple thing to say. Neither of them said it lightly.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the third hour Mr. Zhou sat bolt upright. “Wait.”

“What?”

“Something’s pulling.”

He grabbed the rod. The line went tight. He pulled carefully, and then a bit harder, and for several seconds both men watched in total silence. Then the line went slack.

Mr. Zhou looked at the water. Mr. Lin looked at Mr. Zhou.

“Did you get it?”

“No.”

“Was it a fish?”

“I think so.”

“You think so?”

Mr. Zhou looked at the empty hook. “It was definitely something.”

“Maybe a leaf.”

“It wasn’t a leaf.”

“A very small fish, then.”

“You can laugh. Let’s see what you catch,” said Mr. Zhou.

Mr. Lin raised his eyebrows. He baited his hook with exaggerated confidence, cast it in a long elegant arc into the middle of the pond, and waited. Nothing.

Mr. Zhou smiled into his tea. “Perhaps the fish have changed their preferences.”

“Don’t start,” said Mr. Lin.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the fourth hour the sun had moved round and their tea had been refilled twice and the sunflower seeds were nearly gone. Neither of them was looking at his rod anymore. Mr. Zhou was telling a story about a business trip to Chengdu years ago, and Mr. Lin interrupted to ask which hotel, and it turned out they had both stayed at the same one, four years apart. That led to travel, and somehow travel led to their wives.

“Your wife still likes flowers?” said Mr. Zhou.

“She buys flowers so she has an excuse to rearrange the house.”

“Mine’s the same. She comes home with something and says it’s for the living room. Three days later it’s in the bedroom.”

“And then the hall.”

“Exactly.”

They laughed. Then Mr. Zhou looked at the water. “How are they finding it? Living together?”

“She rings on Sundays. She says he’s tidier than she expected.”

“He isn’t. He copies her.”

“Then it’s working,” said Mr. Lin.

Mr. Zhou turned his flask round. “I think they understand something important. Neither of them expects the other one to stop building their own life just because they’re together.”

Mr. Lin didn’t answer at once. “That was what I worried about. Last spring, when she had the Beijing offer. First I worried she’d go and be too far away. Then I worried she’d stay for the wrong reason. I didn’t want her to think that loving someone meant giving something up.” He looked at his line.

“Yichen was very clear about that. He didn’t want her making her life smaller to keep things easy.”

“He said the same thing to me. At my own table.”

They sat with that for a while.

Mr. Lin turned his cup round in his hands. “I think they have grown up.”

Mr. Zhou smiled. “They have.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly time to go when Mr. Lin asked the question. He was looking at his line, not at Mr. Zhou.

“Have you thought about them getting married?”

“Of course.”

“Do you think they’re ready?”

Mr. Zhou took his time. “I think they know they want to. Whether they’re ready to do it now is for them to decide. Together.”

“That’s what I think too. I don’t want to push them.” Mr. Lin put his rod down across his knees.

“Neither do I.”

“But I suppose fathers think about these things.”

“We do.”

Mr. Lin looked out across the pond. “She’s my only daughter. I know she’s grown up. She has her own home and her own job and her own life. But I still lie awake thinking about whether she’s eating properly. Whether she’s sleeping. Whether she’s remembered an umbrella.”

Mr. Zhou laughed under his breath. “That’s familiar. I think about Yichen the same way. He’s capable. That doesn’t mean he doesn’t need someone to look after him.”

“Do you think he’ll look after her?”

Mr. Zhou answered without any hesitation at all. “I do.”

Mr. Lin looked down at his hands. “He’s always been good to her.”

“And she makes him happy. I don’t think you know how much,” said Mr. Zhou.

The two men looked at each other. There was something comfortable between them now that had taken a handshake over a car bonnet, a nod at a flower market, a graduation, and four hours beside a pond to arrive at. They weren’t talking about their children’s relationship anymore. They were talking about the people their children had become.

“We should let them find their own time,” said Mr. Zhou.

“Agreed. Although I wouldn’t mind if they hurried a bit. Her grandfather asked him at dinner on May Day. In front of everybody.” Mr. Lin picked his rod back up.

Mr. Zhou burst out laughing. “He told us. He said he answered properly.”

“He did,” said Mr. Lin, and looked almost proud, as if he had answered it himself.

✦ ✦ ✦

They packed up with nothing to show for it: two rods, a half-full tub of bait, several empty cups. Mr. Lin looked at the water one last time.

“Next time we come earlier.”

“Or try another pond.”

“That might be better.”

At the gate Mr. Lin’s phone buzzed. He looked at it and turned the screen so Mr. Zhou could see.

Xiaoran: are you still fishing??

Xiaoran: did you catch anything

The two fathers looked at each other. Mr. Lin typed.

Dad (Water Bureau): No fish.

Xiaoran: FOUR HOURS???

Dad (Water Bureau): We had a good conversation.

“She’s going to laugh at us,” said Mr. Zhou.

“Probably.”

Xiaoran: what did you even TALK about for four hours

Mr. Lin considered it for a while. Then he typed: Many things.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening the two families had dinner together at a restaurant halfway between the two houses. The mothers had arranged it; since their husbands had already spent the afternoon together, everyone might as well. Xiaoran arrived with Yichen and said hello to both fathers before she sat down.

“How was the fishing?”

“Very good,” said Mr. Zhou.

“Did you catch anything?”

“No.”

She turned to her father. “Dad?”

“No.”

“Not even one?”

“Not even one.”

Yichen sat down beside her, trying hard not to smile.

“Then what did you do for four hours?”

Her father picked up his teacup. “We talked.”

“About what?”

“Work.”

“And?”

“Family.”

“And?”

“Life.”

“That’s not a conversation. That’s four years of conversation,” said Xiaoran.

“Your father and I have a great deal in common,” said Mr. Zhou, and Yichen laughed out loud.

She leaned towards Yichen under the noise of the table. “Do you think they actually talked about fishing?”

“Not much.”

“Do you think they talked about us?”

“Probably.”

“What do you think they said?”

“That you’re stubborn.”

She gasped. “How do you know?”

“Because it’s true,” he said, and she kicked him under the table, and he caught her ankle between his and held it there.

Across from them, the fathers had started up again. Now they were arguing about whether the pond deserved a second chance. Her father was smiling. Yichen’s father was listening, and adding something now and then, and they both looked completely at ease. Xiaoran watched them, and leaned her head on Yichen’s shoulder.

“I think they like each other.”

“Yes.”

“More than I expected.”

“They’ve had four hours to get used to it.”

She looked at them a while longer. Her grandfather’s question from May Day came back to her: marriage, and timing, and families. And she thought that maybe this was another part of it that she hadn’t thought about before. Not just two people choosing each other. Two families, slowly getting used to each other, over a pond.

Her father caught her looking. “What?”

“Nothing.”

He looked at Yichen. “Take her fishing next time.”

“All right, Uncle.”

“Why?” said Xiaoran.

“Because apparently,” said her father, “somebody in this family needs to catch a fish.”

“Only if you promise we’ll actually catch something,” she told Yichen.

“I’ll make no promises,” he said.

At the end of the meal, while the mothers were arguing over who would pay, Mr. Zhou turned to Mr. Lin and asked whether he was free next weekend. Xiaoran heard it. She looked at Yichen. He looked back at her. Neither of them said a word. They both knew the answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night they stayed at his parents’ house, because it was his mother’s turn. Xiaoran was getting ready for bed in the guest room when her phone buzzed.

Dad (Water Bureau): Yichen’s father is a good man.

Dad (Water Bureau): We should go fishing again.

Xiaoran: did you catch anything in the end??

Dad (Water Bureau): No.

Xiaoran: then why go again

Dad (Water Bureau): We still have things to talk about.

She looked across the room. Yichen was sitting on the bed with his phone. She went and sat down beside him, close, and showed him.

He read it and smiled. “They’re becoming friends.”

She tucked herself against his shoulder. “Four hours and not one fish.”

“At least they had a good time.”

“I think our fathers are going to be difficult now.”

“Why?”

“Because now they’ve got each other.”

He laughed. She tucked herself in closer under his arm. Downstairs, through the floor, they could hear his father on the phone to somebody, and every so often, quite distinctly, the word pond.

chapters.desc: They put their photographs on the wall, and argue about whether the first one is straight.
chapters.title: The Frames Go Up
chapters.epigraph: “Yes. It feels like you.”
chapters.content:
The first photograph went up crooked. Lin Xiaoran saw it at once. Zhou Yichen, on the other side of the living room with her father’s toolbox in one hand, saw nothing wrong at all.

“Done,” he said.

She stepped back from the wall and tilted her head. “Wait.”

“What?”

“Something’s wrong.”

He looked at the frame. “It’s straight.”

“No, it isn’t.”

He looked again. By any reasonable measure it was straight. He picked up the spirit level off the bookshelf, held it along the top of the frame, and showed her the bubble, sitting exactly in the middle.

“Xiaoran.”

“Yichen.”

“It’s straight.”

She went up to the wall and pointed at the right-hand corner. “That side’s higher.”

He came and stood beside her and looked at it. Then he reached up and moved the frame by perhaps a millimetre.

“Now?”

She stepped back. Two steps left. One step right. “Hm.”

He waited.

“Better,” she said.

“Good.” He put the screwdriver back in its place in the toolbox.

“But maybe a little lower.”

He shut his eyes. She grinned at him.

“Just a little,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

It had started three days before. They’d been sitting on the living-room floor with a heap of photographs she’d had printed: trips, university, the last two years in the flat. She wanted to put some up. Not too many. She didn’t want it to look like an exhibition, or for every wall in the place to be covered in their faces. Just enough to make it feel lived in.

He had said yes, and they’d spent a whole evening choosing.

The one from Suzhou, of her under the trees in the sun, looking away from the camera. The one from their sixth anniversary, on a Monday night in December: him in the black shirt, one sleeve pushed higher than the other, taken across a restaurant table while he was in the middle of saying something. One from university that Luo Jiayi had taken outside the sports centre after a game, him in his university kit with his arm round her shoulders. And a handful of small ones: the night market, a café, a blurry picture of their hands, one of the two of them laughing so hard neither of them was looking at the lens.

They’d bought frames in different sizes, mostly plain wood and black. She’d laid them out on the floor in a rough shape. And now, two hours into Sunday afternoon, they were still putting them up.

“That one goes here.” She was holding the Suzhou photograph against the wall by the bookshelf.

He came over. “Slightly left.”

She moved it. “Here?”

“Yes.”

“What if the anniversary one goes next to it?”

He looked at the photograph in her other hand. “The black shirt?”

“Yes.”

“That one’s just me.”

“Is that bad?”

“No.”

“Then what?”

“Nothing,” he said, smiling.

“You’re making fun of me.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He took the black-shirt frame out of her hand and held it against the wall beside Suzhou. “Like this?”

She stepped back. The two pictures sat next to each other: her under the trees, him across a table. She looked at them.

“Yes, like that,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The university photograph took longest. It had faded a little. His hair was shorter in it, and his face younger, and he had one arm slung loosely round her shoulders. She was smiling at the camera. Neither of them looked posed. Jiayi had taken it on the steps of the sports centre after a home game, when everyone was still sweaty and tired and the team was trickling out to the car park.

Xiaoran held it for a while before she gave it to him.

“Do you remember this?”

“Yes.”

“You were annoyed.”

“By two points.”

“Exactly.”

He smiled. “You were trying to cheer me up. You said it didn’t matter because the team had played well.”

“That’s true.”

“And then you bought me noodles.”

“Because you were hungry.”

“I was. I liked that day,” he said.

“So did I.”

He put it on the wall below the other two. She looked at it there: the two of them at nineteen, next to the two of them now. They’d been students then. They’d met at a vending machine between lectures and spent their afternoons in the library and planned their days round training. Now there were work rotas, a shopping list on the fridge, rent, a shared calendar that his away games filled with red. The photographs were the same people. Everything round them had changed.

“Yichen?”

“Mm.”

“Should we put up one of the really old ones?”

He knew which one she meant before she’d finished. Their first proper photograph together: their first winter, outside the school gate, both of them in uniform and far too many scarves. She was smiling too brightly. He was looking at her and not at the camera. The print was small and slightly out of focus, because Tang Meilin had taken it on an old phone with her gloves on.

He looked at the empty bit of wall by the front door. “Then it should go there.”

“Why there?”

“So we see it every time we go out. So we don’t forget where we started.” He was already reaching for the next frame.

She stood still for a while after that, with the little frame in her hands, and he let her.

✦ ✦ ✦

His phone rang while he was drilling the next hole.

“Are you home?” said Fang Ze.

“Yes.”

“Have you still got my charger?”

Yichen looked over at the dining table. “I think so.”

“Can I come and get it?”

“Later.”

“Why later?”

“We’re doing something.”

“Doing what?”

Yichen looked at the wall. “Putting up photographs.”

There was a pause. “Of you and Xiaoran?”

“Some.”

“How many?”

He looked at the floor. “Quite a few.”

“You’re building a shrine,” said Fang Ze, delighted, and Yichen hung up on him.

“Who was that?” said Xiaoran.

“Fang Ze. He wants his charger.”

“Good. When he comes, we can ask him if they’re straight.”

“No,” said Yichen.

✦ ✦ ✦

By five the wall was nearly done. It wasn’t symmetrical, but it was balanced enough to look as if they’d meant it. There was one left on the table: a small picture from Suzhou of the two of them at a café, sharing a dessert. She was laughing. He was looking at her with an expression that it would have been impossible for anyone to miss.

“Where should this go?”

He pointed to a gap near the middle.

She held it there and shook her head. “No. Next to the other Suzhou one.”

“All right.”

She moved it. Stepped back. Moved it again. Tilted her head.

“Little higher.”

He moved it.

“Perfect,” she said, and he drilled the hole before she could change her mind.

Fang Ze arrived twenty minutes later with a bag of snacks and stopped dead in the living-room doorway.

“Oh.”

“What?” said Yichen.

“You really did it.”

“Do you like it?” said Xiaoran.

Fang Ze went up to the wall. He stopped at the university one. “Is this after we lost to East Campus?”

“Yes.”

“You look miserable.”

“I wasn’t.”

“You were.”

“That’s what I said,” said Xiaoran.

Fang Ze moved along. “Ah. The black shirt.”

“You remember?”

“Of course I remember. You showed it to every single partner at the Herons’ Christmas dinner.”

Yichen turned to look at her.

“It was a good photo,” said Xiaoran.

“It is. You both look so young,” Fang Ze agreed. He looked at the little one by the front door.

“We were young,” said Yichen.

Fang Ze stepped back and looked at the whole wall. “Actually, this is nice.”

“Really?” said Xiaoran.

“Yes. It feels like you.”

“What does that mean?”

“Not very organised. But everything’s got a place.”

“That’s a compliment,” said Xiaoran.

“It is. By the way. That one’s crooked.” He found his charger on the counter and put it in his pocket. At the door he turned round.

She whipped round. “Which one?”

He pointed. It was the first one they had hung, the one she had already made Yichen move twice.

“Don’t,” she said.

Fang Ze left laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterward she stood in front of the wall while the light from the balcony went gold and then grey. She looked at every picture, slowly. She was quiet for so long that Yichen came and stood behind her and put his hands on her waist.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing. I like it.” She leaned back against him.

“Good.”

She pointed at the one by the door. “That’s where we started. That’s when we were working things out. That’s when we knew each other so well we didn’t have to explain anything. And that’s now.” At the university one. At the black shirt. At Suzhou.

He looked at it over her shoulder.

“Do you think we’ll keep adding to it?”

“Probably.”

“What next?”

“Whatever you take a picture of.”

“That’s not very imaginative.”

“I’m sure you’ll have ideas,” he said.

She looked at the empty stretch of wall at the end. “There’s still room.”

“Yes.”

She turned round in his arms. “Maybe one from our wedding.”

Something changed in his face. Not surprise. More like recognising something they had already talked about, on the sofa and in the car and once at three in the morning standing in front of him in a shape he could see.

“That would be nice,” he said.

“And one from a trip after that. And one when we’re old.”

“How old?”

“Old enough to complain about our backs.”

“That sounds likely,” he said, and she laughed.

“And maybe we’ll have so many we’ll need another wall.”

He looked round the living room. “Then we’ll find another wall.”

She looked satisfied with that. Then she got her phone out. “We should take a picture of the wall.”

She took one. Then she looked at the screen. “You’re not in it.”

She turned the camera round and held it up and leaned back against him, and took one of the two of them in front of the wall, with all the other versions of them behind. She looked at it and smiled.

“Perfect.”

He looked at it over her shoulder and, for once, didn’t ask her to delete it. She saved it. Then she took his hand and pulled him towards the kitchen, and on the way past the front door she reached out without looking and pushed the little frame, slightly, to the left.

chapters.desc: The first lease renewal with her name on it, and the first time she asks him not to choose for her.
chapters.title: The Renewal, Again
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll ask first. Then I’ll tell you what I think is best.”
chapters.content:
The reminder came up on Lin Xiaoran’s phone at seventeen minutes past nine on a Tuesday morning in November.

Lease renewal – decision required within 14 days.

She read it while brushing her teeth and swiped it away. She read it again over coffee. Then she opened the agreement, and finally she looked across the kitchen at Zhou Yichen, who was by the counter doing up his shirt cuff.

“Yichen. The lease is up.”

“I know.”

“You know?”

“The notice came last week.”

“And you didn’t tell me?”

“I thought we’d talk about it at the weekend.”

“Well, we should probably talk about it now. He’s offering another year. Four percent more.” She turned the screen round.

“I saw.”

“Four percent.”

“Yes. We can negotiate. I’ll ring him.” He came over and read it over her shoulder, then handed the phone back.

She looked up at him. “Why you?”

“About the rent.”

“I can ring him.”

“I know you can. I was only going to ask if he’d keep it at the same rate.” He looked puzzled.

“Okay,” she said.

“I’ll call him at lunch,” he said, and picked up his coffee and kissed her temple and went to find his keys.

She didn’t say anything else. But the conversation stayed with her all the way to work. Not the rent, and not the landlord. The way he’d said it, so naturally, as if the renewal had already become his job.

It would be the first renewal with her name on it. He had renewed this lease every autumn since their first year at university, three times on his own, the way he did everything with forms: quickly, correctly, alone. Last November, when she moved in, he had done it again: added her name, rung the landlord, checked every clause, set up the transfer. She had been happy to let him. She’d been carrying boxes. She’d been four months into a new job.

It hadn’t been an argument. She hadn’t minded. He was efficient and responsible, and he had never once made her feel she couldn’t have done it herself. But somewhere along the way it had become automatic. Yichen did the flat’s paperwork. Xiaoran did everything inside it that made it feel like theirs. They had never decided that. They had just fallen into it. And sitting at her desk at Morrow at lunch with the agreement open in another window, she found that she didn’t want to fall into it again. Not because she didn’t trust him. Because she wanted to be in the decision before it was made.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he got home that evening she was on the sofa with her laptop and a spreadsheet.

He put his keys in the bowl. “What’s this?”

“The flat.”

He came and looked. She’d laid their current rent beside a handful of listings nearby, with columns for size, location, commute, deposit, maintenance fees, and lease terms.

“You’ve been busy.”

“I looked at lunch. I’m thinking about whether we should renew.” She moved over to make room, and he sat down next to her.

“Are you thinking of moving?”

“I’m thinking about whether. There are three places worth looking at. One’s cheaper but further from the metro. One’s more expensive, but maintenance is included. And one’s about the same as ours, but it’s got a proper study.”

He read through it properly, asking questions: had she checked the commute from the third one, did the second one want two months’ deposit or three. He pointed out something about the cheaper one she hadn’t noticed. It was exactly the conversation she’d wanted.

And then he said, “I’ll set up viewings for the two that look best.”

Her fingers stopped on the trackpad.

“Yichen.”

“Mm.”

She took a breath. “Don’t choose for me.”

It came out more firmly than she’d meant. He went still. The only sound was the hum of the air conditioner.

He didn’t look angry. He didn’t even look defensive. But his face had changed.

“What did I do?” he said.

She rubbed her thumb along the edge of the laptop. “You keep saying you’ll do things. You’ll ring the landlord. You’ll decide which places are worth seeing. You’ll do the forms.”

“I was trying to help.”

“I know you were.”

She turned to face him properly, and pulled her knees up on the sofa so they were against his leg.

“That’s why it’s hard to explain. You’re not doing anything wrong. You’re not making me agree with you. But sometimes you go so fast from seeing a problem to fixing it that I don’t get a chance to decide what I want,” she said.

He didn’t say anything. He was listening.

“I don’t want you to stop helping. I don’t want us splitting everything down the middle to prove we’re independent. But this is our home. I want to be part of deciding what happens to it. I don’t want to be the person who gets shown two options after you’ve already worked out which one’s better.” She looked down at the screen.

He was quiet. Then he nodded slowly.

“That’s fair.”

“It is paperwork.”

“But it’s not only that. It’s where we live. It’s our money and our mornings and how long it takes us to get to work. If we move, it should be because we both want to. I’m sorry.” He looked round the room: the shelves, her lemon tree on the balcony, the photographs on the wall. He turned back to her.

Her face softened. “You don’t have to apologise for wanting to help.”

“I should apologise for assuming I knew how you wanted me to help. I don’t want you to feel like a guest in a home that’s yours.” He took her hand.

“I don’t.”

“Good. But I can see how I might have made you feel a bit like one. Without noticing.”

She leaned her head back against the sofa. “I think I’m still getting used to living together.”

“It’ll be a year next week.”

“I know. But sometimes I realise there are things we’ve never actually talked about. We just do them because one of us started first. And then it’s a habit.”

“Like the lease.”

“Exactly.”

“Would you rather we look at the options together first? And then decide whether to renew?”

“Yes.”

“Then that’s what we’ll do.”

“And we both talk to the landlord. Not just you.”

“All right.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re agreeing very quickly.”

“I’m learning. Thank you for telling me,” he said, and she laughed, and he lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles.

She climbed into his lap then, laptop and all, and put her arms round his neck and her face in his collar, and stayed there until the spreadsheet had gone to sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

They spent two evenings looking at flats. Not because they’d decided to move. Because they wanted to know.

The first one had a beautiful living room and a kitchen Xiaoran loved on sight, but the bedroom was smaller than the photos had suggested. He watched her measuring it with her eyes.

“Too small?”

“Maybe.”

“The wardrobe could go there.”

“Then the bed would be right against the window.”

“Would that bother you?”

“A bit,” she said, and he nodded, and didn’t argue.

The second had an excellent study, but the building was old and the lift had a handwritten sign on it that said TEMPORARILY. She stood at the bottom of the narrow stairwell and looked up. He looked at her.

“Remember the water bottles?”

“Don’t remind me.”

They didn’t like either. On Saturday they saw the third. It was a little more than they paid now, but the layout made sense. The kitchen had real counter space. The living room got the afternoon light. And the study was twice the size of theirs, with room for two desks. She stood in its doorway.

“This is nice.”

He came up behind her. “It is.”

She went to the window. “My desk could go here.”

“And I could have the other side.”

She turned round. “You never work in our study. You always work at the dining table.”

“Our study’s got my trophies in it. They watch me,” he said.

She laughed, and turned back to the window, and imagined it: two desks facing each other, two work schedules, coffee cups, cables, and the occasional argument about whose papers had spread onto whose side. It felt possible. But she wasn’t ready to decide.

“Let’s think about it.”

“Let’s,” he said, and he didn’t ask her to choose that afternoon, or that evening either.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning they sat at the dining table with both laptops and made a list of what mattered. Location. Cost. Space. Commute. How long they were tied in. He added one more line at the bottom: Next year.

“What does that mean?”

“Whether we think our work’s going to change. I might be travelling more next season. You might be too.”

“If Gao Yan gives me the Hangzhou account.”

“Exactly.”

She looked at it all. Their flat was still the most sensible. It was close to both their routes. It was familiar. They’d made it home. The four percent was annoying, but it wasn’t unreasonable next to the others.

“I think I want to renew. For another year,” she said.

“You’re sure?”

“Yes.”

“I agree.”

“But I want to negotiate the rent.”

“Of course.”

“And I want them to include the air-con service.”

“Good point.”

“And the water heater’s been making that noise.”

“I’ll add that,” he said.

She met his eyes.

“We’ll add that,” he said.

“Better,” she said, and smiled.

“Do you want to ring him?”

She thought about it. “Let’s do it together.”

The call took twenty minutes, most of them about the water heater. Xiaoran did the talking. She introduced herself, confirmed they wanted to stay, and said they’d like to discuss the increase and the maintenance. Yichen sat next to her with his chin on his hand, listening. When the landlord asked what exactly was wrong with the water heater, he leaned in and murmured, “The clicking. In the mornings,” and she repeated it. The landlord agreed to send someone to look at it before the new lease started, and came down to two and a half percent.

It wasn’t everything they’d asked for. But it was fair.

She hung up. “Well.”

“Well?”

“We’re staying.”

“Looks like it,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat back and looked round the flat. The photographs on the wall: university, Suzhou, the black shirt, the little blurry one by the door. The sofa. The table. The mugs they’d bought together. All the small things that had collected without either of them noticing.

“I like this place,” she said.

“So do I.”

“Next year we talk about it earlier.”

“Agreed.”

“And maybe we should write down who does what. In the house.”

“Would that help?”

“Maybe. But not like a scorecard.”

“It won’t be.”

“And if one of us is busy, the other one helps.”

“Of course. Anything else?” He found her hand on the table.

She pretended to think about it. “Don’t choose for me.”

“I’ll remember.”

“Even when you think you know what’s best?”

He considered that honestly. “I’ll ask first. Then I’ll tell you what I think is best.”

She laughed, and squeezed his hand, and didn’t let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening, putting the signed copy away, she noticed he’d done something else. He had filed the new agreement in their folder, the one with both their names on the front. And on the paper calendar on the fridge, on the date of the renewal, he had written in his small slanted hand:

Lease renewed – both agreed.

She looked at it for a while. Then she turned round. He was on the sofa with his book.

“Yichen. Why did you write both agreed?”

He looked up. “So that next November I remember.”

She went over and sat down next to him with her feet tucked under her and leaned against his side. He put his book down on the arm of the sofa.

“For what it’s worth,” he said, “I never wanted you to feel I was deciding things for both of us.”

“I know.”

“I do things fast. Sometimes I forget that deciding something together takes longer.”

“Sometimes,” she said.

“I’ll try to ask before I start arranging everything. And you’ll tell me when I forget.”

She lifted her head. “I just did.”

“You did,” he said, and laughed.

She kissed him. Then she put her head back on his shoulder and pulled his arm round her, and he picked up his book again one-handed and read with her leaning on him, and on the fridge, under a dumpling-shaped magnet that had moved house with them, the calendar said both agreed.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Lin Xiaoran is loud, dramatic, cries easily, and can get lost walking somewhere she’s been twenty times. Zhou Yichen is calm, patient, and very hard not to notice. He fell for her almost right away, and he has been spoiling her ever since.

From their last years of high school to university in Shanghai, The Softest Kind of Love follows the two of them through first dates and bad fights, exams and families, and the slow work of growing up without growing apart.

Main chapters tell the story in order. Side stories are small moments you can read whenever you like.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
This is a gentle romance, but a few chapters include:

• A crude, sexualized remark made about Xiaoran by a classmate (The One Time Zhou Yichen Lost His Temper)

• A physical fight between students (Xiaoran, Don’t Fight)

• A sports injury with some blood and a hospital visit (Don’t Scare Me Like That Again, Don’t Limp. I’ll Cry Again.)

• Hurtful rumours and a brief break-up scare (Should We Break Up?)

• Dieting and skipped meals after hurtful online comments (The Day Zhou Yichen Found Out Lin Xiaoran Was Dieting)

• Mild language and lots of crying

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
I wanted to write the kind of love story I like to read before bed: no cheating, no misunderstanding that drags on for twenty chapters, nobody secretly dying. Just two people who like each other a lot and keep choosing each other, even on the days one of them is being impossible.

Xiaoran is a bit of everyone who has cried over a math test or sulked because their boyfriend was too popular. Yichen is the person a lot of us wish we had, or wish we were—someone who notices when you’ve gone quiet.

Some chapters are silly. Some are soft. A couple of them made me cry a little while writing. Thank you for reading any of them at all.

— 甜慕
